Enlarged as were Shemitic notions of the dimensions of God's universe, modem astronomy, hy the grandeur and sublimity of its rcYelations, gives definite shape to what were then only vague and shadowy eonceptions. entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Cliaos an emblem of the unrenm,ed soul. I. WITHOUT LIFE: being dead in trespasses and sins (Ephes. ii. 1); absolntely void" in the sense of being untenanted by lofty thoughts, pure emotions, holy ,·olitions, spiritual imaginations, such as are the inmates of sinless and, in great part also, of renewed souls. III. WITHOUT LIGHT: shrouded in darkness (Ephes. iv. 18); walking, perhaps, in the sparks that its own fire has kindled (Isa. 1. 11), but devoid of that tme light which is from heaven (John i. 9). IV. Yet NOT WITHOUT Goo. As the Spirit brooded over chaos, so does God's Holy Spirit hover over fallen souls, waiting, RB it were, for the forthcoming and insonnding of the commanding word to introduce light, order, life.

entries.title: GEN 1:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -" Beginning" is a word familiarly on our lips ; but, for the most part, wo mean only rearrangement, or the commencement of one link in the chain of e,ents. But who can conceive the beginning of creation? Who can travel back in thougl,t to the first moment of its existence, and look into the eternity beyond ? The Bible carries us back to that beginning, the first moment when the universe existed. How far back was the starting-point of time we know not, nor in what form the universe came into being, whether completed, or in germs to be developed in the course of ages. Only we are taught that before that "beginning" the universe was not, anrl that "the worlds were framed by the word of God" (Heh. xi. 3)-their substance, nnd the laws by which they are governed. With this the conclusions of science agree. They point out that the forces of nature tend to extinction, and hence roust have had a beginning. To the question what was that beginning, the Bible gives the answer. 1. What was before the " beginning"1 God was ; he created all (Ps. xc. 2); nnd if it surpass our power to conceive an eternal self-existent Being, still less can we realise life, power, law coming into existence without a cause. And "in the beginning was the Word;" and the Holy Ghost, through whom Christ offered himself (Heh. ix. 14). But further, before the beginning the Lamb was slain (Rev. xiii. 8)-i. e. the necessity for redemption was foreseen and the plan provided-and we were chosen (Ephes. i. 4), and a kingdom prepared for us (Matt. xxv. 3-!). Thus, redemption was no afterthought, no repairing of failure; but God's purpose from eternity, and therefore that which is best. 2. What was the II beginning"? The creation of o. field on which God's plans were to be carried out and bis perfections manifested. And in the course of his work the creation of beings to whom and in whom he might make himself known, who might glorify him here and enjoy him for ever, 3. We mark tlien-At the beginning God brought forth what had been ordained in eternity-his plan complete to the end-our salvation-redemption a~ well as creation. "Very g·ood" (Gen. i. 31) went far beyond the things then existing on the earth. And if it be urged, How is II very good" consistent with sin?- An enemy has sown tares and marred the Creator's work-the world is a ruin. Oh, faithless I why fearful? If God could give life to dry bones (Ezek. xxxvii. 6), if he could of stones raise up children to Abraham, can he not out of. seeming ruin raise up a more glorious temple? But thou sayest, How can this be? Canst thou solve 01:e of the least mysteries of crention? And is it strange thou canst not solve that mystery into whicn angels desire to look? Enough to know II where sin abounded," &c. (Rom. v. 20); to remember," we see not yet," &c. (Heh. ii. 8); and humbly to wait our Fathel"'s time and way. 4. For persrinal enco1tra9ement. Our state fore- 1,cen and provided for from the beginning. Thns our right to trust God's promis~~ THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (<11, I. 1, 2. depends not on anything in us, but is part of his original plan, Our Lord'e call to sinners is in closest agreement with what was ordained II in the beg'inning." 11 \VhosoeYer will" (Rev. xxii. 17) but echoes the word which called the uni\•erse into being.-lll. Yen,. 1-5.-A true and firm foundation of revelation and fnith mnst be laid in a Di,·ine doctrine of "Genesis,'' the beginnings out of which have come both the world of nature and the world of grace. In this book we are taught what is the order by which all things must be ti;ed, Coming forth from Elohim, from the lufinite Personality; flowing in his appointed course. The genesis of lieaven and eartli becomes the genesis of tlie human family. Out of the natural cliaos is brought forth the Eden of rest and beauty. Out of the moi·al waste of a fallen humanity is formed by the gracious work of a Divine Spirit, through a covenant of infinite wisdom and l~ve, n seed of redeemed and sanctified human beings, a family of God. The genesis of the matenal creation leads on to the genesis of the invisible creation. The lower is the type and symbol of the higher. The .first day is the true beginning of days. See "·hat is placed by the sacred writer between that evening and morning. J. THE COMING FORTH OF THE EVERLASTING, UNSEARCHABLE SECRET OF THE DIVINE NATUr.E INTO MANIFESTATION. "God cre,ated." The word employed denotes more than the bare summoning of existence out of nothingness. The analogy of human workmanship (" cutting," 11 carving," "framing") suggests the relation between creation and the God of creation. The heaven and the earth reflect their Maker. '\Vorks embody the mind, the spirit, the will, the nature of the workman. Althoug·h the name Eloliim, in the plural form, cannot be taken as an equivalent of the Trinity, it points to the great fundamental fact of all revelation, the Divine Unity corning forth out of the infinite solitude of eternity, and declaring, in the manifold revelations of the visible and invisible worlds, all that the creature can know of his fathomless mystery. II. HERE rs A GLIMPSE INTO GoD'B ORDER AND METHOD. "In tlie beginning," the immeasurable fulness of creative power and goodness. Formless void, darkness on the face of the deep, apparent confUBion and emptiness, within a limited sphere, the earth ; at a certain epoch, in preparation for an appointed future. Chaos is not the first beginning of things; it is a stage in their history. The evening of the first day preceded the morning in the recorded annals of the earth. That evening was itself a veiling of the light. Science itself leads back the thoughts from all chaotic periods to previoUB developments of power. Order precedu disorder. Disorder is itself permitted only as a temporary state. It is itself part of the genesis of that which shall be ultimately II very good." III. THE GREAT VITAL FACT OF THE WORLD'S ORDER IS TIIE INTIMATE UNION DETWEEN THE SPIRIT OF GOD AND THAT WHICH IS COVERED WITH DARKNESS UNTIL HE ll!AKES rr LIGHT. The moving of the Spirit upon the face of the waters represents the brooding, cherishing, vitalising preseuce of God in his creatures, over them, around them, at once the source and protection of their life. 11 Breath;" 11 wind," the word literally means, perhaps as a symbol at once of life, or living energy, and freedom, and with an immediate reference to the creative w<>rd, which is henceforth the breath of God in the world. Surely no candid mind can fail to feel the force of such a witness in the opening sentences of revelation to the triune God. IV. To us THE BEGINNING OF ALL THINGS IS LIGHT, The word of God "commands tbc light to shine out of darkness." 11 God said, Let there be light," or, Let light be. The going forth of Gorl'a w<>rd upon the universe very well represents the twofold fact, (1) that it is the outcome of his will and nature; and (2) that it is his language-the expressi~n of liimsel.(, Hence all through this Mosaic coemogo~y God is represented as epeakrng to creation, that we may understand that he speaks in creation, as he is also said to look at that which cornea forth from himself to behold it, to approve it, to name it, to appoint its order and use. Snch intimate blending of the personal with the impersonal is the teaching of Scripture as distinguiehc>d from 1111 mere human wisdom. God is in creation and yet above it. Man is thus invited to seek the personal pr~ence as that which is higher than nature, which his own per• sonal life requires, that it may not be oppressed with nature's greatness, that it may ho light, nnd not d[lrkne8B, There is darkness in creation, darknc.;s in the clcep wutors of tlie world's history, darkness in the human soul itself, ur:til God Rpcah an,! 1mm hears. Lialit is not, physically, the first thing created; but it is tho first fact of the Divine days-tbnt is, the beginning of the new order. For what we have to do with is not the infinite secret of creation, but the manifestation of tl,e vi.WJle world, " God manifest." The first day in the history of the earth, as man can recvl it, must be the day when God removes the covering of darkness and says " Let there be light." The veil uplifted is itself a commencement. God said that it wa.i goocl. His own appointment confirmed the abiding distinction between light anrl darkness, between day nnd night; in other words, the unfolding, progressive interchange of work and rest, of revelation and concealment, the true beginning of the world's week of labour, which leads on to the everlasting sabbath. How appropriately this first day of the week of creation stands at the threshold of God's word of grace I The light which he makes to shine !n our hearts, which divides our existence into the true order, the good and the evil separated from one another, which commences our life; and the Spirit is the light of his own word, the light which shines from the face of him who was "the Word," "in tlie be(]innin(J witli G0cl," " without whom nothing was made that was made."-R.

Afterwards it is the particular arrangement effected, or condition induced, by the creative worcl that evokes the Divine commenclation; here it is the creature itself-" perhaps ns the one object in nature which forms the fittest representation of the Creator himself, who is Light, nnd in whom is no darkness at all (I John i. 6), and of the trne Light, which lighteth every man (John i. 9)" (Macdonald). entries.title: GEN 1:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Day two. The work of this clay consisted in tho formation of that immense gaseous ocean, called tho atmosphere, hy which the earth is cncirclccl. And God said, Let there be CL firmament (i-akiya, an expanse, from i·akah, to beat out; LXX., 11r,piwµa ; Vulgnte, .firmamentum) in the midst ofthe waters. To affirm with Knobel, Gescnius, and others that the Hebrews supposed the atmosphe1ic heavens to be a metallic substance (Exod. xxiv. 10), a vault fixed on the water-flood which surrounds tho earth (Prov. viii. 27), firm as a molten looking-glass (Job xxxviL 18), borne by the highest mountains, which are therefore called the pillars nnd foundations of heaven(~ Sam. xxii. 8), and having doors and wmdows (eh. vii. 11 ; xxviii. 17; Ps. lxxviii. 23), is to confound poetical metaphor with literal prose, optical and phenomenal language with strict scientific statement. The Vulgatc and English translations of i·akiya may convey the idea of solidity, though it is doubtful if 11r,piwµ.a (LXX.) does not signify that which makes firm as well as that which is made firm (McCaul, Wordsworth, W. Lewis), thus referring to the well-known scientific fact that the atmosphere by its weight upon the waters of the sea keeps them down, and by its pressure against our bo(lies keeps them up ; but it is certain that not solidity, but expansiveness, is the idea represented by rakiya (cf. Scottish, ra:x, to stretch ; Job xxxvii. 18 ; Ps. civ. 2 ; Isa. xl. 22). "The firmament, expanse of liquid, pure, Transparent, elemental air, diffused In circuit to the uttermost convex Of this great round." {Milton, 'P[lr, Lost,' Bk. vii.) And let it divide the waters from the waters. What these waters were, which were designed to be parted by the atmospheric firmament, is explained in the verse which follows.

entries.title: GEN 1:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God made the firmament. HO\V the present atmosphere was evolved from the chaotic mass of waters the Mosaic narrative does not reveal. The primary intention of that record being not to teach science, hut to discover religious truth, the thing of paramount ·importance to be communicated was that the firmament was of God's construction, This, of course, cloes not prevent us from believing that the elimination of those gases (twonty-one parts of oxygen nnd seventy-nine of niti·ogen, with a small proportion of carbonic acid gas and a.qneous vapour) which compose our atmoepliere wa.s not effected by natural means ; and how far it may have been 1tssistc•l by the action of the light upon the condcnsin" mass of the globe is a problem in the soln~ tion of which science may legitirnatdy take an interest. And divided the waters which were under the firmament Crom the waters which were above the firmament. 'l"he upper waters are not the ma terfal of the stars (Delitzsch, Wordsworth), althou"h Jupiter is of the same density as water, a~d Saturn only half its density; Lut the waters floating about in the higher spaces of the air. The under waters arc not the lower atmospheric vapours, but the oceanic and terrestrial waters. Ho;v the waters arn collected in the upper reaches of the atmosphere, Scripture, no less than science, explains to be by means of evaporation (Gen. ii. 6; Job xxxvi 2i; xxxvii. 16). These latter passages suggest that the clouds are balanced, suspended, upheld by the buovancy of the air in exact accordance with scientific principles. And it was so. Six times these words occur in the creation record. Sublimely suggestive of the resistless energy ofthe Divine word, which speaks, and it is done, commands, and it staudeth fast, they likewise remind us of the sweet submissiveness of the creature.to the all-wise Creator's will, and, perhaps, are designed as well to intimate the fixed and permanent character of those arrangements to which they are nttached.

entries.title: GEN 1:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God called the firmament heaven. Literally, the heights, shamayim, as in ver. 1. "This," says Principal Dawson, "may bo regarded as an intimation that no definite barrier separates our film of atmosphere from the boundless abyss of heaven without;" and how appropriate tho designation "heights" is, as applied to the atmosphere, we a.re reminded by science, which info1·ms us that, after rising to the height of forty-five miles above the earth, it becomes imperceptible, nnd loses itselfin the universal ether with which it is surrounded. And the evening and the moming were the second day. For the literal rendering of this clause see on ver. 5. It is observable that in connection with the second day's work the usual formula, "And Goel saw that it was good," is omitted. The "cai ,ic,v i, 9,o, or& ca~ov" of the Septuagint is unsupported by any ancient version. Tho conceit of the Rabbis, that an expression of the Dil'ine approbation was omitted because on this day the angels foll, requires no refutation. Aben Ezra accounts for its omission by making the second day's work terminate with vcr. 10, Lange asks, "linJ tho pro• 16 TIIE nooK OF GENESIS. [en, r. G-8, rhetic author somo nnticipation that tho hlne ,-ault "-..s merely an arpcaranco, whilst t.hc savans of the Septuagint had no such anticipation, and therefore proceeded to <loctc,r the rassage I" The explanation of Cnlviu, Dehtzsch, Macdonald, and Alford, though declared by Kalisch to be of no weight, is probably the concct one, that tha l\·ork begun on the second dny was not properly terminated till tho middle of tho third, at which plnce, nccordingly, the expr<'ssion of Divine approbation is introduced (see vcr. 10). HmnLETICS. Yer. 7.-T/u at,;nosp/1,eric Ji,r1(UL1nent. I. Tm,: cnEATURE OF Gon. I. From God it re.ceh·ed its being (ver. 7).. Not h~re alone, but.in othe~ parts, Scripture declares ihe firmament to be the Dn-me handiwork (Ps. Xl.l[. 1; c1v. 2). Whence we may note-(1) That not it, tlie creature, should receive our worship, but lte, its Maker who is God o,er all, blessed for ever. (2) That since the firmament was mad~ hy God, it must bdr,ng to him. If at the present moment it is the special abode of the prince of the power of the air (Ephes. ii. 2), it must be a usurped dominion. The air with all its beams and showers, quite as much as the earth with all its trees and flowers, is God's property (Gen. xiv. 22; Ps. xxiv. 1, &c.). (3) That in all its mo,·ements it only carries out tlie will of its Creator. The air does nothing of ii.self. Under the reign of law as all created things are, the law that reigns is itself benealh the rule of God. The Hebrew mind never mistook things for persons or creatures for the Creator (Ps. cxlviii. 8) ; it is only modern science that degrade~ ihe Creator from his throne, and puts the creature in his seat. 2. From God it received its function (ver. 6),-to divide between the upper and the lower waters,- "·hich ,vas-(1) Simple, i. e. in the sense of not being complex. Though its uses are manifold, they are all contained in this, that it floats up and sustains the vapours rising from the earth at a sufficient distance from the terrestrial waters. (2) Necessary. ,vithout a clear body of atmospheric air between the waters, human life could not have existed. And equally without the watery clouds swimming in the atmosphere, both vegetable and animal life would perish. "Were the air absolutely dry, it would cause the water in plants to evaporate from their leaves more rapidly than it could be supplied to them by the soil and the roots. Thus they would Rpeedily become flaccid, and the whole plant would droop, wither, and die." Similarly, "were the air which man draws into his lungs entirely free from watery fluid, he would soon breathe out the fluiils which fill up his tissues, and would dry up into a ·withered and ghastly mummy" (' Chemistry of Common Life,' vol. i. p. 13). (3) Beneficent,. Collecting the vapours of the earth in the form of clouds, it is th·IS enabled to throw them down again in the shape of rain, snow, or dew, according liS it is required. 3. From God it received its name. (1) Suitable. "Heights," significant of the reality. (2) Su.ggestive. "The love, the power, the majesty of God, his thoughts, his ways, his purposes when compared with man's, are set forth to us by the height of the heaven above the earth." II. THE SERVANT OF ~IA..'<'. 1. Indispensable. Without the air man could not live. His physical being would perish without its oxygen. Without its pressuro his bodily structure would fall to pieces. 2. Valuable. The uses of the atmosphere to man as a resident on earth are manifold. It supports animal and vegetable life around him. It conveys, refracts, and decomposes light. It transmits sound. It draws up noxious vapours from tl1e soil, and dispersea them by its winds. It assists him in a variety of his mechanical, chemical, commercial, and scientific enterprises. 3. Willing. Great as are its powers of service and its capacities of rebellion when excited with tempest, for the most part it is meek and docile, ever ready to acknow• ledge me.n as its master, and to execute his slightest wish. 4. Unwearied. Eve, since it received its appointment from God to minister to the happiness of man U has unrestingly performed that tas~, and betr~ys n? more ~igns of_weariness to-day n,nn it did at the first. 5. GratuWJus. It gives 1ls i;erv1ccs, as its great Creator gi,•es his blessings, without money and without price. Let us learn-1. To be thankful for the air we breathe. 2. To admire God's wisdom in tl1e wonderful adjustmenti, of the air. 3. To make the beet use we can of that life which tLe air supports and aubserves. OB. I. 9-13.) entries.title: GEN 1:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Day t!iree. 'l'ho distribution of land and water and the production of vegetation on this day onga~ed the formative eneTgy ol' the word of Eloh1m. And God said, Let the waters under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear. To explain tho second part of this phenomenon us a consequence of the first, the disclosure of the solid ground by the retirement of the waters from its surface, and not rather vice versa, is to reverse the ordinaryprocesses ofnature. Modern analogy suggests that the breaking up of the hitherto universal ocean into seas, lakes, and rivers was effected by the upheaval of the land through the action of subterranean fires, or the subsidence of the earth's crust in consequence of tho cooling and shrinking of the interior mass. Ps. civ. 7 hints at electric agency in connection with the elevation of the mountains and the sinking of the ocean beds. " .At thy rebuke they (the waters) /led : at the voice of thy thunder they hasted away (were scattered). The mountains rose, the valleys sank (lwa/3aivouc11v op11 1<ai KaTa• /3aivoucr, ,,..8,a-LXX. ; ascendunt montcs, et descendunt campi-Jerome) to the place which thou hadst established for them" (Perowne). The gathering of the waters Into one place implies no more than that they were, from this day forward, to be collected into one vast body, and restrained within bounds in a place by themselves, so as to admit of the exposure of the earth's soil. The " place founded for them " was, of course, tho depths and hollows in the earth's crust, into which they were immediately withdmwn, not through direct supernatural agency, but by their own natural gravitation. The configuration of the dry land is not described ; but there is reason to believe that the original distribution of land and water was the same, 01· nearly the same, ns it is at present. Physical geographers have observed the.t the coast lines of the great continents nnd the mountain ranges genero.lly run from north-eost to south-west, ond that these Jines are in reality parts of great circles, tangent to the polar circle, ond at right angles to a line drawn from tho sun's centre to tho moon's, when these bodie~ aro either in conjunction or in opposition. These circles, it hns further been remarked, a1·0 "the lines on which the thin crust of B cooling globe would be most likely to be rupturecl by its intemnl tido.l wave." Hence, though considerahly mo,lified by tho mighty revolutions thro.tgh which at successive periods the earth !ins posse,!, "these, with certain subordinate lines of frndurc, haw determined the fonns of coutinout~ l'1oui tho UEK lsSl8, beginning" (Dawson, '0. W.,' p. 131; cf. 'Green's Geology,' p. 512). And it was so. Though the separation of the dry lam! from the waters and the distribution of both were effected by Divine agency, nothing in the Mosaic narrative obliges us to think that these works were instantaneously completed. "There is truly no difficulty in supposing tliat the formation of the hilh kept on through the succeedillg creative days" (Lange). "Generally the works of the single creative days consist only in lay• ing foundations; the birth process that i~ introduced in each extends its efficacy beyond it" (Delitzsch). "Not how lo1VJ, but how many times, God created is the thing intended to be set forth" by the creati.e days (Hoffman). Scripture habitually repre• sents the world in an aspect at once natural and supernatural, speaking of it as natura and c,·eatura, ,;,vcr,, and n,.,.,, (cf. ::Hartensen's 'Dogma.ties,' § 63) ; and although the latter is the viewexhibited with greatest prominence, indeed exclusively, in the Mosaic cosmogony, yet the fonner is not thereby denied. Not immediateness, but certainty of execution, is implied in the "it was so" appended to the creative fiat.

entries.content: -A.nd God called the dry land Earth. In opposition to the firmament, whichwas named" the hei&hts" (shamayi1n), the dry land was styled "tne flats," ".A.rctz" (cf. Three terms arc cmployed to describe the vegetation here summoned into existence. The first clause describes its specific nature-" fruitbearing ;" the second, its peculiar charactcristic-enclosing the seed in its fruit; the third, its external appearance-rising above the ground. "This division is simple and natural. It proceeds upon two concurrent marks, the structure and the seed. In the first the green blade is prominent; in the second, the stalk ; in the third, the woody kxture. ln the first the seed is not conspicuous ; in the second it is conspicuous ; in the third it i., enclosed in a fruit which is conspicuous" (l\Iurphy). The phrase "a~tcr his kind," appended to the second and third, seems to indicate that the different species of plants '\"<'ere already fixed. The modern clogma of the origin of species by development would thus le declared to be un- 1.nhUcal, a~ it has nc t yet been proved to be scicutifi~. The utmost that can be claimed e.£ csL,\.lisLcd io thut "species," qna Rpl·cies, have tho po"·er of val'iation nlong the line of ccrtnin eharncteristies belonging to thomaelves, but not that any absolutely new species has ever been developed with power indefinitely to multiply its kind. Yer. 12.-And the earth brought forth grass, ttd herb yielding aoed after his kind, and tho tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after hla kind. It i9 noticon.ble that the vcgetntion of tho thil,l day sprnng from the soil in tho same natural manner in "'hich all subsequent vngotation has done, viz., by growth, which scorns to resolve tho well-known problem of whether the tree was bcforo tho seed, or tbo soed before the tree, in favour of the latter.alternative, although in the order of nature the parent is always before the offs:pring. Believing that " if it were given to her to look beyond the abyss ofgeolo~callyrecorded time,'' she might "witness tne evolution of living protoplasm from not living matter," science yet honestly affirms "that she sees no reason for believing that the feat (of vitalising dead matter) has been perfonncd yet " (Huxley's 'Brit. Association Address,' 1871); and Scripture is emphatic that, if it is protoplasm which makes organised beings, the power which manufactures protoplasm is the Ruach Elohim, acting in obedience to the Divine Logos. The timo when the earth put forth its verdure, viz., towards the clos1.> of the third day, after light, ail·, earth, and water hn.d been prepared and so adjusted as to minister to the life of plants, was a signal proof of the wisdom of the Creator and of the nah1ralness of his working. Has modern geological research nny trace of this third day's vegetation I 'l'he late Hugh Jlfillcr identified the long-continued epoch of profuse vegetation, since then unparallelec!. in rapidity and luxminnce, which deposited the coal-measures of the carboniferous system, with tho Intter ha.If of this Jlfosaic day. On these grounds Professor Dana concludes that tlie latter part of the .Azoic age of geology corresponds with the latter half of the third creative day. In the Creation Series of Chaldeau tablets are two fragments, which George Smith conjectures have a referenr,e to tho first part of the third day's work. The one is- I. When the foundation of the ground of rock (thou didst make) 2. The foundation of the ground thou didst call ... 3. Thou didst l,eautifv the heaven . 4. To the face of the heaven ... 5. Thou didst give . . . The other, which is much more mutiJ,.1,r,l and obscure, describes the god Sar (or Assur) as saying- 7. Above the sea which is the sea of ... B. In front of the esara (firmament) which I.have made. 9. Below the place I strengthen it I0. Let there be made also e-lu (earth 1) for the dwelling of [man!] ('Chahlcan Genesis,' p. 63.) HO:\IILETICS. Vers. !J-12.-Sea, land, and vegetation, contrasted and compared. I. Cox- TRASTED; in respect of - 1. Their constitiitions;-sea being matter liquid and mobile, land matter solid and dry, vegetation matter organised and living. All God's creatures have their own peculiar natures and characteristic structures. Each one's nature is that which makes it what it is. A change of constitutional characteristics would be equivalent to an alteration of being. The nature nnd strncture of each nre assigned it by God. Whence may be gathered-(!) that if all creatures are not the same, it is because God has so willed it; (2) that God has so willed it, for this among _other reasons, that he delights in variety; (3) that no separate creature can be other than its individual nature will allow; (4) that to wish to be different from what God has made us is to be guilty of a foolish ns well as sinful discontent; and (5) that a creature's highest function is to act in accordance with its God-assigned nriture. 2. '!'heir sitmitions; 'l\•hich were all different, yet all adapted to their respecth·e natures nnd uses, and all wisely appointed. The waters were gathered into the earth's hollows, the lands raised above the ocean's smface, the plants spread upon the ground. It is the nature of water to seek the lowesl levels; nnd, collected into ocean, lake, nnd river beds, it is of infinitely greater value than it would have been had it continued to oYersprend the globe. Similarly, submerged beneath the waters, neither could the lancl haYe been arrayed in verdure, or made n habitation for the beasts, much less a home for man; nor could the plants have grown without a dry soil to root in, while their beauty would have been concealed nnd their utility destroyed. And then each one h:is the place assigned it by God, out of which it cannot move, aud ngain~t which it need not fret. The place founded for the waters has received them, and God lias set a bound to them that they cannot pass. The dry land still maintains its elevation above the sea; nnd, ns if in obedience to the Divine Creator's will, the waves are continually building up terraces and rni~ed beaches in compensation for those they are taking down. Nor does it seem possible to shake off the vegetation from the soil. Scarcely has n square inch of ground been recovered from the waters, than it begins to deck itself in green. Let us leurn here (1) that every creature of God, man included, has its own plnce; which is (2) best suited to its nature, functions, and uHcs on the earth; and (3) nssigned it by God. Also, (4) that to vacate that place would be to run counter to God's ordinance and to God's wisdom, as well as to its own nature and usefulness; and (5) that it becomes every one to abide in that sphere of life in which he hns bern phced liy God ro11tcntcclly, cheerfully and diligc1,tly seeki,,g to glorit'y L' ~ 20 THE BOOK OF GENESlS. (OH. I. 9-18. hie Creator. 3. Their operati<mi; which nro as diven1ified as nre their natures and plnces. The sea moves, the land rests, the phmt g-rows. 'l'he sen fertilises and beautifies the soil, the soil sustains and nourishes tho plant, the plnnt decorates the land and gi'<"es food to man and beast. The sea fills the clouds the clouds fill the ri,•ers nnd th~ stronn:is, the rivers and the streams slake the thirst of the valleys, the vnlle~'S yield their substance to the corn and the wine and the oil nnd these again deliver up their treasures to their master-man. The sea divid~s the land int~ con_t~nent.s, which, in turn, are broken up int~ c~untries by rivers; and thus nnt1onaht1~~ are formed, and peace promoted by d1vis1on. As the great highway of the nat10ns, too, the 11ea holps to diffuse abroad the blessings of civilisation and to teach men their interdependence. So, likewise, the land has its specific fundtions in the economy of na~nre, being assigned to support, sustain, enrich, instruct, and comfort wan. And different from both are tl1e uses of the plants. All which is fitted to suggest wisdom. (1) That each separate creature has its own separate work to do, for which it has been fitted with appropriate powers-a lesson of diligence. (2) That there are many different ,rnys of serving God in this world-a lesson of charity. (3) That God does not wish all his creatures either to be or to serve alikea lesson of contentment. (4) That the best way to serve God is to be ourselves and use the powers we possess, without condescending to imitate our neighboursa lesson of indi,·iclua!ity. (5) That though each separate creature has its own nature, pince, and power, yet each is subservient to the other, and all to the whole-- a lC'sson of co-operntion. II. Coru:rARED, in respect of - 1. Their natures, ns being God's creatures. Land, sea, and vegetation all owe their existence to his Almighty fiat, and all equally proclaim themselves to be his handiwork. Hence they are all God's property-the earth with its fulness, the sea with its treasures, the plants with their Yirtues. Consequently man should (1) reverently worship him who made the sea 'lnd formed the dry land, and caused the gra.ss to grow; (2) thankfully receive those highly sernceable creatures at God's hand; and, (3) remembering whose they are, and that himself is but a steward, faithfully employ them for their Creator's glory. 2. Their charaders, as being obedient to the Divine word. "Gathered be the seas," said- the word, and the seas were gathered. "Let the dry land appear," and it appeared. "Let the grass grow," and the grass grew. Let the land, sea, and plants be our teachers. Obedience the first duty of a creature. Nothing can compensate for its want (1 Sam. xv. 22). And this obedience must be prompt, complete, and continual, like that of sea, land, and vegetation. 3. Their varieties. The seas were di\'ided into oceans, lakes, rivers; the land iuto mountains, hills, and valleys; the plants into grasses, herbs, and trees. God loves diversity in unity. As in a great house there are 'l"'essels of small quantity and vessels of large quantity (Isa. mi. 24), so in the world are the creatures divided into more important and Jess. In society men are distributed into ranks an~ classes according to their greatness and ability; in the Church there are "babes" and there are "perfect.men" in Christ; there are those possessed of many talents and much grace, and those whose endowments and acquirements are of smaller dimensions. 4. Their qualifie,i, as being all good in their Creator's estimation. The highest excellence of a creature is to be appro'l"'ed by its Maker, not simply commended by its fellow-creature ; to be good in the judgment of God, and not merely in thi, sight of men.

entries.content: -And the evening and the morning were the fcnrtb day. The Scripture references to this day's work are both unmcrous and iustructh·e (cf. Job ix. 9; xxxvii.31; Ps. viii ; xix. ; civ. ; c:tlvii.). The Hebrew writers supply no information as to the astronomical theories which were prevalent in their time; yet. "from other sow·ces wo have facts leadiug to the belief that even in the time of l\loses there was not a little practical astronomy in the East, and some good theory, The Chaldea11s at II very early period had ascertained the principal circles of the sphere, the position of the poles, nnd the nature of the nf,parent motions of the heavens ns the rcsu ts of revolution on nn inclined axis. The Egyptian astronomers, whom we know through '!'hales, 640 n.o., taught the true nature of the moon's light, the sphericity of the earth, nnd the position ofits five zones. Pythagoras, CiS0 D.o., knew, in addition, the obliquity of the ecliptic, the identity ofthe evening and morning star, and the earth's revolution round the sun" (Dawson, '0. W.,' p. 207). Modern astronomy, though po~sessed of highly probable theories as to the formation of the universe, is still unable to speak with absolute precision with !egard to this fourth day'e wc.rk. Yet thore ine not wanting indirect corroboraLions of I.ho truth of tho Mosaic narrative from both it and geology. According to the sacred writer, tlie presently existing atmosphere, the distribution of land nnd water, tho succession of dny and night, nnd the regular alternation of tho seasons, wore established prior to the introduction of animal lffe upon the earth ; and Sir Charles Lyell has demonstrated nothing more successfully than the dominion of " existing causes " from the Eozoic era downwards, and the sufficiency of these causes to account for all the changes which have taken place in the earth's crust. Again, geology_ att~sts_ the prevalence on our ~lobe in prelustonc times of a much more uniform and hicrh temperature than it now possesses, 80 late as the Miocene era a genial tropical climate having extended up beyond the Arctic circle, and in the earliest eras of the history of the globe, in all probability, the entire sphere being so favoured with excessive heat, Different causes have been suggested for tllis phenomenon ; ns, e. (!,, the greater heat of the cooling globe (the earliest geologists), a. different distribution of land and water (Lyell), va1iations in the eccentricity of the earth's orbit (Herschell and Croll), cl1anges in the earth's axis (Evans, Drayson, Bell), and thegreaterintensityofthe sun's beat (Sir W. Thomson, ' Trans. Geolog. Soc.,' Glasgow, 1877). The Biblical nanative, by distinctly teacl1ing that the sun was perfectedon the fourth day, renders it intelligible that his influence on the surface of the eurth wns t11en at its greatest, causing tropica! cl1matcs to prevail ~n,\ tropical \'f';cd~- tion to abound, both ofwhich have g.,-aclnally disappeared from tho polar regions in coneequoncc of the sun's diminished heat. It remains only to note that lhe Chaldeon Genesis preserves a striking reminiscence of this day's work ; the obve1·se of the fifth creation tablet reacling- 1. It was delightful, all that was Ji.,ed by the great gods. 2. Stars, their appearance (in figures) of animals he arranged. 3. To fix the.year through the obsen·ation of their constellations. 4. Twelve months (or signs) of stnrs in three rows he arranged. 5. From the day when the year commeme~ unto the dose. 6. He marked the positions of the, 1nnderingstars (planets) to shine in their courses. 12: TI1~ god Uru (the ~oon)•he c;used ·to rise out, the night he overshadowed, 13. To fix it also for the light of the night, until the shining ofthe day. . . . . . . . . 19. When the god Shamas (the sun) in the horizon of heaven in the east. 20. . . . formed beautifully an,1 . • 21. . . to the orbit Shamas was perfected. "It appears that the Chaldean record contains the review and expression of satisfaction at tho head of each tablet, while tl,,, Hebrew has it at the close of each act " (' Chalclean Genesis,' pp. 69-73).

entries.title: GEN 1:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie cele.stial lwninarie.~. I. Display the DtVI:'.'.;E w1s001I. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Pa. xix. 1). M. Comte belie.ed they declared no other glory thun that of Hipparchus, Kepler, Newton, and their successors. Nc\\"ton ngreed with the Hebrew poet (vid. Expos. on ver. 16). The astronomical argnment in behalf of tht'ism has ahvays been impressive, if not absolutely eonclnsive. Certainly, granting the Divine existence, nowhere does God's glory shine out more conspicuously ; nnd perhaps the attribute which most imperiously arrests attention is that of wisdom. This would seem to be the aspect of the Divine glory which n contemplation of the midnight heavens discovered to the writer of Ps. ci,-. (vid. ver. 24, which is introduced after a poetic version of the fourth day·s work) and of Ps. cxxxvi. (vicl. ver. 7 in the same connection; cf. Prov. iii. 19; viii. 27; Jer. Ii. lo). Many things about the orbs of heaven evince their Creator's "·isdom: these specially-1. Their formation, ns explained by the highly credible teacl1ings of physical astronomy, 2. Their t•arieties--consisting of sun, moon, planets, comets, nebulm. 3. Their motions: in elliptical and parabolic orbits. 4. Their dispositions: the suns, moons, nnd planets in systems; the stars in constellations, clusters, gala:xies. II. Attest the DIVINE GOODNESS. Displuyed chiefly by the threefold pnrpose tho celestial orbs were designed to serve :-1. To give light 11pon tlie eartlt. Even the sta,•s could scureely be dispensed with without u sense of loss. Feeble us their light is, owing to their immense distance from the earth, they ure yet invaluable to voyagP-rs nnd travellers (Acts uvii. 20). Still less could the moon's light, so pale 11h11 ailvery in its whiteness, bo spared. The night without its chaste be:1111s would 24 THE BOOK OF GENgsrn. [en. r. J.t-10. he shrouded in thick gloom, while with th<'m nn ai of cheerfulness is imparted to the ,larkened enrth. And, of course, least of nil could the S'ltn be wanted (for 'The Value of Light' vu/,. p. 13). 2. To distin{jltish day and night. 'l'he beneficence of this arrangement appears by reflecting on the inconvenience of either of the other two alternatives, perpetual day and perpetual night. The disadvantnges of the latter have been indicated; those of the former are scnrcely less numerous. The alternnt!on of dnrkness-(i) Introduces variety in nature, which is always pleasing. Contmuous day would be in danger of becoming monotonous, at least in"this mundane world, if not in the celestial (Isa. Ix. 20; Rev. xxii. 5). (2) Meets thenecessities of creature life, by supplyingconstantly-recurringperiods of repose, which are eminently beneficial for the growth of plants, animals, and man. "Vegetable sleep is tlint relaxation of the vital processes which is indicated by the folding together and drooping of the leaves as night approaches" (Leo Grindon, 'Life: its Nature,' &c., p. 306). The animal tribes generally, with the exception of the wild beasts (Ps. eiv. 20), seek repose with the shades of evening. And man, without the recuperative slumber which darkness brings, would speedily e:xl1aust his energies. (3) Solemnises the mind of man, by suggesting tl,oughts of his frailty, of his end in the sleep of death, but also of his resurrection to the light of a better morning. 3. To mark tirnes and seasons. That the different seasons of the year are somehow connected with the cekstial bodies is perhaps nil that the Mosaic narrative can be made to teach. But we know them to be dependent on the earth's revolution round the sun. And the fact that God has so arranged the earth's relation to the sun as to produce tlicse seasons is n signal proof of the Divine goodness. Another is that God has so fixed and determined their movements as to enable man to measure time by their means. V17ithout the help of sun, moon, and stars chronology would be impossible. III. Proclaim the DIVINE POWER. More than any otherscience, astronomy ennbles us to realise the physical omnipotence of the Deity. Imagination becomes bewildered by the effort to represent the quantity of force required to propel a globe like our earth through the depths of space at the immense velocity of 65,000 miles nn hour. What, then, must be the strength of that arm which, in addition, hurls Jupiter, equal in weight to 1400 earths, along his orbit with a velocity of 29,000 miles an hour? And not Jupiter alone, but suns immensely greater, at rates of motion that transcend conception. Well said Job (eh. mi. 14). Yet, perhaps, the Divine power is as much e,inced by the perpetuation of these celestial masses nnd movements as by their first production. Not only has God made the sidereal firmament, with :its stupendous o-lobes and amazing velocities, but he ha~ so established them that since the begin- ~ing they ha,e kept on their mystic paths without rebellion and without confusion (Ps. c:x.hi:i. 5). IV. Reflect the DIVINE BEAUTY. Perhaps glory is the better word. The counterpart of glory in the Creator is beauty in the creature. The celestial luminaries were approved as good, doubtless, for their uses, but likewis~ for the~selve_s, as_bei~g o~ incomparable splendour. " God bath made everythmg ~eautJful m h_1s time (Eccles. iii. 11). Nothing that God does make can be otherwise than beautiful; and by their splendour, their order, their unity, they seem to mirror forth the majesty, 1u,d purity, and oneness of him to whom they owe their being. HOMILIES BY VARIOUS AUTHOns.

entries.title: GEN 1:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Dayfi,1:e. The waters ancl the Rii·, separated on the second day, ore on this filled with their respective inhabitants. And God said. Nature never makes an onward ruovement, in the sense of nu absolutely new departure, unless under the impulse of the w01·d of Elohim. These words distinctly clnim that the creatures of the sea and of the air, even if evolved from material elements, we1·e produced in obedience to Divine command, and not spontaneously generated by tlie potentia vitre of either land, sea, or sky. Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature. Literally, swarm with swarmers, or crawl with crnwlers. The fundamental signification of shai·atz is to creep or swarm, and hence to multiply (Gesenius); or, vice versa, to multiply in masses, and hence to swarm or abound (Furst ; cf. eh. viii. 17; Exod. i. 7; viii. 3). The sheretzim, though including small aquatic creatures that have short or no legs, nre obviously "all kinds of living creatures inhabiting either Janel or water which are oviparous and remarkable for fecundity" (Bush). We .mo.y, therefore, understand the creative fio.t of the fifth day 11s summoning first into existence the insect creation (in Lev. xi. 20-23 defined as flying sheretzim), the fishes of the sea (sheretzim of the waters, Lev. xi. 9, 10), and the reptiles o.nd saurians of sea nncl land (sheretzim of the lanrl, Lev. xi. 41, 42). Dowson concludes that "the prolific animals of the fifth day's creation belonged to the three Cuvierian sub-kingdoms of the mdinta nrticulata, mollusca, and to the classes of fish and reptiles among the vertebrata. That hnth life. Nephesh chayyah; literally, oliving breath. Herethe creatures of the sea are distinguished from all previous creo.tions, and in particular from vegetation, as being possessed of a vital principle. This does not, of comsc, contrndicl the wcll-knomi truth tl1at plants are living organisms. 011Jy the life principle of the animal creation is different from that ofthe vegetable kingrl.om. It may be impossible by the most acnte microscopic analysis to differentiate the protoplasmic cell of vegetable matter from that of animal organisms, and plants may appear to be possessed of functions tlvi.t resemble those of animals, yet the two are generically different-vegetable protoplasm never weaz. inganimal texture, and plant fibre neverissu. i.ngfrom the loom ofanimal protoplasm. That which constitutes an animal is the possession of respiratory organs, to which, doubtless, there is a reference in the term nephesh. from naphash, to breathe. And fowl that may fly. Literally, let "winged creatures" fly. The fowls include all tribes covered with feathers that can raise themselves into the air. The English version produces the impression that they were made from the waters, which is contrary to eh. iL 19. The correct rendering disposes of the difficulty. entries.title: GEN 1:24

entries.content: -Day six. Like clay three, this is distinguished Ly a double creative net, the production of the higher or land animals and the creation of man, of the latter of which it is perhaps permissible to see a mute prediction in the vegetation which closed the first half of the creative week. And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind. In these words the land animals are generically characterised as nephesh cha'Y"Jah, or animated bein~ ; in the terms which follow they are subdivided into three well-defined species or classes. Cattle. Behemah; literally, the dumb animal, i. e. the larger grasseating quadnipecls. And creeping thing. Remes; the moving animal, i. e. the smaller animals that move eitherwithoutfeet or with feet that are scarcely perceptible, such as worms, insects, reptiles. Here it is landcreepers that are meant, the remes of the sea having been created on the previous day. And beast of the earth (chay11ah of the earth) after his kind. 1. e. wild, roving, carnh•orous beasts of the forest. In these three comprehensive orders was the earth commandc<l.to produce its occupants ; which, however, no more implied that the animals '\Vere to be developed from the soil than were the finny tribesgeneraten bytho sen. Simply in obedience to tho Divine call, and as the product of creative energy, they were to spring from the plastic dust as being essentially earth-born creatures. And it was so. Modern evolutionists believe they con e;onccive-thcy have never yet been able to demonstrate-the modus operandi of the ~uprcme Artificer in the execution of this part of the sixth day's work. Revelation has not deemed it needful to do more than simply 11tate that they were-not, by an evolutionary process carried on through inconceivably long periods of timo, developed from the creatures of the fifth day, butproducc(l directly from the soil by the fiat of Elohim.

According to the witness of geology, "the quadrupeds did not all come forth together. Large and powerful herb,',. vom first take the field, with only a few carnivora. These pass away. Having already explained the significanco of the term Elohim, as snggesting the fulness of the Divine personality, and foreshadowing the doctrine of the Trinity (ver. 1), other interpretations, such as that God takes cou11scl with the angels (Philo, Aben Ezra, Delitzsch), or with the earth (Maimo11iJcs, l\I. If any distinction cloes exist between them, perhaps t.•elem (image) denotes the shadow outline of a figure, nnd damuth (likeness) the correspondence or rcseD1blanc~ of that shadow to the figure. The early Fatl1ers were of opinioD that the words were expressive of separate ideas: image, of the body, which by reason of its beauty, intelligent aspect, and erect stature was an adwnbration of God ; li:J~eness, of thesoul, or the intellectual and moral nature. As to ,~hat iD man constituted the ima:,o Dei, the reformed theologians commonly lield it to have consisted (1) in the spirituality of his being, as an intelligent and free agent ; (2) in the moral integrity and holiDesa of his nature ; and (3) in his dominion over the creatures (cf. entries.content: -Provision for the sustenance of tlic newly-appointed monarch and his subjects is next made. And God said, Behold, I havo given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, o.nd every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding sead; to yon it shall be for meat. Of the three cla'sses into which the vegetable creation was divided, grass, herbs, and trees (ver. 12), the two last were nssiipied to man for food. lliacdonald thinks tnat witl1out this express conveyance man would haYe been warranted to partake of them for nourishment, warranted by the necessities of his naturo. Tho same reasoning, hon·ever, would havc entitled him to kill the lower animals if he jud&ed them useful for his supP.ort. Murphy with more truth remarks, "Of two things proceeding from the same creative hand, neither has any original or inherent right to interfere in nny wny with the other. 'l'he abRolnte right to each lies in the Creator alone. The one, it is t1110, may need tho other to support its life, as fruit is needful to man ; and, therefore, the just Creator cannot make one creature dependent forsubsistcnco on onother without granting to it the nso of that other. But this is a matter between Creator and creature, and not by nny means between creature and creature." entries.title: GEN 1:24–31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -1'/ie sixth day. We pass from the sea and air to the earth. We are being led to man. Notice- I. THE PREPARATION IS coMrLETE. Defore the earth receives the human being, it brings forth all the other creatures, and God sees that they are good-good in his sight, good for man. II. THE PURPOSE OF THE WORK IS BENEVOLENT. Cattle, creeping thing, beast of the earth. So man would see them distinguished-the wild from the domestic, the creeping from the roaming, the clean from the unclean. The division itself suggests the immense variety of the Divine pro:vision for man's wants. III. The incompleteness of the earth when filled with the lower creatures is A TESTIMONY TO THE GREATNESS 01!' MAN'S SPIRITUAL NATURE j for in comparison with the animal races he is in many respects inferior-in strength, swiftness, and generally in the powers which we call instinct. Vegetable, marine, animal life generally, the whole earth filled with what God II saw to be good," waits for the rational and spiritual creature who shall be able to recognise their order and wield dominion over them, Steps and stages in creation lend up to the climax, the paragon of animals," the god-like creature, made to be king on the earth.-R.

Here is the end of:all our endeavour and desire-'--to be perfect men by being like God. Let us be thankful that there is a God-man in whom we are able to find our ideal realised. We grow up into him who is our Head. We see Jesus crowned with glory and honour. When all things are put under him, man will see the original perfection of his creation restored. 6. Man is taught that lie need not leave the earthly spl.ere to be like God. There has been a grand preparation of his habitation. From a mere chaotic mass the earth has by progressive stages reached a state when it can become the scene of a great moral experiment for man's instruction. The god-like is to rule over all other creatures, that he may learn the superiority of the spiritual. Heavenly life, communion, society, and all that is included in the fellowship of man with God, may be developed in the condition' of earth. Grievous error in early Church and Eastern philoaopl;ty-confusion of tlie material and evil Purity does not require an immateiial ·mode of existence. Perfection of man is perfection of his dominion over earthly conditions, matter in subjection to spirit. Abnormal methods, asceticism, self-crucifixion, mere violence to original constitution of man. The '' second Adam " overcame the world not by forsaking it, but by being in it, and yet not of it. 7. God's commandments to man are commandments of Fatherly love. "Behold, I have given you," &c. He not only appoints the service, but he provides the sustenance. 11 Seek ye.first tlte kingdom of God," &c. Here is the union of creative power and providential goodness.
