entries.title: GEN 2:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Thus tho hee.vens and the earth we1·e finished. Literally, And finished were the heavens and the earth, the emphatic position being occupied by the verb. With the creation of man upon the sixth day the Divine Artificc1·'e labours were brought to a termination, and his work to e. completion. The two jclcas of cessation and perfection are embraced in the import of calah. Not simply had Elohim paused in his activity, but the Divine idea of his universe had been realised. The finished world was a cosmos, ammged, ornamented, and filled with organised, sentient, and rational beings, with plants, animals, and man ; and now the resplendent fabric shone before him o. magnificent success - "lo ! very good." This appears to be by no means obse1;1rcly hinted at in the appended clo.use, and all the host of them, which suggests the picture of o. wiJite.ry armament arranged in marching ordei:. Tsebaam, derived from tsaba, to go forth e.s a soldier (Gesenius), to join together for service (Furst), e.nd applied to the angels (arparia ovpav,o,, Lukeii 13. 1Kingsx.xii. 19 ; 2 Chron. xviii. 18 ; Pa. cxlviii. 2) and to tho celestialbodies (ovvaµE,, TWV ovpavwv, Matt. xxiv. 29. Isa. xxxiv. 4 ; xl. 26 ; Dan. viii. 10), here includes, by Zeugma, the material heavens and earth with the angelic and human races (cf. Feh. ix. 6). If the primary signification of the root be splendour, glory, like tsavah, to come forth or shine out as a star ('l'. Lewis), then will the LXX. e.nd the Vulgo.te be coITect in translating 1riic o1<oaµo, avrwv a.nd omnis ornatus eorum, the conception being that when the heavens and the earth were completed they were a bl'illiant array.

entries.title: GEN 2:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And on the seventh day God (Elohim) ended his work whioh he had ma.de. To avc1t the po~sibility of imagining that any portion of the seventh de.y was consumed in working, which the English version seems to favour, tho LXX., the Samaritan, nncl Sy1inc versions insert the si:cth day in the text instead of the seventh. Calvin, Drusius, Lo Clerc, Rosenmiillcr, nnd Kalisch translate had .finished. Other, nnderstalHI the sense to be declared the wo1·k to be finished, while llaumgarten and Delitzsch regard the resting as included in the Cf)ffipletion of the work, and Von Bohlen thinks "the language is not CJ_uite precise." Rut cala.h followed by rnin signifies to cease from prosecuting any work(Exod. xxxiv. 33; I Sam. x. 13 ; Ezek. xliii. 23), and this was, negatively, the aspect of that sabbatic rest into which the Creator entered. And he rested on the seventh de.y from all his work which he had me.de. Shavath, the primary idea of which is to sit still, depicts Elohim as desisting from his cl'eative labonrs, ancl assuming a postw·e of quiescent repose. The expression is a pure anthropomorphism. " He who fainteth not, neither is weary" (Isa. xl. 28), can be conceived of neither as resting nor as needing rest through either exhaustion or fatigue. Cessation from previous occupation is all that is implied in the figure, and is quite compatible with continuous activity in otherdirections. John v. 17 represents the Father ns working from that period onward in the preservation and redemption of that world which byhis preceding labours he had created and made.

entries.title: GEN 2:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God blessed the seventh day The blessing (cf. eh. i. 22, 28) of the seventh day implied-I. That it was thereby declared to be the special object of the Divine favour. 2. That it was thenceforth to be a day or epoch of blessing for his creation. And-3. That it was to be invested with apermanence which did not belong to the othersu clayseyery one of which passed away and gave place to asuccessor. And sanctified it. Literally, declared it holy, or set it apart for holy purposes. As afterwards Mount Sinai was sanctified (Exod. xix. 23), or, for the time being, invested witha sacred character as the residence of God ; and Aaron a.nd his sons were sanctified, or consecrated to the priestly office(Exod. x.xix.44); and the year ofJubilee wns sanctified, or devoted to the purposes of religion (Levit.. :s:xv. 10), so here was th~ seventh dny sanctified, or instituted in the interests of holiness, and as such prochinied to be a holy day. Because that iu it he had D2 !1.5 Tl:IE BOOK OF GENESIS. [ell, IJ. 1--3, rested from all hie work whioh God hnd rreated and made. Litemlly, createdtomah, t',1c exact import of which bes been variouslX explained. The "Jv ijp(aro o6,0( ,ro,ij,ra, ' of the LXX. is obviously incorrect. Calvin, Ainsworth, Bnsh, et alii take the second verb mnJ>hatice, as intensiiying the action of the first, end conveying the idea of a l)erfoct rreation. Rnlisch, A1ford, and others explnin the second as epe:r:cgetic of the first, as in the simifar phrases, "spoke, saying, literally, spoke to speak" (Exod. n. 10), and "la- 1,oured to do " (Eccles. ii. 11). Onkelos, the Yulg,,te (quod Dezu; ci·eavit ut faceret), Cakin, Tayler Lems, &c. understand the infiuiti,e in e tdic sense, es expressive of the purpose for which the heavens and the earth were at first created, viz., that by the six days' work they might be fashioned into a cosmos. It has been observed tliat the usual concluding formula is not appended to the record of the seventh day, and the reason has perhaps been declared hy Augustine: "Dies nut.em septimns sine vespera est, nee habet occasum, quia senctificasti eum ad J>ern1Ansionem sempit.ernam" ('Confess.,' xiii. 36). But now wl1at was this seventh day which received Elobim's benediction! On the principle of interpretation applied to ihe creative days, this must be regarded ns a period of indefinite duration, correspomling to the lmman era of both Scripture and geology. But other Scriptures (E.J::od. xx. 8 ; xx:iii 12 ; Dent. v. 12, &c.} ~hO\~ that the Hebreu-s were enjoined by God to observe a se.cnth day rest in imitation of himself. There are also indications that sabbatic observance was not unknown to the patria.rchs (eh. xxix:. 27, 28), to the antediluvians (eh. viii 6-12), and to Cain end Abel (eh. iv. 3). Profane history likewise vouches for the veracity of the stat.ement of Josephns, that " there is not any city of the Grecians, nor any of the barbarians, nor any nation u-hatsoever, whither ourcustom ofresting on the seventh day bath not come" ('Contra Apionem,' ii 40). The ancient Persians, Indians, and Germans esteemed the number seven as sacred. Bythe Greeksand Phenicians a sacred character was ascribed to the seventh day. The Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians, and other nations of antiquity were acquaiut.ed with the bebdomadal division of time. Travellers J1ave detected traces of it nmong the Afric.'lll nnd American aborigines. To account for its exu.ience among nationsso widely apart, both chronologically and geo- /traphically, recourse has been had to some violent hypotheses ; as, e. g., to the number of the primary planets known to the ancients (Humboldt), the division of a lunar month into fo•J..r nearly equal periods of seven days (lielei; Baden PO\HSll, &c.), Jei.·ish example (JC111ephus). Its true grncsis, however, must be sought for in the primitirnobscrvnncoofa seventh day rest in accordance with Divine appointment. Precisely as we reeson that the early nnd widespread provalenco of sncri• fice can only be explained by nn authoritativo revelation to tho first parents of tho human family of such a mode of worship, so do we conclude that n seventh day sabbath must 111\Ve been prescribed to man in Eden. The question then al'ises, Is this sabbath also referred to in the Mosaic 1-ecord of the seventh day I The popular belief is that the institution of the weekly Sabbath alone is tho subject spoken of iu the opening verses of the present chapter; and the language of Exod. xx. 11 may at first sight appenr to wa1Tant this conclusion. Amore careful consideration of the phraseology employed by Moses, however, shows that in the mind of the Hebrew law~ver there existed a distinction between Gods seventh dny and man's sabbatb, end that, instead of identifying the two, he meant to teach that the first was the reason of tho second; as thus-" In six days God made .•.. and rested on the seventh day ; wherefore God blessed the (weekly) sabbatb day, and hallowed it." Here it is commonly assumed tbat the words are exactly parallel to those in eh. ii. 3, and that the sabbath in Exodus corresponds to the seventh day of Genesis. But this is open to debate. The seventh day which God blessed in Eden wns the first day of human life, and not the seventh day; and it is certain that God di.d not rest from his labours on man's seventh day, but on man's first. We feel inclined then to bold with Luther that in Gen. ii. 3 Moses says nothing about man's day, and that the seventh day which received the Divine benediction was God's. own great ieonian period of sa!Jbatic rest. At the same time, for the reasons above specified, believing that a weekly sabbatb was prescribed to man from the beginning, we have no difficulty in assenting to the words of Tayler Lewis:"'And God blessed the seventh day.' Which seventh day, the greater or the less, the Divine or the human, the ieonian or the astronomical 1 Both, is the cosy answer; both, es commencing nt the same time, so far as the one connects with astronomical time ; both, as the greaterincludingthe less ; both, as being (tbo one as represented, the other as typically representing) the same in essence and idea.'' It does not appear necessary to refute the idea that the weekly sabbatb had no exist.ence till the giving of the law, end that it ie only here proleptically referred to by Moses. In addition to tho above-mentioned historical t.estimonies to the antiquity of the Sabbath, the Fifth Tablet in the Chaldean Creation Series, aft.er referring to the fourth day's work, proceeds:- OH, II, 1-:J,] 'l'IIE noorr OF GENJ<.:srn. 37 "On theseventh dny henprointcd a. holy dny, And to conso from nil business he commo.ndetl. Then iirose thesun in thehorizon of heaven in (glory)," thus <tpparently affirming that, in the opinion of the early Babylonians, the institution of the sabbath was coeval with the crea.tion. (Vid. 'Records of the Past' vol. ix. p. 117,)

entries.title: GEN 2:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: Tlte two sabbatlis: the Divine and the human. I. THE SABBATH oir Gon. A period of-1. Cessationfrom toil, or discontinuance of those world-mBking operations which had occupied the six preceding days (Heh. iv. 4). Never since the close of the· creative week has God interfered to fundamentally rearrange the material structure of the globe. The Deluge produced no alteration on the constitution of nature. Nor is there evidence that any new species have been added to its living creatures. 2. Holy delight. On the seventh day Elohim rested and was'' refreshed" (Exod. xxxi. 17); which refreshment consisted partly in the satisfaction he experienced in beholding the cosmos-a satisfaction prefigured and anticipated by the solemn pauses intervening at the end of each creative day, accompanied by the 11 good," 11 lo I very good," of Divine approbation; and partly in the pleasure with which he contemplated the peculiar work of blessing his creation which lay before him, a work which also had its foreshadowings in the benedictions pronounced on the Jiving creatures of the fifth day, and on man on the sixth. 3. Beneficent activit?J. Even man, unless where his intellectual and moral faculties are dormant, finds it difficult to rest in indolence and inactivity. Absence of motion, with cornpleto negation of effort, may constitute the refreshment of the physical system. The mind seeks its rest in change of occupation. Still less can the supreme Intelligence, who is pure Spirit, rest in absolute inaction; only the Divine energy is now directed towards the happiness of his creatures (Pa. cxlv. 9). Having finished his creative labours, what else could Elohim do but outpour his own blessedness upon his creatures, in proportion to their capacities to receive it? His nature as God necessitated such communication of good to his creatures (Ps. =iv. 8; James i. 5, 17). The capacities of his creatures for such blessing required it. Hence God's rest may be said to have been man's birthright. He was created in that rest, as the sphere of his existence. 4. Continuous duration. That which secures its perpetuity is the Divine resolution to bless it, i. e. constitute it an era of blessing for man, and in particular to sanctify it, or devote it to the interests of holiness. And in this Divine determination lies the pledge of man's salvation. Without it God's rest might have been broken into by man's sin, and the era of blessing ended. But, because of it, man's sin could not change the character of God's seventh day, so as to prevent it from dropping down gifts and exercising holy influences on the creature for whose sake it was appointed. Tlie seC'ltrity of the worlcl as a cosmos may also be said to be involved in the permanence of God's sabbath. So long as it continues nothing shall occur to resolve the present goodly· framework of this globe into another lightless, formless, lifeless chaos, at least until the Divine purpose with the human race has been fulfilled. II. THE SADDATH OF MAN. 1. Of Divine in$titution (Exod. xx. 8; Levit. xix. 30; Pa. cxviii. 24). That God had a rig·ht to enact a weekly sabbath for man is implie,l in his relation to man as Creator and Lawgiver. For man, therefore, to withhohl the seventh portion of his time is to be guilty of disobedience against God as ,1 moral Governor, ingratitude towards God as Creator 1rnd Preserver, robbery of God as the original Proprietor of both man's powers and time's days. As an institution of God's appointing, the sabbath deserves our honour and esteem. To neglect to render this God counts a sin (Isa. )viii. 13). 2. Of sacred character. Among the Israelites its sanctity was to be recognised by abstinence from bodily labour (Exod. xx. 10; xxxiv. 21, &c.) and holy convocations (Levit. xxiii. 3). That this wn~ the manner of its observance prior to the giving of the law may be judged from the regulations concerning the manna (Exod. xvi. 22). That from the bcginnin!,; it wns a day of rest and religious wor8hip may be reasonably inferred. That it wa~ ao used by Christ nnd his apostles the Gospels nttest (Luke iv. lG). That the s:inu; 1:harncter was held to nttach to the first clay of the week aftP.r Cliri~t's rest11Tection 38 THE nooK OF GENESIS. Lr,11, JI. 1-3, may ~e deduced from the practice of the apostolic Church (Acts xx. 7). The sancbty_ o~ the sabbnth m~r. be profaned1_positively, by prosecuting one's ordinary labours m 1_ts_ hours (Is.a. lvm. 1~ ;_ Jer. ;1v11. 24); negatively, by neglecting to devote them to D1vme worship and spmtual 1mpro-vemcnt (Ezek. xliv. 24). Christianity has not obliterated the distinction between the sabbath and the other days of the "'eck_; not even by elevating them to the position of holy days. An nttempt to eqnahse the seven days always reRults in the degradation of the seventh never in !he elevation of the other six. 3. Of ben_eficent <f:esi,gn (Mark ii. 27). Th~ snbbath 1s adapted to the wants of man physically, mtellectually, socially politically. Innumerable facts and testimonies establish the beneficial influence ~f 11. seventh day's rest from toil upon the manual labourer, the professional thinker tho social fabric, the body politic, in respect of health, ,vealth, streugth, happin~ss. It is howe,er, chiefly man's elevation as a religious being at which it aims. In th~ riaradisaiacal state it was designed to hedge him round and, if possible, prevent his fall ; since t.he trngedy in Eden it has been seeking his reinstatement in that rinrity from which he fell. 4. Of permanent obligation. •Implied in the terms of its institution, its permanence would not be affected by the abolition of the Decalogue. 'l'he Decalogue presupposed its previous appointment. Christianity takes it up, just as Judaism took it up, as on6 :if God's existing ordinances for the good of man, and seeks through it to bring its higher influences to bear on man, just as Judaism tsought, through it, to operate with its inferior agency. Till it merges in the rest of "·hich it is a shadow by the accomplishment of its grand design, it must abide. III. Tm: CONNECTION OF THE TWO. God's rest is-I. The reaso1i of man's sabbath. The Almigl1ty could have no higher reason for enjoining a seventh day's rest upon l,is creature than that by so resting that cr~ature would be like himself. 2. The 1Jatlern of man's sabbath. A.s God worked through six of his days and rested on the se,enth, so should man toil through six of his days and rest on the_ seventh, As God did all his work in the six creative days, so should all man's labour be performed in the six days of the week. As God employs his rest in contemplation of his finished work and in blessing his creature man, so should man devote his sabbath to pious meditation on his past life and to a believing reception of God's gi:Cis of grace and salvation. 3. The life of man's sabbath. Whatever blessing comes to man on his weekly day of rest has its primal fountain in the rest of God. As man himself is God's image, so is man's sabbath the image of God's rest; and as man lives and moves and has his being in God, so does man's sabbath live and mov~ and have its being in God's rest. 4. The end of man's sabbath. The reinstatemen~ of man in God's rest is the purpose at which man's sabbath aims, the goal towards wl1ich it is tending. God's rest remains on high (Hcb. iv. 9), drawing men towards it. Man's weekly sabbath will ultimately lose itself in God's eternal rest.

entries.title: GEN 2:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -These are the generations is the usual heading for the different sections into which the Rook of Genesis is divided (vid. eh. v. 1; Yi. 9 ; x. 1 ; xi. 10, 2i; xxv. 12, l 9 ; xxHi. 1 ; xxxvii. 2). Misled by the LXX., wlio render toldoth by ;, {3/{3~oc: y11,i,uw~, Ranke, Ticle, H::ivernick, Tuch, Ewald, nnd 8tiihelin disconnect the entire verse from the second section, which says 11othi11g about the origination of the heavens on<l the earth, and append it to the preceding, iu which their creation is described. Ilgen improves on their suggestion by transferring it to the commencement of eh. i, as an appropriate superscription. Dreschler, Vaihinger, Ilohlen, Oehler, l\Iacdonald, et aliidivide the verse into two clauses, and annex the former to what precedes, commencing the ensuing narrntive with the latter. All of these proposals are, however, rendered unnecessary by simply observing that toldoth (from yaladh, to bear, to beget; hence begettings, procreations, evolutions, developments) does notdescribe the nntecedcnts, but the conscquents, of either thing or person (Rosen., Keil, E:allich). The toldoth of Noah are not the genealogical list of the patriarch's nncestry, but the tabulated register of his posterity ; and so the generations of the heavens and the earth refer not to their original production (Gesenius), but to their onward movements from creation downwards (Keil). Hence with no incongruity, but with smgular propriety, the first half of the present verse, ending with the words when they were created, literally, intheircreation, stands at the commencement of the section in which the forward proivession of the universe is traced. The pomt of departure in this subsequcnt cvolution of the material heavens and earth is further specified as being in the day that the Lord God (Jehovah Elohim) made the earth and the heavens; r,ot the heavens and the earth, which would Lave signified the universe ('1,W. on eh. i. 1), and carried back the writer's thought to the initial act of creation ; Lut the ea1ih and the atmospheric firmament, which indicates the period embracing the second and (possibly) the third creative days as the terminus a quo of the generations to be forthwith recorded. Then it wns thnt the heo.vcns nnd the enrth in theirdevelopment took a clenrnnd decided step forward in the direction of man and the human family (wes it in the appearance of vegetation !) ; and in this thought perhnpe will be found the koy to tbo si~1ificance of the new name for the Divine Demg which is used exclusively throughout the present section-Jehovah Elohim. From the frequency of its use, and the circumstnnce that it never has the article, Jehovah may be regarded as the proper personnl name of God. Eithe.r falsely interpreting Exod. xx. 7 and Levit. xxiv. 11, or following some encieut superstition (myste1ious names of deities were used generally in the Enst; the Egyptian Hermes had a name which (Cic. 'de Natura Deorum,' 8, 16) durst not beuttered: Fiirst), tl1e le.ter Hebrews invested this nomen tetragrammaton with such sanctity that it might not bepronounced (Philo, •Vit. Mosis,'iii. 6191 529). Accordingly,itwa.s theircustom to write it in the sacred text with the vowel points of Adonai, or, if that preceded, Elohim. Hence considerable doubt now exists as to its correct pronunciation. Etymologically viewed it is a. future form of havah, an old form of hayah; uncertainty as to whnt future has occasioned many different suggestions as to whatconstituted its primitive vocalisation. According to the evidence which scholam have collected, the choice lies between (1) Jahvch (Gesenius, Ewnld, Reland, Oehler, Macdonald, the Samaritan), (2) Yehvch or Yebeveh (Furst, W. L. Alexander, in Kitto's 'Cyclopeclia '), and (3) Jehovah (Michaelis, l\Ieyer, Stier, Hoelmann, 'fregelles, Murphy). Perhaps the preponderance of authority inclines to the first ; but the common punctuation is not so indefensible as some writers allege. Gesenius admits that it more satisfactorily accounts for the abbreviated syllables 1il~ and pthan the pronunciation which be himself favours. l\Iurphy thinks that the substitution of Adonai for Jehovah was facilitated by the agreement of their vowel points. The locus classicus for its signification is Exod. iii. 14, in which God defines himself as" I am that I am," and commands Moses to tell tho children of Israel tlmt Ehyeh had sent him. Hengstcnberg encl Keil conclude that absolute self-existence is the essential idea re11rcscnted by the name (cf. Exo<l. iii. 14; owv, LXX.; Rev. i. 4, 8; o WV 1tni o,"jv 1tai olpxoµ,vo,·, vid. Furst, 'Lex. sub nom.'). Baumgarten and Delitzsch, laying stress on its future form, regard it as = the Becoming One, with reference to the revelation, rather than the cssenct>, of the Divine nature. Macdonald, from the circumstance that it was not used till after the fall, discovers a pointing forward to Jehovah es oipx611wo, in connection with redemption. m. H. 4--7.] Tirn BOOK OF GENESI8. 41 Others, (loriving from o. hiphil future, take it ne denoting "ho who cnusos to be, tho Fulftller," and find in this nn explanation of Exod. vi. 8 (Exoll). Mny not nll these ideas be more or less involved in the fulnesa of the Divino nnme I As distinguished from Elohim, Deus omnipotem, the mighty One, Jehovah is the nbsolnte, self-existent One, who manifests himself to man, and, in particular, enters into distinct covenant engagements for his redemption, which he in due time fulfils. In the present section the names o.re conjoined partly to identify Jehovah with Elohim, and partly because the subject of which it treats is the history of man. Yer. 5.-And every plant of the field before it was (literally, not yet) in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew (literallr, had not yet sprouted). Following the LXX., the Euglish Version suggests an intention on the writer's part to emphasise the fact that the vegetation of the globehere comprehended under the general te11ns, shiah, sltrub, and eseb, herb - was not a natural production, but, equally with the i,-eat earth and heavens, was the creation of Jehovah Elohim-a rendering which has the sanction ofTaylerLewis; whereas the m-iter's objectclearly is to depict the appearance ofthe earth at the time when the man-ward development of tho heavens and the earth began. Then not a single plant was in the ground, not a green blade was visible. The land, newly spnmg from the waters, was one desolate region of bleak, bare lava-hills and extensive mud-flats. Up to that point the absence of vegetation is o.ccounted for by the circumstance that the presently existing atmospheric conditions of the globe had not then been established, for the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and the ordinary agricultural operationson which its production was afterwards to depend had not then been begun, and there was not a man to till the ground.

entries.title: GEN 2:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -But there went up a mist· from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground. 'The dry land having been sepnmted from tho wo.ters, and the atmospheric occ:nn uplifted above them both, vaporous exhalations began to ascend to the o.erial regions, and to return ago.in in the shape of rain upon the ground. Jehovah thus caused it to rain upon the ground, nnd so prepared it for the vegetation which, in obedience to the A!- mighty fint, sprung up nt the close of the third day, o.lthough tlte writer docs not mention its appenrnnco, but leaves it to bo inferred from the preceding section. 'l'hat soon after its emergence from the waters the land should be "dry, sterile, nnd snndy" will not be thought remarkable if we remember the highly igneous condition of our i,lnn~t at the time when the dry larnl wns uphenvecl and tl:c wnlcrs g.:~hercd into the subsiding valley,1. Nothing would moro naturally follow that event than the steamin" up of vapours to float in the aerial sea. I~ fact, the rnpidity with which evaporation would be carried on would very speedily leave the newly-f?nned land hard and dry, baked and caked mto a crust, till the atmosphere, becoming overcharged with a'lueous vapour, returned it in the shape of rain. To talk of insuperable c:,ifficulty and manifest dissonance whern everything is clear, natural, and harmonious is to speak at random, and betrays an anxiety to create contr::ulictions rather than to solve them.

entries.title: GEN 2:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Lord God (.Jcho,ah Elohim) formed man of the dust of the ground. Literally, dust from the ground. He,·e again, Bleek, Kalisch, and the thcoJoc,ians of their school discover contrariety bcttr~en this account of man's creation and that which has been given in the preceding chapter. In thatman is represented as having been crc,itcd by the Divine word, in the Divine image, and maleand female simultaneously; whereas in this his creation is exhibited as a painful process of elaboration from the clay by the hand of God, who works it like a. potter (asah; LXX., 1r>.ciaa10), and, after having first constructed man, by a subsequent operation forms woman. But the first account does not assert that Adam and Eve were created together, and gins no details of the formation of either. These are supplied by the present narrative, which, beginningwith the construction of his body from the fine dust of the ground, designedly represents it as an evolution or de,elopment of the material universe, and ends by setting it bcforo us as animated by the breath of God, reserving for later treatment the mode of Eve's production, when the circumstances that led to it have been described. And (the Lonl God) breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Literally, the breath of !ins. "The formation of mnn from the dust and the breathing of the breath of life must not be understood in 11 mechanical sense, as if God first of nil constructed a human figure from the dust" (still less docs it admit of the idea that man's physical nature was evolved from the lower animals), "and then, hy breathing his breath of life into the clod of earth which be had shaped into the form of n man, macle it into a li,·i..ng being. The words nro to be understood 9w1rp,1rw,. Ily an net of Divine omnipotence man arose from the dust ; and in the snme moment in which the dust, by ,;rtue of crcntfre omnipotence, shaped itself into a human form, it was P<'rvadecl by the Divine breath of life, and created a living being, so that we cannot say the body was earlier th,rn the soul" (Dolitzsch). And man became 11 42 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (':11. II. 4-7. living soul. Nephcsh cltayyah, in eh, i. 21, 30, is employed to designote the lower animals. Describing a boing animated by a ,/,vx•i or life principle, it does not necessarily imply thnt the basis of the life principle in man nnd the inferior animals is the samo. The distinction between the two appears from the difference in the mode of their creations. 'l'he beasts arose at tho o.lmighty fiat completed beings, eYery one a ru1i~esh cha'!fYah. '' The origin of their soul wns coincident with that of their corporeality, and their life was merely the indiYiduo.lisatiou of the uniYersal life ":ith ,..-hich nll ma.ttcr wns filled at the beginning by the Spirit of God" (Delitzsch). Man rcccind his life from n distinct act or Dinne inbroathing ; ccrtninly not an in• breathing of atmospheric air, but nn inflatus from the Runch Elohim, or Spirit of God, a comnrnuicatiou from the whole pe1·sonality of the Godhead. In effect man was thoroby constituted n -nepheslt cha'!fYah, like the lower animals ; but in him the life principle --,onferred R personality which was wnntmg in them. Thus thereis no real contradiction, scnrcely even an 'apparent dissonance," between tho t,vo ~ cco£mts of man's crea~ion. The second exhibits the foundation of thnt likeness to God nnd world-dominiou nscribc,l to him in the first.

entries.title: GEN 2:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -In accordance with a well-known chnracteristic of Hebrew composition, tho writer, h11ving carried his subject forward to a convenient place of rest, now reverts to a point of time in the six days antecedent to IIHln's appearance on tho earth. In anticipation of his arrival, it was needful thnt a suitable abodo should bo prepared for his reception. .Accordingly, haviug already mcntiouecl the creation of plants, trees, and flowers, the narrative proceeds to describe tho construction of .Adam s early homo. And the Lord God (Jehovah Elohim) planted-i. e. specially prepared-a garden (gan, n placo protected by a fence, from qanan, to cover ; hence a gnrden: cf. Deut. ii. 10 ; 1 Kings xxi. l! ; Isa. Ii. 3 ; LXX., ,rapaorn10~·; Vulgetc, pamdiaus; whc11c.a English, pnrndiso, Luke x:..,iil. 43) eastward (mekedein, literally, from the front quarter, not from lhe beginuing,-a,ro apxik, Aquila; EV ,rpwro,~·. Theodotion ; a principio, Yulgate, - Lut in the region lying towards tho east uf Palestine- LXX., 1<aT' at•«To:1-a,) in (not of, ns Murphy, who rentlern " in the cast of Eden") Eden (delight ; Greek, ,;0011i1: cf. Hedencsh, or Heclcn, the Lirlhplace of Zoroaster-l,alisch). The won! is not merdy descriptive of tho beauty and fertility of tho garden (paradiS'lts voluptatis, Yulg., er. ,rapcifoo-o'° n1~ Tpv~•a·, LXX. (Joel ii. 3). On the ground of possessing similar qualities, othor districts 11ml places were subsequently termed Edens : cf. 2 Kings xix. 12 ; Isa. xxxvii.12; Ii. 3; Ezek. xxvii. 23; s\mos L 6), but likc"·ise il'<lir:1tes its loralily, whid1 44 THE TIOOK OF GlrnESIS. [en. 11. 8-17. is Rfterwar<ls more exactly defined (vers. 10, 14). In the menn time it is simply noted thnt, this enchanting paradise having been sperinlly prcpnro<l by Jehovah, there he put the ma.n (Adnm) whom he ha.d formed. Yer. 9.-And out of the ground ma.de the Lord God (Jehovah Elohim) to grow every tree tha.t ie pleaeant to the sight-literally, lovely to see ; i.. c. beautiful in form and colour-and good forfood. In the preparation of man's pristine abode respect was had to ornamentation as well as utility. E,·ery ~pecies of vegetation that could. minister 1o his corporeal necessities was provided, Flowm-s, trees, and shrubs regalecl his senses l\;i11 their frngrance, pleased his eye with their exquisite forms nnd enchanting colours, nnd grntifie<l. his palate ,dth their luscious fruits. Hence the garden of the Lord became the highest ideal of earthly excellence (Isa. Ji. 3). In pnrticular it was distinguished by the presence of two trees, which occupied a central position among its multifarious 1)roductions. The tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and e~i.l. That these were not two separntc trees, but only one tree distinguished by different names, has been maintained, though mth no weightier reason than the statement of Eve in eh. iii 3. The opinion of 'Witsius, Luther, Kennicott, and Hengstenberg, that classes of trees, and not individual trees, are meant by the phrases "tree of life " and " tree of knowledge," is predudccl by the bnguage of Jehovah Elohim iu eh. ii -I7 and eh. iiL 24. As regards their significance, consistency requires that they should both be explained on the same principle. This, accordingly, disposes of the idea that the tree of life (literally, the tree of the lives: cf. (v~ov Tijc ,wik, Rev. ii 7; :x::x. 19) is simply a Hebraism for a living tree, as by 110 sort of ingenuity can the tree of knowledge be transformed into a k1w10ing tree. Jt likewise militates against the notion that the two trees were styled from the peculiar effects of their fruits, the one conferring physical immortalityon Adam's body(Scotus, Aquinas, Fairbairn, Kalisch, Luther), and the other imparting moral and intellectual intuitions to his soul (Josephus, Kalisch). But even if the life-giving properties of the one tree could be demonstrated from eh. iii. 24, proof woulcl still be required with regard to the other, that the mere physical processes of manclucation and digestion could be followed by results so immaterial as those of "rousincr the slumberiug intellect, teaching HRsou t; reflect, and enabling the judgment to distinguish between moral good and moral Evil" (Kalisch). Besides, if this was the im• mdiate effect ofeating the forbidden fruit, it is ditfkult to perceive either why it should han 1,een proJi;Hted to our first parent.Ii at all, it being "for thoir good to have their wits shnrpcnrd" (WillEt); or in what I'll• spect they suffered lo~s through listening to the tempter, and did not rnther gain (Rabbi Moses) ; or wherein, being destitute of both intellectual and mornl discernment, they could be rcgnrded as either ~uilty of transgression or responsible for obedience. Incapacity to know good and evil may be. a characteristic of unconscious childhood and unreflecting youth (Dent. i. 39 ; Isa. vii. 16 ; Jonah iv. 11), or of debilitated nge (2 8nm. xix. 36), but is not conceivable in the case of one who was created in God'e imege, invested l\;th world-dominion, e.nd himselfconstituted the subject of moral government. Unless, therefore, with ancient Gnostics and modem Hecrelians, we view the entire story of the probation as an allegorical representation of the necessary intellectual and ethical development of human nature, we must believe that Adam was acquainted with the idea of morn! distinctions from the first. Hence the conclusion seems to force itself npon our minds that the first man was possessed of both immortality and knowledge irrespective altogether of the trees, and that the true charac;ter which belonged to these trees was symbolical or sacramental, suggestive of the conditions under which he was placed in Eden. "Arbori autem vit:e nomen indidit, non quod vitam homini confe1Tet, qua jam ante prreditus erat ; sed ut symbolum ac memo1;a1e esset vital divinitus acceptre " (Calvin). For a further exposition of the exact significance of these trees see below on vers. 16,17.

entries.title: GEN 2:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The precise locality of Eden is indicated by its relation to the great watercourses of the region. And ariver (literally, a flowing water, applicable to large oceanic floods-Job xxii 16; Ps. xxiv. 2; xlvi. 6; Jonah ii. 4-as well as to nnn·ow streams) went out (literally, going out) of Edon to we.ter the garden. To conclude from this that the river had its source within the limits of the garden is to infer more than the premises will warrant. Nothing more isimplied in the language than that a great watercourse proceeded through the district of Eclen, and served to inigate the soil. Probably it intersectetl the garden, thus occasioning its remarkable fecundity and benuty. And from thence (i. e. either on emerging from which, or, taking IO in its secondary sense, outside of, or ata distance from which) it was parted (literally, divided itself), and became into four heads. Roaltim, from rosh, that which is highest; either principal waters, arms or branches (Tayler Lewis, Alford), or beginnings of rivers, indicating the sources of the streams (Gesenius, Keil, Macdonald, Murphy). If the second of these interpretetions be adopted, Eden must ho looked for CII. JI. 8--17.] nm BOOK OJ!' GENESIS. 45 in I\ spot whero some great flowing water is subdivided into four separate streams ; if tho former be rcg1trcled as the proper exegesis, then nny grcnt river which is first formed by the junction of two streams, and afterwords disperses its watersin two different directions, will meet the requirements of the case. Vora. 11, 12.-The name of the ftrst(river is) Pishon, or "the full-flowing." This is the first of those mnrks by which the river, when discovered, must be identified. It waspal)lably a broad-bosomed stream. A second 1s derived from the region through which it flows. That is it which compasseth (not necessarily surroundin15, but skirting in a circular or circuitous fash1on-Num. xxi. 4; Judges xi. 8) the whole land of Havilah. Havilah itself is dcscriued by three of its productions. Where there is gold. J. e. it is a gold-proclucing country. And the gold ofthat land is good. Ofthe purest qualityand largest quantity. There also is bdellium. Literally bedolach, which the manna was declared to resemble (Exod. xvii. 14 ; Num. xi. 7). The LXX., supposing it to be a precious stone, translate it by av0pa! in the present passage, and by ,rpvaraXXo, in Num. xi. 7-a view supported by the Jewish Rabbis and Gesenius. The m1tjority of modern interpreters espouse the opinion of Josephus, that it was an odorous and costly gum indigenous to India, Arabia, Babylonia, and Baetriana. The third production is the onyx (shoham, from II root signifying to be pale or delicate in colour, like the finger-nails), variously conjectured to be the beryl, onyx, sardonyx, sardius, or emerald. From this description it appears that Havilah must be sought for among the gold-producing countries of Asia. Now among the sons of Joktan or primitive Arabs (Gen. x. 29)-" whose dwelling was from l\Iesha, as thou goest, unto Sephar, a mount of the east"-are Ophir and Havilah, whence Gesenius concludes that India, including Arabia, is meant. Other countries have their advocates, such as Arabia Felix, Suaiana, Colchis, &c.; and other rivers, such as the Ganges (Josephus, Eusebius), the Phasis (Relnnd, Jahn, Rosenmiiller, Winer), the Indus (Schulthess, Kalisch).

entries.title: GEN 2:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the name of the second is the Gihon, or ft the bursting," from tl'A, to break forth. "Deep-flowing," T. Lewis renders it, connecting it with w,riavnt, and identifying it with Homer's (3a0vpf,ooi; ·o~,- avoi;. The same is it that compaHeth the whole le.nd of Ethiopia (Cush). Under the impression that th 1 African Cush was weant, tho Alexandrine Jews discovered the Gihon in tho Nile - e.n opinion in which they havo been followed by Schulthess, Gesenius, Fiirst, Berthenu, Kalisch, and others. But Cush, it is now known, describes the entire region between Arabia and the Nile, nnd in particular the southern district of the former lying between tho Persian Gulf and the Rerl Sea. Hence Tayler Lewis finds the Gihon in the ocean water sweeping round the south coast of .Arabia. Murphy detects the name Kush in the words Caucasus and Caspian and, looking for the site of Eden about the sources of the Euphrates and the Tigris in Armenia, thinks the Gihon may have been the leading stream flowing into the Caspian. Delitzsch advocates the claim of the Araxis to be this river.

entries.title: GEN 2:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the name of the third river is the Hiddekel, or "the darting," from 1[1 nnd S~;i. a sharp and swift arrow, referring to its rapidity. It is unanimously agreed that this must be identified with the Tigris ; in the present lan~age of the Persians designated tir, which signifies an arrow. H is styled in Aramaic diglath or diqlah. That is it which goeth towards the east of Assyria. Its identity is thus placed beyond a question. And the fourth river is Euphrates, or ft the sweet," from an unused root, parath, signifying to be sweet, referring tc the sweet and pleasant taste of its waters (Jer. ii. 18). Further description of this great water was unnecessary, being universally known to the Hebrews as "the great river" (Dent. i. 7; Dan. x. 4), and "the river" par e:ccellence (Exod. xxiii 31 ; Isa. vii 20). The river still bears its early name. In the cuneiform inscriptions deciphered by Rawlinson it is called "Ufrata." entries.title: GEN 2:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -T!te (Jarden of Eden. I. A SCENE OF BEAUTY. Whether situated in Ar'!1cnia. or Bt1byloni~ (sec Exposition), it was _a fair sl?ot in a sunny region of delights (Eden). Tine beauty was-1. Luxuriant. Milton has lavished all tl11J wealth of hie creative genius in on attempt to depict "t.he happy rural seat of the first pair" (' Par. Lost,' bk. iv.). Yet it is questionable if even he has succeeded in re. producing the gorgeous spectacle, the endlessly diversified assortment of lovely forrn8 and radiant colours that seemed to compress "in narrow room nature's whole wealth," entitling Eden to be characterised as "a heaven on earth." 2. IJiiinely prepared. Jehovah Elohim caused it to spring up and bloom before the wondering eye of man.. All the world's beauty is of God. Tlie flowers and the herbs and the trees have all their symmetry and loveliness from him. God c:lothes the lilies of the field ; the raiment, outshining the glory of royal Solomon, in which they are decked is of his making. If nature be the loom in which it is woven, he is the all-wise i,~avr,,, or"INeaver bywhom its wondro11s mechanism is guided and energ;uerl. Let us rejoice in the earth's beauty, and thank God for it. 3. Eaxeptional. We arc scarcely warranted, even by eh. iii. 17, to suppose that, prior to the fall, the whole world was a •paradise. Rather, geologic revelations give us reason to believe tliat from the first the earth was prepared for the reception of a sinful race, dea.th antl defo1mity ha.ving been in the world anterior to man's arrival upon the scene (cf. Bushnell, 'Nat. and Super.,' eh. vii.), and that the Edenic home was what the Bible says it was-a fair spot, specially planted and fenced about, for the temporary residence of the innocent pair, who were ultimately, as transgressors, to be driven forth to dwell upon a soil which was cursed because of sin. Let it humble us to think that the earth is not a paradise solely because of human sin. 4. Prophetic. Beside,; being a picture of what the world would have been, had it been prepared for a. sinless rnce, it was also a foreshadowing of the renova.ted earth when sin shall be no more, when "this land that was desolate shall have become like the garden of Eden." Let it stimulate our hope and assist our faith to anticipate the palingenesia of the future, when this sterile and disordered world sliall be refitted with bloom and beauty. II. A SPHERE OF WORK. Adam's work wae-1. God-assigned. So in a. very real sense is every man's life occupation appointed 1.,y God. "To every man his work' is the law of God's world as well as of Christ's kingdom. This thought should dignify "the trivial round, the common task," and enable us, "whether we eat or drink, or whatsoever we do, to do all to the glory of God." 2. Pleasant. And so should all work be, whether arduous or easy, especially to a Christian. To he sure, Adam's work was light and easy in comparison with that which afterwards became his lot, and that which now constitutes ours. But even these would be joyous and exhilarating if performed by the free spirit of loYe, instead of, as they often are, by the unwilling hands of hondmen, 3. Necessary. Even in a state 0£ innocence it was impossible that man could he sufl'e-red to live in indolence ; his endowments and capacities were fitted for activity. Hia happiness and snfety (against temptation) required him to be employed. And if God who made him was ever working, why should he be idle? The same arguments forbid idleness to-day. Christianity with emphasis condemns it. "If a man will not work, neither shall he eat." III. AN ABODE OF INNOCENCE. This abode was-1. Suitable. It was not su.iti>.ble for sfoners, just as the world outside would not have been adapted for a pair who were sinless ; but it was peculiarly approprinte for their innocence. He who appointeth to nil men the bounds of their habitation always locates men in spheres that are exactly suited to their natures and needs. 2. Provisional. Their possession of it was contingent on their remaining sinless. If their souls continued pure, their homes would continue fair. It is man's own sin that defaces the beauty and m:irs the happiness of man's home. When men find themselves in positions that are not compatible with their happiness al;l.d usefulness, it is sin that has placed them there_. 3. Quit'kl;,; lost. How long they continued innocent is usele~s to conjecture, thou,: n probably it was not long. Mor!! important is it to observe that uot much w..s THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CR. II. 8-17 rrqnired to depri,·e them of their lovely homo-one act of disobedience I See th111 <langer of even one sin. 4. Ultimauly recoverable. This truth wns taught by the i,taiioning· of the chC'rnhim nt its gate (q. v.). Rev. xxii. 1 tells us it has been regained for us by Clirist, nn<l will in the end be bestowed on us. TV. A HOME OF HArPINEss. 1. Everything ""'as absent that might mnr mnn's felic!t~·. _No sin, no error, no sorrow. 2. Everything was present that could minister to !us enJoyment. There wns ample gratification for all the different parts of his complex nature. (1) For his bodily senses, the fair scenes, melodious sounds, crystal strnams, and \uscions fruits of the garden. (2) For his mental powers, tho study of the works of God. (3) For his social affections, a loving nnd lovely partner. (4) For his spiritual nature, God. To reproduce the happiness of Eden, ~o far ns thnt is possible in II sinful world, there is needed (a) communion with a gracious God: (b) the felicity of a loving and a pious home; (c) the joy of lifeph)·sical, intellectual, moral. V. A PLACE OF rRODATION. This probation wns-1. Necessary. Virtue that stands only because it has ne,•er been assaulted is, to say the least of it, not of tho highest kind. Unless man had been subjected to trial it might have remained dubious whether he obeyed of free choice or from mechanical necessity. 2. Easy. The specific commandment which Ado.m was required to observe was not severe in its terms. The limitations it prescribed were of the smallest possible descriptionabstinence from only one tree. 3. Gracious. Instead of perilling the immortality of Adam and his poste1ity upon every single act of their lives, he suspended it upon tJ1e observance, doubtless for only a short space of time, of one easily-obeyed precept, "·hich he bad the strongest possible inducement to obey. If he maintained his intC'grity, not only would his own holiness and happiness be confirmed, but those of his descendants would be secured; while if be failed, he would involve not himself alone, hut all succeeding generations in the sweep of n terrific penalty. The clearr.ess "·ith which that penalty was made known, the certainty of its execution, and 1.he severity of its inflictions, were proofs of the grace of God towards bis creature ma.n.

entries.title: GEN 2:8–17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.Jfon's first dwelling-place. The description of Eden commences an entirely new stage in the record. We are now entering upon the history of humanity as such. I. The first fact in that history is a state of II PLEASANTNESS." The garden is planted by God. The trees are adapted to human life, to support it, to ~ratify it; and in the midst of the garden the two trees which representthe twomost important facts with which revelation is about to deal, viz., immortality and sin. II. OUTSPREAD BLESSING. The BIVEB breaks into four fountains, whose description carries us over enormous regions of the world. It is the river which went out of Eden to water the garden ; so that the conception before us is that of an abode of man specially prepared of God, not identical with Eden in extent, but i? character; and the picture is carried out, as it were, by the channels of the outflowrng streams, which bear the Eden life with them over the surface of the earth, so that the general effect of the whole is a proplUX?J of blessing, Eden-like beauty, and pleasantness, ovCT the whole ext,ent of the world. III. THE PREPARED GARDEN WAITED Fon ITS INHABITANT. 11 And the Lord God took the man, and put him into thegarden of Eden" (literally, made him to rest !nthe i:;-arden) "to dress it and to keep it." Perhaps the simplest view of these words 1s the most significant. Man is led into a life of pleasantness, with only ~ueh demands upon him as it will be no burden to meet; and in that life of J:!Ure happmess n!1d free activity he is ruade conscious, not of mere dependence upon his Creator for existence, not of laws banging over him like threatening swords, but of a Divine eomme.ndment which e.t on~e ga\'e libnrty and restrained it, which surrounded the one tree of knowledge of good and evil with its circle of prohibition, not as an arbitr~ry test of obedience, but as a Divine proclamation of eternal righteousness. "Evil 1s death,' Thou alrnlt not eat of it," for this reason, that "in the day that thou eatest thereof thon shalt surely dio." It is not a subjection of a new-made creature to a test. It would be a harsh demand to make of Adam, unless he understood that it was founded on the nature of things. IV. '.rHE TREE OF Lill'!!: AND THE TREE OF DEATH STAND TO0ETHER in the midst of the garden. They hold the same position still in every sphere of human existence. But the book of Divine grace, ns it teaches us how the sin-stricken, dying world is restored to a paradise of Divine blessedness, reveals at the last, in the vision of the Christian seer, only the tree oflife beside the water oflife; the evil cast out, and the death which it brought with it, and the ncw-macfo inhabitants " taking freely" of "the pleasures which arc for evermore."-R.

entries.title: GEN 2:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie tree of life and the water oflife. These two features of Eden claim special attention. I. THEIR RECURRENCE IN SCRIPTURE. They link the paradise of unfallen man to that of redeemed man. Actual channels of life and blessing, they were also figures of that salvation which the history of the world ,vas gradually to unfold. But sin came, and death ; present possession was lost. \Vhat remained was the promise or a Saviour. We pass over much of preparation fvr his coming: the selection of a people ; the care of God for his vineyard ; the ordinances and services foreshadO\ving the gospel. Then a time of trouble: Jerusalem a desolation; the people in captivity ; the temple destroyed ; the ark gone ; sacrifices at an end. "Where is now thy God?" \Vhcre thy hope? Such the state of the world when a vision given to Ezekiel (Ezek. xlvii. 1-12), reproducing the imagery of Eden, but adapted to the need of fallen man. Again we have the stream ; now specially to heal. Its source the mercy-seat (comp. Ezek. xliii. 1-7; xlvii. 1; Rev. xxii. 1). And the trees;. not different from the tree of life (Ezek. xlvii. 12: "It shall bring forth new fruit'') ; varied manifestations of grace ; for food and for medicine. But observe, the vision is of a coming dispensation. Again a space. Our Saviour's earthly ministry over. The Church is struggling on. The work committed to weak bands ; the treasure in earthen vessels. But before the volume of revelation closed, tho same symbols are shown in vision to St. John (Rev. ::a.ii. 1, 2). The "river of water of life" (cf. "living water," John iv. 10), and the tree whose fruit and leaves are for food and healing. Meanwhile our Lord had said, "Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness." A link to connect this with Gen. iL is Rev. ii. 7 (cf. also Rev. xii. 11). And again, the word used for "tree" in all these passages is that used for the cross in Gal. iii. 13 and 1 Pet. ii. 24. ll. THEIR SPIRITUAL SIGNIFICANCE. The tree with its fruit and leaves are the manifestation of Christ to the soul-to sinners pardon, to the weak support and guidance, to saints communion. And the stream is the gospel (the four-parted river in Eden has been likened to the four Gospels), spreading throughout the world, bringing healing, light, and life ; enuhling men to rejoice in hope. But mark, the drops of which that stream is composed are living men. The gospel spreads from heart to heart, and from lip to lip (cf. John vii. 38). Forming part of that healing flood are preachers of the gospel in every place and way; and thinkers contending for the faith; and men mighty in prayer; and those whose loving, us.eful lives set forth Christ; and tho sick silently preaching patience; and the child in his little ministry. There is helping work for all. The Lord hath need of all. To each one the question comes, Art thou part of that stream? Hast thou realised the stream of mercy, the gift of salvation for thine own need? And canst thou look at the many still unhealed and be content to do nothing? Thou couldst not cause the stream to flow; but it is thine to press tho "living water" upon others, to help to save other!! Art thou doing this? Is there not within the circle of thy daily life some one in grief whom Christian sympathy may help, some anxious one whom a word of faith may strengthen, some undecided ono who may be influenced? There is thy work. Let the reality of Christ's gift nnd his charge to thee so fill thy heart that renl longing rnny l~nd to earnest prnyer; tl,rn a w:iy will bo opencd.-M. GliN!iSIS, 60 'l'lIE DOOK OF GENESIS. (en. 11. 18-26,

Tho portrait l1ere clolincatcd of tho first man is something widely different from that of an infantile snvago slowly groping his way towards the "'Ossession of o.rticulute speech and intel- [igiblo lnngunge byimitation of the so\lllds of nnimals. entries.title: GEN 2:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: --And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept. This was clearly not a sleep of weariness or fatigue, in consequence of arduous labours undergone, but a supernatural slumber, which, however, may have been superinduced upon the natural c,,ndition of repose, Lightfoot, following the LXX., who translate tardemah (deep sleep) by ecstasy, frurn,rn;, im:igines that the whole scene of Eve's creation was presented to Aclam's imagination in a Divinely-inspired clream, which bas at least the countenance of Job iv. 13 Such a supposition, however, is not rcquiretl to account for Adam's recognition of his bride. There is more of aptness in the observation of Lange, that in the deep sleep of Au.am we have an echo of the creative evenings that prececled the Divine activity. "Everything out of which some new thing is to come sinks down before the event into such n deep sleep," is tlrn farseeing and comprehensive remark of Ziegler. And he took one of his ribs (tsela = something bent, from tsala, to incline ; hence a rib), and closed up the flesh (literally, flrsh) instead thereof. Wbether Atlam was create,[ with a superfluous rib, or his bocly was mutilated by tho abstraction of a rib, is nquestion for the curious. In the first, Calvin fimfa nothing "which is not in a.ccordance with Divine providence," while he favours the latter conjecture, nod thinks that Aclam got n rich compensation-" quum so integrum vidit in uxore, qui prius t:intum climiclius crat." Luther inclines to think that Adam's language in ver. 23 implies that not the bar~ rib, but the rib with the accom]Janying flesh, was oxtracted.

"The word implies 1he solemn bestowrucnt of her in the bonds of the marriage coYenant, which is henoo called the co,·enant of God (Prov. ii. li); impl~ing that he is the Author of this sacred institution" (Bush). On awaking from his ~lumber .Adam at once recognised the Divine intention, nncl joyfully welcomed bis bride. Yer. 23.-And Adam sa.id. Eitb.er as being possessed, while in a sinless stnte, of a power of intuitivc perception whieh has bceu lost through the fall, or as speaking under Divine inspiration (vide Matt. xix. 4---o). This now. Literally, this tread, step, or stroke, meaning either this time, looking back to the previous re,icw of the animal creation, as if he wished ro say, At last one hru; come who is suitable to be my partner (Calvin); or, less probably, looking forward to the ordinary mode of woman's production, this time she is supernaturally formed (Bush). "The thrice repeated thi.i is characteristic. It vividly points to the woman on whom, in joyful astonishment, the man's eye now rests with the full power of first love" (Delitzsch). Instinctively he recognises her relation to himself. Bone of my bone, and flesh of my flesh. entries.title: GEN 2:25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And theywere bothnaked. Not partially (Pye Smith), but completely destitute of clothing. Diodorus Siculus and Plato both mention nakedness as a feature of the golden nge anil a characteristic of the first men (vide Rosenmiiller, Schol·ia in loco). The man and his wife. The first pllir of human beings a.re henceforth recognised in their relationship to one llnother ns husband and wife. And theywere not ashamed. Not because they were wholly uncultivated and their moral insight undeveloped (Knobel, Kalisch); but because theirsoulswere llrrayed in purity, and "their bodies were made holy through the spirit which a.nime.ted them" (Keil). "They were naked, but yet they were not so. Their bodies were the clothing of their internal glory; and their internal glory was the clothing of their nakedness" (Delitzsch). It is not surprising that tho primeval history of mankind should have left its impress upon the current of tradition. The Assyrian tablets that relate to man llre so fragmentary and mutilated that they can scarcely be rendered intelligible. So far ns they have been deciphered, tho first appears on its obvcrse side " to give the speech of the Deity to the newly-create,! pnir (man antl woman), instrncting them in their duties," In which cnn be cletcctecl n refcrcnco to something which is eaton Ly the stomach, to the cluty of clnily invocation of the Deity, to the do.uger of lenving Gocl's fcnr, in which alone they can be holy, and to the propriety of trusting only a. friend ; and on its reverse what resembles a. discourso to the first woman on her duties, in which occur the words, ff With the lord of thy beauty thou shalt be faithful : to do evil thou shnlt not approach him" ('Chalde:m Genesis,' pp. 78-80), '.l.'ho Persian legend describes .Mcschia and Meschiane, the first parents of our race, as living in purity and innocence, and in the enjoyment of happiness w~ich Ormuzd promised to render perpPtunl 1f they persevered in virtue. But Ahriman, e.n evil demon (Dev), suddenly appeared in the form of a serpent, and gave them of the fruit of a wonderful tree. The literature of the Hindoos distinguishes four ages of the world, in the first of which Justice, in the form of a. bull, kept herself firm on her four feet ; when Viltue reigned, no good which the mortals possessed wns mixeu with baseness, and man, free from diseo.se, saw all his wishes accomplished, nnd o.ttaincd an age of 400 years. The Chinese also have their afae of happy men, living in abundance o food, and surrounded by the peaceful beasts(' Kalisch on Genesis,' p. 87). In the Zenclavesta, Yima, the first Irnnic king, lives in a secluded spot, where he and his people enjoy u11i11tcrruptcd hnp1,incs~, in a region free from sin.ifolly, ,.iolence, poverty, deform, ity. The Teutonic Edclas have a glimpse of tl,o same truth in their magnificent clrinking balls, glittering with burnished golcl, where the primeval race enjoyed a life of perpetual festivity. Traces ofa similar belief arc found among the Thibctans, Mongolians, Cingalese, ancl others (Rawlinson's •Hist. Illustrations of Scripture,' p. 10). The Weatern traditions are familiar to scholars in the pages of Hesiod, who speaks of the golden nge when men were like the gods, free from labours, troubles, cares, ancl all evils in general ; when the earth yiclcled her fruits spontaneously, and when men were beloved by the gods, with whom they hehl uninterrupted commnnion (Hesiorl, ' Opern et Dies,' 90). Ancl of Ovid, who adcls to this picture the element of moral goodness as a characteristic of the aurea II!t<U ('Met.am.,• i. 89). .Macrobius (' Somn. Scipionis,' ii. 10) e.lso depicts this period u one in which reigned simplicit<U mali nescia et adhuc astutuz ine:cperta (Macclonalcl, ' Creation and the Fall,' p. 147). ff These coincidences affect the originality of the Hebrew WTitings as little as the frcqu~nt resemblance ofMosaic and heathen laws. They teach us that all such narratives have a common source; that they are reminiscences of primeval traditions modified by the different nations in accordance with their individual culture" (Kalisch),.

entries.title: GEN 2:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie fi1·st marriage. I. THE LONELY MAN. 1. Nobly born. Sprung from the soil, yet descended from above. Fashioned of the dust, yet inspired by a celestial breath. Allied to the beasts, yet the offspring of God. 2. Comfortably placed. His native.country a sunny region of delights (Eden, eh. ii. 8) ; his home a beautiful and fertile garden (eh. iii. 5); his supplies of the amplest possible description (eh. i. 30; ii. 16); his occupation light and pleasant (eh. ii. 15); his restrictions slight nnd trivial (eh. ii. 17) ; his p1ivileges lnrge (eh. ii. 16). 3. Richly endowed. With immortality (eh. ii. 17), intelligence (eh. ii. 19), social capacities and instincts (eh.ii. 18), the faculty of speech (eh.ii. 20). 4. Highly exalted. As God's offspring, he was invested with world-dominion (eh. i. 28; Ps. viii, 6), symbolised in his naming of the creatures (eh. ii. 20). Yet-5. Essentially alone. Not as entirely bereft of companionship, having on the one hand the society of Jehovah Elohim, and on the other the presence of the animals ; but in neither the Creator nor the creatures could he find his other self-his counterpart and complement, his consort and companion. On the one hand Jehovah Elohim was too high, while on the other the creatures were too low, for such partnership as Adam's nuturc crn,·cd. And so Adam dwelt in solitude apart from both. "But for Adam there was not found an help meet for him." II. THI!: PROVIDED PARTNER. 1. Divinely fasliioned (ver. 22). (1) Woman was the last of God's creative works; presumublv, therefore, she was the best. "Eve's being made after Adam puts an honour upon that sex us the glory of the man (1 Cor. xi. 7). If man is the head, she is the crown-a crown to her husband, the crown of the visible creation" (M. Henry). (2) Woman was not made till everything wns in the highest stute of readiness for her reception. Before her creation, not only must there be a home for her reception, provision for her m!linten!\nce, and serrnnt11 54 Trm TIOOK OF GENRSiS. [err. n. 18--25. to attend npon l1er bidding; there must likewise be a husband thnt feels the need of l1er sm••ct society, that long-s for her coming, nnd tl1r,t can npprccinte her worth. Hence he who llC'C'ks n pnrtner should first find n house in which to lodp;e her, tho lll<'nns to rnpport hn, but specially the. love whn_ewilh to cherish her. (3) Womnn wn~ formed out of ~ncr_ 1111d ~10re prccwus nrntcnal than mnn, hcing co11slructed 0£ a nh taken from l11s s1do. 'The man was dust refined, hut the woman was dust double refined, one remo,e further from tho earth" (M. Henry). '!'his wns not because. of any s_npi:iosed excell~nce :esidi_ng in the matter of .a human body. It "·a~ designed to md1cate w_oman s unity w!l11 mnn as part of lmnself, nnd womnn'R claim upon man for nffectwn and protection. She wns made of a rib taken from his side-" not made out of his hend, to rule over him; nor out of his feet to be trampled on by him ; but out of his side, to be equal with him; under hie arm' to be protected ; and near his l1eart, to be beloved" (Henry). (4) Woman wns const;·ucted with the greatest possible care. The entire operaticn was carried through, not only under God's immediate superintendence, but exclusively by God's own hand, Adnm 11cither saw, knew, nor took part in the work. God cast him into a deep sleep, "that no room might be left. to imagine that he had herein directed the Spirit of the Lord, or been his counsellor" (Henry). '!'hen by God's own hnnd Adam's side was opened, n rib extracted, the flesh closed in its stead, and finally, the rib thus removed from Adam's side- "Under his forming hands a creature grew, :Man like, but differ~nt sex; so lovely fair, That what seemed fair in all the world, seemed now Mean, or in her summed up, in her contained, And in her looks ; . . . . , Grace was in all her steps, heaven in her eye, In every gesture dignity and love" (Milton, 'l'ar. Lost,' Dk. ,iii. 469). 2. .Divinely presented (ver. 22). "The Lord brought her unto the man." ""'herein we have exemplified the three great causes of marriage. (1) The father's consent, in God's giving. (2) The woman's consent, in Eve's coming. This was no forced marriage; the woman comes freely. (3) The man's consent, in Adam's receiving. 'And Adam said, Tl1is is at last bone of my bone'" (Hughes). And without these human marriages are sinfully contracted. Love for the bride is one of the signs which God vouchsafes of his approval of a marriage ; the bride's affection for the bridegroom is another; while a third is the approbation and the blessing of tLe parent.a of both. III. TIIE WEDDED PAIR. 1. Jfarried by Goel. 11 God is tl1e best maker of marriages" (Shakespeare). Nay, unless God unites there is no real mar1iage, but only an unhallowed connection, legitimised by man's laws, it may be, but not sanctioned by God's. As tl1is wedding was of God's arranging, so likewise was it of his cclebruting. What celestial benedictions were outbreathed upon the young and innocent pair, as they stood there before their Maker, radiant in beauty, tremulous with joy, full of adoration, we are left to imagine. Happy they whose nuptials arc first sanctioned and then ccfobrated by the living God I 2. United in love. This first marriage was certainly something more than a social or a civil contract; something otl1er than a union of cor,venience or a diplomatic alliance; something vastly different from a legalised connubium. It was the realisation of what our Laureato pictures as the ideal uarriage :- " Entb fulfils Defect in each, and always thought in thought, Purpose in purpose, will in will, they grow, Tho single, pure, and perfect anim:i.l ; Tho two-cell'd heart beating, with one full sL!okc, Life" (' Princess,' vii.). B. Clothed in innocence. Never had bridal pair so beautiful and radiant npparcl. ']'he unclotl1cd bodies of our first parents we can imagine were onawnthed in ethereal 1md transfigul'ing liglit; in their caee the outshining of their holy souls, which, us yet, ott. rt. IR-2u.) Ttm DOOK OF GENESJR. 55 wrro tho undimmed nml unmarred image of their Maker, capable of receiving and reflecting his glory. Alns, never bridnl pair has stood in robes so .fair I The beauty of holiness, the lustre of iunocence, the radiance of purity lrnvc departed from the souls of men. Never till we stand in the celestial Eden, where they neither marry nor are given in marriage, will garments of such incomparable splendour b'3 ours. Menntime, let ns thank God there is a spotless raiment in which our guilty sou)3 may bo arrayed, and in which it were well that every b1irlal pair were decked. Happy they who, when they enter int_o maITicd life, can say, 11 I will great_ly rejoice in tl,c Lord, my soul sl,all be joyful m my ~od; for he hath _clothed me with the ;:\'armenw of salvation he hath covered me with the robe of nghteousness, as a bndegroom decketh him self with ornaments, and ns a bride adorneth herself with jewc!R." 4. Housed in paradise. United by the hand of God, they began their married life in Eden. 11 Ancl thero these bVllin upon the skirts of time Sat sicle by sicle, full summ'cl in all their powers, Dispensing harvest, sowing the to-be. Self-reverent each, and reverencing each ; Distinct in indiviclualities, But like each other, ev'n as those wl10 love" (Tennyson's 'Pdnces.~,' vii.). And so may any wedded pair be housed in Eden wl,o, putting on the Lord ,Jesus Christ, fill their home, however humble, with the light of love. Hm.IILIES BY VAilIOUS AUTHORS.

entries.content: -T!te tnie life of man. The commencement of human society. First we see man surrounded by cattle, fowl, and beast of the field, which were brou,!!;ht to him by God as to their lord and ruler, that he might name them as from himself. (Cf. the three assaults upon the Second .Adam (Matt. iv. 1; Luke iv. 1), which were essentially the same.) entries.content: -Confession having thus been made by both delinquents, and the arch-contriver of the whole mischief discovered, the Divine Judge proceeds to deliver sentence, And the Lord God said unto the serpent. Which he does not interrogate as he did the man and woman, "because (1) in the animal itself there was no sense of sin, and (2) to the devil he would hold out no hope of pardon" (Calvin); "because the trial has now reached the fountain-head of sin, the purely evil purpose (the demoniacal) having no deeper ground, and requiring no further investigation" (Lange). Because thou haet done this. I. e. beguiled the woman. The incidence of this curse hns been explained as -1. The serpent only (Kalisch). 2. The devil only (Macdonald). 3. Partly on the serpent and partly on Satan (Calvin). 4. Wholly upon both (Murphy, Bush, Ca.ndlish). The difficulties attending these different interpretations have thus been concisely expressed : --,- " 1. Quidam statuunt maledictionem latam in serpentem solum, quia hie confertur cum aliis bestiis, non in diabolum, quia is antea maledictus erat. 2. Alii in diabolum so!um, quin. brutus serpens non poterat jus~ puniri. 3. Alii applicant ver. 14 ad serpentem, ver. 16 in diabolum. At vero tu et te idem sunt in utroque versu. 4. Alii existirno.nt eam in utrumque latam " (Medus in 'Poli Commentar.,' quotod by Lange). The fourth opinion seoms most nccorclnnt with the lnngu~e of the malediction. Thou art ouraed. The cursing of the irrationlll creaturo sho11ld occasion no more GENESIS, difficulty than the cursing of the earth (ver, 17), or ofthe fig tree (Matt. xi. 21). Creatures can be cursed or blessed only in accordance with their natures. The reptile, therefore, bciug neither a moral nor responsible creature, could not be cursed in the sense of being rnado susceptible of misery. entries.title: GEN 3:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The searching question. We can picture the dread of this question. Have you considered its love-that it is really the first word of the gospel? Already the Shepherd goes forth to seek the lost sheep. The Bible shows us - 1. The original state of man ; what God intended his lot to be. 2. The entry of sin, and fall from happiness. 3. The announcement and carrying out God's plan of restoration. THE GOSPEL DEGJNS not with the promise of a Saviour, but WITU SHOWING MAN IIIS NEED. Thus (John iv. 15-18) our Saviour's answer to II Give me this water'' was to convince of sin: 11 Go, call thy husband." That first loving call has never ceased. Men are still straying, still must come to themselves (Luke xv. 17). \Ve hear it in the Baptist's teaching; in the preaching of St. Peter o.t Pentecost; and claily in his life-giving work the Holy Spirit's first step is to convince of sin. And not merely in conversion, but at every stage ho repeats, "\Vhere art thou? 11 To welcome God's gift we must feel our own need; o.nd the inexhaustible treasures in Christ are discerned us we mark daily the defects of our service, o.nd how far we are from the goal of our striving (Phil. iii. 13, 14). Hence, even in o. Christian con- ~reg11tion, it is needful to press "Where o.rt thou? 11 to leo.d men nearer to Christ. We want to stir up easy-going disciples, to mo.ke Christians consider their calling, to rouse to higher life and work. Our Saviour's co.II is, "Follow me." How ure you doing· this? You 11re pledged to be his soldiers; what reality is there in your 70 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. r. 8-19, figli~ing? How many are c_ontent_ m_erely to do as others do I What do ye for Chnst?_ You have,)'Ot\r Bible; lB 1t studied, prayed over?
