entries.title: GEN 3:9–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.The word of God in tlie moral cliaos. These verses bring before us very distinctly the elements of man's sinful state, and of the redemptive dispensa, tion of God which came out of it by the action of bis brooding Spirit of life upon the chaos. • I. THE WOUD OF Goo ADDRESSED TO THE PERSONAL CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE BEGINNING OF THE NEW WORLD. "The Lord God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Wl1ert art thou?" Before that direct intercoarse between the Spirit of God and the spirit of man there is no distinct recognition of the evil of sin, and no separation of· its moral and physical consequences. The " Where a1·t, thou 1" begins the spiritu11l work. I!. THE PROCESS OF THE WORK OF GoD IN THE CONSCIENCE IS ONE THAT LEADS US FROM THE OUTSIDE CIRCLE OF BESPONSlBILITY TO THE INNERMOST CENTRE Oil' CONVICTlON AND CONFESSION. "I was naked," "Iwas afraid," "I hid myself," "The woman gave me of the tree," "I did eat;" so at last we get to the central fact-I broke the commandment, I nm guilty towards God. Each lays the blame on another-the man on the woman, the woman on the serpent. But the main fact is this, that when once the voice of God deals with us, when once the Spirit of light and life broods over the chaos, there will be truth brought out, nnd the beginning of all new creation is confession of sin. After all, both the transgressors admitted the fact: "I did eat." Nor do they dare to state what is untrue, although they attempt to excuse tl1emselves; for there may be a true confession of sin before there is a sense of its greatness and inexcusableness. IIL The transgression being clearly revealed, next comes THE DIVINE CONDEMNA· TION. It is upon the background of judgrnent that redemption must be placed, that it may be clearly seen to be of God's free grace. The judgment upon tlie serpent must be viewed as a fact in the sphere of man's world, not in the forger sphere of the superkuman suggested by the later use of the term "serpent." God's condel"!lnation of Satan is only shadowedfortli here, not actually described. The cursed animal simply represents the cursed agent or instrument, and therefore was intended to embody the curse of sin to tlie eyes of man. At the same time, the fifteenth verse must not be shorn of its spiritual appfication by a merely naturalistic interpretation Man's inborn detestation of the serpent brood, and the serpent's lurking enmity ao-ainst roan, as it waits at his heel, is rightly taken as symbolically representing (1) tl~e antagonism between good and evil introduced into the world by man's foll ; (2) the necessity that tliat antagonism should be maintained; and (3) the purpose of God that it should be brought to an end by the destruction of the serpent, the removing out of tho way both of the evil principle and of the besetments of man's life which liave a1isen out of it. This ".first promise," as it is called, was not given in the form of a promise, but of a sentence. Are we not reminded of the cross, which itself wnl! tl-e carrying out of a sentence, but in which wae included the redeeming mercy of Uod? Life in dP.atli i.> "J1e myatery of Christ's sacrifice. "It pleased the Lord t~ Vil. Ill. 8-19.] TIIE BOOK OF GENESIS. 71 bruise Mm" (Isa. !iii. 10), "Througl, death he destroyed kim that ltad the power of death," &o. (Heh. ii. 14). It must have been itself like a. revelation of redeeming love ·thnt God pronounced sentence farst upon the serpent, not upon man, thereby teaching him tha.t he wll!I in the sight of God a victim of the evil power, to be delivered by the victorious seed of the woman, rather than an enemy to he crushed nnd destroyed. Tho sentence seemed to say, Thou, the serpent, art the evil thing to be annihilated,' man shall be saved, though wounded and bruised in the heel ; the "woman's seed" shall ho the conqueror,-which was the prediction of a renovation of humanity in a pecond Adam, a dim forecasting of the future, indeed, but a certain nnd unmistakable proclamation of the continuance of the race, notwithstanding sin and death; and in that continuance it was declared there should be a realisation of entire deliverance. The sentence upon the woman, which follows that upon the serpent, as she was the first in the transgression, is a sentence which, while it clearly demonstrates the evil of sin, at the same time reveals the mercy of God. 'rho woman's sorrow is that which she can and does forget, for "joy that a man is born into the world." Her desire to her husband and her submission to his rule do come out of that fall of her nature in which she is made subject to the conditions of a fleshly life; but from the same earthly soil spring up the hallowed blossoms and fruits of the affections, filling the world with beauty and blessing. So have the law of righteousness and the law of love from the beginning blended together in the government of God. In like manner, the sentence upon the man is the same revelation of Divine goodness in the midst of condemnation. The ground is cursed for man's sake. To tliee it shall bring forth thorns and thistles, i. e. thy labour shall not be tLe productive labour it would have been-thou shalt put it forth among difficulties and obstacles. Thou shalt see thine own fnoral perversity reflected in the stubborn: barrenness, the wilderness growth of nature. Yet thou shalt eat the herb of the field, and depend upon it. With sweat of thy face all through thy life thou shalt win thy bread from an unwilling earth. And at last the dust beneath thy feet shall claim thee as its own ; thy toil-worn frame shall crumble down into the grave. It was (1) a sentence of death, of death in life; but at the same time it was (2) a merciful appointment of man's most peaceful and healthy occupation-to till the ground, to grow the corn, to eat the bread ; and it was (3) a proclamation of welcome release from the burden II when the dust shall return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return to God who gave it." There is no allusion in any of these sentences to spiritual results of transgression, but that is only because the whole is a representation of the fall, olJjectively regarded. Just as the serpent is spoken of as though it were only an animal on the earth, so man's sin is spoken of as though it were only his life's error, to be paid for in his life's suffering; but as in the former case the deeper spiritual meaning lies behind the form of the serpent, so in the latter the condemnation which brings toil and suffering and death upon man's bodily frame brings upon his whole nature that which the external infliction symbolises and sets forth. The life goes down into the dust, but it is the life which by sin had become a smitten, cursed thing; that hiding of it in the dust is the end, so far as the mere sentence is concerned. We must, however, wait for the revelation which is to be made in the new man,-the life coming forth again,-which, though but dimly promised, is yet suggested in the story of paradise. Adam gave 11 new name to his wife when she became to him something more th1m "a help-meet for him." He called her, first, woman, because she was taken.out of man. He called her, aftenrnrcls, "Eve," as the life-producing, 11 because she was the mother of all l·iving." The coats of skin-which were not, like the fig-leaves sewn together, man's own devico for hiding shame, but God's preparation for preserving that reverence between tho sexes so vital to the very continuance of the rac!l itself-betokened again the mingling of mercy with judgment; for, apart altogether from any theory as to the slain trnimals whoAe skins were employed, the Divine origin of clothing is a most significant fact. When we are told that "the Lord God made them coats of skins, and clothed them," we must interpret the language from the standpoint of the whole mirrative, which is that of an objective representation of the mysteries of man's primeval life. It would !!ot be in harmony with the tone of tlrn whole book to say in what metho(l such Divine interposition was brought about. To the Biblical ,vriters a spiritur1l guidance, 72 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. Ill. 20-H,. • work of God in the mind of man, is just as tmly God's own act as though it were altogether apart from any humn.n a&"ency. The origin of clothing wn.s an inspiration. Perhaps it is not putting too much into the language to see in such a fact nn allusion to other facts. Man is directed to use skins; might he not have been directed to slay animals? If so, might not such slaughter of animals have been first connected with religious observances, for as yet there is no allusion to the use of animal food, eave in the indirect form of dominion over the lower creation? In the fourth chapter in the extra paradisaic life, the keeping of herds and flocks is mentioned as a nati:.rat sequel. Doubtless from the time of the fall the mode of life was entirely changed, as was its sphere. Before sin man was an animal indeed, but with his animal nature in entire subordination; after his fall he was under the laws of animal life both as to its support and propagation. Death became the ruling fact of life, as it is in the mere animal races. Man is delivered from it only as he is lifted out of the animal sphere and becomes a child of God. The expulsion from Eden was part of the l~ivine sentence, but it was part of the redemptive work which commenced immediately upon the fall. The creature knowing good and evil by disobedience must not live for ever in that disobedience. He must die thnt he mny be released from the burden of his corruption. An immortality of sin is not God's purpose for his creature. Therejdre the Lord God shut up Eden.-R.

entries.title: GEN 3:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Unto Adam also and to hie wife did the Lord God make coats (catlinoth, from cathan, to cover; cf. x•rwv; Sanscrit, katam,· English, cotton) of skin ('or, the skin _of a man, from iir, to be nnked, hence a l11de). Jonathan), but tunics prepared from the skins of animals, slaughtered possibly for food, as it is not certain that tho Edenic man was 11 vegetarian (eh. i. 29), though more probably slain in sacrifice. Though said to have been made by God, " it is not proper so to understand the words, as if God had been a furrier, or a servant to sew clothes" (Calvin); God being said to m11.ke or on. m. 20-24.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 73 do wl111t be gives orders or instructions to be mnde or done. Willet end Macdonald, however, prefer to think that the garments were nctunlly fashioned by God. Bush finds in tho mention or Adam end bis wife an intimo.tion that thoy were furnished with different kinds of npparel, and suggests that on this foct is bnsed the prohibition in Deut. xxii. 5 against the interchange of raiment between the sexes. And clothed them. " I. To show them how their mortal bodies might be defended from cold nnd other injuries. 2. To cover their nakedness for comeliness' sake ; vestimenta horwris (Chaldee Paraphrase). 3. To teach them the lawfulness of using the beasts of the field, as for food, so for clothing. 4. To give a rule that modest and decent, not costly or sumptuous, apparel should be used. 6. That they might know the difference between God's works and man's invention-between coats of leather and aprons of leaves; and, 6. To put them in mind of their mortality by their raiment of dead beasts' skins-talibus indici oportebat peccatorem ut essent mortalitatis indicium : Origen" (Willet). 7. "That they might feel their degradation-quill vestes ex ea materia confect::c, belluinum quiddam magis saperent, quam linere vel lanere-and be reminded of their sin" (Calvin). "As the prisoner, looking on his irons, thinkcth on bis theft, so we, looking on our garments, should think on our sins" (Trapp). 8. A foreshadowing ,:,f the robe of Christ's righteousness (Dclitzsch, Macdonald, Murphy, Wodsworth, Candlish; cf. Ps. cxxrii. 9, 16 ; Isa. lxi. 10 ; Rom. xiii 14; Ephes. iv. 24; Col. iii. 10). Bonar recognises in Jehovah Elohim_at the gate of Eden, clothing the first transgressors, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, as the High Priest of our salvation, l1ad a right to tho skins of the burnt offerings (Levit. vii. 8), nnd who, to prefigure his own work, appropriated them for covering the pardoned pair.

entries.title: GEN 3:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Lord God said. Verba fri.sultantis (Augustino) ; ironica reprobatio (Calvin). But "irony nt the expense of 11 wretched, tempted soul might well befit Satan, but not the Lord" (Delitzsch), and is altogether inconsistent with the footing of grace on which man was placed immedintely upon his foll. l3ehold, the man is become 11e one of ue. Not the nngels (Kalisch), but the Divine Persons (cf. eh. i 26). It is scarcely likely that Jehovah alludes to the words of tho tempter (eh. iii. 5). To know good and evil. Implying 11n acqunintanco with good and evil which did not belong to him in the state of innocence. The lunguage seems to hint thnt none-sided ucqunintnnce with good nnd evil, such ns that possessed by the first Jluir in the garden und the unfallon nnacls an heaven, is not so complete a knowledg~ of the inherent beauty of the one and essential turpitude of the other as is acquired by beings who pass through the experience of a fall, and that the only way in which a finite being can approxima.te to S11ch a comprehensive knowlec.lge of evil as the Deity possessea without personal contact-can see it as it lies everlastinglyspread out beforehis infinite mind-is by going down into it aml learning what it is through personal experience (cf. Candlish, in loco). And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever. On the meaning of the tree of life vide eh. ii. 9. Neither (1) lest by eating of the fruit he should recover that immortal life which he no longer possessed (Kalisch), as "it is cert.a.in that man would not have been able, had he even devoured the whole tree, to enjoylife against the will of God" (Calvin) ; nor (2) lest the first pair, through participation of the tree, should confer upon themselves the attribute of undyingness, which would not be the l;w,j aiwv,oc of salvation, but its opposite, the oX,9pov aiwv,ov of the accursed (Keil, Lange, T. Lewis, Wordsworth); but either (3) lest man should conceive the idea th:.t immortality might still be secnred by eating of the tree, instead of trusting in the promised seed, and under this false impression attempt to take its fruit, which, in his case, would havo been equivalent to an attempt to justify himself by works instead of faith (Calvin, :Macdonald); or (4) lest he should endeavour to partake of the symbol of immortality, which he could not &,,,"'llin do until his sin was expiated and himself purified (cf. Rev. xxii. 14 ; Candlish). The remaining portion of the sentence is omitted, anakoloutha or aposiopesis being not infrequent in impassioned speech (cf. Exoci xxxii. 32; Job xxxii 13; Isa. xxxviii. 18). The force of the ellipsis or expressive silence may be gathered from the succeeding words of the historian.

entries.content: -Tlte dispensation of redemption. Notice- 1. THE MEBCY WITH JUDGMENT. He did not destroy the garden; he did not root up its trees and flowers. 11. He II DROVE OUT THE MAN" into hie curse that he might pray for and seek for and, at last, by Divine grace, obtain once more bis forfeited blessing. Ill. entries.title: GEN 4:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Lord said unto Ca.in. " Probably soon after the event, at the next time of sacrifice, and at the usual place of offering" (Bonar). Where is Abel thy brother1 "A question fi.tred to go straight to the murderer's conscience, and no less fi.tt,ed to ronse h.iB wrathful jealousy, as showing how truly Abel was the beloved one" (ibid). Whether spoken by Adam (Luther), or whispered within h.iB breast by the still small voice of conscience, or, as is most probable, utrered from between the cherubim, Cain felt that he was being examine.J. by a Divine voice (Calvin). And(inreply) he ■aid (adding falsehood, effronrery, and even profanity to murder), I know not: amI my brother's keeper 1 'fhe inquiry neither of ignorance nor of innocence, but the desperate resort of one who felt himself closely tracked by avenging justice and about to be convicted of his crime. "He showeth himself a lyer in saying, 'I know not ;' wicked awl, projane in thinking he could hide his sin from God ; unj'll,8t in denying him.self to be his brother's keeper; obstinate and deaperate in not confessing l, is sin " <Willet: cf. r~. x. ).

entries.title: GEN 4:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Satislied thnt tho guilty l\·ntri• cide is resolved to mako no acknowledgment of his deed, the omniscient Judge pIQceeds to chnrge him with his sin. And he-i. e. Jchovah-eaid, What hast thou done1 Thus intimating his perfect cognisance of the fact which his prisoner was attompting to deny, What a revelation it must have been to the inwardly trembling culprit of tho impossibility of eluding the besetting God I (Ps. cxxxix. 6). The voice of thy brother's blood (literally, bloods, i e. of this nnd all subsequent me.rtyrs-Chald. Par.) crieth unto me. A common Scriptural expression concerning murder and other crimes (eh. xviii. 20, 21 ; xix. 13 ; Exod. iii. 9 ; Heb. xii. 24 ; James v. 4). The blood cryin~ is n symbol of the soul crying for its nght to live (Lange). In this instance the cry wa.s I\ demand for the punishment of the murderer; and that cry he.s reverberated through all lands and down through all il"es, proclaiming vengeance against the shed'aer of innocent blood (cf. eh. ix. 6). "Hence the prayer that the earth may not drink in the blood shed upon it, in order that itmay not thereby become invisible and inaudible " (Knobel). Cf. Job xvi. 18 ; Isa. x:xvi. 21 ; Ezek. xxiv. 7 ; also Eschylus, 'Chcephorre,' 310, 398 (quoted by T. Lewis in Lange). From the ground. Into which it had disnppeared, but not, as the murderer hoped, to become forgotren.

entries.title: GEN 4:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Convicted, if not humbled, the culprit is speechless, and can only listen in consternation to the threefold judgment which pronounced him "cursed in his soul, vagabond in his body, and unprosperous in his lnbours" (Willet). And now-either at thu time, already (cf. Josh. xiv. 11; Hosea iL 10), or for this cause, because thou hast done this (eh. iii 14 ; cf. eh. xix. 9 ; Exod. xviii 19)-art thou cursed. Theforst cursi pronounced against a human being. Adam and Eve were not cursed, though the serpent and the devil were. If we may not conclude that Cain was thereby for ever excluded from the hope of salvation if he should repent, still less must we explain the DivinE judgment down to a simple sentence ol banishment from Eden. The fratricide wa1 henceforth to bear the displeasure and in, dignation of his Maker, whose image in Abel he had slain ; of which indignation and dis, pleasure his expatriation was to be a symbol Different explanations have been offered o; the clause, from the earth, or ground, Ad, ham.ah, which, however, cannot mean mori than the ground, which already had beeE cursed (eh. iii. I7 ; Lange), since " the cur111 of the soil a.nd the misery of man cannot weJ: be compared with each other" (Kalisch); 01 simply away from the di.strict, the scene 01 his crime (Kalisch Speaker's, Rosenmiiller, CB. IV. 1-lG.] THE BOOK OF GRNESTS. Tuch, Gerlach, Delitzech), as if nil that the aentence implied was banishment from Eden; but must involvo in addition the idea that Lho curse wns to lenp upon him from the earth, or ground, in goneral (Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Knobel, Alford, Murphy). Which bath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand. The terrible significance of this curse is further opened in tho words which follow. The earth was to be against him - 1. In refusing him its substance. • When thou tilleat (literally, shale till) the ground, it shall not henceforth yield (literally, add to give) unto thee her strength. Neither a double curse upon the entire earth for man's sake (Alford), nor a doom of sterility inflicted only on the district of Eden (Kalisch) ; but a judgment on Cain and his descendants with respect to their labours, Their tillage of the ground was not to prosper, which ultimately, Bonar thinks, drove the Cainites to city-building and mechanical invention. 2. In denying him a home. A fugitive and a vagabondliterally, moving and wandering; "groaning and trembling" (LXX., erroneously), "banished and homeless" (Keil)-shaU thou be in the earth. ".As robbers are wont to be who have no quiet and secure restingplace" (Calvin) ; driven on hy the agonising tortures of a remorseful and alarmed conscience, and not simply by "the earth denyiny to him the expected fruits of his labour" (Delitzsch). The ban of wande1ing, which David pronounced upon his enemies (Ps. !ix. 12; cix. 10), in later years fell upon the Jews, who "for shedding the blood ofChrist, the mostinnocent Lamb ofGod, arevngabonds to this day over the face of the earth" (Willet). Thus the earth was made the minister of Gotl's curse, not a partaker of it, 8ll some have strangely imagined, as if by drinking up the blood of .Abel it had become a pnrticipant of Cain's crime (Delitzsch).

entries.title: GEN 4:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Convicted, if not humbled, the culprit is speechless, and can only listen in consternation to the threefold judgment which pronounced him "cursed in his soul, vagabond in his body, and unprosperous in his lnbours" (Willet). And now-either at thu time, already (cf. Josh. xiv. 11; Hosea iL 10), or for this cause, because thou hast done this (eh. iii 14 ; cf. eh. xix. 9 ; Exod. xviii 19)-art thou cursed. Theforst cursi pronounced against a human being. Adam and Eve were not cursed, though the serpent and the devil were. If we may not conclude that Cain was thereby for ever excluded from the hope of salvation if he should repent, still less must we explain the DivinE judgment down to a simple sentence ol banishment from Eden. The fratricide wa1 henceforth to bear the displeasure and in, dignation of his Maker, whose image in Abel he had slain ; of which indignation and dis, pleasure his expatriation was to be a symbol Different explanations have been offered o; the clause, from the earth, or ground, Ad, ham.ah, which, however, cannot mean mori than the ground, which already had beeE cursed (eh. iii. I7 ; Lange), since " the cur111 of the soil a.nd the misery of man cannot weJ: be compared with each other" (Kalisch); 01 simply away from the di.strict, the scene 01 his crime (Kalisch Speaker's, Rosenmiiller, CB. IV. 1-lG.] THE BOOK OF GRNESTS. Tuch, Gerlach, Delitzech), as if nil that the aentence implied was banishment from Eden; but must involvo in addition the idea that Lho curse wns to lenp upon him from the earth, or ground, in goneral (Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Knobel, Alford, Murphy). Which bath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand. The terrible significance of this curse is further opened in tho words which follow. The earth was to be against him - 1. In refusing him its substance. • When thou tilleat (literally, shale till) the ground, it shall not henceforth yield (literally, add to give) unto thee her strength. Neither a double curse upon the entire earth for man's sake (Alford), nor a doom of sterility inflicted only on the district of Eden (Kalisch) ; but a judgment on Cain and his descendants with respect to their labours, Their tillage of the ground was not to prosper, which ultimately, Bonar thinks, drove the Cainites to city-building and mechanical invention. 2. In denying him a home. A fugitive and a vagabondliterally, moving and wandering; "groaning and trembling" (LXX., erroneously), "banished and homeless" (Keil)-shaU thou be in the earth. ".As robbers are wont to be who have no quiet and secure restingplace" (Calvin) ; driven on hy the agonising tortures of a remorseful and alarmed conscience, and not simply by "the earth denyiny to him the expected fruits of his labour" (Delitzsch). The ban of wande1ing, which David pronounced upon his enemies (Ps. !ix. 12; cix. 10), in later years fell upon the Jews, who "for shedding the blood ofChrist, the mostinnocent Lamb ofGod, arevngabonds to this day over the face of the earth" (Willet). Thus the earth was made the minister of Gotl's curse, not a partaker of it, 8ll some have strangely imagined, as if by drinking up the blood of .Abel it had become a pnrticipant of Cain's crime (Delitzsch).

entries.title: GEN 4:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Cain saidunto the Lord, My punishment (or my sin) is greater than I can bear. Or, than can be borµe away. Interpreted in either way, this is scarcely the language ofconfession, "sufficiens confessio, sed intempestiva" (Chrysostom); but, as the majority of interpreters Rre agreed, of desperation (Calvin). .According to the first rendering Cain is understood as deploring not the enormity of his sin, but the severity of his punishment, under which he reels and staggers as one amazed (Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Calvin, Keil, Delitzsch, Murphy, Alford, Speaker's, Kalisch). .According to the secc,nd, from the terrific nature of the blow which had descended on him Co.in awakens to the conviction that his sin was too heinous to be forgiven (margin, Septuagint, Vulgate, Theodotion, .Arabic, Syriar., Onkelos, Sam11ritl\n, Gesenius1 Wor:!n·ofth). GENESIS. The first of these is favoured by the remaining portion of his address, which shows that that which had paralysed his guilty spirit was not the wickedness of his deed, but the overwhelming retribution which had leapt so unexpectedly from its bosom. The real cause of his despair was the sen• tence which had gone forth against him, and the articles of which he no,v recapitulates. Behold, thou hast driven me this day-" Out of the sentence of his own conscience Cain makes a clear, positive, Divine decree of banishment" (Lange)- from the face of the earth. Literally, the ground, i. e. the Janel of Eden. "Adam's sin brought expulsion from the inner circle, Cain's from the outer" (Bonnr). And from thy face shall I be hid. Either (1) from the place where the Divine presence was specially manifested, i. e. at the gate of Eden, which does not contradict (Kalisch) the great Biblical truth of the Divine omnipresence (cf. Exod, xx. 24); or, (2) moro generally, from the enjoyment of the Divine favour (cf. Deut xxxi. 18). "To be hidden from the faCJl of God is to be not regarded by Go,l, or nrit protected by his guardian care" rC:Alvfa). And I shall be a fugitive and a vagabond. ".A vagabond and a runngate" ('Iyndale, Coverdale, 'Bish<>ps' Dible'). Vagus et p;·ofugua (Vulgate,; vagus et infestus agitationibua (Tremellius and Junius). In the earth. The contemplation of his miserable doom, acting on his guilty conscience, inspired him with a fearful apprehension, to which in closing he gives expression in the hearing of his Judge. And it shall come to pass, that every one--not beast (Josephus, Kimchi, Michaelis), but person-that fl.ndeth me shall slay me. ".Amongst the ancient Romans a ma.n cursed for any wickedness might be freely killed (Dionysius Halicarnass., 1. 2). Amongst the Gauls the excommunicated were deprived of any benefit of law (Cresar. 'de Bello Gallico,' I. 6 ; cf. nlso Sophocles, '<Edip. Tyrannus ')" (.Ainsworth). The apprehension which Cain cherished has been explained as an oversight on the part of the narrator (Schumann and Tuch) ; as a mistake on the part of Cain, who had no reason to know that the world was not populated (T. Lewis) ; as referring to the bloo,l aven~~rs of the future who might arise from Dis father's family (Rosenmiiller, Delitzsch) ; and also, aDll perhaps with as much probability, as indicating that already, in the 130 years thnt had gone, .Adam's descendants were not limitod to the two brothers nnd their wives (Ho.vernick).

entries.title: GEN 4:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The condemnetl fratricitle's apprehensions were allayed by II special act of grace. And the Lord said unto him, N!erefore (the LXX., Symm., 1'he0Jotio11 il 82 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. 1v. 1-10. Ylllgatc, Syriac, Dnthius, translate Not so- .,;,x oi'•rw(', ,1eq11aqitam, reading ,:;,_N~ in- Eknd of P~) whosoever slayeth Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him eevenfold. I. e. fully, sevenfold vengeance-complete vengeance (cf. Levit. mi. 28). In the case of Caiu's murderer there was to be no such mitigation of the penalty as in tho case of Cain himself; on the contrary, ho would bo .,.isitcd more severely than Cain, as being guilty not alone of homicide, but of transgressing the Dinne commandment which said that Cain was to live (Willet). As to why this special privilege was granted to Cain, it was not because "the early death of the pious Abel was in reality no punishment, but the highest boon" (Kalisch), nor because banishment from God's presence was the greatest possible punishment, "having in itself the significance of a social human death" (Lange), nor because it was needful to spare life for the increase of posterity (Rosenmiiller); but perhaps - 1. To show that " Vengeance is mine ; I will repay, saith the Lord." 2. To prove the riches of the Divine cleme!lcy to sinful men. 3. To serve as a warning again,,--t the crime of murder. To this probably there is a reference in the concluding clause. And the Lord set a ma.rk upon-gave a sign to (LXX. )-C&in, lest a.ny 11ntliu him should kill him. Commentators are divided as to whether this was a visible sign to repress avengers (the Rabbis, Luther, Cal- Yin, Piscator, &c.), or :i.n inward nssurance to Caill himself t!iat he should not be destroyed (Aben Ezra, DatheJ. Rosenmilller, Gesenius, Tuch, Kalisch, 1Jollt2sch). l11 support of the former it is urged that an external badge would bo moro likely to repel assailants ; ,vhile in favour of tho latter it is pleaded .that of seventy-six times in which oth occurs in the Olcl '.l.'estamcnt, in scvehtyfive it is translated ti,gn. If thero wns a visible mark upon tho fugitivo, it is impos• sible to say what it was; that it was a shaking (LXX.), or a continual fleeing from place to place (Lyra), or e. horn in the head (Rabbis), a peculiar kind of dress (Clericus), are mere conceits. But, whatever it was, it was not a sign of C:i.in's forgiveness (Josephus), only a pledge of God's protection. Cf. the Divino prophetic sentenco against the Jcwish Cain (Ps. !ix. 11).

entries.title: GEN 4:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Co.in went out from the preaence of the Lord. Not simply ended his interview and prepared to emi&rate from the abode of his youth (Kalisch) ; out, more especially, withdrew from the neighbourhood of the cherubim (vide on ver, 14). And -dwelt in the land of Nod. The geographical situation of Nod (Knobel, China!) cannot be determined fwther than that it was on the east of Eden, and its name, Nod; or wandering (cf. vers. 12, 14 ; Ps. lvi. 8), was clearly derived from Cain's fugitive· and vagabond life (vide Michaelis, 'Suppl:,' p. 1612; and~ cf. Furst, 'Lex.,' sub voce), "which shi:Jw• eth, as Josephus well conjectureth, that Cain was not amended by his .punishment, but waxed worse and worse, giving himself to rapine, robbery, oppression, deceit" (Willet).

entries.title: GEN 4:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Care for our bretlwe:n,. How terrible this question to the murderer I ~e thought,_ ~erhaps, his aC't ~as hidden,, and stro"e to put it out of mind. Perhaps <'hd not ant1c1pate effect of Ins stroke; but now brought face to face with his sin. ""·'here is Abel?". He knew not. He knew where the body lay; but that wns not ~bel. , Had sent hun whence he could not call him back. "Where is thy brother?" 1s God s word to each of us. It e.xpresses the great· law that wo are responsible for each ot,her's welf~re. "Am I my brother's_ keep_er ?" some would n~k. Assuredly )'es. God has kmt men together so that all our hfe through we requmi each other's help; and we cannot avoid influencing each other. And has created n bond of. brotherhood (cf. Acts xvii. 26), which follows from our calling him "Father.II \\'hat doing for good of mankind? Not to do good is to do harm; not to eave is to kill. Love of Christ works (Rom. x. 1; 2 Cor. v. 14). I. ,vE ARE CALLED TO CARE FOR THOSE AFAR OFF. "Who is my neighbour?" We might answer, ,vi10 is not thy neighbour? Everywhere our brethren. Thousands passing away daily. Abel, a vapour, the character of human life (Ps. ciii.15). ViThither are they going? And we know the way of salvation. Light is given to no one for himself only (Matt. v. 13, 14). We are to hold it fo1th; to be as lights in the world (Phil. ii. 15). It is God's will thus to spread his kingdom. Are we nnswE'ring the call? Test yourselves (cf. 1 John iii. 17). Deliver ue from bloodguiltiness, 0 God. Thank God, the question speaks to us of living men. There are fields still to be reaped. The heathen, our brethren, claim a brother's help. .How many varieties of Cain's answer:-You cannot reclaim savages ; you just make them hypocrites; we must look e.t home first. And the lost masses at home are our brethren. Oh, it is in vain to help them; they will drink ; they hato religion; th~y only think what they can get from those who visit them. Test these objections. Single out in thought one soul; compare hie case with yours. You have instruction, ordinances, influences; &.Dd he the darkness of heathenism, or surroundings of vice. Yet Christ died for that soul Can you let it depart without some effort, or even earnest prayer? II. WE ARE CALLED TO CARE FOR THOSE AROUND us. For their sake, watchfulness and self-restraint (cf. Rom. xiv. 15). We teach more by what we• do than by whatwe say. The loving life teaches love; the sel.fieh, ungodliness. Inconsistencies of Christians hinder Christ's cause. What art thou at home? le thy life pointing heavenward? "None of ue liveth to himself." "Where is thy brother?"-M.

entries.title: GEN 4:9–15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.The condemnalion andjud,qment oftliefirst murderer. Notice- !. The Divine APPEAL TO CONSCIIlNCE, affording opportunity to repentance and confession, and therefore to the exercise of mercy. II. TnE BLINDING EFFECT OF A GREAT SIN. The man who Knew that God knew all persisting in a lie, and insulting the Divine majesty at the very throne of judgment, i. e. defying God by the monstrous extravagance of self-assertion, which is the effect of indulged sin, not only hardening the heart, but filling it with a mad despe-4tion. So we find great criminals still, to the very last, adding sin to sin, us thougn they had come to think that the deeper they BWik into it the more chance tliey had of escaping its punishment, or by daring the whole extremity might the sooner know the worst. III. There is great significance in the INTIMATE CONNECTION BET FORTII BETWEEN THE CRIME AND PUNISHMENT OF CAIN AND TIIE EARTH AND THE GROUND. The blood speaks from the ground, crying to God. Cain is cursed from the ground. The ground opened her mouth to receive the brother's blood. The ground refuses to serve the murderer. On the earth he shall be a fngitive and vagabond. From the face of the earth he is driven. His/unishment is greater than he can bear. Surely all that iB intended to place in vivi contrast the righteoueness of God o.nd the un• righteousness cf man ; the one witnessed by the Bteadfast eatrth, with its unbroken l\\WB1 ita pure, unfnllen, peaceful etate, with its communities of creaturea inno•;1JJ1t of Rli ain; tho other witnesse<l by the curae<l, wnndering, suffering, hungcr-pinollc,}, rniserable IDnn, flying from hie neighbour, flying from himself. IV. AIJ in the expulsion of man from Eden, so in the cxpul~ion of Cain from society, thero is MERCY MINGLED WITH JUDGMENT. The mark set upon Cain by the Lord was at once the mark of rejection and the mark of protection; it threatened sevenfold vengeance on the murderer of the murderer; it was an excomm•mic11tion for the sake of the sinner as well as for the sake of the community. We must not expect to find in these primeval records more than a dim intimation of the Divine mind. But here, at the outset of the human race, there is the germ of that distinction and separation among -mankind on the moral and spiritual gronncl which really is the essential fact of the kingdom of God. "The blood of sprinkling sp011keth better things than that of Abel." Yet it is a good thin~ that God should say to us, in however fearful a manner, that that which i~ destructive of human society, which rises up against a brother's life, which hates and works out its hatred in cruel act, shall be, can be, separated from the world into which it has come, and cast out. We must look at the whole narrative from the side of tho Abel element, not from the side of the Cain element; and the blessed truth contained in it is that God purgea society of its evil men and evil principles, and makes its very martyrs' blood to be a consecration of the earth to proclaim his righteousness. We have not to answer the question, How about Cain? He is protected from violence. He is permitted to repent and return, though for a time an outcast. Out of the conflict of the two worlds will come forth the purpose of God-evil separated, good eternally triumplmnt.-R.

entries.title: GEN 4:17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Domiciled in Noel, whither, impelled by woman's love, his wife had accompanied him, the unhappy fugitive began to seek, if notto find, relief from the gnaWU1g agonies of remorse in the endearments of conjugal felicity and the occupations of secular industry. And Cain knew hia wife. Who must have been his sister, and married before the death of Abel, ns "after that event it can scarcely be supposed that any woman would bo willing to connect herself with such a miserable fratricide" (Bush). Though afterwardsforbidden, tho tendency ofDivinelegislation on the subject of marriage being always in the direction of enlarging rather than restricting the circle of prohibited relationships, the tmion of brothers and sisters at the first was clearly indispensable, if the race ,vas to .multiply outwards from a common stock. " Even in much later times, and among very civilised nations, such alliances werenotconsideredincestuous. The Atheninn law mnde it compulsory to marry the sister if she had not found a husband at a certain age. Abraham married his half-sister, Sara\1; and the legislator Moses himself was the offs;erin~ of II matrimony which he Inter interd1cte<1 as unholy" (Kalisch). And she conceived. For even from the unbelieving and unth11nkful, the disobedient and the reprob11te, God's providential mercies are not entirely withhold (Ps. cxlv. 9 ; Matt. v. 45). And bare Enooh. Ohanoch, "dedicated," initiated," from chana.ch,to instruct (Prov. xxil. 6) and to consecrate (Deut. xx. 5 ; 1 Kings viii. 63). Canillish detects in the name the impious pride of the first murderer; with more charity, Keil and Kalisch sec " promise of the renovation of his life. The latter think~ that Cain called his son "Initiated" or "Instructed" to intimate that ho intendeJ to instruct him from his early years . in tho duties of virtue, and his city "Dedicated " to signify that he now recognised that ' '' the firstling of his social prosperitybelongs to God." If Luthcr's conjecture be correct, that the child received its name from its mother, itwill touchingly express that young mother's hope that the child whom God ha:! sent might be an augury of blessing for their saddened home, and her resolution both to consecrnte him from his youth to God and to instruct him in God's feo.r and worship. And he builded. Literally, was biiildinrr, L e. began to build, " but never finished, leading still a nma,,aate life, and so often constrained to leave the work, as the ginnts did who built the tower of Babel" (Willet). A city. Yater, Hartmann, 11nd Bohlen discover in the city-building of Cain 11 " m3L-J. !;'roof of the mythical contents of the narrative," an ndvnnced state of civilisation "utterly unsuitnble to so early 11 period ;" but ancient tradition (Phrenicisn, Egyptian,and Hellenic) is unanimous in ascribing to the first men the invention of 11griculture and the 11rts, with the discovery of metals, the origin at music, &c. (vide. Hnvernick's 'Intr,, ,' § 1~). 88 TitE BOOK OF GEN~SlS. [en, 1v. 17-28, Of course the -,,p which Cain orected was not n city accordi~g to modern ideas, but a keep or fort, enclosed with a wall for the defence of those who dwelt within (Murphy). It was the first step in the direction of civilisation, and Kalisch notes it !IS a deep trait in the Biblical account that the origin of cities is ascribed not to the nomad, but to the agriculturi~t. Impelled by the necessities of Ins occupation to have a fixed residcnoo, he would like,nso in course of time be constrained by the multiplication of hia household to insure their protection and comfort. It is possible also that his attempt to found a cit,· may have been dictated bv a desire to bid defiance to the curse which doomed him tn a wandering life ; to create for his family and himself a new point of interest outside the holy circle of Eden, and to find an outlet for those energies and powers of which, as an early progenitor of the race, he must have been conscious, and in the restless activity of which obliTion for his misery could alone be found. If so, it explains the action which is nert recorded of him, that he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch. I. e. he consecrated it to the realisation of these his sinful hopes and schemes.

entries.title: GEN 4:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Years passed away, the family of Cain grew to manhood, and, in imitation of their parents, founded homes for themselves. And unto Enoch (whose wife probably would also be his sister, few caring at this early stage to intermarry with the accursed race) was born Irad. Townsman, citizen, urbanus civil,u (Keil, Lange); fleet as a wild a.'IS (Murphy); ornament of a city, from Ir, a city (Wordsworth). And Irad begat Mehnjael. Smitten of God (Keil, Ge,enius, Murphy), the purified or formed of God (Lange). And lllehnjael begat l'!Iethusael. .Man of God (Gesenius, Lange), man e.sked or man of El (Murphy), man of prayer (Keil). And :M:ethusael begatLamech. Strong youth (Gesenius, Lange); man of prayer, yonth (Mnrphy); king, by metathesis for melech (Wordsworth). The resemblance between these names and those in the line of Seth has been accounted for by supposing a eommingling of the two genealogies, or one common primitive legend in two forms (Ewald, Knobel). But-1. The similarity of the names does not necessarily imply the identity of the persons. Cf. Korah in the families of Levi (Exod. vi 21) end Esan (eh. xxxvi 5); Hanoch in those of Reuben (eh. xlvi 9) and Midian (eh. xxv. 4); Kenaz in those of Esau ({:h, mvi 11) and Judah (Num. xxxii 12). 2. The similarity of the names only proves that the two collateral branches of the same family did not keep entirely apart. 3. The paucity of names at that early period may have led to their repetition. 4. The names in the two lines arc only similar, not identical (cf, with Irad, Jared, descent; with Mehujaol, Mnha.laloel, praise of God; with Methusael1 Methuselah, man of the sword). 5. The particulars rolated of Euoch a.nd Lamech in tho line of Seth forbid their identification with those of the samo name in the liue of Cain.

entries.title: GEN 4:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And L&mooh took unto him two wives. Being the first polygamist of whom mention is made, the first by whom " tho ethical aspect of marrio.ge, as ordained by God, was turned into the lust of the eye and lust of the flesh " (Keil). 'l'hough afterwards permitted because of the hardness of men's hearts, it was not so from the beginning. This was " a new evil, without even tho pretext that the first wife had no children, which helditsground untilChristianity restored the original law-Matt. xix. 4-6 " (Inglis). The names of Lamech's wives were suggestive of sensual attractions. The name of the one Adah, tho Adorned (Gesenius), and the name of the other Zillah, the shady or the tinkling (Keil), the musical player (Lange), the shadow (Wordsworth). "Did Lamech choose a wife to gratify the eye with loveliness 1 end was he soon sated with that which is so short-lived as beauty, and then chose another wife in addition to Adah 1 But a second wife is hardly a wife; she is only the shadow of a wife" (ibid.).

entries.title: GEN 4:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Adah bare .Tabal. Either the Travelleror ihe Producer, from yabhal, to flow; poetically, to go to walk; hiphil, to produce ; descriptive, in the one case, of his nomadic life, in the other of his occupation or his wealth. Ke was the father-av, father ; used of the founder of a family or nation (eh. x. 21), of the anthor or maker of anything, especially of the Creator (Job xxxvi.ii 28), of the master or teacher of any art or science (eh. iv. 21)-of such as dwell in tents, and ofsuch as have cattle. Mikneh, literally, possession, from kanah, to acquire, as in ver. 1; hence cattle, DB that was the primitive form ofwealth (cf. pecus,puunia); by which may be meant that Jabal wa.a the first nomad who introduced the custom of living in tents, and pasturing and breeding not sheep merely, but larger quadrupeds a.s well, for the sake of wealth.

entries.title: GEN 4:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw

entries.title: GEN 4:17–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlt,eprogress of tlie race. I. ITS INCREASE n~ POPULATION. Starti?g from a single pair in Eden in the course of seven generations _the human family mn.st have attained to very considerable dimensions. At the birth of Se~h, Ada!I• was 130 years old, and in all probability had other s_ons an~ daught~rs besides Cam d 1i· if If Lamech the seventh from Adam m the lme of Cam, was conteman w e:tl Enoch the'seventh from Adam in the line of Seth, at least 600 years poraneous w1 1 , . if Ab h • t k · 1 1 d d awa Sm • ce the race becran to multiply; and " ra am s s oc m ease ia passe Y o • • • h J'k t' • ht • t than 400 ea.res amounted to 600,000, Cam's posterity m t e i e ime-m1g a;1se. o the like Jultitude" (Willet). If to these the descendants of .Seth be adde~, it will at once appear that the earth's population ~n the time of La~ech was cons1derabl! over 1,000,000 of inhabitants. Let it remmd us of the reality and po,vcr of God a blessing (eh. i. 28). 11. 1TB ADVA_NCEHENT IN INTELLIGENCK. "It is a curious fact that while all on. 1v. 17-26.J THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 91 modern writers o.<lmit the great antiquity of man, most of them maintnin the very recent development of his intellect, and will hardly contemplate the pos,ibilit,y of men equal in mento.1 capacity to ourselves having existed in prehistoric (?) times'' (Wo.llace, Brit, Assoc. Address, 1876). For prehistoric write antediluvian, nnd the sentiment is exactly true, The circumstance that we have no remains of antediluvian civilisation is no sufficient evidence that such did not exist. Speaking of certain earthworks of g_reat antiquity that have been discovered in the Mississippi valley,- cnmps, or works of defence, sacred enclosures, with their connected groups of circle~, octagons, squares, ellipses, polished and ornamented pottery, &c.,-the same distinguished writer says," The important thing for us is, that when North America was first settled by Europeans, the Indian tribes.inhabiting it had no kno·.vledge ortradition of ai:iy races preceding themselves of higher civilisation. Yet we fmd that such races existed ; that they must have been populous, and have lived under some established government; while there are signs that they practised agriculture greatly, as indeed they must have done to have supported a population capable of executing euch gigantic works in such ,ast profusion." The exhumation by Dr. Schliemann on the plains of Troy of three successive civilisations, of which two were not known to have previously existed, and the third (the Ilium of Homer) had been almost regarded by archreologists as fabulous, is conclusive demonstration that the absence of all traces of primeval civilisation is no more a proof that such civilisation did not exist., than is the absence of all traces of the third day's vegetation a proof that it did not exist. The passage under c.onsideration unmistakably reveals that the human intellect in those early times was not asleep. Within the compass of ten verses we read of the building of cities, of the laying out of farms und the acquisition of property, of the beginning of the mechanical arts and the manufacture of metallic weapons, of the rise of music and the cultivation of poetry. It may strike one as peculiar that this great intellectual development is represenlc,l as taking place exclusively in the line of Cain. From this some have inferred that the Bible means to throw disparagement upon human industry, commercial Rnd agricultural enterprise, and all kinds of mechanical and inventive genius, and even sanctions the idea that religion is incompatible with business talent, poetical genius, and intellectual greatness. There is, however, no reason to suppose that this advancement in intelligence was confined to the Cainitic branch of the Adamic race. The prophecy of Enoch (vide Expos.) and the incidental allusion to metallic weapons in the name of Methuselah (man of the dart) suggest that the Sethitic line kept pace with their ungodly contemporaries in the onward march of civilisation, though that was not their chief distinction. Let us leam-1. That there is no essential antagonism betweenintelligence and piety. 2. That in God's estimation righteousness is of much higher value than material prosperity. 3. That where, as in the Cainitic line, there is no true godliness there is apt to be too intense devotion to culture or business. III. ITS DECLENSION IN WICKEDNESS. 1. ,ve can trace it in their names. Enoch, lrad, :Mehujael, Lamech being suggestive of qualities, principles, characteristics euch ns are approved by the spirit of worldliness ; and Adah and Zillah (uide Expos.) being indicative of sensual attractions. 2. Their works proclaim it. It would be wrong to say that cities are necessarily evil things. On the contrary, they are magnificent monuments of man's constructive genius, and immensely productive of man's comfort, A city too is atype of heaven's gathering of redeemed hum::rnity. Still it cannot be doubted that the need for cities was a proof of sin, as the building of the first city was an act of sin. The acquisition of property, and the uprise of such ideas as the rights of property, are likewise indications of a state of life that is not purely innocent (cf. Acts iv. 32). A.nd though certainly it cannot be sinful either to mnke or to handle a. harp, or to cultivate poetry, yet when we put all these things together-beautiful wi,es, iron weapons, musical instmments, and warlike ballads, if notbncchanaliansongs-it is not difficultto perceive adeepening of that devotion to the things of this life which invariably proclaims 11 departuro from the life of God. 3. Their immoral lives attest it. A growing disregard for the marriage lnw is evinced by the polygamy of Lamech ; in the manufacture and use of offensive weapons we see the rising of n turbulent nnd lawless spirit; and these THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [ctt. IV. 17-26, two thing~, licentiousness and lawlessness, ahvays mark tho uownward progress of ab age or reople. IV. TS PROGRESS IN RE!:IGION; at least in a section of its population, the godly line of Seth, in whom the piety of Abel was revived. Yet the narrative would seem to ind_icate that even ~hey were I!ot entirely free from the prevailing wickedness of the times. In the third generation the pressure of the worldly spirit upon the company of the faithful was so great that they felt obliged, as it were, in self-defence, to buttress their piety by a double wall of protection ; viz., separcuwn from tliei,• ungodly associates in tlu! world by the formation of a distinct religious community, and by tM institutwn ofst,atedsoci,al worship (eh. iv. 26). And without these declen- 1,ion in trne religion is as certain as with them advancement is secure. They are the New Testament rules for the cultivation of piety (2 Cor. vi. 14-18; Ephes. iv. 11-13; Heh. x. 25). Lessons :-I. The downward progress of sin. 2. The danger of intellect and <'i,·i!isation when divorced from piety. 3. The only right use of earth and earthly 1lii:igs is to make all subservient to the life of grace. 4. The danger of conformity to the world. 5. The only safety for the people of God, and especially in these times of great intellectual activity and mechanical and scientific skill, is to make deep and wide the line of distinction between them and the world, and steadfastly to maintain the public as well as private ordins.nces of religion. HOMILIES BY VARIOUS AUTilORS.

entries.title: GEN 4:16–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The kingd<im of God contrasted with tlie kingdom of this wr.,,.Zd, Society without the Lord. The banished Cain and his descendants. I. MULTIPLICATION apart from Divine order is no blessing. IL CIVILISATION without religion is a. chaos of conflicting forces, producing \·iolence, bloodshed, working out its own ruin. Compare France in the seventeenth und eighteenth centuries. Arts of life ma.y grow from a mere natural root. Music, mechanical skill, scientific discovery, and invention, in themselves contain no moral life. Luxury turns to corruption, and so to misery. III. RELIGION IS THE DASIS OF SOCIAL PROSPERITY. It is the true defence against the " inhumanity of man." Lamech, with his artificial protection against violent revenge, suggests the true safety in the presence of the Lord and observance of his commandments.-R.

entries.title: GEN 5:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - The dedicated and initiated childgrewup,likea.n Old TestamentTimothy -let us hope, .to possess, illustrate, and proclaim the piety which was the distinguishing characteristic ofthe holy line. At the comparatively early age of sixty-fivebe begat (" forbidding to ma1Ty" being unknown then) Methuselah. Man of a dart (Gesenius), man of military arms (Fiirst), man of the missile (Murphy), man of the sending forth-sc. of water (Wordsworth), man of growth (Delitzsch). And Enoch walked with God (Elohim). T1ie phrase, used also of Noah, (eh. vi. 9), o.nd by lllicah (eh. vi. 8. Cf. the eimilar expressions, " to walk before God," eh. xvii. 1 ; Ps. cxvi. 9, and " to walk after God," Deut. xiiL 4 ; Ephes. v. 1), portrnys nlifo of singularly elevated piety; not merely o. constant realisation of the Divine presence, or even a perpetual effort a.t holy obedience, but also "a. maintenance of the most confidential intercourse with the personal God" (Keil). It implies a situation of nenrness to God, if not in place at leo.st in spirit ; a cha.rac~r of likeness t~ God (Amos iii. 3), a.ml a life of converse with God. Followina tb~ LXX. (d,qpforq<rE ol 'Ev,ax r,; Otrp°), th~ wntcr to the Hebrews llescribes it 11s 1t life that was " plc,ising to Go,\," as springing from the root of faith (Hcb. xi. 5). Yot though pre-eminently spiritual and contemplative, Jude tells us (vers. 14, 15) the patriarch's life had it~ active and aggressive outlook towards the evil times in which he lived. After he begat Methuselah. "Which inti mates that he did not begin to be eminent for piety till about that time, ; at first he walked as other men" (Henry). Procopius Gazcus ~oes beyond this, and thinks that before Ins son's birth Enoch was "a wlcke,l liver," but then repented. The bistorinn's language, ho,vever, does not necessarily imply that his piety was so late in commencing, and it is more pleasing to think that from his youth upwards he was "as a shining star for virtue and holiness" (Willet). Three hundred ye2,:rs. As his piety began early, so likewise did it continue long ; it was not intermittent and fluctuating, but steadfast and persevering (cf. Job xvii. 9; Prov. iv. 18; 1 Cor. xv. 58). And begat sons and daughters, "Hence it is undeniably evident that the state and use of matrimony doth very well agree with the severest course of holiness, and with the office of a prophet or preacher" (Poole). And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. " Ayear of years" (Henry) ; " the same period as that of the revolution of tha earth round the sun. After he had finished his course, revolving round him who is the true light, which is God, in the orbit of duty, he was approved by God, and taken to him'· (Wordsworth). Modern c1itics have discovered in the age of Enoch traces of a mythical origin. They conclude the entire list of names to be not older than the tirno of the Babylonian Nabonassar, o.nd believe it to be not improbable that "the Babylonians regulated the calendar with the assistance of a.n Indian astrologer or ganaka (arithmetician) ofthe town of Chanoge" (Yon Bohlen). nut " it would. be strange indeed if just in the life of Enoch, which represents the purest and sublimest unity with God, a heathen and astrological element were intentionally introduced;" and, besides, "it is almost generally admitted that our list contains no astronomical numbers ; that the years which it specifics refer to the lives of individuals, not to periods of the world.; anJ that none of all these figures is in any way reducible to n chronological system" (Kalisch). And Enoch walked with God. "Non otiosa ravro~oyia," but an emphatic repetition, indicative of the ground of whatfollows. And he wns not. Literally, and not he (cf. eh. xii. 36 ; Jer. xxxi. 15 ; ,ea, oux Eupirr- «Ero, LXX.). "Not absolutely ho was not, but relntively he w:is not extnnt iu the sphere of sense." "Non amplius inter mortales npparuit"(Roscnmiiller). "If this plmlse Joes not Jcnoto l\lmihilation, much less doc~ the 96 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, V, 1-82, phrase 'and he died.' The one denotes absence from the world of sense, 11.nd the other indicatos t.ho ordinary way in which the soul depar~ from this :world" (Murphy). For God (Eloh1m) took him. Cf. 2 Kings ii. 8, 5 9, 10, where the same word MR~ is u~e~ or ~lijah's translation; or, µ,r;o,,,m, aurn,, o 9,o,;, LXX.). Though the "Titer to tho Hebrews (eh. xi. 5) adopts the paraphrase of the LXX., yet his language must be accepted as com•eying the exact sense of the "·ords of Moses. Analysed, it teaches (1) that the patriarch Enocn did not see death as diJ all tho other worthies in the catalogue; and (2) that in some mysterious way "he was taken up from this temporal life and tr~nsfi~rc? into life eternal, as those of the faithful will be who shall be alive at the coming of Christ to judgment" (Keil). The case of Elijah, who was also taken up, and who afterwards appeared in glory on the mount of transfiguration (l\[att. xvii.; Mark ix. ; Luke ix.), appears to determine the locality into which Enoch was translated (which h:alisch willingly leaves to antiquaries to decide) to be neither the terrestrial Eden (certain Popish writers) nor the heavenly paradise where the pious dead are now assembled-sheol (Delitzsch and Lange), but the realm of celestial glory (Keil). That the departure of the good man was witnessed by his contemporaries we may infer from what occurred in the case of Elijah ; and, indeed, unless it had been so it is d.iilicult tosee how it could have served the end for which apparently it was designed, which was not solely to reward Enoch's piety, but to demonstrate the certainty and to stimulate tl1e hope of immortality. That the memory of an event so remarkable should have survived not merely in Jewish (Ecclus. :tliv. 16) and Christian tradition (Jude 15), but also in heathen fable, is nothing ru.'lrvellous. The Book of Enoch, compiled probably by a Jcw in the days of Herod the Great, describes the patriarch as exhortinghis son Methuselah and all his contemporaries to reform their evil ways ; as penetrating with his prophetic eye into the remote future, and exploring all mysteries in earth and heaven; as passing a retired life after the birth of his eldest son in intercourse with the angels and in meditation on Divine matters; and as at length being translated to heaven in order to reappear in the time of the Messiah, leaving behind him 11 number of writings on religion and morality. "The Book of Jubilees relates that he was carried into paradise, where he writes down the judgment of all men, their wickedness nnd eternal punishment" (Kalisch). Arabic legend declares hinl to havo ken the inventor of writin_g and arithmetic, 'J'hePhrygian aageAnnacus{"Ava~or: "nomen detortuw ab CLanoch ") is said by Stephamis Dyzantinus, and Suid11S, who corrupts the name into Nannacus, to have lived bofore the flood of Deuciilion, to hiivo attainod 11n age of moro than 800 yearn, to have foreseen the flood, gathered di tho people into 11 temple and made supplicRtion to God, and finally to have been tmnslatcd into heaven, ff Classical writers 111s0 mention such translations into heaven ; they assign this distinction among others to Hercules, to Ganymede, and to Romulus (liv. i. 16: "needeinde in terris fuit "). But it was 11warded to them either for their v11lour or their physical beauty, 11nd not, as the transl11tion of Enoch for ff II pious and religious life." Nor i; ff the idea of a trnnslation to heaven limited to the old world ; it was familiar to tho tribes of Central America ; tho chronicles of Guatemalarecord four progenitors ofmankind who were suddenly raised to heaven ; and tho documents add that those first men came to Guate.me.le. from the other side of the sea, from the East" (cf. Rosenmiiller e.nd Kalisch, in loco).

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The shortest life was followed by the longest, Methuselah begetting, e.t the advanced age of 187, Lamech,-strong or young man (Geseniua) ; overthrower, wild man (Furst); man of prayer (Murphy),-continuing after his son's birth 782 years, nnd at last succumbing to tho stroke of death in the 969th year of his age, the year of the Flood. Lamech, by whom the line was canied forward, was similarly far advanced when he begat a son, at the age of 182, and called his name Noah,-" rest," from nuach, to rest (cf. eh. viii 4),-not ff The Sailor," from tho Latin no, and the Greek vaii, (Bohlen), but e.t the same time explaining it by saying, This same shall comfort-nacham, to pant, groan, Piel to comfort. "Nuach and ruzcliam are stems not immediately connected, but they both point back to a common root, nch, signifying to sigh, breathe, rest, lie down" (Murphy)-ns COD.• cerning our work and toil of our h11nds. To say that Lamech anticipated nothing more than that the youthful Noah would assist him in the cultivation of the soil (Murphy) is to put too little into, and to allege that " this prophecy his father uttered of him, e.s ho that should bo a figure of Christ in his building of the ark, and offering ofsacrifice, whereby God smelled e. sweet savour of rest, and said he would not curse the ground anv more for man's sake, eh, viii. 21 " (Ainsworth), is to extract too much from his language. Possibly he had nothin~ but e. dim, vague expectation of somegood thrngthe destruction of sinners in the Flood (Chry• sostom), the use of the plough (R. Solomon), the grant of animal food (Kalisch), the invention of the arts and implements <>f husbe.mlry (Sherlock, Rush)-that God was a.bout to 011. v. 1-32.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 97 bestow upon his wonr'/ heritage ; or at most e. hope that the promise would be fulfilled in his son's do.y (Bono.r), if not in his son himself (Ce.lovius). The fulfilment of that promise he connects with a recall of tho penal curso which Johovo.h had pronounced upon the soil. Because of the ground which the Lord-Jehovah, by whom the curse had been pronounced (eh. iii. 17)- he.th cursed. 'l'he clauso is not a Jchovistic interpola~ion (Bleck, Davidson, Colcnso), but o. proof " that tho Elohistic theory is unfounded " (' Speaker's Commentary'),

entries.title: GEN 5:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Noah was five hundred years old. Literally, a son of 600 :t~ars, i. e. going in his 500th ytar (c,~· eh. vu. ~.; xvii. 1). The "son of a year (Exod. xn. 6) means "strictly within the first year of the life" (Ainsworth). And Noah begati. e. began to begot (cf. eh. xi. 26)-Shem, -name (Gesenius), fame (Filrst)-Ham, -cham; hot (Gesenius, Murphy), da!k• coloured (Fiirst)-and Ja~heth-sp~eadmg (Gcsenius, Murphy) ; beautiful, denoting the white-coloured race (Furst). That the sons al'e mentioned in the order of their ages (Knobel, Kalisch, Keil, Colenso) may seem to be deducible (1) from the fact that they usually stand in this order (cf. eh. vi. 10 ; vii. 13 ; ix. 18; x. 1 ; 1 Chron. i. 4) ; (2) from the circumstance that it is commonly the eldest son's birth which is stated in the preceding list, though this is open to doubt ; (3) from eh. x. 21, which, according to Calvin, Knobel, Keil, and others, describes Shem as Japheth's elder brother ; and eh. ix. 24, which, according to Keil, affirms Ham to be the younger son of Noah; (4) from eh. x. 2--31, in which tho order is reversed, bul not otherwise altered. But there is reason to believe that Japhcth was the eldest and Ham the youngest of the patriarch's children (Michaelis, Cliuke, MurJjhy, Wordsworth, Quarry). According to eh. xi. 10 Shem was born 97 years before the Flood, while (eh. vi. 11) Noah was 600 years ol<l at the time of the Floo<l. Hence, if Noah began to beget children in his 500th year, and Shem was born in Noah's 503rd year, the probability is that the firstborn son was Japhcth. In accordance with this eh. x. 21 is understood by LXX., Vulgate, Michaelis, Lange, Quarry, and others to assert the priority in respect of atte of Japheth. In the narrative Shem is pfaced.first as being spiritually, though not physically, the firstborn. The data for this deduction, as stated by Sir Charles Lyell, are chiefly the discovery, in recent and postpliocene formations ofallegedgreatantiquity, of fossil human remains and flint implements along with bones of the mammoth and other animals long since extinct (' Antiquity of l\Ian,' chs. i.-xix.).
