entries.title: GEN 5:1–32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -1'he antedilu:viansaints. I. DESCENDANTS OF ADAM. As such they were-1. .A sinfulrace. Adam's son Seth was begotten in his father's image. Though still retaining the Divine image (1 Cor. xi. 7) as to nature, in respect of purity man ]Ja6 lost it. Inexplicable as the mystery is of inherited co~ruption, it is ~till 11: fact tb,i.t the moral deterioration of the head of the human family has transmitted itself to all the members. The doctrine of human depravity, however unpleasant and humbling to carnal pride, is asserted in Scripture (Gen. vi. 5, 12; viii. 21; Job xv. 14; xxv. 4; Ps. xiv. 2, 3; Ii. 5; Isa. liii. 6; Rom. iii. 2:J), implied~ the universal prevalence of sin and death (Rom. v. 12-21), assumed 1~ the doctrmes o~.regeneration, which is declared to be ne<'essary absolutely and umversally (John m. 3), and redemption, of which one part of the design was to deliver men from th.e power as well as guilt of sin (Ephes. v. 25--27; Titus ii. 14; Heb. ix. 12-14; xiii, 12), and abundantly confirmed by experience, which testifh~s that "the wicked are estranged from the womb, and go astray as so?n as they be born, s~eaking lies" (Ps. lvi~..3). 2. A long-lived race. Whether theu_ remarkable longevity ":'as due to the 0;1gmal vigour of the p1"imus R()1TW, or to the mfluenc~ ?£ the tree o! hfe, or to the emmency of the Setbites' piety, 1t was-(1) A gre_at pny1/ege, affordmg to themselves ~~l?le opportunity for self-cultivation and family trarnmg; to the world enlarged fac1ht.1es for advancement in intelligence and civilisation; and to the Church the means of transmitting truth from age to age, and of drawing more closely together the bonds of. religious c0mmunion. (2) An unexpected privilege. Upon the mind and heart of cu. v. 1-32.) 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. 99 Adam in particular it mnst have come with much surprise to find that life, which had been forfeited by sin, :prolonged towell-nigh a millennium of years ; atid this impression, though perhaps 1t might become less as patriarch succeeded patriarch, wonl<I not, we think, entirely disappear. And eo let ns hope they came to recoguise it as (3) a gracious privilege, clue not to any secondary cause whatsoever, but primarily cmcl solely to the infinite mercy of Goel, who had given them the promise of a woman's seed to sustain their faith and hope. And as such also (4) a suggestive privilege, emblematic of the immortality they had lost by sin, but received again through grace. 3. A dying race. Though a sinful, they were yet a pardoned race ; but though a pardoned, they were yet a m<>_rtal race. A portion of the original penalty remains to remind man of hie past history and present condition; and so although the Sethites "lived many hundred yeares, yet none of them filled up a thousand, lest they should have too much flattered themselves in long life; and seeing a 'lhoueand is a. number of perfection, God would have none of them to attain to a fuousand that we might know that nothing is perfect here" (Willet). II. ME~BERS OF' TIIE CnuncH OIJ' Goo. Great as was the former distinction, it is completelyeclipsed bf this. It is a great thing to be born, but a greater to be born again. To be in Gode 'Yorld is.much, to be in God's Church i? ~ore. To be ?f the line of Adam by nature 1e questionable honour, to be of Adams line by grace 1s unquestionable glory, These ten names from Adam to Noah represent the leaders of the Church of God in the primeval age of the world. Whether distinguished by rare talent, great wealth, or high position, whether they invented arts, built cities, and composed hymns like the Cainites, is not said. Their chief distinction lay in- 1. Tlieir possessicn of faith in God. Not perhaps all with the ea~e tenacity,_b~t all with tlie same reality, they clung to the pronuse of the woman s seed. This 1t was which made them members of the antediluvian Church. Wituout faith it is impossible to please God (Heh. xi. 6). 2. Their observance. of religious worshi:p- From the beginning of the world the practice of sacrificial worship was mamtained by believers. For two generations it appears to have been privato rather than public in its character. In the days of Enos, according to one of the interpretations of eh. iv. 26, the Sethites began to worship God in social assemblies, as a mea.ns at once of foBtering their own piety and of defending themselves against the rising tide of ungodliness; and we cannot doubt the godly practice would continue -till the number of believers became eo small that Noah could discover no one of like heart and spirit with himself to participate in his devotions. 3. Their nonconformity to the world. According to another reading of eh. iv. 26, in the third generation the holy seed began to make clearer and more distinct the lines of demarcation between themselves and the Cainites by calling themselves by the name of Jehovah, i. e. by adopting to themselves the appellation of the worshippers of the Lord. The fact tha.t «the sons of God " are mentioned in eh. vi. 1 lends a ~anction to this view. If it was so, doubtless the assumption of this particular title was o:r;ily a sign or symptom of a great religious movement that began to effect the age,:...:.:a nioveinent of eepaiation in heart and life from the unbelievers of the time,-and that with a greater or. lesser intensity perpetuated itself through each successive generation, not even dying away when there was only one man to be aifocted by it, 4. Tlieir witness-bearing against the widcedness of the imgodly world. This comes out not indeed here, but in other Scriptures, in connection with two patria.rche, Enoch and Noah; the first of whom prophesied of the coming of the Lord (Jude 14), and the secorid of whom was a preacher of righteousness to the men of hie generation (2 Pet. ii. 5); and what was true of them was doubtless characte:rietic in a measure of them all. They were unquestionably prophets, priests, and kings in their families and in relation to their contemporaries, 5. Tlieir eminently godly lives. As much as this is implied in what has been nlready said. But of two of them it is distinctly stated that they walked with God: of Enoch, that before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God; and of Noah, that he was a. perfect man and an upright; and though not perhaps entitled to say that all of them lived nt the same spiritual elevation as did those two fathers, yet we are fairly warranted to conclude that all of them maintained n holy Wl\lk and conversation in r,. rapidly degenerating age. 11 2 100 THE BOOK OP GENESIS. [err. v. 1-32. III. PROGENITORS OF THE PROMISED BEED. This was the chief distinction of those i;aintly men, and tho r<'al reason why their names and ages have been eo carefully preserred to the Church of God. They were all links in the chnin leading on to the woman'1, seed. So to speak, they were the ten first heralds sent out to proclnim the appr0ach 0£ .t:he king; the ten fi_rst shadows or adumbrations of the great Prophet, Priest, and Krng to whom the faith of the Church was looking forward. True, it is not mnc-h tl,at we know about them beyond their names, and certainly there is consider- :'ble rag:ueness and uncertainty about their import; but still, accepting those menn- J11gs wl11ch have the greatest probability in their favour, it is interestino- to note how they all indicate points of character or features of history which ~et in Christ. Adam we know was a prophecy of Christ, the second Adam, in more than his name (1 Cor. :~x. 45). Abel, the first martyr, prefigured him in dying by a brother's hand. Seth, the Substituted.One, was a_shadow of him ~ho took our room and stead (Rom. Y. 8); Enos, the Frail OnP,, of him who, as to his human nature, was as "a tender l'lant, and a root out of a dry ground" (Isa. liiL 2); Cainan, Possession, of him who was the gift of God (2 Cor. ix. 15). :Mahalaleel, Praise of God, of him who "was not ashamed to call us brethren, Sa};ng, I will declare thy name unto my brethren, in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee" (Heh. ii. 11, 12); Jared, Descent, of him who came down from heaven (John vi. 38); Enoch, the dedicated nnd instructed child who walked with God, and was translated that he should not see death, of him who for his people "sanctified himself" (John xvii. 19), "in whom were hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col. ii. 3), who with _regard to hi~ Father could say, "I do always those things that please him" (John viii. 29), and who, after accomplishing his Divine mission on the earth, was received up into glory (Acts i. 11); Methuselo.h, Man of the Dart, of him of whom the royal psalmist sang, "Thine o.rrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies " (Ps. xiv. 5); Lamech, Strong Youth, of the strong One whom David saw in vision raised up for Israel's help (Ps. l.xxxix.. 19); Noah, Rest, of him in whose sacrifice God smelled a sweet savour of rest (Ephes. v. 2). Lessons.~1. As descendants of Adam, let us remember we are sinners, and, repenting, believe the gospel; let us measure our daye, and, observing their shortness, apply our hearts unto wisdom; let us think of our mortality, and prepare for the narrow house appointed for all the living. 2. As members of the Church of Christ, have we the marks that distinguished these antediluvian saints? 3, As the spiritual posterity of Jesus Christ, do we reflect him as his progenitors foreshadowed him?

entries.title: GEN 5:22–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Enoch. I. The CHABA.CTEB of his piety, 1. Walking with God, 2. Witnessing for God. II. The EXCELLENCE of his piety. 1. It began in early boyhood. 2. It flourished in evil times. 3. It grew in spite of scanty privileges. 4. It continued to the close of life. III. The BEWA.BD of Enoch's piety. He was trnnslated that he should not see death. 1. A visible proof of immortality. 2. A solemn confirmation of the gospel. 3. A striking prophecy of Christ's ascension.

entries.title: GEN 5:24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Walking with God. Whole chapter a reproof of the restless ambitions of men. Of these long lives the only record is a name, and the fact, "he died." Moral of the whole," Dust thou art" (cf. 1 Cor. xv. 50). Yet a link between life here and life above. Enoch translated (Heh. xi. 5). The living man passed into the presence of God. How, we need not care t? know. _But we know why. He "walked with God." Who would not covet this? Yet 1t may be ours. What then was that life? Of its outward form we know nothing. But same expression (eh. vi. 9) tells us that Noah's was euch. Also Abraham's, "_the frie!ld of God" (c)1. xvii. 1); and St. Paul's (Phil. i. 21); and St. John (1 John 1. 3) claims" fellows1np with the Father" not for himself only (cf. John xiv. 23). I. ESSENTUL FEATURES OF A. WALK WITB Goo. Not a life of austerity or of contemplation, removed from iDterests or careM of world. Noah's was not; nor Abra- TIIE BOOK OF GENEfHS. 10! ham's, Nor LI life without fault, Elijah was " of like passions as we are;" and David ; and St. John declares, 1 John i. 8-10. 1. It is a life of faith, i. e. a life in which the word of God is a real power. Mark in Heh. xi. how faith worked in different circumstances. To walk with God is to trust him as a child trusts ; from belief of his fatherhood, 11nd that he is true. With texts before us such as John iii. 16; 1 John i. 9; ii. 2, why are any not rejoicing? Or with such as John iv. 10; Luke xi. 13, why are any not aRking and receiving to the full? God puts no hindrance (Rev. iii. 20). Ilut (1) too often men do not care. To walk with Goel is of less importance than to be admired of men. (2) If they do care, they often v,ill not take God's way. The simple message (2 Cor. v. 20; 1 John v. 11) seems too simple. They look for feelings, instead of setting God's message before them and grasping it. 2. To walk with God implies desire and effort for the good of men. Jn an ungodly world Enoch proclaimed the coming judgment (Jude 14; cf. Acts xxiv. 25). Spiritual selfishness often a snare to those who have escaped the snare of the world. It is not the mind of Christ. It springs from weakness of faitl1. Knowing the gift so dearly purchased, so freely offered to all, our calling is to persuade men. Not necessarily as teachers (James i. HJ), but by intercession and by loving influence. Ill. ENOCH WAS TRANSLATED. But apostles and saints died. Yet think not th::t their walk with God was less blessed. Hear our Lord's words (John xi. 26), and St. Paul (2 Tim. i. 10). Hear the apostle's desire (Phil. i. 23). Enoch walked with God on earth, and the communion was carried on above. Is not this our Saviour'8 promise? (John xiv. 21-23; xvii. 24). Death is not the putting off that which is corruptible ; it is separation from the Lord. Assured that we are his for ever, we may say, 11 0 death, where is thy sting?"-M.

entries.title: GEN 5:24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A great example and a great reward. Notice the three distinctions in tliis patriarchal prophet. I. Hrs distinguished PIETY-walking with God ; faith giving him knowledge, confidence in God, enjoyment of God. II. Hrs comparatively snonT LIFE, and therefore speedy deliverance from the imperfection and suffering of this world, though his son lived the longest antediluvian life, and .perhaps was a disciple of his father, teaching his doctrine. Those who "initiate" (Enoch) great moral movements are seldom long-lived men. III. Hrs distinguished END-translation. God took him because he loved him. The anticipation of the resurrection was itself a prophecy. The seventh from A.dam is taken to heaven without death, though all the rest died, however long they lived, as though to vivify the promise of the redeeming seed. It seems better to su]ilply the word "died" rather than "was." "And he died not; for God took lii·m" -referring to the common formula of the patriarchal history, "and he died." Walking with God is walking to God. Those who are like Enoch in their life will not be very different from him in their end; for the peace and triumph of n good man's end is little short of translation. The first of the prophets is thus gloriously signalised. Was it not like a special blessing from the beginning of tho world on the life of consecrated ministration to God? Walking with God may be the description of any kind of service, but especially of the prophets'.-R.

Cf. Judges v. 7; vi. 17; Song of Sol. i. 7 (A. V.). Though an Aramaic particle, " it must never be forgotten that Aramaisms arc to be expected either in the most modern or in the most ancient portions ofScriptui·e" (' Speaker's Commentary')-is flesh. Not "transitory beings·" (Gesenius, Rosenmiiller, Tuch), or corporeal beings (Kalisch), but sinful beings; bashai· being already employed in its ethical significa,tion, like aap~ in the New Testament, to denote "man's materiality e.s remlcrcd ungodly by sin" (Keil). "The doctrine of the carnal mind (Rom, viii.) is merely the outgrowth of the thought expressed mthis passage" (Murphy). Yet his days-not the mdividual's (Kalisch), which were not immediately curtailed to the limit mentioned, a.nd, even after the Flood, extended far beyond it (vide eh. xi.) ; but the i-aces, which were only to be prolonged in gracious respite (Calvin)-shall be an hundred and twenty years. Tuch, Colenso, aud others, suyposiug this to have been so.id by Qod in Noah's 600th year, find a respite only of 100 years, instea<l of 120; but the historian does not assert that it wo.J then God either formed or aunow1ced this determination.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - ihere were. Not became, or nrose, ns if the giants were the fruit of the previously-mentioned meselliances ; but already existed contemporaneously with the sons of God (cf. Keil, Havernick, and Lange). Gi&nta. Nephilirn, from naphal, to fall ; hence s.upposed to describe the offspring of the daughters of men and the fallen nngels (Hoffman, Delitzsch). Tho LXX. translate hy yiyavrE~ ; whence the "giants" of the A. Y. and Vulgate, which Luther rejects ns fabulous ; but Kalisch, on the strength of Num. xiii. 33, accepts ns tho cortaiu import of the tenn. More probable is the interpret- 11tion which understands them ns men of violence, roving, hwless gnllnnts, "who fall on other~;" robbers, or tyrants (Arinila, Roseurniillcr,Oescnius,Luther, Calv:in, Kurtz, Keil, Murphy, 'Speaker's Commentary'). That they were "monsters, prodigies" (Tuch, Knobel), may berejected, though it is not unlikely they were men of large physical stature, like the Anakim, Repbaim, an,l others (cf. Norn. xiiL 33). In the earth. Not merely ou it, but largely occupying the populated region. In those days. Previously referred to, i. e. of the mixed marriages. And also-i. e. in addition to these nephilim-after that,-i. e. after their uprising-when the sons of God came in unto the daughters ofmen, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men. Ha'gibborim, literally, the strong, impetuous, heroes (cf. eh. x. 8). "They were probably more refined in manners and exalted in thought than the.ir predecessors of pure Cainite descent" (Murphy). Which were of old. Not " of the world," as a note of character, taking olam as equivalent to aiwv, but a note of time, the narrator reporting from his own standpoint. Men of renown. Litel'!l.lly, men of the name; "the first nol.Jihty of the world, honourable robbers, who boasted of their wickedness" (Calvin) • or gallants, whose names were often in men's mouths (Murphy). For contrary phrase, "men of no name," see Job xxx. 8.

entries.title: GEN 6:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God (Jehovah, which shouhl have been rendered 'the LorJ. ') sa.w-indicative ofthe long-continued patience (Calvin) of the Deity, under whose imme<liate cognizance the great experiment of the primeva1 age of the world was wrought out- that the wickedness (ra'ath; from the root 1·aa, to make a loud noise, to rnge, hence to be wicked) of man (literally, of thr- Adam: this was the first aggravation of the wickedness which God beheld ; it was the tumultuous rebellion of the being whom he had created in his own image) was great (it was no slight iniquity, but a 'lride-sprcn,l, firmly- rooted, and deeply- staining corruption, the second aggravation) in the e&rth. This was the third aggravation; it ,ms in tha world which he had made, and not only in it, but pervading it so ''that integrity rossessed no longer a single corner" (Calvin). And that every im&gination-yetzer, a device, like pottery w11re, from yatza, to fashion as 11, potter (eh. ii. 7; viii. 19). Cf. yotzer, a potter, used of God (Ps. xciv. 9, 20). Heb. ix. l:l (T. Lcwis)-of his he&rt-lev, the heart, tht1 104 TUE BOOK OF GENESlS. !t,&t of the affections and omotions of tho mind. Cf. Judges xvi. 15 (love); Prov. xxxi. 11 (confidence) ; Prov. v. 12 (contempt) ; Ps. civ. l li (joy). Here "the feeling, or deep mother heart, the state of soul, lying below all, and givinR"mornl character to all (Lewis). Cf. the psychological division ofHob. iv. 12was only evil continually. Literally, every day. " If this is not totnl depravity, how can language express it!" Though tho phrnse does not mean "from infancy," yet "the general doctrine" (of man's total and universal depravity) "is properly and consistently elicited hence" (Calvin). 'ler. 6.-Aud it !'epented the Lord. Yinnah,em; from naham, to pant, to groan ; Niph., to lament, to grieve becauso of the misery of others, also because of one's own actions; whence to repent (cf. German, re11,en; English, ni,e: Gesenius) ; ="it grieved him at his heart." " Verbum nostr:e prontatz accommodatum" (Chrysostom) ; "non est perturbatio, sod judicium, quo irrogntur prena ;" nnd again, "prenitudo Dei est mntandorum immnta.- bilis ratio" (Augustine). "Dens est immutabilis; sed cum ii, qnos curat, mutantur, rnntat ipse res, prout iis expedit quos curat" (.Justin Martyr: Latin Version). " The repcnt:mce here ascribed to God docs not properly belong to him, but has reference to our understanding of him" (Calvin). "The repentance of God does not presuppose any rnriableness in his nature or purposes" Keil). "A peculiarly strong anthropopathic expression, which, however, presents the truth that God, in consistency with his immutability, assumes a changed position in respect to changed man" (Le.nge). Th&t he h&d made man on the earth. I. e. that he had created man at all, and in particular that he had settled him on the earth. .And it grieved him at his heart. A touching indir.ation that God did not hnto mnn, nnd a clenr proofthRt,, though tho Divine purpose is immut&\Jlc, the Divine nature is not impassible.

entries.title: GEN 6:1–8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -"11te days tlwJ, were before the flood" (Matt. x.xiv. 38). I. SIN JNCilEASINCJ. 1. Licentwusness raging. The special form it assumed was that of sensuous gratification, leading to a violation of the law of marriage. In the seventh age Lamech the Cainite became a polygamist. By and by the sons of God, cap• tivated by the charms of beauty, cast aside the ~onds_of self-restraint, and took t!iem wives of all whom they chose. (1) They roamed with ungodly women,-beautiful, perhaps talented and accomplished, like the Adahs, Naamahs, and Zillahs of the rnco of Cain but unbelieving and ungodly,-which, as the professing followers of Jehovah, t.J,ey should not hav_e done. Holy Scriptu~e forbids the u;1ion o~ believ_ers with unbelievers (2 Cor. v1. 14). (2) They m'.1me~ to please. theu fancies_, }eavmg a!together out of reckoning, as necessary quahficat10ns m their partners, spmtual nffimty, iutellectual compatibility, and even general suitability, and fixing their eyes only on what charmed the senses, physical loveliness. (3) They married as many wives as they desired. Lamech, the first polygamist, was satisfied with two ; the degenerate sons of Seth, having yielded to self-indulgence, only limited their wives by the demanda Qf their passion. 2. Violence prevalling. Those who begin by breaking the laws of OH, VI. 1--8.] TllE BOOK OF GENESIS. 105 God nre not likely to end by keeping those of man. From the beginning a characteristic of thC' wicked line (witness Cain and Lamech), lawlessness at length passed over to the holy seed. What with the Nephilim on the one hand (probably belonging to the line of Cain) and the Gibborim on the other (the offspring of the degenerate Sethites), the world was overrun with tyrnnts. Sheer brute force was the ruler, and the only code of morals was" Be strong." Moral purity alone has a God-given right to occupy the supreme seat of influence and power upon the earth. After tlrn,t, intellectual ability, Mere physical strength, colossal statnre, immense bulk, were designed for subjection and subordination. The subversion of this Divinely-appointed order results in tyranny; and, of all tyrannies, that of strong, coarse, passion-driven unimalism is the worst. And this was the condition of mankind in these antediluvian ages. And what was even a worse symptom of the times, the people loved to !tave it so. Those lawless robbers and tyrants and these reckless, roving gallants were men of name und fume, in everybody's mouth, as the popular heroes of the day. As mere physical beauty was woman's pathway to marriage, so was sheer brute force, displaying itself in feats of daring and of blood, man's road to renown. 3. Corntption deepening. Most appalling is the picture sketched by the historian of the condition of the Adam whom God at first created in his own image, implying-(1) Complete extinction of the higher nature. Through persistence in the downward path of sin it had at length become lost, swallowed up, in the low, carnal portion of his being called the "flesh." (2) Complete supremacy of evil-evil in the imaginations, evil in the thoughts, evil in the heart, nothing but evil; and that not temporarily, but always; nor in the case of one or two individuals merely, but in the case of all, with one solitary exception. (3) Complete insensibility to Divine influences. Hence the withdrawal of God's Spirit. There was no use for further striving to restrain or improve them ; they were '' past feeling" (Epbes. iv. 19). II. Goo REPENTING. l. A mysterio1is fact. ",ve do not gain much by attempting to explain philosophically such states or movements of the Divine mind. They are strictly uppqra-ineffable. So the Scripture itself represents them-Isa. lv. 9" (Tayler Lewis). What is here asserted of the Divine thoughts is likewise true of the Divine emotions; like the Deity himself, they are past finding out. 2_ A real fact. The language describes something real on the part of God. If it is figurative, then there must be something of which it is the figure; and that something is the Divine grief and repentance. These, however, are realities that belong to a realm which the human intellect cannot traverse. As of the Divine personality man's personality ie but an image or reflection, so of the Divine affections and emotions are man's affections and emotions only shadows. Man repents when he cha.nges his mind, or his attitude, or his actions. God repents when his thoughts are changed, when his feelings are turned, when his acts are reversed. But God is "of one mind, and who can turn him i' " He is "without variableness and shadow of turning; " "the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever." Hence we rather try to picture to ourselves the Divine penitence as expressive of tl,e changed attitude which the immutable Deity maintains towards things that are opposite, such as holiness and sin. 3. An instructive fact, telling us (1) that the Divine nature is not impassible; (2) that sin is not the end of man's creation; and (3) that a sinful man is a disappointment to God. 4. An ominous fact. As thus explained, the grief and penitence of God describe the effect which human sin ever have upon the Divine natnre. It fills him with heart-felt grief and pity. It excites all the fathomless ocean of symputhy for sinning men with which his infinite bosom is filled. Ilut at the same time, un<l notwithstanding this, it moves him to inflict judicial retribution. "And the Lord said, I will destroy man." III. GRACE OPERATING. 1. In restraining sinners. It was impossible tlrnt God could leuvo men to rush headlong to their own destruction without interposing obstacles in their path. In the way of these npostates of the bumnn race he erected quite II series of barriers to keep them back from perdition. He gave them (1) a g·ospel of mercy in the promise of the woman's seed; (2) a ministry of mercy, raising up nnd maintaining n succession of pious men to preach the gospel, and warn them against the wnys of sin; (3) n Spirit of mercy to strive within them; (4) n pro• vidence of mercy, (a) mensuring out to them a long term of years, yet (b) solemnly tOG THE BOOK OF GENESlS. [cu. VI. 1-B. rcmin<ling them of their morlality, and finally (c) giving them a reprieve, even after they were sentenc<'<l to destruction. 2. /11, saving believers. (1) Accepting them l\ll he ncccpted Nonh ; (2) preserving them amid the general defection of the times, as he _did Noah, who without Divine assistance must have been inevitably swept u~·ny m the g·enernl current of ungodliness; (3) providing for their safety against the coming jndgment. They "'ere nil removed by death before the flood came, and Noah was delivered by the ark. Lessl)'ll,S :-1. The terrible degeneracy of human nature. 2. The danger of mixed marriages. 3. God may pity, but he must likewise punish, the evil-doer. 4. The day of grace has its limits. 5. l£ a soul will go to perdition, it must do so over many mercies. 6. God ne,er leaYes l1imsclf wilh:rnt a witness, even in the worst of times. HOMILIES BY VAIUOUS AUTHORS.

entries.title: GEN 6:1–8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The wod.: of sin, The moral chaos out of which the new order is about to be evolved. ·we find these features in the corrupt state depicted. I. ILL-ASSORTED MARRIAGES. The sons of God--i. e. the seed of the righteous such men as the patriarchs described in eh. v., men who walked with God, and wer; his prophets-foll away from their allegiance to the Divine order, and went after the daughters of the Cainites. The self-will and mere carnal affections are denoted by the expression ".ill whom they chose." . II. VIOLENCE ANJl MILITARY AMllITION. The giants were the "nephiliip," those who assaulted and fell upon their neighbours. The increase of such men is. distinctly traced to the corrupt alliances. III. TEE WITHDRAWAL by judgment of THE DIVINF. SPIRIT from man, by which ma~- be meant not only the individual degeneracy which we see exemplified.in such a case as Cain, driven out from the presence of the Lord, given up to. a reprobate mmd, and afterwards in Pharaoh; but the withdrawal of prophecy and such special spiritual communications as had been given by such men as Enoch. IV. TnE SHORTENING OF HUM.AN LIFE. Since the higher moral influence of Christianity has been felt in society during the last three centuries, it is calculated that the average length of human life has been increased twofold. The anthropomorphism of these verses is in peifect accordance with the tone of the whole Book of GenesiJl, and IB not in the least a perversion of truth. It is rather a revelation of truth, as anticipating the great central fact of revelation, God manifest in tl,e flesh. But why is God said to have determined to destroy the face of the earth, tl,e animal creation with the sinful man? Because the life of man involved that of the creatures round him. "The earth is filled with violence." ' To a large extent the beasts, creeping things, and fowls of the air participate in the disorder of the human race, being rendered unnaturally savage and degenerate in their condition by man's disorderly ways. Moreover, any destruction which should sweep away a whole race of men must involve the lower creation. The defeat of a king is the defeat of his subjects. In all this corruption and misery there is yet, by the grace of God, one oasis of spiritual life, the family of Noah. _He £o~nd grace not becau~e l,e earned it, but because he kept what had been given him, both through his ancestors and by the work of the Spirit in his own heart.-R. Giants in health and life are often giants in wiekedneBs. II. THE UNHOLY AJ,LIANCES OF THE SETHITES AND CAINITES. Nothing BO demoralising a.s marriage with .an evil woman. Its bad effects are commonly transmitted to, and intensified in, posterity. III. THE DEP.RAVITY INDUCED DY TllF. FALL, which was universal in its extent, and gradually deepening in its intensity. Lessons :-1. The inherent evil of our natures: 2. The curse clinging to ungodliness. 3. The true function of worldly sorrows and of frequent and early deutL.-W. It. OR. entries.title: GEN 6:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Probation, appobation, and reprobati011,. "And the Lord said, My spirit shall not nlways etrivo with man," &c. The life of man, whether longer or shorter, is a time during which the Spirit of God strives with him. It is at once in judgment and in mercy that the strife 1s not prolonged; for where there is continued opposition to the will of God there is continual laying up of judgrnent against the day of wrath. The nllottcd time of man upon the earth IS sufficient for the required probation, clearly manifesting the direction of the will, the decided choice of the heart. Here ie- I. THE GREAT MORAL FACT OF MAN'S CONDITION IN HIS FLESHLY STATE. The striving of God's Spirit with him. 1. In the order of the worl<l and of human life. 2. In the revelation of truth and positive appeals of the Divine word. 3. In the constant nearness and influence of spiritual society. 4. In the working of conscience and the moral instincts generally. II. THE DIVINE APPOINTMENT OF SPIRITUAL PRIVILEGE at once a righteous limitation and a gracious concentration. That which is unlimited is apt to be undervalued. Not always shall the Spirit strive. 1. Individually this is testified. A heart which knows not the day of its visitation becomes hardened. 2. In the history of spiritual work in comm1tnities. Times of refreshing generally followed by withdrawments of power. The limit of life itself is before us all. Not always can we hear the voice and see the open door. Ill. THE NATURAL AND THE SPIRITUAL ARE INTIMATELY RELATED TO ONE ANOTHER I~ THE LIFE OF MAN. He who decreed the length of days to his creature did also strive with the evil of hie fallen nature that he might cnst it out. The hundred nn<I twenty years are seldom reached; but is it not because the evil is so obstinately retained ? Those whose spirit is most in fellowship with the Spirit of God are least weighed down with the burden of the flesh, are strongest to resist the wearing, wasting influence of the world. IV. THE STRIVIN0 OF Goo's SPIRIT WITH us MAY CEASE. What follows? To fall on the stone is to be broken, to be under it is to be crushed. The alternative i~ before every human life--to be dealt with as with God or against him. "Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker I" The progressive revelations of the Bible point to the winding up of all earthly history. Not always strife. Be ye reconciled to God.-R.

entries.content: -And God said unto Noah, The end. Yi?. Of all flesh. Jansen of Holland, in 1609, proved by actual experiment that a ship constructed after the pattern of the ark, though not adapted for sailing, would in reality carry a cargo greater by one-third than any other form of like cubical content. The diffi.culty of building a vessel of such enormous magnitude, T. Lewis thinks, may be got over by remembering the extreme simplicity of its structure, the length of time allowed for its erection, the physical constitution of the builders, and the facilities for obtaining materials which may have existed in abundance in their vicinity. Bishop Wilkins (' Essay towards a Philosophical Character and Language'), Dr. A. Clarke, and Bush are satisfied that the ark was large enough to contain all the animals directed to be taken into it, along with provision for a twelvemonth ; but computations founded on the number of the species presently existing mlllit of necessity be precarious ; and besides, it is at least doubtful whether the Deluge was universal, or only partial and local, in which case the difficulty (so called) completely vanishes.

entries.title: GEN 6:9–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The building of the ark. I. Tm~ MAN AND HIS cONTEMPOnARIBS. A common saying, and one possessed of a show of wisdom, that a person seldom rises far .above the average goodness, or sinks far below the average wickedness, of the age in which he lives. Yet it is precisely in proportion as individuals either excel or fall beneath their generation that they are able to affect it for good or evil. All epoch-making men are of this stamp. Noah, it is obvious, was not a man whose character was ·shaped by his contemporaries. In respect of three things, the contrast between him and them was as great and decided as could well be imagined. I. Legal standing. Noah was a just man, i. e. a sinner justified by his believing acceptance of the gospel promise of the woman's seed; while they were corrupt, or had declined into in.fidelity. 2. Spiritual characte/'. Noah was perfect in the sense that his heart was right with God, and his nature wns renewed by Divine grace ; they were wanting in all the essential characteristics of true being, " alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that was in them, because of the hardness of their hearts." 3. Outer walk. As a consequence the daily life of Noah was one of eminent piety....;,a walking with God1 like that of Enoch; while theirs was one of impious defiance of the laws of God, anct ruthless oppression of the rights of men. Learn (1) that it is quite possible to be pious in the midst of evil times; and (2) that only a life of close communion with God will prevent one from being overborne by the wickedness of his age. II. THE EVENT AND ITS OCCASION. The event was-1. .Appalling in its forrn. The destruction of a world by n flood of waters. "In the beginning," at God'8 command, the goodly fabric had risen from the waters (eh. i. 2; 2 Pet. iii. 5), radiant in beauty, swimming in asea of light, rejoicing its Crentor's heart (eh. i. 31) ; now it was about to return to tho dark and formless matrix whence it sprang. If the world's birth woke music among the morning stars (Job xx:xviii. 7), surely it« destruction was enough to make the angels weep [ 2. Universal in its sweep. Without engaging at present in any controversy as to the actual extent of the Deluge, we mu.y notice that Elohim represents it as destructive of the entire human race (Noah and his family exceptACl). Considering the impres~ion made upon our he:nts hy the 112 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [err. vr. 9-22, report of some sudden accident (the explosion of n mine, the sinking of I\ ship, the collision of a train), in which a number of lives arc lost, it is not wonderful tlll\t the eeho of this stnpendous catnstrophe should hllve vibrnted through the world (see 'Tr_a<litions of the Deluge l . 3. SttJ?ernatural in its origin. It was not an or<lmary occurrence, but a d1shnctly nnraculous phenomenon. 11 Behold, 11 even I <lo _hrin_g a flood of water~ ~pon t)ie ~arth:" 4. Punitive in its purpose. It~ r0!nh11tJYc character was d1stmctly implied m the form of its announcoment- ,, I will destroy." All temporal calamities arc not of this description. That all snffe1ing is p~nal was the mist:~kc ~£ ~ob's friends (Jo~ h•. 7, et passim), though 11ot .?.£ Job h1msel~1 and certainly _1_~ 1s not the tea.clung of the Bible (cf. Job xxxm. 29; Ps. xc1v. 12; Rom. vm. 28; 2 Cor. 1v. 17). But this was - 5. lilelanclwly in ?°t,; occasion-the total, absolute, and radical corruption of the earth's inhabitants. Through unbelief and disobedience they had ruined the morn! nature which God had gfren them; and now there was no help for it but that they should be swept away. 6. Inevitable in it,; comi1l{J, Implied in one interpretation of the words" the end of all flesh" (vule Expos.). Sin ever canies its own retribution in its bosom; not merely, howeYer, in recoiling upon itself with inward misery, sense of loss, weakness, depravation; but likewise in necessitating the infliction on the part of Elohim of positive retribution. 7. Near in its approach. "Behold, I am bringing l" as if it were already at hand. Sec here (1) the danger of sin; (2) the certainty of retribution; (3) the righteousness of the wrath of God; (4) the mercy of God in making this knovm to siriners, as he foretold the Flood to the ante<liluvians. III. THE COMMISSION AND ITS EXECUTION. 1. It related to the safety ofthe Ohm·ch (rnr. 18). A.t that time the antediluvian Church was small, consisting only of Noah an<l. his family (eh. vii. 1), and in all probability uninfluential and despised, by the Gibborim and Nephilim of the day ridiculed and oppressed. Endangered by the immorality and violence of the times, it was likewise imperilled by the impending Del~fe. Yet God. never leav:es his peop.~e unprotecte~ or unprovided for (Deut. xx:.xm. 12 ; Ps. XDJ.V. 15; xlv1. 5; Zech. 11. 5; 2 Pet. n. 9). The Church of God and Christ is imperishable (Isa. !iv. 17; Matt.. xvi. 18; xviii. 14). That was symbolised to Israel by the burning bush (Exod. iii. 2), and to all postdiluvian time by ihe ark. It was impossible that Go,l could be unconcerned about the safety of the believing remDant in antediluvian times. The commission which came to Noah concerned the rescue of himself and children. 2. It was IJivinely given (vers. 131 14). Sal,ation is of the Lord (Ps. iii. 8; Jonah ii. 9). Manifestly only God could have provided for the safety of Noah and his family. Directions from any other quarter, or even expedients devised by himself, must have proved both futile and presumptuous. So, whatever instructions may be given to man with a view to salvation must come from God, if they are to be successful. Schemes of redemption may be beautiful, ingenious, attractive, hopeful ; if they are not God's schemes they are worthless (Isa. :xliii. 11 ; Hosea xiii. 4). 3. It was minutely detailed (vers. 14-16). The plan which God proposed to Noah for the salvation of himself and house was building of an ark according to Divinely-prepared specifications. In its construction there was no room left for the exercise of inventive genius. Like the tabernacle in the wilderness, it was fashioned according to a God-given pattern. And so, in all that concerns the salvation of sinful men, from first to last the plan is God's, admitting neither of addition nor subtraction, correction nor improvement, at the hands of the men themselves. 4. It was believingly received(Heh. xi. 7). Perhaps the last device that would ever have suggested itself to the mind of Noah, very likely ridiculed by Lis contemporaries as an act of folly, probably at times regarded with considerable misgivings by the patriarch himself, and certainly an undertaking that would involve immense labour, patient endurance, heroic self-sacrifice, it was yet accepted in n spirit of meek and unquestioning faith. A.nd so should it be with us. When God speaks we should hear. When he directs we sho1 1ld obey. 5. It was obediently carried throwJh (ver. 22). This was the best test of his faith. Where obedience is absent, faith it1 not present. Faith always discovern its existence by obedience (Heb. xi. 8). Learn-(1) God's care of his people. (2) The sufficiency of God's pbn of salvation. (3) The wisdom of implicitly following God's directions. OH, vr. 9--22.] 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. 113

entries.title: GEN 6:9–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Riglieeousness and .Pea.ce. The description of Noah is very similar to that of Enoch, just and perfect m his generation, that is, blameless in his walk before men, which is saying much of one who lived in a time of universal corruption. And he walked with God, i. e. devout and religious, and, from the analogy of the preceding use of the words, we may say, a prophet. He preached righteousness both with lip and life. To this good and great prophet the announcement is made of the coming judgment. "The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him, and he will show them his covenant." The earth is filled with violence through men, and therefore with man must be destroyed. With the message of judgment there is also the message of mercy, as at the first. THE ARK, AN EMBLEM OF SALVATION BY GRACE, AS AFTERWARDS (cf. 1 Pet. iii. 19-22). The offer of salvation was a trial of-faith. God did not himself provide the ark ; it was made by the hands of men, of earthly materials, with ordinary earthly measurements and appointments, and prepared as for an ordinary occasion. There was nothing in the visible ark to stumble faith; but, as it was connected with a positive commandment and prophElcy, it was a demand on the simple faith of the true child of God, which is of the nature of obedience. We cannot doubt that this Divine message to Noah was the Bible of that time. It appealed to faith as the word of God. And, as in all times, with the written or spoken word there was the unwritten law, the lex non scripta; for we are told that" Noah did according to all that God commanded him, so did he." In this primitive dispensation notice these things :-1. The righteousness of God is the foundation. 2. The accordance of the world with God's heart, as at once commanding righteousness and hating violence, is the condition of its preservation. 3. The mercy of God is connected with his special revelations in and by the men who have found grace in his sight. 4. The provisions of redemption are embodied in an ark, which is the symbol of Divine ordinances and the associated life of believers. 5. The salvation of man is the real end and aim of all judgments. 6. With the redeemed human race there is a redeemed earth-creatures kept alive in the ark to commence, with the family of God, a new life. 7. While we must not push the symbology of the Flood too far, still it is impossible to overlook the figure which the Apostle Peter saw in the ark floating on the waters-the Church of Christ as washed by the Holy Ghost in those waters, which represent not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of o good conscience toward God.-R.

entries.title: GEN 7:1–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The al'k entered. I. Tlll!: INVITATION OF J1moVAll. "Come thou nnd nll thy house into the nrk." 'l'his invitation wae-1. Timely. It was n·iven ou the fini~liing of the ark, und thcrefuro not too soon; also seven days before tl~e Flood, I 2 116 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [err. VII. 1-10. and therefore not too late, God's interventions in his people's behalf nre nlways opportune : witness the exodus from E~ypt, the deliverance nt the Red Sen the rlestruction of Sennacherib's army; Christ s walking on the sea, sleeping in the boat, rising from the dead. 2. Specud. It was addressed in particular to Noah. "Come thou." "The Lord knoweth them that are his." "The Good Shepherd calleth his own sheep by name,!'-n~ l~adeth them out." So is the invitation of the gospel of the 1mme personal and md1vidual description (Matt. xiii. 9; Rev. iii, 6). Men are not 1mmmoned to believe in masses, but as individuals. 3. Comprehensive. "And all thy house." Whether Shem, Ham, and Japheth were at this time believers is not known. The noticeable.circumstancEl is th_at the invitation was not addressed immediately to them, but mediately through _their father. If Noah stood alo~e in his piety, their summo!"ls to enter the ark reminds us of the ad_vantage of belongmgto n pious family, and bemg even only externally connected with the Church (cf. Luke xix. 9 · Acts XYi. 32). 4. Gracious. Given to Noah certainly, in one sense, because of his'piety, (eh. ,ii. 1). But since his godliness was the fruit of faith, and his faith nothing more than a resting on the Divine covenant or promise, it was thus purely of grace. So is God's invitation in the gospel all of grace (Gal. i. 6; Epbes. iii. 8). 5. Urgent. Only seven days, and the Flood would begin. There was clearly not much time to lose. Only a seyenth of the time given to the men of Nineveh (Jonah iii. 4). But not e,en se,en days are promised in the gospel call (Matt. x.x.iv. 36; Rom. xiii. 12; Phil. iY. 5; James,. 9). II. Tm: ODEDIENCE OF NoAH. "And Noah did according unto all that the Lord commanded him." This obedience was-1. Immediate. It does not appear that };oah trifled with the Dinne summons, or in any way interposed delay; and neither Hhould sinful men with the invitation of the gospel (2 Cor. vi. 2; Heh. iii. 7). 2. Believing. It bad it.s inspiration in a simple credence of the Divine word that safety could be secured only within tl1e ark ; and not until the soul is prepared to accord a l,earty trust to the statement that Christ is tbe heaYen-provided ark of salvation for a lost world does it yield to the gospel call, and enter into the safe shelter of bis Church by believing on his name (Epbes. i. 13). 3. Persor,,al. Noah himself entered in. Had be not done so, not only would his own salvation have been missed, but bis efforts to induce others to seek the shelter of the ark would have been fruitless. So the first duty of a herald of the gospel or minister of salvation is to make his own calling and election sure, after which his labours in behalf of others are more likely to be efficacious (1 Cor. iL 27; 1 Tim. iv. 16). 4. Influential. The entire household of the patriarchfollowed his example. Itis doubtful if at this time any of them were possessors of bis faith. Yet all of them cornplied with the heavenly invitation, probably impelled thereto by the example and exhortation of their parent. When tl:e head of a household becomes aChristian he in effect brings salvation to the house. He brings all its in.mates into at least a nominal connection with the Church, encircles them with an atmosphere of religion ernanating from his own character and conduct, and frequently through Divine grace is honoured to be the instrument of their salvation (Luke xix. 9; Acts xL 14; xvi. 31). 5. Minute. Noah's entry into the ark in all particulars corresponded with the Divine invitation. The animals went in two and two as God commanded. Men are not expected or allowed to deviate from the plain pr~scriptione of the word of God concerning the way of faith and salvation (Acts x. 33). Leam-1. The unwearied diligence of God in saving men. 2. The personalnature of God's dealings with men. 3. The extreme solicitude with which he watches over them, who are hie. 4. The indispensable necessity of obedience in order to salvation.

entries.title: GEN 7:1–6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God the Sa'IJWUr invitingfaith. "Come thou and all thy house into the ark " &c. Covenant mercy. A type of the Christian Church, with its special privilege and defence surrounded with the saving strength of God. I. DIVINE PnEPARA;ION. Providence. The ark. 1. Human agency under inspired ihrection. 'fhe word of God. The institutions of religion. The fellowship of eaints. 2. A preparation mnde in the face of antl in spite of an opposing world. The history of the Church from the beginning. 3. The preparation is safety and peace to those who trust in it, notwithstanding the outpoured judgment. II. DIVINE ll'Al'l'IIll'ULNEBB. 11 Come tlwu; for thee have I seen righteous." Not the merit of man is the ground of confidence, but the Lord's grace. I have seen thee righteous because I have looked upon thee as an obedient servant, and have counted thy faith for righteousness. Faithfulness in God is an object of man's trust as connected with hie spoken word and the preparation of his mercy. III. DIVINE SUB'FIOIENOY. The weak creatures in the ark surrounded by the destroying waters. A refuge opened in God. Ilis blessing on the household. His redemption succouring the individual soul, the life and its treasures, family peace and prosperity, &c. The ark a type of the prepared salvation, carrying the believer through the flood of earthly cares and troubles, through the deep waters of death, to the new world of the purified heaven and earth, wherein dwelleth righteousnese.-R. Vcrs. 7-16.-Realised salvatwn. "And Noah went in," &c. "And the Lord shut him in" (vers. 7, 10, 16). I. The OONTRAST between the position of the BELIEVER and that of the UNBE· LIEVER. The difference between a -true freedom and a false. 11 Shut in" by the Lord to obedience, but also to peace and safety. The world's judgment shut out. The restraints and privations of a religious life only temporary. The ark will be opened hereafter. II. TnE METHOD OF' GRACE ILLUSTRATED. He that opens the ark for salvation shuts in his people for the completion of his work. We cannot shut ourselves in. Our temptation to break forth into the world and be involved in its ruin. The misery of fear. Are we safe? Perseverance not dependent upon our self-made resolutions or provisions. By various means we are shut in to the spiritual life. Providentially; by ordinances; by bonds of fellowship. We should look for the Divine eeal.-R.

entries.content: -And they that went in, wenl in mo.le o.nd femalo of all flesh, as- God (Elohim) had commanded him. This ovi- ,lently closed an Elohistic passage, according to Colenso, as the ensuing clt\use ns· manifestly belongs to the .lehovisticintcrpolator.; but the closo connection subsisting between the tl'ro clauses forbids nny such dislc,cntion of tlio narrative as that suggested. And the Lord (Jehovah)shuthimin. Literally, shut behincl hiin, i. o. closed up the door of the ark after him (fr}\Elo-E r~v ic,fjwrov [tw9w uvrou, LXX.) ; doubtless miraculously, to preserve him both from the violence of the waters and the ra,,<re of men. entries.title: GEN 7:17–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Andtha:6.oodwasfortydays upon the earth. Referring to the forty days' and nights' rain of. ver. 4 (uaaapci1<ovra i,µipac ,cai TEO'O'Upai:ovra VvKra,, LXX.), duringwhich the angmentationof tlie waters is described in a threefold degree. And the waters increased. Literally, grew great. The first degree of increase, marked by the floati711J of the ark. And bare up ~he ark, and it wasliftup above the earth. L1!erall:)'.', it was h,i.gh, from up<>n the earth, 1. e. 1t rose above it. And the waters prevailed. Literally, were strong; from i~}, to bo strong ; whence the Gibborim of eh. vi 4. And were increased greatly on the earth. Literally, became g1•eat, greatly. TheSifCond degree of increase, marked. by the goi711J of the ark, And the ark went-i. e_. floated a.I.on"'• ,cal hn~•pEro, LXX. (Ps. c1v. 26)- upo; 'the face of the waters. And the waters prevailed exceedingly. Literally, and the watera became strong, exceedi711Jly.. The third degree of increase, marked by the submergence of the, monntains. And all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven were covered. A clear assertion of the uni~ersality of the Flood (Keil, Kalisch, Alford Bush Wordsworth); but the la.n• guage does not necessarily imply more th:i.n that all the high hills beneath the spectator's heaven were submergecl (cf. eh. xli. 57 • Exod. ix. 25 ; x. 15 ; Deut. ii. 26 i 1 Ki~gs x. 24 ; Acts ii. 6 ; Col. i. 25, for ID• stances in which the universal terms all and every must be taken with a limi~ed signification) • while it is o.lmost certain that, hau the ;arrator even designed to record only the fact that all the heights within tli. , visible horizon had disappeared beneath t:t rising waters, ho woulr~ lrnv~ done so by snying thnt " nil the !ugh hills under tho wholo hcnvcn woro covered." A general expression for the e.nima.1 creation, of which the particulars are then specified. Both of fowl, and of cattle, and of beast, and of every creeping thing that creepeth on the earth. Literally, in fowl, and in cattle, &c. (cf. ver. 14). And every mo.n. I. e. all the human race (with the exception of the inmates of the ark), which is further characterised as all in whose nostrils was the breath of life. Literally, the breath of the spirit of lives, i. e. all mankind. A clear pointing backwards to eh. ii. 7, which lee.de Davidson to ascribe vers. 22, 23 to the Jehovist, although Eichhorn,Tuch, Bleck, Vaihinger, and others lee.ve them in the fundamento.l document, but which is rather to be regarded as a proof of tl1e interne.l unity of the book. Of all that was in the dry le.nd,-a further specification of the creatures that perished in the Flood,-died. It is obvious the construction of vers. 21, 22 may be differently understood. In the worcl3 which follow, which wear the aspect of an unnecessary repetition, it is re~arded in its relation to the Divine thrcatemng.

The straits to which the ad\"0cates of the documentary hypothesis are sometimes reduced are remarkably exemplified by the fortunes of these veTscs (21- 23) in the attempt to assign them to their respective authors. Astruc conjectures that ver. 21 was taken from what he calls monumentum B, ver. 22 from " monument" A, and ver. 23 from monument C. Eichhorn ascribes vers. 21, 22 to e.n Elohistic author, nnd ver. 23 to a Jehovistic. Ilgen assigns vers. 21, 22 to the first, and ver. 23 to the second Elohist. Bleek, e.11 three tn the Elahist; nncl Davidson ver. 21 to the Elohist, vcrs. 22, 23 to the Jehovist. entries.title: GEN 7:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Was the Flood universal 1 I. THE BIBLICAL ACCOUNT. Unquestionably the language of the historian appears to describe a complete submergence of the globe beneath a flood of waters, and is capable of being so understood, so far as tixegesis can determine. Unquestionably also that this was the writer's meaning would never have been challenged had it not been for certain difficulties of a. scientific nature, ns well as of other kinds, which were gradually seen to attach to such hypothesis. But these difficulties ha.ving arisen in men's minds led to a closer and more careful investigation of the Scriptu10 narrative,when it was found-I. That the language of the historian did not necessarily imply that the catnstrophe described was of universal extent (vide Exposition). 2. Thnt, if it had been only partial and local in its operation, in all probability the same, or at least closely similar, terms would have been selected to depict its appearance, as observed by a. spectator. 3. That the purpose for which, according to the inspired record, the Deluge was sent could have been completely effected without the submergence of the entire globethat purpose being the destruction of the human race, which, it is believed, had not 120 TllE llOOR: OF GENEStS. ten. vn. 11-24. nt that time overspread tho earth, but was confined to a limited region contiguous to the vnlley of the Euphrates. That this last conjecture is not of recent origin but was early entertained by theologians, is proved by tho facts that Aben Ezra 111 confuteth ,~he ~pinion of som~ who in h_is days hold the Deluge not to have been unive~al (" 11let); that Bishop Patnck notes (ch. vii. 19) that II there were those anciently, and they have their successors now, who imagined the Flood was not nniversal,-aAA' lv fj oi ,..;,.f civ91"",ro, ,jlrovv,-but only there where men then dwelt·" that Matt. Poole writes, "Peradventure this Flood might not be universal over the ~·hole ea~h, but only over al~ the habita~le world, where either men or beasts lived, wlnch wns 11B much as either the meritorious cause of the Flood men's sins or the end of it, the destruction of all men and beasts, required" (Syno psis eh. vii: 19) ; and that Bishop Stillingfleet in his 'Origincs Saerai' remarks "I ca~not see nny necessity, from the Scriptures, to assert that the Flood did sp~ead itself over all the surface of the earth. That all mankind (those in the ark excepted) were destroyed by it is most certain, according to the Scriptures; but from thence follows no necessity at all of asserting the universality of it as to the globe of the earth, unless it be sufficiently proved that the earth was peopled before the Flood w~ic_h I ?es_pair of ever seeing proved" (vide 'Quarry on Genesis,' p. 184). Thi~ opm10n, 1t 1s almost needless to observe, has been adopted by the majority of modem scholars. 4. That subsequent Scriptural references to this primeval catastrophe are at least not decidedly at variance with the notion of a limited Deluge. Gen. ix. 15 places emphasis on the fact that the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all.flesh, i. e. all mankind. Isa. !iv. 9, pointing back to Gen. ix. 15, says that as God swore in the days of Noah that the earth would be no more inundated as to carry off the entire population, so did he swear then that he would not rebuke Israel. The language does not, as Wordsworth thinks, imply the universality of the Deluge. 2 Pet. ii. 5; iii. 6 refers to the destruction of the apxafoc rcirrµoc, i. e. the world of men, the ,ccirrµoc ltrr,{3wv specially mentioned in the former of these passages. So far then as Scripture is concerned we are not shut up to the necessity of regarding the Deluge as universal. II. ScIENTIFIC DIFFICULTIES. 1. .Astronomical. It is urged that, as there is no sufficient evidence of any general subsidence of the earth's crust, the theory proposed by some harmonists, that the land and water virtually exchanged places (this was supposed to be borne out by the existence of shells and corals at the top of high mountains), having now been completely abandoned (that the outlines of the great continental seas have been substantially the same from the beginning-11ide eh. i. ver. 9, Expos.), the entire surface of the globe could be covered only by a large increase of water being added to the earth's mass. Kalisch supposes eight times the aggregate of water contained in all the seas and oceans of the earth ; that this must ha,e produced such a shock to the solar system as to have caused a very considerable aberration in the earth's orbit, of which, however, no trace can be detected ; and that, consequently, it is unphilosophical to imagine that such a disturbance of the entire stellar world as would necessarily follow on that event would be resorted to in order to destroy a race of sinful beings in one of the smallest planets of the system. But-(1) Biblical science, which recognises an incarnation of the Word of God in order to save man, will always hesitate to pronounce anything too great for the Ahnighty to permit or do in connection with man. (2) It is gratuitous to infer that because a general subsidence of the earth's crust cannot now be traced, there was none. .Absence of evidence that a thing was is not equivalent to presence of proof that a thing was not. Witness the third day's vegetation and antediluvian civilisation. (3) If even the earth's surface were covered with water, it is doubtful if it would be much more in effect than the breaking out of a profuse sweat upon the human body, or the filling up with water of the indentures on the' rough skin of an orange, in which case it is more than probable that the apprehended disturbance of the solar system would prove in great part imaginary. 2. Geologi,cal. At one time believed to afford incontestable evidence of a universal deluge in the drift formations, the diluvium of the earlier geologists (of late, with better reason, ascribed to the influence of a glacial period which prevailed over the greater part of Central and Northern Europe in prehistoric times), geolr,gica) OH. Vil, 11-24.J 'tHE BOOK OF GENESlS. 121 science Is now hclcl to teach exactly the opposite. The extinct volcanoes of Languedoc ancl Auvergne are believed to have been in operation long anterior t-0 the time of man's appearance on the earth, the remains of extinct animals being found among thoir scorim; and yet the lava cones are in many instances as perfect as when fir11t thrown up, while the clross lies loose upon their sides, which it is scarcely supposable would be the case had they been subjected to any cataclysmal immersion such as is presupposed in the Deluge. But here the mistake is that of imagining the Noachic Flood to have been of any such violent torrential character. On the con• trary, the Scripture narrative represents the waters as having risen and subsided slowly, and the whole phenomenon to have been of such a kind as, while destroying human life, to effect comparatively little change upon the face of nature; and, besides, careful scientific observers have declared that the volcanic scoriai in question is not so loose as is sometimes alleged (Smith's 'Bib. Diet.,' art. Noah). 3. Zoological. This refers to the difficulty of accommodating all the animals that were then alive. So long of course as Raleigh's computation of eighty-nine distinct species of animals was accepted as correct, the task impoBed upon apologists was not of a very formidable character. But of mammalia alone there are now known to exist 1658 different species, thus making about ~000 ancl upw~rds of individual~ (the clean beasts being taken in sevens or seven pairs) that requued to be stalled in the ark; and when to these are added the pairs of the 6000 birds, 650 reptiles, and 550,000 insects that are now recognised by zoologists, the difficulty is seen to be immensely increased. An obvious rem11rk, however, in connection with this is that there is a tendency among modern zoologists unnecessarily to multiply the number of species. But in truth a prior difficulty relates to the collection of these multitudinous creatures from their respective habitats. If the entire surface of the globe was submerged, then must the fauna belonging to the different continents have been conveyed across the seas and lands towards the ark, and reconducted thence again to their appropriate settlements in some way not described and impossible to imagine; whereas if the inwidated region extended (through the subsidence of the earth's crust) to the Mediterranean on the west, and the Indian Ocean on the south and east, it is apparent that neither would this difficulty have proved insuperable, nor would the collection of the animals have been rendered unnecessary, the devastated country being so wide that only by preservation of the species could it have been speedily replenished. III. The CONCLUSION, therefore, seems to be that, while Scripture does not imperatively forbid the idea of a partial Deluge, science appears to require it, and, without ascribing to all the scientific objections that are urged against the universality oE the Flood that importance which their authors assign to them, it may be safely affirmed that there is considerable reason for believing that the mabbul which swept away the antediluvian men was confined to the region which they inhabited.

entries.title: GEN 7:23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The Deluge. I. A STRIKING TESTIMONY TO 'l'HE DIVINE FAITHFULNESS. 1. In respect of threatenings agai11,st the wicked. Whether the faith of Noah ever betre.yed symptoms of we.vering during the long interval of waiting for the coming of the Flood it is impossible to say ; it can ecnrcely be doubted that the men who for six scoro years had seen the sun rise and set with unwearied regularity, that had watched the steady and continuous movement of nature's laws e.nd forces throughout the passing century, oftentimes exclaimed, "Where is the promise of his coming, for all things continue as they were from the beginning?" And yet God kept hie word, and fulfilled his threatening. "The flood came, and took them all nway" (Matt. xxiv. 39). Cf. the Dh•ine threntenings against Babylon (Jer. Ii. 33), against Tyre (Isa. x.xiii. 12), against Jerusalem (2 Kings xxi. 13; Jer. xxvi. 18), against the Jews (Deut. xxviii. 49). Let impenitent sinnerij thereby be reminded that there is one more word of doom which he will yet cause to come to pass (Pa. ix. 17 ; 2 Thess. i. 8; 2 Pet. iii. 10). 2. In respect of promi,ses to the saints. At the same time thllt he foretold to Noah the destruction of his licentious and violent contemporaries, he distinctly promised thut he would establish hie covenant with Noah, and preserve both him and his o.mid the genera.I overthrow. And that too he implemented in duo time nnd to the letter. Let the saints then learn to trust the preciollll promises of God 122 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [err, vn. 11-24. ~2 Pet, i. 4) which haYc been given to enable them to escapo the co1T11ption thnt is m t.he world through lust (Tiic 111 "o"/l-'i' i11 im6uµ.iv 1/JBopai;, i. e. the destruction thnt is already operating in tho world and coming out of, as it is cnrried in, the wodd's lust). Ii. A sIGNA~ DISPLAY o_v THE D~YINE POWER. l. bi controlling his creatures, p) _In coll~cting the anim,als, which he did, doubtless, by making uso of their msbncts winch led them to apprehend the coming danger. VideJob xxxix.-xli. for God's power over the animal creation. (2) In usi1i(/ the powers ofnatm·e--breaking up the flood-~a.~ of th~ deep, and ope_ning the wmdows of heaven. The phenomenon we.s d1stmctly rn1racnlous; but 1f God made the world, causing it to stand together out of ihc water and through ihe water, the supernatural character of the Deluge should not occasion difficulty. Nor should the power of God be overlooked in tlie ordinary phenomena of nature. "Nature is but another nnme for nn effect whose cause is God." In the miracle God reveals what he is always silently and impercept.ibly doing in the natural event. Nothing hoppens in the realm of providence without the concurrence of Almighty power (Amos iii. 6; Matt. x. 29). Let God's power exhibited over nature's forces remind us of bis ability to bring the present terrestrial economy to an end as he has promised (2 Pet. iii, 10, 11). (3) In destroying the lives of men. In every caso life is 11 gift of God, and can only be recalled by him (Deut. xxxii. 39; 2 Sam. ii. 6). Yet, unless when God interposes to destroy on a large scale,-e. g. by famine, pestilence, war, acoident,-his absolute and unchallengeable control o,er men's lives (Ps. xxxi. 15) is apt to be forgotten. And with what infinite ease he can depopulate the fairest ond most crowded regions he has often shown ; witness, in addition to the Flood, the destruction of the cities of the plain (eh. xix. 24, 25), of the first-born in Egypt (Exod. xii. 29), of the army of Pharaoh (Exod. xiv. 27), of the host of Sennacherib (2 Kings xix. 35). 2. In pmiishing his enemies. That appalling visitation is fitted to remind us. tho.t God is able to execute ,engeance-(1) On thegreatest sinners. Having castdownthe sinning angels, and drowned the world of the ungodly, and burnt up the filthy Sodomites, it is scarcely likely that any criminal will be beyond hls power to apprehend nnd chastise (2 Pet. ii. 9; Jude 15). (2) b~ the severest forms. Having all the resources of nature at l.iis command,-the gleaming thunderbolt, the sweeping flood, the sleeping volcano, the tempestuous hurricane, nil the several and combined potencies of fire, air, earth, and water,-he can never want a weapon wherewith to inflict upon bis adversaries" the tribula.tion a.nd wrath, indignation and anguish,'.\ ho has decreed for their portion (Rom. ii. 8, 9 ; 2 Thess. i. 8, 9 ; Hev, xx. 15 ; xxi. 8). (3) .At the most unexpected times. Few things connected with the Noachic Del1;1ge are more impressive and paralysing to the mind thnn the suddenness of the surpnsal with which it sprang upon the wicked generntion that for 120 years had been disbelieving its reality and ridiculing the warnings of the patriarch. _"So ALSO SHALL TEE COMING or THE So~ OF MAN DE." (4) Witli tlie most inevitable certainty. Tempted by their long lives to imagine that the penalty of death was ca_ncelled or had become inoperative, or at least would not really be put in force agamst them, these men of the first acre were recalled from their delusive reasonings. The Deluge wa1, God's proclamatio; that the penalty was still in force against sinners, God's explanation of what that penalty meant, God's ce~ification tbat that penalty_ ~as sure. 3. In protecting his people. The ark floatmg on the waters was a visible sermon to all time coming of God's ability to save them who believe and obey him. And, like the shelter enjoyed by Noah, the salvation which God besto:ws upon his people is (1) gracious-flowing from the Divine mercy ; (2) free-with no condition attached except that men shall, like Noah, believe and obey; (3) adequate-containing all that is required for their spiritual necessities, as _the. ai;~ held abundant provision for the voyage; (4) aecure-" the Lord shut him _m. So says Christ, "I give unto them eternal life, and they shall never pensh " (John :x. 28). III. A SOLEMN ATI'EBTATION OF THE DIV:NE HOLINESS. Proclaiming-!. That th4 Di,vine character was holy. A deity who is himself subject to imperfection _is inconceivable. But sinful men are prone to forget that God is of purer eyes than to look upon iniquity. In this laet age of the world God has discovered that to men by 8onding forth an imngc or likeness of himself in the peraon of his Son, who wo.s holy, ho.rmless, undeliled, and separate from sinners (cf. John xiv. 9). In the first aga ha announced the same great truth by the water-flood. 2. That the Di,vine law WC!-! holy. That, besides being himself personally pure, ho requires sinless obedience at the hands of his creatures, the Almighty has in every separate era or epoch of human history taken pains to inform men ; in Edenic times by the forbidden tree ; in 1rntediluvinn by the Deluge; in Mosaic by Mount Sinai; in Christian by the cross of Cal• vary. 3, That the Di,vine government was holy. That from the first the world has been governed in the interests of holiness is unmistakably the doctrine of Scripture. If any in Noah's time believed either that God was indifferent to righteousness, or that it was possible for "the throne of iniquity to have fellowship" with him, they must have been terribly undeceirnd when the crack of doom waa heard above their heads0 So will it be when the righteous Judge reveals himself a second time in flaming fire to render unto every man according to his deeds. Lessons •-1. "It is impossible for God to lie" (Heh. vi. 18). 2. "There is nothing to~ hard for the Lord" (Gen. xviii. 14). 3. "It is a fearful thing to fall ir:to the hands of the living God" (Heh. x. 31).

entries.title: GEN 7:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie bdiever's safet1J. Parable of the ten virgins speaks of a final separa• tion. •"The door was shut.' There our thoughts are turned to those without; here, to those within. The time was come when the choice must be made. " Come thou nnd 1111 thy house into the ark." The broad and narrow way. The confinement of the ark or the freedom of home; and, in view of the flood, the frail vessel or the mountains. Trust in Christ or trust in self (cf. Rom. x. 3). He chose the way of faith. God shut him in (cf. Isa. xxvi. 3). He knew he was eafe. The world saw no good in it. The pause of seven days (ver. 10) illustrates the present state. Believers rejoicing in their safety ; the world unconvinced of danger. I. CHRIST OFFERS SAFETY TO ALL. The ark was prepared that all might be saved. The condemnation was because they did not care (John iii. 19). There was room and welcome for nil who would come (cf. Luke xiv. 22). Noah did not preach impossible things. When Jericho was destroyed Ra.bah was saved. When Sodom, Lot. God bids all seek and find refuge in Christ (Rom. iii. 22). II. CHRIST IS A REFUGE FROM THE CONVICTION OF SIN. How many are livin~~ witho~t serious concern. Not rejecting the gospel; they hear it, and approve, a1io. think that all is well. Like St. Paul, 11 alive without the law." God's commanc• ments not understood ; his holiness not known. Let such a one be led to see how God's law reaches to the springs of life and feeling, and to feel the working of the law of sin" in his members ; then what a flood. " Who will show us any good ?" Good deeds cannot give pence. Worldly good as wormwood. Conscience repeat9, He bas been knocking, and I bav:e not opened (Prov. i. 26). Yet, hark I his voice again: "Come unto me." It is not too late. Even now, if thou wilt, the Lord will shut thee in. III. THE SAFETY OF THOSE WHO BELIEVE, whom God shuts in. Who shall lay anything to their charge? Who shall condemn ? Who shall separate ? (Rom. viii. 33-35). The flood is without. Noah is weak and helpless as the world. Hi8 safety is God's refuge. The Christian is surrounded by evil influences, messengers of Satan. Temptations to worldliness or to spiritual pride ; cares and anxieties hindering prayer; suggestions of unbelief, and hard thoughts of God ; the fainting of nature because so little progress made. But in Christ is safety. Coming to him daily as we are; with weak faith, with many perplexities, with the marks of many falls. His word is, "I will never leave thee nor forsake thee." In the trials of lib "we 11re more than conquerors through him that loved us."-M; 124 Tlil ·BOOR OF GENESIS. (en. vm. 1-14.

entries.title: GEN 8:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God. El-Ohim, i. e. God in 'bis most univerea.l relation to his creatures. The supposition of two different accounts or histories being intenning_led in the narrative of the Flood (Bleek, Eichhorn, Hupfcld, Kalisch, Alford, Colenso) is not required for a sufficient explanation of the varying use of the Dinne names. Remembered. From a root signifying to prick, pierce, or print, e. g., upon the memory; hence to remember. "Not that there is oblivion or forgetfulness with God, but then God is said to remember when he showeth by the effects that he hath taken ea.re of man" (Willet). He remembers man's sins when he punishes them (Ps. xxv. 7 ; cf. 1 Kings ::i::ni. 20), and his people's needs ..,-hen he supplies them (et: Neh. v. 19). The expression is an anthropopathism desi~ed to indicate the Dinne compassion as ,vcll as grace. Calvin thinks the remembrance of which Moses speaks " ought to be referred not only to the external aspect of things (i. e. the coming deliverance), but also to the inward feeling of the holy man," who, through grace, was privileged to enjoy " some sensible experience of the Divine presence" while immured in the ark. Noah, -d. the Divine remembrance of Abraham nnd Lot (eh. rix. 29), the request of the Hebrew psalmist (Ps. cxxxii. 1)-and every living thing,-chayyah, or wild beast (vide rh. i. 25; vii. 14)-and all the cattle that was with him in the ark. A touching indication of the tendemP-ss of God towards his creatures (et: Dent. xxv. 4; Ps. x:xxvi. 6; cxlv. 9, 15, 16; Jonah iv. 11). As a proof that God remembered the lonely inmates of the ark, he at once takes steps to accomplish their deliverance, which steps are next enumerated. And God made a wind - ruach.
