entries.title: GEN 8:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the waters returned from oft' the earth oontinua.lly. Literally, going and returning. "Moro and more" (Gese-. nius). The first verb expresses the continnance and self-increasing state of the action involved in the second ; cf. eh. xxvi 13 ; 1 Sam. vi. 12; 2 Kings ii. ll (Fii.rst). Grauually (Murphy, Ewald). The expression "denotes the turning-point after the waters had become calm" (T. Lewis). May it not be an attempt to represent the undulatory motion of the waves in an ebbing tide, in which the water seems first to advance, but only to retire with· greater vehemence, reversing the movement of a flowincr tide, in which it first retires and then ~vances-in the one case retu;ning to go in the other going to return1 The LXX.', as usual, indicates the visible effect rather than the actual phenomenon: rcai EVEOioov TO iiowp ,ropd,opEVOV a,ro Tij~ rii'"- And after the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters were abated. Literally, 1oere cut off, hence diminished ; imminutre sunt (V~lgate) ; ,iXaTTovoiiro To ii8wp (LXX. ). The first stage was the quieting of the waters ; the second was the commencement of an ebbing 01· backward motion ; the third was a perceptible diminution of the waters.

entries.title: GEN 8:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the ark rested. Not stopped sailing or floatin"', got bei:aJ~ed: and re; mained suspended over (Kitto s Cyclop., art. Ararat) but actually grollllded and settled on (Tayler Lewis) the place in-. dicated by ~l,I (cf. ver. 9; also Exod. x. 14; Numb. x. 36; xi. 25, 26; Isa. xi. 2). In the seventh month, 011 the seventeenth day. of the month. /. e. exactly 150 days from\ the commencement of the forty days' min, reckoning thirty days to n mouth, which seems to confirm the opinion expressed (eh. vii. 24) that the forty days were includetl in the 150. Supposing the Flood to have begun in Jlfarchesvan, the eecon~ 1;nonth of the civil year (about the begrnnrng of November), "we have then the 1·emorknb]o coincidences that on the 17th day of Ab1b ,11bout tho beginning of April) the ark rested on Mount Aro.rat, the Israelites passed over tho Red Sea, o.nd our Lord rose again from tho dead" (' Speaker's Commentary'). U;eon the mountains. I. e. one of the mounto.ms. "Pluralis numerus pro singulari ponitur" (cf. eh. xxi. 7; xlvi. 7; Judges xii. 7; vide Glass., 'Philo!. Sacr. Tract.,' i. cap. xiv. p. 866). Of Ararat. 1. It is agreed by 11ll tl1at the term Ararat describes a region. 2. This region has been supposed to bo the island of Ceylon (Samaritan), Aryavarta, the sacred land to the north of India (Von Bohlen, arguing from Gen. xi. 2); but "itisevident that these and·such liketheories have been framed in forgetfulness of what the Bible has recorded respecting the locality" (Kitto's 'Cyclopedia,' art. Ararat). 3. Tho locality which appears to have the countenance of Scripture is the region of Armenia (cf. 2 Kings xix. 37 ; Isa. xxxvii. 38 ; Jeremiah Ii. 27 ; Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, Vulgate). 4. In Armenia three different mountains have been selected as the site on which the ark grounded. (1) The modern Ararat, which rises in Northern Armenia, about twelve miles south ofEriva.n, in the form of two majestic cones, the one 16,254, and the other 12,284 feet (Parisian) in height above the level of the sea (Hieronymus, Fiirst, Kalisch, Keil, Delitzsch, and Lange). All bl!.t universal tradition has decided that the loftiest of these two peaks (called Macis in Armenian; Aghri-Dagh, i. e. the difficult or steep mountain, by the Turks; Kuchi Nuch, i. e. the mountain of Noah, by the Persians) was the spot where the sacred vessel first felt the solid land. 'fiavellers describe the appearance of this amazing elevation as of incomparable and over]Jowcring splendour. "It appeared as if the highest mountains in the world had been piled upon each other to form this one sublime immensity of earth and rocks and snow. The icy peaks of its double head rose majestically into the clear and cloudless heavens; the sun blazed bright upon them, and the reflection sent forth o. radiance eq,uel to other suns" (Ker Porter's 'Travels, i. 132; ii. 636). "Nothing co.n be more beautiful than its shape, more awful than its height. All the surrounding mountains sink into insignificance when compared to it. It is perfect in all its po.rts; no hard, rugged feature, no unn11tura1 prominences ; everything is in harmony, and all combines to render it one of the sublimest objects in nature" (Morier's 'Journey,' i. 16 ; ii. 312, 346). The ascent of the Kara Dagh, or Greater Ararat, which the Armonians believe to be gua.rded by angels from the profane foot of man, after two unsuccessful attempts, was nccomplished in 1829 by Professor Parrot, " G~npun1 nptl f\vo years lntQr1 in 1834, l>y the Russian traveller Automonolf. In 1856 five English travellers, Majors Stewart and Fra1.er, Rev, Walter Thursby, l\Iessrs. Theobald and Evans, performed the herculean task. The latest successful attempt was that of Prof. Bryce of Oxford in 1876 (vide 'Transca.ucasia and Ararat:' London: llfacmillan and Co., 1877). (2) An unknown mountain in Central Armenia between the Araxe, and lakes Van and Urumio.h (Vulgate, super mon,tes Armenire; Gesenius, Murphy,Wor<lsworth, Bush, 'Speaker's Commentary'). (3) A peak in the Gorclyiean mountains, or Carcluchian range, separating Armenia on the south from Kurdistan (Chalclee Paraphrase, Onkelos, Syriac, Calvin),nearwhich isa town called Naxuana., the city of Noah (Ptolemy), Idshenan (Moses Chorenensis), and Nachidshenan, the first place of clescent (the Arme• nians), which Josephus translates by ci,ro/3ar11p,ov, or the place of descent. Against the first is the inaccessibleheightofthemountain; in favour of the thircl is the proximity of the region to the starting-place of the ark.

entries.title: GEN 8:10–12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Hoping and waiting. I. The PATIE?.CE of Noah's hope. l. Patience a characteristic of all true hope (Rom. viii. 25). 2. Faith in the Divine covenant is the secret of hope's patience (Heh. xi, 1). 3. The patience of hope is al~ays proportioned to the brightness of faith's vision. II. The EAGERNESS of Noah's hope. 1. While waiting God's time he kept a steady outlook for the coming of the promise. 2. He employed different methods to discover its approach-the raven and the dove. 3. He sanctified the means he used Ly devotion. Ill. The nEWAilD of Noah's hope. In due time the dove retumed with an olive leaf, which was-1. .A timely answer. 2. An intelligible answer. 3. A joyous answer; ::md-4. A sufficient answer.

entries.title: GEN 8:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The returning ofthe waters, or the recall ofDivinejudgments. I. Goo's JUDGMENTS HAVE THEIi!. SPECIFIC PURPOSES. I. Separation-the elimination of _the righteous from the wicked. Under the present condition of the world there 1s n strange intermingling of the good and the evil. The tares and the wheat, the drawnet with good and bad fish (Matt. xiii.) are suggestive emblems of this mixed state of society. The grand object contemplated by Christianity is the elimination of the saintly element from that which is corrnpt. For this end it lays a special injunction on the former to withdraw themselves from the company and contagion of the latter (2 Cor. vi. 17; 2 Thess. iii. 6; 1 Tim.. vi. 5). Only it forbids_ men, unde~ cover of real or pretended zeal for righteousness, to attempt any forcible separation of the commingled elements (Matt. xiii. 30). Yet what the ha.nd of man cannot do the J1and of God can-winnow the chaff from the wheat. He did so by the Flood. Ha did so by the incarnation (Matt. iii. 12). He will do so at !he ~econd advent (M~tt. xiii. 30 ; xxv. 32). 2. Condemnation-the infliction of retribution on th_e finally impenitent. Undisguisedly was this the design of the fe11 cata.strophe which overtook "the world of the ungodly" in the time of Noah. It was sent for the specific purpose of punishing their evil deeds. And so have all ~ivine ju~gments of a like k~nd, what we misname accidents,-catastrophes, floods, fammes, pestilences, &c,,-aternble ou look of wrath and judicial retribution to t),em w~o forget to humbl? themselves beneath the mighty hand of God. So certamly will the last great JUdgment, of which Noah's flood was a prophetic symbol and warning, have 11s its specific purpose the coinplete clestructio11 of the fin.ill,)' impenitent (Rom. ij, 5; 2 1'hcsa. i. 7 i Heb, OH, VIII, 1-14.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS.. 129 x. 27 ; 2 Pet. iii. 7). 3. Preservation-the salvation of the faithful. This may bo Rnid to be the aim of nil those minor troubles and afflictions that befall God's people on the earth (Rom. viii. 28; 2 Cor. iv. 17). It is specially so when on a larger scale he interposes to inflict his judgments on the world (Isa. xxvi. 9). When he overthrows the wicked (whether nation or individual) suddenly as in a moment, it is with nn eye to the deliverance of his people. Examples-Pharaoh, Goliath, Haman, Herod, Belshazz11r. It was so with Noah. The destruction of the antediluvian sinners was necessary, if the remnant of the primitive Church was to be saved. Elo may it be said that the future overthrow of the wicked is indispensable, if the eternal hafpiness of the redeemed is to be secured. II. Goo a JUDGMENTB HAVE THEIR APPOINTED TIMES. 1. Their times of coming. The hour of the commencement of the Flood was both fixed and announced 120 years before the event. Though not revealed, as in the case of the Noachic Deluge, the date of every event is as truly predetermined (cf. Gen. xviii. 14; Exod. ix. 5; Job vii. 1 ; Eccles. iii. 1 ; Jer. viii. 7; Acts xvii. 26). And God's judgments always keep their set times of coming, as the Flood came in the ~redicted hour for its arrival. 2. Their times of continuance. The flood of waters lingered on the earth for a season, but not for ever. From the moment when the first rain-drop fell from the leaden sky, after the Lord had shut the patriarch with his family and living creatures into the ark, till it could be said the earth was dry, one year and ten days passed away. So have all God's judgments, at least here, their limits. Upon sinful men his wrath is not poured out without measure. 3. Their time-s of recall. In the future world we do not read that there will be any recall of the Divine judgments ; everlasting punishment (Matt. xxv. 46), fire that never shall be quenched (Mark ix. 43), everlasting destruction (2 These. i. 9) are some of the expressions employed to depict the fire-deluge of eternity. But here on earth God's judgments, being only for a set time, are subject to recall; and as they cannot anticipate the hou.., appointed for their coming, so neither can they linger beyond the moment assigned for their departure. Their recall too is, as in the case of Noah's flood-(1) .An act of grace (Gen. viii. 1). "God remembered Noah." '' It is of the Lord's mercies we are not consumed" (Lam. iii. 22; cf. 2 Kings xiii. 23; Mark i. 41). (2) An act of power (vers. 2, 3). As in order to roll back the tide of waters he sent forth a wind and stopped up the flood-gates of the deep and the windows of heaven, so is he able to lay his hand upon all the powers and forces of the material universe, and make them cease their working as easily as he set them in operation. III. Goo's JUDGMENTS HAVE THEIR APPROPRIATE SIGNS. 1. Signs oftheir approach, which are commonly-(!) Tlie growing wickedness of man, as in the days of Noah (eh. vi. 11, 12). When an individual or II nation is becoming mature in sin, then tqat individual or that nation is becoming ripe for judgment. So it was with Pharaoh, and afterwards with Israel, with Babylon, Nineveh, Greece, Rome. So will it be in the end of the world (cf. Rev. xiv. 15). (2) Prelusive chastisementsfrom God, again as in the days of Noah (eh. vii. 10). The Deluge began with a ro.in-shower, which gradually became more violent as the days passed, and withthe bursting forth of subterranean floods, which swelled the rivers, lakes, and oceans; all which must have been ominous indications that the long-threatened judgrnent was at last approaching. So the full outpouring of God's wrath is commonly heralded by anticipatory inflictions. 2. Signsoftheir departure, which are usually-(!) The accomplishment of their mission. Immediately it could be said, "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life died " (eh. vii. 22), it was added, "And God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged" (ver. 1). (2) The mitigation of their violence. The quieting of the waters (ver. 1) was the first symptom of the passing of the storm to Noah; and so, when God's retributive judgments are about to be withdrawn, their severity begins to relax. (3) The removal of their causes. The second sign to Noah was the cessation of the rain and the retirement of the floods (ver, 2). Sc-, ~h~n God's judgrnents are about to disappear, the agencies that brought them nre v1s1oly .recalled. (4) The ar-.-ival of little foretastes of deliverance. Such was the grou_ndmg of the ark to Noah and his imprisoned family (ver. 4). (5) The peruptible return of tl1e previo11s condition of uffairs. This was symbolised by the reappearance of the mountain-tops (,·er. 5), GENESIS. ,t 130 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cJt. VIII, 1-14, IV. Goo's JUDGMENTS IIAVE THEIR INTERESTED 0BSER'7ERS, Possibly the wicked are indifferent to the Divine judgments when they happen to be abroad upon the earth; but not so the righteous, to whom everything connected with them is of the utmost importance. Observers of God's judgments should be like Noah-I. Hopefulexpecting them to pass.' Had Noah not anticipated the complete removal of the waters, he had not made a sing·le experiment to discover how that removal wns progressing. Let the saints learn from Noah to cherish hope in God. 2. Pmyerful. There is good reason for believing that Noah sent forth the raven nnd the dove on the day of weekly rest, and after solemn relig-ious exercises (vide Expos.). The s~int's inquiries _into G_?d's judgments shoul_d always _be conducted in a spirit of devot10n. 3. lnteU'l{Jent-1. e. capable of readmg the signs of the times. When the do,e came home to Noah with the fresh-gathered olive leaf, 11 he knew that the waters were abated from off the earth" (ver. 11). So God ever vouchsafes to de,out souls, who seek them by faith, llppropriate and adequate signs of his movements, which it becomes them to study and interpret. 4. Patient-seeking neither to ??trun Go~•~ leading nor to anticipate God's directing, but, like Noah, calmly waiting the D1vme order to advance to the new sphere and the new duty which the passing of his judgments mayreveal. Noah waited fifty-seven days after the drying up of the waters before he left the nrk, and then he only did so o.t God's command; wherefore, "be ye not unwise" by being over-hasty, 11 but understanding what the will of the Lord is" (Ephes. v. 17). HOMILIES BY VARIOUS .AUTHORS. Ver. !.-God's infinite care. In the experience of Christians the joy of first belienng is often followed by a time of discouragement. Freshness of feeling seems to fade. The " law of sin" makes itself felt. Yet it is just the training by which firmer faith and fuller joy are to be reached. Deep must have been the thankfulness of those in the ark ; safe in the midst of the flood. But their faith was tried. Five months, and still no abatement.. Noah may well have had misgivings (cf. Matt. xi. 3). But God had not forgotten him (cf. Mark vi. 48; John x. 14). He remembered not Noah only, but every creature in the ark (cf. Luke xii. 6). He ,;aves to the uttermost (Heh. vii. 25). The time of trial wae a prelude to complete deliverance (cf. .Acts xiv. 22). I. THERE ARE TIMES WHEN BELIEVERS ARE TEMPTED TO FEEL FORGOTTEN. When troubles gather, end prayers seem unanswered, it is hard to keep faith firm. The warning Heh. xii. 6, 7 often needful Christiane would fain be led in smooth ways. .And when their course ie irksome and discouraging they sometimes see the wind boisterous, and begin to sink. Still more surely does the feeling follow sin. The disciple has forgotten to watch ; has trusted to his own strength; has ventured into temptation, and fallen. Then God is felt to be afar off (cf. Exod. xxxiii. 7). And there are times of discipline, when spiritual freedom seems denied, and the soul eannot cry .Abba, and prayer seems choked (of. Isa. xlix. 14). ~erhaps it is to teach lrnruility; perhaps to show some root of evil; perhaps to excite more hunger for communion with God. II. BuT Gon DOES NOT FORGET. .A creature's love may fail (Isa. xlix. 15), a creature's watchfulness may faint, but not God's, He made us; can he forget our wants? His purpose is our salvation; will he neglect any step? He gave hie own Son for us; is anything else too great for his goodness? Not even thy coldness and unbelief can make hirn cease to care. III. Goo's CARE EXTENDS TO THE LEAST. Our Lord welcomed (1) those of small account (Matt. xxi. 16; Mark x. 49; Luke xviii. 16), and (2) the undeserving (Luke vii. 39; xv. 10; xix. 7). He cares also for small matters (cf. Luke xii, 28-30). What treasures of wisdom and love surround us on every aide I These are r.ot beneath his care. Will he not fulfil? (Rom. viii. 28). IV. FREEDOM THROUGH THE WORK OF THE HOLY SPIRl'l'. God's time not always what we should choose (cf. John vii. 6). Noah a prisoner of hope. God showed that the hope was well founded, The agent of deliverance II a wind "-the same word, both in Hebrew and in the LXX., as is used in Gen. i, 2 for the Spirit of God OH, VIII, 1-14.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 131 DoubUess the agent in drying up the water was a wind. But in the spiritual lesson we nre reminded of the Holy Spirit. His work at first brought life on the earth ; and his work prepared for repeopling it, and completed the work of Noah's deliverance. And his work gives us freedom, showing us the work of Christ, and our position as children of God.-M.

entries.title: GEN 8:1–5
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Grace and providence. The powers of material nature are obedient servants of God, and those who are the objects of his regard, remembered by him, are snfely kept in the midst of the world's changes. "All things work together for their good." There is an inner circle of special providence in which the family of God, with those whose existence is bound up in it, is under the eye of the heavenly Father, and in the hollow of his hand. "And the ark rested" (ver. 4). We speak of the cradle of the human race being set on Mount Ararat ; is it not well to remember-1. The new world came out of an ark of Divine grace. Religion is the real foundation of society. 2. The waves of the flood bore the ark to its restingplace. So the waters of affliction, though they heave ~ur vessel an~ trouble our hearts with fear, carry us onward to a new and often h1~her standpoint of knowledge and faith. 3. _While the_ flood bore the ark, God himself chose out t~e spot where it should end its awful Journey. The Ararat of the new world was like the paradise of th_e ~rat man-t'!ie nursery of a rising humanity ; .b1;1t whereas i:n the_ st~te of innocence 1t 1s a g·arden, m the case of the redeemed man 1t 1s a mountain, with its steep, rough places, its heights _and ?-ep~hs, its trials and dangers. T~e humanity which started from Ararat earned with 1t at once the good and the evil of the old world which had passed away, and the mountain symbolised the complex treasury of possibilities, ming·led with liabilities, which were laid up in the rescued race.-R.

entries.title: GEN 8:6–12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The dispensations o/rigliteo1tsness and love. The raven and the dove. \Vhile this passage has its natural, historical fitness, we ce.nnot overlook its symbolical significance. It seems to setforth the two administrations of God, both of them going f.1rth from the same centre of his righteousness in which his people are kept safe. The one represented by the carrion bird, the rave,n, is THE ADMINISTRATION OF JUDG· MF.NT, which goes forth to and fro until the wnters are dried up from off the earth- Ending n resting-place in the waters of destruction, though not a permanent rest; returning to the ark, as the beginning and the end of judgment is the righteousness of God. The dove is the emblem of DIVINE GRACE, spiritual life and peace. It ca(i. not find rest in the waters of judgment until another seven days, another perioJ of gracious manifestation, has prepared the world for it ; then it brinKS with it the olucked-off olive leaf, emblem of retiring judgment and revealea mercy; and when yet another period of gracious manifestation has passed by, the dove shall return no more to the ark, for the ark itself is no more needed-the waters are abated from off the face of the earth. So we may say the rnven dispensation was thnt which preceded Noah. Then followed the first sending forth of the dove unto the time of Moses, leading to a seven d!lys' period of the ark life, waiting for another mission of grace. The dove brought back the olive leaf when the prophetic period of the old dispensation gave fuller promise of Divine mercy. But yet another period of seven days must transpire before the dove is sent forth and returns no more to the ark, but abides in the earth. After the two sacred intervals, the period of the law and the period of the prophets, which were both immediately connected with a. special limited covenant such as is represented in the ark, there followed the world-wide missio~ of the Comforter. The waters were abated. The " Graceand Truth" took posseasion of man's world, cursed by sin, redeemed by grace.-R.

entries.title: GEN 8:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Noah builded an altar. Mizbeach, a place for slaying sacrifices, from zabach, to slaughter animo.ls (eh. x:xxi. 54), to slay in sacrifice (Levit. ix. 4; I Sam. i. 4), as f!ur11ac1Tr,pt0v, from f!{mv, is the first altar mentioned in lustory. The English term (from altus, high) signifies a high place, because the altar was commonly a raised structure or mound of earth or stones (Exod. xx. 24). Keil thinks that altars were not required prior to the Flood, the Divine presence being still visibly among men at the gate of Eden, " so that they could turn their offerings and their hearts towards that abode." Poole, Clarke, Bush, and Inglis hold that the antedilu,ian sacrifices presupposed an altar. Unto the Lord. Jehovah, the God of salvation. And took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl Vide eh. vii. 2. " Seldom has there been a more liberal offering in proportion to the meanR of tbe giver. His whole stock of clean animals, wherewith to fill the world, was seven pairs of each" (Inglis). And offered. By Divine appointment, since his service was accepted ; and "all religious services which arc not perfumed with the odour of faith are of an ill savour before God" (Calvin); but "God is peculiarly well pleased with froo-will offerings, and eurely if ever an occa1;ion existed for the exe1 cise of grateful and adoring sentiments, tho prosent W1II one" (Bush). :Burnt offering•. entries.title: GEN 8:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: And the Lord (Jehovah) smelled --is is done by drawing the nir in and out through the nostrils ; from the root ruach, to broothe ; hi~h., to smell-a sweet savour, Reach hannichoach, litero.lly, an odour ofsatisfaction, acquiescence, or rest; from nuach to rest, with nn allusion to Noah's nam~ (vi.de eh. v. 29) ; lu1µ:qv ,i,woiac (LXX.) ; (cf. Levit. ii. 12; x:xvi. 31 ; Num. xv. 3 ; Ezek. vi. 13). The meaning is that the sacrifice of the pntrinl'Ch was o.s acceptable to God as refreshing odours are to the senses of a man; and that which rendered it acceptable was (1) the feeling from which it sprang, whether gratitude or obedience ; (2) tho truths which it expressed-it was tantamount to an acknowledgment of personal guilt, a devout recognition of the Divine mercy, an explicit declaration that he had been saved or could only be saved throug:h the offering up of the life of another, and a cheerful consecration of his redeemed life to God ; (3) the great sacrifice of which it was a type. Pau1, by using the language of the LXX. (Ephes. v. 2), shows that he regarded the two as connected. And the Lord said in his heart. I. e. resolved within himself. It is not certain that this determination on the part of Jehovah was at this time communicated to the patriarch (cf. eh. vi. 3, 7 for Divine inward resolves which were not at the moment made known), unless the correct reading be to his (Noah's) heart, meaning the Lord comforted him (cf. Judges xi.x. 3 ; Ruth ii. 13 ; Isa. xl. 2 ; Hosea ii. 14), which is barely probable. I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake. Literally, I will not add to curse. Not a revocation of the curse of Gen. iii. 17, nor a pledge that such curse woulu not be duplicated. The language refers solely to the visitation of the Deluge, and promises not that God may not sometimes visit particular localities with n flood, but that another such world-wide catastrophe should never overtake the human race. For the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth. Oh. vi. 5 assigns this as the reason for man's destrnction ; a proof ofinconsistency between tho Elohistic author and his Jehovistic euitor (Bleek). ff Hie inconstantiai videtur Deus accusari posse" (Luther). ff God seems to contradict him-' self by having previously declared that the world must be destroyed because its iniquity was desperate" (Calvin). Lowis). Others connect it with "for mnn'a sake," as explanatory not of the promise, but of the past judgment (Murphy), or as stating that any future cursing of the ground would not be for man's sake (Jacobus). 'rhe truo solution of the difficulty oppears to lie in the clause "from his youth," as if God meant to say that whereas formerly he had visited man withjudicial extermination on account of his absolute moral corruption, he would now have regard to the circumstance that man inherited his depravity through his birth, and, instead of smiting man with punitive destruction, would visit him with compassiono.te forbearance (Keil, 'Speaker's Commentary'). Tayler Lewis regards the expression as strongly anthropopathic, like eh. vi. 6, and indicative of the Divine regret at so calamitous an act as the Deluge, although that act was o.bsolutely just and necessary. Neither will I again smite any more every Eving thing, as I have done. There should be no more deluge, but-

entries.title: GEN 8:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - While the earth remaineth. Literally, as yet, all the days of the earth, i. e. henceforth, so long as the earth continues, iii expressing tho ideas of repetition and continuance (vide ver. 12). Seed-time and harvest,-from rootssignifyingto scatter, e. g. seed, and to cut off, specio.lly grain; ,11ripµ,a 1eai 9,p,uµ,iic (LXX.)-and cold and heat,-,J,uxo,a:ai KaiJµ,a (LXX.)-andsummer and winter. Properly the cutting off of fruits, from a root meaning to cut off, hence summer ; and the time when fruits are plucked, hence autumn (including winter) ; the import of the 1·oot being to gather, to pluck off; fllpo, 11:ai fop (LXX.). The first term of ench pair denotes the first half of the year, and the second term of each pair the second half. And day and night (cf. eh. i. 5) shall not cease. Hebrew, lo yishbothu, shall not snbbatise, or keep a day of rest ; i. e. they shnll continue ever in operation nnd succession. This Divino promise to conserve the orderly constitution and course of nature is elsewhere styled "God's covenant of the do.y and of the night" (cf. Jer. xxxiii. 20, 26). TRADITIONS OF THE DELUGE. 1. The Babylonian. (1) From the Chaldeo.n monuments. As deciphered from the eleventh tablet of the Izdubnr series, the story of the Flood is briefly this :-Izdubar, whom George Smith identifies with Nimrod, the founder of Babylonia, is informed by Hasisadra, whom tho same authority believes to represent Noah, of a Div'J1e commandment which he had received to construct a ship after a. specified pattern, in which to save himself aml "the need of all life," because the city Surippak wherein he dwelt was to be destroyed. After first atterr.pting to excuse himaelf, as he explaius to Izdnbar, on the ground that "young and old will deride him," Hasisadra builds the ship, and causes to go up into it "all my male servanta and my female servants, the beast of the fieltl, the animal of the field, the sons of the people, all of them," while the gocl Shamas makes a flood, causing it to rain heavily. The flood destroys all life from the face of the ea1th. Six days and nights the storm rages; on the seventh it grows calm. Twelve measures above the sea rises the land. The ship is stopped by a. mountain in the country of Nizir. After seven days Hasirndra sends forth a dove, "which went and turned, an,l a resting-place it did not find, mcl it returnecl ; " then a swallow, and finally a raven. On the decrease of the waters he sends forth the animals, and builds an altar on the peak of the mountain, aml pours out a libation (' Chaldean Genesis,' eh. xvi. ; 'Records of the Past,' vol. vii. 133-141). (2) From Berosus. The god Kronos appeared to Xisuthrus, the tenth king of Babylon, in 11 vision, and warned him of an approaching deluge upon the fifteenth day of the month Dcsius, by which mankintl wouhl be clestroyed. Among other things the god instructed him to build a vessel for tho preservation of himself antl friends, and specimens of the different animals. Obeying the Divina admonition, ho built a vessel five stodia in length and two in breatlth, and conveyed into it his wife, children, and frientls. After the flood had been upon the earth he three times sent out binls from the vessel, which returned to him the secon,l time with mud upon their feet, and the third time returned to him no more. Finding that the vessel had grountled on o. mountniu, Xisuthrns disembarked with his wife o.nd children, antl, having constructccl au l\ltur, offered sacrifices to the gods, in rew11rtl for which ho was raised immediately to heaven (' Chaltle,1n Genesis,' eh. iii. ; Kalisch, p. 202 ; 'Encycloped:a llritannica,' nrt. Deluge, ninih edition). 2. The Et]yptian. Though commonly 184 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, VIII, 15-22. alleged to be entirely unknown in the Nile vn1ley, it is certain that the germs of the Deluge story are to be discovered even there. According to the Egyptian historian lllanetl,o, quoted by Eusebius, Thoth, the first Hermes, erected certain pillars with inscriptions, which,qftm·theDelugt,weretranscribed into book-s. Plato also st.ntes in the Timreus (chap. v.) that a certain Egyptian priest informed Solon that the gods, when wishing to pnrifr the earth, were accustomed to overwhelm it hy a deluge, from ~hich the herdsmen and shepherds saved themselves on the fops of the mountains. Josephus(' Ant.,' I. iii. 9) certifiesthat Hieronymus the Egyptian refers to the Flood. A conception altogether :mnlogous to that of Genesis is likewise to be found in a myth belonging to the archaic period of Seti I., which represents Ra, the Creator, as being disgusted with the insolence of mankind, and resolving to exterminate them (vide Inscription of the Destruction of 1\[ankind, ' Records of the Past,' vol. vi. p. 103). In short, the Egyptians believed not that there was no deluge, bnt that there had been several The absence ofany indications of this belief in the recovered literature of ancied Egypt is not sufficient to set aside the above concnrrent testimonies to its existence (Kitto, 'Bible Illustrations,' vol. i. p. 150; Rawlinson's 'Historical Illustrations of 0. T. ;' 'EncycL Britan.,' art. Deluge, ninth edition). 3. The Indian. Through the theft of the sacred Vedas by the giant Hayagrivah, the hnm.an race became fearlally degenerate, with the ei.:ce1)tion of sev,m saints and the good King Satyavrata, to whom the Divine spirit Vishnu appeared in the form of a fish, informing him of bis purpose to destroy the earth by a flood, and at the same time to send a ship miraculously constructed for the preservation of himself :md the seven holy ones, along with their wives, and one pair of each of all the irrational animals. After 6<:ven days the rain descended, when Satyavrata; confiding in the promises of the god, saw a huge ship drawing near, into which he eutercd ns directed. Then the god appeared in the form of n fish a million miles long, with an immense born, to which the king :made the ship fast, and, drawing it for many years (a night of Brahma), at length landed it upon the highest peak of Mou11t Himavau. When the flood abated the god arose, struckthedemonHnya,grivah,recovered tho sacred books, instructed S11tyavrato. in a.11 heavenly sciences, and appointecl him the seventh Ma.nu, from whom tho second population of the earth descended in a supernatural manner, whence man is style(! :Mnnudsha (born of Manu). Vide Knli~ch, p. 203 ; .Auberlen's 'Divino Revelation,' p. 169 (Clark's ' For. 'l.'hcol. Lib.'). 4. The Gi·ecian. It is sufficiont here to refer to the well-known story of Deuce.lion and Pyrrha, first given in Pindar, and afterwards related by Apollodorus, Plutarch, Lucian, a.nd Ovid, whose account bears so close a resemblnnce to the Biblical narrative o.s to suggest the probability of access to Hebrew or Syrian sources of information. The previous corruption of manners and morals, the eminent piety of Deucalion, the determination "genus mortale sub undis perd.e:re," the constructionof a boatbyDivine direction, the bursting of the storm, the rising' of the waters, the uni Ve!sal ocean in which "jamque mare et tellus nullum discri.men habebant,'' the subsidence of the flood, the landing of the boat on Pnmassus with its double peak, the consultation of the Deity " per sacras sortes," and the answer of the god as to how the earth was to be repeopled " ossaque post tergum magnre jac; tate parentis,'' aredetailed with such ,graphic power as makes them read "like a~plified reports of the record in Genesis." Indeed, by Philo, De11calion was distinctly regarded as Noah. Cf. Ovid, ' Metamorph.,' lib. i. f. vii. ; 'Kalisch on Genesis,' p. 203 ; Kitto's 'Bible Illustrations,' p. 150 (Porter's edition); 'Lange on Genesis,' p. 294, note by Tayler Lewis ; Smith's 'Dictionary of the Bible,' art. Noah. 5. The American. Traditions ofthe Flood appear to be even more numcrou& in the New World than the Old. The Esquimaux in the North, the Red Indians, the Mexicans and the Brazilians in tho ccntral parts of America, and the Peruvians in tho South have all their peculiar versions of the Deluge story. Cha.sewee, the ancestor of the Dogrib Indians, on the Ma.ekensio river, according to Franklin, escaped in a canoe from a flood which overflowed the earth, taking with him all manner of four-footecl bea.sts and birds. '!'he Asteca, the Mixtr,ee, tbo OU. VIII. 16-22.] 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. 135 Z11potees, and other nations inhabiting Mexico nJI hnve, according to Humboldt, their Nonhs, Xisuthrns, or Manus (called Coxcox, 'feocipnctli, orTezpi), who eaveshimself by II raft, or in II ship, which lands upon the.summit of Colhuacnn, the Ararat of the Mexico.ns. The legends of the Tamanacks relate that a man and woman saved themselves from the Deluge, and repeopled the earth by casting behind them the fruits of th.e llfauritia palm tree (Kalisch, p. 205 ; Anberlen's ' Divine Revelation,' p. 171 ; Smith's 'Dictionary,' art. Noah). What, then, is the conclusion to be drawn from this universal diffusion of the Deluge story i The theory of Schirren and Gerland, as stated by tho writer of the article Deluge in the 'Encyclopedia Britannica,' is that the Deluge stories were originally ether-myths, descriptive of the phenomena of the sky, which havebeen transferred from the celestial regions to the earth; but, as Kalisch justly observes, "the harmony between all these accounts isan undeniableguarantee that the tradition is no idle invention;" or, as is forcibly stated by Rawlinson, of a tradition existing among all the great races into which ethnologistshave dividedmankind,-the Shemites, the Ha.mites, the Aryans, the Turanians,- " but one rational account can be given, viz., that it embodies the recollection of a fact in which all mankind was concerned." IIOMILETICS.

entries.title: GEN 8:15–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Th.e saint and the Saviour. I. THE SAVIOUR'S INJUNCTION TO THE SAINT (ver. 15). The command which God addressed to Noah and the other inmates of the ark to go forth and take possession of the renovated earth may be regarded as emblematic of that·Divine instruction which shall yet be given to the saints to go forth and take possession of the new heavens and the new earth, when the great gospel ship of the Christian Church, now floating on the troubled sea of life, shall have landed with its living freight upon the coasts of bliss. The Divine command to Noah was an order to pass-1. From a situation of comparative peril to a positiO'I!, of perfect safety. Though, certainly, before the bursting of the storm the only available ahefter was that afforded by the ark, "all flesh and all in whose nostrils was the breath of life " that remained without having perished, yet even in8ide tbo ark must have seemed.to the inexperienced voyagers to be at the best of only doubtful security. But now whatever danger had been connected with their twelve months' drifting across a trackless sea was at an end. And so, though only within the shelter of the Christian Church can safety be enjoyed, yet atthe beet it is not entirely free from peril. What with temptations and afflictions, 11 fears within and foes without," there always is a risk of making shipwreck of the soul (1 Tim. i. 19); butwhen life's voyage has been finished, and the new heavens and the new earth have been revealed, the salvation of the saints will be complete. 2. From a period ofpatienthoping to a season ofdelightful enjoving. It is doubtful if we always sufficiently realise the greatness :of the strain to which the faith of the patriarch was subjected when be was shut up within the ark and left there for o.ver a twelvemonth without any direct communication from God, with nothing for his faith to rest upon but the simple promise that he and his should be saved. Af the best it was only little foretastes or eamests of God's complete salvation which he enjoyed : first in being sheltered from the storm ; next in being floated above the waters ; then in touching land upon Ararat ; and again in getting signs of the approaching deliverance. Throughout the entire period he could only live in hope and pati~ntly endure. But here at length was the time of foll fruition come. Go forth from the ark. And so it is with Christ's saints nniversnlly. Here are only earnests of tho inheritance (Ephes. i. 14); there alone is the inheritance itself (Col. i. 12). Now is the time for hoping and waiting (Rom. viii. 25); then is the season for seeing and enjoying (1 John iii. 2). Here the saints rest upon the promise as their guarantee (2 Tim. i. 1; Heb. iv. 1) ; there the so.ints behold and experience its renlisation (Heh. vi. 12). 3. From a condition of restrained activit'IJ to a spltere ofhighe1· andfreer service. Not thatNotih's life within the ark could ln any s•)nse have been one of idleness, and neither are the lives oc Christians en the earth md in the Church belo,v; but Noah entered on another o.nd B nobler kind of work when he left the nrk thlln tl1at which bud engaged his powers within its precincts, nnd so do they who nrc counted worthy of attaining ta Christ's THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CR, VIII, 16-22. 1dngdom nnd g-lory. Here, like Noah's, the saint's powers ofservice are limited nnd confined ; there they shall attain to greater freedom and fuller scope (1 Cor. xiii. 9 --12; Rev. iY. 8). II. THE SAINT'S RESPONSE TO THE SAVIOUR (ver. 18). The command to leave the nrk which G?d addre_sscd to Noah wa~ obeyed-1. lininediately. We can imng-ine that everything was in n state of readiness for departure when the mnrching orders came, so thnt there was no need to interpose delay. So was it with tho Hebrews when the Lord led them forth from Egypt (Exod. xii. 11); so should Christians be always ready for their Master's summons, whether to pass from affliction (Isa. Iii, 11) or into it (eh. xxii. 1; Acts xxi. 13), to enter upon a new 8phere of work (Isa. vi. 8) or re_tire _from an old ~me into silence (1 Kings xvi\, 3) ; to go down into the grave (2 Tim. ff. 6) and wait for the apocalypse of the samts (Job xiv. 14) or to go up into glory and partake of the inheritance of the saints in light (Matt. ~iv. 44). 2. Universally. Not the patriarch alone, but all his family and all the creatures came forth; so did all God's people come forth from the house of bondage (Exod. x. 26); and so will nil Christ's redeemed ones who have entered into the salvation ark of ~is Church emerge at last into tI1e light and felicity of he~ven (Isa. Ii. 11 ; Luke xn. 32; 1 Cor. xv. 22; 1 Thess. 1v. 14). 3. Joyfully. This we may infer. After the twelve months' isolation, and confinement, and comparatfre peril we need not doubt that Noah and his family exulted with delight, and that even the lower creatures were not strangers to agreeable sensations. It was a picture of the happiness which even here the saints enjoy in the Divine interpositions on their behalf • but especially of the universal thrill of gladness which God's redeemed family, and even "the creature itself," shall experience in the J>alingenesia of the heavens and the earth (Isa. mv. 10; Rom. viii. 19-23). 4. Finally. They were never more to return to the ark, because never again should there be a flood. Itwas a delightful symbol of the completeness and finality of God's salvation when the saints shall have been landed on the heights of bliss (Rev. x.xi. 4 ; xx:.ii. 3-5). III. THE SAUIT'S WORSHIP OF THE SAVIOUR (ver. 20), As Noah's first act on stepping forth from the ark was to build an altar unto the Lord, so the saint's first work on reaching heaven will be to worship; and this worship will be-1. Believing. This was implied in the very thought of offering up a sacrifice to Jehovah, but specially so in the circurustances in which the patriarch was then placed. The visible symbol of the Di,•ine presence had retired to its original dwelling-place in the heavens, and yet Noah had as little doubt as ever he had that there was a God to worship. The building of an altar, therefore, just then and there was an explicit declaration of his faith. Without faith there can be no worship of God either here or there, on earth or in heaven (Heh. xi. 6). 2. Thanliful. The offering of Noah was designed as an expression of his gratitude for the Lord's mercy, and so should the worship of the saints on earth be characterised by the same spirit (Phil. iv. 6), as we know the adorations of the saints before the throne are (Rev. vii. 12). 3. GenerOUJJ. Noah took of every clean beastand every clean fowl, i. e. one of seven or one of fourteen (vide Expos.), in either case a munificent tribute to the God of his salvation. How seldom is the like liberality exhibited by Christ's worshippers on earth I What a blessed thought it is that among the saints above there will be no temptation to such meanneRB as is often practised by the saints below I 4. Sincere. It was no merely formal service that the patriarch presented. The burnt offering was e. symbolic declaration of his self-consecration-body, soul, and spirit--to the God who had redeemed him. Of this sort is the service which Christ expects and believers should render on the earth (Matt. xvi. 24; Luke xiv. 26; Rom. xii. 1 ; 1 Cor. vi. 20). Of such kind will be the worship of the saints in heaven (Rev. x:x:ii. 3). IV. THE SAVIOUR'S BESPONSE TO THE SAINT (vers. 21, 22). As the sacrifice of Noah was well-pleasing unto God, so will the y;orship of the s~ints fi_nd acceptance_in his sight. And this accep_tance of the sacnfices of the glonfied, hke the reception of Noah's offering-I. Will consist in the cherishing, by God of a feeling of sweet complacency towards the worshippers. As from the burning victims upon Noah's altar there came up into the Divine nostrils a 6avour of rest, so from the spiritual aacri.ficee of Christians even here there ascends an odour of e. sweet smell unto God (Phil. iv. 18), while in the npper fanctuary the services of the redeemed go up con• THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 137 tinunlly before Goel like tho smoke of incense (Rev. viii. 4). 2. !Vilt be bcued upon the odour of the sacrifice of Christ, of which Noah's w1s the type. It was not the actual service of Noah, considerecl as an opus operatum, that producecl the feeling of complacency in Goel (Micah vi. 7), but the sacrificial work of Christ, to which the fnith of the patriarch had an outlook (Ephes. v. 2). For the sake of that offering up of himself once for nil in the encl of the world that was to be accomplished by the woman's seed, nncl which Noah's faith truly, however dimly, embraced, God accepted him and hie. That same offering is the ground or basis on which all the saints' sacrifices are accepted either on earth (1 Pet. ii. 5) or in heaven (Rev. v. 6). 3. Will express itself through the perpetuation of the worshipper's safety. (1) By averting all evil. "There shall be no more curse" (Rev. xxii. 3), as God determined in his heart (ver. 21), and afterwards expressed to Noah (eh. ix. 15), never more to curse the ground or flood the earth. (2) By securing all good, which was symbolised by the confirmation of the covenant of day and night. Lessons :-1. Live in a state of readiness for the glorious appearing of the Son of man (Titus i. 13). 2. Expectantly wait for thi: manifes~atio_n of the sons of God (Rom. viii. 19). 3. Learn the nature of the samt'e sernce m the heavenly world (Rev. v. 8). 4. Note the security for the perpet1Iity of heaven's blessedness- Christ's sacrifice and God's covenant.

entries.title: GEN 8:13–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Rest and restoration. Noah (Rest) comes forth from the ark in the sahbath century of his life, the six hundred and first year. He liven after the Flood 350 years, the half week of centuries; his life represented a rest, but not tlie rest, a half sabbath, promise of the rest which remains to the people of God. I. AN EXAMPLE OF FAITH. 1. Not until God spake did Noah dare to do more tl,an lift off the covering and look. 2. At the heavenly word the family, redeemed by grace, takes possession of the redeemed habitation. II. THE REDEEMED LIFE IN ITS NEW APPOINT?.IENT. Go forth of the ark into the new world. 'l'here is the keynote of the Bible. Man redeemed is man Iiving by every word of God. 1. By Divine commandment going into the prepared refuge. 2. By Divine commandment taking down old bounds and occupying new places. 3. Goingforth into a promised land rejoicing in a pledgedfuture. 4. Carrying with him all lower creatures into a new, progressive, God-blessed inheritance. The whole creation groaning and travailing, the whole creation participating in the Divine deliverance.-R.

entries.title: GEN 8:20–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The sanctification of the earth. The sweet savour of man·s burnt offerings-(!) not the offerings of caprice, but the fulfilment of Divine commands, (2) the reciprocation of Heaven's communications-(3) ascends from the earth-built altar and fills the Lord with satisfaction. In return for that obedience and devotion the curse is removed, the earth -is sealed with the saving strength of God in a covenant of peace. I. RELIOIOUS LIFE IS ACCEPTABLE TO Goo when it i~ (1) grateful acknowledg·- ment of his mercy; (2) humble obedience to his own revealed will; (3) consecration of place, time, life, possessions to him. II. UNION and COMMUNION between God and man is the foundation on which all earthly happiness and security rest. Ill. The FORBEARANCE AND MERCY OF Goo in his relation to those whose hearts are yet full of evil is at once probation aud grace. The ground is not cursed any more fur man's sake, but, the more evidently, that which falls upon the ground may fall upon man himself. The higher revelations of God in the post-Noachic period were·certainly larger bestowments of grace, but o.t the same time they involved a larger respon3ibility. So the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews reasons as to the punishment of those who trample underfoot the covenant of the gospel. The progressirn covenants which make up the history of God's grace recorded in the Scriptures am progres11ive separations of the evil and the good, therefore they point to th,it complete and final separation in which God's righteousness shall be eternally glorified.-R. 188 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. entries.content: -But-1~, an adverb oflimitation or exception, ·as in Lcvit. xi. 4, introducing a restriction on the foregoing precept-flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof. Literally, with its soul, its blood; the blood being regarded as the seat of the soul, or life principle (Levit. xvii. 11), and even as the soul itself (Levit. xvii. 14). The idea of the nnity of the soul and the blood, on which the prohibition of blood is based, comes to light everywhere in Scripture. In the blood of one mortally wounded his son\ flows forth (Lam. ii. 12), and he who voluntarily sacrifices himself p0nrs out his soul unto death (Isa. liii. 12). The murderer of the innocent slays the soul of the blood of the innocent (,J,ux,jv a'iµa-co~ a0wou, Deut. xxvii. 25), which also cleaves to his (the murderer's) skirts (Jer. ii 34 ; cf. Nor can it bo said to be e:s:clusively peculiar to Holy Scripture. In ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics the hawk, which feeds on bloods, represents the soul. Virgil says of o. dying person, "purpnream vomit ille animam" (' .&neid,' ix. 3'19). The Greek philosophers taught that the blood was either the soul (Critins), or the soul's food (Pythagoras), or the soul's sent (Empedocles), or the soul's producing cause (the Stoics) ; bnt only Scripture reveals the true relation between them both when it cleclarcs the blood to be. not the soul absolutely, but the means of its self-attestation (vide Delitzsch's 'Bib. Psychology,' div. iv. sec. xi. ). Shall ye not eat. Not referring to, although certainly forbidding, the eating of flesh taken from a living animal (Raschi, Cajetan, Delitzsch, Luther, Poole, Jamieson)-a fiendish custom which may havo been p1uctised among the antedi!uviaus, ns, according to tru,cllers, it is, or was, among modem Abyssiniuns; rather interdicting the flesh of slaughtered 140 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. Literally, he shedding, i. e. wilfully and unwarmntably; nnd not simply accidentally, for which kind of mnnslaughter the law afterwards provided (vide Num. xxxv. 11) ; orjudwially, for thnt is commanded by the presentstatute. Man's blood. Literally, blood of the man, humo.n blood. By man. Not openly and directly by God, but by man himself, acting of course as Gotl's instrument and ai;ent-an instruction which involved the settmg up of the magisterial office, by whom the sword might be borne (" Hie igitur fons est, ex quo manat totum jus civilo etjus gentium." -Luther. Cf. Nurn. xxxv. 29-31; Rom. xiii. 4), and equally laid a basis for the law of the goel subsequently established in Isrnel (Deut. xix. 6 ; Josh. xx. 3). The Chaldeo paraphrases, "with witnesses by sentence of the judges." The LXX. substit•1tes for "by man" civri rou a'iµarot;: abroii-an interpretation followed by Professor Lewis, who quotes Jona hen Gannach in its support. Shall. Not merely a permission legnlising, but an imperative command enjoining, capital punishment, the reason for which follows. For in the image of God made he man. To apply this to the magistracy (Bush, Murphy, Keil), who are sometimes in Scriptnre styled Elobim (Ps. lxxxii. 6), and the ministers of God (Rom. xiii. 4), and who may be said to have been made in the Divine image in the sense of being endowed with the capacity of ruling and judging, seems forced and unnatural ; the clause obviously assigns the original dignity of man (ef. eh. i. 28) as the reason ,vhy the murderer cannot be suffered to escape (Calvin, Poole, Alford, 'Speaker's Commentary,' Candlish, Lange)

entries.title: GEN 9:7

entries.title: GEN 9:1–7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -New arrangements for a new era. I. PROVISION FOR THE INC,P,EASI!! OF 'l'HE HUMAN FAMILY. 1. The proximate instrumentality - the ordinance of marriage (vers. 1, 7), which was - (1) .A. Divine institution appointed by God in Eden (cf. eh. ii. 22, and Matt. xix. 5). (2) A sacred institution. Every ordinance of God's appointment, it may be said, is in a manner holy ; but a special sanctity attaches to that of marriage. God attested the estimation in which be held it by visiting the world's corruption, which had principally come through its desecration, with the waters of a flood. (3) A permanent institution, being the same in its nature, uses, and ends that it had been from the beginning, only modified to suit the changing circumstances of man's condition. Prior to the fall it was exempt from any of those imperfections which in human experience have clung to it ever since. Subsequent to the melancholy entrance of sin, there was superadded to the lot of woman an element of pain and sorrow from which she had been previously free; and though anterior to the Flood it had been grossly abused by man's licentiousness, after it, we cannot doubt, it was restored in all its original purity, though still with the curse of sorrow unremoved. 2. The originating cause-the Divine blessing (vers. 1, 7), without which-(1) The marriage bed would not be fruitful (Ps. cxxvii. 3). Cf. the casP. of Rachel (eh. x.x.x. 2), of Hannah (1 Sam. i. 11), of Ruth (Ruth iv. 13), (2) The married life woitld not be holy. What marriage is and leads to when dissociated from the fear of God had already been significantly displayed upon the theatre of the antediluvian world, and is abundantly declared in Scripture, iloth by precept (eh. xxiv. 3; x.xviii. 1; Exod. xxxiv. 16; Deut. vii. 3, 4; Josh. xxiii. 12, 13; 2 Cor. vi. 14) and example; e. g., the Israelites (Judges iii. 6, 7), Samson (Judg·es xiv. 1-16), Solomon (1 Kings iii. 1), Jews (Ezra ix. 1-12). (3) The marriage tie would not be sure. As ungodliness tends to violate the marriage law by sins of polygamy, so, without the fear of God, there is no absolute security that the bond may not be broken by adultery and divorce (cf. eh, xix. 5, 8; xxxv. 22; 2 Sam. xi. 1-5; Mark vi. 17, 18). II. PROVISil>N Fon TUE PROTECTION OF THE HUMAN FAMILY. 1. Against the world of animals. (1) In Eden such protection was not required, wllil having been constituted lord of the inferior creation, and the beasts of the field never rising to dispute his c.uthority, bis rule being characterised by gentleness and love (eh. ii. 20). (2) After the fall such protection was incomplete. A change having passed upon the master, there is reason to suppose that a corresponding change transpired upon the servant. The moral order of the world having been dislocated, a like instability would doubtless invade those economical arrangements that depended on man for THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [OH, IX, 1-7, thc:-ir <1uccessful Rdministration. As man sank deeper into the mire of corruption, bis supremacy over tho beasts of the field would appear to have been more frequently and fiercely disputed (eh. vi. 11). But now, the Flood having washed away the sinning race, (3) such protection was henceforth to be rendered secure by imbuing the brute nature with an instinctive dread of man which would lend the animals "x> ackno,dedge his supremacy, and rather flee from his presence than assail }:j9 dominion. The operation of this law is pro,•ed to-day by the facts that man retains unquestioned his lordship over all those domesticated animals that are useful to him; that there is no creature, however wild and ferocious, that he cannot tame; and that wherever man appears with his civilising agencies the wild beast instinctive!) retires. 2. A~·ainst. the world ~f men. Ever si~ce the fall man has required to be protected agamst himself. Pr10r to the Flood 1t does not appear that even crimes of murder and bloodshed were publicly avenged. Now, however, the previous laxness, if it was such, and not rather Divine clemency, was to cease, and an entirely new arrangement to come into operation. (1) The law was henceforth to inflict CAPITAL PUNISHMENT on its murderers; not the la.w of man simply, but the law of God. Given to Noah, this statute was designed for the universal family of mnn until repealed by the Authority that imposed it. Not having been exclusively a Jewish statute, the abrogation of the Mosaic economy does not affect its stability. Christ, having come not to destroy the fundamental laws of Heaven, may be fairly presumed to have left this standing. Inferences from the spirit of Christianity have no .alidity as against an express Divine commandment. (2) The reasons for the law were to be the essential dignity of man's nature (ver. 6; cf. homily on the greatness of man, eh. i. 26) and the fundamental brotherhood of the race (ver. 5), a point which appears not to have received sufficient prominence in prediluvian times (cf. Acts rni. 26). (3) The ezecuti,on of the law was neither to be retained in the Dinne band for miraculous administration, nor to be left in that of the private individual (the kinsman) to gratify revenge, but to he intrusted to society for enforcement by means of a properly-constituted tribunal. This was the commencement of social government among men, and the institution of the magisterial office, or the power of the sword (vule Rom. xiii. 1-5). III. PROVISION l"OR TITE SUSTENANCE OF THE BUMAN FAMILY. 1. The rule. It is not certain that animal food was interdicted in Eden; it is almost certain that it was in use between the fall and the Flood. At the commencement of the new era it was expressly sanctioned. 2. The restriction. While the flesh of animals might be used as food, they were not to be mutilated while alive, nor was the blood to be eaten with the flesh. Note the bearing of the first of these on the question of Yinsection, which the Divine law appears explicitly to forbid, except it can be pro\-ed to be indispensable for the advancement of medical knowledge with a view 10 the healing of disease, and, in the case of ext4nding a permission, imperatively requires to be carried on with the least possible infliction of pain upon the unresisting creature whose life is thus sacrificed for the good of man; and of the second of these. on the lawfulness of eating blood under the Christian dispensation, see Expos. on ver. 4. 3. The reason. (1) For the rule, which, though not stated, may be judged to have been (a) a concession to the moral weakness of man's soul, and (b) a provision for the pbyi,ical infirmity of man's body. (2) For the restriction- (a) to prevent crue1ty to animals; (b) to fence about man s life by showing the criminality of destroying that of the beast; (c) to assert God's lordship over nil life; (d) because of its symbolic value as the sign of atoning blood. Le-ssons:-1. God's clemency towards man. 2. God's care for man. 3, God's g·oodness to man. 4. God's estimate of man.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God spake---in continuation of the preceding discourse-unto Noah, and to his sons with him, saying.

entries.title: GEN 9:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And I, behold, I establish-literally, am causing to rise up or stand; aviar71µ, (LXX. )-my covenant (cf. eh. vi. 18) with you, and with your seed after you. I. e. the covenant contemplated all subsequent posterity in its provisions, and, along with the human family, the entire animal creation.

entries.title: GEN 9:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And with every living creature -litemlly, every soid (or breathing thing) that liveth, a generic designation of which the particulars are now specified-that is with you, of the fowl, of the cattle, and of every beast of the earth-literally, in fowl, &c. ; i. e. belonging to these classes of animals (cf. eh. i. 25, 30; vi. 20; viii. 17)- with you; from all that go out of the ark, -not necessarily implying(' Speaker's Commentary,' Murphy), though in all probability it was the case, that there were animals which Jiad never been in the ark; hut simply an idiomaticphrase expressive of the totality of the animal creation (Alford)-to everybeast of the earth. I. e. wild beast (eh. i. 25), the chayyah of the land, which was not included among the animals that entered the ark (Murphy); or living creature (eh. ii. 19), refeITing here to the fishes of the sea, which were not included in the ark (Kalisch). 'fhat the entire brnte creation was designed to be embraced in the Noachic covenant seems apparent from the use of the prepositions-:;! describing the classes to which the' animals· belong, as in eh. vii. 21 ; )r,> indicating one portion of the whole, the terminus aquo, nnd? the terminus ad quemin their enumeration (vicle Fiirst, 'Hebrew "teL,' sub ~. p. 715; cf. Keil in loco). Kalisch thinks the language applies only to the animals of Noah's time, and not to those of a later age, on the ground that "the destiny of the animals is everywhere connected with that of the human race;" but this is equivalent to their being included in the covena.nt.

entries.title: GEN 9:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And I will establish my covenant with you. Not form it for the first time, ns if no such covenant had existed in antediluvian times (Knobel) ; but cause it to stand or permanently establish it, so that it shall no more be in danger of being overthrown, as it recently has been. The word "my" points to a covenant already in existence, though not formally mentioned until the time of Noah (eh. vi. 18). The promise of the woman's seed, which Conned the substance of the covenant during the interval from Adam to Noah, was from Noah's time downwards to be enlarged by a specific pledge of the stability of the earth and the safety of man (c£ eh. viii. 22\. Neither shall all flesh-including the human race and the animnl creation. Cf. ;b::i--',:::i, mankind (eh. vi 12'., the lower c;e;tur~s (eh. vii. 21)-be cut off any more by the waters of a. flood. Literally, the flood just passed, which would no more retum. Neither shall there anymore be a flood (ofany kincl) to destroy the earth. Re~ons might be devastated and tribes of animals and men swept away, but never again woul,l there be a universal destruction of the earth or of man. V_er. 12.-And God said, This is the token -m~ (vida eh. i. 14; iv. 15)-of the covenant which I make-literally, mn giviTII] (cf. eh. xv-ii. 2)-between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations. Le'd6r6th (vide eh. vi. 9); '6lam (from 'alam, to hide, to conceal), pr. that which i,s hidden; hence, specially, time of which either the beginning or the end is uncertain or undefined, the duration being usually determined by the nahtro of the case (vide Gesenins, 'Heb. Lex.,' s1tb voce), Here the meaning is, that so long as there were circuits or generations of men upon the earth, so long would this covenant eudure.

entries.title: GEN 9:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -I do set. Literally, I hav6 given, or placed, an indication that the atmospheric phenomenon referred to had o.lready frequently appeared (Syriac, Arabic, Aben Ezra, Chrysostom, Calvin, Willet, Murphy, Wordsworth, Kalisch, Lange). The contrary opinion has been maintained that it nowfor the first time appeared (Bush, Keil, Delitzsch), or at least that the histori11n thought so (Knobel) ; but unless there had been no rain, or the laws of light and the 144 THE BOOK OF GEN'ESIS. [CH. IX. 8-17, ntm!'spberic conditiom of the earth had been different from what they are at present, it must h•ve been a frequent spectacle in the primeval hc•vens. My bow. I. e. the rainbow, ,-o{ov (LXX.), (cf. Ezek. i. 28). The orrlinari- rainbow consists of a series of successiYe •zones or bands of polarised light, forming little concentric circles in the sky, nnd haring a common centre almost always hdow the horizon, and di1tmetrically opposite to the sun. It is produced by the refraction and reflection of the sun's light through the spherical raindrops on which the rays fall, and, accordinglyt must always appear, with a grcater or a lesser degree of visibility, "·h e11 the two material agencies come in contact. The part of the sky on which the rninhow is thrown is much ·more bright within tlum without the bow. The outer spnce is dark, almost bla.ck; and the inner space, on the contrary, melts into the violet almost insensibly (Nichol's 'Cyclopedia of the Sciences,' nrt. Rainbow). It is here sti-led God's bow, es being his workmansl{ip (cf. Ecdus. xliii. 12), and his seal appended to his covenant (eh. ix. 17). In the cloud. j~~. that wh,:ch veils the heavens, from a root signifying to cover (Gesenius). And it shall be for a token. riii:-t~ =Eic tITJl'•iov (LXX.). In Greek mythology the rainbow is designated by a name (Iris) which is at least connected with ,ipo,, to spee.k, and ,ip,1,,71, peace; is represented as the da~hter of Thaumas (wonder), and Electra (brightness) the dano-hter of Oceanus; is assigned the office of m~ssenger to the king and queen of Olympus; and is depi~te~ as set in-~ea,en for a sign (Homer, 'IL, ::a. 27; XTIL 547, 548 ; xxfr. 14.4, 159 ; Virgil, '1En.,' iv. 694 : ,-_ 606; Ovid, 'Met.,' i. 270; xi. 585). The Persians seem to have associated the rainbow mth similar ideas. An old picture, mentioned by Stolberg, represents a win~ed boy on a rainbow with_ an old ma1;1- kneeling in a posture of worship. Th~ HIDdoos d_escribe the rainbow as a warlike weapon ID the hands of Indra.s their god, "with which he hurls flashing darts upon the impious giants ;" but also as a symbol of peace exhibited to man "when the combat of the heavens is silenced." By the Chinese it is regarded as the harbinger of troubles an~ misfortunes on earth, and by the old Scandinavians as a bridge uniting earth and heave!! (' Kalisch on Genesis,' pp. 2_23! 224). ~1tional reflections of the Biblical narrative, they do not " account for the application in the Pentateuch of the rainbow to a very remarkable purpose," or "explain _why the New Testament represents the raIDbow as an attribute of the Divine throne," or "whr, angels are sent as messengers on earth ' (Kalisch) ; bvt are themselves accounted for and explained by it. The institution of the rainbow as a sign clearly negatives the idea !(.Aquinas, Cajet~n) that it WD.ll origin11lly and naturally a ~ign ; which, if it was, "it was a lying sign, ' since the Flood came notwithstanding its prognostications (Willet). Of a covenant. " The bow in the hands of man was an instrument of battle (eh. xlviii. 22; Ps. vii. 12; Prov. vi. 2; Zech. ix. 10); but the bow bent by the hand of God bas become a symbol of peace" (Wordsworth). Between me and the earth.

entries.title: GEN 9:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it shall come to pass, when I bring a cloud over the earth. . Literally, in my clouding a cloud, i. e. gathering clouds, which naturally signify store of rnin (1 Kings xviii. 44, 45). Clouds are often used to denote afflictions and dangers (cf. Ezek. x.xx. 3, 18; xxxii. 7; xxxiv. 12; Joel ii. 2). That the bow shall be seen in the cloud. Literally, and the bow is seen, which it always is when the sun's rays fall upon it, if the spectator's back is towards the light, and his face towards the cloud. Thus at the moment when danger seems to threaten most, the many-coloured arch arrests the gaze.

entries.title: GEN 9:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And I will remember (cf. eh. viii. 1). .An anthropomorphism introduced to remind man that God is ever faithful to his covenant engagements (Calvin). "God is said to remember, because he maketh us to know and to remember" (Chrysostom). My covenant (vi,de on ver. 11), which is between me and you and every living creature of all fiesh; and the waters shall no more become a 11ood-hayah with le= to become (cf. eh. ii. 7); literally, shall no more be (i. e. grow) to a flood; or, "and there shall no more be the waters to the extent o a flood "-to destroy all fiesh.

entries.title: GEN 9:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the bow shall be in the cloud; and I will look upon it, that I may romember the everlasting covenant. Literally, the covenant of eternity. One of those pregnant Scripture sayings that have in them an almost inexhaustible fulness of meaning, which does not at first sight disclose itself to the eye of the unreflecting reader. In so far as the Noachic covenant was simply a promise that there should be no recurrence of a flood, the covenant of eternity had a corresponding limit in its duration to the period of this present terrestrial economy. But, rightly viewed, the Noachic covenant was the original .Adam.ic covenant set up again in a different form ; and hence, when applied to it, the phrase covenant of eternity is entitled to retain itq highest and fullest significance, 1111 a covenant reaching from eternity to eternity. Between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth.

entries.title: GEN 9:17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God said unto Noah, Thu OH, IX, 8-17,l 'rHE BOOK OF GENESIS. 145 IB the token of the covenant. Murphy thinks thnt Goel hero elirecteel the patriarch's o.ttention to nn nctnnl ro.inbow; it seems more no.tum! to conclude thnt from the beginning of the interview (eh. viii. 20) the o.rk nltnr, nnel worshippers were encircleel by 'its vnl'iegnted o.rch. Kalisch compares with the rninbow the other signs which God subsequently appended to his covenants ; as e. g., circumcision (eh. xvii. 11), the p;ssovcr (Exod. xii. 13), the sabbath (ibid. xxxi. 13). 'fhe Noachic covenant being universal, the sign was also universal-" dpa, p,pcnrwv av0po!1rwv" (II., xi. 27), a sign to men of many tongues. The later covenants being limited to Israel, their signs were local and provisional, and have now been supplanted by the higher symbolism ofthe Christian Church, viz., baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the Christian sabbath. Whieh I han established. The different verbs used in thia passage in connection with n•7,;1 may be here brought together. 1. tm (~er. 12) re• presenting the covenant as a gift of Divine grace. 2. 0.1p (Hiph.; vers. 9, 11, 17) exhibiting the covenant as something which Goel has both causeel to stand and raised up when fallen. 8. i:;)t (ver. 15) depicting the covenant as always present to the DiTine mind. Tuch, Stahelin, and Delitzsch detect an idiosyncrasy of the Elohist in using the first and second of these verbs instead of rrJf, the favourite expression of the J ehovist. But rrJf is used by the Elohist in eh. xxi. 27, 32, while in Deut. iv. 18 the Jehovist uses C'i?v• lletween me and all :flesh that is upon the earth.

entries.title: GEN 9:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tkecovenant renewed. I. THE AUTHOR OF THE COVENANT. God. This is evident from the nature of the case. In ordinary language a covenant signifies "a mutual contract between two (or more) parties" (Hodge, 'Syst. Theo!.,' vol. ii. p. 355); cf. eh. xxi. 27 (Abraham and Abimelech); Josh. xxiv. 25 (Joshua and Israel); 1 Sam. xviii. 3 (Jonathan and David); 1 Kings xx. 34 (Ahab and Benhadad); "comprehending a promise made by the one to the other, accompanied with a condition, upon the performance of which the accepter becomes entitled to the fulfilment of the promise" (Dick's 'Theo!. Leet.,' xiv.). Applied, however, to those transactions between God and man which took their rise subsequent to the £all, a covenant is an arrangement or disposition originated by God under which certain free and gracious promises are made over to man, which promises are ratified by sacrifice and impose certain obligations on their recipients, while they are usually connected with institutions illustratiye of their nature (cf. 'Kelly on the Covenants,' lect. i. p. 12). But, taking either definition of the term, it is obvious that the initial mowment in any such trnnsaction must belong to God ; and with special emphasis does God claim to be the sole Author of the covenant established with Noah and his descendants (vers. 9, 11, 12, 17). II. Tim PARTIES 'l'O THE COVENAN'l', i. e. the persons interested in the covenant; viz., Noah and his posterity. But Noah and his sons at that time were-1. The Tieads of the race. Hence the covenant may be said to have possessed a worldwide aspect. Because of their connection with Noah the entire family of man had an interest in its provisions. 2. 1'/ie fathers of the Church. As believers Noah and his family had been saved; and with them, in the character of believers, the covenant was made. Hence it had also a special outlook to the Church, for whom it had a bhissing quite distinct from that which it conferred upon the world as such. III. THE SUBSTANCE OF THE COVENANT. Calling it so frequently as l1e does II my coven11nt" (eh. vi. 18; vii. 9, 11), the Author of it seems desirous to connect it in our thoughts with that old covenant which, more thnn sixteen centuries earlier, he h11d established with mankind immediately after the fall. Now that covenant was in substance an arrangement, disposition, proposal, or promise of mercy and salvation; and that has been the essential element in every covenant that God has made with man. So to speak, God's covenant is just another name for his formal conveyance to mankind sinners of the free gift of Christ and his salvntion. IV. THE FORM OF THE 0OVENANT. While in every age essentially the same, the form of the covenant has been changing with the changing eras of human history. When we speak of a change of dispensation, the thing meant is a change upon the outwnrd forrn or mode of representing- the covenant-a dispensation being a Pivinll OEKF.Sl8, i, 146 THE DOOK OF GENERIS. [en. ,x. 8-17. arrangement. for commnnicltting blessing. In prediluvian times tho form which:the covenant asrnmcd was the promise of the woman's seed. From the Deluge 011wa1•ds it was a promise of forbearnncc-" Neither shall nil flesh be cut off any more b7 the waters o~ n flood; n_either shall there be any more a flood to destroy tho earth.' In thC' pntnarchal era it became the promise of a son "in whom nil the families of the earth ~hould be ble~sed" (eh. xii. 3; xviii. 18; xxii. 18). Under the I\'Ioauic clispcns11trnn the pro1rn_se of n prophet like unto Moses (Deut. xviii. 15); during the mona_rchy the I?rom1so of II king to sit upon David's throne (2 Sam. vii. 12); in !ho time of lsarnh the _prom_ise of a sn~ering servant of the Lord (Isa. xlii., !iii.); m the fnlncss of the times 1t assumed its permanent form, viz., that of the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ as the "·oman's seed, ns Abraham's child, ns David's son, os Jel1ov.ih's scr,ant. V. THE SEAL OF' TIIE COVENANT. Covenant transactions under the old or Leviticnl dispensation were invariably accompanied with the offering up of sacrificial victims as a public attestation of the binding character of the arrangement. The covenant which God made with Noah had also its sacrificial seal. 1. The meritorious sa1:rijice. The propitiatory offering of the Lord Jesus Christ, on the sole ground of which he is well pleased with and mercifolly disposed towards the race of sinful man. 2. The typu:al sacrifice. The offering of Noah upon Ararat after emerging from the ark. YI. THE SIGN OF THE COVENANT. The rainbow, which was-1. A universal sign. The covenant having been made with the entire family of man, it was in a manner rcq11isite that the sign should be one which was patent to the race; not limited and local and national, like circwncision, afterwards given to the Hebrews or Abrahamidai, hut universal, ubiquitous, cosmopolitan ; and such was the rainbow. This was a first mark of kindness on the part of God towards the family which he had taken into covenant with himself. 2. An attractive sign. Such as could not £ail to arrest the gaze of those whose special interest it was to behold it. Nothing is more remarkable than the quickness with which it attracts the eye, and the pleasurable feelings which its sight enlcindles. In its selection, then, to be a sign and symbol of his covenant, instead of something in itself repulsive or even indifferent, we can detect nnotl1er proof of kindness on the part of God. 3. A seasonable sign. At the ,ery moment, as it were, when nature's elements are threatening another deluge, the signal of heaven's clemency is hung out upon the watery sky to rebuke the £ears of men. Another token of special kindness on the part of God. 4. A. suggestive sign-suggestive of the covenant of grace. Possibly this was the chief reason why the rainbow was selected as the sign of the covenant; a further display of kindness on the part of God. VII. THE PERPETUITY OJ!' THE COVENANT. 1. To eternity (ver. 16). In so far RB it was a spiritual covenant with the believing Church, it was designed to be unto, as it had actually been from, everlasting. 2. For perpetual generations (ver. 12). In so far as it was a providential covenant with the race, it was designed to continue to the end of time. Lessons:-1. The exceeding riches of Divine grace· in dealing with men by way of a covenant. 2. The exceeding faithfulness of God in adhering to his covenant, notwithstanding man's sinfulness and provocation. 3. The exceeding hopefulness of man's position in being placed beneath a covenant of mercy.

entries.title: GEN 9:8–17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - The new Noaclli,e covenant establislied. I. It is o. COVENANT OF r,Jf'E. It embraces all the posterity of Noah, i. e. it is-1. T!te new foundation on which humanity rests. 2. It passes through man to all flesh, to all living creaturec. 3. The sign of it, the rainbow in tlie cloud, is also the emblem of the salvatiQ11, which may be said to be typified in the deliverance of Noah and his family. 4. The bockground is the same element wherewith the world wae destroyed, representing the rigliteomness of God os against the sin of Jllan. On that righteousness God sets tlie ,i,gn of love, which is produced by the rays of light-the sun being the emblem of Divine goodnese - radiating from the infinite centre in the glorious Father of all CU.
