entries.title: GEN 9:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The bow in the cloud. With deep joy and yet with awe must Noah have looked around him on leaving the ark. On every aide digns of the mighty destruction; the earth scarcely dried, and the busy throng of men (Luke xvii. 27) all gone. Yet signs of new life; the earth putting forth verdure, as though preparing for a new and happier chapter of history. His first recorded act was sacrifice-an acknowledgment that his preserved life was God's gift, a new profession of faith in him. Then God gave the promise that no such destruction should again befall the earth, and so ordered the sign that the rain-clolld which might excite the fear should bring with it the rainbow, the pledge of the covenant. But as eh. vi. 18 foreshadowed the Christian covenant (1 Pet. iii. 21) in its aspect of deliverance from destruction, the text points to the same in its bearing on daily life and service. The Godward life and renewal of the will which the law could not produce (Rom. viii. 3) is made sure to believers throllgh the constraining power of the love of Christ (cf. 1 John iii. 3; Rev. xii. 11). .And if clouds should cause fear, and God's face be hidden, and the energy of dedication grow languid, we are reminded (Rom. vi. 14; Gal. v. 24). And in the vision of the glorified Church (Rev. iv. 3) the rainbow again appears, pointing back to the early sign, connecting them as parts of one scheme, and visibly setting forth the glory of God in his mercy and grace (cf. Exod. xxxiii. 19; xxxiv. 6; John i. 14). [ THE 'JOVENANT WAS MADE WITH NOAH AND HIS SEED AS CHILDREN 01" JJ'AITH. They had believed in God's revealed way of salvation and entered the ark (cf. Num. xxi. 8). The root of a Christian life is belief in ufinished redemption (2 Cor. v. 14; 1 John v. 11); not belief that the doctrine is trne, but tmst in the fact as the one ground of hope. Hast thou acted on God's call; entered the ark; trusted Christ; none else, nothing else? Waitest thou for something in thyself? Noah did not think of fitness when told to enter. God calleth thee as unfit (cf. 1 Tim. i. 15). Try to believe; make a real effort (cf. Matt. xv. 28; Mark i.x. 23). II. TrrE POWER OF A CHRISTIAN LIFE j FAITH AS A HAIJIT OF THE MIND. Look to the bow. "Looking unto Jesus." The world is the field on which God's grace is shown; we are the actors by whom his work is done. How shall we do this? Beset by hindrances-love of the world, love of self, love of ease. \Vo cannot of ourselves (cf. Luke xxii. 33, 34; Rom. xi. 20). We are strong only in trusting to the power of the Lord (cf. 2 Cor. xii. 10 ; Phil. iv. 13). III. IN THIS THE HOLY SrmIT IS OUR HELPER, His offic1J is to reveal Christ to the soul. His help is promised if sought for.-M. L2 148 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (err, IX, 18-29,

entries.content: - And he drank of the wine. P.1 .; "perhaps so called from bubbling up and fermenting;" connected with 11.! (Gesenius). entries.title: GEN 9:25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said. Not in personal resentment, since "the fall of :Noah is not st all connected with his prophecy, except as serving to bring out the real character of hi8 children, and to reconcile him to the differ• ent destinies which he was to announce as awaiting their respective races" (Candlish) ; but under the impulse of a prophetic spirit (Poole, Keil, Lange, Candlish, Murphy, ancl expositors generally), which, however, had its historical occasion in the foregoing incident. The structure of the prophecy is perfectly symmetrical, introducing, in three poetical verses, (1) the curse of Canaan, (2) the blessing of Shem, and (3) the enlargement of Japheth, and in all three giving promi:.Jence to the doom of servitude pronounced upon the son of Ham. Cursed. Tbe second curse pronounced upon a human being, the first having been on Cain (eh. fr. 11). Colenso notices that all the curses belong to the Jehovistic writer; but vide eh. xlix. 6, 7, whichTuch and Bleek ascribed to the Elohist, though, doubtless in consequence of the "curse," by Davidson and others it is now assigned to the Jehovist. That this curse was not an imprecation, but a prediction of the future subjection of the Canaanites, has been maintained (Theodoret, Venema, Willet), chiefly in consequence of its falling upon Canaan ; but (1) as the contrary "blessing" implies the inheritance of good in virtue of a Di,inc disposition to that effect, so does "cursing" import subjection to evil by tho same Divine power ; and (2) if we eliminate the moral element from the doom of Canaan, which clearly referred to a conclition of temporal servitude, there seems no reason why tho language of Noah should not be rogarcled ns a solemnly pronounced and Divinely guaranteed infliction ; while (3) ns the curse is obviously aimed at the nations and peoples descending from the execrated person, it is not inconsistent to suppose that many indhidunls amongst those nations and peoples might attain to a high dcgreo of tempornl ancl spiritual prosperity. Be Canaan. (1) Not Ham, the father of Canaan (Arabic Version) ; nor (2) all the sons of Ham, thou"h concen~ted in Canaan (Hii.vernick, Keil, Mu.~phy); but (3) Cana:u, alone, though indirectly, through him, HaRl also (Calvin, Bush, Kalisch, Lange, et alii). For the formal omission of H"-m many different reasons have been assignc,1. (1) Because God had preserved him iii the ark (Jewish commentators). {2) Becm.s~ if Ham had 150 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (cu. ix. 18-29 bcon m11ntione,l all his other sons would have boon implicRterl (Pererius, Lange). (3) Becanse the sin of HRm was C'omparatively trifling (Bohlen). For the cursing of Canaan inst.cad of Ham, it has been urged- (1) That lie was H11.m's youngest son, e.s Ham was Noah's (Hoffman and Delitzsch); surely a very insufficient l'Cll.son for God cursing any one ! (2) That he was the real perpetrator of t:he crime (~ben Ezra, Procopius, Poole, Janueson, Lewis, &c.). (3) That thereby tl,e greatness of Ham's sin was ei-inc.ed (Cnhin). {4) That Canaan was already walking in the steps of his father's impiety (Ambrose, Merc.erus, Keil). (5) That Noah foresaw that the Ca.naanites would abundnntlv desen•e this visitation (Calvin, Wordsworth, Murphy, Kalisch, La.nge). We incline to think the truth lies in the last three reasons. A servant of servants. A Hebraism for the superlative degree ; cf. "1":ing of kings," "holy of holies," "the i;ong of son!!"S" (vide Gesenius, § 119). I. e. "the last e~en among servants" (Calvin) ; "a servant reduced to the lowest degree of bondage and degradation " (Bush) ; " vilissima servitute pressus" (Sol Glass); "a most base and vile servant" (Ainsworth) ; "a "·orking servant" (Chaldee); "the lowest of slaves" (Keil); ,raic oidrqc (LX.X.), which " conveys the notion of permanent hereditary servitude " (Kalisch). Keil, Hengst.cuber", and Wordsworth see an allusion to this condition in the name Canaan (q. v., supra), which, however, Lange doubts. She.ll h11 be to his bretbren. A prophecy which was afterwards abundantly fulfilled, the Canaanites in the time of Joshua having been partly exterminated and partly reduced to the lowest form of slavery by the Israelites who belonged to the family of Shem (Jash. ix. 23), those that remained being subsequently reduced by Solomon (1 Kings ix. 20, 21); while the Phenicia~s, along with the Carthaginians and Egyptians, who all belonged to the family of Canaan, were 611Ljected by the Japhetic I'ersians, Macedonians, and Romans (Keil).

entries.title: GEN 9:20–29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The future unveiled. I. A PAGE FROM HUMAN HISTORY. The prominent figure an old man (of 620 years or upwards)-always an object of interest, as one who has passed through life's vicissitudes, and worthy of peculiar honour, especially if found walking in the paths of righteousness and peace ; an old saint who had long been distinguished for the elevation of his piety, who had long maintained his fidelity to God in the midst of evil times, who had just enjoyed a special deliverance at the hand of God, and who up to the period referred to in our text had brought neither stain upon his piety nor cloud upon his name ; the second head of the human family, and in 11 manner nlso the second head of the Church of God; an old disciple, ~vho probably had seen Seth, the son of Adam, and walked with Enoch, ·and spoken with Methuselah, and who lived, as the Scripture tells us, to the days of Abram; clearly one of the most distinguished figures that, looking back, one is able· to detect upon the canvas of time. Well, in connection with this venerable patriarch we learn-1. That he engaged in a highly honourable occupation. (1) It was to his credit that he had an occupation. Being an old man, he might have reasoned that his working days were done, and that the evening of lifo might as well be spent in leisure and meditation. Having threo stalwart sons, he might have deemed it proper to look to them for aid in his declining years. Ann. knowing himself to be an object of Heaven's peculiar care, he might have trusted God would feed him wiLhout his working, since he had saved him without his asking. But from all these temptations--to idleness, to dependence, to presumption-Noah was de1ivered, and preferred, as all good Christians,should do, to labour to the last, working while it is culled to-day, to depend upon themselves rather than their friends and neighbours, and to expect God's nssistnnce rather when they try to help themselves than when they leave it all to hitn Then, (2) The calling lie cngagP,d in was an honest one, lb2 ':tiiE BOOK OF GENESIS. ten. It. 18--29. I He was a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard (vide Exposition on vine cultivation). God's peopl~ sho~1ld be careful in selecting honest trades and professions for themsel\'cs nnd their children (Rom. xii. 17). No social statnR, or public estimation, or p~ofitable returns c~n render that employment honourable which, either in its nature or l!1 th~ ma~n~r of Its carrying; on, ,iolates the law of God; while tha.t calling bas a special g.ory m itself and a special value in the sight of Heaven which however bumble and unremunernth·e, respects the rights of men and the rules of God'. 2. That Ju irulul,ged in a per.fecUv legitimate gratijication. "lle drank of the wine." Thero ,ms ~ot)1ing v.Ton;s· !n. Noah eating of the ripe grapes w,hich grew upon his vines, or drmkmg of their JUICe when transformed mto wine (et. Deut. x.xv. 4; 1 Cor. ix. 7). The sinfulness of making fcnnented liquors cannot be established so long as fermentation is a natural process for the preservation of the produce of the grape and Scripture, in one set of passages, speaks of its beneficial influence upon man'~ physical system (Judges ix. 13; Ps. civ. 15; Prov. xxxi. 6; 1 Tim. v. 23), and God himself ern_p~oys it as a sy~bol of the highe~t and choicest blessings, both temporal and sp1ntual (Gen. xxvu. 28, 37; Prov. 1x. 2; Isa. xxv. 6; Matt. x.xvi. 28, 29), and Christ made it at the marriage feast of Cana (John ii. 9, 10). Nor is the drinking of wines and other fermented liquors condemned in Scripture as a violation of the law of God. That there are special seasons when abstinence from this as wP.11 as other gratifications of a physic:il kind is a duty (cf. Levit. x. 9; Jndgcs xiii. 4, 14; Ezek. xliv. 21; Dan. i. 5, 8, .16; Rom. xiv. 21; 1 Cor. x. 28), and that it is competent to any Christian, for the sake of his weaker brethren, or as a means of advancing his own spiritual life, or for the glory of '1od, to renounce his liberty in respect of drinks, no intelligent person will doubt. But that total abstinence is imperatively required of every one is neither asserted in Scripture nor was it taught by the example of Christ (Matt. xi. 19), and to enforce it upon Christian men as a term of commnnion is to impose on them a yoke of bondage which Christ has not sanctioned, and to supplant Christian liberty by bodily asceticism. 3. That he jell beneath a pitifully sad humiliatwn. (1) He drank to the extent of intoxication. Whatever extenuations may be offered for the action of the patriarch, it cannot be regarded in any other light than a, sin.• Considering the age he had come to, the experience he had passed through, the position which he occupied as the head of the race and the father ofthe Church, he ought to have been specially upon his guard. While permitting man a moderate indulgence in the fruit of the vine, the word of God especially condemns the sin of drunkenness (cf. Prov. xxiii. 20; Isa. v. 11, 22; Luke :xxi. 34; Rom. xiii. 13; 1 Cor. v. 11; vi. 10; Gal. v. 21; Ephes. v. 18; 1 Thess. v. 8). (2) His immodesty. The veil of modesty in which God designs that every sinful human being should be wrapt should be jealously guarded from infringement by any action either of ourselves or others. Lessons:-1. "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor. :x. 12). Remember Adam, Noah, Abraham, David, Peter. 2. "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with t!Je Spirit" (Ephes. v. 18). There is scarcely a sin to which intoxication may not lead ; there is no infallible cure for drunkenness but being filJed with the Spirit. 3. "Be sure thy sin will find thee out" (Num. mii. 23). "There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed; neither hid that shall not be known." II. A REVE:LATION OF BUMAN CHARACTER. On the threshold of the new world, like the Lord Jesus Christ in the opening of the gospel dispensation (Luke ii. 35), the patriarch Noah appears to have been set for the fall and rising again of many, and for n sign to be spoken against that the thoughts of many hearts might be revealed. All unconsciously to him his vine-planting and wine-drinking become the occasion of unveiling the different characters of his sons in respect of-1. Filial piety, which Shem and Japheth remarkably displayed, l,ut of which Ham, the youngest son, appears to have been destitute. There was nothing sinful in Ham's having witnessed what should never have been exposed to view, and there is no reason to credit any of the idle rabbinical legends which allege that Ham perpe• trated a particular outrage upon his father ; but Ham was manifestly wanting· in that filial reverence and honour which were due to his aged parent, in that he gazed with delight upon the melancholy spectacle of his father's shame - in singular contrast to the respectful and modest behaviour of Shem an<l Japheth, who "wont on. 1x. 18--29.) 'fliE BOOK OF GENESIS. 158 with their faces bnckwo.rd," so tho.t "they saw not their father's nakedness.'' 2. Tender charity. In addition to the mocking eye which gloater! over the patriarch's infirmity, there was present in the heart of Ham an evil and m'1.liciouR spirit, which led him to inflict another and a severer indignity upon his father's fame. The faults of even bad men are required by religion to be covered up rather than paraded in public view. Much more the indiscretions, failings, and sins of good men. Most of all the faults of a father. But, alas, instead of sorrowing for his father's overthrow, Ham obviously took pleasure in it; instead of charitably trying to excuse the old man, nay, without even waiting to ascertain whether an explanation of his conduct might be possible, he appears to have put the worst construction on it; instead of doing what he could to hide his father's sin and shame, he rushes forth and makes it known to his brothers. But these brothers, with another spirit, without offering any apology for their father's error, perhaps instinctively perceiving it to be altogether unjustifiable, take the first loose garment they can find, and, with a beautiful modesty as well as a becoming piety, casting it around their shoulders, enter their father's presence with their faces backward, and cover up his prostrate form. Let the incident remind us-(1) That if nothing can extenuate a father's falling into sin, much more can nothing justify a son for failing in respect towards his father. (2) That it is a sure sign of depravity in a child when he mocks at a parent's infirm ities and publishes a parent's faults. (3) That filial piety ever seeks to extenuate and to bide rather than to aggravate and blaz'3 abroad a parent's weaknesses and sins. (4) That children in the eame family may be distinguished by widely different dispositions. (5) That a son may have pious parents and experience many providential mercies for their sakes, and yet be at heart a child of the devil. (6) That that which makes one son differ from another in the same family is Divine grace ; and (7) that the characters of children, and of men in general, are oftentimes revealed at the most unexpected times, and by the most improbable events. III. A DISCLOSURE OF HUMAN DESTINY. Awaking from bis wine, the patriarch became aware of what had taken place. Discerning in the conduct of his sons an indication of divergence in their characters, recognising in their different characters a repetition of what had taken place at the commencement of the first era of the world's history, viz., the division of mankind into a holy and a wicked line, foreseeing also, through the help of inspiration, the development of the world's population into three different tribes or races, ho foretells, acting in all under the Spirit's guidance, the future destinies that should await them. His utterance takes the form of a prediction, in which he declares-I. The degradation of Canaan. " Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brethren." (1) So far as Ham was concerned this judgment was severe, as being imposed upon his youngest and probably his best beloved son; appropriate-he for whose sake it had been inflicted having been his father's youngest son ; merciful, as falling not on all his race, but only upon one son and his descendants. N.B.-God's judgments upon sinful men are always proportioned in severity to the guilt which brings them, adjusted to the natures of the sins for which they come, and mixed with mercy in the experience of the persons on whom they fall. (2) So far as Canaan was concerned the doom of servitude was sovereiunly imposed. There is no evidence that Canaan was at all connected with the incident that happened in his grandfather's tent. That the penalty of his father's offence was made to fall on him of all his father's sons was in virtue of that high prerogative which belongs to God alone of assigning to men and nations their lots on earth (cf. Ps. l:xxv. 7 ; Isa. xli. 2; Dan. v. 19; iv. 35; Acts xvii. 2G). Richly merited. Whether Canaan had begun by this time to display any of the dispositions of his father cannot certainly be known; but in after years, when the prophecy was nearing its accomplishment, it is well known that the peculiar sins for which tho Canaanites were destroyed or subjected to bondage were allied to those which are referred to in the text (vide Levit. xviii. 27). Exactly f11lfilled by the subjugation of the land of Canaan under Joshua and David, though here it should ho noted that the enslavement of the African negro, who, though a Hamite, is not a C[Lllaanite, was a daring defiance of those limits within which the supreme Judge had confined the sentence pronounced upon the Hamite race. Mercifully cancelled by the later promise which was given to Abraham, and is now fulfilled in the iBcarnation of the Lord ,T\.'SIIS Christ-of a seed in whom all the families of the earth should be 154 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. 1x. 18-29, bles8ed (Gen. xxii. 18). 2. The exaltatwn of Shein. "Dle~sed be Jehovah, the Elohim of Shem," &c., in which description was the promise of II threefold exalta.tion. (1) To S?tJn·ernacy iii tM Chu.rck, ns being possessed of the knowledge of the true relig·ion, as being en'riched with the fulness of blessing that is in Jehovah Elohim, BB being- the Divinely-appointed medium tl1rough which the first promise of the woman's seed was to be fulfilled, and he wns to come whose name should be above every name. (2) To dominion in tlte ,corld. In virtue of the religious ascendancy eonferred upon him, Shem was to be possessed of power to influence other nations for good, and in particular to receive into his service, for education ns well as for 11ssistance, the descendants of Cannan. (3) To ,•e,wwii tlii-ouglwut all time. .As mueh as this perhaps is hinted at in the name Shem; and to this day the glory which encircled the Shemitic nations of antiquity has not faded, but continues to shine down the eenturies with undiminished lustre. 3. TM enlargement of Japlieth. "God shall enlarge Japhetb, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant." .A promise of-1. Territorial expansion. While the Shemite tribes should remain in a manner concentrated in the valley of the Tigris and Euphrates, the Japhethites should spread themselves abroad westward as the pioneers of civilisation. 2. Spi,ritual enruhment, by being broug·ht ultimately to share in the religious privileges and blessings of the Shemites-a prediction which has been abundantly fulfille<l by the admission of the Gentiles to the Christian Church. 3. .Civilising influence. .As Canaan wns subjected to Shem in order, while he served, to· be instructed in the faith of his master, so does he seem to have been placed beneath the sway of Ja~1heth, that .Tnpheth might lead him forth to a participation of the pecnlia.r blessings w]!ich he has been commissioned to bestow upon the other nations of foe earth. entries.title: GEN 9:18–29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The threefold distribution of tlie human race-into the Shemitic, Hamitic, and Japhetic families. The fall of Noah was through wine; not, indeed, a forbidden product of the earth, but, like the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good end evil, representing a tremendous responsibiliiy. I. Tm;: FERTILITY OF SIN. It was out of drunkenness that the widespread curse of the Hamitic nations came forth. And the drunkenness is closely connected with other sins-(1) shameful degradation both of f<'-tlier and son, (2) alienation .of brethren, and (3) human slavery. What a picture of the forthcoming· results· of intemperance and self-indulgence I 11. THE CONTRAST IlETWEEN THE BLESSING AND THE CURSE IN THEIR WORKING ou·r. Noah's prediction of the blessing on Shem and Japheth and the curse upon Ham may be taken as nn outline of the religious history of the world. ,L The Shemitic races are the source of religious light to the rest. "Blessed be tlie Lord God of Shem." "Jelwvali," the Shemitic revelation, is the foundation of all other. 2. The Japltetic races are the great colonisers and populators of the world, overflowing their own boundaries, dwelling in the tents of Shern, both as inquirers after Shemitic light and in friendly co-operation with Shemitic civilisation. 3. The Hamitic races are servants of servants unto their brethren, paitly by their degradation, but partly also by their achievements. The Plicenician, Assyrian, Egyptian, Ethiopian, and Canaa.nitish races, although by no means always in a lower/olitual state than the rest of the world, have yet been subdued by Japhetic an Shemitic conquerors, and hnnded down their wealth and acquirements to the Northern, Western, alld Enstern world. III. THE RENOVATION OF THE EARTH UNDE.B THE NEW COVENANT. .After the Flood Noali lived the half week of centuries, and thus laid firmly the foundations of a new earth. Yet, prolonged as was that life of him who had "found grace in the eiJes of the Lord," it came to an end at last. lie died. The one became the tliree. 1. The blessing /uzn-ded on. The type of rest and comfort was spread through the redeemed earth. And from l1enceforth we have to deal not with the small beginnings of the rescued race, but with the vast multitude of human beings. 2. New sphere of trial. under the light of the new covenant again the new race were placed upon their trial tl1at again the redeeming mercy of him who willeth not the death of bis creatures may be made :manifest in the midst of the teeming earth, with its threefold liu.maiiity, apreading ea~tward, westward, northward, and southward.-R. -----------------------------------

entries.title: GEN 10:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now these are the generations ofthesons ofNoah (cf. eh. v. 1; vi. 9), Shem, Ham, and J'apheth. Not the order of age but oftheocratic importance (vide eh. v. 32). And unto them were sons bom (cf. eh. ix. 1, 7, 19, 22) after the flood. An indication of the punctum temporis whence the period embraced in the present section takes its departure.

entries.title: GEN 10:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The sons of J'apheth are first mentioned not because Japheth was the eldest of the three brothers, althon~h that was true, but because of the greater distance of the Japhetic tribes from the theocratic centre, the Hamites having always been much more nearly situated to and closely connected with the Shemites than they. The immediate descendants of Japheth, whose name, 'Ia1rtTo!:', occurs again in the mythology of a Japhetic race, were fourteen m number, seven sons and seven grandsons, each of which became the progenitor of one of the primitive nations. Gomer. A peoplo inhabiting "the sides of the north" (Ezok. xxxviii. 6); the Galatm of the Greeks (Josephus, 'Ant.,' i. 6) ; tho Chomarii, a nation in llactriana on the Oxus (Shulthess, Kalisch); but more generally tho Cimmerians of Homer (' Odyas.,' xi. 13-19), whoso nbodes were the shores of the Caspian and Euxini, OR, X. 1-82.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 157 whonco they eoem to ha.ve oprerid themselves over Europa ns for wost as the Atlantic, loaving traces of their presence in the Cimbri of North Gennnny a.nd the Cymri in Wa.les (Keil, Lange, Murphy, Wordsworth, 'Speakor's Commentnry '). And Magog. A fierce 1tnd wa.rliko people presided over by Gog (an appellative name, liko the titles Pharaoh and Cresar, nnd corresponding with the Turkish Chak, the Tnrtnnan Kak, and the Mongolian Gog: Kalisch), whose complete destruction wns predicted by Ezekiel (chs. xxxviii. xxxix.) ; generally understood to be the Scythians,whose territory Jay upon the borders of the sea ofAsoph, and in the Caucasus. In the Apocalypso (eh. xx. 8-10) Gog and Magog appear as two distinct nations combined against the Church of God. And Madai. The inhabitants of Media (Mada in the cuneiform inscriptions), so called because believed to be sit11ated 11'Epi µ,u71v .-,jv 'Auiav (Polyb. v. 44) on thesouth-west shore of the Caspian. And Ja.van. Identical with 'Iawv (Greek), Javana (Sanscrit), Juna (Old Persian), Jounan (Rosetta Stone); allowed to be the father of the Greeks, who in Scripture a1e styled Javan (vide Isa. !xvi. 19; Ezek. xxvii. 13 ; Dan. viii. 21 ; x. 20 ; Joel iii. 6). And Tubal, and Muhech. Generally asso- ;iated in Sc_~pture as ti-i~utaries of M3:gog \Ezek. x.xxvu1. 2, 3 ; X.."'l:XlX. 1); recogmsed as the Iberians and Moschi in the north of Armenia, between the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Bia.ck Sea (Josephus, Knobel, Lange, Kalisch). And Tira.s. The ancestor of the Thracians (Josephus), of the Tyrrheni, a branch of the Pelasgians (Tuch), of the Asiatic tribes round the Taurus (Kalisch), in support of which last is a circumstance mentioned by Rawlinson, that en the old Egyptian monuments Mashuash and Tuirash, and upon the Assyrian Tubal and Misek, stand together ns hero, Tiras occurs nowhere else in Sclipture.

entries.title: GEN 10:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the sons ofJa.va.n; Elieha.h. The isles of Elishah arc praised by Ezekiel (x:xvii. 7) for their blue and purple ; supposed to have been Elis in the Peloponnesus, famous for its purple dyes (Bochart) ; 1Eolis (Josephus, Knobel); Hellas (i\Iichaelis, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch) ; without doubt a maritime people of Grecian stock ('Speaker's Commentary'). And Ta.rshish. Tarsus in Cilicia (Josephus); but rather Tartessus in Spain (Eusebius, Michaelis, Bochart, Kalisch). Biblical notices represent Tarshish as a wealthy and .flourishing seaporttown towards the west (vide 1 Kings x. 22; Ps. xlviii. 7 ; lxxii 10 ; Isa. Ix. 9; 1xvi 19; Jer. x. 9 ; Ezek. xxvii. 12). entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -By these were the isles of the Gentiles. Sea-washed coasts as well ns islands proper (cf. Isa. xiii. 4 with Matt. xii. 21). Isaiah (eh. x.x. 6) styJes Cannan lll1 islo (cf. Peloponnesus). Tho expression signifies mnritime countries. Divided in their lands ; every one e.fter his tongue. Indicating a. time posterior to the building of Babel (eh. ::i:i. 1). After their families.. 'Ev rai~'f>v;\aic aurwv (LXX.); in their tribes or cla.ns, 11 lesser subdivision than the ne::i:t. lu their nations. The division here exhibited is fourfold: (1) geogrnphical, (2) dialectical, (3) tribal, and (4) nntionn.l. The first de.fines the terl'itory occupied, and the second the language spoken by the Japhethites ; the third their immediate descent, ond the fourth the nntional group to which they sevornlly belonged. V~r. 6.-And the sons of Ham. 'l'hcso who occupy the second place, thnt the list might conclude with the Shemites as the 158 1'HE DOOK OF G~~F.SlS. [CR. X. 1--81 line of promise, number thirty, of whom only four were immediate descendants. Their territory generally embraced the southern portions of the globe. Henoe the name Ham has been connected with c,r.,0, to be mirm, though Kalisch declares it to be not of Hebrew, but Egyptian origin, appearing in the Chme ofthe Rosetta Stone. The most usual ancient name of the country was Kein, the black land. Scripture speaks ofEgypt as the land ofHnm (Ps. lxxdii. 51; cv. 23; cvi. 22). Cush. Ethiopia, including Arabia" quai mater est," and Abyssinia "qnai coloma" (Michaelis. Rosenmiillcr). The original settlement of Cush, however, is belie,ed to have been on the Upper N'ile, whence he afterwards spread to Arabia, Babylonia, India (Knobel, Kalisch, Lange, Rawlinson). Murphy thinks he may haYe started from the Caucasus, the Caspian, and the Cossaci of Khusistan, and migrated south (to Egypt) and east (to India). Josephus mentions thnt in his day Ethiopia was called Cush ; the Syriac transla.tcs av,ip A,f!io,J, (Acts nii. 27) by Cuschaeos; the ancient Egyptian name of Ethiopia was li:eesh, Kish, or Kush (' Records of the Past,' i,. 7). The Cushites are described as of a black colour (Jer. riii. 23) and ofgreat stature (Isa. xlv. 14). And ]l[izra.im.. A dual fonn probably designed to represent the two Egypts, upper and lower (Gesenius, Keil, Kalisch), though it has been discovered in an,:,ient Egyptian as the name of a Hittite chief (circa B.C. 1300, contemporary with Rame,ses II.), mitten in hieroglyphics M'a,zrima, Ma being the sign for the dual The old Egyptian name is Kemi, Chemi, with obvious reference to Ham ; the name Egypt beingp::-obably derived from Kaphtah, the land of Ptah. The singular form Mazor is found in later books (2 Kings xix. 24; Isa. rix. 6; xxxv. 25), and usually denotes Lower Egypt. And l'hut. Phet (Old Egyptian), Phaiat (Coptic); the Libyans in the north of Africa (Josephus, LXX., Gesenius, Bochart). Kalisch suggests Buto' or Butos, the capital of the delt;a of the Nile. And Canaan. Hebrew, Kenaan ('Dide on eh. ix. 25). The extent of the territory occupied by the fourth son of Ham is defined in vers. 15---19.

entries.content: -And the sons of Cush; Seba. Meroe, in Nubia, north ofEthiopia(Josephus, Ant.,' ii. 10). And Havile.h. EbiH (LXX.); may refer to an African tribe, the Avalitae, south ofBabelmandeb (Keil, Lange,Murphy), or the district of Ohanian in Axabia Felix (Rosenmiiller, Kalisch, Wordsworth). entries.title: GEN 10:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Cush begat-not necessarily as immediate pro~enitor, any ancestor being in Hebrew styled a. father-Nimrod ; .the rebel, from maradh, to rebel; the name of a person, not of a people ;-Namuret in ancient Egyptian, Though not one of the great ethnic heads, he is introduced into the register of nations as the founder of imperialism. Under him society passed from the patriarchal condition, in which each separato clan or tribe owns the sway of its natural head, into that (more abject or more civilised according n.s it is viewed) in which many different clans or tribes recognise the sway of one who is not their natural head, but has acquired his ascendancy and dominion by conquest. This is the principle of monarchism. Eastern tradition has painted Nimrod as a gigantic oppressor of the people's libertiesand an impious rebel against the Divine authority. Josephus credits him with having instigated the building of the tower of Babel. He has been identified with the Orion of the Greeks. Scripturo may seem to convey a bad impression of Nimrod, but it does not sanction the abrnrdities of Oriental legend. He began to be a mighty one-Gwbor (vide eh. vi. 4) ; what he had been previously being expressed in ver. 6in the earth. Not i71'1 riji; -yijt (LXX.), as if pointing to his gigantic stature, but either among men generally, with refer• ence to his widespread fame, or perhnps better "in the land" where he dwelt, which was not Babel, but Arabia (vide ver. 6).

entries.title: GEN 10:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -He was a mighty hunter. Originally doubtless of wild beasts, which, according to Bochart, was the first step to usurping dominion over men and using them for battle. "Nempe venationum prmtextu collegit juvenwn robustam manum, qunm talib118 exerr:itue ad belli labores induravit" (' Phaleg.,' !iv. 12). Before the Lord. 1. 'Evavrlov ~-vplou (LXX.), in n spirit of do- on. x. 1--112.J THE BOOK OF GF.NESIS. 159 fianco (Augustine, Keil, Murphy, Bush). 2. Comm Deo, in God's sight, ns an nggrnvation of his ein-cf. eh. xiii. 3 (Cajctan). 3. As a superlative, declaring his excellence-cf. eh. xiii. 10 ; xxx. 8 ; xxxv. 6; 1 Sam. xi. 7 ; John iii. 3; Acts vii. 20 (Aben Ezra, Kimchi, Kalisch, 'Speaker's Commentary'). 4. With tho Divine approbation, na one who broke the way through rude, uncultivated nature for tho institutions of Jehovah (Lange). Cf. eh. xvii. 18 ; xxiv. 40 ; 1 Sam. xi. 15; Ps. xli. 12. Probably the first or tho third conveys the sense of the expression. Wherefore it ia said, Even as Nimrod the (n) mighty hunter before the Lord. The precise import of this is usually determined by tho view taken of the previous phrase.

entries.title: GEN 10:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - And the beginning of hie kingdom. Either his first kingdom, as contrasted with his second (Knobel), or the commencement of his sovereignty (Keil, Kalisch), or the principal city of his empire (Rosenmiiller) ; or nll three may be legitimately embraced in the term reshith, only it does not necessarily imply that Nimrod .built any of the cities mentioned. Was Babel. Babylon, "the land of Nimrod" (Micah v. 6), the origin of which is described in eh. xi. 1, grew to be a great city covering an area of 225 square miles, reached its highest glory under Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. iv, 30), and succumbed to the Medo-Persian power under Belshazza.r (Dan. v. 31). The remains of this great city have been discovered on the east bank of the Euphrates near Hillah, where there is a square mound called "Babil" by the Arabs (Rawlinson's 'Ancient Monarchies,' vol. i. eh. 1). And Erech. The Orchoe of Ptolemy, identified by Rawlinson as Wurka., about eighty miles south of Babylon. And Accad. 'Apxa.o (LXX.); the ciiy Sittace on the river Argade (Bochart) ; Sakada, a town planted by Ptolemy below Ninus (Clericus); Accete, north of Babylon (Knobel, Lo.nge); identified with the ruins of Nifi'er, to the south of·Hillah (Keil) ; with those of Akkerkoof, north of Hillah(Kalisch). Rawlinson does not identify tbe site ; George Smith regards it as "the capital ofSargon, tho great city Agad.i, near •tho city of Sippara on the Euphrates, nnd north of Babylon" (' Assyrian Discoveries,' eh. xii.). And Calneh. Calno (Isa. x. 9) ; C11nneh (Ezek, xxvii. ?.3) ; Ctesiphon, cast of the Tigris, north-east of Babylon (Jerome, Euse\Jius, Boche.rt, Michaelis, Kalisch); identified with the ruins of Niffer on the east of tho Euphrates (Rawlinson). In the land of Shinar, Babylonia., ns distinguished from Assyri11 (Isa. xi. 11), the lower part of Mesopotamia, or Cho.ldrea.

entries.title: GEN 10:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Out of that land went forth ABBhur, the son of Shem (ver. 22; LXX., Vulgate Syriac, Luther, Calvin, Michaelis, Dathe, Rosenmiiller, Bohlen); i. e. the early Assyrians retired from Babylon beforo their Cushito invaders, and, proceeding northward, founded the cities after mentioned ; but the marginal rendering seems preferable: "Out of that land went (Nimrod) into Asshnr," or Assyria, the countrynorth-eastofBabylon, through which flows the Tigris, and which had already received its name from the son of Shem (the Targums, Drusius, Bochart, Le Clerc, Do Wette, Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch, Lange, et alii). And bnilded Nineveh. The ea.pita! of Assyria, opposite j\fosul on the Tigris, afterwards became the largest and most flourishing city of the ancient world (Jonah iii. 3; iv. 11), being fifty-five miles in circumference (Diod., ii. 3), and is now identified with the ruins of Nebbi-yunus and Kouyunjik (Layard's' Nineveh,' vol. ii.pp.136 ff.). And the city Rehoboth. Rehoboth-i1-, literally, the streets of the city (cf. Platrea, a city in Dceotia), a town of which the site is unknown. And Calah. The mounds of Nimroud (Layard and Smith), though Kalisch and Murphy prefer Kalah Shergat (about fifty miles south of Nineveh), which the former authorities identify with Asshnr the original capital of the country.

entries.title: GEN 10:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Resen, i. e. Nimrond, be• tween Kalah Shergat and Kouyunjik (K1• lisch); but if Calah be Nimroud, then Resen may be Selamiyeh, a village about half way, between Nineveh and Calah, i. e. Kouyunjik and Nimroud, ut supra (Layo.rd). The same. Resen (Kalisch), which will suit if it was Nimroud, whose remains cover a parallelogram about 1300 feet in length and 900 feet in breadth ; but others apply it to Nineveh with the other towns as forming one largo composite city (Knobel, Keil, Lange, Wordsworth). Is a. great city. With this the record of Nimrod's achievements closes. It is generally supposed that Nimrod flourished either before or about the time of the building of the tower of Babel ; but Prof. Chwolsen of St. Petersburg, in his 'Ueber die Ueberreste der .A.ltbabylonischen Literatur,' brings the dynasty of Nimrod down a.s late as 1500 B.c., relyin<> principally on the evidence of an origintl work composed by Qu.t'ami, a native Babylonian, aml translated by lbn-wa'hschijjah, o. descendnnt of the Chaldreans, and assigned by Chwolsen to one of the earlier periods of Babylonian history, in which is mentioned the name of Nemrod, or Nemroda, as the founder of II Canaanite dynasty which mled at Babylon (vide an excellent paper on this subject in 'l'umer's 'Biblical nncl Oriental Studies,' Edin., A. and C. Black, 1876). Perhaps the hardest difficulty to explain in connection with the ordinary date assigne,l to Nimrod is the foct that in eh. xiv., which speaks of the reigning monar,;:hs m. the 160 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [on. x. 1-B2, Euphrntes rnllcY, there is no account taken of Jlineveh and its kin~-B circumstanco which has bP~n supposed to import that the founding of tl1c cnpital of Assyria could not have been anterior to the days of Abraham, But early Babvlonian texts confirm what eh. xiv. seems to imply-the fact of an Elamite conquest of Babylonia, n.c. 2280, by Kudurnanhundi (Kudurlngamar, the Chederlaomer of Genesis), who car.-ied off an image of the goddess Nana from the city Erech (v£de 'Assyrian Discoveries,' eh. xii. ; 'Records of the Past,' .ol. iii.), so that this difficulty may be held to have disappeared before the light of archreological discovery. But at whatc,cr period Nimrod flourished, the Biblical narrn.ti,e would lead us to anticipate a commingling of Hamitic and Shemitic tongues in the Euphrates valley, which existing monuments confirm (cf. 'Records of the Past,' vol. iii p. 3).

entries.title: GEN 10:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Mizraim begat l,udim. .An African tribe, a colony of the Egyptians, like the next seven, which are "nomina non singulorum hominum sed populorum" (Aben Ezra, Michaelis, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch, Murphy); probably referred to in connection with Tarshish and Put (Isa. I.xvi 19), with Kush and Put (Jer. xlvi. 9), and in connection ,,ith Put (Ezek. xxvii 10 ; xxx. 5), Lud (ver. 22) mi.s Shemitic. And Anamim. Not elsewhere mentioned; the inhabitants of the Delta (Knobel). And Lehabi.m. Lubim (2 Chron. xii 3; Dan. ii. 43; Nahum iii. 9); Libyans (Dan. xi. 43); probably the Libyans west of Egypt (Michaelis, Kalisch, Murphy). And Naphtuhim. Nephthys, near Pelusium, on the Lake Sirbonis (Bochart); the Libyan town Kapata (Kalisch); the people of llliddle Egypt (Knobel).

entries.title: GEN 10:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Pathrusim. Pathros in Upper Egypt. And Casluhim. The Colchians, of Egyptian origin (Bochart, Gesenius); the inhabitants of the primitive Egyptian town Chemnis, later Panoplis (Kalisch). Out ofwhom came Philisti.m. The Philistines on the Mediterranean from Egypt to Joppa, who had five principal cities - Gaza, .A.shdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. They are here described as an offshoot from Casluhim. The name has been derived from an Ethiopic root falii&a, to emigrate ; hence '' immigrants" or "emigrants." Jer. xlvii 4 and Amos ix. 7 trace the Philistines to the Caphtorim. Michaelis solves the difficulty by transposing the clause to the end of the ,crse ; Bochart by holding the Casluhim and Caphtorim to have intermingled; Keil and Lange by the conjecture that the original tribe the Casluhim was subsequentlystrengthened by an immigration from Caphtor. Against the Egyptian origin of the Philistines the possession of a Shemitic tongue and the non-observance of circumcision have been urged ; but the first may have been acquired from tho conquered Avim whoae laud they occupied (Dent. ii. 23)1 and the exodus from Eip'pt mny ho.ve taken place prior to the inst1tut;o11 ofthe rite in question. And Caphtorim. CappaJocia(Bochart),Syrtis Major (Clericus), Crete (Calmet, Ewald), Cyprus (Michaelis, Rosenmiiller), Coptos, Kouft or Keft, a few miles north of Thebes (Kalisch).

entries.title: GEN 10:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Canaan begat Bidon his firstborn. .A. famous commercial nnd maritime town on the coast of Syria (1 Kings v. 6 ; I Chron. xxii. 4 ; Isa. xxiii. 2 4 12 • Ezek. xxvii. 8); here includiug Tyre: FroU:: the mention of the circumstance that Sidon was Canaan's firstborn, we may infer that in the rest of the table the order of seniority is uot followed. And Heth. The father of the Hittites (eh. xxiii. 3, 6), identified by Egyptologers with the Kheto., a powerful Syrian tribe.

entries.title: GEN 10:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Jebusite. Settled nt and around Jerusalem (Josh. xv. 8; Judges xix. 10, 11 ; I Chron. xi. 4, 5). And the Amorite. On both sides of the Jordan, though dwelling chiefly in the Judrean mountains (eh. xiv. 7; Josh. x. 5), to which the name "mountaineer " from ·" Amor " elevation (Gesenius), is ;upposed to ref:.r. And the Girgasite, The u me , nly is preserved (Josh. xxiv. 11).

entries.title: GEN 10:17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Hivite. "Villagers" (Gesenius) ; "settlers in cities" (Ewald) ; their localities are mentioned in eh. xxxiv. 2; Josh. ix. 1, 7; xi. 3; Judges vi. 3. And the Arkite. Inhabitants of Arka, a city of Phrenicia (Josephus) ; afte'rwards called Cresarea Libani ; its ruins still exist at Tel Arka, at the foot ofLebanon. And the Sinite. The inhabitants of Sin. Near Arka are a fortress named Senna, ruins called Sin, and a village designated Syn,

entries.title: GEN 10:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Arvadite,-d.welt in Arvad, Aradus, now Ruad (Josephus)-and the Zemarite,-Simyra, a city of Phrenicia (Bochart,:Michaelis, Gesenius, Kalisch) whose ruins are still called Sumrah-and the Kamathito. The inhabitants of Hamath, called Hammath Rabbah (.Amos vi. 2) ; Epiphaneia by the Greeks ; now Hamnh. And afterwards-i. e. subsequent to the formation of these distinct tribes by the confusion of tongues-were the families ofthe Canaanite& spread abroad.

entries.title: GEN 10:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the border of the Canaanites was from Bidon (its northern boundary), as thou comest-i. e. as thou goest, in the direction of-to Gerar,-between Kadesh and Shur (eh. xx. I)-unto Gaza (now called Guzzeh, at the south-west corner of Palestine) ; as thou goest, unto Sodom, and Gomorrah, and Admah, and Zeboim (vide eh. xix. 24), even unto Laaha-Callirrhoe (Hieronymus, Jerusalem Targum, Josephus, Rosenmiiller, Keil, Kalisch); possibly a vari, OD, X, 1-82.J THE BOOK OF GENEBIB. 161 ation of L11ish e.nd Leshem, 11 Sidonfon city near tho sources of the Jordan (Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 10:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -These are the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongu~s1 in their oountries, and in their nations (vute ver. 5). Yer. 21.-Unto Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, -as Ham of Canaan (eh. ix. 22; vide ver. 24)-the brother of Japheth the elder. Either the eldest brother of Japheth (Syriac, .Arabic, Yulgate, Gescniua, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch) ; or the brother of Japheth who was older (LXX., Symmachus, Onkelos, Raschi, Aben Ezra, Luther, Clericus, Michaelis, Dathe) ; or the elder of Japheth's brothers, as distinguished from Ham the younger, i. e. the son who was older than Ham, but younger than Japheth (Murphy, Quarry; vide eh. v. 32). Even to him were children born.

entries.title: GEN 10:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - The children of Shem were twenty-six in number, of whom five were sons. Elam. Elymais, a region adjoining Susiana and Media, stretching from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea ; the people first met with as Persians. And Asshnr. The ancestor of the .Assyrfans (vide ver. 11). And Arphaxad. A region in the north of Assyria; the .Arrhapacitis ofPtolemy (Rosen• mliller, Keil, Kalisch). The explanation of the name is " fortress of the Chaldmans" (Ewald) ; "highland of the Chaldmans" (~nobel), And Lud. The Lydians of Asia Minor, to which they e.ppear to have migrated from the land of Shem (Josephus, Bochart, Keil, Kalisch). And Aram. "The high land ;" Mesopotamia being the Aram of the two rivers, and Syria the Arnm of Damascus. Yer. 23.-And the children of Aram; Uz, from whom was named the land of Uz (Job i. 1), south-east of Palestine, a tract of the Arabia Deserta. And Hnl. In Armenia (Josephu~); that part called Cholobetene, or house of Hui (Bochart) ; the Hylatm of Syria, near the Emesenes (Delitzsch) ; Crelesyria (Michaelis) ; Huleh, near the sources of tbe Jordnn (Murphy). And Gether-of uncertain situation-and Mash-traced in Mons Masius of Armenia (Boche.rt). Yer. 24. -And Arphaxad begat Sa.lab. Tho nr,tion descended from him has not been identified, though their name, ff Extension," may imply that they were early colonists. And Salah begat Eber. The father of the Hebrews or" Emigrants" (vide ver. 21). Yer. 25.-And unto Eber were born two sons: the name ofonewas Peleg. "Division," from palag, to divide ; cf. 1Ti>.ayoc and pelagus, a. division of the sea. For in his days waa the earth divided. At the confusion of tongues (Bochart, Roso,nmiiller, Keil, Lange, Murphy) ; at an earlier separation of the earth's population (Delitzsch), of which there is no record or trace. And his brother's name was Joktan. Father of the Arabians, by whom he is called Kachtan.

entries.title: GEN 10:26–30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Joktan bega.t Almode.d. Usually said to be Yemen. And She• leph. The Salapenoi of Ptolemy, belonging to the interior of Arabia. And Haza.rma.veth. Hadramant, south-east of Arabia (Bochart, Michaelis). And Jera.h. Contiguous to Hadramaut. And Hadoram. .Adramitm of Ptolemy, or the Atramitm of Pliny (Bochart). And Uza.l. .Awzal, the capital of Yemen (Bochart). And Diklah. The palm-bearing region of .Arabia Felix (Bochart) ; a tribe between the mouth of the Tiber and the Persian Gulf (Michaelis). And Oba!, and Abim.ael, whose settlements a.re not known. And Sheba. Vide supra, ver. 7. And Ophir. In .Arabia; probably in Oman, on the Persian Gnlf (Michaelis, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch, Keil), though it has also been located in India (Joscphus, Vitringa, Gesenius, Delitzsch). The gold of Ophir cele• brated (1 Kings iL 27, 28; 2 Chron. ix. 10, 13, 21). And Havilah. The Chaulan in Arabia. Felix, but vide supra, ver. 7. And Jobab. The Jobabit:e of Ptolemy, near the Indian Sea (Michaelis, Rosenmiiller) ; but more probably a. tribe in Arabia Descrta if Jobab =Arabic .jebab, e. desert (Bochart, Gesenius, Kalisch). All these were the sons of Joktan. And their dwelling was from Meeha. The seaport of Muza (Bochart) ; Messene, at the mouth of the Tigris (Michaelis, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch). As thou goest into Zephar. Zafar or Dhafari, on the coast of the Hadramut. The difficulty of identifying a seaport town with a mountain is got over (Kalisch) by reading ff to the" instead of a. monnt Qf the east-the thu, riferous range of hills in the vicinity. Vcrs. 31, 32.-These are the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations. The pedigree of the Shemite tribes is closed with the customary formula (vide ver. 6) ; that which follows being the concluding formula for the entire table of nations. These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations (literally, according to their Th6ldoth, or historical developments), in their nations: and by these (literally, from these) were the nations divided (or, did the nations scatter themselves) in the earth after the flood.

entries.title: GEN 10:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The ethnological ,·egister. I. PROCLAIMS TRE UNITY OF THE RACE. 1. It declares a.11 the successive families of mankind to have sprung from a common stock. Diverse as they now are in their geographical situations, ethnic relations_ GENEUB, K physical capabilities, national peculie.ritiee, according to the doctrine of thie genell• logical table they nil trace their origin to Noe.h and his sons. 2. It condemns nil those theories which derive man from eever11l pairs. Equally the heathen superstition which assigned to each particular region its own .Autocltthones and the modern scientific dogma of vnrieties of species and distinct centres of prdpngation is here condemned. ~ven no:w ethnolog1st~, archre~logiste, nnd philologists of the highest repute lend then sanction to the sublime sentiment of the grent Mars' hill prencher that "God h1 ~th made of ol?-e blood all nations of men for to dwell upon all the foe~ of the earth. The anatomical strncture of the human frame, especially of the brnin and skull,_ the physiological properties and funct~ons P?Bsessed by the body, tho psycholog:ical natu_re of i:nan, and the power of mdefimte propng·ation, which are the same m all nations, with the ascertamed results of comparative grammar which ha,e alre.ady traced back all existing languages to three primitive branches tend in a po':erful degree to confi1;11 the ~octrine ~hich this table t~ac_hes. ~- It implies certam other truths on which Scnpture with equal emphasis msists such as the brotherhood of man, the universnl corruption of the race, and tho ~ecessity and unfrersa.lity of Christ's redemption. II. ATTESTS THE mnsroN of the RACE. 1. It asserts the/act of the division. It i;tates ihat in the days of Peleg the earth's population was divided. The means employed are described in the succeeding chapter. 2. It confirms the truth of this division. Had the confusion at Babel not occurred, and the subsequent dispersion not followed, this t.able could not have been written. Its existence as a literary document in the time of Moses authenticates the fact which it reports. 3, It defines the e:tieni of this division. It shows that the scattered race were to be split up into nations, families, tongues. • III. ILLUSTRATES THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE RACE. The geogrnphical distribution of the earth's population wai:-1. .Effectedin an orderly manner. They were neither scattered promiscuously nor suffered to wander and settle at hazard. Divided into tribes and nations according to their tongues and dialects of speech, they were allocated to distinct portions of the earth's surface. 2. Specially adapted to the cltaracters and destinies of the several natwns. The operation of purely natural principles makes it impossible that tribes can permanently settle in countries that are either incapable of yidding to them a maintenance or affording an outlet to their powers. More extensive infonnation would doubtless enable the suitability of each locality in tbie t.able to the occupying people to be exhibited ; but in broad outline it is perceptible even here-Japheth, whose destiny it was to spread abroad, being established on the coasts of the Euxine, the Caspian, and the Mediterranean; Ham finding rest in the warmerclimates, whose enervating influences tended largely to de-elop hie peculiar character, and ultimately to lay him open to subjection by the more vigorous rnces of the North; and Shem, whose function in the Divine economy it was to conserve religion and religious ~t~, being ~oncentrated mainly in the Tigris and Euphrates valley. 3. The result ofIhmne appointment. Moses (Deut. mii, 8) and Paul (.Acts xvii. ~6) conspire to. r~present the allocation of. territory to the different races of mankind as the handiwork of God (the special .means employed for the breaking up of th~ originally ~ite~ family o~ Noah's sons is detailed in the ensuing chapter); the import of which IB, that nations he.ve a Godassigned title to the count:i,es _which they occ~py. f· The Divinely:order~d distribution of the earth's population lB capable of being disturbed by the sinful interference of man. Instances of this e.ppear in the present table, e. g. the intrusion of the Cushite into Shinar, and of the Canaanite into what originally belonged to Shern. IV. PREDICTS THE FUTURE OF THE RACE, As it were, the separntion of tl1c earth's population into races and the mo:ing of them ?ut~ard to tl~eir respective habitations was the starting of them on the Imes along whwh 1t was designed they should accomplish their respective destinies and common work. They were meant to overspread the globe; and this was the in~tiation o~ a grea~ movcf!lent which would only terminate in the complete occupation of their God-given heritage. Lcsscm.B :-1. 'fhe equal rights of men. 2. The sinfulness of wars of aggression. 8, The hopefulness of emigration

entries.title: GEN 10:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Nimrod. 1. His ancestral pedigree-a Cushite. 2. His e:nly occupat.ion -11 hunter of wild beasts, a pioneer of civilisation. 3. His rising ambition-he began to be n "Gibbor," or mighty one. 4. His regal authority-the beginning of his kingdom was Babel. 5. His extending empire-out of that land went he forth into Asshur. 6. His posthumous renown: "Wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod."-W.

entries.title: GEN 10:15–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: --The Canaanites. I. DESCENDANTS OF A WICKED FATHER. II. b- IIERITons OF AN AWFUL CURSE. III. POSSESSORS OF A FAIR DO)!AJN. IV. Ui:!URPEI\B OF ANOTHER'S LAND. Lessons:-1. Wicked men and nations may greatly prosper. 2. Prosperity sometimes leads to greater wickedness. 3. The greatest prosperity cannot turn aside the punishment of sin.-W.

entries.title: GEN 10:25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Peleg, or the division of the people. I. WHE!l IT TOOK PLACE. In the fourth generation after the Flood. II. How IT WAS EFFECTED. 1. By the Divine interposition. 2. By the confur;ion of tongues. III. FoR WHAT IT WAS DESIGNED. 1. To punish sin. 2. To separate the Church. 3. To occupy the earth. IV. BY WHAT IT WAS REMEMBERED. The naming of Eber•s son. Learn-1. To read well the signs of the times. 2. To understand well the cause of God's judgments. 3. To remember well the gift of God's mercies.-W.

entries.title: GEN 10:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Nations. I. THEIR ROOTS. Individuals. II. THEIR RISE. 1. As to time, after the Flood. 2. As to ca11Se, Divine impulse. 3. As to instrumentality, variation of speech. III. T1rnrn CHARACTERISTICS. 1. A common head. 2. A common tongue. 3. ..1 common land. IV. THEIR DESTINIES..To overspread the earth.-W.

entries.title: GEN 11:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Ancl the whole earth. I. e. the entire population oftheglobe, and not simply the inhabitants of the land of Shinar (Inglis ; cf. eh. ix. 29}. Was. Prior to the dispersion spoken of in the preceding chapter, though obviously it may have been,subsequent to thnt event, if, ns the above-named author believes, the present paragraph refers to the Shcmites alone. Of one language. Literally, of one lip, i. e. one articulation, or one way of pronouncing their vocables. And of one speech. Literally, one (kind of) word.s, i. o. the matter as well as the form of human speech was the same. The pl'imitive language wns believed by the Rnbbins, the Fathers, and the older theologians to be Hebrew ; but Keil decla1·es this view to be utterly untenable. Bleck shows thnt the family of Ahraham spoke in Ammnie (cf. Jegu-sahaduth11, eh. xxxi. 47), and that the patriarch himself acquired Hebrew from the Canannites, who may themselves hnve o.dopted it from tho early Semites whom they displaced, While regnl'lling neither the Aramaic, Hebrew, nor Arabic 11s the original tongue or mankind, he thinks the Hebrew approaches nearest the primitive Semite language out of which all three were developed.

entries.title: GEN 11:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Ancl it came to pass, as they journeyed. Literally, in theirjourneyings. The root (Vj:)l, to pull up, as, e. g., the stakes of a tent when a camp moves, Isa. x.,:riii. 20) suggests the idea of the migration of nomadic hordes (et: eh. xii. 9 ; xxxiii. 17). From the eut. .tlb or,.'ente (AncientVersions. Calvin, et alii), meaning either that they started from Armenia, which was in the eOJ!t respectu terrce Canaan (Luther), or from that portion of the Assyrian empire which was cast of the Tigris, and called Orientalis, as distinguished from the Occidentalis on the west (Bochart) ; or tho.t they fi.nlt travelled westwards, following the direction or the Euphrates in one of its uprr branches (Bush) ; or that, having ronme to the east of Shinar, they ultimately returned occidentem versus (Junius). 'l'he phrase, however, isadmittmlto bemore correctly rendered act orienten~ (Drusius, Lange, Keil, Murphy), ns in eh. xiii. 11. Kalisch interprets gener- 11Jly in oi'i,mte, 11greeing with Luth~r thl\t 11 2 IG4 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. iu. 1-9. the migrittions Pre yfowcd by the writer as tnking rlnce in the east; while T. Lewis prefers to rend from one front part (the originnl meaning of kedent) to anotheromrnrds. That they found a plain. i"l~Jt~; not n •~_l_lcf be!ween mom~tain ranges, as· in Deut. nu. , ; Ju.. 11; rs. c1v. 8, bnt a widelyextended plain (,r,viov, LXX.), like tlrnt in 'l'l'hich Babylon was situated (Herod., lib. i. 178, .,,,,a, EV ...,oiq, µ•ytiXq,; cf. Strnbo, lib. ii. 109). In the land of Shinar. Babylonia (cf. eh. x. 10). The derivation of the term is unl"T!own (Gesenius), though it probably meant the land of the two rivers (Alford). Its absence from ancient monuments (Rawlinson) suggests that it was the Jewish name for Chaldrea.. And they dwelt there. Yer. 3.-And they s&id one to another. Literally, a numto hisneighbour; a,,0pw7roc ,rp .,,.X,1crio1, a&rov (LXX. ). Go to. A hortatory expletirn =come on (Anglice). Let us make brick Nilbenah lebenim; literally, let us brick bricks; r.X,v0tvuwµtv ,rXiv0ovc (LXX.) ; la:terifecimus la:teres (Calvin) ; lehenah (from laban, to be white), being so called from the white and chalky clay of which bricks were made. And burn them thoroughly. Literally, burn them to a burning; venisrephah lisrephah, a second alliteration, which, however, the LXX. fails to reproduce. Bricks were usually sun-dried ; these, being designed to be more durable, were to be calcined through the agency of fire, a proof that the tower-builders were acquainted with the art of brick-making. And they had-literally, and there was to tlwm--brick for stone. Chiefly because of the necessities of the place, the alluvial plain of Babylon being void of stones and full of clay ; a proof of the greatness of their crime, seeing they were induced to undertake the work nonfacilitate operis, nee aliis commodis, q= se ad manum o.fferrent (Calvin) ; scarcely because bricks would better endure fire than would stones, the second destruction of the world by fire rather than water being by this time a common expectation (Com. aLapidc). entries.content: -And the Lord said-within himself, and to himself (vide ver. 8); expressiva of the formation of a Divine resolution (cf. eh. vi. 7)-Eehold, the people-Cl)l, from root signifyingto bincl to"ether, expresses the idea of association; 11l, from a root signifying to swell (Lange), to flow together (Gesenius), to gather together (Fi.irst), conveys the notion of a confluxus homimim. T. Lewis connects it with the sense of interiority, or exclusion, which is common in the Chaldee and Syriac-is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do. One race, ono tongue, one purpose. The words indicate unity of effort, as well as concentration ofdesign, on the part ofthe builders, and a certain measure of success in the achievement of their work. And now nothing will be restrained from them. Literally, there will not be cut off from them anything; ov~ ·~~Ei,/m ,i,r' avrwv ,rav-;a (LXX.); non desistent a coqitationibus suis (Yulgate, Luther) ; i. e. nothing will prove too haru for their daring. entries.title: GEN 11:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -So (literally, and) the Lord scattered them abroad (ns the result of the confusion of their speech) upon the face of all the earth : and they left off to build the oity. I. e. 11s 11 united community, which does not preclude tho idea of tho Babylonians subsequently finishing tho structure. Ver. 9,-Therefore is the name of it called Eitbel. For Balbel, confusion (11vn:v11,,, LXX., Josephus), from Balal, to confound; the derivation given by the sacred writer in the following clause (cf. for the elision of the letter l, totaphah for tophtaphah,, Exod. xiii. 16, nnd cochav for covcav, Gen. x.-uvii. 9). Other uerivationssuggested are Bab-Bel, tho gato or C?Urt of Belus (Eichhorn, Lange), nn explanation of the term which Fiirst thinks not impossible, and Kalisch declu.res 16R THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, XI, 1-9. "can sCR.rcely be overlooked;" and Bab-iJ,, the gate of God (Rosenmiiller, Gesonius, Colenso) ; but the first is based upon n purely mythical personage, Bel, the imllginary founder of the city ; and the second, if even it were supported by evidence, whicl1 it is not, is not so likely es that given by llfoses. Beo&11Be the Lord did there confound -ho"" is not explained, but has been conjectured to be by &n entirely inward process, nz., changingthe ideas associatedwith words (Koppen) ; by aprocesa wholly outward, viz., an alteration of the mode of pronouncing words (Hoffman), though more probably by lJoth (Keil), or possibly by the first insensibly leading to the second-the language of all the earth : and from thence did the Lord scatter them. As the result not simply of their gromng discord, di.ssensio aninwrum, per quam factum sit, ut qui tui-rem struebant distracti sint in contraria studia et consilia (Vitringa) ; but chiefly of their diverging tongues-a statement which issupposed to conflict with the findings of modern philology, that the existing differences of language among mankinJ are the result of slo1" and gradual changes brought about by the operation of natural causes, such &S the influence of loc:i.lity in changing and of time in corrupting human speech. But (1) mo- Jcrn philology hwi as yet only succeeded in explaining the growth of what might he called the sub-modifications of human ~re~ch, and is confessedly unable to account for what appears to be its main division into a Shemitic, nn Aryan, and a Turanian tongue, which may have been produced in the sudden and miraculous way described ; and (2) nothing prevents us from regarding the two events, the confusion of tongues and the dispersion of the nations, &S occurring simultaneously, and even acting and reacting on each -0ther. As the tribes parted, their speech wonld diverge, Rud, on the otherhand, as the tongues differed, those who spoke the same or coguate dialects would draw together and draw apart from the rest. We may even suppose that, prior to the building of Babel, if any of the human family had begun to spread themselves abroad upon the surface of the globe, a slight diversity in human speech had begun to show itself; and the truthfulness of the narrative will in no wise be endangered by admitting that the Divine interposition at Babel may have consisted in guickening & natural process which had already commenced to operate; nay, we are rather warranted to conclude that the whole work of subdividing hwnan speech was not compressed into nmoment of time, but, after receiving this special impul~e, was len to develop and complete itself as tho nations wandered farther aud ever farther from the plains or Rhinar (cf. Kurtz, ' Hist. of thQ Old Coven:u:t,' vol. i. pp. 108-117 (Clark'A For. Theol. Lib.), 11nd 1 Qua11-y on Genesis,' pp. 195-206). • CHALD..EAN LEGEND OF TIIE TOWER I.JI! BAnEr..·-Berosus, indeed, docs not refer to it. nnd early writers arc obliged to have rocoms~ to somewhat doubtful authorities to confirm it. Eusebius, e. g., quotes Abydenus as snying that "not long after the Flood, the ancient race of men were so puffed up with their strength and tallness of stature that they began to despise nnd contemn tl,10 gods, and laboured to erect that very lofty tower which is now called Babylon, intending thereby to scale the heavens. But when the building approached the sky, behold, the gods called in the aid of the winds, and by their lielp overturned the tower, and cast it to the ground ! The name or'the ruin is still called Babel, because until this time all men had used the same speech ; but now there was sent upon them a confusion of many anu diverse tongues" (' Prae~v.,' ix. 14}. But the diligence of the late George Smith ha~ been rewarded by discovering the fragment of an .Assyrian tablet (marked K. 3657 in British Museum) containing an account of the building ofthe tower, in which the gods are represented as being angry at the work and confounding the speech of the builders. In zol. i., lines 5 and 6 (according to W. St. C. entries.title: GEN 11:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The tower-builders of Babel. I. THE IMPIETY OF 1'Hlmt DESIGN, I. ..tl.m'bition. They were desirous of achieving fame, or "a name" for themselves, Whether in this there wae a covert sneer at the exaltation promised to the Sliemitcs, OH. XI. 1-0.] 'NIE BOOK OF GENESIS. 167 or aimlllY o, diepl11.y of th!lt lust of glory which natively resides within the fallen hcBrt., 1t was essentially a guilty purpose by which they were impelled, In only ona direction is ambition perfectly legitimate, viz., in the direction of moral and spiritual goodness, as distinguisl1ed from tempornl and material greatness (cf. 1 Cor. xii. 31). Only tl1en may the passion for glory be exuberantly gratified, whc,n its object is the living God instead of puny o.nd unworthy self (cf. Jer. ix. 23, 24; 1 Cor. i. 29, 31). 2. Rebellion. Setting its head among the clouds, " exalting its throne above the stars," it wns designed to be an act of insolent defiance to the will of Heaven. The city and the tower of Babel had their origin in deliberate, determined, enthusiastic, exulting hostility to the Divine purpose that they should spread themselves abroad over the face of the whole earth. And herein lies the essence of all impiety: whatever thought, counsel, word, or work derives its inspiration, be it only in an infinitesimal degree, from antagonism to the mind of God is sin. Holiness is but another name for obedience. II. TrrE MAGNITUDE 011' THEIR ENTERPRISE. The undertaking of the tower-builders was-1. Sublimely conceived. The city was to ward off invasion from without, and to counteract disruption from within. Gathering men of a common tongue into n common residence, engaging them in common pursuits, and providing them with common interests was the sure way to make them strong. If this was the creative idea out of which cities sprung, the Cainites, if not pious, must at least have been possessed of genius. Then the tower was to touch the skies. Unscientific perhaps, but scarcely irrational; "an undertaking not of savages, but of men possessed with the idea of somehow getting above nature." .And though certainly to aspire after such supremacy over nature in the spirit of a godless science which recognises no power or authority superior to itself was the very sin of these Bnbelites, yet nothing more convincingly attests the essential greatness of man than the ever-widening control which science is enabling him to assert over the forces of matter. 2. Hope· fully begun. The builders were united in their language and purpose. The place was convenient _for the proposed erection. The most complete preparations were made for the structure. The work was commenced with determination and amid universal enthusiasm. It had all the conditions of success, humanly speaking---one mind, one heart, one hand. 3. Sudilenly abandoned. "They left off to build the city." So the most prosperous undertakings often terminate in miserable failure. The mighty enterprise was mysteriously frustrated. So have all such wicked combinations in times past been overthrown. Witness the great world empires of Babylon, Persia, Greece, Rome. So in the end will the great mystery of iniquity, of which that early Babel was the first type. III. TuE INSPECTJON OF THEI!l. WORK. 1. No work ofman can hope to escape the !ye of God. Even now he is minutely acquainted with the thoughts, nnd words, and works, and ways of every individua} on the earth (Prov. xv. 3 ; Heh. iv. 13), while there is. a day coming when II there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed" (Matt. x. 26). 2. Every work ofman shall beJudged at the bai· of God (Eccles. xii. 14; 1 Cor. iii. 13). The Divine verdict upon human undertakings will often strangely conflict with the judgments of men. IV. THE CONFUSION OF THEI!l. TONGUES. 1. .As a fact in the experi,mce of the builders, it was-(1) Unc!tallengeable. They could not understand one another, so that they could not doubt that a change of some kind had passed upon their speech ; and observation convinces us that as men have now a variety of tongues, something must have broken up the original unity of speech. (2) Myste:rious. It is not likely that these primitive builders understood how their language had been transmuted. Modern philology has no certain word to utter upon the subject yet. (3) Supernatural. It was effected by the immediate agency of God. If even natural causes had begun to operate, they were quickened by the Divine action. Believers in a God who made the tongue of man should have no difficulty in believing· in a God who changed the tongue of man. 2. .As a judgment on the persons of the builders, it was-(1) Unexpected in its coming, as are all God's _judgm_ents, like the Flo?d and l~ke the corning o-fthe Son 0£ man. (2) Deserved by its subJects. Caught, as 1t were, m the very act of insubordination, guilty of nothing short of treason against the King of heaven, they were visited with summary and condign chastisement. So are all God's punishments richly merited by those on whom they fall. (3) Appropriate in its clutracte'!'. 168 'l'IlE BOOK OF GENESIS. ton. XI. 1-9. It 'l\'as fitting thnt they who had abused their oneneaa of speech, which wae designed for their good, to keep _th~m in _the Church, should be punished ~ith variety of tongues. (4) Effectual in its design. Sent to scatter them abroad, it succeeded in its aim. Man's designs often fail; God's never. V. THE DISPERSION OF THEIR RANKS. 1. Judi,c,ial, in its character. In its inci- ?CDCe on the builders it wore a punitive aspect.. Providences that are full of bleesmgs for the good are always laden with curses to the wicked. 2. Beneficial in its PU;?J?OSif; '.fhe scattering of t~e earth's population over the surface of the g-lobe wne origmauy mte!1d~d f~r ~hat it has eventually tun!e? out ~o be, a blessing for the race. 3. Unlimued in its extent. Though the or1gmal dispersion could not have ?arried the tribes to an)'. remote distances from Sh~nar, the process then hegun was mtended not to rest until the earth was fully occupied by the children of mon. VI. THE MEMORIAL OF THEIR FOLLY. This was-1. .Exceedingly expi·essii•e. The unfinished tower was designated Babel, or Confusion. It is well that things should be called by their right names. The name of Babel was an epitome of the foolish aim and end of the builders. The world is full of such monuments of folly. 2. Selj-ajfixed. So God often compels " men of corrupt minds " and " reprobate concerning the faith" not only to manifest, but also to publish, their own folly. 3. LO'll,fl· enduring. It continued to be known as Babel in the days of Moses and long afteran emblem of that shame which shall eventually be the portion of all the wicked. Learn-1. The sinfulness of ambition. 2. The folly of attempting to resist God. 3. The power of God in carrying out his purposes. 4. The mercy of God in dividing the nations. 5. The ability of God to regather the divided nations of the earth. HmULIES BY VARIOUS AUTHORS. ,ers. 1-9.-0rder broughtforth. We are now to trace the rise of the kingdom of God among the nations. Already in the case of Nimrod, the mighty hunter before the Lord, that is, by pennission of Divine providence, the antagonism between the 1.ingdom of God and the kingdoms of this world has been symbolised. Now we find the concentration of the world's rebellion and ungodliness in the false city, type of the worldly power throughout the Sciiptures. It is on the plain of Shinar to which the early migration from the East directed the course of mankind. We are not told at what time the settlement in Shinar took place. As the account of the confusion of tongues is intioduced between the larger genealogy and the lesser, we may infer that its object is to account for the spread of nations. Whether we take this Babel to be Nimrod's Babel or an earlier one is of very little consequence. The whole narrative is full of Divine significance. Notice- I. MAN's BillEL IS A LYING PRETENSION. It rests on an attempt to substitute hie o,rn foundation of society for God's; it is-1. False safety-the high tower to keep above the flood. 2. False ambition-reaching unto heaven, making a name with bricks and mortar. 3. False unity-" lest we be scattered abroad." These nre the characteristics of all Babel despotisms. Material foundations to rest upon ; lying structures built upon them. II. Goo's KINGDOM IS NOT REALLY HINDERED DY MAN'S REBELLION. He suffers the Babel structure to be reared, but by his judgments scatters both the men and their projects, making the rebellious conspiracy against himself prepare the way for hie ultimate universal triumph. So it has been all through the history of the world, and especially i=ediately before the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. The confusion of tongues was a judgment and at the same time a mercy. 'fhoee that are filled with such ambitions and build upon such foundations are not fit to dwell together in one place. It is better they should be divided. The investigations into comparative grammar and the genesis of human language point to some primitive seat of .the earliest form of speech in the neighbourhood indicated. It was certainly the result of the false form of society with which men began, the Nimrod empire, that they could not remain gathered in one community; and as they spread they lost their knowledge of their original language, and were confounded because they understood not one another's speech. It is remarkable that in the beginning of the kingdom of Christ, the true city of God which shall overspread the world, the Spirit besto.ved the gift of tongues, as if to signify that the Babel of man's lying ambitions was to on. :11. 1-9.J THE BOOK O:B' GENESIS. 169 oease, nnd in the truth of the gospel men would be united ae one family, 11 under• etanding ono anoUrnr'e epeech."-R Vor. 1.-Unity of [<11T1,guage. 1. The original birthright of the human race. 2. The )oat inheritllnce of sinful men. 3. The ultimate goal of the Christian dispensation. 4. The recovered heritage of redeemed humanity.-W.

entries.title: GEN 11:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Note-1. The benefit of a wandering condition. It sometimes prevents the rise of sinful thoughts nnd wicked deeds. So long as the primitive nomads '(,Vere trnvelling from station to station they did not think of either rebellion or ambition. So Israel followed God fully in the wilderness. 2. The danger of a settled state. Established in the fat plain of Sl,inar, they wanted a city and a tower. So Israel in Canaan waxed fat and kicked, So Moab, having been at ease from hi~ youth, retained his scent unchanged. So comfortable surroundings often lead men from God.-W.

entries.content: -Ancient brickmakers. I. IN SHINAR. Examples of (1) ingenuity, (2) earnestness, (3) perseverance, (4) unity in sin. II. IN EGYPT (Exod. v. 7). Illustrations of (1) the bondage, (2) the degradation, (3) the misery, (4) hopelessness, of sin.-W.
