entries.content: -The tower of Babel. I. .A. MONUMENT OF MAN's-1. Sinful ambition. 2. Laborious ingenuity. 3. Demonstrated feebleness. 4. Stupendous folly. II. A MEMORIAL OF GoD's-1. Overruling providence. 2. Resistless power. 3. Retributive juatice. 4. Beneficent purpose.-W.

entries.title: GEN 11:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God's city or man's city. "And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and n tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth." In the world after tLe Flood we trace the outlines of the gospel dispensation. To Noah was revealed" good will toward men ;" the acceptance of sacrifice ; faith us the condition and channel of blessing; nnd work, to sprend the knowledge of and trust in his name, i. e. whnt he is pleased to reveal concerning himself. But" the carnal mind" was there resisting the Spirit. Noah and his seed were to replenish the earth (eh. ix. 1; cf. Mark xvi. 15). They were promised snfety from beasts, of whom, if separated, they might be afro.id (eh. ix. 2; cf. Matt. x. 29, 31; Luke :x:. 19). Here was a trial of faith and obedience (cf. Exod. xxxiv. 24). But men had not faith, would not trust, would not go forth at his word. Their calling was to seek God's city (Heb. xi. 10-16), to Jive as citizens of it (Phil. iii. 20). They chose n city for themselves ; earthly security, comforts, luxuries. Called to glorify God's name, their thought was to ma'lte a name for themselves. Self was the moving power. The name of God is the trust of his people (Ps. x.x. 7 ; Prov. xviii. 10) ; a centre of unity to all his children in every place. They tru,sted in themselves; would be like God to themselves. The tower, the work of their own hands, was to be their centre of unity; and the nnme of it came to be Babel, i. e. confusion (cf. Mntt. xv. 13). Love draws mankind together. Self-seeking tends to separation. God bade them spread that they might be united in faith and in ,vork. They chose their own way of union, and it led to dispersion with no bond of unity. I. WE ARE CALLED TO BUILD THE CITY OF GoD (Heh. xii. 22). To prepare the way for Rev. xxi. 3. The gifts of Christ are made effectual by the work of men. That city, built of living atones (1 Pet. ii. 5), cemented not with slime, but by unity of fnith (Ephes. iv. 3). And a tower, a centre of unity, the "good confession" (Rom. xiv. 11 ; Phil. ii. 11). And to obtain a nnme, to be confessed by the Lord before tho angels, to be acknowledged ushis"brethren," and stamped with the "new name." And a promise given, as if pointing to Bnbel: "Your labour is not iu vain in the Lord." II. MANY HAVE NO MIND 'I'O BUILD. They Jove ease and have no earnestness, triflers with time, or direct their earnestness to earthly prizes-a name among men. III. EVEN BELIEVERS ARE OFTEN THUS HINDERED. There may be spiritual selllshness along with really spiritual aims. The multitude of cares may distract the soul. Temptations may wear the garb of zeal, or of charity, or of prudence. W ntch 8.Ild pray. God's faithfulness will not £nil (1 Cor. x. 13).-M. 170 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. ,·er. 5.-Tlie ct'.ties of men and, the city qf God (Gen. xi. 6; Heh. xi. 16). I, THElR DtTILDERS. entries.title: GEN 11:26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Tere.h lived seventy years, e.nd bege.t Abram. First named on account of his spiritual pre-eminence. If Abram was Terah's eldest son, then, as Abram was seventy-five years of age when Terah died (eh. xii. 4), Terah's whole lifo could only have been 145 years. Bnt Terah lived to the age of 205 years (eh. xi. 32); therefore Abram was born in Tcrah's 130th year. This, however, makes it surprising that .Abraham should have reckoned it impossible for him to have a son at 100 years (eh. xvii. 17); only, after having lived so long in childless wedlock, it was not strange that he should feel somewhat doubtful of any issue by Sarai. Kalisch believes that S:ephen (Acts vii. 4) made a mistake in sayinl!; Terah died before his son's migrati0n from Charran, and that he really survived that event by sixty years ; while the Samaritan text escapes the difficulty by shortening the life of Terah to 145 years. And Nahor, who must have been younger than Haran, since he married Haran's daughter. And He.ran, who, as the eldest, must have been born in Terab's seventieth year. Thus the second family register, like the first, concludes after ten generations with the bu-th of three sons, who, like Noah's, are mentioned not in tho order of their ages, but of their spiritu.~l pre-eminence. What guarantee then do we possess that in every iustance the registered son was the firstborn1 Jn the casa of Arphaxad this is almost implied in the statement that ho was born two years after the Flood. But if the case of Eber were parallel with that of Terah, and Joktan were the son that he begat in his thirty-fourth year, then obviously the birth of Peleg, like that ofAbram,may have happened sixty yelll'B later; in which case it is apparent that any reckoning which proceeded on the minute verbal accuracy of the registered numbers would beentirely nt fault. Tho palpable artificiality also of these later t.'tblcs renders them oven Jess worthy of credit than the Hebrew. The introduction by the LXX. of Cainan 11s the son of Arphaxad, though seemingly confirmed by Luke (Luke iii. 35, 36), is clearly an interpolation. It does not occur in the LXX. version of l Chron. i. 24, and is not found in either the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Targums or the ancient versions, in Josepbus or Philo, or in the Codex Beza of the Gospel of Luke. Its appearance in Luke (and probably also in the LXX.) can only beexplained as an interpolation. Wordsworth is inclined to regard it as authentic in Luke, and to suppose that Cainaan was excluded from the Mosaic table either to render it symmetrical, as Luke's table is rendered symmetrical by its insertion, or because of some moral offence, which, though necessitating his expulsion from a Hebrew register, would not prevent his ro11ppearance in his proper place under the gospel.

entries.title: GEN 11:10–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -From Shem to A.fo·am. I. THE s;c/ABATION OF THE GODLY SEED. The souls th:it constitute the Church of God upon the earth are always, as these Hebrew patriarchs-I. Known to God; and that not merely in the mass, but as individuals, or units; nor simply superficially and slightly, but minutely and thoroughly. He knows the fathers they descend from, thP families they belong to, the names by which they are designated, the number of years they live, and the children they leave behind them on the earth (cf. Ps. i. 6; 2 Tim. ii. 19). 2. Separated by Cod. This was one of the great ends contemplated by the division of the people which happened in the days of Peleg, which was designed to eliminate the Shemites from the rest of mankind. Then the migration of the sons of Eber contributed further to the isolation of the children of the promise. And, lastly, the selection of the 1,on, not always the firstborn, through whom the hope of the gospel was to be carried on tended in the same direction. So God afterwards separated Ierael from the nations. So be still by his providence and bis word calls 011t and separates his people from the world (cf. 1 Kings viii. _53; 2 Cor. vi. 17). 3. H?noured_ before G?d_; by being selected as the vessels of his grae;e, the channels _of his prom10e, the mm1sters of his gospel, and the messengers of bis covenant, w~1le others are passed by; nnd by being written in God's hoe:~. of remembrance, wh1I~ ot~~rs are for&'~tten (cf. 1 Sam. ii. 30 • Ps. xci. 15 • Mai. m. 16 ; Matt. x. 32; 2 Tim. 11. 20; Hev. 111. 5). II. THE 'sHOBTENING ~F HUMAN LIFE. A second characteristic of the postdiluvian era. 1. A patentfact. Even Shem, the longest liver of the men of this period, did 11ot continue on the earth so long as La.mech, the shortest liver of the previous age, OH, XI. 10-26.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS 17S by 177 years; while the life of Arphaxad was shorter than that of his father by 162 years, and the days of Tera.hat the close dwindled down to 205 years. 2. A potent sermon. Whether the comparative brevity of life immediately after the Flood we.a due to any change in the physical constitution of man, or to the altered conditions of existence under the Noachic covenant, or to the grndnal deterioration of the race through the lapse of time, or to the direct appointment of Heaven, it was admirably fitted to remind them of-(1) The reality of sin. With its penalty descending so palpably e.nd frequently it would seem impossible to challenge the fact of their being e. guilty and condemned race. (2) Tlie necessity of repentance. Every death that happened would sound like a trumpet-call to sinful men to tnrn to God. (3) Tlie vanity of lije. The long terms of existence that were meted ont to men before the Flood might tempt them to forget the better country, even an heavenly, and to seek a permanent inheritance on eartl,; it would almost seem apparent to these short livers that no such inheritance could be obtained below. Alas that the shortness of man's career beneath the sun is now so familiar that it has well nigh ceased to impress the mind with anything I (4) Tlie certainty of death. When men's lives were counted by centuries it might be easy to evade the thought of death. When decades came to be enough to reckon up the longest term of existence, it could scarcely fail to remind them that "it was appointed unto all men once to die" III. THE NEARING Oil' TH!l: GOSPEL PROMISE. Ten generations further down the stream of time do we see the promise carried in this second genealogical table. It was-1. .A vindication ofthe Divinefaithfulness in adhering to his promise. Already twenty generations had come and gone, and neither was the promise forgotten nor had the holy line been allowed to -become extinct. Ever since Adam's day in Eden the covenant-keeping Jehovah had found a seed to serve him, even in the darkest times, and had been careful to raise up saints who would transmit the hope of the gospel to future times. It was a proof to the passing generations that God was still remembering his promise, and was intending to make it good in the fulness of the times, 2. A demonstration of God's ability to keep his promise. Not once through all the bygone centuries had a link been found wanting in the chain of saintly men through whom the promise was to be transmitted. It was a clear pledge tl111t God would still be able to supply the necessary links that might be required to carry it forward to its ultimate fulfilment.

entries.title: GEN 11:10–26

entries.title: GEN 11:10–32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Divine traditions. A genealogy of Shem and of Terah, in order to set forth clearly the position of Abraham e.nd the.t of his nephew Lot, and their connection with Ur of the Che.ldees and Canaan. The chosen family is a.bout to be separated from their country, but we a.re not told that there was no light of God shining in Ur of the Chaldees. Probably there was the tradition of Shem's knowledge handed down through the generations. Arphaxad was born two years after the Flood; Salah, thirty-seven years; Eber, sixty-seven years; Peleg, one hundred and one years; Ileu, one hundred and thirty-one years; Serug, one hundred and sh:ty-three years; Nabor, one hundred and ninety-three years; Terah, the father of- Abraham, two hundred and twenty-two years-no great length of time for traditions to be preserved. The call of Abram was not merely his separatiou from idolatry, but his consecration to the special vocation of founding the religious institutions which were to be connected with his family.-R. 174 THl:1: BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. xr. 27-89. PART III. THE PATRIA.ROHAL .A.GE OF THE WORLD. CH. XI. 27--L. 26. § 7. THE GENERATIONS OF TERAH (CH. XI. 27-XXV. 11). Yer. 2i.-Now (literally, and, intimating the close connection of the present ~ith the preceding section) these are the generations -the commencement of a new subdi,ision of the history (Keil), and neither the winding-up of the foregoing genealogy(' Speaker's Commentary') nor the heading only of the brief paragraph in vers. 2i--32 (Lange; 1:ide eh. ii. 4)-of Tera.h. Not of Abram ; partly because mainly occupied with the career not of Abram's son, in which case "the generations of Abram" would have been appropriate, bnt of Abram himself, Terah's son; rrnd partly owing to the subsidiary design to indicate Nahor's connection, through Rebekah, with the promiseJ. seed (cf. Quarry, p. 415). Terah begat Abram, "Father of Elc,ation," who is mentioned first not because he happened to be Terah's eldest son (Keil), which he was not (vide eh. :ri. 26), or because Moses was indifferent to the order in v,hich the sons of Terah were introduced (Cal-rin), but because of his spiritual preeminence as the head of the theocratic line (Wordsworth). Nahor, "Panting," not to be confounded with his grandfather of the same name (ver. 25). B:a.ran, "Tarrying," the eldest son of Terah (ver. 26), and, along ,,ith Abram and N.nhor, reintroduced into the narrative on account of his relationship to Lot and Milcah. That Terah had other sous (Calvin) does not appear probable. And B:a.ran begat Lot. tiiS ; of uncertain etymology, but may be =Cl~~, a concealed, i. e. obscure, low one, or perhaps a dark-coloured ob.e (Fiirst).

entries.title: GEN 11:28
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And B:a.ran·• died before his father. Literally, upon tlie face of his father; lvw1rrnv roii 1ra-rpoc av-roii (LXX); while his father -was alive (MDI1ster, Luther, Calvin, Rosenmiiller); perhaps also in his father's presence (Keil, Lange), though the Jewish fable may be discarded that Terah, 0.t this time an idolater, accused his sons to Nimrod, who cast them into a furnace for refusing to worship the fire-god, and that Haran perished in the flames in bis father's sight. The decease of Haran is the lint recorded instance 9f the natural death of a son before his father. In tho land of his nativity. 'Ev -r-g y-g ,J__ ly,vv,)O,, (LXX.). In Ur ofthe Che.ldees. Ur Kasdim (eh. xi. 81; xv. i; Neh. ix. 7). The Kasdim -formerlybelieved to have been Shemites on account of (1) Abram's settlement amona them, (2) the preservation of the nam~ Kesed among his kindred (eh. xxii. 22), (3) the close affinity to a Shemite tongue of the language known to modern philolo~sts as Chaldee, an Aramrean dialect dilfermg but slightly from the Syriac (Heeren), and (4) the supposed identity or intimate connection of the Babylonians 1,ith the .Assyrians (Niebuhr)-are now, with greater probability, and certainly '1ith closer adherence to Biblical hi.story (eh. x. 8-12), regarded as having been a Hamite race (Rawlinson, Smith) ; an opinion which receives confirmation from (1) the statement of Horuer('Ociy~s.,'i. 23, 24), that the Ethiopians were diviclcc! and dwelt at the ends of the earth, towartis the setting and the rising sun, i. e., accordmg to Strabo, on both sides of the Arabian Gulf; (2) tho primitive traditions (a) of the Greeks, who regarded Memnon, King of Ethiopia, as tho fow1der of Susa (Herod., v, 54), 0.nd the son of 'a Cissian· woman (Stmbo, xv. 3, § 2; (b) of the Nilotic Ethiopians, ·who claimed him as one of their monarchs; and .(c) of the Egyptians, who identifted him with their King Amunoph III., whose statue became known as the vocal l\Icmnon (vide Rawlinson's 'Ancient Monarchies,' vol. i. p. 48); (3) the testimon;r ofl\Ioses ofChorene (' History of .Armenia, i. 6), who connects in the closest way Babylonia, Egypt, and Ethiopia Proper, identifying Belue, King of Babylon, with Nimrod, and making him the son of llfizraim, or the grandson of Cush; and (4) the monumental history of Babylonia, which shows the language of tho earliest inscriptions, according to Rawlinson " dilforing greatly from the later Babylonian,'' to havo been that of a Tur:mian peoplo (cf. 'Records of the Past,' vol. iii. p. 3). Tho term Ur has been explained to be identical with 'Ir, a city (Rawlinson); the Zend Varc, a fo1-tress (Gesenius); U1·, the light country, i. e. tho land of the sun-rising (Fiirst); and even Ui·, CR. :u. 27-3~.] 'rH:m BOOK OF GENESIS. 175 fire, 'rith epM!al reference to the legendary furn!lco already referred to (Talmudists). Whether n district (LXX., Lange, Kalisch) or n. city (Josephus, Eusebius, Onkelos, Drusius, Keil, Mnl'}!hY, 'Speak~r's C?m• mentary '), its exo.ct site 1s uncert11rn. Rival claimants for tho !1onour of representing it hnve appeared in (1) a Persian fortress (Persicum Castcllum) of the name of Ur, mentioned by .Ammianus Marccllinus (lxxv. c. 8) ns lying between Nisibis and the Tigiis (Bochart, Michaelis, Rosenmiiller, Delitzsch) ; (2) the modem Orfah, tlie Edessa of the Greeks, situated "on one of the bare, rugged spurs which descend from the mountains of Armenia into the .Assyrian plains" (Stanley's 'Jewish Church,' i. 7); and (3) Hur, the most important of the early cspitals of Chaldrea, now the ruins of Mugheir, at no great distance from the mouth, and six miles to the west, of the Euphrates (Rawlinson's '.Ancient Monarchies,' i. 15, 16; Smith's '.Assyrian Discoveries,' xii. 233 ; ' Records of the Past,' vol. iii. p. 9). Yet none of them is. quite exempt from difficulty. .A military fort, to take the first-named location, does not appear a suitable or likely place for a nomade horde to settle in ; while the second has been reckoned too near Charran, the first place of encampment of the emi1-'Tants ; aml the third, besides being exceedingly remote from Charran, scarcely harmonises with Stephen's speech before the Sanhedrim (.Acts vii 2). Unless, therefore, Stephen meant Chaldrea when he said Mesopotamia (Dykes), and .Abra.ham could speak of Northern Mesopotamia as his country (eh. xxiv. 4), when in reality he belonged to Southern Babylonia, the identification of Ur of the Chaldees with the Mugheir ruin though regarded with most favour by archreologists, will continueto be doubtful ; while, if the clan march commenced at Etlessa, it will always require an effort to account for their coming to a halt so soon after sta.rting and so near home ; and the Nisibis station, though apparently more suitable than either in respect of distance, will remuin encumbered with its own peculiar difficulties. It would seem, therefore, as if the exact situation of the patriarchal town or country must be left undetermined until further light can be obtained.

entries.title: GEN 11:29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abram and Nahor took them wives (cf. eh. vi. 2) : the name of Abram's wife was Sarai. "My princess," from sarah, to rule (Gesenius, Lange) ; "Strife" (Kalisch, Murphy): "Jah is ruler" (Furst). The LXX. write l:apa, changing afterwards to l:,ip{,a to correspontl with Sarah, That Sarai was Iscah (Josephus, Augustine, •Jerome, Jonathan) has been. inferred from eh. xx. 12; but, though receiving apparent sanction from ver. 31, this opinion "is not supported hy any solid argument" (Rosenmi.iller). And the name of Na.hor's wife, Milca.h (Queen, or Counsel), the daughter of Haran, i. e. Nahor's niece. Marriago with a half-sisteT or a niece was afterwards forbitlden by the Mosaic code (Levit. xviii. 9, 14). The father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah, whose name" Seer" may have been introduced into the narrative like that of Naarnah (eh. iv. 22), as that ofan eminent lady connected with the family (Mnrphy). Ewald's hypothesis, that Iscah was Lot's wife, is pure conjecture.

entries.title: GEN 11:30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - But Sarai was barren; she had no child. Perhaps in contrast to :\Iilcah, who by this time had begun to have a family (Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 11:31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Terah took-an act of pure human volition on the part of Tcroh (Kalisch); under the guidance of Gocl's ordinary providence (Keil) ; but more probably, ns .AbJRm was called in Ur (i·,:de infra), prompted by a knowledge of his son's call, ancl a desire to participate in his son's inheritance (Lange)-Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife. The Samaritanreads, "ancl 1Iilcah his daughter-in-law, the wives of Abram ancl Nabor his sons," with an obvious intentioa to account for the appearance of Nahor as a settler in Charran (eh. uiv. 10) ; but it fa better to understand the mi=tion of Nahor and his family as having taken place subsequent to Terah's departure. And they went forth with them. I. e. Lot and Sarai with Terah and .Abram (Keil) ; or, better, Terah and .Abram withLot aud Sarai (Jarchi, Rosenmiiller, Murphy, 'Sreaker's Commentary'); though best is the inttrpretation, " and they went forth with each other" (Lange, Kalisch). For the reflexive use of the personal pronoun vide eh. iii. i ; x.-tii. 3, and cf. Gesenins, 'Gram.,' § 124. Other readings are, "and he Jed them forth" (Samaritan, LXX., Vnlgate, Dathius), and "and they (the unnamed members of tho family) went forth with those named " (Delitzsch). From Ur of the Cha.ldees, to go into the la:id of Canaun. Expressive of the Divine destination, rather the.n of the conscious intention of the travellers (Heb. xi. 8), though Canaan was not at this time unknown to the inhabitants of the Tigris and Euphrates valley (vide eh. xiv. 1-12). And they came into Haran. Charran, Kappa,, Carrao, in north-west Mesopotamia, about twenty-five miles from Edessa, one of the supposed sites of Ur, and celebmted as tho scene of the overthrow o[ Crassus by the Parthians (n.c. 63). And dwelt there. Probably in consequence of the growing infhmity of Terah, the period of their sojourn being differently computecl 176 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [OH, XI, 27-81, according as Abram is regarded as having been born in Torah's 70th or 180th.year. Yer. 32.-And the daya of Terah were two hundred and ftva years. So that if Abram 11-,,s born in Ternh's 70th year, Torah must have been 145 when Abram left Haran, e.nd must he.ve survived that departure sixty years (Kalisch, Dykes) ; wherees if Abrom wa.s born in his father's 130th year, thon Torah must havo Jied beforo his son's departure from Hiiran, which ngreos with Aots vii. 4. And Terah died in Harl\n, HOl\lILETICS.

entries.title: GEN 11:31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie migraJ:ion of tlie Terachi-tes. I. THE DEPARTURE OF THE EMIGRANTS. Th~ attendant circumstances of this rnigration:-t_he gathering of the clan, the mustermg of the flocks, the farewells and benedictions exchanged with relatives and friends, the hopes and fears of the adventurous pilgrims-imagination may depict, die_reaEc;ms wh~ch p_rornpted i~ ma~ be conjectured to have been-I. The sp_iri_t oj ernigra,twn, which smce the d1spers1on at Babel had been abroad among the pr1m1tive populations of mankind. The arms of a Trans-Euphratean state had already pene• trated as far west as the circle of the Jordan, and it has been surmised that this Teracbite removal from Chaldiea may have been connected with some largermovement in the same direct.ion. 2. The oppression ofthe Hamues, who, besides being the most po,~erful and enterprising of the early tribes, and having seized upon the fattest settlements, such as Egypt, Canaan, and Chaldiea, had wandered farthest from the pure Noachic faith, and abandoned themselves to n degraded polytheism, based for the most part upon a study of the heavenly bodies. That the Cushite conquerors of Southern Babylonia were not only idolaters, but, like Nimrod, their leader, destroyers of the liberties of the subject populations, bas at least the sanction of tradition. 3. The awakening of religious life in the breasts of the pilgrims. That Abram had by this time been called we are warranted on the authority of Stephen to hold, and though Terab is expressly said to have been an idolater in Ur, it is by no means improbable that be became a sharer in the pure faith of bis distinguished son. At least it lends a special interest to this primitive migration to connect it with the call of Abram. II. THE JOURNEY OF THE EMIGRANTS. Though upon the incidents and experiences of the way, as upon the circumstances and reasons of the departure, the inspired record is completely silent, yet the pilgrimage of the Chaldrean wanderers was-1. Prom an id-Olatrous land,, which could not fail to secure, even had it not already received, the Divine approbation. Not that flight from heathen countries is always the clear path of duty, else bow shall the world be converted? But where, as was probably the case with the Teracbites, the likelihood of doing good to is less than that of receiving hurt from the inhabitants, it is plainly incumbent to withdraw from polluted and polluting lands. 2. 13y an unknown way. Almost certainly the road to Canaan -was but little understood by the exiles, if even Canaan itself was not entirely a ter,a incognita. Yet in setting forth upon a path so uncertain they were only doing what mankind in general, and God's people in particular, have always to do in life's journey, viz., travel by a way that they know not; while for comfort they had the sweet a~surance that their path was steadily conducting them from idols and oppression, and t:le certain knowledge that they were journeying beneath the watchful and loving superintendence of the invisible Supreme. Happy they :whose path in life, though compassed by clouds and darkness, ever tends away from sm and 1ilavery, and never lacks the guidance of Abram's God I 3. To a better country._ In comparison with the rich alluvial soil of Southern Babylonia, the lancl of Canaa~ might be only a bleak succession of barren bills; but, in respect of liberty to worship God, anywhere, in the eyes of men whose hearts were throbbing with new-found faith, would seem superior to idolatrous Chaldrea. Without endorsing Luther's fancy, th~t Shem and his followers bad already withdrawn to Palestine, and that Terah and his family were setting forth to place themselves beneath the patriarch's rule, we _may reasonably suppose that, like the Pilgrim Fathers of a later age, they were seeking a new land where they might worship God in peace. III. THE HALTING OF THE EMIGRANTS. In the absence of definite info1mation as to the motives which induced it, this sudden stoppage of their joume1 at Haran ii! CTH. XI. 27-32.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 177 usunlly ascribed to either-!. The irresolution of Terah, who, having hecome wearied by the fatiguos and perils of the way, and having fo1rnd a comfortable location for himself and flocks, preferred to bring his wanderings to a· close, as many a noble enterprise is wrecked through weak-kneed vacillation, and many a Christian pilgrimage broken short by faint-hearted indecision; or-2. The unoelief of Terah, who, in the first flush of excitement produced by Abram's call, had started on the outward journey with strong faith and great zeal, but, as enthusiasm subsided and faith declined, was easily persuaded to halt at Haran-an emblem of other pilgrims who begin their heavenward journey well, but pause in mid career through the cooling of their ardour and declining of their piety; or-3. The infirmity of Terah, who was now an old man, and unable further to prosecute his journey to the promised land, thus making the delay at Haran a beautiful act of filial piety on the part of Abram, and on that of Terah an imperious necessity. See in this migration of the Terachites-1. An emblem of the changefulness of life. 2. An illustration of God's method of distributing mankind. 3. An example of th~ way in which an overruling Providence disseminates the truth. 4. A picture of many broken journeys on the face of earth.

entries.title: GEN 11:29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Two weddings. L THE TWO BRIDEOrtOOMs-Abram and Nabor. 1. Younger sons in Terah's family. 2. Eminent men in Ur of the Chaldees. 3. Favoured saints in the Church of God. Marriage is honourable in all. II. THE TWO DRIDES-Sarai and Milcah. 1. Near relations of their husbands. Though permissible at that early stage of the world's history, the inter.narriage of relatives so close as half-sister and niece is not now sanctioned by the law of God. 2. Attractive ladies in themselves. As much as this may be inferred from their names. It is both allowable and desirable to seek as wives women distinguished for beauty and intelligence, provided also they are noted for goodness and piety. 3. Descendants of the holy line. Doubtless this was one cause which led to the choice of Abram and Nahor. So Christians should not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. III. TrrE TWO II0MES, Formed it might be at the same time, and under similar benignant auspices, they were yet divided. 1. And from the first in their constitutions. This was of necessity. 2. And afterwards in their fortunes. Sarai had no child ; Milcah was the mother of o. family. "Lo, children are the heritage of the Lord." 3. And eventually in their locations. Nabor and Milcah remained in Ur, and ultimately moved to Haran ; Abram and Sarai pitched their tent and established their home in Canaan. So God parts the families of earth.-,v.

entries.title: GEN 12:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now the Lord. Jehovah= the God of salvation, nn indication tlmt the narrative is now to specially- concern itself with the chosen seed, and the Deity to discover himself as the God of redemption. The hypothesis that vers. 1-4 were inserted in tbe fundamental document by tl1e Jehovist editor is not required for a satisfactory explanation of the change of the Divino no.me at this particular stage of the narrative. Had said. Literally, said. In Ur of the Chaldees, according to Stephen (Acts vii. 2), reverting, after the usual manner of the writer, to the original point of departure in the Abrahamic history (Aben Ezra, Mede, Piscator, Pererias, Calvin, Willet, Rosenmiiller, Dathius, Alford, Murphy, 'Speaker's Commentary'); or in Harau, after Terah's death, as the first call given to the patriarch (LXX., Chaldee, Syriac, Raschi, Lyra, Keil, Kalisch, Dykes), or as a repetition of the call addressed to him in Ur (Clarke, Wordsworth, Inglis). Luther conjectures that the call in Ur was given "fort(l,sse per patriarcham Shem;" but if the authority of Stephen be recognised, this was the occasion of the first theophany vouchsafed to Abram; Get thee out. Literally, go for thyself, a frequent Hebraism, expressive of the way in which the action of the verb returns upon itself, is terminated and completed (cf. eh. xxi. 16; xxii. 2; Isa. xxxi. 8; Cant. ii. 11 ; vule Ewald's 'Hebrew Syntax,' § 314) ; hence, though not necessarily emphatic, it may oe equivalent to "Go thou," whoever else remains behiud (Jarchi, Ainsworth, Bush). Of thy country. A proof that the elate of the call was while Abram was in Ur (Calvin), though if Ur was at Edessa (vid6 aupra) the patriarch could scarcely have been said to be from home. And from thy kindred. At Ur in all probability Nabor and Milcah were left behind ; at Haran, Nahor and his family, if they had nlready arrived thither, and according to soma (Kalisch, Dykes) Teroh also. And from thy father'• houae. I. e. if they will not accompany thee. No Divine interdict forbade the other members of the fan1ily of Tcrah joining in the Abrahamic emigration, cm. x11. 1-5.J TIIE BOOK OF GENESIS. 179 Unto a (litcrully, the) land that I will show thee. 'l1irough a. revelation (La.nge), or simply by ~ho gui<lancc of providence.. The !tmd itself 1s loft unnamed for the tnal of tho patriarch's faith, which, if it sustained the proof, was to be rewarded by the exceedinggreat and precious promises which follow: -according to ono arrangement, seven in number, ono for each clanso of the next two verses (Cajeta.n, Willet) ; according to nnother, four, corresponding to the clauses of the second verse, the last of which is expanded in the third (Keil) ; according to a third, six, forming threo pairs of parallels (Alford); according to a fourth, and perhaps the best, two, a lower or personal blessing, comprising the fi;st thr_ee particul~rs, nnd a higher or public blessmg, embracmg the last three (Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 12:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And I will make of thee a great nation. A compensation for leaving his small kindred. 'fhe nation should be great (1) numerically (Keil, Rosenmiiller), (2) influentially (Kalisch, Inglis), (3) spiritually (Luther, Wordsworth). And I will bless thee. Temporally (Pererius, Murphy), with every kind of good (Rosenmiiller), in particularwith offspring (Vatablus); but also spiritually (Rupertus, Bush), in the sensA, e. g., of being justified by faith, as in Gal. iii. 8 (Candlish). The blessing was a recompense for the deprivations entailed upon him by forsaking the place of his birth and kindred (Murphy). And make thy name great. Render thee illustrious and renowned (Rosenmiiller); not so much in the annals of the wol'ld as in the history of the Church (Bush); in return for leaving thy father's house (Murphy). So God made David a great name (2 Sam. vii. 9 ; cf. Prov. xxii. 1 ; Eccles. vii. 3). And thou shalt be a blessing. I. e. "blessed," as in Zech. viii. 12 (Chahlee, Syriac, LXX., Dathe, Rosenmiiller, Gesenins) ; or "a typo or example of blessing," so that men shall introduce thy name into their formularies of blessing (Kimchi, Clericus, Knobel, Calvin) ; but, best, "a source of blessing (spiritual) to others" (Tuch, Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch, Murphy). The sense in which Abram was to be a source of blessing to others is explained in the next verse. First, men were to be either blessed or cmsed of God according ns their o,ttitude to Abram was propitious 01· hostile. And I will bless them -grace expecting there will bo many to bless (Delitzsch)-that bless thee, and curse (with a jmlicial curse, the word bein~ the same as in eh. iii. 14; iv. 11) him-only an individual here and there, in the judgment of the Deity, boi.ug likely to inherit this malediction (DeliItsch)-that ourseth (liternlly, treateth ligl<tly, or despiseth. The verb ia nppliecl in eh. viii. 11 to tho diminntion of tho waters of the flood) thee. The Divine Being thus identifies himself with Abr~m, and solemnly engages to regard Abram's friends and enemies as his, as Christ rloes with his Church (d. Acts i. 4). And in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Not bless themselves by thee or in thy name (Jo.rchi, Clericus); but in thee, as the progenitor of the promised seed, shall all the families of the ground (which was cursed on account of sin, eh. iii. 17) bo spiritually blessed-cf. Gal. iii. 8 (Calvin, Luther, Rosenmiiller, Keil, Wordsworth, Murphy, 'Speaker's Commentary'). Thusth0 second sense in which Abram was constituted a blessing lay in this, that the whole fulness of the Divine promise of salvation for the world was narrowed up to bis line, by which it was in future to be carried forward, and at the appointed season, when the woman's seed was born, distributed among mankind.

entries.content: -So (literally, and) Abram departed-from Ur of the Chaldees, or from Haran (vide supra) - as the Lord had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him. Lot's name being repe&ted here because of his connection with the ensuing narrative. And Abram was seventy and five years old-literally, a 8on offive years and seventy years (cf. eh. vii. 6)-when he clepa.rted-literally, in his goi711J forth upon thesecond stage ofhis journey-from Haran.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abram took (an important addition to the foregoing statement, intimat• ing that .Abram did not go forth as a lonely wanderer, but accompanied by) Sarai hi3 wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the substance - ree1.1Sh, acquired wealth, from racash, to gain (cf. eh. xiv. 11, 16, 21; YV. 14), which consisted chiefly in cattle, Lot nnd Abram being nomads-that they had gathered (not necessarily implying a protracted st11y, as some allege), and the souls -here slaves and their children (cf. Ezek. xxvii. 13)-that theyhacl gotten-" not only as secular property for themselves, but as brethren to themselvcs, and as children oftha one heavenly Fnther" (Wordsworth); that they had converted to the law (Oukelos) ;that they had proselyted (Raschi, Targnm Jonathan,and JerusalemTargum)-in Haran; and theywent f~rth to go in:to the landofCan~n; -a proleps1s (cf. eh. x1. 31, q. v.)-and into the land of Canaan they came--a distance of 300 milesfrom Haran,from which theircours0 must have been across the Euphrates in one of its higher affluents, over the Syrian desert, southwards to Lebanon and Dam1LScus (cf. eh. xv. 2), where, according to Josephus, the patriaroh reigned for some considerable time, "being come with o.n army from the land of the Chuldreans" ('Ant.,' L 7), and a village smTiV~ll to his day callc,l "abr-J.ham's N 2 180 THE 13OOK OF GENESIS. [en. xn. 1-li. habitation." Quarry, p. 420),

entries.title: GEN 12:1–5
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The preparations of grace. We may call this the genesis of the kingdom of God. I. It is FOUNDED in the word of the Divine covenant, the faith given by Divine grace to individuals, the separation unto newness of life. II. The one man Abram gathers round him a small SOCIETY, kindred with him by the flesh, but bound to him doubtless by spiritual bonds as well. Thus God has sanctified the family life by making it as the nidus of the spiritual genesis. When the new kingdom began its course in the Messiah, he drew to himself those who were previously associated by neighbourhood, relationship, and familiar intercourse in Galilee. The Divine does not work apart from the human, but \vith it and by it. III. 'l'he PROMISE was that of Abr11.m should be made a great nation, that he should be blessed and a blessing, and his blessing should be spread through all families of the earth. The structure which Divine grace rears on the foundation which itself lays is a structure of blessed family and national life. IV. The land of CANAAN may not have been indicated with positiYe certainty to the migrating children of God, but it was enough that he promised them a land which he would hereafter show them. "A land that I will show thee." There was the certainty that it ,vas a better land: Get thee out of thy country, because I have another for thee. The day-by-day journey under Divine direction was itself a help to faith to make the promise definite. The stay at Haran, from whence the pilg·rimage might be said to make a true start, wus itself a gathering of "souls'' &nd "substance" which predicted a lurge blessing in the future. ·when once we have followed the word of God's grace and set our face towards Canaan ,ve soon begin to get pledges of the future blessings, laid-lip riches of soul and substauce, which assure us of the full glory of the life to come. V. Even in that first beginning of the kingdom, that small Church out of Ur of the Chaldees, there is the evidence of that individual vAI:IETY OF CHARACTER A:ND ATTAINMENT e.nd history which marks the whole way of the people of God. Lot was a very different man from Abram. As the story of this little company of travellers develops itself we soon begin to see that the grace of God does not obliterate the specialities of human cha.racter. Out of the varieties of men's lives, which to us may seem incapable of reconciliation, there may yet be brought the onward progress of a Divine order and a redeeming purpose.-R. Vet. 1.-The voices of God at t!te opening ofthe worl<£s eras. I. .AT THE OPENING OD' CREATION. "And God said, Let there be light." II. A•r '!'HE OPENING OF REDEMPTION. "And God said, I will put enmity between thee and the womnn," &c. Ill. A.·1• 'l'IIE OPENING OF THE OLD DISPENSATION. "And Go l said to Abram, Get thee out of thy country." 182 TilE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cm. x11. 1-3, IV. AT THE orENING OF THE CDRISTIAN EllA, "And God snid, This is my beloved Son." V. AT THE OPENrNG OF 1'HB ETERNAL STATE God will say," Come, ye blessed of my Fnthcr.''-~r. Yer. 1.-Ab,-aham caJ,led. "Now the Lord God had snid unto Abrnhnm, Get thee o_ut o~ _thy country," &~. The record of Abraham's life is second only in beautiful s1mphc1ty to that of Chnst. There are certain coJTespondences between the two. I. A 8Ullfl!ONS WAS GIVEN TO ABRAHAM, It w11s from the Lord. We know not tho form. It wos explicit.. He was to leave all. It was nn unmistakable summons and it wns repeated. Such calls are genernlly opposed to cnrnnl inclinations'. Dangers beset the one who should respond to the call, for " the Canaanite was then in the land." II. THE SUMMONS "WAS SUSTAINED llY A PROMISE of guidnnce to tlie land. The first call was to a land, the second to a definite pince. God did not nt first tell .Abraham that he would give him the knd, but only "show" it. God docs not reveal all the riches of his grace at once. The promise was sufficient. Abraham went forth from the plain of Chaldea to the land which God would make through him nnd his descendants the most renowned in the world. Ever listening to a voice unheard by others Abraham was led. Sublime faith of the patriarch; he looked for "a city that bad foundations."-H

entries.title: GEN 12:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abrakam useful. "And thou sbnlt be a blessing." This is part of the sixfold promise given to Abraham. He was to be II blessing to all nations. It is a very great joy to a devout soul to becorue a blessing temporally or spiritually to others. I. EVERY MAN OF FAITH JS ACENTRE OF DLESSING. Men wllo yield to their carne.l natures cannot bless others. The Christian should not incidentally, but intentionally, bless others. "Where a man is corrupt bis working will be injurious ; purity is a benediction to man.kind. JI. A DEVOt'T A!\'ll FAITHFUL MAN IS A llLESSING CHIEFLY TO THOSE WHO CAN RECEIVE Hrs INFLUENCE. The light of the sun causes one substance to decay, another to fructify. The life of a servant of God may only provoke a sneer and oppoeitio'n in some souls; but in otllers joy, thankfulness, love, and effort at imitation. To some nn apostle was "a savour of death unto death." III. THE lfliSURE OF OUR FAITH IS THE MEASURE OF THE DLESSING WE SHALL T.ll.ANSMIT TO OTHERS. We sometimes binder the operntion of God's promise by our self-righteous humility, which ignores the fact that God often uses the "weak things of the world to confound the things that are mighty.'' There must be faith in God's continued working. He can make the future fruitful in proportion to our faith. Look nt what he ma.de of Paul, Luther, Wesley, and Whitfield because they were all men of strong faith. JV. To llE A DLESSING THROUGH THE POWER AND FAVOUR OF GOD JS TilE HIGHEST HONOUR IN THE WORLD. It was God who "made" Abraham a blessing; be gave him the power, fostered his faith, and perpetuated hie influence. What honour could Abraham have comparable w-ith this? It is probable tha~ Abrah~m thought li~tle o~ the honour which would come to him; but God adapted his promise to the.t winch he knew to be the desire of the secret soul of Abraham. Seeing II longing in the heart to lift men to a higher level, he gratifies it by making Abraham a blessing. All should cherish such desires. Tbe help we ca.n give to o.thers morally is far greater than that we can bestow materially. To live an aimless life is a disgrnce and ~in, but to live to bless others is Divine.-H.

entries.content: -And Abram paSBed throughlilomlly, passed over, or travelled about as a pilgrim (cf. Hob. xi. 9) in-the land unto (or as far as) the place of Sichem. A prole:psis for the place where tho city Shcchem (either built by or named after the Hivito prince, eh. xxxiv. 2) was afterwards situated, viz., between Ebal and Gerizim, in the middle of the land ; " the most beautiful, perhaps the onlyvery beautiful, spot in Central Palestine" (Stanley's 'Sinai and Palestine,' T. 234). The modern name of Sichem is Na.blus, a corruption of Neapolis. Unto the plain. )i,~, from ,~~ or , 11::t, to be strong, 11 strong,hardy tree: the terebinth,as opposed to the oak, )i~~, from'~1$(Celsius, Michaelis, Rosenmiiller, Keil); the oak,as distinguished from i"l~~, the turpentine tree, or terebinth (Gesenius, Kalisch, Murphy). Butit seems demonstrable that these and the other cognate terms, ,1~, i"l~~. are frequently used as synonymous for o.uy large, strong tree (cf, eh. xxxv. 5; Jndges ix. 9; xxiv. 26; Josh. rix. 33 with Judges iv. 11), though commonly Ji'll~, oak, is opposed to i"l~~, terebinth, as in Isa. vi. 13; Hosea iv. 13. The translation of )i'~ by plain (Targwns, A. V.) is inaccurate, though "the truth is it was both a plain and setwith oaks" (Willet). OfMoreh. Like Mamre (eh. xiii. 18), the name of the owner of the oak-grove (Murphy, Kalisch, Alford); probably apriestly character (l\Ioreh signifying a teacher, Judges vii. 1; 2 Kings xvii. 28; Isa. ix. 15) whoinstitutedthe Divine cultus in the locality (Luther) ; though it has also been regarded as the name of the place (Calvin),which maybeheregiven to it byanticipation (Wordsworth), being derived from raah, to see, and equivalent to the place of vision (Samaritan), because God there appeared to the patriarch (Fagius), and showed him the land of Canaan (Masius, Lyra). Knobel renders " the onk of the teacher," comparing it with "the oak of the witches" (Judges ix. 37). The LXX. translate by v,i,,,x~v, lofty, and the Vulgate by illustrem. And the Canaanite was then in the land. A sig11 of post-Mosaic authorship (Tuch, Bleek, Colenso); an interpolation (Aben Ezra; rather (1) o. proclamation of the miserable exile in which the pntrinrch lived (Luther) ; or (2) areminder to Ab1'll.Dl of his heavenly country, sooing he \Ills II stronger in his earthly one (Calvin); or, better, (3) an intimation of the fact that already the Canaanites were in possession of the land which bore their name (Kalisch), or perhaps simply (4) a declaration that the land was not a stretch of nnoccupied territory, but a populated region (Hengstcnberg), thus making thefulfilment of the ensuing promise all the more difficult, and all the greater a trial to the faith of the patrfr1rch (Keil, Murphy, Wordsworth, .Alford); or (5), but not so good, an explanation of the previous selection of the oak of Moreh as his habitation (Lange, Havernick, vide Introduction, § 18). -

entries.title: GEN 12:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Lord appeared. The first mention of a theophany, though Acts vii. 2 alleges that such a Divine manifestation had previously occurred in Ur of the Chaldees. Though not a direct vision of Jehovah (John i. 18), that there vrns some kind of outward appearance may be inferred from the subsequent Divine manifestations to the patriarch (eh. xviii. 2, 17, 33 ; xxii. 11-18), to Hagar (eh. xvi 7-14; x.ri. 17, 18), and to Jacob (eh. x=i 11-13; x:xx:ii. 24-30). On the relation of the angel of Jehovah to Jehovah vide eh. xvi 17. Unto Abram. "Jam preno fatigato Abraha isto duro exsilio et perpetuis migrationibus " (Luther). And said, Unto thy seed-to himselfGod gave '' none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on" {Acts vii. 5) ; the land was promised to his seed " when as yet he had no child "-will I give this land Now occupied by the Canaanites. Undoubtedly a great promise, that the Canaanites should be dispossessed, and their wuntry given to the offspring of a childless old man already over seventy-five years. The apparent improbability of its ever being accomplished rendered it a strong trial to the patriarch's faith. And there bnilded he analtar. "Constituit certum locum, in quo conveniat ecclesia, auditma vcrbum Dei, facturn preces, laudatura Deum, sacrificaturaDeo' (Luther). "Altare forma est Diviui cultu~; i.nvocatio nutem substantia etveritas" (Calvin). "The rearing of an altar in the laud was, in fact, a form of taking possession of it on the ground of a ri~t secured to the exerdso of his faith" {tlush). "It is often said of Abraham and the patriarchs that they built altars to the Lord ; it is never sahl they built houses for themselv~s" (Wordsworth). entries.title: GEN 12:6–10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Thepromised land. I. WANDERINGS. Entering Canaan from the north, the Chaldman emigrant directs his progress steadily towards the south, rerno,ing from station to station till he reaches the furthest limit of the land. This wandering life to the patriarch must have been (1) unexpected. Leaving Ur at the Di-vine command, and journeying many hundreds of miles, he must have eagerly anticipated rest in Canaan; but instead he finds that he must journey still. So is life to God's people always full of disappointments. Yet was it also (2) in.ei,-itable. The land was in possession of the Canaanites, and, even though it had been free and untenanted, it was famine-stricken, both of which circumstances necessitated frequent removal. .And for causes not dissimilar must the saints ever wander, the world for the most part belonging to their enemies, and the produce of earth being insufficient to meet their souls' needs. Then to the patriarch himself it was meant to be (3) prophetic. The promised land being designed not so much for a possession in itself as for an emblem of the better country towards which his spirit with its new-found faith was travelling, it was not intended that life in Canaan for the father of the faithful should be one of absolute repose, but rather one of wandering and unrest ; and of that he had a foretaste, or earnest, immediately he stepped across tLe borders of the land. And still further was it purposed to be (4) emblematic. In the fortunes of .Abram it was contemplated that God's believing people in every age should behold, in main characteristic at least, an outline or shadow of their own. .AI3 to him the land of Canaan was not the better country, but only its anticipation, so to them is it not so ruucb a type of heaven as of the visible Church, and the patriarchal wanderings an emblem not of the beatific life of the redeemed in glory, but of the experiences of the saints on earth. II. TmALS. Along with ceaseless peregrinations, more or less exacting in their nature, trials of another and severer sort entered into the texture of the patriarch's experience -in the promised land. The peculiar circumstances in which he found himself were such as to make a vehement assault upon his faith. 1. Hi,; cliildless e:ondition seemed to render all but impossible belief in the mighty nation of which Jehovah talked. And so are saints sometimes tempted to indulge a suspidon of the Divine goodness and veracity, because of the absence of certain creature comforts which they see G0d bestowing upon others. 2. The occupation ofthe land appeared to negative the idea of its ever becoming bis; and not unfrequently because a saint cannot discern how a promise is to be fulfilled, he begins to challenge the Divine resources, and ends by impeaching the Divine faithfulness. 3. The prevalence of famine was calculated to excite doubts in his mind as to whether after all the land was worth either having or desiring; and in this life the saints are not unacquainted with temptations, arising from the pressure~ outward circumstances, such as extreme THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 185 poverty or long-continued affliction, to admit the apprehension that after all the blessings of religion cmd the glories of the future life may not be worth the sacrifices made to secure them. III. CoNSOLA'l'IONS, If a field of wanderings and a scene of trials, the promised land was likewise a place of consolation. Abram enjoyed-I. The comfort of the JJivine presence. Though unseen, the companionship of Jehovah was understood by the patriarch to be a grand reality on which he might depend; and so says Christ to his believing people, 11 Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world." 2. The joy of lJivine manifestations. As'Jehovah appeared to Abram, probably in t!HJ form of a man, so already has God appeared to his Church in the person of the man Christ Jesus; and so does Christ promise still to appear spiritually to his people, and to disclose to them the treasures of hi8 grace and love (John xiv. 21). 3. The consolation of lJivine worship. Wher'lver Abram wandered he built an altar and called upon the name of the Lord who had appeared unto him; and without any altar may the saint at any moment enter into closest communion with the Lord Jesus Christ, who in the fulness of the times was manifested to take away our sins, and who is ever ready, through the medium of his Holy Spirit, to interpose for his people's aid. Learn-1. That a saint's wanderings are o.f God's appointing. 2. That a saint's trials are of God's permitting. 3. That a saint's consolations are of God's sending. HOMILIES BY VA.RIOUS AUTHORS.

entries.title: GEN 12:6–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Revelations. We here enter upon the more specie.I history of Divine appearances. Hitherto the word is described simply as a word-" The Lord said;" now we connect with the word distinct appearances. The plain of Moreb will be ever memorable as the first scene of such revelations. The altar which Abram .erected was to the Lord who appeared unto him, i. e. in commemoration of the vision. Thus the long line of theophanies commences. 1'b.e great lesson of this record is the worship of man proceeding from the gracious revelation of God. True religion is not a spontaneous prod)lct of man's nature, but rather a response to God's grace. He appears; the believer to whom the vision is vouchsafed raises an altar not "to the unknown God," but to the God who has appeared to him. .Another point in the record is the connection of the promise with the revelation. The Lord appeared, and when be appeared he gave his word of promise: "Unto thy seed will I give this land." .Are we not reminded thus early in the history of religion that for its maintenance there is required not only a revelation to the mind and heart by the Spirit, but also a seat of its institutions and community? Religion without a people of God dwelling in the land of privilege, and bound together by the sacred bonds of a Divine fellowship, is no true religion at all. .Abrum builds altars at the various stages of his pilgrimage, still going south. .Although we are not told of a distinct vouchsafement of God in connection with every altar, we may well suppose, especially as the II mountain" is specified, that the altars marked out not mere resting-places, but the scenes of specie.I comnnnion with Jehovah.-Il.

entries.title: GEN 12:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie first wanderer and the second, or Cain ancl Abram compared and contra.sted. I. COMPARED. Each wandered-I. From the place of bis nativity- Cain from Eden, Abram from Ur. 2. Accompanied by his wife, who in each instance was his sister. 3. In obedience to the word of Jehovah. He who called .Abram had previously banished Cain. 4. Beneath the protection of Heaven-Cain defended by his scarred brow, Abram shielded by the arm of God. 5. To the close of life; neither finding a permanent habitation on the earth. II. CONTRASTED. While both wandered-I. The one, Cain, trnvelled from God ; the other, Abram, journeyed with God.. 2. The one roamed across the face of earth; the other wallrnd within the borders of the promised land. 3. The one fled beneath the curse of Heaven; thJ other was o'ercanopied by Heaven's favour. 4. The one wue t1n emblem of the sinner seeking rest and finding none ; the other was a picture of the saint, who must travel through the world to his home. 186 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cH, XII,,6-9 Lessons :-1. There are wanderings and wanderings among men upon the earth. 2. He who would not become a fugitive like Cain must, liko Abram become, a pilg·rim. 3. They who choose the lot of Abram need never fear the doom of Cain.-W.

entries.title: GEN 12:6–20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The strength and weakness o.f_ Abmin. I. A1'HREEFOLD SOURCE or BTRE!\'GTH. 1. His enjoyment of gracious visits from God. 2. His exercise of faith in God. 3. Ilis cultivation of communion with God. II. A THREEFOLD SOURCE OF WEAKNESS. 1. An unwarrantable fflar of man. 2. A heedless reliance on worldly policy and craft. 3. entries.title: GEN 12:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abrali,am worsliipping. "And there he builded an altar unto the Lord who appenred unto him." Abraham is at length Divinely informed that he is in the land hereafter to be his. He was at the spot where the great temple, to be set up by his descendants, would stand. Here he builds an altar. It was doubtless a very plain altar of rough stones, but large enough for the sacrifices to be offered. It would have little attraction in the eyes of many, but it would be approved of by God. I. IT WAS REARED ENTIRELY IN THE HONOUR OF Goo. There was no self-glorifying in it. It was erected as a spontaneous act of gratitude. The m_en of Babel by the tower-building sought to get themselves a name; Abraham by his altarbuilding seeks to honour God's name. His act was a prot~st against the prevalent and surrounding idolatry. This was the first altar reared in Canaan to the great I AM. II. IT WAS AN EXPRESSION OF ABRAHAM'S DESIRE TO ACKNOWLEDGE THE DIVINE GUIDANCE Th' HIS PAST LIFE. He found it a joy to be under the leadership of God. "Wherever Abraham had his tent God he.d his altar," In how many families is the altar in need of repair I In many it has not even been set up. Ill. IT EXPilESSED ABRAHAM'S DEPENDENCE ON THE MERCY REVEALED THROUGH A rnoPITIATORY SACRIFICE. He evidently believed in an atonement. He offered an heifer, goat, ram, turtle-dove, and pigeon. After the rude manner of that day he offered sacrifices for his own sins and for those of his household. He found that God wns brought nearer through the sacrifice, even as we discover that fact through the Christ of Calvary. • ' IV. IT EXPRESSED ALSO Al!RAHAY's READINESS TO CONSECRATE HrnSELF ENTIRELY TO Goo. An altar that failed to express this would have been a mockery. God is not flattered by an outward show of reverence. He must have inner and absolute consecration if we are to know the heights of spiritual power. V. lT EXPRESSED THE PATRIARCH'S FAITH IN THE FULFILMENT OF THE DIVINE PRO· MISES. Abraham was already in the land of promise, nnd could leave the future to his God. He v,as, by rearingthat altar, taking possession of.the land for himself, and of the world for God, even as Columbus, with befitting pomp, planted in the newlydiscovered continer.t a cross, and named the land San Salvador, thus consecrating it to the holy Saviour.-H.

entries.title: GEN 12:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.Abraham's altar. "And there he builded an altar unto the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord." There is a solemn word (Matt. x. 32, 33). Tim distinction is not between Christians and heathen ; it is within the visible Church. To confess Christ is more than professing Christianity. It must be in the life, not merely in religious services. No doubt these have their use; without them spiritual life would wither and die, like a light und~r a ve_ssel. They _are as food; but "the life is more than meat." The world ncqmesces m surr serv1cE}s as respectable and proper. B~t it is a poor ~hristianitr that raises no opposition. _A ChriRtian life may constram respect, but 1t must differ from worldly (1) .as to its objcc!r-jirst the kingdom of God; (2) as to its means-God's promises and help trusL&d to as real. Mark Abraham's example: dweltamong Canaanites on sufferance; they idolaters. Prudence would suggest keeping his religion secret. Many try to keep their faith secret• afraid to confess it, but unwilling to give it up. In vain; fuith ashamed of brings no comfort or strength. Abram did not hide his faith. Wherever he sojourned he built an altar; confessed whom he trusted. We are told on. xrr. 10-20.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. IR1 -1. Ilo built o.n nltnr, i. e. mode open confession of his faith. 2. "Called on the name," &c., i.e. spoke to God as n living person, n ree.l helper. I. WHAT 1s IT TO 0ONFESB Goo? I. In the l,eart; firmly to believe what he hns revealed. His promises were given to be trusted. The fool puts away belief (Pe. xiv. 1). It moy be from dislike of truth (cf. Rom. i. 28); it may be despondingly (cf. Gen. xiii. 36), afraid to take God at hie word. The voice of trne wisdom, Ps. lxii. 1, 2. 2. In the life; acting upon "ye are not your own." We cannot go for without being tried: ia business, in companionship, in bearing what we do not like, in resisting self-will and self-seeking, in standing firm against the world's scorn or well-meant persuasions. Passing events constantly put the question whom we serve (cf. Dan. iii. 15; Acts v. 28, 29). And not merely in matters that seem gree.t. Little things show whom we have first in our hearts II. CLOSELY CONNECTED WITH THIS IS CALLING ON THE NAME OF THE LORD. '\Ve must look below the surface. Among professing Christians some prayer is a matter of course; but is it used as a real means to obtain? It is one thing to believe the doctrine of God's providence, and of the use of prayer, and another to pray as a practical power and to feel our Fnther's care. Yet St. Paul connects prayer and peace (Phil. iv. 6, 7). When Hannah had prayed she was no more sad (1 Sam. i. 18). The Bible has many encouragements to pray, but not one warning against asking too much. III. EFFECT OF THIS ON THE CBARA(')TER. Abraham's character as eminently faithful was built up by exercising faith. He walked with God not by any con• straining power, nor by reason of special manifestations; then he would be no example for us. Each acknowledgment of God increased his communion. Each altar marked a step in hie own life, and a work in the world. He who is faithful in little gains more power (cf. Matt, xiii. 12).-M. EXPOSITION,

entries.title: GEN 12:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And there was e. famine. :iv,, from a root signifying to huuger, the primary idea appearing to lie in that of an ample, i. e. empty, stomach (Gesenius, Fiirst). 'fhe term is used of individuals, men or nnimals (Ps. xx.xiv. 11; 1. 12); or of regions (Ps. xli. 55), In the land. Of Canaan. which, tl1ough naturally fertile, was, on ac: count of its imperfect cultivation, subject to visitations of dearth (cf. eh. xxvi. 1 ; xli. 56), especially in dry seasons, when the November and December rnins, on which Palestine depended, either failed or were scanty. 'l'he occun-ence of this famine just at the time of Abram's entering the land was an additional trial to his faith. And Abram went dowu to Egypt. :Mizraim (vide eh. x. 6) was lower than Palestine, and celebrated then, as later, as a rich and fruitful country, though sometimes even Egypt suffered from a. scarcity of corn, owing to a failure in the annual inundation of the Nile. Eichhorn notes it as an authentication of this portion of the Abrahamic history that the patriarch proposed to take himself and his household to Egypt, since at that time no corn tmde existed between tho two countries such as prevailed in the days of Jacob (vide Havcra1ck's Introduction, § 18). The writer to the Hebrews remarks it us an instance of the patliarch's faith that ho did not return to either Haran or Ur (Heb. xi. 15, 16). To sojoum there. To tany as 11 stranger, but not to dwell. Whether this journey was undertaken with the Divine sanction and ought to be regarded as an act of faith, or in obeclience to his own fears and should be reckoned as a sign of unbelief, does not appear. Whichever way the patriarch elected to act in bis perplexity, to leave Canaan or reside in it, there was clearly a. strain intended to be put upon his faith. For the famine was grievous (literally, heavy) in the land.

entries.title: GEN 12:11–13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass (liternlly, itwas), when he was come near to enter into Egypt (that he had bis misgivings, arising probably from his own eminence, which could scarcely fail to nttmct attention among strangers, but chiefly from the beauty of his wife, which was calculated to inflame the cupicJ..ity and, it might be, the violence of thewarm-blooded Southrons,and)that be said unto Sarai his wife. The armngemeut here referred to nppears (eh: xx. 13) to hnvo been preconcerted on first sottin~ out from Ur or Haran, so that Abram's alldress to his wife on o.pproachin"' Egypt may bo viewed as simply a reminder of their provious cornpact. Behold now, I know that thou art e. fair woman to look upon. Literally, fair of aspect (cf. 1 Sum. xvii. 42). Though now upwards of sixty-five years of ago, she was still in middle life (eh. xxiii. 1), and her 188 '!'HE BOOK OF GENEStS. ton. xt,. 10-20, constitution had not been impaired by be11ring children. Besides, the clear complexion of Sarnh would render her specially attractive in the eyes of the Egyptians, whose women, though not so dark as the Nubi~s and Ethiopians, were yet of a browner tinge than the Syri1ms and Arabians. Monumental evidence confirms the nssertion of Scripture that a fair complexion was deemed a high recommendation in the age of the Pharaohs (vide Heng; stenberg's 'Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 200). Therefore (literally, and) it shall come to pass, when (lit.erally, that) the Egyptians-notorious for th&ir licentiousness (vuie P. Smith's 'History of the World,' _vol. i. eh. vi. p. 71)-shall see thee, that (literally, and) they shall say, This is his wife: and they will kill me-in order to possess thee, counting murder a less crime !han adultery (Lyra). An unreasonable anxiety, considering that he had hitherto enj?yed_ the Divine protection, however natural 1t nught seem in new of the voluptuous character of the people. But (literally, and) they will save thee alive-for either compulsory marriage or dishonourable use. Say, I pray thee, -translated in ver. 11 as "now;" "verbum obsecrantis vel adhortantis" (Masius)-thou art my sister. A half truth (eh. xx. 12), but a "l"l"hole falsehood. The usual apologies, that he did not fabricate, but "cautiously conceal the truth" (Lyra), that perhaps he acted in obedience to a Divine impulse (Mede), that he di~sembled in _order to protect his wife's chastity (Roscnmuller), are not satisfactory. On the other hand, Abram must not be judged by the light of NcwTest3:m~nt revelation. It is not necessary for a Chnstlan in every situation of life to tell all the truth, especially when its part suppression involves no deception, and is indispensable for selfpreservation; and Abram may h:ave deeme_d it legitimate as a means of secunng both his own life and Sarah's honour, though how he was to shield his wife in the peculiar circumstances it is difficult to see. Rosenmiiller suggests that h~ knew t~e pre!imina_ry ceremonies to marnage reqlllred a considerable time and counted upon being able to leave Egypt before any injury ~-as_ done to Sara:11, The only objection to th1S_ lS that t~e. hlStorian represents him as being less sohc1t~us about the preservation of his wi~e•s chast_1ty than about the conservation of his own life. That it may be well (not with thee, though doubtless this is implied, but) withme for thy eake (the import of which is declared in !he words which follow); and my soul shall live because of thee. "No defence can be offered for a man who, merely ~hro~gh d_rea~ ~f danger to himself, tells a he, nsk.s his w1fe_s chastity, puts temptation in the way.of his neighbours,andbetraysthechargetowhich the Divine favour had summoned him" (Dykes).

entries.title: GEN 12:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.Abraham and, carnal poli,cy. "Say, I pray thee, that thou art my sister: that it may be well with me." These words were partially true (eh. xi. 20). Abraham had real ground for saying that Sarah was hie sister, but he hid the fact that she was his wife. He asked her to consent to llil equivocal statement and to repeat it. I. CONTEMPLATE THE NATURE OF CARNAL POLICY. A truth which is part alie is ever a dangerous lie. The temptation to this carnal policy came (I) from his mingling with the worldly Egyptians on equal terms, (2) from his very prosperous state, and (3) from his having lately come from a religious observai:ice _ii:1 which he had_ ~ad bigh spiritual revelations. Possibly he presumed upon his v1s1ons and the D1vme promises. David fell also shortly after he had attained the kingdom and been delivered from great dangers. - II. SEE BOW ALL CARNAL POLICY IS SURE IN THE LONG RUN 'l'O FAIL. Abraham did not foresee all the consequences of bis equivocations. He even ma.de the path clear for Phare.oh to ask for Sarah. He bad afterwards to know that hie name was a byword among the Egyptians. (I) He lost self-respect; (2) he had to be rebuked by a Pharaoh, and (3) to feel that God was dishonoured by his a.et. Abraham repeated his sin. That God d_elivered A~rab:tm should teach us that we are not to reject others, who have committed a special em, as past hope. God does not cast ue off for one si..-tful action. Still Divine forbearance and love should never lend to presumption and to a tampering with carnal policy.-H.

Sublime deeds of spiritual heroism are not to be expected at the hands of believers who con• form to the world. The true champions of the faith, who by their personal behaviour can illustrate its godlike character, are only to be found among those who walk as strangers and pilgrims on the earth, and do not stray from God's commandments. 2. .After havin_g committed a great sin. The recoil which Abram's spirit must have experienced when, in the light of God's merciful interposition, he came to perceive the heinous nature of the tr~ns_gTession i_nto which his fea~s had betrayed him in Egypt, had doubtless somethmg to do with the lofty elevation of soul to which he ~oon afterwards climbed upon the heights of Bethel. So oftentimes a saint, through g-race, is profited•by his backslidings. The memory of the matter of Uriah had its influence in ripening the piety of David, and the recollection of the judgment-hall of Pilate assisted Peter to a height of spiritual fortitude he might not otherwise hava attained. 3. After all, God's kindnesses to .Abram and Sarai were the principal instrumentalities that quickened the better no.ture of the patriarch ; and so it is generally in proportion as we meditate upon and partake of Di,ine mercy that our hearts are ennobled and enabled. It is the love of God in Christ that constrains a saint to holy and unselfish deeds. II. How IT WAS occASIONED. 1. By the danger of collision between himself and Lot. The strife which had arisen between his nephew's herdsmen and his own was liable, unless promptly extinguished, to communiqate its be.d contagion to l1imself and Lot. But the patriarch, with that insight which belongs to simple minds, discerned a method of avoiding so unseemly a calamity, and, with that self-forgetful heroism which ever characterises noble souls, had the fortitude and magnanimity to put it into execution. It indicates an advanced stage of Christian maturity whe1 what might prove temptations to sin are, by spiritue.l discernment and unshrinking self-sacrifice, transformed into occasions for holy acting and suffering.· 2. If the present history shows that good men may become rich, and sometimes in dubious ways, it also reveals that wealth has its dangers. The character of Lot was demonstrably injured by prosperity; while if Abraru escaped corruption through wealth, that wealth was indirectly the power which deprived hirn of his kinsman. It is a poor bargain when one grows rich at the expense of bis better natwe, as did Lot; or even, like Abram, at the expense of affection. Better remain poor Olld keep friends than become rich and lose friends I (2) To the quarrels of their servants. Though possibly occasioned by devotion to their masters' interests the contention of the herdsmen was wrong. A peaceful mind antl a quiet heart are indispensable pre-requisites to grace's motions. Heavenly virtue cannot prosper in an atmosphere of wrath 11nd contention. The conciliatory disposition of the elder of the two travellers was nn admirable preparation for, almost a foreshadowing of, the magnanimous act that followed ; as the perpetuation of the strife or the indulgence of anger on the part of Abram would have rendered it impossible. IV. IN WHAT rr WAS DISPLAYED. 1. A sublime ad of self-r(';7l,unciation. entries.title: GEN 13:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie cltoice of Lot. I. THE EXCELLENCE OF LoT's CHOICE. 1. Beaut,'jul. Viewed from the Bethel plateau, at the moment perhaps gilded with the shimmering rad.iance of the morning sun, the Jordan circle was a scene of enchanting loveliness ; and in yielding to the fascinations of the gorgeous panorama that spread itself out on the distant horizon it cannot be affirmed that Lot committed sin. The Almighty Maker of the universe loves beauty, as his works attest (Eccles. iii. 11), and hath implanted the like instinct in the soul of man. Hence, so far from being a signal of depravity, the capacity of admiring and appreciating mere physical and external ·grace and symmetry betokens a nature not yet completely disempowered by sin; and so far from its being wrong to surround oneself with objects that are pleasing to the eye, it is rather incumbent so to do, provided always it can be accomplished without sin. 2. Prodztctive. As there is no sin in having elegant mansions, fair gardens, and fine pictures to look upon, so neither i11 there evil in desiring fertile fields instead of barren rocks to cultivate. Sentenced to eat bread in the sweat of his brow, the Christian is not thereby required to prefer a tract of moorland to a farm of rich alluvial soil. llfonkish asceticism may enjoin such self-mortification on its devotees; Christianity invites men to enjoy the good things which have been freely given to them by God. The well-watered fields of the Jordan circle were as open to the choice of Lot as were the bleak Judrean hills. 3. S1tggestive. Already it Im.I recalled to his memory the luxuriant plains of Egypt which he had lately visited, and to his imagination the resplendent Eden of man's primeval clays; and doubtless it was such a region as could scarcelyfail to inspire a devout mind with lofty thoughts, pure emotions, and holy aspirations, so leading the entranced worshipper from nature up to nature's God, Since the human soul cannot choose but be insensibly affected for g·ood or evil by its material as well 11.B moral environment, it is well, when Divine providence gives .us the election, that we select for our abodes scenes and places that shall elevate and refine rather than deteriorate and depress. IL 'I'm: DRAWBACKS 01!' LoT's CHOICE. 1. Bad neighbours. The inhabitants of tl1c Jordanic Pentapolis were sinners of an aggravated type. And while it may not be possible to avoid all contact with wicked men (1 Cor. v. 10), it becomes God's people to keep as far aloof as possible from the ungodly, and especially from transgressors like the Sodomites. Mingling with and marrying into the families of the ungodly ruined the antedilnvian world. '!'he chief injury done to the Church of Christ arises from n throwing down of the wall of separation between it and the world. Separation from and nonconformity to the world, and much more the wicked _Portion of it, is the duty of believers (Rom. xii. 2; 1 Cor. vi. 17). 2. ~Moral co11t,1minatio1i. Though Lotwas II good man,his piety would not prevent the gradual deterioration of his nature through the evil influence of his neighbours. There is li contagion, for good or evil, in example which is well nigh irresistible. "He that THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (en. ,nn. 10-18, walketl, "·ill, \\"isc men shnll he wise; but the companion of fools ~hnll ho destroyed," 3. Ritter s01-i·o10. Precisely in proportion to the eminence of his religious olum\ctet would this be inevitRble. The immoralities and infidelities of the Sodomites would plunge him into grief, if they did 11ot cause "rivers of water" to rnn down his eyee: And so it e,·entnnlly came to pass (2 Pet. ii. 8). ITJ. '.l.'".'E sJNFUL'NEss OF Lo-r's cnotcE. 1. Aoo.rici<>us in us origin. Thus it wns Rsin agamst God. Had no dra·wbacks attended it, bad it in all other respects been commende.b\e and prudent, the lust of cupidity out of wliich it sprang would have condemned 1t. Few things are more f-requently and emphaticaHy reprehended in the ~•.ord of God ~l_1_an the inordinate_de~ire of possession (Luke _xii. 15;_Ephes. v. 3; Col. m. 5; Heb. xm. 5). 2. Selfi.~h in its cliara,cter. Thus, besides being a sin against God, it was an offence against his uncle. Had Abram and Lot stood upon~ platform of equality, religious principle should have dictated to Lot the propriety of either returning the right of choice to Abram, or himself selecting what he believed to be the inferior quarter (Rom. xii. 10; Phil. ji, 3); but Abramwns Lot's superior in. age, and therefore entitled to take precedence of one who was younger; Lot's uncle, and; in Yirtue of that relationship, deserving of his nephew's honour; Lot's guardian and benefactor, and, as a consequence, worthy of acknowledgment and gratitude at the hands of one whom he had enriched ; and, what :was more important for the settlement of the question, the actual heir ancl owner of the lnnd, to whom accordingly belonged the prerogative of claiming not its fattest portion only,. but its entire domain. All these considerations rendered Lot's choice offensive in the extreme. K Dangerous in it,s issue,s. As such it w.as a sin against himself as weU as against God. Even though evil shonld not come of it, it was not open to Lo,t, as a good man, t.o esta.blish himself where injury to his spiritual interests was possible. That he did not reckon the moral bearings of his choice was an aggravation rather than an extenuation of his sin. He had time to calculate the chances of material prosperity: he should also have counted up the moral hazards before he elected to drive his flocks and herds to Sodom. Lessons:-1. .All is not gold that glitters; hence the supreme· unwisdom of judging either thing11 or peraons according to appearance. 2. In every man's lot there -is Ii crook; hence the propriety of moderating our desires concerning everything. 3. H is possible to pay too dear a price for material prosperity. "What shall it profit'a man if he shall gain the whole world and lose his own soul?" 4. Itis II poor outcome of piety which prefel"!l self-interest to the claims either of affection or religion: the ma.n who loves himself better than his· neighbour is still devoid of_ the spiri_t of Christ. 5. In the long run the spirit of selfishness is certain to overreach itself and nccomplish its own ruin.

entries.content: -The choice ofLot. I.·WHAT LoT TOOK INTO ACCOUNT. 1. His owri worldly circumstances· and, 2. That while it may be right, in life's actions, to take our worldly mterests into account, it is wrong and dangerous to take nothing else. 2. Vera. 10 13.-Sodom and tlie Sodomites, or tlie place a'Tl,(l, tlie people. 1. The pl,ysical be'auty of the Jordan valley. 2. The moral corruption of its inbabitonts. Lessons.-1. The weakness of nature as a moral educati;,r. 2. The true design of nature ll.B a more.I educator.-W. • • \"er. '!1.--Theparting of thefriends. I. The BADNESS of this parting.
