With rnag• nunimity on the part of Abram. 4. With meanness on that of Lot. Lessons :-1. It is sad when brethren cannot dwell together in unity. 2. It id better that brethren should sepnrate than quarrel.-W. , Ver. 11.-Lot's unwise clioue. "Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan." To Lot no doubt this seemed but a matter of prudence, n choice of pastnre~, yet it stamped his after life. He was a godly man. We miss the point if Wll tbink of him as. careless. .The lesson is for God's people. At first guided by his uncle, but· time came·when he must act a.lone. Pastures of Ilethel not sufficient. Strife between the herdsmen. God uses little things to work his will. In every lifo times when choice must be made. Perhaps definite and distinct, e. g. leaving home, or cJ1oice of ii profession ; perhaps less marked, as in the choice of friends and asso· ciates, or the· habits· imperceptibly formed. We must be thus triecl ; neetlfol for 01ir training (James i. 12). A sevenfold blessing "to him that overcometh " (Rev. ii., iii.). I. EVIL OF LOT'S CH(!ICE. He chose the best pasture. Why should he not? The fault lay in•the motive, t~e want of spiritual thought in a secular matter. He bro!rn no positive law, but looked only to worldly good. The evil of Sodom was rlisre• garded. No prayer for .guidance; no thought how he could best serve God (cf. James i. 14). II. EFFECT OF Lo1''S CHOIOE. 1. No real happiness. His soul vexed (2 Pet. ii. 8). His life ; fretting at evil which he had not resolution to escape from. 2. Real injury. His character enervated.' From dwelling in plain came into the city ; fonned connections there.. Irresolute and lingering when warned to flee. His prayer for himself only'. Was saved" as by fire" (1 Cor. iii. 15). We are tried daily, in the valley or oh the mountain. We cannot avoid trials; not good for us ii ,ve could. The one way of safety: ((Seek first the kingdom of God." There is an evil terribly \videspread--'of seeking first the world; thinking not to neglect God, but putting Christianity into comers of the life. What saith the world? Haste to be rich, or great; take thine ease; assert thyself; be.high-spirited. And the customs of society and much of education repeat the lesson. Bat what saith Christ? Look unto me. Not at,stated times, but always. '.l'he cause of much dispeace, of many spiritual sorrows (1 Tim. vi. 10), is want of thoroughness in taking Christ as our guide. Lot was preserved. Will any say, "l ask no more"? "Remember Lot's wife." How narrow the line between his hesitation and her looking back I The grain may sprout through thorns (Matt. xiii. 22), but the thorns are ever growing.-M.

entries.content: -Going to Sodom. I. How IT MAY HAVE LOOKED TO LoT. 1. As a matter of business it was good. 2. In its morn! aspects the step wns dangerous. But-3. Perhaps a studied reference to the a.et of Lot, which Moses describes in similar language (,;er. 10), and possil.,ly designed to su~o-est the greater satisfaction wl1ich would be m1- 11a.rted to the soul of Abram by the survey about to be ma.de. And look from the place where thou art. Between Bethel and Ai, ou one of the mountain peaks (cf. eh. xii 8 ; xiii. 3), from whid1 a commanding view of ,,]most the entire country could be obtained. Northward-towards "the hills which dinde .Iudrea from the rich plains of Samaria"- and southward-as far as to the Hebron ra.nge-anil eastward-in tl1e direction of the dark monntain wall of Moab, down through the rich ravine which leads from the central hills of Palestine to the valley of the Jordan, and across that very "circle " into which Lot has already departed with his flocks-and westwaril-literally, towards the sea. entries.title: GEN 14:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The capture of Lot, or Nemesi,s pursuing si,n. I. AN EXAMPLE OIi' Tim r.11·rna l'I:uITS OF WAR. 1. War is sometimes justifiable in its origin and objects. ,rl,en undertaken to achieve or preserve national independence, to vindicate the liLerties and secure the rigl,ts of men, or to repel the aggressions of ambitious de~pot~, even war with all itR bloody horrors may become an imperious and fierce neu,ssitv. It is difficult to determine whether on either side the campaign in tl,e vale of·Siddim was entitled to be so cliaracterised. The kings of the Pentapoli~ were figl,ting for emancipation from a foreign yoke, and so far perhaps were entitled to be regarded :u; having right upon theirside; yet they had themselves been invaders of a land which had originally been assigned to the tribes of Shem. But however tl,e question of right may be settled as between these ancient warriors, it is certain tl,eir successors on the battle-fields of earth have much more frequently had the wrong upon their sides than the rigl,t. 2. Victory does not alwavsfavour those wlio seem to /,ave the best cause. 'l'he maxim of the great Napoleon, that God is alwuyR on the side of tl,e strongest battalions, is as wide astrny from the exact truth on this important subject as is the prevailing sentiment that God always defends the right. The doctrine of Scripture is that the Lord of Hosts is independent of both regime11ts and rifles can save by many or by few, and giveth the victory to whomsoever he will; and that' not always does he choose to render those arms triumphant which are striking for the holiest cause, but sometimee, for reasons of hie own (it may be to cbastise a nation for its sins, or to move them to faith and prayer, or to teach them 11ome important lesson), permits the wrong to trample down the rigl1t. The history CR. XIV. 1--12.) 'fHE BOOK OF GENESIS. of Isrnel nnd the records of modem warfare supply numerous examples, 3. Disastrous and ter1·ible are tlie usual concomitanta of war. Not that God does not frequently overrule the hostilities of contending nations, and evolve from the murderous designs of monnrchs results the moat beneficial, making war the pioneer of civilisation, and even of religion ; but th'l immediate effects of international strife are ever ruinous and appalling-fruitful fields devastated, fair cities sacked, valuable property destroyed, lives of men wasted, a nation's blood and treasure poured 011t like water, lamentation, mourning, and woe commissioned to many home,i, and a hurden of care and sorrow laid on all. All this WIIB exemplified in the present instance. 4. IV/ten wa.1· arises tlte innocent largely suffer with the guilty. Harl the campaign against the kings of the Pentapolis not been prepared, it is probable that tbe Rephaims, Zuzima, Emims, 1-Iorites, Amalekites, and Amorites would not hani suffered at the hands of Chedorlaomer, and it is certain that Lot would not have hePn made a prisoner by the victorious monarch. Now, so far as the primal reason of this invasion was concerned, all these were innJcent of any offence against the Asiatic king, and yet they were amongst the victims of his wrath against the rebels of the Jordan circle. II. AN INSTANCE OJ! DIVINE RETRIIlUTIO:)(. 1. Deserved. Although Lot was a righteous man, he had egregiously sinned, (I) in choosing the Jordan circle as his portion, (2) in making his abode in Sodom, (3) in continuing amongst the inhabitant~ when he ascertained their ungodly charactu. Consequently God avenged himself upon his erring servant by allowing him to lose bis property, and to come near the losing of his' life as well in the sacking of foe city. So " the face of the Lord is set against them that do evil." 2. Unexpected probably as to its cause, Lot thinking he had committed nothing worthy of chasti,Jement, for sin has a strange po"·er of obscuring the moral vision and deadening the voice of conscience; almost certainly as to its time, God's judgments for the m,,st part taking rncn unawares (cf. Ps. lx::riii. 18, 19), and evil-doers being commonly snared in an evil time, like the fishes of the sea (Eccles. ix. 12), walking like blind men because they have sinned against the Lord (Zepk i. 17) ; and more than likely as to its form, those who anticipate the outpouring of Divine indignation being seldom able to discern beforehand the special character it will assume. 3. .Appropriate~ Lot bad chosen the Jordan circle as the most advantageous locality for thriving in his flocks and herds, and Chedorlaomer's armies swept his folds and stalls entirely clean. He had elected to live among tho filthy Sodomites, and so be is compelled to ·fare as they. G_od's recompenses to evil-doers (whether saints or sinners) are never unsuitable, though man's often are. 4. Merciful. He might have lost his life in the general massacre of the city's inhabitants, but be onlylost his property, or rather itwas not yet lost, although, doubtless, Lot imagined that it was; only pillaged and carried off along with himself, his wife, and daughters. So God ever mingles mercy with judgment when dealing with his people. 5. Premonitory. Though all retribution is not designed to admonish anrl reprove, this was. The vengeance taken on the wicked at the day of judgment will be purely punitive; that which fa.Us upon transgressors while on earth is aim£'d nt their amendment. Unhappily, however, as in the case of Lot, it is sometimes inefficacious. Instead of taking warning at what might have proved his rnin, Lot was no sooner rescued than he returned to Sodom. So great providential jt1d,;mcnts and great providential mercies are often equally despised. HOMILIES BY VAHIOUS AUTHORS. Ch. xiv.-The kingdom of God in its relation to the contending powers of tl.i,s world. I. Goo's JUDGMENTS ARE ALREADY BEGINNIN"Cl TO JJ'ALL. War is made by confederate kings or princes against the people of the wicked cities of the plain, who by their propinquity would naturally be leagued together, but by theircommon rebellion ogainst Chedorlaomer were involved in a common danger. Notice the indication of the futme judgment E;iven in the course of the narrati,e-" the vale of Siddim woe full of slime-pita. ' God's ,·engeance underlies the wicked, ready to pnrst forth on them in due time. u. THE UNl'AlTIIl'UL LOT IS INV('L\'KI) IN THE JUDGllENT. lie I\Dd his good~ o.re 206 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [on. XIV. 13-lG. taken. For whilo before it is said he pitched his tent near to Sodom, now we find that he is in Sodom. • III. The MEDIATION OF ABRAM, representattve of that of God's people in the world,' pr0cures the deliverance of the backsliding. He has already succeeded in drawing strength to himself ; and doubtless Abram the Hebrew represented a nuoleus of higher life even in that land of the idolatrous and degenerate which was recognised 11s in some sense & refuge to which men could appeal. IV. The VICTORY OF THE CIIILD OF Goo, with his small company, over the great army of heathen is typical. It represents, like the victory of Dnvid over Goliath, &c., the supe1ior might of the spiritual world (cf. 1 Cor. i. 27-31). V. The HOMAGE PAID To ABRAM as the conqueror both by the heathen king of Sodom and the priest-king of Salem is typical of the superior position of the covenant people. Abram gnve tithes to Melchizedek (cf. Heb. vii. 1-7) as an acknowlcdgment of the superiority of the position of Melchizedek, but Melchizedek blessed Abram as the possessor of ihe promise. The idea is that Mclcbizedek was the priest of a departing dispensation, .Abram the recipient of the old and the beginning of the new. VI. .ABRA~I's STRICT SEPAUTJON from the worldly power, which he rested on mi oath of faithfulness to God, shows that he is decidedly advancingin spiritunl character. The contrast is very striking between his conduct and that of Lot. He. at the same time does not attempt to enforce his own high principle upon others.. The Church of God has suffered much from its attempts to apply its own high rules to the world instead of leaving the world to find out for itself their superiority and adopt them.-R.

entries.title: GEN 14:13–16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The kinsman deliverer, or .Abram'smilitary expeclitum. I. ABRAlI's ELEVATED PIETY. 1. Self-forgetful magnanimity. Had the patriarch possessed a le11s noble soul, the tidings of his nephew's capture would almost certainly have kindled in his breast a secret feeling of complacency. But not only in his behaviour on the occasion was there the complete absence of any such revengeful dispositiGn as gloatswith satisfaction over the punishment of awrong-doer, there was something like a manifest unconsciouaness of having ever suffered injury at Lot's hands at all. 2. Brotlierly compassion. If he did sometimes admit to himself that his nephew had scarcely acted .handsomely towards him, any feeling of resentment with which that reflection may have been associated was completely swallowed up by the sorrow which he felt for that nephew's fate. After all Lot was his dead brother's son, and was a child of God as well, and he could not choose but be affected by the melancholy news. Besides being self-forgetful, the piety of Abram was sympathetic. 3. Active benevolence. Meekly patient of injuries when inflicted on himself, the patriarch was ever ready to redress the wrongs of others, even of the undeserving. Nor was his philanthropy of that weakly benevolent sort which is always going to do some act of kindness to others, but never does it, or is so unaccountably slow in doing it that it comes to be practically of littlo use, or that would willingly extend a helping hand to the unfortunate if it could only be done without much trouble; on the contrary, it was prompt, decisive, energetic, and carried through with much lo.hour, and at considerable risk to his own person11l safety. II. ABRAM'S MILITARY GENIUS. 1. Unexpectedly evoked. The last thing which ordinary minds would o.nticipe.to as an element in the character of one so good, pious, benevolent, and magnanimous as Abram the Hebrew, there is yet no essential incong·ruity between the talents of a soldier and the graces of a Christian ; while as for the patriarch suddenly discovering all the qualities of II great commander, it is perhaps sufficient to reply that hitherto the crisis had not 11nived to call them forth. The annuls of warfare, both ancient and modern, attest that true military genius has not always been confined to professors of the soldier's 11rt, but has oftentimes been discovered, of the mrest kind, in persons who, till summoned forth by Providence, have been engaged in peaceful callings. 2. Brilliantly displayed. In the gallant exploit of the patriarch are exhibited the tactics that from time immemorial have been adopted by all greatgenerals-by Miltiades andThemistocles of Greece, by Julius Creaar, by Belise.rius, the general of Justinie.n, by Oliver Cromwell, by Napoleon, by Stonewall Jackson and Sherman of America, and again by Von Moltke of Prussiacelerity of movement, suddenness of attack, skilful division of forces, outflanking and THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. XII', 13-16. ontmnrC'hing o[ the enemy (ef. Limge, p. 405). 3. Completely successful. The foo WRS defeated, the prisoners and spoil were recRptured, nnd it does not appear that Abrnm or his allies lost II man. That generalship is the best which accomplishes Its object at the least expense of soldiers' blood and subjects' treasure. III. ADllAM's WONDER-WORKING FAITH. It afforded-!. A snj}lcient ground on "·hic-h to go to "·ar. The question as to Abram's right to mingle in this contest in thr Sodom valley is fairly nnswered by replying that Abram hau. the right (1) of ~atural affection_to attempt _the rescue of his relative, (2) of II sacred humanity to liberate the captive and punish the oppressor, and (3) of faith. Already God had gi,·e!J him th_e _Ian~, and we ai:e fully warranted in regarding him as ncting in this heroic expedition m the c11pamty of (under God) lord-paramount of the soil. 2. Tiu 11Rcessttry power with which to prosecute the war. Possessed of military g·enius though the patriarch was, it is not supposable that he entered upon this campaign against the tmined armies of the conquering kings, pursuing them along a difficult and dnngerons track, without first casting himself on the Almighty arm as his ~trength. And if that Almighty arm;·ln order to auccour him, took the way of <leYe]oping- the capabilities for warfare which hnd hitherto been lying dormant in his 8oul, it was none the less true that the help which he received was Divine. • 3. The ~:plendid victory which resulted from the war. \Vhether the writer to the Hebrews (c-h. xi. 34) thought of Abram when he spoke of faith's heroes subduing kingdoms and ,rnxing nlinnt in the fight, it is apparent that Isaiah (eh. xli. 2, 3) ascribed the triumph of the son of Terah to the grace of God, which thus rewarded the faith which, in obedience to a Divine impulse, sprang to the relief of Lot. IV. ABRAM'S TYPICAL CHARACTER. The symbolic foreshadowing of the great kinsman Deliverer is too obvious to be overlooked. 1. In his person the Lord Jesus Christ, like Abram, was the kinsman of those whom he delivered, 2. The work he undertook, like that of Abram, was the emancipation of his brethren. 3. As in the case of Abram, that work consisted in despoiling the principalities and powers of evil. 4. The motive by which he was impelled on this arduous warfare was, like that which inspired the patriarch, love for his kinsmen. 5. The promptitude of Christ in coming to the aid of men was typified by Abram's celerity in hastening to the rescue of Lot. 6. As the campaign of Abram, so the warfa,re of Christ was carried through at great expense of toil and suffering to himself.· 7. In the faith of Abram ·was shadowed forth the calm reliance of the Saviour that all he did was in obedience to his Father's will. 8. The success with which the patriarch was rewarded was emblematic of the bigher -victory of Christ. Learn-I. To imitate the piety of Abram. 2. To admire in him, if we cannot in onrseh-es, the possession of superior abilities. 3. To covet earnestly the_wondorworl..ing faith which he displayed. 4. To trust in the great kinsman Dehyerer of which he was the type.

entries.title: GEN 14:17–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Visited by kings. I. THE KING OF SALEM. 1. Hu exaUedperso11,, Neither a supramundane being, an angel, the Holy Ghost, o_r;cbrist; n~r one o~ the early patriarchs, such as Enoch or Shem; but a C_anaa!11tie~ (Shem1te ?) prince, whoee capital was Salem (Jerusalem), and who umted ·m hie person the. double function of priest and monarch of hie people ; probably the last official repreeen~ative of the primitive religion, who here advances to meet and welcome the new faith in ihe person of Abram, as at a later period John Daptist recognised and Bl\luted on. XIV, 17-24.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 211 Christ. 2, His twofold desiynati<m. Melchisedeck, king of S,tlem, i. e. kii:g of righteousness and king of peace (Heh. vii. 2) ; descriptive of-(1) Personal excellence. Pious in spirit nnd peace-loving in disposition, he was not only fitted to be a type of the Meek a.nd Holy One, but admirably qualified to be a governor of men and a minister of religion. Happy' the land whose throne is filled by purity and love, and the Church whose teachers illustrate by their lives the religion they profess I (2) Regal sway. Righteous in principle, as a consequence his kingly rule was peaceful in administration; thus again constituting him an eminent foreshadowing of H,o righteous King and Princo of peace, as well as an instructive pattern and guide to earth's rulers. When righteousness and peace occupy the throne they seldom fail to reign throughout the land. (3) Priestly work. The specific function of his sacerdotal. office being to make peace between God and sinful men, probably hy means of sacrifice, and thus to cover with righteouane.~s as with a garment those who wore exposed.to condemnation, he a third time symbolised the great King-Priest of the New Testament Chnrch; while at the same time he seemed to proclaim this important truth, that they who labour in the priest's officeshould diligently strive for the salvation of souls. 3. His mysterwus appearance. Of unknown parentage, of unrecorded genealogy, of unchronicled existence, the uniquepersonality of this grand old ldng-priest flashes meteo'r-like across the path of the conquering patriarch, emerging from the gloom of historical obscurity, and almost instantaneously vanishing into inscrutable seclusion. Spirit-taught writers of later times diilcerned in this ancient figure, so-enigmatical and mysterious, a Divinely-appointed type of the c,crliving High Priest, "the Son who is consecrated for evermore." 4. His regal !tospitality. Whatever additional significance attached to the banquet on the pbin of Shaveh, it was clearly designed as a refreshment fo; the victoriou8 patriarch and his wearied soldiers. So· should earthly monarchs gratefully and sumptuously reward those who at the risk of their lives maintain the cause and vindicate the rights of the oppressed within their, borders. So does heaven's King provide for his toiling followers. 5. His priestly benediction. (1) The blessing conferred on Abram was not simply the expression of a wish, but the actual conveyance by Divine authority of the good which it proclaimed ; and so is Christ invested with supreme power to bless and save. (2) The ascription of praise to God was a sincere declaration of the patriarch's gratitude for.the heavenly succour vouchsafed in connection with his military expedition ; and so should God's redeemed ones, whom be has delivered out of the hands of the enemy, cherish a lively recollection of Divine mercies, and offer heartfelt thanksgivings through the one Mediator. 6. His public recognition. In presence of the king of Sodom and hie people, his confederates and their forces, as well as of his own domestics, the patriarch delivered into the hands of Melchisedeck a tenth part of the spoils. Designed as a solemn act of worship to Jehovah, it was both an.acknowledgment of the claim which God's minister had upon his countenance and support, and a symbol of the service,-the voluntary devotement of a liberal portion of their substance,-which should by a.II saints be yielded to him who has been constituted a Priest for ever after the order of Melchisedeck. entries.title: GEN 14:18–20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.A Icing-priest. "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God. And he blessed Abraham," &c. \Vhen the king of Sodom was beaten in a. war with Chedorlaomer, Lot was involved in the overthrow. Chedorla.orner was a warrior of great power, and his very name was terrible. Five confederate kings had in vain resisted him "·ith his three auxiliaries. He whom kings could not oppose the simple patriarch Abraham, with armed herdsmen, will attack and conquer. His kinsman Lot is in cnptinty; Abraham will deliver him or die in the attempt. How nobly shines the character of Abraham in this determination. Lot had separated from him through a misunderstanding, and had chosen the most fertile district, and left .Abraham· the least promising, yet Abraham forgets a.II, when his relative is in danger. .At great risk he undertakes his deliverance. He armed his " trained servants," pursues the enemy, comes upon them "by night," divides bis small band into three companies, :md makes ·an assault at once on the right, the Cl'ntre, and flank of the enemy. He routs and pursues them, smiting many and taking much spoil. •He accomplishes above all his one desire, the restoration of Lot to liberty. As Abraham returns, ll ushed with conquest, he is met at the gates of Salem hy Melcihizedek, bringing to him bread, wine, and the Divine benediction. ' I. THE DE~IGNATION AND CHARACTER OF MELCHIZEDEK, lid is king and prie~t. His name means, krug of righteousness. He dwells in Salem, the placo of peace. He did not go out to war, and had no pnrt in the quarrel between Chedorlaomer and the lil:ing of Sodom. lie had lost no relatives, and had no reason for fighting. Had cunning foes attacked his city of peace, he would doubtless have driven them off if possible. A kin~ of righteousness, he would not think it his duty to submit to unrio-hteousness. He was, however, left unattncked by the fierce Chedorlaomer, and took care to provoke no quarrel. Perhaps he was not assailed because universally respected as a man of peace and a priest of God. 'J.i1is reason may have availed in that early age, and in respect to the first war of which we have any account, btlt it is not certain that it would be accounted a sufficient reason now. Various have heen the speculations as to who Melchizedek was. Some believed that he waa Enoeh come back to earlh, or Job, the tried one; others, that he was Shem, the best son of Noah. This is possible, as, according to calculations made, Shem 1111rvived Abrahum forty years; but it is improbahle, hccauBe l\toRes wonld have ~poken of on. xtl". 17-24.J '!'HE BOOK OF llENESlfl. 213 Shem hy his proper name, nnd because that would not upply wliid, i~ said of Melchizedek, in Heh. vii. 3-thnt he was "witliout father, without mother, witl10ut descent, having neither beginning· of dnye, nor end of life." We know the ancestry of Shem, but not thnt of Melchizedek. The difficult passage, the third of the seventl1 chopter of Hebrews, means, probably, merely this-that his descent was 1,ot known, nnd that his priesthood wns not inherited or derived from others, b11t one resting in his individual character. Thus Nooh, Job, Hobab or Jethro, and nalaarn actAcl as independent priests, and their..offerings were recognised by God. Melchizede,:C, in his maintenance of the worship of God, came to be accepted as a priest, and hi~ life was like a star shining omid the general heathenism of C,,naan. He also came like a streak of light, neither the coming nor the going of which could ea~ily Le discerned, We are told of him that he was" without beginning of days or encl of life,". Some have therefore thought that Melchizedek was an angel or a pre-incarnation of Christ; if so, Christ would have been the type and the antitype. Ilut that which is thought to be spoken of the man refers to his office; it was without definite beginning or ending. The Leviticnl priesthood had a definite beginning and ending; that of Melchizedek is never ended. The one stood in camn\ ceremonies, the other in the power of o. holy charo.cter. The Levitical was introduced because of tl,e unfitness of all to become "kings and priests unto God;" but that of Melchizedek, being according to character, has no "end of days." It foreshadowed the priesthood of Christ, whose work never passeth away, but who abideth a priest continually. Melchizedek was a type of Christ, the one great High Priest, the holiest of all on earth, and who enters for us into the holiest place. The omissions concerning parentage or the beginning of his priesthood were probably designed by God, that in Melchizedek-the most prominent of patriarchal priests-there might be a more significant typo of him who is n Priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. This would explain the force of the prophecy in Ps. ex., and the words in Heh. Tii. Indeed the Levitical priesthood could not supply a perfect type, for it had no one who was at once a priest and king. Moses claimed not to be priest or king. Davi,! ventured not to intrude into the priestly office. Solomon, ut the dedication of the temple, when he blessed the people, gave sacrifices for the priests to offer, but he slew them not. Uzziah attempted to intrude into the priestly office, but was stricken with leprosy. Under the Jewish dispensation there was no one who in his person could represent the twofold character of Chiist as the only High Priest and uni,·ersal King. Under the patriarchal dispensation, and in Melchizedek, there is this very plai11 type of Christ in his priestly and regal character. Melchizedek may never have iurngined how great was the dignity put upon him ns a type of Christ_ Living a quiet, pure, and devoted life, he becomes accepted by his fellows as a priest of the Most High, und becomes the type of him who was the Saviour of the world. II. THE SIGNIFICANCil IN THE Rl!:COilDED ACTS OF MELC!lIZEDEK. 1. Refreshing the weary. "Brought forth bread and wine," that Abraham might eat and be strengthened. Possibly part of the wine was poured out as an oblation. When those who met wished to seal a friendship, they brake bread or partook of a mertl together. Thus the Lord's Supper is the indication of our union with Christ-of a friendship on his prtrt for us sinners, cemented by his suffering. lie grt,-e himself to be the Bread of Life for us, We are in I\ spiritual sense to eat of his flesh and drink of his blood, or we have no life in us. Christ oft thus comes forth to meet the wenry pilgrims and soldiers of the cross. ,ve must remember that it is the previous weary march, the confusion and the conflict, that fits us for the cnjoymenL of the sucred ordinance of the Lord's Supper. We have had to battle with temptations of various kinds, and come stained with the dust nnd blood of brtttle to the table of our Lord, and here he meets us and refreshes us. ,ve begin here to see the meaning of nil the conflict and burden of life. His word acquires more meaning, and his Spirit rests upon us with greater power, us, just outsido the gates of tlw leavenly Jerusalem, we sit and rest awhile ere pursuing our way and battling ngai,1 with sin. What thoughtfulness there was in this act of l\Ielchizedek ! Single 11ct1 like these tell what is the character of a man. How it hints nt the thoughtfu\nes~ of Christ for us in nil our spiritual struggles! 2. l\lelchizedek also "blessed" Abralu1m. He pronounced upon him the blessin!! which belongs to nn unselfish 214 TilE BOOtt OE' GENESIS. trn. XII', 17-24. performance of duty. God's blessing is Abraham's great reward, cmd n mnn was its rnoutl1piece. Because God's npproYal was his reward he would not retain the spoil, although nr~ed by _the kin~ of Sodom to keep the goods, and simply hand over tl11l' persons of his cuptn-e subJects. The approval of God expressed through conscience or the words of the good should be the Christinn's one desired reward. The blessing ":ill always come in the wny of duty. 3. Melchizedek claimed the honour of the 'l'Jctory for God. "Blessed be the most high God, who hath delivered thine enemies into thine hand." Before the king of Sodom Abraham is reminded of his dependence on God; thus before the world the Christinn shows forth his dependence on the Spirit's help and "on the Lord's death till he come." We may never be ashamed to confess Christ. Abraham readily recognised the claim of God. He gtwe r,s a thank offering a tenth part of all he had taken. That which he gnve, was !1is by custom and right. He gi'l'es it to God. God would not accept that whicrr 1s ,nnng, hy force, from another. He would say, "Who hath required this nt your hand?" "I hate robbery for burnt offering." God only accepts that which is righteously and willingly offered. If taxes are imposed men pay them, but often when it is left to tl1eir conscience they neglect their duty. Better, however; that :io tenth or titbings, no ratings and taxings, should be paid thnn that God'.s cause should be sustained unwillingly. As God gives us all we possess in love, as he irnstains and pardons us in love, the lenst we can do is to love him and readily s.erve in return. We sliould devote all we are and have to Christ. Talents and possessions are his, and should be held in stewardship as from \1im. Let us not, howc'l'er, make the mistake of thinking that it is by our gifts or good works we are saved. Many err here. It is only through Christ that our doings or persons can he accepted, even as Abraham's gifts were through Melchizedek. Christ is our Priest and Sacrifice. Do not attempt to slight him. Trust in Ilia merits, work, and intercession. Let him have the pre-eminence. Christ must rule in our hearts and lives. The will must be given into his bands. Life must be held as a gift frorri him, nnd eternal life will be his certain bestowal hereafte.r.. 4. Melchizedek gave to Abrnham cheering words nnd stimulus. ·This was more almost than the refreshment. Here, as we meet in communion with. one another and with Christ, we have grent joy. Christ cheers us. We feel we can go forth boldly, and thl\t when sin meets us we can, in Christ'sstrength, say, "Stand aside;" when hopes are cut off, ns Lot was from his home, we can recover them through the cross. Thus our arms are nerved and hearts made strong for the future conflict. All the joy, however, is only a foretaste of that which will be ours when Christ shall meet us at the gate of the New Jerusalem, and shall lead us in to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Melchizedek, and all those who have been faithful to him. What will be our joy when we shall enter to abide in the "city of peace" with the "King of righteousness" for ever I May none of us know what will be the bitter pain of those who shall vainly call from without, because the door is shut, and the Master has entered in witli those who were rcady.-H.

entries.title: GEN 14:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Mdchizedek blessi,ng .Abraham. "And he blessed him, and said, "Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth." Wherever in Scripture Melchizedek is spoken of, it is as a type of Christ (Ps. ex. 4 ; Heh. v., vi., vii.). We may so regard him here, and consider his act in its typical light; Outwardly the transaction was of little mark. A band of men unde~ Clied?rluomer carried off Lot, along with other spoil, from Sodom. Abram, on le~mmg this, arme_d his household, pursued the invaders, routed them, and set the captives free. On Ins return Melchizedek, the head of a tribe near the line of march, came out to offer refreshment to his men· and as priest of his tribe he blessed Abram. Whether the type was understood' by Abram or Melchizedek matters not. These things are written for our learning. We see in them Christ bestowing bis blessing. I. THE OCCASION OF THE llLESSING. After conflict. Our Lord the antitypo of Melchizedek, as Kmg of peace (Isa. ix. 6; cf. Luke ii. 14; John xiv. 27). Yet the Cliristian life is emphaticallyone of warfare (Ephes. vi. ff--13 ; 2 Tim. ii. 3; cf. G~n. :u::xii. 24; 1 Pet. v. 8; also Rev. ii., iii.-" to him that overcometh," f!z-c.). ~ue nat11re of th11t fight is against .temptations to unbelief. The fight of faith (1 Tun, l,'}1, XIV, 17-24.] 'l'HE BOOK OF GEN£S1S. 216 vi, 12), 'l'ho ronewal undcr Christ of the battle lost in Eden (2 Tim. iY, 7 ; 1 ,Job v, 4). Circumstances may vary, The trial mny be apparent or not. There mQy be no outward suffering, no visible hindrance. But what a struggle is implied in 2 Cor. x. 5. It is the struggle against unbelief; to resist the power of things seen ; to overcome "How can these things be?" to realise habitually the "city which hatli foundations" (cf. Phil. iii. 20); to rest on God's promises in simplicity (Phil. iii. 7). As often as this struggle is honestly waged a blessing is bestowed (James i. 2; cf. Matt. vii. 13; xvi. 24; Acts xiv. 22). We naturally love spiritual ease, but trial is better (Ps. cxix. 71). II. THE SOURCE OF THE DLESSINO. "The most high God, possessor," &c. 1. All blessing is froni God. We acknowledge this ; but Isa. x. 13 is a nntural feeling. Wc instinctively look to second causes; yet without this "looking upward" we cannot truly pray, "Thy will be done;" we cannot really live a Godward life. Compare Melchizedek's wc,rds with our Lord's (John xiv. 13-16; xvi. 23), and their fulfilment in his receiving for meri (Pa. lxviii. 18) all needful gifts-forgizeness, sonship, right to pray, mee.nB of grnce, opportunities of work. 2. All creation used by him as means of bestowing his blessing (cf. Rom. viii. 28). Sorrows (Rom. v. 3; Heh. xii. 11) and joys (Rom. ii. 4) 11re alike instruments of good (cf. Ps. cxvi. 12; cxix. 67). III. THE FRUIT OF THE BLESSING. Closer walk with God. The e,ents of this chapter were followed by mqre vivid spiritual manifestations to Abram. And thn~ our spiritual life advances. The blessing is God's free gift; but throngh conflid ,vith evil the soul is prepared to receive it (cf. Ps. xcvii. 10). As in natural life powers a·re increased by exercise, or rather by God's gift on this condition, so in the spiritual the conflict of self-denial, our Saviour's blessing, and the" spirit of adoption" are inseparablylinked together. "Grace for grace" should be the Christian's n10tto ; ever pressing onwards. And 11s we c11n assign no limits to God's blessing, so neither is there any limit to our nearness to him.-M.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie Church militant. I. THE ENEMIES OF THE CHURCH. Like Abram's -1. Numerous. 2. Formidable. 3. Exulting. II. THE TRIUMPH OF THE CHURCH. Like Abram's-!. Certain. 2. Complete. 3. Final. III. THE 1'11ANKSGIVINO OJ!' THE CHURCH. Like Abram's-1. Due to Gou most high. 2. Offered through the priest of the most high God. 3. Expressed in selfconsecration to the service of God.-W.

entries.title: GEN 14:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abraliam's independent spirit. "And Abraham said to the king of Sodom, I have lift up my hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth, that I will not take from a thread even to II shoelatchet," &c. When Lot chose the plains of Sodom he knew not wh11t trials awaited him there. The king of Sodom was attacked and defeated. He escaped, but many of his subjects were either slaughtered or made captive. Lot was carried away by the invading host. Abraham delivers him. On his return, flushed with victory, he is met by two persons-Melchizedek and the king of Sodom. To the first he gives tithes, as :, thank offering ; from the second he will not receive anything for all the risk ho had run in the conflict. If Abraham had taken all the spoil, it would only have been in accordance with the genernl practice of that age; but a principle, and not a custom, is his guide. I. entries.title: GEN 15:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A.nd Abram said, Lord God. Adona.i Jehovah,; the :Ii.nit use of these terms in combination, the second, which usually l1as tl,e vowel-points of the first, king he1·e written with the vocalisation of Elohim. Adonai, an older plural form of Adcnim, plumlis e.xcellentire (Gesenius), though by some the tormination is regarded as a suffix (Ewald, Fiirst), is a term descriptive of the J?ivine sovereignty, from adan = dun, or dwi, to rule or judge ; connected with which is the Phrenician adon, an 11011, orary epithet of deity, and recognised as such in Deut. x. 17 (vide Fiirst, •Hebrew Lexicon,' sub voce). What wilt thou give me, seeing I go - literally, and I going = iyw 8, ,i,ro)..voµa, (LXX., Jonathan); e.x hac vita discedam (Rosenmiiller) ; but this, though the word " go " is sometimes used in the sense of" die" (Ps. xxxix. 14), does not seem necessary-childless-solitary, desolate, hence devoid of offspring, as in Levit. eh. xx. 20, 21 ; Jer. xxii.· 30 - and the steward-Ben-.llfeshek; either (1) the son of running (from shakak, to run)'= .filius discursitatis, i e. the steward who attends to my domestic affairs (Onkelos, Drusius); or, and with greater probability, (2) the son of possession (from mashak, to hold), i. e. the possessor of my house, or heir of my property (Gesenius, Fiirst, Delitzsch, Jreil, 1folisch)-ofmyhouse is this Eliezer ofDamascus. Literally, Dammesek Eliezer. The paronomasia of this utterance is apparent, and was obviously designed to impart a touch of pathos to the patriarch's grief by pointing out the coincidence that the Ben- Meshek of his house was either Dammesek (Damascus) in the person of Eliezer (Delitzsch, Keil), or the Damascene Eliezcr (Onkelos, Syriac, .Aben Ezra, Calvin, Lange, Murphy), or Dammesek-Eliezei· as one word (Kalisch).

entries.title: GEN 15:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abram said, Behold; to me thou hast given no seed : and, lo, one born in my house (literally, tli,e son of my house, i. e. Eliezer) is mine heir. The language of the patriarch discovers three things : (1) a natural desire to have a child of his own ; (2) a struggle to hold on by the promise in face of almost insuperable difficulties; and (3) an obvious unwillingness to part with the hope that the promise, however seemingly im_possible, would eventually be realised. This unwillingness it was which caused him, as it were, so pathetically to call the Divine o.ttention to his childless condition ; in response to which he received an assurance that must have thrilled his anxious heart with joy.

Yer, 6.-And he (Jehovnh, or "the Won! of tho Lord") brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them (a proof that Abram's vision was not n dream): and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be. And he counted it to him. 'E>-.oyi119f1 avrcp (LXX.), which is followed by nearly ell the ancient versions, and by Paul in Rom. iv. 3 ; but the suffix ';J (a feminine for a ~euter, as in Job v. 9 ;Ps. xii. 4 ; xxvii. 4 ; vule Glass,' Phil.,' lib. iii. cp. i. 19), clearly indicates the object of the acUon expressed by the verb Ji;;,, to think, to meditate, and then to imputeT (>-.07//;oµa,), followed by ~ of pers. and acc. of the thing (cf. 2 Sam: xix. 20 ; Ps. xxxii. 2). The thing in this case was his faith in the Divine promise. For righteousness. il~l~ = ,ic oiKmo11vvf1v (LXX.); neither for· merit and justice (Rabbi Solomon, Jarchi, Kalisch), nor as a proof of his probity (Gesenius, Rosenmiiller) ; but unto anrl with a view to justification (Rom. iv. 3), so that God treated him as a. righteous person (A Lapide), not, however, in the sense that he was now "correspondent to the will of God both in character and conduct" (Keil), bnt in the sense that he was now before God accepted and forgiven (Luther, Calvin, :Murphy, Candlish), which "passh-e righteousness," however, ultimately wrought in him an "active 1ighteousness of complete conformity to the Divine will" (' Speaker's Colllmentary ').

entries.title: GEN 15:1–6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Under the sta?'S with God. I. DEJECTED BEFORE Gon. 1 Appre- 1 iensive of dange1·. Victorious over the Asiatic monarchs, Abram nevertheless dreaded their return. Signal deliverances are not seldom followed by depressing fears; e. g. David (1 Sam. xxvii. 1) and Elijah (1 Kings xix. 10). Having emancipated the people of the land by breaking "the yoke of their burden, and the staff of their shoulder, the rod of their oppressor," he yet feared an outbreak of their hostility. The enmity of those they serve is not an infrequent reward of patriots: witness Moses (Exod. xvii. 4) and Christ (John x. 31). 2. Disappointed in hope. Notwithstanding repeated assurances that he would one day become a mighty nation, the long-continued barrenness of Sarai appears to ba'l"e lain upon bis heart like a heavy burden. Partaking to all more or less of the nature of a deprivation, the lack of offspring was to Abram an acute grief ond serious affliction. The pent-up yearnings of his nature, rendered the more intense by reason of the promise, could not longer be restrained. In language full of pathos he complains to God about his childless condition. So "hope deferred maketh the heart sick" (Prov. xiii. 12). 3. Anxious abo11t t!te promise. He could not discern the possibility of its fulfilment, with years rapidly advancing on himself and Sarai. It is doubtful if any saints, more than Abram, can predict beforehand how the Divine promises shall be accomplished. Yet a recollection of whose promises they are should enable them, us it n,ight have assisted him, to perceive that not a single word of God's can foll to the ground. But, owing partly to limitations in the human mind o.nd imperfections in the human heart, doubts insensibly insinuate themselves against even the clearest nnd the strongest evidence. And when danger, disappointment, and doubt conjoin to invade the soul, dejection must inevitably follow. II. Com.roRTED DY Goo. I. A s!tieldfor his peril. Divinely given, oil sufficient, ever present. "I," Jehovah, "nm," now and always, "thy shield "--i. e. thin~ impregnable defence, And the like protection is vouchsafed to Abram's chi!Jreu when imperilled: as to character, Divine (Prov. xxx. 5); ns to extent, complete, universal, defending from all forms of evil, warding off assaults from all qut1rter~ (Pa. v. 12) ; a.s to duration, perpetual (Ps. cxxi. 8). 2. A solace for liis sorrow. Happy a.s the birth of an heir in Sarai's tent would make him, Jehovah gives him to und6rstand tlrnt not that was to be hi~ recompense for the trials be had passed 218 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [et,. x.v. 1- -6, tbroug-h, the sacrifices he had made, and the feats he had performed since Jeavinr1 Ur, but hin:iself. God's saints are prone to seek their happiness in God's gift~ rather than rn the Giver. Here they are recalled along with Abram to the sublimo tb?ught that G?d h!mself _is his people's best reward, and that the possession and enJoyment of Ins fnendslup should abundantly compensate for the absence of creature comforts,_however dearly prized and ardently desired. 3. A son /01' his heir. lns~ad of ~hezer,.whom _in his _perplexity h_e thought of adopting as his son, a ventable child of his own 1s promised. Let samts learn how blind is human reason and how feeble faith becomes when it tries to walk by sight; let them also notic; and consider how sure arc God's promises, and how inexhaustible nre God's resources. III. BELIEYING IN Goo. 1. The obJect of Abram's fnith. That at this stage of the patriarch's history attention is so markedly directed to his faith can only be explained on the supposition that he now for the first time clearly and implicitly received, embraced, and rested in the promise of a seed, and consequently of a Saviour. And the faith which justifies and saves under the gospel dispensation has an outlook nothing different from that of Abram. The object which it contemplates and appropriates is not simply the Divine promise of salvation, but the specific offer of a Sanour. God is the Justifier of him who believes in Jesus (Rom. iii. 26). 2. The ground of Abram's faith. Neither reason nor sense, but the solemnly given, clearly stated, perfectly snfficient, wholly unsupported word of God. And of a like description is the basis of a Christian's faith-God's promise in its naked simplicity, which promise (of a Saviour, or of salvation through Jesus Christ) bas, like that delivered to Abram, been solemnly announced, clearly exhibited, declared to be perfectly sufficient, but left wholly unsupported in the gospel (John iii. 36). 3. The acting of Abram's faith. It was instantaneous, accepting and resting on the Divine promise the moment it was explicitly made known; full-hearted, without reservation of doubt or uncertainty, implicitly reposing on the naked word of God; and conclusive, not adm.iiting of further opening of the question, "being fully persuaded that God was able also to perform that which he had promised" (Rom. iv. 21). IV. ACCEPTED WITH Gon. Whatever exegesis be adopted of the clause, "it was counted unto him for righteousness,'' the transaction which took place beneath the starry firmament is regarded in the New Testament as the pattern or model of a sinner's jnstification, and employed to teach-I. The natureofjustification, which is the reckoning of righteousness to one in himself destitute of such excellence, and, on the ground of sncb imputed righteousness, the acquittal in the eye of the Divine law of one otherwise obnoxious to just condemnation. Possessing no inherentrighteous, ness of his own, Abram had the righteousness of another (not at that time revealed to him) set to his account, and was accordingly justified or declared righteous before God. 2. The conditwn of justification, which is not works, but faith, Abram having been accepted solely on the ground of belief in_tb~ Divine promise (Ro~. i_v. 2-5)_; not, however, faith as an opus operatum or mentor1ous act, but as a subJechve cond1, tion, without which the act of imputation cannot proceed upon the person. 3. The time of justification, which is the instant a soul believes, whether that soul be cognisant of the act or not Abram again being justified, according to the Scripture, from the moment he accepted the Divine promise, though it is not said that Abram at the time was aware of the indemnatory act passed in his favour in the court of heaven. Lessons :-1. God's saints may sometimes be cast down in God's presence (Ps. xliii. 5). 2. It is God's special character and care to comfort those wl!o are cast down (2 Cor. vii. 6). 3. God's promises are the wells of comfort which he has opened for the solace of dejected saints.

entries.title: GEN 15:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -What the Lord is to his people. I. A SHIELD against--1. The charges of the law (Isa. xiv. 24). 2. The accusations of conscience (Rom. xv. 13). 3. The force of temptation (Rev. iii. 10). 4. The opposition of the world (Rom. viii. 31), 5, The fear of death (Heb. ii. 15). •II. A REWARD-1. For sufferings patiently endured (2 Tim. ii. 12). 2. For sacrifices cheerfully made (Matt. xi:x. 28). 3. For service faithfully accomplished (Rev. ii. 28). Lessons :-1. Admire the exceeding richness of Divine grace. 2. Appreciate the fulness of Divine salvation. 3. Realise the height of Divine privilege ar.corde<l to the saint.-W. •

entries.title: GEN 15:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Faitli and Righteousness, "And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Even by itself this passage claims attention. How does the idea of righteousness come into it at nil? What is meant by " counting" or " imputation " ? And what is the connection between belief and imputed righteousness? But it does not stand alone. (1) In Ps. cvi. 30 (cf. :t-lum. :xxv. 7) the same" counting" takes place on an act of an entirely different character; and (2) it is thrice quoted in the New Testament as an example of the action of faith in the spiritual life. Imputation must not be explained away. Its meaning is seen in Levit. vii. 18; xvii. 4; 2 Sam. xix. 19. There is here the germ of II the Lord our righteousness." In Rom. iv. 3-5, 23-25, St. Paul refers to it as an instance of justification by faith, connecting it with "the reward ;'' and this again with forgiveness and acceptance (Ps. :x:xxii. 2), the psalm almost repeating the worJs of the text (see o.lso Gal. iii. 6). We need not suppose that now for the first time Abram was accepted of God, or that he alone was counted righteous. Mark, Abram beliend not merely the particular promise, but "in the Lord." This instance is specially noticed by St. Paul as an instance of faith, because from the nature of the case there was no opportunity of action. I. THE WORKING OF FAITH-simple belief of what God hns said, because he is true; casting all care upon him. No merit in this. Faith is the channel, not the source of justification. By the look of faith the dying Israelites lived (Num. xxi. 9)1 but the healing was from God. God offers salvation freely (John vii. 37; Rev. :x:xii. 17), because he loves us even while in our sins (EJ?hes. ii. 4). What hinders that love from being effectual is unbelief. Many "believe 11 lie"-e. g. that they must become better ere they can believe (cf. Acts xv. 1). Primary lesson of practical Christianity is that we must begin by receiving, not by giving; must learn to believe his word because it is his word. This delivers from the spirit of bondage (Rom. viii. 15), und enables to ask with confidence (Rom. viii. 32). And this faith is counted for righteousness. II. FArrlI GROWS BY USE. It is the gift of God (Ephes. ii. 8), but it is given according to laws. Sometimes it springs up suddenly-e. g. Nnthanael, St. Paul, the Philippian jailer; but usually it is like the growth of the seed, hardly to be tracedll gradual growth from efforts to live by faith, Let none think, I can believe when I will, The endeavour delayed will meet with many difficulties, suggestions of doubt, 220 1:'lrn BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, XV, 7-iJt, or hal~its of indecision. And let none despise the trai11ing which prepares the soul to lehe,·e. It may seem to be labour in vain, yet the Holy Spirit may be workin!( unseen to prepare the soul for life and pence. • _III. FA~TH LEADS TO !IOLINE:SS. It renders possible a service w.bich cannot otherwise be gH·en. The faith wluch was counted to Abram for rio·hteousness formed the character :diich _enabl~d him afterwards to offer up Isaac (cf Jamee ii. 21-23). Thns growth m holiness 1s the test of real faith, There is a faith which has no power (cf. James ii. 19; 1 Cor. xiii. 2; 2 Tim. iv. 10). It is with the heo.rt that man belie-ves unto righteousness (cf. Ps. b::xxiv. 6, 7; Prov. iv. 23).-M.

entries.title: GEN 15:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he (Jehovah, or tl1c Word of the Lord) said unto him (after the act of faith on the part of the patriarch, and the act of imputation or justification on the part of God, and in explication of the exact nature of that relationship which had been constituted between them by the spiritual. tr>1nsaction so described), I am the Lord tha.t brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldeea (ride eh. xi. 2S), to give thee this land to inherit (or, to possess) it. Yer. 8.-And he said, Lord God {A<Wnai .Tehovah; Tide ver. 2), whereby shall I know tha.t I sha.11 inherit it 1 Not the language ul' doubt, though slight misgivings are not incompatible with faith (cf. Judges vi. 17; :! Kings XL 8; Luke i 34), and questioning wiih God "is rather a :proot of faith than a sign of incredulity" (Calvin); but of desire for a sign in confirmation of the grant (Luther), either for the strengthening of his uwn faith (Chrysostom, Augustine, Keil, 'Speaker's Co=ent:i.ry '), or for the sake of his posterity (Jarchi, Michll,€lis), or for some intimation as to the time and mode of taking 11ossession (Morphy). Rosenmiiller conceives the question put in Abram's mouth to be only a device of the narrator's to lead up to the subject following.

entries.title: GEN 15:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said unto him, Take me (literally, for me, i. e. for my use in sa~rifice) a.n heiier of three yea.re old. So nghtly (LXX., Syriac, Samaritan, .Arabic, Josephus, Bochart, Rosenmiiller, Keil); not three heifers (Onkelos, Jarchl, Kimehi, et aJ,ii). And a she goat of three years old, a.nd a ra.m of three years old. These offerings, afterwards prcscribed by the law (Exod. xxix. 15; Num. xv. 27 ; xiL 2; Deut. =i. 3), were three in number, and of three years ea.eh, to symbolise him who was, and is, and is to come (Wordsworth) ; perhaps rather to indicate the perfection of the victim in respect of maturity (Murphy). Cf. Ganymede's offering (in 'Lucian's Dialogues') of a three years old ram for a ransom. And a turtle-dove, and a young pigeon-also prescribed by the law (Levit. i. 14; Luke ii 24).

entries.title: GEN 15:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he took unto himRll these, and divided (a word occuning only here in Genesis, and supposed by Michaelis to hava been taken by Moses from the ancient document from which he transcribed this portion of his work The word is afterwards found in Cant. ii. 17, and Jer. xxxiv. 18) them in the midst,--,µfoa (LXX.) ; in equa.l parts (Onkclos)-and laid each piece one age.inst another : but the birds. divided he not. So afterwards in the Mosaic legisla.tion (Lcvit. i. 7). Wordsworth detects in the non-dividing of the birds an emblem of "the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of peace a.nd love, which is a. Spirit of unity," a.nll of "Christ's humnn spirit, which was not divisible." Kalisch, with more probability, recognises as tho rea.son of their not being divided the fac~ that such division was not required, both fowls being regarded as one part of the sacrifice only, and each, as the ha.If, being placed opposite the other. Wordsworth numbers seven parts in the sacrifice, and sees a symbol of completeness a.nd finality, the number seven being the root of shaba, to swear (Gesenius, p. 802) ; Kalisch reckons four, which he regardsas "denotingperfection, but rather the external perfection of form than the internal one of the mind," and pointing ''to the perfect possession of the Holy Land." The ritual here described is the same wl1ich was afterwards observed among the Hebrews in the formation of covenants (cf. eh. xxxiv. 18), and appears to have extensively prevailed among heathen nations (cf. 'Iliad,' b. 124, "opK1a 7r111rd raµo,,r,,;;" am! the Latin phra.se, "fredus icere ").

entries.title: GEN 15:11

entries.content: -And when the fowls-literally, and the bird ofpi·ey, a collective singular with the article, as in eh. xiv. 13, symbolising the Egyptians and other adversaries of Israel, a.s in Ezek. xvii. 3, 7, 12; xxxix. 4, 17; Rev. xix. 17, 18 (Knobel, Rosenmiiller, Lango, Keil, Kalisch), which may beregarded as probable if the divided victims represented Israel in affliction, which is doubtful (vide supra). It does not appear necessary to attach a.ny special significance to the descent of the vultures, which aro alwnys attracted towards carrion, and the introduction ol which here completes the naturalness of the scene-came down upon the carcases (the <lH. XV. 7-21.] 'rHE BOOK OF GENESIS. 221 LXX. intcl'polates, brl ra ~,xornµ.~µ.ara), Abram drove them away. Literally, cauaed them to be blown away, i. e. by blowing. " Though .Abram is here re.Presented as the instrument, yet the effect 1s to be ascribed primarily to the tutelar agency of omnipotence " (Bush ; cf. Exod. xv. I0 ; Ezek. xxi. 31). The net of scaring the voracious birtls has been taken to reprcsent the ease with which .Abrom or Israel would ward off his enemies (Jonathan, Targums, Rosenmiiller, Ilnsh) ; the averting of destruction from the Israelites through .Abram's merit (Kalisch, Keil) ; .Abram's religious regard for and observance of God's treaty (Wordsworth); the patiiarch's expectation that God was about to employ the sacrificial victims for some holy purpose (.Alford) ; simply his anxiety to preserve the victims pure and unmutilated for whatever end they might have to serve (Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 15:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And when the sun was going down. Literally, was about to go down (cf. Gesenius, § 132). The vision having commenced the previous evelllllg, an entire day bas already passed, tho interval being desi~ed to typify the time between the promise and its fulfilment (Kalisch). A deep sleep-tardemah (cf. .Adam's sleep, eh. ii. 21); ;KaTaa,, (LXX.); a supernatural slumber, as the darkness following was not solely tlue to natural causes-fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkneas-literally, an horror, a great darkness, i. e. an overwhelming dread occasioned by the dense gloom with which he was encircled, nnd which, besides being designed to conceal the working of the Deity from mortal vision (Knobel), was meant' to symbolise the Egyptian bondage (Grotius, Calvin, Rosenrniiller, Keil, Kalisch), and perhaps a.lso, since Abram's faith embraced a larget.sphere than Canaan· (Heb. xi. 10, 14, 16), and a nobler seed 'than Sarah's sou (John viii. 66), the sufferings of Christ (Wordsworth, Inglis) -fell upon him.

entries.title: GEN 15:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said unto Abram, Know 'of a surety-literally, knowing know (cf. eh. ii. 17; vide Ewald's 'Hebrew Syntax,'§ 312)-that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land which is not theirs (literally, wt to them, viz., Egypt, or Egypt and Canaan, according to the view which is taken of the point of departure for the reckoning of the 400 years), and shall serve them (i. e. the inhabitants of that alien country) ; and they (i. e. these foreigners) shall affl.ict themthree different stages of adverse fortune are described :- (1) exile; (2) bondage; (3) o..ffliction (Murphy) ; or the two last clauses depict the contents of the first (Kalisch)- four hundred years. The duration not of their nfiliction merely, but either of their bc?::!~be and affiiction, or more probnbly of their exile, bondage, and affliction ; either a round number for 430 (Calvin, Rosenmi.illcr, Keil, AHord), to bo reckoned from the data of the descent into Egypt (Kalisch, Lange), as Moses (Exotl. xii. 39) and Stephen (Acta vii. 6) seem to say, antl to be reconcilecl with the statement of Paul (Gal. iii. 17) by reg"rding the death of Jacob as the closing of the time of promise (Lange, Inglis) ; or an exnrt number dating from the birth of Isaac (Willet, Murphy, Wordsworth), which was thirty years after the call in Ur, thus making the entire interval correspontl with the 430 yearn of Paul, or from the persecution of Ishmael (Ainsworth, Clarke, Bush), which occurrctl thirty years after the promise in eh. xii. 3.

entries.title: GEN 15:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And also that nation (the name of which he docs not reveal, in case of seeming to interfere with the free volition of his creatures, who, while accomplishing his high designs and secretpurposes, arc ever conscious of their moral freedom), whom they shall serve, will I judge :-i. e. punish after judging, which prediction was in due course fulfilled (Exod. vi. 11)-and afterward shall theycome out with great substance-recush (cf. eh. xiii. 6 ; vide Exod. xii. 36).

entries.title: GEN 15:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And thou she.It go to thy fathers in peace (cf. eh. xxv. 8; xu:v. 29; xlb:. 33). Not a periphrasis for going to the gra,e (Rosenmiiller), since .Abram's ancestors were not entombed in Canaan; but a proof of the survival of departed spilits in a state of conscious existenceafter death (Knobel, Murphy, Wordsworth, 'Speaker's Commentary,' 111glis), to the company of which the patriarch was in due time to bo gathered. The disposaI of his remains is provided for in what follows. Thou shalt be buried in a good old age. Yer. 16.-Ba.t in the foa.rth generationnraprp oi YEVHj (LXX.) ; but, more correctly, the .fourth generation, calculatin:s 100 years to a generation. "Caleb was the fourth from Judah, and JIIoses from Len, antl so doubtless many others" (Bush). Drs. Oort and Kuenen, reckoning four generations as a far shorter space of time than four centuries, detect a contradiction between this verso and ver. 13, anti an evitlence of the free use which the ancient and uncritical Israelitish author matle of his mnterials (' Bible for Young People,' vol. i. p. 158). On the import of ii"I vide eh. vi. 9-they shall come hither again (literally, shall i·eturn hither): for the iniqa.ity or the Amorites is not yet full. Literally, for not completed the iniquity of tl,e Amorites (vide eh. xiv. 7; here put for the entiro population) until then (the same word as "hither," which i! ';.s nsunl signification).

Gesenius, p. 869 ; Keil in loco)-nd a burning 11;-mp-a lnmp of fi_re, or fiery torch, cmergmg from the smokmg stove ; an cmhlcm of the Dinne presence (cf. Exod. xiic. 1S)-that passed between those pieces-in ratification of tlie ~ovcn~nt. Ycrs. 1S-21.-In that day tbe Lord made ~ cove1!'ant-1itemlly,_ cut a covenant (cf. 0 o«a ,,µ,•nv, fredus were). On-the import of Tl'"!f •11ule ~h. ix. 9)-with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt-the Nile (Keil, Kurtz Hen~tcnberg, Kalisch) rather than th~ Waay el Arish, or Brook of Egypt (K=bel, Lange, Clarke), at the southern limits of the country (Numb. =xiv. 5; Josh. xv. 4;.Isa. xxvi.i. 12)-u.nto the great river, the river Euphrates. The ideal limits of ·the Holy Land, which were practically reached under Dand auu. Solomon (vide l Kings iv. "21; 2 Chron. ix. 26), and which embraced the following subject populations, ten in number, "to convey the impression of universality without exception, of unqualified completeness" (Delitzsch). The Kenites,-inhabiting the mountainous tracts in the south-west of Palestine, near the Amalckites (Numb. xx:iv. 21 ; l Sam. xv. 6; =vii. 10); a people of uncertain origin, though (Judges i. 16; iv. 11) Hobn.b, the brother-in-law of Moses, was n Kenite-and the Kenizzites,-mentioricd only in this passage; a peop1e dwelling apparently in the same region with the Kenites (Murphy), who probably became extinct between the times of Abraham and Moses (Dochart), and cannot now be identified (Keil, Kalisch), though they have been connected with Kena.z tlie Edomite, eh. xxxvi. 15, 42 (Knobel)-and the Kadmonites,- nevcr a,,.-.ain referred to, but, as their name implies, an Ea.,tcrn people, whose settlements extended townrds tho Euphrates (Kalisch)-- and the Hittites,-the dcscendl\nts pf. Heth (vitk eh, x. 15); identified with the Khota and Kntti of the Egyptian and .Assyrian monuments, and supposed by Mr, Gladstone to be the Kheteians ofthe 'Odyssey;' apowerful Asiatic tribe who must have oady established themselves on the Euphro.tes, and spread from thence southward to Canaan and Egypt, nnd westward to Lydia and Greece, carrying with them, towards the shores ofthe ..Egcan Sea, the art and culture of Assyria and Babylon, already modified by the forms and conceptions of Egypt. Th~ .northern capital of their empire was Carchemish, about sixteen miles south of the modern Birejik ; and the southern Kndesh on an island of the Orantes (Prof. Sayce i~ 'Frli.zcr's Magazine,' August, 1880, art. 'A forgotten: Empire in Asia Minor ')--and th(I Perizzites, and the Rephaima (vide eh. xiii. 7 ; xiv. 6), and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgaehites, -and the .Tebusites {vide. eh, x. 16-19). The boundaries of the Holy Land as here defined are regarded. by some (Bohlen) as·.contradictory of those designated in Numb.. xxxiv. 1-12. But (1) the former may be viewed e.s the ideal (or poetical), and the latter as the act!lal (and prosaic), .limits of the couptry assigned to Israel (Hengstenbreg, Keil) ; or (2) the. former may represent the. maxima, and theJatter the minima, of the promise, which admitted ofa larger or-a smaller fµlfilment, 11ecording as Israel should in the sequel prove fit for its occupation (AugustinA, Pererius, Willet, Poole, Gerlach, Kalisch, and others) ; or, (3) according to a certain school of interpreters, the former may point to the wide extent of country to be occupied by the Jews on occasion of their restoration to their own land, as distinguished from their fu-st occupation on: coming up out of Egypt, or their.second on-1·eturni:ng from Babylon; or (4) the rivers may be· put for the countries with which thepromisedland was coterminous (Kurtz, Murphy) ; or (5) ,strict ~cographical accuracy may not have "been· mtendcd in defining the lim_its of the land of promis, (' Speaker's Commentary,' lngli~).. •

entries.title: GEN 15:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Taken into covenamL I. TnE BLESSING OF THE COVENANT. 1. The ultimate blessing, to which, in both the commencement and close of the present section, the prominence is assigned, was a splendid inlieritance-the land of Canaan for hie descendants, and for himself the better country, of which that ~arthly posse11sion was a type. 2. The medwte blessing, through which alone the las.t· cou}d be reached, w;i.s a distinguished seed-a numerous posterity to occupy the lanq, and a 1iving Sa.viour to secure for himself the better country. 3. The proximate ble~oing, to be enjoyed wl,ile as yet tl1e second and the third were unfulfilled, wn.s r1, celestial alliance by whicli Jehovah himself engaged to be his sliiclu and e:1:cec<ling greut reward. It is obvious thllt these llre the blessings which the gospel confers on believers-ll hellvenly_Friend, an llll-sufficient Saviour, a future inheritance; whence the Abrnh11mic covenant WllS nothing different from the covenant of grace. II. THE nEASON OF TBE COVENANT. The essential idea in a covenant being a visible pledge for the fulfilment of a promifl'e, the necessity for such a guarantee on the present occasion, it is apparent, could not Ii~ with God. On the contrary, the proposal on the part of God to bind himself by a superadded engagement to implement bis own gracious and spontaneous promise was an explicit condescension, if not to the feebleness of the patriarch's faith, at least to the weakness of his human nature. Perhaps the recollection of who Jehovah was, and what he had already accomplished in bringing Abram from Ur, should have proved sufficient to authenticate the premise; but it would almost seem as if human nature, in its innocent no less than in its fallen state, instinctively craved the assistance of external symbols to enable it to clearly apprehend and firmly grasp the unseen and spiritual blessings that are wrnpt up in God's promises. In the garden of Eden the tree of life was Adam's sacramental pledge of immortality ; after the Flood the many-coloured rainbow was a sign to Noah; in the Hebrew Church material symbols of unseen verities were not awanting; while in the Christian Church the passover and circumcision have been repllleed by the Lord's Supper and baptism. The reasons that required the institution of these external signs may be held as having necessitated the solemn ritual which ,vas exhibited to Abram. III. T1rn SYMBOLS OF TBE COVENANT. 1. The sacrificial mctims. Seeing that these were afterwards prescribed in the Mosaic legislation, which itself was a shadow of the good things to come, to be employed as propitiatory offerings, it is impossible not to regard them, though not necessarily understood as such by Abram, as types (not of Israel, Abram's seed after the flesh simply, nor of the Church of God generally, i. e. Abram's seed according to the spirit, though perhaps neither of these should be excluded, but) of Abram's greater Seed, whose perfect, Divinely-appointed, and substitutionary sacrifice alone constitutes the basis of the everlasting covenant. 2. The imokin(J furnace and,· the bm"fl,ing lamp. CompaTed with the smoke and fire that afterwards appeared on Sinai when Jehovah descended to covenant with Israel, am! the pillar of cloud and fire thllt led the march of Israel from Egypt, these at onco sugg·est their own interpretation. They were emblems of God's presence, and may be viewed ns suggesting (1) the combination of justice and mercy in tlrn Divine character, and (2) the twofold attitude in which the Deity exhibits himself to men according as they are his enemies or friends. IV. THE IMPORT OF THE COVENANT. Partly through visible sign, partly in spiritual vision, partly by audible words, the patriarch was instructed llS to-1. The ob:jective basis of his own j11sti,fi,cation, which was neither personlll merit nor faith considered as an opus operatitm, but the Divinely-appointed sacrifice which God was graciously pleased to accept in propitiation for humllll sin. 2. The true smtrity for God)sful- -fi.lrnent, of the promise, which was not 11ny outward sign or token, but the everlasting covenllnt which in mysterious symbol had been unfolded to him. 3. The interval of discipline allotted to tlte heirs of tlie land; for his descendllnts three generations of exile, servitude, and affliction, to prepare them for receiving Canllan in the fourth ; and for himself a continual.sojourning, without a final settling within its borders ; in both cases emblematic of the saint's experience after justification and before glorification. 4. Tlie ultimate assumption of the inheritance by his seed-a Divine voice solemnly foretelling their return from captivity, ns it aftenvnrds declared that his spiritual descendants should be emancipated and brought back to their celestial ilbode, and II Divine vision unfolding to his gaze the wide extent of territory they ehotild eventulllly possess-perhaps the limits of the earthly land melting llway, 11s his spirit stood entranced before the gorgeous panorama, into the confines of the better country. 5. His oum certain passage to the heavenly Canaan, for which he was even at tl1at time looking-a prolllise which belongs individually to 1111 who are the children of Abram by faith in Jesus Christ. See from this subject--!. The fulness of Divine blessing which the covenant cont11ins. 2. The depth of Divine condescension which the covenunt reveals. 3. The glorious sernrities which the coven11nt idiorrls, THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, XV, 7-21

entries.title: GEN 16:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children (litera.lly, bai·e not to him, notwithstanding ,the promise; the barrenness of Sarai being introduced ns the point of departure for the ensuing narrative, and 'emphasised as the cause or occasion of the subsequent transaction): and she had-literally, to her (there was)-an handmaid, an Egyptian (obtained probably while in the house of Pharaoh (eh. xiL 16)-whose name was Hagar-" flight," from hagai·, to flee. Cf. Hcgirah, the flight of l'lfahomet. Not her original designation, but given to her afterwards, either because of her flight from Egypt (Ambrose, Wordsworth), or because of her escape from her mistress (l\Iichaelis, Bush, ' Speaker's Commentary'). Though not the imaginary or mythical (Bohlen), it is doubtful if she was the real (Ainsworth, Bush), ancestor of the Hagarenes (1 Chron. v. 10, 19, 20 ; xxvii. 31 ; Ps. lxxxiii. 6, 8),

entries.title: GEN 16:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the Lord bath restrained me from bee.Ting. Literally, hath shut me up (i. e. my womb, eh. x:x. 18; a,JIJ;.,xuae µ•, LXX.) from bearing. Her advancing age was rendering this every day more and more nppnrent. I pray thee go in unto my maid (cf. eh. xxx. 3, 9). It is so far satisfactory that the propo~al to make a secondary wife of Hagar diJ not originate with Abram ; though, as Sarai's guilt in making it cannot altogether be e:;cused,,so neither can .A.bram bo entirely freed from fault in yielding to her solicitations. I,t may be that I may obtain children by her. Literally, be built '1tp by her; from banah, to build, whence ben, a son (Deut. xll:v. !) ; Ruth iv.'11). Calvin notes that Snrai's desire of offspring was not prompted by natural impulso, but by the zeal of foith which made her ,vish to secure the promised benediction. As yet it had not been clearly intimated that Sarai was to be the mother of Abram's child ; and hence hor recourse to what was II prevalent practice of the times, while unjustifiable in itself, was a signal proof of her humility, of her devotion to her husband, nud perhaps 'also of her faith in God. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai. " Tho faith of both was defective ; not indeed with regard to the substance of the promise, but with regard to the method in which they proceeded" (Calvin).

entries.title: GEN 16:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw

XXV, 6), she is here improperly called a wife IJU<epneterDeile,gem in alienum tho• rum inducitur (Calvin), from whom the pilgash or concubine differed (1) in power over the family, which belonged solely to the trno wife, not to the secondary ; (2) in the manner of espousal, which in the case of the former was accompanied with solemn rites of espousal an<l liberal gifts of dowry ; and (3) in privilege of issue, the offspring of the secondary wife having no title to inherit.
