entries.title: GEN 16:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The captw·e of tlie runaway, or Hagar and tlie angel of the Lord. I. THE FUGITIVE ARRESTED, 1. Tlie agent of her capture. The angel of Jehonh (vidtl Exposition), whose appearance to Hagar nt this particular juncture was donbtless-(1) Unexpected. Those who flee from duty seldom anticipate the encounterirw of God in their career (Jonah i. 3). (?) Instantaneous. The Invisible Supn'me, ~-ho ever compasses our paths, only reqmres to either open his creatures' eyes, or veil his uncreated glory in a fi~i~e form, to make his presence known (Ps. cxxxix. 7; Luko xxiv. 15). (3) Familiar. Though here mentioned, 11ngelic visitation need not now hav~ occurred for the first time. Hagar probably had learnt something in the patnarch's household of the character,existence, and form ofthis celestial visitant. (4) Opportune. Whether reginded in this light or not, the present Divine manifestation to Hagar wo.s highly seasono.ble, as God's visits to men ever are, in both the worlci o.nd the Church. 2. Theplace oflier capture. (1) In the wilderness, a very different locality from Abram's tent. But all regions nre equally ncccssible to God's providence and grace; and God's angel of mercy nnd salvation can find his way to dis• consolate wanderers ncross the wilderness of a bnrren world ns easily as to eminent eaints within the sacred precincts of the Church. (2) On the way to Shur, i. e. going bnck to Egyptian worldliness and idolntry. Her ch:-.nccs of reaching the Inn,! :230 THE BOOK 01'' GENESIS. [en. XVI. 7-16. of Ham were indeed small, considering· her bodily condition ; but thither 'ivas·her, destination, and hence her arrestment by the angel of the Lord was a specio.l meroy. So Divine grace interposes to prevent those who have been onco enlightened from relapsing· to ~heir ol~ n~tuml con~itio~ of worldliness and sin. (3) By a foun!ain ofwafer, bss1do v.•luch it may be 1magmed she had cast herself in sheer exhaustion . a'.1 emblem of tho~e.springs ?f refreshment, or wells of ~aca, which God has pro• nded for ~h~ spmtually d1sconsolate, and one of winch was being opened b.--: Jehovah's ns1t for the comfort of the unhappy bondmaid. _II. TnE ll'OUN'DLING IN~RROG;'TED. l. The qu_estion ofthe angel.· (1) The.designat10ns used, Hagar, Sarai s maid, reveal the minuteness of tlie Divme knowledge.. God is acquainted with the names and the homes, tl1e conditions in life, and the con• stituent elements in the history of all men (Ps. cxxxix. 1-5). (2) The refei•ence to Hagar's original condition of servitude implies disapprobation of her union with Abram. No transaction can be safely pMsed as blameless until it has been reviewed and judged by God. (3) The inquiries addressed to Hagar were designed to convict l1er of sin. \Vhence had she come? From Abram's house, where the naine of God was worshipped ; from the presence of Sarai, who had a lawful claim upon her ser~ vice; from the land of Canaan, the inheritance of Abram's seed, of which, as she fondly hoped, she was about to become the mother-in all which she wat1 clearly committing wrong. Then whither was she going? Back again to Egypt, as the ultimate goal of her flight, while in the mean time she was exposing herself and her unborn child to serious peril. Doubtless these and other considerations of a similar sort arose within the breast of Hagar as she listened to Jehovah'e qJI.estionings. Vi'hen God examines souls they are truly, minutely, and completely searched. 2. 1'he answer of Hagar. (1) Promptly given. There was no sign of hesitancy or reluctance. The utmost frankness and cordiality should characterise a sinner's dealings ~ith God. (2) Briefly expressed. "She was fleeing from the face of Sarai her mistress." Comprehensive brevity should signalise our responses to·God's interro~ gations. (3) Honestly declared. She had run away. If it was wrong, she made no attempt at concealment. Guileless acknowledg·ment of sin is a true mark of contrition. • III. THE wANDERE& DIRECTED. 1. To return to Abram's house. The tent of Sarai, though to Hagar's quick Southron blood a place of,humiliation, was neverthe• less for her the true place of safety, both physically and .epiritual)y. The first connsel that God's word and spirit give to those who flee from. duty', forsake -the company of saints, and venture out upon perilous and sinful courses is" to stand•in the ways, and ask for the old paths" (Jer. vi. 16). 2. To submit to'Sarai's yoke. Her alliance v-ith tlie patriarch could not in God's sight alter her' original position as IL slave. Though soon to be the mother of Abram's seed, she was still a bondwoman, whose duty was submission, however galling to her hot blood, and however unreasonable it might seem in the case of one wl1ose child might yet inherit Canaan. God's people are required to abide in those stations in life in which they have been called, until they can be honourably released from them (1 Cor. vii. 20-22), and to endure those afflictions which God in his providence may impose, rather than impetuously and sinfully endeavour to escape from them (Matt. xvi. 24). IV. THE DISCONSOLATE COMFORTED. 1. The richness of the offered consolation. (1) A gracious assurance-that she was an object of the Divine regard, ns this very visit proved ; of the Divine observation, since the Lord knew her condition ; and of the Divine compassion, for already he had heard her affliction-than which no sweeter consolation can be offered to either penitent bachlider or dejected sufferer. (2) A comfortaUe promise-that she should live to be the mother of Abram's seed, that her unborn babe should be a son, and that her son should develop into n bold, courageous, and prosperous man, and that through him she herself, an Egyptian slave-girl, should become the ancestress of a numerous and mighty people. God is ahle, even in respect of material and temporal benefits, to compensate for life's sorrows and tribulations, and to make up in one direction for what he takes awny in another. (3) An important instructwn--to name her child "Ishmael" when it should be born; partly as a memorial to herself of the Divine mercy, and partly ne 11 rcininder to her child of the sure Source of pro~pority, both personal and nntional, on. XVI. 7-16.] 'rHEl BOOK OF GENESIS. 231 temporal and spirit1ml. God's people should remember the right hand of the Most High (Pa. Ixxvii. 10), and seek advancement from him nlone (Ps. lxxv. 6, 7). 2. The efficacy of the offered consolation. (1) Adoriny gratitude. Hagar was amazed at the Divine condescension in pennittin&'. her to see God and yet live-a mercy denied to Moses on the mount (Exod. xxx1ii. 20) ; and the Divine grace which had imparted life and hope to her soul through this celestial visitation. (2) Mercy r,m,,embered. Hagar called the well Beer-lahai-roi, i. e. the well of seeing and living. The Divine loving-kindness is worthy of memorials, which also shoulc1 be written on the tablets of the heart when they cannot be expressed in words or enshrined in deeds. (3) Cheerful submistrion. Hagar returned to Abram'a house, submitted to Sarai's l1and, and in due time gave birth to Ishmael. The best evidence that grace has comforted thehuman heart is prompt compliance with the will of God. See in the angel's appearance to Hagar-1. An adumbration of the incarnation of our Lord Jestis Christ. 2. An illustration of God's care of those who are within his Church. 3. An indication of the kind of people that most attract the Divine notice and compassion. 4. A revelation of the tenderness with which he deals wilh sinners. 5. A proclamation of God's gracious readiness to forgive the erring.

entries.title: GEN 16:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God pleading with wanderers. "Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence earnest_ thou? and whither wilt thou go?" . She knew not, cared not. Undisciplined smarting under effects of her own wilfulness (vcr. 4), she thought only of escaping pain-a type of those weary, yet unconverted (cf. Jer. ii. 13; v. 3). But God saw her. The Shepherd sought her (cf. Gen. iii. 9; Luke xv. 9). Though not of the chosen race, and having no claim upon his care, of his own mercy be calls her (cf. Ps. cxlv. 9; Ephes. ii. 4; TitUB iii. 5). The angel of the Lord; in ,er. 13 culled the Lord; the messenger of the covenant (Mai. iii. 1)-sent to carry out the lt'uther's purpose (cf. John iii. 17; Luke iv. 18). The same who speaks in the voice of awakened conscience, thnt he may give peace (cf. Matt. xi. 28). "Hagar, Sarai's mnid," expresses God's full knowledge of her (cf. Exod. xxx.ili. 12; John x. 3). The name distinguishes the individual. She n stranger, n slave, n fugitive ; yet God's eye upon her; nil her life before him (cf. Ps. cxxxix. 1-4). A word for those following theit- own ways, feeling as if hidden in the multitude. Nothing glaring in their lives; men see nothing to find fault with ; will God? (cf. Ps. xciv. 7). He knowsthee altogether; thywhole life, the selfishness underlying a fair profession, the unconfessed motives, the little duplicities, the love of worldly things; or it may be thy spiritual pride and self-trusting. He sees thee through. But wilt thou seek to escape the thought of liim? For what does he search thee out? Is it not to bring thee to peace? A word of comfort to him who is cast down because o.f weakness in faith, little progress, want of spirituality. Ho sees all (cf. Luke xiL 5). Not ns man-men see the failures; God sees the battle, the longing desire for better things, the prayers (Pa. xxviii. 1; c:xxx. 1), the searching of heart, the sorrow because of failure. Even in the wilderness he is present to help (Gnl. vi. 9). I. "WHENCE CAMEST THOU ?" Is the wilderness better thnn the home thou hast loft? (cf. Isa. v, 4). Thou hast left s1ifety and plenty (cf. Nnm. xxi. 5), impatient of God's discipline A goodly possession was thine-the plare of a child (1 John THE DOOK OJ<' GENESIS. [en. XVII. 1-14. iii. I), the right always to pray (Luke xviii. 1; John xv. 7; Heb. iv. 16 i James iv. 2), the promise of g-uidance (Ps. nxii. 8;. Isa. :xu. 21), For what hast thou g·lven up all tl1is? Is thy present lot better? In deepest love these questions are asked. God pleads by providen~e (Ps. c:xi:x, 67)1 by the entering of the word (Pa. cxjx. 130; Hob. iv. 12), by the "still small voice" of the Holy Spirit. II. " \\'HITHER WILT THOU Go?" How many have never really considered.. Hast thou renounc~d thy heavenly portion? God forbid. Then is thy life heavenward? Are thy sms blotted out? Hast thou accepted the free gift of so.lvo.tion? I am not sure of that. And why not? Is it not that thou hast not cared enoug·h to entertain the question as a practical one? (cf. Ezek. xx. 49; :x:x.:xiii. 32). Meanwhile thou art not standing still. The day of grace is passing away (of. Jer. viii, 20). St.ill Cl1rist pleads (Rev. iii. 20). But day by day the ear becomes more dull and the aims and habits of life more bard to change. 11 Return," was the Lord'~ word to Hagar. Take again thy place in God's family (of. Luke :xv. 20), Fear not to bear thy cross. There is a welcome and joy in heaven over every returning wandercr.-M.

entries.title: GEN 17:1–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlu covenant renewed. I. THE COVENANT CONFIRMED. 1. Tlie time. " When Abram was ninety years old and nine," i. e. thirteen years .after Ishmael's birth. Mark the penalty of striving to anticipate Divine promises. Human inge~ nuity, even when not directly sinful, can only retard, not accelerate, Jehovah's.purpose. 2. The Autlior. "El Shaddai," i. e. the Being who, though ordinarily operating silently and invisibly in nature, is able to break through nature in order to accomplish his designs. Nature is not superior to God, but vice versd-the Almighty transcends his own handiwork; and much as Nature. discloses of God's eternal power and Godhead in her ordinary workings, she does not by means of these reveal· the infinite fulness of his Divine resources. 3. The condition. "Walk before me, and be thou perfect," i. e. follow holiness as well as trust my word. Though grace is the prime mover in all Heaven's bargains or contracts with sinful men1 they nre invariably conditioned by man's obedience to and trust in the Divino Covenanter. The meaning briefly is, that if God's grace does not oonquer man's unbelief and sin, man's unbelief and sin will ultimately cancel God's grace. II. THE COVENANT EXPLAINED. 1. J.'he promiseofa seed. An old promise recapitulated, since God gives "line upon line," "precept upon precept" (Isa. xxviii. 10); with little additional clearness of definition, beyond the hint, conveyed by the words "nations" and "kings,'' that something more than Ishmael and his descenda~ts wne to be expected, since the Revealer of the Father (the Word of Jehovah, Chnst, tho Word of God) only discovers truth to the human mind as it can bear (Mark iv. 33). 2. The promi.se ofa land. Thi6 too was an old promise redelivered, with the old particularity of description and the old solem?ity of donation_; partly :to inform_ the hearer's mind, partly to allay whatever anxwus thoughts might remo.m, but clnefly to prepare for the imposition of the obligations that were about to be d~clared. Covenant mercies, at least in God's contracts, always go before covenant duties. 3. J.'he promise of a bless-ing. Thie too had been included in the gracious provision.a of the covenant from the first; but now a slight advance is made in the elucidation of its nature. The blessing is to be distinctly Rpiritual. Jehovah is to be n God to Abram and hie Reed. Hence the inference which Paul drawa (Gal. iii. 14-18) was deaigned to be deduced by the patriarch,-that the true and proper recipients of the covenanted merciea were not to be his natural, but spiritual descendants. See the pro• rninence in respect of clearness of revelation which God assigns to things spiritual. III. THE COVENANT ATTESTED. 1. The imposition of a. new name. (1) Its signifi• cance.· Instead of high-father, a peraonal appellation descriptive of the eleva.tion of his rank aa a chieftain, or of his .character a.a a man, he was henceforth to be styled father of a multitude, a federal or representative designation, defining his relation to both his natural and apiritual descenda.nta. It were well if narnea alwa.ys were thus suggestive and symbolic; but only names aasigned by God, directly or indirectly, can be relied on as expressive of reality, (2) Its intention. ' This was to indicate that God's covenant waa made not with Abram the Cha.ldrean chieftain, but with Abraham the believer.. •It was thus a symbol of the new position before God which Abraham occupied, and the new nature which as abeliever in GodAbraham possessed; i. e. of. Abraham's justification and regeneration. It was also a reminder that God's covenant was made not with the offspring of Abram as a man, i. e. with his natural descendants, except, indeed, provisionally and typically; but. with the children of Abraham the believer,i. e. with his spiritual posterity, all of whom, like himself, must have new names, i. e. occupy new positions and possess new natures, in other words, be justified and regenerated children of God by f(l.ith in Jesus Christ. 2. The attachment of a new sign. (1) Its nature. Circumcision. On the origin of the rite of circumcision see Exposition. (2) Its import. As regarding the grand blessing of the covenant, the promise of a seed, it was designed for a sign that that seed was to be'not a- child of the flesh, but achild of the promise; not the offspring of nature, but the gift of·grace. Hence it served as nn adumbration of the sinless humanity of the Lord Jesua Christ, and an intimation of the holy character of his seed. Then, a..~ administered to the patriarch, it was intended as a practical declaration of his faith in the coming seed, and a symbolic representation of his personal devotement to holiness. In every one of these respects its place has been supplied by the Christian rite of baptism, with only this difference, that baptism is a visible token of faith not in a coming, but a crucified end risen, Saviour. (3) Its incidence. The ceremony was appointed to be administered first to Abraham, and then to all bis household, including Ishmael and his male domestics, and subsequently to all his posterity through the promised son. So the obligations of the covenant rest on all within the Church, encl descend from nge to age upon believers. 'HOMILIES BY VARIOUS AUTHORS.

entries.content: -God's call to believers. "And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the Lord appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect." In what sense are we to take this? None can keep God's law perfectly (Ilom. vii. 23). And why at this point in Abram's history the emphatic "I am?" &c. The character of his life was faith (cf. Heb. xi. 6) resting on the promises made him (Gen. xii. 7; xiii. 16;•xv. 5). The last of these was a special instance of faith. But the triumph wasfollowed by a fall-impatience, would not wait God's time (cf. Ps. uvii. 14; mi. 15). An instance of a common fault -partial faith (cf. Matt. iv, 4; xiv. 28-31). The result was disappointment. Thirteen years passed. Must we not connect this with his fault? Want of faith delayed the blessing (cf. Num. xiv. 33). Then came the word of the Lord-a gentle rebuke (cf, Matt. viii. 26), and a precept: "Walk before me," &c. Return to thy first faith; let it be perfect, not partial (cf. Prov. iii. 5; Matt. xvii. 20). I. A LESSON FOR DELIEVERS. Watch lest faith grow cold. Some like not to retain God in their thoughts. They hide themselves from him amid the v11nities of the world, But his people, who have known his love (1 John iii. 1), why should they ever shrink from opening their whole heart to him? Yet, imperceptibly perhaps, there is a change, The faith is held, but the sunshine is gone. The desire to tell all to God is not there, Why? The man has set his heart upon something, and cannot trust God's love; or he is drawn to something he cannot approve, nnd listens to TH~ BOOR OF GENESIS. [tl!. :n'11. 1-14. what can be said for it (cf. Rom. :tiv. 4) _; or he has £~lien into self-sufficiency. Then reser,e towards God. The hidden hfe becomes disordered. 'No longer tho desire that he should know all and guide all. And thus uneasiness, reserve, distance.. Then follow ~Ian~ to quiet the uneasiness-;busin_ess, cere!'1ony, t~eology, or work m some other dnection. But no real commumon with God m all tins,· II. THE REMEDY. "Walk before me." Recognise the evil. Believe the cause, De not faithless. Bear in mind God's presence (cf. Ps. lxii. l-,-7). Seek not to hid~ from him, or to justify self. And" be perfect," i'. e. matured; not in any high 01 strange attainment, but in that which a child may learn_:_in trusting God's truth and love ; in bringing thoughts, wants, and wishes before him. Towards this active obedience and following Christ are means; and, above nil, sincerity and a reol definite dedication of the life to God. ' • III. ENCOURAGEllENT. "I am the Almighty God "-all-powerful (Isa. !ix. 1· Luke i. 37) and all-loving (Ps. xxxvii. 5; Rom. viii. 32). This, really .believed' would remove anxious care. \Vhat is it that leads thee to seek another way? Th~ consciousness of having wandered. Has he not made provision for this? (1 Tim. i. 15; 1 John ii. 1). Or is it that the blessing long desired is not given.?. Sarne power, some opportunity for God's work, and still the door is closed; or -it may be some spiritual gift, some token of growth in grace, and still the evil of thy nature is nnsubdned. De patient (James i 4). Thy Father in heaven w:ill not fail thee (Rom. vi. 14). Walk before him. Tell him all that is in. thy mind. In hie time thou shalt find peace (Phil. iv. 6; 1 John v. 4; Rev. xxi. 7).-M VerA. 1, 2.-Tlte true life of faitli set furth. I. COMMENCING WITH GRACIOUS AP· PEARANCE OF Goo TO HIS CREATURE. 1. The revelation one in a.continued series ofpro• qressive manifestations. 2. Accompanied with direct promise; which in the form of covenant appeals to reciprocal fellowship and confidence. 3.. Embracing both present and future blessedness. The blessing upon the earthly lot, as preparatory tv the higher blessedness, a foundation on which the higherlife is built up., II. The METHOD of the life of faith. Walk before me; be perfect, &c. 1. Constant reference to God-his will, hie truth, his covenant. 2.. Di,stinction from the world. Abram the pilgrim. Walk among the heathen; and yet before me. The coni;ciousness of a chosen aim a great preservative. The sust11ining fovour o,f• God. Development of the Divine in the human. 3. A life which is worked out as a trust for others. The representative man holds a special position -towards God not for his own sake alone, but as the depositary of the blessing. Great help to walk before God and be perfect, that we are called to be the channel through which blessings flow. Confinnation of the covenant will be sent to us in the way, when there is lack of promise in appearances, notwithstanding the evidence of our own infirmity. We walk in the light towards a future which shall abundantly rew11rd patient continuance in well doing.-R. EXPOSITION, Yer. ]5.-A.ll God said unto Abraham, As for Sarai thy wile,-who, nothaving hitherto l.ocen mentioned in any of the promises, is IJOW expressly taken into covenant, and accor,lingly receives a ne,v name (cf. ver. 5; eh. xxxii. 28; Rev. iii. 12)-thou shalt not call her name Sarai,-" my princess" (Gesenius) • "princely, noble" (lkenius, Rosenmiiller ' Keil Delitzsch); "the heroine"' (Knol;~l); ,', strife, contention" (Ewald, Mm·phy), with special reference to her struggle against sterility (Kalisch)-but Sara~- " princess" (Gesenius), the meaning bemg that, whereas formerly she ,vae Abram's princess ouly, she wa.s henceforth to be recognised as a princess generally, i. e. a~ the mother of the Church (Joromo,. On ihe contrary, the Biblicn.l narrative expressly mentions that its observanoe by the pe.triarch and his household was due to a Divine command, andwas connected withareligious significance which was altogether foreign to the Egyptians and others by whom that rite was practised. .Among the reasons for its ndoption by the heathennations of antiquity have been assigned, among the Ethiopians, a prophylactic design to ward off cettain painful, and often inclll'ltble, disorders i among the Egyptians, a regard· to clee.nliness ; and perhaps among the priesthood of the latter country a semi•religious idea (the deification of the generative powers) was associated with a practice which was commonly regarded as enhancingproductivity; butthe import ofthe ceremony aS enjoined upon the.father of the faithfulwas aswidelyaspossible'removedfrom everyone of the~o_ideas, being ~onnectedwi.t~ spiritual conceptions of. which the heathen worldwas entirelyignorant. That a heathen cnstomshould have b~en adopted ·by Jehovah nnd elevated to the :ra11k and connected with the spintual significance of a. religious sign will not occur as e. difficulty to ·thos11 who remember that the rainbow, a. well-known natural phenomenon, was selected as the sign for Noah's covenant, and that Christian baptism is a similar transformation of a previously existing ceremony by which Gentile proselytes were admitted to the Hebrew Church.

entries.title: GEN 17:15–27
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The covenant completed. I. THE ADMISSION OF SARAI. 1. The changed name. As on enteringwithm the covenant the name of A_bramwas changed to Abraham, so, to signalise the receptio~ of hi~ ap~use, Sarai was tranaf~rm~d into Sarah (vide Exposition), the trans_fonna~wn hav1!1g m her ca_ae the earn!/. s1gmficance as it had in Abraham's. In partwular 1t proclaimed that, like Abraham, Sarah was now a justified and regenerated believer in the Divine promise.. N. B. There is only one gate of entrance to Christ's Church, !i.z., faith or conversion. 2. Tlie' gu'f,rctn~eed blessing. What is here affirmed of Sarai LB that she should not only be received into the Church but made a sharer of Abraham's blessing, i. e. become entitled to all the gracious pr ovisions of the covenant. The blessing of Abraham belongs to· all who are possessed of Abraham's faith. Christ's salvation is the common property of believers. And to all it is certain, as it w11s to Sarai. The "yea" concerning Sarai has now become for Christ's people " yea and amen." .3. Tlte promised son. This was the first intimation that Sarai was to be the mother of the seed. The Eternal never hastens. God's disclosures of his own plans are ever slow, gradual, progressive, and mostly regulated by_the faith .o~ the recipients. Wh~n ~he_ fu~ess of th,e time arrives he is able to be rmnute, e:xphc1t, emphatic, as he was m mt1matrng Isaac a birth: (1) by tl1e time-a year hence, and (2) by the name-Isaac. 4. The rejoic-ing /t,usband. The laugh of gladness which escaped the patriarch, though partly owing C'H. XVU. 115--27.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. to,the reiterated promise of a son, was chiefly due to the announcement that Sarah 'IY'IIB to. be its mother. It was the joy of a husband in the happiness of a beloved wifo, long tried, but at length about to be rewarded ; itwas also the joy of a believing nusband in the well-founded assurance of his wife's interest in the covenant of grace. II. TnE EXCLUSION OF IsnMAEL. 1. The prayer of Abraham-(1) Reveals a note of sorrow. The displacement of Hagar'e child by the son of Sarah, though for Sarah's sake thrilling him with joy, appears to have raised a tender sympathy in his breast for the disappointment which was to fall upon the lad and his mother. For years he had himself no otherthoughtthan that Ishmael mightbe the seed, and now he cannot put aside the cherished hope without regret. Let fathers learn that though it is beautiful to feel for children's griefs, it is dangerous to constmct plans for children'E greatness. (2) Breathes an earnest spirit. Deeply concerned for the welfare ot h_is son, Abraham was also filled with longing that God would listen to his prayer. If there is anything about which a parent's heart should be sincerely passionate, it is the happiness and prosperity of his offspring; and if there is one season more than another in wbioh a parent'B heart should be possessed by strong emotion, it is when pleading for his children nt a throne of grace (Ps. l.xxviii. 2). (3) Craves a heai-enly blessing. Though Ishmael was to be denied the honour of serving as a medium for the transmission of the blessings of the covenant to future ages, his father supplicated for him a personal participation in those blessings. The chief ambition of a parent should be the .conversion and spiritual advancement of his children (3 John 4). 2. The answer of God-(1) Assures tlte praying father of acceptance. Ishmael, though not admitted to the succession of the holy seed, shoul!l, not be excluded from the gifts of grace. If Hagar's child, though born of the flesh, should become possessed of faith, he too would share in the spiritual benediction of the covenant. Let parents be encouraged to pray for their children. (2) Promises great temporal prosperity to the son. Abraham had sought spiritual life for Ishmael; God bestowed Ill addition temporal renown. So God did with Solomon (1 Kings iii. 11), and still does with saints (Ephcs. iii. 20). III. THE ACQUIESCENCE OF ABRAHAM. This was signified by the patriarch's observance of the rite of circumcision, in regard to which his obedience was-1. Immediate. There was no delay, no reluctance, no considering the question, but instantaneous compli1mce with the Divine directions. On the self-same day as God explained to him the provisions and conditions of the covenant, he declared his consent before God by the acceptanoe of the sugg·ested sign. His behaviour in this resp"'ct should be taken as a model by believers. 2. Cheerful. The rite of circumcision was of course attended with pain and something approaching to personal humiliation, and yet self-abasement and suffering were joyously assented to in view of the coming gift of the covenant. So should. Chiistians delightedly accept tribulation and any sort of bodily indignity that God may impose, considering them as nothing in comparison with the eternal weight of glory. 3. T½_rough-going. Prompt as to its time, willing in its spirit, the obedience of Abraham ,vas also minute in its performance. The appointed ordinance was administered to himself, his son Ishmael, and every male domestic in his house, as God had said unto him. So God's people aro required to observe all things written in the book of the covenant.

entries.title: GEN 17:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -"Thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be," &c. " Mother of nations;" "kings of peoples shall be of her." I. EXALTATION OF THE LOWLY. A. pilgrim and stranger, made a princess. A mother of nations, though once desolate, mourning, ready to murmur, The lamentation turned into laughter. II. THE FREEDOM OF DIVINE GRACE. The blessing unexpected, apart from creature strength, notwithstanding blind and foolish attempts to obtain blessing in ollr own way-the Ishmael, not the Isaac. Though many things "said in ou·r heart," the one thing Divinely purposed the only true fulfilment of that heart's desire. III. FORIWLEAMS OF TIIE COMING GLORY. Tho seed of the woman, specially repIO• 1,,enting the promise of God,_supernaturally giYOn, coming ns the royl\l seed, sou of a 240 TilE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. xrnr. 1-15. princess and forerunner of kings of peoples. God-gh·en heir, God-given inheritance. The birth of the child of promise, so manifestly Divine, points to the yot greater glory; "Unto us a Son is bom,"-R.

entries.title: GEN 18:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the Lord-Jehovah, the Divine nnme employed throughout tho present nnd succeeding chapters, ,Thich are aecordingly assigned to the JchoTist (Tuch, Bicek, Daridson, Colenso), with the exception of eh. xix.. 29, which is commonly regarded as a f~1cnt of the original Elohist's narration (1,'ide i1\fra)-appeared unto him. The absence of Abraham's name has been thought to favour the idea that the present chapter should haTe begun at eh. xvii. 23 (Quarry). That the time of this renewed Divine manifestation 'l"as shortly after the incidents recorded in the preceding chapter is apparent, as also that its object was the reassurance of the patriarch ·concerning the hirth of lsaAc. In the plains of Me.mre. Literally, in the oaks of Mamre (vide eh. xiii. 18). And he sat in the tent door. Literall_,, in the opening of the tent, a fold of which was fastened to a post near by to admit any air that might be stirring. In the heat of the day. I. e. noontide (cf. 1 Sam. xi 11), as the cool of the day, or the \\ind of the day (eh. iii. 8), means eventide. " The nsnal term for noon is Tsoharim (eh. xli.ii. 16), that is, the time of •double or greatest light,' while a more poetical expression is ' the height of the day' (Prov. iv. 18), either because then the sun has reached its most exalted position, or because it appears to stand still in the zenith" (Kalisch). Among the Orientals the hour of noon is the time of rest (cf. Cant. i. 7) and the time of dinner (eh. xii.i.i. 16, 25). In this case the patriarch had probably dined and was resting after dinner, since, on the arrival of his visitors, preparations had to be commenced for their entertainment. Yer. 2.-Alld he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him. :Kot in addition to (Kalisch), but including (Keil), Jehovah, whose appearance to the patria~ch, having in the previous verse been arst generally stated, is now minutely described. That these three men were not manifestations of the three persons of the Godh~ad (Justin Martyr, Ambrose, Cyril), bnt Jehovah accompanied by two created angels (Keil, et alii), may be inferred from eh. xix. 1. When first perceived by the patriarch they were believed to be men, itl'llr,gers, who were approaching his tent, and indeed were already close to it, or standing hy him. AJ,d when he eaw them (i. e. understood the.1 one of them was Jehovah, Jarchi rightly explaining that the wortl translated abovn "looked " i. e. with the bodily vision, no,v implie~ an act of mental perception), he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground. The expression denotes the complete prostration of the body by first falling on the knees, and then inclinina the head forwards till it touches. the ~und. As this was a mode of salutation practised by Orientals towards superiors generally, such as kings and princes (2 Sam. ix. 8), but also towards equals (eh. xxiii. 7 ;· xxxiii. 6, 7; xliL 6 ; xii.ii. 26),' as well 11.'1 towards the Deity (eh. xxii. 6; 1 Sam. i. 3), it is impossible to affirm. with certainty (Keil, Lange) that an act of worship was intended by the patriarch, and ·not simply the presentation of human and civil honour (Calvin). If Heb. xiii. 2 inclines to countenance the la.tter interpretation, the language in which Ab1·aham immediately addresses one of the three men almost leads to the conclu~ion that already the patriarch had recognised Jehovah,

entries.content: -And said, My Lord-Adonai, .literally, Lord, as in·ch. XV; 2, q. v. (LXX., ,cvpu ; Vulgatc, Domine,· Syriac, Onkolos, Kalisch, Alford, Lango), though the term may have indicated nothing more than Abraham's recognition of the superior authority ofthe Being addressed (Murphy). The readin~s Adoni, my Lord (A. V.., Dathius, Rosenmiiller), and AdonlU, my lords (Gesenius), are incorrect-if now I ha.ve found favour in thy sight - not implying dubiety on Abraham's part as to his a.cceptance before God (Knobel), but rather postulating his already conscious enjoyment of the Divine favour as the ground of the request nLout to be preferred (Delitzsch, Lange), 'l'hoso who regard Abraham as unconscious of the Divinity of him to whom he spake see in his language nothing but the customary formula of Oriental address (Rosenmliller ; cf. eh. xxx. 27 ; 1 Sam. xx. 29 ; Esther vii. 3)- paes not away, I pray thee, from thy eerv&nt. The hospitality of the Eastern, a.nd even o~ the Arab, has been frequently remarked by travellers, Volney describes the Arab. as dining at his tent door in order to invit<1 passers-by(' Trav.,' i. p. 314). "Whenever our path led ue near an encampment, as was frequently the case, we always found some active sheikh or venore.blo patriarch sitting 'in his tent door,' and ns soon as we wero witttin hail wo heard the earnest words of welcome nnd invitation which the Oltl Testament Scriptures had rendered long ego familiar to us : 'Stay, my lord, stay. Pabs not on tiH thou hast-eaten bread, and rested under thy servant's tent. entries.content: -Let a little we.tar, I pre.y you, be fetched, e.nd wash your feet. Feet washing was a neccssnry part of Oriental 'hospitality (cf. eh. xix. 2; xxiv. 32; xliii. 24). Dr. Robinson e.nd party on arriving at Ramleh repaired- to the abode of a wealthy Arab, where the ceremony was performed rn. the genuine style of ancient Oriental hospitality" (vide Kitto's 'Bible Illnstrations,' vol. i. p. 230). entries.content: -And Abraham ran unto the herd, e.nd fetcht a co.If tender and good,-the greatness of the honour done to the strangers was evinced by the pet"Sonal activity of the patriarch, and the offering of animal food, which was not a common article of consumption among Orientals- and gave it unto e. young man ;-i. e. the servant in attendance (cf. eh. xiv. 2!)-a.nd he he.ated to dress it.

entries.title: GEN 18:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Andhe took butter,-il~)?~, from the root Non, to curdle or become thick, signifies curdled milk, not butter (/3ovrvpov, LXX.; butyrum, Vulgate), which was not used among Orientals except medicinally. The word occurs seven times in Scripture with four letters (Deut. xxxii. 14; Judges v. 25; 2 Sam. xvii 29 ; Isa. vii. 15, 22 ; Prov. xxx. 33; Job xx. 17), and once without N (Job xxix. 6; vide Michaelis, 'Supplement,' p. 807)-and milk,-:170, wilk whilst still fresh, or containing its fatness, from a root signifying to be fat (cf. eh. xlix. 12; Prov. xxvii 27)-and the ea.If which hei. e. the young ma.n-had dressed, and set it before them; e.nd he stood by them under the tree,-a custom still observed among the Arabs, who honour their guests not by sitting; to cnt with, but by standing to wait upon, them-and they did ee.t. Not seemed to eat (Josepbus, Philo, Jonathan), nor simply ate nftor au allegorical fashion, as fire consumes the materials put into it (Justin Martyr), but did so in reality ('rertullian, Delitzsch, Keil, Kurtz, Lange). Though the angel who appeared to Mnnoah (Judges xiii. 16) rofusod to partake of food, the risen Saviour ato with his disciples (Luke xxi,. 43}. Physiologically inexJ?licable, this latter action on the part of Chnst Wtl.S uot a mero </)a,voµ.,vov or simulntion, but a veritable manducation of material food, to which Christ nppealetl in confirmation of the reality of his resurrection ; and the acceftance of Abraham's hospitality on the part o Jehoval1 and his angels mny in like manner hnve been designe,l to prove that their visit to his tent at Ma.mre was not a dream or a vision, but 11 genuine external manifestation.

entries.title: GEN 18:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And they said unto him (i. e. the Principal One of the throe, speuking; for the other'!, intc!'rog,itcd Alm1h:1rn ,\nring tl1ll THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. XVIII. 1-15. proi;(l'ess, or perhaps at the closo of, the meal saying), Where is Sarah thy wife I (thus in• dicating that thei1· visit hodaspecial referenco to her). And he Hid, Behold, in the tent. It is obvious that if at first Abraham reguded his ,isitors only as men, by this time a suspicion of their truo character must have be1;Un to dawn upon his mind. How should ordinary travellers be aware of his wife's name 1 and why should they do so unusual a thing, nccording to Oriental manners, n.s to inquire after her! If thus far their behm·iour could not fail to smprise the 11atriarch, what must have been his astonishment at the subsequent communication! Yer. 10. - And he said (tho Principal Guest, as above, who, by the very nature and tem1s of his announcement, identifies himself \\ith Jehovah), I will certainly return unto thee according to the time of life. Literally, at the tim,e reviving; i. e. when the year shall have been renewed, in the next year, or rather spring (vule Ewald, 'Heb. Synt. ,' § 33i ; Rosenmiillcr, Drusius, Keil, Kalisch, Lan"c, Ainsworth, 'Speaker's Commentary'); though other interpretations of the phrase l1aYe been suggested, as, e. g., " according to the time of that which is horn," i. e. at the end of nine months (Willet, Calvin, Bush, Murphy). And, lo, Sarah thy wife shall h.ave a son. I. e. at the time specified. And Sarah heard it in the tent door, which was behind him.

entries.title: GEN 18:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age. Literally, gone 1'nto days, i. e. into years. This was the first natural impediment to the accomplishment of Jehovah's promise; the second was peculin.r to Sarah. And it ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women (vide Levit. xv. 19, 25).

entries.title: GEN 18:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Therefore (literally, and) Sarah laughed within herself- Abraham had laughed in joyful amazement (eh. xviL 17) at the first mention of Sarah's son ; Sarah Jauuhs, if not in unbelief (Calvin, Keil, 'Speaker's Commentary,' Wordsworth), at least with a mingled feeling of doubt and delight (Lange, Murphy) at the annonncemcnt of her approaching maternity-saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also1-literally, and my lord, i e. my husband, is old. The reverential 6Ubmission to Abraham which Sarah here displays is in the New Testament cornmended 118 a pattern to Christian wives (l Pot. iii. 6). Yer. 13.-And the Lord said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh,~-i question which must have convinced Abmhnm of the Speaker's omniscience. Not only had .ho heard tho silent, inaudible, inwarcl cachin- • nation of Samh's spirit, but he knew tho tenor of her thoughts, and the purport of" her dubitations--aaying, Shall I of a surety bear a child, which (literally,. and I) am old t Sarah's mental cogitations clearly showed th,at the temporary obscurntion of her faith proceeded from a strong realisation of the weakness of nature, which-made conception and pregnancy impossible to one like her, who ,vas advanced in years; antl accordingly• her. attention, as woll as that· of her husband; was directed to the Divine omnipotence as the all-sufficient guarantee for the accomplishment of the promise. Yer. 14.-Is any thing too hard for the Lord 1 Literally, Is anyW01°d too wo.nderfal, i. e. impossible, for Jehovah i µ,j aovvarq<1u• '1iapd T<f 0uj pijµa (LXX.), with which may be compared Luke i. 37. A.t the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life (vule supra, ver. 10), and Sarah shall have a son.

entries.title: GEN 18:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Then Sarah (who.had overheard the conversation, and the: charge preferred against her, and who probably riow appeared before the stranger).denied1 saying, I laughed not. Sarah's conduct will admit-of no other explanation than that which.the sacred narrative itself gives. For she was afraid. Tho knowledge that hersecret·thoughts had been deciphered must have kind.led in her.brelllltthe suspicion that her visitor was none other than Jehovah.. With this a sense of guilt would immedistely 3.Sl!ail )1or consci~nco for having cherished..even,a moment any .dou!it of the Divine worcl In the consequent confusion of soul she tries what ever seems to lie the first impulse of "detected transgressions, viz., deception-(cf. oh. iii 12, 13). And he said, Nay; bilt thou didst laugh. With a directness similar to that which he employed in dealing with the first culprits in the garden, not contending in a multiplicity of words, but solemnly announcing that what she said wiul false. The silence of Sarah was anevidence ofher conviction;. her subsequent conception was a proof of her repentance and forgiveness.

entries.title: GEN 18:1–15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Noont:ide at Mamre, or angels' visits. I. THE ·AnnrvAL OP 'rllE ETI\aNGERB. 1. The appearance they p_esented. Seeming)y three men, th?Y were in reality three angels or more correctly, Jehovah accompamed by two celcstrnl attendants, who at an udcx;ected moment, were making for Abraham's tent. So are the homes of 'RaintR ofltiincs visited by angels unawnrcs (lleb. i. 14), nnd, grcator honour ne. xvm. 1-15.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 243 still, by him who claims the angels as bis ministers (Ps. viii. 4; Isa. !vii. 17). 2. Tlie reception eliey obtained. Immediately that Abraham discerned their approach, be hastened to accord them most respectful and courteous salutation, in true Oriental fashion, foiling on hisknees and bowing till bis head touched the ground ; an illustration of that beautiful politeness towards one's fellow-men (if as yet he only regarded hie visitors as men), or of that reverential self-abasement before God (if already he had recognised the superior dignity of the principal figure of the three) which ought especially to characterise God's believing and covenanted people (see Ps. xcv. 6; 1 Pet. iii. 8). 3. The invitation tliey received. Probably oppressed bythe sultry heams of the noonday sun, if not otherwise travel-stained and weary, they were, with genuine Arab-like hospitality, entreated by the patriarch to avail themselves of such refreshment and repose ae hie cool-shaded, well-furnished tent might be able to afford. And this invitation of the patriarch was-(1) Humbly proffered, as if their acceptance of it would be more an act of grace conferred on him than a benefit enjoyed by themselves. (2) .Mod,estly_described, as if it were only a trifle after all that he was asking tl:iem to accept, while all the time his liberal heartwas devising liberal things. (3) Piously enforced, by the consideration that he recognised in their arrival at his tent a special call to 'the discharge of the duty of hospitality. (4) Promptly accepted, without apologies or deprecations of any sort, but with the same generous simflicity as it was offered. "So do as thou hast said.'' l . THE EN'l'ERTAINMENT OF ';l'HE STRANGERS. Jn the banquet which Abraham extemporised for his celestial guests beneath the umbrageous oak at Mamre were three things which should be studied by all who would use hospitality. 1. Joyous alacrity. That the patriarch's invitation was no mere conventional remark which was meant to pass unheeded by those to whom it was addressed was proved by the expeditious cordiality with which he set about the preparations needed for the proffered repast, enlisting Sarah's_ practised hands in baking cakes, and commissioning n trusty servant of the house- to kill and dress a young and tender calf selected by himself from the flocks: Here was no reluctance or half-heartedness with Abraham in the work of kindness to which Providence had called him. So ought Christians to manifest a spirit of cheerfulness and a habit of promptitude in doing good (Rom. xii. 8, 13; 2 Cor. ix. 7f 2. -unstinted liberality. Modestly characterised as a little repast, it was in reality a sumptuous banquet which was set before the strangers. Abraham entertained his guests with prirrcely munificence. The modem virtue of stinginess, or niggardliness, supposed by many to be a Christian grace, had not been acquired by the patriarch, and should with ae much speed as possible be unlearned by Christ's disciples. Hospitality towards the saints and_ beneficence towards all men, butespecially towards the poor, should be practised with diligence, nnd even with a holy prodigality, by all who are of Abraham's seed (Luke xiv. 12-14; Rom. xii. 13; 1 Tim. iii. 2; Heb. xiii. 2). 3. Personal activity. Though the master of a large household, with 300 trained domestics, and the noble Eliezer at their head, the patriarch does not think of relegating the important work of preparing the entertainment to hie subordinates, but himself attends to its·immedinte execution. Indeed, in nil the bustling activity which forthwith pervades the tent his figure is always and everywhere conspicuous. And when the meal is ready he reverently serves it with hie own hand; again a true pattern of humility, ne if he had caught up by anticipation the spirit of our Saviour's words (Matt. xx. 26); and a true preacherof Christian duty, saying thatin God's work personalservice is ever better thanlabouring by proxy. III. THE COMMUNICATION OF THE STRANGERS. The noonday meal over, or perhaps while it was advancing, the principal of the three guests, who certainly by this time was recognised as Jehovah, made an important announcement to the patriarch, which, however, was specially intended for Sarah, who was listening behind the dark fold of the camel's-hair tent, viz., thnt next year the promised seed should be born. That announcement was-1. Autlioritatively made. It wne made by him who is the faithful and true Witness, with whom it is impossible to lie, and who is able also to perform that which he has promised. 2. Unbelievingly received. The laugh of Sarah wee altogether different from thnt of Abraham (eh. xvii. 17). While Abraham's w11s the outcome of fuith, here w11e the fruit of lutcnt <loubt nn<l incredulity. entries.title: GEN 18:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -" Samh laughed within herself." 1. The incongruity between a Divine promise and the sphere of its fulfilment is temptation to unbelief. 2. A disposition to measure the reality and certainty of the Divine by a human or earthly standard is 1mre to lead us to irreverence and sinful doubt. 3. '!'here may be an inward and con- 1ealed working, known to God though not outwardly expressed, which is still both e.n insult to him and an injury to us. 4. The root of unbelief is in the ground of the soul. Sarah laughed because she was not prepared for the gracious promise. She was afraid of her own thoughts because they were not such as became her, and did dishonour to God's sufficiency and love. "She denied, saying, I laughed not." A more receptive and spiritual mind would have both risen above the incongruity and been incapable of the dissimulntion.-R.

entries.title: GEN 18:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -" Is anything too hard for the Lord?" I. TAKE IT AS THE QUESTIO:-f WHICH Gon ASKS OF MAN. 1. Remonstrance. The history of Divine manifestations proves that nothing is demanded of faith which is not justified by the bestowments of the past. 2. Invitation. We connect the question with the promise. He opens the gate of life; is it too hardfor him to give us the victory? "At the time appointed" his word will be fulfilled. He would have U'!- rest on himself. "Delieve that he is, and that he is the rewarder," &c. 'What he is, what he says, are blended into one in the true faith of his waiting children. II. TAKE THE QUESTION AS ONE WHIC!l MEN ASK OF ONE A..~OTHER. 1. When they set forth the goodness of Divine truth. 'l'he possibility of miracles. The hardness oE the world's problems no justification of unbelief. 2. When they proclaim a gospel of supernatural gifts, a salvation not of man, but of God. Why should we doubt conversion? \Vhy should a regenerated, renewed nature be so often mocked at? 3. "When they would encourage one another to persevere in Christian enterprise. The methods may be old, but the grace is ever new. 'l'he world may laugh, but the true believer should see 1111 things possible. The times are rur measures. Eternitv is God"s.-R. .

entries.title: GEN 18:17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Sodom's doom revealed. I. THE REASON OF THE REVELATION. 1. Abralrn.m's new posit-ion. Having been lately taken into covenant with God, allied "by tLe holy tie of a celestial friendship to Jehovah, the patriarch seemed in the Lord's eyes to occupy a footing of intimacy before him that demanded the disclosure of Sodom's impending doom. That footing the patriarch no doubt owed to Divine grace-sovereign, unmerited, free; but still, having been accorded to him, it is, by a further act of grace, represented as laying God himself under certain obligations towards bis servant. So" the secret of the Lord is with them that fear him, and he will tihow them his covenant" (Ps. :x:.xv. 14). 2. Abraham's new prospects. About to become the head of a great nation, it was natural to suppose that Abraham would be profoundly interested in all that concerned mankind. As the head of the Old Testament Church too, which had just been constituted (eh. xvii.), there existed a special reason for Lis being properly instructed as to the impending judgment of Sodom. Upon him would devolve the interpretation to the men of his day of the i:ignificance of that event. Rightly viewed, this is one of the proper functions of the Church on Ott. XVIII. 16-22.1 TltE BOOK OF GtNESI8. 247 cnrth-to explain God's judgments to the unbelieving world. Hence "the Lord God docth nothing but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets" (Amos iii. 7). 3. Abmham'e new responsibilities. These were the cultivation of personal nnd family religion, which devolved upon him with a new force and a heavier degree of obligation than they did before in consequence of his new standing as a Church member. God having graciously nssigned this position within the Church in order that he might command his children and his household after him, by means of religious instruction as well as through the influence of personal example, to fear God, it was needful that he should be informed 11B to the ground, at lea~t, of thE> coming judgment on the cities of the plain. II. THE REASON OF THE RETRIBUTION. This was the wickedness of Sodom, which was-1. Exceedingly heinous as to its character. Minutely detailed in the ensuing chapter, it is here only indirectly mentioned as something grievous in the sight of God. All sin is inherently offensive in the eyes of the Almighty ; but some forms of wickedness are more presumptuously daring or more intrinsically loathsome than others, 'and of such ~ort were the sins of Sodom (eh. xix. 1). 2. E:r,ceedingly ahundant as to its measure. It was "multiplied" iniquity of which the Sodomites were guilty; ·and this not simply in the·sense in which the sins of all may be characterised as beyond computation (Ps. xix. 12 ; xl. 12), but in the sense that their hearts were set in them to do evil (Eccles. viii. 11), so that they worked all manner of uncleanness with greediness (Ephes. iv. 19). 3. Exceedingly clear as to its comtnission,. Though God speaks of making investigation into the sins of Sodom, this was really unnecessary. The moral degeneracy of the inhabitants of the Jordan valley was one of the "all things" that are ever "naked and manifest" unto his eye. So nothing can hide sin from God (2 Chron. xvi. 9; Prov. xv. 3; Amos ix. 8). 4. Exceeclingly JJatent as to its ill desert. This was the reason why Goel employed the language of ver. 21. He meant that though the guilt of Sodom was great, ha would not let loose his vengeance until it should be seen to be perfectly just. Nothing would be done in haste, but all with judicial calmness. Lessons:-1. The impotence of anything but true _religion to purify the heart or refine a people. 2. God is specially observant of the wickedness of great cities. 3. When great cities sink to a certain depth in their wickedness they are doomed to perish. 4. When God's judgments overtake a nation they are ever charncterist)d by justice.

entries.title: GEN 18:16–33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abraham'& intercession (_or Sodom. The whole wonderful scene springs out of the theopbany. Abrahams faith has given him a special position with the Lord. "Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?" &c. The true priesthood and mediatorship is friendship with God. The grnce of God first gives the likeness and then exalts it. The Lord knew Abraham because Abraham knew the Lord. The superior angel, the Lord, remains behind his comp1mions that Abrnham 1night have the opportunity of intercession; so the Lord lingers in his providence that he may reveal bis righteousness and mercy. As to the pleading of the patriarch and the answers of the Lord to it, we may take it- I. As it bears on the CHARA<TrEr. OF Goo. 1. He is open to entreaty. 2. He is unwilling to destroy. 3. He spurcs for the sake of righteousness. 4. He "does right" 11s "Judge of the earth," even though to the eyes of the best men thcra is awfnl mystery in his doings. IT. As it reveals the CHARACTERISTICS OF PATRIARCHAL PIETY. 1. It wus bold with the boldness of simplicity and faith. 2. It was full of true humanity while deeply reverential towards God. Abrnhum was no fanatic. 3. It waited for and humbly accepted Divine judgments nnd appointments not without reason, not without the exercise of thought and feeling, but all the more so as it prayed and talked with Goel. 4. The one living principle of the patriarchal religion wns that entire confidence in God's righteousness and love, in separating the wicked and the good, in both his judgments and his mercy, which is the essence of Christianity 11s well. " The right" which the Judge of 11ll the earth will do is not the right of mere blind 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cFI, XVIII. lA-22, l11w, or rough human 11dmi11istration of law, but. the rig·ht of him who discornelh between the eYil ond the good, "too wise to err, too g·ood to be unkind."-R.

entries.title: GEN 18:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God's ru.le in the family. "For I know him, that he will command his childre_n and his housel!old ofter him, and they shall keep the way of the Loni." The promise to Abr:aham mc~uded-(1) understanding of God's acts; (2) tho.t he should become a m1:ghty nation; (3) that h~ should be ancestor of the promiseq Seed; (4) that he lumself should be a blessing to others, O.f these points two at least are not confined to him personally, but belong to all who will. 'l'o know what 90d d_oeth _a man must be taugl!t of the Spirit (1 Cor. ii. 14? cf._ Isa. vii. 12). There 1s a,W1de difference between seemg an event, oreven foreseeing 1t, and understanding God's lessons therein. To be able in everything to mark the love, and care and wisdom of God ; to walk with him as a child, accepting what he sends not m~rely as inevitable, but as loving; to learn lessons from all that happen11, and through the works of his hands to see our Father's face-this is peace, and this is what the v.isdom of this world cannot teach (Matt. xi. 25; 1 Cor. i. 20, 21). Again, .Abraham was to be not merely the ancestor of a nation, but the father of a spiritual family by influence and example (Matt. iii. 9; Gal. iii. 7). In this his calling is that of every Christian (Dan. xii. 3; Matt. v. 13, 14). Text connects. the godly rule of a family with both these blessings. Christianity is not to be a selfish, but a diffusive thing (Matt. v. 15; xiii. 33); and the influence must needs begin at home (cf. Num. x. 29; ActR i. 8), among those whom God has placed with us. I. THINGS NEEDFUL FOR Tnrs WORK. 1. Care for liis own soul. I£ tliat is not cared for a man cannot desire the spiritual good of others. He may desire and try to train his children and household in honesty and prudence ; to make them good members of society, successful, respected; and may cultivate all kindly feelings; but not till he realises eternity will he really aim at training others for eternity. Might say that only one who has found -peace can fully perform this work. A man aroused with desire that his family should be saved. But, he cannot press the full truth as it is in Jesus. 2. Love for tlie souls of othe:rs. Christians are sometimes so wrapped up in care for their own souls as to have few thoughts for the state of others. Perhaps from a lengthened conflict the mind has been too much turned upon its own state. But this is not the mind of Christ (1 Cor. x. 24). It is not a close following of him. It tells of a halting in the" work of faith" (2 Cor. v. 13, 14 ; cf. Rom. x. 1). 3. Desire to advance the kin[Jdom of Clirist. When a mo.n has this Le sees in every ono a soul for which Christ died (cf. John iv. 35), and those with wLom he is closely connected must chiefly call forth this feeling. IL THE MANNER OF THE WORK. Family worship; acknowledgment of God as ruling in the household; his will a regulating principle and bond of union. Let th_is be a reality, not a form. Let the sacrificial work of Christ be ever put forward m instruction and in prayer. Personal example-constantly aiming at a holy life. To pray in tLe family and yet to be evidently making no effort to live in the spi_rit of the prayer is ~o do positive evil ; enc?uraging the belie~ t!iat God may be_worslupped with words, without deeds; and tendrng to separate relig10n from daily hfe. Prarer in private for each member-children, servants, &c. ; and watchfulness to deo.1 with each as God shall give opportunity (Prov. xv. 23). Let prayer always accompany such efforts.-M.

entries.title: GEN 18:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.Abraham and family training. "For I know him, that he will c_ommand l1is cl1ildren and his household after him," &c. Under the shady terebmth celestial visitants partake, or appear to do so, of a meal hastily provided by the patriarch. 'l'he whole narrative is given in such a way that,-after the mnnner of tl1e iime,-to God are ascribed human passions, desires, hesitancy, and resolve. Hence God is described ae resolving, on two grounds, to reveal to Abraham that which he is about to do in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah: (1) that Im would become a great and mighty nation; (2) that he would direct his household to follow in the ways of righteousness and truth. Notice- 1. THE VALUE GOD PLACES ON EARLY BPIItl'l'UAL 'l'RAINING. Chil<lren and servants are both to be bronght under spiritunl iufluence. The heart will not become p11ro naturully, ~!1y more tlmn the bo~t le~t _to itself_wo~ld '!lake headway against a st~<mg current. lho set of the world-tide 1s IIl &n evil duect1on. Abmham had no wntten book to aid him in his work. His unwritten Bible was the tradition of God's dealings with the rnce and with himself. He could tell of the promises of God and of the way of approach to him by sacrifice. Evidently there had been careful training in this respect; for when Jenae was going with hie father to the mount of sacrifice he noticed that,although the fire and wood were carried,theyhad no lambfora burnt offering. II. GOD NOTICES HOW SPIRITUAL TRAINING IS CARRIED ON. " I know him." He could trust Abraham, for he would "command," &c., not in the dictatorial tone3 of a tyrant, but by the power of a consistent life. Many children of reli"'ious parents go back to the world because of the imperious style of training they h~ve received. In tro.ining,,every word, look, and act tells. In many homee there is, alas, no training given and no holy example set. Parents are held accountable for failure, and ehould therefore be firm and loving in training. They should not readily delegate to others the work of training, either in secular or religious knowledge. Sunday-school teaching should supplement, not supplant, home training. III. Goo MADE THE BEST0WMEN'l' OF INTENDED BLESSINGS CONTINGE,IT ON THE FAITHFUL DISCHARGE OF DUTY. "Thatthe Lord may bring upon Abraham that which he bath spoken of him." If Abraham had not been faithful his name would have died out, and there would have been no handing on of the narrutive of his devoted life and tenacious hold of the Divine promises. Isaac followed in his father's steps and was a meditative man. •Jacob cherished the promises and handed them on to his sons. The Jews preserved n knowledge of God when all other races were sunk in polytheism. From them cnme the One who was the Saviour of the world. All, however, depended on the right training of Isaac. The rill flowed to the strenmlet, the streamlet to the creek, the creek to the river, the river to the ocean. Influence ever widened, and God's aim with respect to Abraham was carried out. Let nll stril'e so to act that the chnracter of the life may not undo the teachings of the lip.-H.

entries.title: GEN 18:23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abraham drew near. I. e. to Jehovah; not simply locally, ~ut also spiritually. The religious use of WJ~ as a performing religious services to God, or a J1ious turning of the m~d to God, is found 1n Exod. xxx. 20; Isa. xxu. 13; Jer. xxx. 21; and in n sirnilnr sense lnil;w is employed in the New Testnment (cf. Heb. iv. 16; x. 22; Jemes iv. 8). TheJonathan'l'argum explains, "and Abraham prayed." And said. Commencing tho sublimest net of human intercession of which Scripture preserves e. record, being moved thereto, if not by an immetliate rcg11rd for Lot (Lnnge), at le11st by a sense of compassion towards the inhabitants of Sodom, "communis erga qui?uzue populos mise1·icordia" (Calvin), which was heightened and intensified by his own previous experience of forgiviug grace (Keil). Wiltthou also destroy the righteous with the wicked 1 The question presupposes that God had, according to the resolution of ver. 17, explained to the patriarch his intention to destroy the cities of the plain. The object the patriarch contemplated in his intercession was not simply th~ preservation of any godly remnant that might be found within the doomed towns, but the rescue of their eutire popnlntions from the impending jndi:ment,-only he does not at first discover his complete design, perhaps regnrding such an absolute reversal of the Divine purpose a, exceedin~ the legitimate bounds of creatur~ supplication; but with what might be characterised as holy adroitness he veils his ulterior aim, and commences his petition l\t e. point somewhat removed from that to which he hopes to come. Assuming it as settled that the fair Pentapolis ia to be destroyed, he practicnlly asks, with e. strange mixture of humility and boldness, if Jehovnh has considered that this will involve asad commingling in onegigantic overthrow of both the Jighteous e.nd the wicked.

entries.title: GEN 18:24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - Peradventure there be firty righteous within the city. entries.title: GEN 18:23–33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abraliam's intercesswn. I. THE OBJECT OF HIS INTERCESSION. Not simply the rescue of Lot from the doomed citiee, but the ealvation of the citiee tLemselves, with their miserable inhabitants. A request evincing-I. Tender sympatky. Cll. XVllI. 23-33.] TllE BOOK OF GENESIS. 2f>l Though doubtloss tho righteous character of the impending retribution hart been expl11ined to him, its appalling severity was such as to thrill his feeling heart with nnguish, which would certainly not be lessened, but intensified, if he allowed his thoughts to dwell upon the future into which thl\t overwhelming calamity woulr! forthwith launch its unhappy victims. 2. Unselfish clw,1-ity. Not blindly shutting his eyes to the miseries of the Sodomites, as many would have done, on the plea that they were richly merited, or that they were no concern of his, or that it was little he could do to nvert them, he actively bestirs himself, if possible, to prevent them. Nor does he se.y that, having delivered them once from the devouring sword of war, without their having profited by either the judgment or the mercy that had then been mensured out to them, he will now leave them to be engulfed by the approaching storm of Almighty wrath; but, on the contrary, he rather seeks a second time to effect their rescue. 3. Amazing cathol-ici,ty. Not content with asking Lot's deliverance, or the rescue of the righteous, he aims at nothing short of the complete preservation of the cities. He solicits not a few of their inhabitants only, but their entire population. One wonders whether to admire most the greatness of the love or the grandeur of the faith herein displayed. II. THE SPIRIT Oil' HIS INTERCESSION. 1. Holy boldness. Abraham "drew near." The expression intimates confidential familie.rity, earnestness of entreaty, unrestrained freedom of discourse, almost venturesome audacity in prayer; all of which characteristics should be found in a believer's prayers, especially when interceding in behalf of others (Heh. x. 22). 2. Reverent humility. Three times he deprecates Jehovah·s nnger, and acknowledges personal unworthiness; o.nd that this self-abasement was not affected, but.real, is apparent from the circumstance that the more his supplication prospers, the deeper does he sink in self-prostration. Gracious souls are ever humble under a sense of God's mercies: Jacob (eh. xxxii. 10), David (2 Sam. vii. 18; cf. Luke vii. 6). 3. Fervent importunity. With a sanctified dexterity he, as it were, endeavours to shut up the heart of God to grant the deliverance be solicits. Nor does he rest contented with the first response to hie entreaty, but with greater vehemence returns to the charge, increasing his demands as God enlarges his concessions (cf. Matt. xv. 22). III. THE L0CJI0 OF HIS INTERCESSION. 1. The argument. The principle on which tl1e patriarch stands is not the grace of the covenant, but the righteousness of the Judge. Hie meaning is that in moral goodness there is a certain dynamic force which opernte9 towards the preservation of the wicked, and which the Divine righteousness itself is bound to tnke into its cal,,;ulations. Where this force reaches n certain limit in intensity, n regard to judicial equit.y seems to require that it shall be nllowed to exercise its legitimate sway-a principle which God admitted to the patriarch when he said that the Amorites were !pared because their iniquity was not full (eh. xv. 16), and which he here endorses by consenting to spnre Sodom if even ten righteous men cnn be found within its gates. 2. The a'fPluation. The patriarch conducts his case with singular directness, going strnight to the logic11l issues of the principle with which he starts; with mn.rvelloue ingenuity pitching the hypothetical number of pious Sodomites so high n.s to insure o favourable response, and grndually diminishing as grnce enlarges, nnd with unwearied assiduity refusing to discontinue his holy nrgument so long as a chance remains of saving Sodom. IV. THE succEss OF HIS INTERCESSION. 1. He got all lie asked. He did not cre.ve the unconditional sparing of the city, but only its preservation on certain suggested conditions. Those conditions too were of his own framing; and yet against them not so much as one single caveat was entered by God. 2. He ceased asking bPjore Gad sfo'fPed giving. Itmay be rash to speculate as to whatwould have happened had Ahrahnm continued to reduce the number on which he perilled the salvation of Sodom; but for God's glory it is only just to observe that it was not he who discontinued nnswering the patriarch's petitions, so much as the patrinrch himself, who felt that he had reached the limit of thnt liberty which God accords to believing suppliants nt his throne. .Lessons:-1. The liberty which snints have to npproach God in prnyer. 2. The Divinely-tnught art of wrestling with God in prayer. 3. The great encouragement which sn.inls have to pray without ceasing. 4. The profound interest which saints should ever take in the welfare of their fellow-men. 2!i2 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [ell, ltIX. 1-11

entries.title: GEN 19:1–11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -'-Waming lights in Sodom. I. THE ·FLICKERING LIGHT OF LoT's PIETY. 1. That the light of Lot's piety was still burning, though he had long been Rnbjected to the moral contamination of the licentious Pentapolis, is apparent from- (1) The practice of lwspitality which he appears to ltave maintained, having probably learnt it while in his uncle's tent. So men often cling to the outward forms of religion when its living power is ceasing to exert an influence upon the heart; and t.hough adherence to the former ii! not to be mistaken for the latter, yet it renders the decline of the latter less rapid and disastrous than it would otherwise be. (2) Tlie l.:indly reception wliicli he extended to !tis celeiltial visitors. If scarcely so elaborate us the sumptuous entertainment of Abrnhnm at Mumre, the banquet of Lot was at least as outwardly reverential and as unaffectedly sincere and earnest. It clearly testified that Lot had not yet become insensible to the practical duties of religion, as at that time understood. Early religious training is exceedingly difficult to erndicate. (3) The couragedusd:efence which he made of kis threatened guests. At the risk of his personal safety lle endeavoured to repel the violence with which the citizens nssniled them ; o.nd by the proffer of a sacrifice, the greatest surely that a parent could make, he sought to beguile the infamous designs which the townsmen cherished. W11atever mny be said of Lot's conduct in this latter action, his behaviour throughout towards the llngels proved that the life of gruce within his soul was not quite extinct. 2. That the ligl1t of Lot's piety, though still burning, was fast fading, may be gathered from 1.he circumstances-(1) 'J'frnt he Imel remained so iong among tltd 25-1 THE DOOK OF GENESIS. [ell. Xllt. 1-11. Sodornius, Unless a process of moral deterioration had been going ort within the soul of Lot, residence among a people so depraved would eventually have becomo tmpossible. Instead of being merely vexed in his righteous soul while in Sodom, he would have taken the earliest opportunity to escape from Sodom. (2) Tliat he had betrotlted his daughters to two of Sodom's dtiz.ens. That his prospective sons-in-law were infected by the bad taint of the city may be inferred from their subsequent behaviour, as well as from the preceding judgmen'tof God .on the universal corruption of the city's inhabitants. Hence Lot should rather have kept his daughters virgins than l1ave su:ffered them to enterinto matrimonial engagements with ungodly suitors. (3) That he actually offered to sacri.fwe his daughters' purity to the. lust of tlie Sodomi,tes. Whatever apology may be offered for so extraordinary a proposal on the part of Lot, nothing can be plainer than that it implied a strange obliquity of moral Yision, and a serious deadening of fine moral feeling. It was a clear proof that the immoral contagion had begunto affect Lot, and that itwas high time for him to leave S~o~ • II. THE wnrn LIGHT OF Sono1i1's IMPIETY. Already well enough known as to its character, the wickedness of Sodom is at length unveiled in all its revolting features and frightful dimensions. The history of that last night in the doomed city proclaimed the sin of Sodom to be-1. Unnatural. In the unbridled licence of their appetites they had far outstripped common sinners; even the natural brute beasts they had left behind; they had sunk to a monstrosity of wi9kedness of which shame forbids to speak. Paul enumerates their sin amongst the forms of impurity by which the heathen world has at times defiled itself (Rom. i. 26, 27). 2. Sliameless. Disp:nsting and repnlsive as their wickedness was, instead of shrinking into darkness and doing it in secret, they openly proclaimed their filthiness, and would have gratified their lusts in public. It is a lower deep in moral degradation when one not only does "those things which are not convenient," but glories in his shame (Phil. iii. 19)...3; Violent. This marked a third degree in the wickedness of Sodom, that, rather than be baulked of their lewd design, the citizenswere prepared to set at nought.the laws of hospitality, which insured the safety of strangers within lhcir city, and, if need were, the rights of property, by breaking into Lot's house, and, still further, thl! liberties of the person, by laying hands on the objec:ts o;f their unhallowed lusts. Ordinary sinners are satisfied if they can gratify an unholy impuJse without an undue expenditure of crime; these were ready to trample on all laws of God aJld man to r,ccomplisb their desire," adding sin to sin" (Isa. xxx. 1). 4. Obdurate. Even "·hen struck with blindness they did not discontinue their impious attempt. They wearied themselves groping about in the darkness, but it was still in an endeavour "to find the door." Common sinners pause when confronted with the just judgments :if Heaven ; these were only maddened into greater fury (Ps. lxxiii. 7). And, to complete the picture, this appalling wickedness was--5. Universal. From all. quar.: I.ere and of all ages they clustered and clamoured round the door of Lot's house. There does not seem to have been any dissension in the multitude. They were all of one mind. CouJd anything more signally attest Sodom's ripeness for destruction? Learn-1. How rapidly a good man can deteriorate in evil company. 2. How completely a nation can resist the ameliorating influences of its good men. 3. How disgustingly repulsive sin is when fully developed.

The expression ff like the laud of Egypt as thou comcst to Zoar" (eh. xiii. 10) is suggestive rather of the southern than of the northern extremity of the lake ns tl10 site of the Pentapolis. It may be 'idded that this opinion has receivecl the ,;unction ofRobinson, Stan1ey, Porter, Thomson (' The Land and the Book'), and other eminent geographers. On the other hand, there are reasons for believing that the true site of the cities wns at the north, and not the south, of the Dead Sen. 1. The circle of the Jordan was visible from the Bethel plateau (eh. xiii 10); the southern extremity of the Dead Sea is not. 2. From the heights nbove Hebron or Mamre, though the nctual circle is not visible, ff yet the depression between the nearer hills nud those of Gilead can be perceived, nnd .Abraham could at onco identiry tho locality whence the smoke arose," after Sodom's burning. 3. Chedorlnomer's route (eh. xiv. 7-14) was from Kadesh to Hnzezon-tnmar, midway up the wcstcm shore of the Deacl Sea, from Haze zon-tamar to the vale of Siddim, ancl from Siddi.m to Dan, the natural conclusion being that on reaching Hazezon-tamar he dicl not tum southward, but continued marching northwards. 4.
