entries.title: GEN 19:24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The judgment of fire. I. 'l'BE DELIVERANCE OF LOT. 1. lilercifully warned. The intimation conveyed by the angels was-(1) Explicit; the city was to be destroyed. The cry for vengeance could no longer be resisted. 'l'he cup of its iniquity was full. (2) Emphatic; there was no dubiety about the announcement. Already the doom had been decreed, and they had como to be the ministers of its execution. (3) Merciful; it was designed to secure the escape of himself and friends from the impending overthrow. "Whatsover thou he.st, bring them out of this place," (4) Timely; there was still ample opportunity for not only getting clear c,ut of the perilous region himself, but for alarming bis daughter's intended husbands. So a.re sinners warned clearly, expressly, grnciously, and opportunely in the gospel to flee from the wrath to come, to escape from the city of destruction. 2. Urgently hastened. Notwithstanding the angel's warning, it is obvious that Lot trifled, probably from a latent apprehension that there was ~lenty of time, i! not fro~ any becret dubiety as to the need for the celestil\l exhortation; and so do smners daily yet on=L s 258 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XIX. 12-28. with the solemn announcen~ent of the gospel, which necessitates that they be vehemently presser!, like Lot, w1th-(l) Earnest admonition. "Arise I'' "Up I" "Get thee out of this place I" (2) Serious caution. " Lest thou be consumed in the iniquity of the city." 3. Grawusly asmted, Even the urgency displayed by the nngels would not have sufficed to rescue Lot, had they not extended to him and his worl<lly-min<led partner a helping hand. Hankering after Sodom, perhaps thinking of the wealth they had to leave, the good man and his wife still lingered and were nt last_ only dragged forth by main force beyond the precincts of the do~med city. It reminds us that few, probably none, would ever escape from the city of destruction if Dfrinc grace were not practically to lay hold of them and drag them forth • and c,en this Divine grace would not do unless the Lord were specially merciful to them as he was to Lot. 4. Minutely directed. To the further prosecution of their journey they were not left without most careful instructions as to how they might secure their safety; and neither are awakened sinners, who have been aroused to see their peril and to start upon the way of life, permitted to struggle on without celestial p:nidance as to how to make their calling and election sure. Like the :fleeing Lot and Lis wife, they are counselled (1) to be in earnest, seeing it is their life for which they flee; (2) to beware of backsliding, since he who looketh back is not fit for the king• <lorn of God ; (3) to indulge in no delay, since so long as one continues in the plain of his natural condition he stands in imminent peril; and (4) to·persevere until he reaches the mount of salvation in Jesus Christ. II. Trm OTIRTHROW 011" SoooM. 1. Supernatural. Whatever the natural forces employed in the destruction. of the fair cities of the Jordan circle, their employment wiih such severity and at such a time, viz., precisely at the moment when the moral rl.egradation of the people showed them to be ripe for judgment, was a signal <lemonstration of the miraculous character of the catastrophe; as indeed the narrative alleges it to have been a phenomenon altogether out of the commoncourse of events: "Jeho,ah rained down fire from Jehovah." 2. Unexpected. It does not appear that the inhabitants of Sodom generally were warned of the approaching fire-storm, though, i.£ Lot's sons-in-law may be accepted as an indication of the temper in which the people at that time were, any such announcement would only have been listened to with mocking incredulity. So was it in thti days of Noah (Matt. ixiv. 38); so will it be in the end of the world (2 Pet. iii. 3, 4). 3. Complete. The cities with their inhabitants, the fields with theirvegetation, were engulfed in the eulphureoue baptism and " turned into ashes." As overwhelming in its kind, though not as sweeping in its extent, as had been the previous submergence of the world by a :flood of water, the devastation sent uvon the fair Pentapolie of the Jordan circle was o. ghastly 1,hadow and premonition of that vengeance of eternal fire which shall yet devour the ungodly (2 Thess. i. 8). 4. Righteowi. It was a just judgment which had been richly merited, as the vi!,it of the angels had convincingly demonstrated. Indeed that previous unveiling of the filthiness of Sodom which had taken place may be viewed as having been designed to supply a visible justification of the righteousness nf the great Judge in consigning them to so disastrous an overthrow. And so before -~be infliction of the great day of wrath upon the impenitent and the ungodly there will be a revelation of the secret characters of all hearts and lives, that" thou mightest be justified when thou speakeet, and be clear when thou judgest 11 (Pe. Ii. 3). 5. Public. In particular, besides being experienced by the unhappy euJferere and observed by the trembling fugitives who bad sought refuge in Zoar, it was witnessed by Abraham, who gat him up early, and, looking towards Sodom, saw the smoke of the country ascending like the smoke of a furnace to heaven-a fit emblem of the terrible publicity which will invest the final judgment of a sinful world (Matt. xxv. 31-46 ; 2 Thess. i. 7-10; Re,. xviii. 9). III. THE FATE OF LoT's WIFE. 1. Intensely melanc!toly. Overtaken by the ~ulphureous storm, she was transfixed where she stood, and in a moment after wrupt in a sheet of saline incrustation. Affecting in itself, her doom was rendered nil the more impressive from the circumstance that she had so nearly escaped. ALs, nearly saved meana wholly lost I 2. Truly deserved. Contrary to the angel's inslructione, she had looked behind. Thus she had brought her tragic fate upon Lerself. Obedience would have saved her; disobedience proved her ruin. Whether Rhe was lost atcrnally it ia not safe to say, but her temporal destruction lrn.d been righteously incurred. 3. Solemnly suggestive. It was doubtless designed to teach many lessons, such as the danger of disobedience, the folly of delay, the severity of the Divine judgments, and the intensity of the Divine displeasure against sin. Lessons:-1. The difficulty of saving a good man (1 Pet. iv. 18). 2. The ability of God to punish sin (Heh. x. 31). 3. The danger of looking back (Heh. x. 26, 27, as). 4. The possibility of being nearly saved, yet wholly lost (Mark xii. 34),

entries.title: GEN 19:23–25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The rigliteousness of God revealed. The judgment of God upon Sodom and the cities of the plain. The deliverance of Lot. The reception of the two angels by Lot was a great contrast to that of ~he three by Abraham. The scene of the Divine judgment is suggestive. The plam of the Jordan was well watered, attracted Lot by its beauty and promise. Early civilisation gathered about such spots, but civilisation without religion is a blasting influence. 1:h~re are hidden fountains of judgment ready to burst forth and pour the fire of D1vme wrath upon the sinners. The man who II pitched his tent towards Sodom" became at last a townsman, 11 vexed with the filthy conversation," yet, but for Divine mercy, involved in its punishment. The whole narrative teaches important lessons, especially on the following points:- I. A TRULY RELIGIOUS LIFE is not a mere secret of the sonl, but HAS ITS APPll:0Pll:IATB PLACE AND SURROUNDINGS, II. THE HOUSEHOLD of the true believer IS A LARGE ENOUGH CIRCLE IN WHICH .TO MANIFEST SINCERITY AND FAITHFULNESS, yet must we take heed that our house is well defended against the invasions of the corrupt world, III. How GREAT A RESULT COMES OUT OFTEN FROM A SMALL BEGINNING OF ERROR I 'fhe selfishness of Lot's first choice of his residence was the seed of evil which multiplied into all the subsequent suffering and wrong. IV. "Behold the GOODNESS and SEVERITY OF Goo "-mingled judgment and mercy, but not mingled in a confused manner, with perfect order. The man who had joined with Abraham in the covenant with Jehovah, who with all his faults wns yet •a believer, is warned, rescued by angels; able by his intercession to obtnin mercy for others. V. The DIVINE JUSTICE which is manifested on the large scale as BETWEEN THF. CHURCH AND THE WORLD is nlso revealed in the smaller sphere of HOUSEHOLDS and families. Lot's wife is an apostate, and becomes involved in the destruction of the wicked. His sons-in-law mock at the Divine warning. His daughters become the incestuous originntors of nations which afterwards greatly trouble the history of the people of God. VI. THE SAME STEADFASTNESS 01!' Goo HAS TWO SIDES OR .ASPECTS OF IT. "The sun was risen upon the earth when Lot entered Zoar." The same day, while the sun was serenely smiling on the city of refuge, the storm of fire and destruction from heaven was gathering over the doomed people and ready to burst upon them. When God destroyed the cities of the ploin, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow."-R.

entries.title: GEN 19:26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The danger of falling back. 11 But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of snlt." Every part of this narrative suggestive of lessons. Reminded how II the righteous scarcely saved," and of the danger of an amiable weakness. In Lot's sons-in-law we see how the world receives the gospel (cf. Ezek. x.x. 49; James i. 24). In his wife, one convinced, but not converted; seeking safety, but with a divided aim (James i. 8), In the angel's help, God's watchful care, even where the need is unknown. Text teaches the responsibility of those who hear the gospel. Dangers surrounding us, but a way of safety (Ps. ci. 1 ; 2 Cor. ii. 16). But not enough to be roused (Matt. x. 22; Hob. xii. 1). Many are ·awakened to flee, yet look back (Luke ix. 62). Lot's wife not deaf to tl,o call ; did pot think it fancy ; really believed; felt the danger, and fled (2 Cor Yi, 17 ; Rev. 8 '.! 260 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. :ox. 20-38, x,·111, 4). But the sun rose; tho valley beautiful; homo attractive; no signs of danger. .Jlust she leaye all; and at once? She paused, That pnuse was death. I. May be roused by ALARM OF CONSCIENCE nnd yet look hack (cf. l\Iatt. xii, 43- 45). Some, intent on the world, think not of the future, Preaching seems only a venerable form_; prayer a_ proper homage to God. But ns to anything moro, no hurry. But n time of anxiety comes, Perhaps a wave of revival or some special o?currence-illness_,..be~eavement,.care, Eternity is brought near: false confidence d1spell_ed (Isa. xxvm. 11). Then m earnest to seek the true refuge (Heb. vi. 18). The Dible read; prayer a real pleading. But the sun 1uises. The immediate cause passes awar, Fears fade away. Then a_ looking back, .Surely some of you can remember times of earnestness. Perhaps m hours of anxious watching or in preparati?n for communion, ?!. God has spoken directly to the soul and'made you feel his presence (Gen. x.xvm, 16, 17). Then the blessedness of accepted salvntion was felt. The message was not a parable then. The Bible and prayer were preciou11 then. But time went on. The immediate influence gone. All as before, Old ways asserted their power; hard to give them up. In mercy the call once more. A"·ake; the storm is at hand, though thou. eeest it not, Pray that the Holy Spirit may transform thy heart. II. May be moved by EXAMPLE OF OTHERS, yet turn back. She felt her husband's earnestness, and went with him, but so far only. We know the power of example. "Then we see those we love affected, we are moved to be as they, So at the preaching of John the Baptist, So at times of n1issions. Have any felt this influence; heen stirred to read and pray? It is well. But has it lasted? For a real saving change there must be a personal transaction with the Lord ae a living Saviour; a laying bold of him, a real desire and effort that the will and whole nature be submitted to him. III. A MIGHTIER POWER STILL l\lAY ACT UPON THE SOUL, While Lot lingered angels laid hold of hands. There are times when God pleads urgently. One refuge after another swept away. Call upon call, sign upon sign, till the will seems conquered. But all is not done (Phil. iii 13). Such pleadings neglected, cease. Observe, God led Lot out of Sodom, not to Zoar. There is work still to be done (2 Pet. i. 10), The qqestion is not as to the past, but as to the present. It will not eave a man that he was once anxious. Look not back. Look to Jesus (Heh. xii. 2). Let earnestness in every part of Christian life testify that you are not looking baek (Heh, x. 30).- M.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Lot went up out of Zoar (probably soon after\ and dwelt 1D the mOUJL• ott. XllL 29-38.J 'flt~ BOOK OF GENESIS. 261 tain (i. e. of Moab, on the enst of the Dead Sen), andhis two daughters-step-daughters, it hne been suggested, if Lot married a widow who wns the mother of the two girls (Starke) -with him; for he feared to dwell in Zoar -from which the panic-stricken inhabitants may have fled towards the mountains ().Iurphy), eitl,~r because at that time it wns shaken by an earthquake (Jerome, Roscnmiiller); or because he dreaded the conflagration which devoured the other cities might spread thither (Poole, Kalisch, Wordsworth), or the rising waters of the Dead Sea which engulfed them might reach to it (Bush) -apprehensions which were groundless and unbelieving, since God had granted Zoar for an asylum (Lange) ; or because he saw the wickedness of the inhabitants, who had not been improved by Sodom's doom (Vatablns,Inglis); orsimply because he was driven by "a blind anxiety of mind" (Cal,in). And he dwelt in a cave,-i. e. in one of tho3e cavernous recesses with which the Moabiti3h mountains abound, and which already had been con.ertcd into dwelling-places by the primith·e inhabitants of the region (cf. eh. ~iv. 6)-he and his two daughters. Yer. 31.-And the firstboru said unto the younger,-showina that she had not escaped the pollution, if she had the destruction, of Sodom. "It was time that Lot hnd left the cities of the plain, No wealth could compensate for the mora\ degradation into which his family hnd sunk" (lnglis)-0ur fo.ther is old,-an indirect confit,nation of the inference (vide eh. xi. 26) that Abram wns younger thtm Hurnn, since Lot, Haran's son, is now an old ruan-o.nd there is not a mo.n in the ear\h-not in the entire world (Origen, frenll!UB, Chrysostom, Kalisch), which is smrcely probublc, since they knew that Zonr hud been spa1·ed ; but either in the district whither they hnd fled (Calvin, Willet), being under the impression thnt, living in so clesolato I\ region, they could have no more intercourse with mankind ; or in the laud of Cannan (Ainsworth, Bush), meaning that there wero no moro godly men with whom they might marry ; or perhups they meant thut no mnn would now care to unite himself with them, the remnunt of a curse-stricken region (Knobel, Keil)-to come in unto us after the manner of all the earth.

entries.title: GEN 19:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Come, let us make our fo.ther drink wiue,-cither, therefore, Lot had not left Sodom totally unprovided (Inglis), or some little time hud elapsed after his escaping to the mountl\in cave, smce his daughters are provided with this intoxicating beverageand we will lie with him. Considering the town in which the do.ughters of Lot bud been reared, the mother of whom they were tho offsp1ing, and the example they had received from their father (vel'. 8)1 "we cnn understand, though we cannot cen.se to abhor, their incestuous condnet" (Kalisch). Their proposal was revolting and unnatural in the extreme. By subsequent Mosaic legislation a translp'ession of such enormity was rendered pnnisll.able by death. Even in the present rnstance the perpetrators were not wholly unconscious or the wickedness of their conduct. The fact that they required a stratagem for the attainmentof their purposeshows that at least they could not calculate on their father's approbation. The entire story bas been regarded as the invention of later Jewish hatred to the Moabites and Ammonites (De Wette), a conjecturu believed by some to be "notimprobable" (Roscnmliller); but if so, how should the same writer exhibit Abraham (eh. xviii. 23) as filled \\ith compassionate tenderness towards the cities of the phin ·1 (Hiivemick). Lot's daughters may be credite,1 "ith whate,•er virtue may be supposed tu reside in this motive for their conduct.

entries.title: GEN 19:37
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the firstborn bare a son, and called his name Koab =Meab, from the father, alluding to his incestuous origin (LXX., which adds x;yov<ra h: roii 1rarp6t; ,,ou; Augustine, Jerome, Delitzsch, Keil); though ]lfo (= water, an Arnbic euphemism forthesemenvirile) and ab has been advanced ns a more correct derivation (Roscnmiiller). The same is the father of the Moabites-who originally inhabited the country north-east of the Dead Sea, between the Jabbok and the Amon (Deut. ii. 20), but were afterwards driven by the Amoritcs south of the Amonunto this day. This phrase, indicatil.1" a ,·:triable period from a few years to a few centuries (cf. eh. xlviii. 13 ; Exod. x. 6 ; Knmb. xxii. 39; Josh. xxii. 3), cannot be rcgardeu as a trace of post-Mosaic authorship (De Wette, et alii), since in Genesis it is always used of events which had taken placo several centuries before the time of Moses, as in eh. xxvi. 33; xxxv. 20; xlvii. 26 (cf. Keil, 'Introduction,' part i. § 2, div. 1, § 38).

entries.title: GEN 19:38
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the younger, she also bare a aon, and called his namo J!en-ammi. I. e. son of my people (LXX., Jerome, Augustine), meaning that her child WQS the oifs-r,ring of her own kind and blood (RosenmiJ.ller), or the son of her relative (Kalisch), or of an unmixed race (' Speaker's Commentary'). The same is the father of the children of Ammon-an unsettled people who occupied the territory between the Jabbok and the Arnon, from which they had ejected the Rephaims or Zamzummims (Deut. ii. 22), and in which they possessed a strong city, Rabbah (2 Sam. xi. 1) ; in their habits more migratory and marauding than the Moabites (Isa. xv., xvi.; Jer. xlviii.), and in their religion worshippers of Molech, "theabomination of the Ammonites" (1 Kings xi. 7)- unto this day.

entries.title: GEN 19:29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The last days of Lot. I. HAUNTED BY TERROR. 1. The te1-ror of DivinefudgmenJ. The appalling spectacle of Sodom's overthrow had no doubt filled him with alarm. And so are God's judgments in the earth designed to put the souls of men in fear (Ps. ix. 20; xlvi. 8-10; cxix. 120). 2. Tlie terrorof men. Dwelling in Zoar, he apprehended an outburst of wrath from the citizens, who probably regarded him as the cause of the ruin which had invaded Sodo)l'.I. So are better men than Lot sometimes overtaken by the fear of mar, (2 Sam. xxii. 5; Ps. xviii. 4), though they should not (Isa. Ji.·12). 3. The terror ofconscience. That Lot enjoyed while in Zoar a calm and undisturbed repose of heart and mind is scarcely supposable. Rather it may be- safely conjectured that after the storm and the fire and the ·earthquake through which he had latelypassed, the still small voice of conscience spoke to him in awe-inspiring accents, unveiling his past life, reproving him of sin, and pierci~g l1im through with many sorrows; and that under the agitations produced by its accusations and reproaches he became s.frnid, and withdrew to the mountains. "Thus conscience doth make cowards of us all." II. SouNDING THE LOWER DEEPS. 1. Descending into unbelief. God had promised to spare Zoar for him, and him in Zoar, and one would have thought Lot had been sufliciently warned of the sin of distrusting God. Yet he is scarcely established in tlie city which God had granted in response to his own prayer than he begins to think it hardly safe to remain within its precinctl3. How inveterate is unbelief I 2. Plung· iilg into sin. The details of the present story clearl)'. show thut .Lot, when. he went to the mountain cave, endeavoured to escape from his terrors not by carryrng them to God's throne but by drowning them in dissipation. The wretched man, who had once been a sai~t in God's Church, must have been in the habit of drinking to excess, else his daughters would never have thought of their abominable stratagem. Oi:ily oue little gleam of virtue can be detected as entitled to be laid to Lot's account, viz., tlmt liis daughters apparently believed that unless their father was drunk he woufd never be brought to assent to their lewd proposal. 3. Sinki;ng into shame. Tw\ce 0\'ercome by wine, he is twice in successio~ d1shono11red by 111s duught~rs; and twice 01·er wliile in his drink stupor be allows himself to commit an act wlnch almost out- Sod~ms Sodom. To what depths a saint may fall when once he turns his back on God I III. DISAPPEAnING JNTO0DLIVION. Notl1i11g could more distinctly mark the Divine diHapprobntion with Lot's conduct than the fact that after this he was suffered--;-!. To live an imncorded life, beir,g J!evcr hcnrcl of again in the pages of Holy Scnpture. tn. :xx. 1-18.J 'l'BE BOOK OF GENESlS. 263 2. To die an unnoticed deatl~. Where and how he met his end the histori,rn does not condescend to state, 3. To mnk into an unknown grave. Whether buried in hie mountain cave or entombed in the Jordan valley no man knoweth unto this day. See-1. The dnnger of turning aside from God and good men (Heh. iii. 12; x. 25). 2. The melancholy end of a worldly life (1 Cor. x. 6; Phil. iii. 19; 2 Tim. iv. 10). 3. The bitter fruits of parental neglect (1 Sam. ii. 27-36; Prov. xxix. 15-17).

entries.title: GEN 19:29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The destruction of Sodom and Gomorral;,. I. TIIE VIsmu JUDGMEt!T. "God o-erthrew the cities in the which Lot dwelt." 1. The reason. 2. The instrumentality. 3. The reality. 4. The lessons of the overthrow. II. TnE UNKNOWN MERCY, "He sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow." To Abraham this was-1. A great mercy. 2. A mercy granted in answer to prayer. But-3. An unknown mercy, there being no reason to believe that Abraham ever saw Lot again, or knew of hie deliverance. Leam-1. That God always mixes mercy with his judgments. 2. That his mercies are not nlways so perceptible to the eye of sense and reason as his judgments. 3. That God's people get more mercies poured into their cups than they arc nt all times cognisant of.-W.

entries.title: GEN 20:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abraham journeyed (vide eh. xii. 9) from thence. Mamre (eh. xviii. l ). In search of pasture, as on a previous occo.sion (Keil) ; or in consequence of the hostility of his neighbours (Calvin) ; or because he longed to escape from the scene of· so terribl~ n calamity as he had witnessed (Calvin, Willet, Murphy); or iu order to benefit as many places and peoplits as possible byhis residence among them (A Lapide); or perhaps being impelled by God, who designed thereby to remind him that Canaan was not intended for a permanent habitation, but for a constant pilgrimage (Poole, Kalisch). Toward the south country. Negeb, the southern district of Palestine (eh. xii. 9 ; xiii. l) ; the central region of Judrea lieing called Hah,o1·, or the Highlands; the eastern, townrds tho Dend Sea, JV[idhbar,· and the western Shephelah, (Lange). And dwelled between Xadesh and Shur (vide eh. xvi. 14 and xvi. 7), and sojourned in Gerar (vide eh. x. 19).

entries.title: GEN 20:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister. As formerly he hnd done on descending into Egypt (eh. xii. 13). That Abraham should a second time have resorted to this ignoble expedient ufter the huznrdous experience ofEgypt und the richlymerited rebuke of Pharaoh, but more especially after the assurance he had lately received of his own accoptance before God (eh. xv. 6), and of Snnh's destiny to be the mother of the promised seed (eh. xvii. 1G), is well nigh c.iaccountable, nnd ulmost irreconcilable 11>ith any degree of faith aucl piety. Yet the lapse of upwards of twenty years since that former mistake may have deadened the impression of sinfulnesswhich Pharaoh's rebukB must have left upon his conscience ; whib altogether the result of that experiment mny, through a common misinterpretation of Divine providence, have encouraged him to think that God would watch over the purity of his. house as he had done before. Thus, though in reality n tempting of God, the patriurch's repetition of his early vcntmo may have had a secret connection with his deeply-grounded faith in the Divine promise (cf. Kalisch in loco). And Abimelech-i. e. Father-king, a. title of the Philistine kings (eh. xxi. 22; xxvi. l ; Psalm xxxiv. 1), as Phuraoh was of the Egyptian (eh. xii. 15), and Hamor of the Shechcmite (eh. x.uiv. 4) monarchs; cf. Padishah (fnthcr-king), a title of the Persiun kings, and Atahk {father, properly puternity), of the Khnns of Boklrnm (Gesenius, p. 6)-king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah. I. e. intoliis hnrcrn, as Phamoh previously hud done {eh. xii. 15), either hnving been fascin11ted by her beauty, which, although she was twenty years older tban when sho entered Egypt, need not have been much faded (vicle eh. xii. 11 ; Culvin), or may have been miraculously rejuvenntc,I when she received strength to conceive seed (Kurtz) ; or, what is as probable, havin1; sought through her au alliance with tho rich and powerful nomnde prince who had entered his dominions (Delitzsch).

But (l) tl1e use of Elohim throughout the present chapkr is sufficiently accounted for byobserving thnt it describes tlie intercourse of Deity with a heathen monarch, to whom the name ofJeho,ah was unknown, while the employmen_t of the latter term in ver. 18 may be ascribed to the fact that it is the covenant God of Sarah who there interposes for her rrotection; and (2) the apparent resemblance between the two incidents is more than cou_nterbal~nced by the points of diversity which subsist between them-came to Abimelech in a dream-the usual mode of self. revelation employed by Elohim towards heathen. Cf. Pharaoh's dreams (eh. xii. 1) and Nebuchadnezzar's (Den. iv. 5), as distin~1ished from the visions in which Jehovah manifests his presence to his people. Cf. the tbeophanies vouchsafed to Abraham (eh. xii. 7; xv. 1 ; xviii. 1) and to Jacob (eh. x:xv:iii. 13 ; xxxii. 24), and the visions granted to Daniel (Dan. vii. 1-28; x. 5-9) and the prophets generally, which, though sometimes occurring in dreams, were yet e higher form of Divine manifestation than the dreams-by night, and said to him, Behold, thou art but a dead man,-literally, behold thyse{f dying, or about to du= av a.1ro9vf,ar:ni; (LXX. ). Dent. xxii 22).

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - But Abimelech had not come near her. Apparently withheld by the peculiar disease which had overtaken him. The statement of the present verse (a similar one to v;hich is not made with reference to Pharaoh) was clearly rendered necessary by the approaching birth of Isaac, who might othernise have been said to be the child not ofAbraham, bnt of the Philistine king. And he said, Lord,-Adonai (vide eh. xv. 2)- wilt thou slay also a righteous nation 1 .Anticipating that the stroke of Divine judgment was nbout to fall upon his people ns well as on himself, with a.llusiou to the fate of Sodom (Knobel), which he deprecates for !,is people at least on the ground that they are innocent of the offence charged against l,im (cf. 2 Sam. xxiv. 17). That Abimelech au<l his people, like Melchisedeck and his subjects, had some lrnowledge of the true liod, and that the Canaanites generally at this period had not reached the depth of rnora degradation into which the cities of the Jordan circle had sunk before their overthrow, is apparent from the narrative. The comparative virtue, therefore, of these tribes mts a proof thnt the hour hnd not arrived for the infliction on them of the doom of extermination, . From which it is clenr thnt the P~ilistine monnrch, equally with the Egyptmn Pharaoh, shrank from the sin of ~dultery. In the integrity of my heart and mnocenoy of my hands have I done this. entries.content: -And God said unto him in a dream,-" It is in full agreement with the nature of dreams that the communication s~ould be made in several, and not in one smgle act; cf. chs. xxxvii. and xli.; Matt. ii." (Lange)-Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart-1·. e. judged from thy moral standpoint. The words do n_ot imJ?IJ: a Divine acquittal as to the essen- ~utl gmlt~ness ~f the ~et, which is clearly rnvolved m the mstrucbon to seek the mediation of God's prophet (ver. 7). entries.title: GEN 20:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now therefore restore the ma.n his wife. Literally, the wife of the man, God now speaking of Abraham non tanquam de homine quolibet, sed peculiariter sibi cha.rum (Calvin). For he is a prophet. Nabi, from naba, to cause to bubble up; hence to pour forth, applied to one who speaks by e. Divine afflatus (Deut. xiii. 2; Judges vi. 8 ; 1 Sam. ix. 9; 1 Kings xxiL 7). The office of the Na.bi was twofold-to announce the will of God to meu (Exod. iv. 15 ; vii. 1), and also to intercede with God for men (ver. 7; Jer. vii. 16; xi. 14; xiv. 11). The use of the term Ne.bi in this place neither proves the.t the sphit of propl1ecy had not existed from the beginning (cf. eh. ix. 25-27), nor shows that the Pentateur.h, which always uses this term, cannot be of greater antiquity than the time of Samuel, before which, according to 1 Sam. ix. 9, the prophet was called a seer (Bohlen, Hartmann). As used in the Pentateuch the term describes the recipient of Divine revcla.tious, and as such it was incorporated in the Mosaic legislation. During the period of the Judges the term Roeh appears to have corn~ into use, and to have held its ground until the reformation of Samuel, when the older theocratic term was again reverted to (vide Hiivernick, § 19). And he shall pray for thee (vide supra), and thou shalt live. Literally, live thou, the imperative being used for the future in strong prophetio assurances (cf. Pa. cxxviii. 5 ; vide Gesenius, § 130). And if thou restore her not, know thou that thou aha.It surely dle,--Iiternlly, rl'I. H. 1--]8.] TRE BOUK OF GENE~JS dylnr, t/101~ shale die (cf, eh. iL 17)-tho11, and all that rtrc thine.

entries.title: GEN 20:8

entries.content: -Therefore Abimelech rose early in the morniug,-nn evidence of the terror into which he l1nd been coat by the Divine commnnicntion, and of his earnest desire to cnn-y out the Divine instnictions-and called all his servants, and told all these things in their ears :-confessed his fault, explained his danger, and affirmed his intention to repair his error ; a proof of the humility of this God-fearing king (Langeland the men were sore afraid. It spoke well for the king's household that they received the communication with seriousness.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Then Abimelech called Abraham, a.nd ea.id unto him (in the presence of his people), What hast thou done unto ue1 -identifying himself once more with hill people, as he had already done in responding to God (ver. 4)-and what have I offended thee (thus modestly allowing that he may himself have unwittingly occasioned the sin of Abraham), that thou hast brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin1 The w-avamen of Abimelech's accusation was that Abraham had led him and his to offend against God, and so to lay themselves open to the penalties of wrong-doing. Thou hast done deeds uuto me that ought not to be done. Literally, deeds which <mght not to be done thou hast done with me (cf. eh. x.uiv. 7 ; Levit. iv. 2, 13; vide mass, 'Philol. T:-act., 1. iii. t. iii. c. vi. ). The king's words were unquestionably designed to convey n severe reproach.

entries.content: -And Abimelech said unto Abraham, What sawest thou,-either, What hadst thou in view 1 (Knobel, Delitzsch, Keil, Murphy, et alii), or, What didst thou see I Didst thou see any of my people taking the wives of strangers and murdering their hu~bnnds I (Rosenmiiller, 'Speaker's Commentary ')-that thou ha.at done this thing 1

entries.content: -And Abraham sa.id (offering as liis first apology for his sinful behaviour the fear which he entertained of the depravity of the people), Beca.nse I thought,-literally, .,aid (sc. in my heart)-Surely the fear of God is not in this place ;-otherwise, there is not anyfear of God, j:)1 having usua.J.ly 11 confirmin" sense with rererence to whnt follows (cf. Dent. iv. 6; 1 Kings xiv. 8; vide Ccsenillll, p. 779)-and they will slay:me for my wife's sa.ke.

entries.title: GEN 20:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And yet indeed she is my sister. This wns the second of the patriarch's extenuating pleas, that lie had not exnctly lied, having uttered at least a half-truth. She is the daughter of my father ('l'erah), but not the daughter of my mother. That Snroh was the grand-daughter of Teroh, i. e. the <laughter of He.rnn, and sister of Lot, in :1ther words, lscah, has been maintained (Josephus, Augustine, Jerome, Jona\h,rn). That she was Ternh's niece, being a brother's daughter adopted by hiin, has received soma support (Calvin); bnt there seems no reason for departing from the statement cf the text, that she was her husband's half-sister, i. e. Terah's daughter by another wife than Abraham's mother (Rosenmiiller, Kalisch, Keil, Knobel). And she became my wife.

entries.title: GEN 20:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, when God ea.need me to wander (or to go on pilgrimages) from my father's house, - Elohim, usually construed with a singular verb, is here joined with a verb in the plural, as an accommodation to the polytheistic standpoint of Abimelech (Keil), as a proof that Elohim is to be viewed e.s e. Plurali3 ftfajestaticus (Kalisch), as referring tn the plurality of Divine manifestations which Abraham had received (Lange), as showing that Elohim here signifies angels (Calvin), or, most likely, as an instance of the literal meaning of the term as the supernatural powers (:\Inrphy). Cf. eh. xxxv. 7; Exod. xxii. 8; 2 Sam. ,ii. 23; Ps. ]\;ii, 12-that I ae.id unto her, This is thy kindness which thou shalt show nnto me. The third plea. which the patriarch presented for his conduct, it had no special reference to Abimelech, bnt was the result of e.n old compact formed between himselt' and Sarah. At every place whither we shnll come, sa.y of me, He is my brother (cf. eh. xii. 13).

entries.title: GEN 20:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abimelech-as Phnraoh did (eh. xii. 16), but ,vith a. different motivetook sheep, and oxen, and men-servants, and women-servants. The LXX. nnd Samaritan insert"a thousand didrachmn.s" after"took," in order to include Sarah's present mentioneu in ver. 16 ; but the two donations are scpar• ated in order to distinguish them as Abraham's gift o.nd SRrah's respectively (Rosenmiiller, Delitzsch), or the sum of money may indicl\te the value of the sheep and oxen, &c. which Abraham receh·ed (Keil, Knobel, Lange, 'Speaker's Commentary'). And gaVll them unto Abraham. To propitiate his favour for the wrong he hnd suffered. Pharaoh's girts were ''for the sake of Sarah" (eh. xii. 16). And restored him Sarah his wife.

entries.title: GEN 20:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abimelech aaid, Behold, my land is before thee : dwell where it pleaseth thee. Literally, in the qood in thine eyes; the generous Philistine offoriug him a settlement within his borders, whereas the Egyptian monarch hastened his departure from the country (eh. xii. 20).

entries.title: GEN 20:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And unto Sarah he said, Behold, I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver. Literally, a thousand of silver, the exactweightofeach piece being uncertain. H sacred shekels (Cesenius, Keil, Kalisch) their value would be over £130, if shekalll 266 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. xx. 1-18. 01"\linary somc'ehat less. :Behold, he-i. e. thy brotl1er; or it, i. e. the present (LXX., Yulgate, Targums, Syrinc)-is to thee a covering of the eyes. Cl~?V. n~c~ (from a root signifying to cover over) has been under- ~toocl as (I) n propitiatorygift= r,µ,) (LXX.), or (2) a veil for the protection of the face; nn<l, according as the subject of the sentence has been regarded as Abraham or the sum of money, the sense of the clause has been gfreu as either (I) he, i. e. thy brother, will he to tb?e a protection, hi<ling thee like a wil, from the voluptuous desires of others (Ahen Ezra, Cajetan, Calvin, Kalisch) ; or (:2: it, i. e. this present of mine, will be to thee n propitiatory offering to make thee oYerlook my offence (Chrysostom, Gesenius, Fiirst, Knobel, Delitzsch, Keil, Murphy) ; or (3) a declaration of thy purity, and so a defence to thee against any calumnious aspersions (Castalio) ; or (4) the purchasemoney of a veil to hide thy beauty, lest others be ensnared (Vnlgnte, Arnbic, Kitto, Clark); or (5) the means of procuring that Lri<la1 veil which married females should 11ever lay aside (cf. eh. xxiv. 65; Dathe, Yitringa, :Michaelis, Baumgarten, Rosenmi.iller). The exact sense of this difficult passage can scarcely be said to have been determined, though of the above interpretations the choice seems to lie between the first and second. Unto all that are with thee, and with all other. entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Auraluzm in Cerar, or two royal sinners. I. THE BIN ?F 1_'IIE HEBREW PATRIARCH. 1. An old S'in repeated. "A?rnham said. of S~rah !us wife, She is my sister." As Abraham explained to Abimelech, it was no sudden nnpulse on which he acted, but a preconcerted scheme w}iich l~e had put in op_eration.. ln_tended for the ex~en_u• ation of his fault this was in reality an aggravation. The )?.atriarch said to himself, "Surely the fear of God is nut in this place, and they will slay me for my wife's sake," without reflecting that he was not only deciding without evidence, but doing an injustice to the monnrch and the people into whose land he was crossing. Leilrn-1. How hard it is to lay aside one's besetting sin. The character of the patriarch, othenvise so noble, appears to have had a natural bias towards deception. 2. How difficult it is to lead a life of faith. One would have thought that by tl1iH time every vestige of carnal policy would have been eliminated from the walk of Abraham. 3. How possible it is for an eminent saint to relapse into great sin. If Abraham illustrated the virtues, he likewise remarkably exemplified the weaknesses of God's believing people. 4. How wrong it is to cherish and act upon uncharitable views of others. True religion always leans to the side of charity in judging of the characters of men. II. THFJ SIN OF THE HEATHEN PRINCE. 1. A common sin. The popularity of an action, though not sufficient to make it good, may serve, in some degree, to extenuate its guilt where it is wrong. 2. An unconscious sin. The narrative distinctly represents Abimelech as a prince who feared God and shrank from incurring his displeasure-a character which all kings should study to possess. Abimelech himself claimed to have perpetrated no offence against the law of God in acting as he did, which shows that the voice of conscience always speaks according to its light. The avowal which be makes of his integrity is ndmittcd by Jehovah as correct-n proof that God judges men nccording to their privileges. Yet it was-3. A weat sin. Implied in the Divine direction to seek the friendly intercession of the patriarch, it was admitted by Abimelech when once his mind was enlightened as to the true character of the deed he had committed. See here-1. A lesson of charity concerning peoples nnd individuals outside th~ visible Church. 2. A proof that men are not necessarily free from guilt because their consciences fail to accuse them. 3, A good sign of true contrition, viz., the acknowledgment of sin when it is pointed out. III. Goo's DEALINGS WITH TH:E PRINCE AND _WITH THE PATRIARCH. 1. With the prince. (1) Restraining grace. God withheld him from proceeding to further sin by doing injury to Sarah, the means employed being disease which was sent upon both the monarch and his house. So God frequently interposes by afflictive dispensations to prevent those who fear him from running into sins of which perhaps they - are not aware. (2) flluminating grace. Appearing in a dream, Elohim disclose,! the true character of his offence, and quickened his conscience to apprehend the guilt nnd danger which had been incurred. Sincere souls who fear God and are faithful to the light they have are never left to wander ih darkness, but in God's time and way are mysteriously guided to the path of safety and duty (Ps. xxv. 12-14). (3) Directing grace. Finding the heathen monarch's heart susceptible of good impressions, God further counselled him how to act in order to obtain forgiveness, viz., to solicit tl,e mediating services of Abraham, who in thii; matter wns a type of henYen's great High Priest nnd Intercessor (Heb. vii. 25). Cf. God's way of dealing with errin~- men (Job xxxii. 14-33). 2. With the patriarch. (1) Protect-ion. A second timJ he shield11d his erring servant from the consequences of his own folly. A mark o~ God's tender pity towards sinful men. (2) Reproof. Besides being much needed, it wns exceedingly severe, and must have been deeply humiliating. God often permits l1is people to be rebuked by the world for their good. (3) Hon01tr. God i, ever better to his people than their desnrts. Not only did he direct Abimelecl1 to ask the help of Abraham, but he constituted Abraham the medium of bestowing blessing-, on Abimelech. So does God honour Al:iroham's seed, Christ, by exalting hiru in 1.hc world's sight as the one Mediator bctw,ien God and man; and Abruhum's children, the Church, by making them the instnments of drawing down blessings on 1.ho world. I.earn-I. That God's dealings with sinning men nr alwnys'adapted to the pccuuor <l,aracters of their respective sins. 2. That God neYer chastises men, either by nflliction or rebuke, for his pleasure, but for their profit, 3, That God never pardu11~ ein without bestowing- blessing on the sinner. Tm: DOOR OF GF.NESfS. (en. u. 1-1~ nmnLIES BY VARIOUS AUTHOUS. Vrr. 2.-Falseliood the f1"ltit of urweluf. "Abrnham said of Sarah liis wife- ~lie is my sister.". Notice ho," imperfectly the obligation of truth recognised in Old Test.~ment t1n:ies. Not only among heathen, or those who knew little c.~ God (,Josh. 11. ?. ; 2 Kmgs x. 18), but godly men among God's own people (eh. xni 7: 1 Sam. xxvn. 10). Yet the excellence of truth was known, and its connectio::i with the fear of God (Exod. xviii. 21; Ps. xv. 2). Not unt.il manifested in Christ does truth seem to be fully understood (cf. John vsiii. 44; 1 John iii. 8). This givM force to" I am the truth." Some see in text an act of fe.ith; trust that God would make the plan (Yer. 13) successful. Bnt faith must rest on God's word. Trust in what God gives no warrant for believing is not faith, but fancy, e. g. to attempt what we ha,·e no reason to believe we can accomplish, or to incur liabilities without rensonable prospect of meeting them. More natural and better to look on it as a breach of truth under temptation ; the failure of a godly man under trial. His words were true in letter (ver. 12), bnt were spoken to deceive, and did deceive. l RooT or, ms FAULT-UNBELIEF; want of all-embracing trust. His faith wns real and vigorous (cf. 1 Cor. x. 12), but partial (cf. eh. xxvii. 19; Matt. xiv. 28). Shrank from trusting God fully. Turned to human devices, and tbns turned out of the wny (Prov. iii. 5). Partial distrust may be found even where real faith. A very common instance is trusting in God for spiritual blessings only. Alarge part of our actions, especially in little things, springs not from conscious decision, but from habitual modes of thought and feeling. We act instinctively, according to whnt fa the natural drift of thought. .Abraham had so dwelt on t~e danger that he forgot the help at band (Ps. miv. 7; Rom. viii. 28). Bold in action, his faith failed when dang-er threatened. To endure is a greater trial of faith than to do. To stand finu a.mid secularising influences, ridicule, misconstruction is harder than to do some greut thing. St. Peter was ready to fight for hie Mastt;r, but failed to endure (Mnrk xiv. 50-71; Gal. ii. 12). So to St. Paul's "What wilt thou have me to do?" tl,e Lord's word was, "I will show him how great things he must suffer." II. Fonr,r or HIS FAULT-UNTRUTH. Contrary to the mind of Christ. May be without direct statement of untruth. May be by true words so used as to convey a ,nong idea ; by pretences, e. g. taking credit unduly for any possession or power; by being ashamed to admit our motives; or by untruth in the spiritual life, making unreal professions in prayer, or self-deceiving. Every day brings numberless trinls. These can be resisted only by the habit of truthfulness, gained by cultivating "truth in the inward parts," aiming at entire truthfulness. Nothing unpractical in this. May be said, 1\1.Jst I tell all my thoughts to every one? Not so. Many things we liave no right to speak; e. g. things told in confidence, or what would give unnecessary pain. Concealment when it is right is not untruth. No doubt questions of difficulty may arise. Hence rules of casuistry. But a Christian should be guided by principles rather than by rules (Gal. v. 1); and wisdom to apply these rightly is to be gained by studying the character of Christ, and prayer for the Holy Spirit's guidance (Luke xi. 13; John xvi. 14).-M. entries.title: GEN 21:1–8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The •·on of promise, or a young child's biograpliy. I. Tm: BinTII OF lsAAC. 1. A surprising phenomenon. " Who would have said that Sarah should have suckled sons?" Motherhood at ninety was certainly unusual, especially when conjoined with paternity at a hundred. In a world presided over by a personal Deity there must always be room for surprises. 2. A miraculous production. That the conception and birth of Isaac were due to Divine interposition-that, in fact, the child of promise was a special supernatural creation-is asserted by Paul as well as Moses (Rom. iv. 17). 3. An accom:p_lishedprediction. Not only the fact of Isaac's birth, but the exact time was 1,pec1fied beforehand. And now the longlooked-for child had arrived. A signal proof of the Divine veracity, it was another pledge to God's people in every age of tl1e Divine fidelity in implementing his gracious word of promise. 4. A joyous inspiration. • Isaac's birth not simply woke laughing echoes in Sarah's tent, but opened founts of song in Sarah's breast; which was not wonderful, considering that the tender infant over which she exulted was the child of her own and .Abraham's old age, the child of promise, the fruit of faith and the gift of grace, and the Heaven-appointed heir of the covenant blessing. 5. A prophetic intimation. Sarah's anthem contained a higher note of melody than that occasioned by a mother's joy ; there was in it too the gladness of a faith that saw in Isaac the harbinger and pledge of another and greater Seed. Like the birth of Isaac, that of Christ was fore-announced by God, waited for in faith, accomplished through Diviue power, and welcomed with bursts of joy. II. 'l'IIE CIBCUMCISION OF ls.Uc. 1. 'fhe import of the rite (see on eh. xvii. 10). It implied the formal reception of the party upon whom it was imposed within the pale of tlie Old Testament Church ; it signified the putting away of the filth of the flesh ; it took the subject of it bound to a holy life. Of a like import is the Christian sacrament of baptism, wliich, however, differs from the Hebrew rite in looking back upon a Cliriot ,L-eady manifested, inGtead of forward to a Christ that was still to come. 2, The authority for the rite. This was exclusively the Divine commandment - the sole reason that can be assigned for the observance of the Christian so.crnments, which in themselves o.re only symbols of spiritual transactions, and have no validity apart from the appointment of Christ. 3. The index to the rite. This wae contained in the name generally given on the occasion of its observance: cf. Abrahn.m (eh. xvii. 5), John the Baptist (Luke i. 60), Jesus (Luke ii. 21). With this ancient custom must be connected the Christian practice of naming children at baptism. III. THE WEANING OF faAAc. 1. A mother's duty fulfil,led. The first duty of a mother is to her babe, and to withhold the eUBtenance God has provided for her babe's necessities is both to violate Divine law and to perpetrate a fraud upon her helpless offepring. Sarah, though a primess, was not above discharging the duties of a nuree-n example which Sarah's d,1ughters should diligently follow. 2. A child}s independence beg-ztn, From the moment of weaning a child may be said to enter on a separate and as it were independent existence, attaining then for the first time to a distinct individuality of being, 3. A father's joy expressed. The interesting event was celebrated by a festal entertainment, at which, if not Shem, Melchieedek and Selah, according to the Rabbis, the inmates of Abraham's household were do~btlees present. "God's blessing upon the nursing of children, and his preservation of them during the perils of infant age, are signal instances of the care and fonderness of Divine providence, which ought to be acknowledged to its praise" (Henry). • f • • • h • I 'Id 2 Th d • Lessons:-1. The nght o parents to reJ01ce m t e1r c u ren. . e uty o~ parents to introduce their children to the Church of God. 3. The propriety of Darents recognising the separate individualities of children.

THE FAITH OF HIS SERVANT, which was evidenced in wniting, hoping, naming the son born unto him, obeying the commandment. III. THE GIFT of God was THE REVELATION of God: bis love, bis power, his purpose, his patience. IV. Taken TYPICALLY, the foreshadowing of the miraculons conception, the kingdom of God, ns originnting in the sphere of human infirmity and helplessness; as being tho introduction of bright hope and cheerful promise into the gloomy barrenness of human life; as the lifting up of man's state into the covonnnt of God, sealed with his appointed ordinance, surrounded with the promised blessings. Isnac was the type of Christ, Sarah of Mary, Abraham of the people and Church of God. V. SARAH'S BONO, the first cradle hymn of a mother's thankful joy, representing the Divine delight in the pure and simple happiness of those who a.re children of God. Abraham rejoiced to see the brightness of the future (John viii. 56). VI. THE WEANING FEAST. All called in to share in the joy. Household joy should be widespread. We may suppose that such a banquet was religious in its charo.cter. If so, not only is it a sanction of religious festivals, but it reminds us that we should connect the events of the family life immediately with the word and ordinance3 of God.-R.

entries.title: GEN 21:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And God said unto Abraham.- probably in e. dream, or night vision (vide ver. 14)-Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thybondwoman ;-who was never i-ecognised by God as Abraham's wife (cf. eh. xvi. 8)-in all that Sarah bath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice. Though Saralt'J counsel was approved by God, it does not fol101v that her conduct was. On a former occasion A.bra.- ham's hearkening unto Sarah's voice had led to sin (eh. xvi 2); this time it would lie exactly in the line of duty. For in Ieaao shall thy seed be called. Literally, in Isaac shall seed (i. e. posterity) be called to thee,· meaning neither, "by Isaac shall thy seed be called, or named " (Hofmann, Kalisch, Ainsworth), nor, "in Isaac shall thy seed be called into existence" (Dreschler); but, "in Isaac shall there be posterity to theo which shall pass as such," i. e. be called or recognised as such (Keil) ; or, more simply, "in Isaac,'' i. e. in the line of Isaac, " shall be called to thee a seed," i. e. e. seed par excellence, the seed already promised (Bicek, Delitzsch, Rosenmiiller, Alford, Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 21:9–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie expulsion of Ishmael. I. THE CAUSE. 1. The persecution oj Isaac. "Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian mocking." That thiii "·as no mere sportive pleasantry may be inferred from the deep feeling it aroused in Sarah, the summary chastisement it brought on Ishmael, and th• seY{lre language in which it is characterised by Paul. The emphasis laid by Sarah on the heirship suggests the probability that Ishmael's offence partook of the nature of wicked, irritating laughter at the position and prospects of Sarah's son, springing partly from envy and partly from unbelief. 2. The apprehensions of Sarah. That Sarah was actuated by personal dislike of Hagar's boy, or inspired solely by maternal jealousy, is a gratuitous assumption. It is more satisfactory to ascribe her seemingly harsh coun. sel to the clearness with which she recognised that Isaac alone was the Heavenappointed heir, and that nothing must be allowed to either damage his position or endanger his prospects. 8. The commandment of God. Considering the patriarch'R former experience of "hearkening to Sarah," his acquiescence in her counHel on this occasion would in all probability have been problematical, had not God interposed to recommend its adoption. It would both secure the happiness of Isaac and remove temptation from the path of Ishmael; while it would serve to educate the patriarch himself for the coming sacrifice on Mount Moriah. To facilitate the patriarch's compliance with the Divine injunction, the promise of future greatness to Ishmael is renewed, and in the end Hagar and her boy are dismissed. II. THE MANNER. 1. With pain to liimself. "The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son." Parental affection must have urged him to retain his first-born son, Conjugal love must have interceded for her who had been to him as a wife. Self-interest may have represented the advisability of still clinging to Ishmael for the fulfilment of the promise, in case the line of Isaac should fail. Yet grace nnd faith triumphed. "All things are possible to him thnt belfoveth." 2. With tenderness towards the outcasts. •Making provision for their immediate necessities, and either then or afterwards adding gifts (eh. x.:xv. G), he sends them away, doubtleBs with many prayers and tears. Nature and grace both enjoin tenderness in dealing with those whom God in his providence calls to suffer. 8. With submission to the will of God. The moment the mind of God was ascertained, internal controversy ceased and determined. The patriarch was never irresolute in following when God fed. Obedience is the first duty of faith. III. TIIE TYPICAL SIGNIFICANCE. 1. Ishmael and Isaac represcntatiYes of Abrnham's natural descendants and Abraham's spiritual posterity; Israel after the flesh and Israel after the spirit; souls in legal bondage anrl souls enjoying spiritual freec!;;:n. 2. Ishrnael's separa• tion from Isaac prefigured the ultimate removal of unbelievers from believers, of the "·orld from the Church, of those in a sl;ate of nature or of legal bondage from those l"l"hO are children of the promise and of the heavenly Jerusalem. entries.title: GEN 21:15–21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Hagar and Ishmael, oi· the fortunes of the outcasts. I. TnE LONELY WANDERERS. 1. Banishedfrom liome. Hitherto the household of Abraham had been to Hagar and her boy such o pleasant and doubtless much-prized abode ; henceforth their connection with the patriarch's encompment was to be completely severed. So God in his mysterious providence and in many different ways frequently bereaves men of the shelter and society of home. 2. Separated from the Church. Practically the expulsion of this Egyptian slave-mother and her son from the household of Abraham, if it did not involve a casting off from God's mercy, amounted to extrusion from the patriarchal Church. 3. Lost in the wilderness. Whether because the region through which they travelled was unfamiliar, or because, impelle.l by indignation and excitement, they simply drifted on with aimless feet, the narrative depicts the unhappy pair as having "wandered," turned neido into unfrequented paths, and become lost; in that touchingly portraying the sad condition of thousnnds of homeless and churchless wonderere to-day, roaming purpose)eijs and pe.rplexed across the trackless waste of life. II. THE FAINTING YOUTH. 1. Perishing thro11gh thirst. Extreme thirst one of the most excruciating torments to which the physical frame con be subjected, and a fellow-creature dying for lock of water, one of tho commonest of God's mercies, a! snd o. spectacle as any on which the eye of man can gaze. 2. Sobbing in angitish. Too exhausted to weep aloud, the poor disheartened Ind moons out his misery. Happy they who, if they cannot relieve, can at least understand and bo affected by their necessities. To recognise :md make complaint of one's spiritual destitution is better tlrnn to be callou~ and indifferent to one's dying condition. 3. Prayinr, to God. Though not certnm thot the " voice " of the lad meant more than the rude cry of his distress, charity mny hope that in the day of his calamity h directe,l his 11rnyer to God. Prayer gcr.crnlly precedes delivernnce. 1' 2 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [nn. xxi. 15-21. III. THE WEEl'ING MOTHER. 1. The i•oict of luatlien superstition. "Let me not see the death of the lnd." To a Christi,111 11iother Hagar s behaviour is simply inexplicable. It is doubtful if Sarah would J.arn been a bow-shot removed from Isaac h1td he been expiril1g. But then Hagar, though she had been Abraham's wife, wus still II poor untutored slave-girl. It may assist us to understand our indebtedness to the humanising in~uences of Christ's religion. 2. The ci-y of maternal affection. "She sat ov~r agarnst_ her boy, a!ld lifted up her voice and wept." Even in the breast of this Egyptian bondmaid nature asserted her supremacy. Everywhere beautiful and sacred is a mother's lo\·e, worthy of being cherished and reciprocaterl hy tho8e who know its sweetness and strength, never failing to bring down retribution on those by whom it is rejected and despised. lY. THE COJ\lFORTING Gon. 1. Sympatht'sin,g witli tlte sorrowful. "What aileth 1hee, Hagar?'' "'hat a glimpse into the infinite pitifulness of the Divine nature I Only when Christ came was it surpassed in clearness and fulness. 2. Lutening to the suppliant. As the prayer of Ishmael came up into the wakeful ear of God, so tl,c cries of dJing- men and perishing souls never foil to do. 3. Consoling the d~jected. As to Hagar the angel spoke words of encouragement, and renewed the formerly-gi,en assurance concerning the future greatness of her son, so God revives tl,e drooping spirits of his people by directing them to his exceeding great and precious promises. 4. Providing for tlie destitute. " God opened her eyes, and sl,e ,-aw a well of water." .And so by the !endings of his providence, the teachings of l,is word, and the illumination of his Spirit does God guide the meek to the wells of sa),ation. 5. Abi,ding with the homeless. "God was with the lad." Ejected fro111 Abraham's house, he was not deserted by Abraham's God. Happy they who amid life's wanderings can count on God's companionship. For desertions of friends and deprivations of goods it will prove ample compensation. Learn-1. To prize the blessing of a home and the privilege of a Church. 2. To c0mmiserate and succour those who ha,e neither. 3. To use God in all the revealed a~pects of bis gracious character. HOMILIES BY VAllIOUS AUTHORS.

entries.title: GEN 21:17
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Hagar, a weary outcast. "What aileth thee, Hagar?" Hagar is sent away from .Abraham's tents. In the wilderness wandering she is lost. In despair sl1e sinks down and weeps. An angel's voice is heard inquiring, "What nileth thee, Hagar?" I. HAGAR MAY BE TAKEN AS REPRESENTING THE SOULS STILL CHRISTLESB. They are- ]. Weary. 2. Thirsty. 3. Apparently man-forsaken and God-forsaken. 4. Their dearest comforts slipping from them, as Hagar's child, by death. 5. Death expecting. JL HAGAR1 B ACT INDICATES HOW SUCH SOULS SHOULD ACT IN TROUBLII. 1. Realise it. 2. Seek deliverance from above. God nenrer to us than we imagine. He feels for us, hears us, helps Ill!, He gives sustenance, cheer, guidance.-H.

entries.title: GEN 21:17–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Gocl's appearance t<> Hagar. The greatest truths in the Bible put hefore us in a setting of human interest and feeling. Our hearts strangely touchod by the picture of the rlesolate woman and the helpless child. The fatherly character of God exhibited. He heard the voice of the lad. All such facts point to the greatest fact, the union of God and man in the man Christ Jesus. We see here- I. Goo's NOTICE OF AND COMPASSION FOR HUMAN BUFFERING: our example. The object of pity apart from antecedents. II. THE WORKING OUT OF DIVINE PURPOSES notwithstanding, nnd to some extent by means uf, human infirmities, errors, and sins. Ishmael must be preserved, and hue his po.rt tu play in the future. III. Taken TYPICALLY, Hagar and Ishmael represent the life of man npart from the covenant of God, outside the circle of special privilege. There is God in the wilderness. The eyes which are darkened with ignorance and self-will may yet be mercifully opened to see the well of water. The Rngel of deliverance follows e,·en thP. hondwomRn and her son. entries.title: GEN 21:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Hagar in the wilderness. "And God opened her eyes, and she eaw a well of water." Hagar in the wilderness. Why? She had no pleasure in her home; would not accept her position there. Hence lehmael's mocking. Compare working of pride in Eden-" Ye sha!l be as gods;" and its result-Adam and Eve driven out. Observe-a soul despising the position of a child of God is driven into the wilderness by its own act. Pride rebels against terms of salvation (Rom. x. 3)- o. free gift to sinners seeking it as such (Mark ii. 17). Hagar felt her misery, liko many who find no peace. "All is Yanity." She eat down and wept. Did she cry to God? He had met her there before. Past mercies should move to trust (Ps. xiii. 6). But pride and unbelief hinder prayer (Exod. xvii. 3-6). But God had not forgotten her (cf. Matt. xviii. 11). "What aileth thee?" Compare our Lord's dealing with those he helped. 1. Himself taking the first step. 2. Requiring a confession of their want. 3. Rousing expectation (John iv. 14 ; vii. 37). I. TnE WELL WAS NEAR HER, BUT SHE SAW IT NOT. So is it with the water of life. Why are so many without peace? The well is beside them; the sound of the gospel is famili:u to them. The Bible is read in their hearing, but it speaks nothing to them (2 Cor. iii. 15). Christ died for all (2 Cor. v. 14). His blood the ransom for all (1 John i. 7). We have not to go to seek a Saviour (Rom. x. 6-8). No sin too deep for cleansing, no sorrow too great for comfort; nothing required to give a right to trust him (Isa. Iv. 1 ; Luke xv. 2). ,vby without peace? The eyes are closed to the truth (1 Cor. ii. 14). Human teaching cannot give life (Ezek. :x:xxvii. 8). What is wanted is not a new fountain, but opened eyes. And it is disbelief of thi~ that keeps so many in anxiety. To them the well is not there; they want God to give it. They look for something they nre to do to find 11 Saviour. Importnnt to know what is wanted-spiritual discernment. 'fo many this seems a mere fancy ; but they whose eyes nre opened know it to be a pnssing from darknesa to light (cf. 2 Tim. i. 10). Words often read become full of new meaning. II. Goo OPENED HER EYES. It is blindness that causes trouble; but as blind cannot see by bis own will, so neither can the nnspiritual. The wny of salvation id before him, but while it commends itself to his reaRon it brings him no joy. Are we then without effort to sit still? No; all is ready on God's part. "Wilt thou be made whole?" Want of will alone hinders. Often men would like to drink, but not at God's foWltain. Make an effort to believe, and power will be given. Ill. WHAT SHE SAW. The well of life ; the revelation of Jesus Christ to the soul -this is peace. Not our own powers or wisdom, not onr own holiness or advnnce in gruce; but trust in him. No more fears. True, the wilderness is there; the work l111s to be done, temptations overcome, sorrows borne, graces cultivated; but we eaµ do all through Christ. Now troubles become helps (Ps. lxxxiv. 6), for they make us flee to Christ (2 Cor. xii. 9). And who can count the blessings revealed to biru whose eyes are opened? A Father in everything-protection, teaching, guidance. Everytliing surrounding him, every event that happens to him, are inlets of everincreasing knowledge of God, whom to know is life eternnl.-M.

entries.title: GEN 21:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God:s care for Ishmael. "And God was with the lad." The enc11mpment of Abraham was the scene of joy and festivity on the occasion of the recognition of Isaac publicly as his heir. It is snid in Jewish lore that Abraham called a number of the patriarchs to the feast, and th11t Melchizcdek, Nabor, and even Nonh were present. Ishmael had been heir-presumptfre up to th11t time. He wns then put in the position of a subject to the son of Sarah. He nnd his mo.her despised the weakling and nursling. They "mocked.'' 'fhis roused the indignation of Sarnh, und she insisted on the banishment of both. Abruhnm was very unwilling to consent to the proposal, for he had gre11t affection for Ishmael. No wonder that be loved him, for he w11s, if not the child of promise, ut leost the son who first roused in his breast the pride and joy of paternity. He seems to have hoped that Ishmuel would be the one through whom th~ greut bleseinge promised to him would he hcstoweJ. 1.'1-IE BOO}{ OF GENESIS. [err. XXI. 15-2]. Hence lie had_ prayed, "0 that Ish!11ael might li':o before thee 11 (eh. :xvii. 18). P~rhnps unbelief had n_iuch to do with the expression of the hope. He indicated his own contentment with that mode of fulfilment of the promises• God however has another. Abraham ev\dently _lo:cd the lad, and now that he is gro,~n to be ~ stalwart youth of about suteen, 1t 1s strongly against his inclination to send him away. Snrnh ins\sts. She in her indignati•m will not even speak of him by his nam"', but caJis lmn ~ontemptuously "the son of this bondwoman" (eh. x.xi. 10). Abrnh?m ~·as very grieved (ver. 11), but lie can see thnt there is no prospect of nny peace m his encam~ment !lnl~ss he shou~d do_as Sarnh wishes. Two jealous women sre enough to embitter !us hfe, and brmg discord eventuaJly amon"' his retainers. For typical reasons the banishment was permitted by God (ver. 12) and Abraham sends both away, lnden probably not only with trinkets, which shall suffice for barter hut with a flask of water and strings of small loaves. Abraham had thus to sacrific~ his o"·n inclinations in Ishmael, his son after the flesh, as afterwards his will in offering up Isaac, his chi!~ of promise. Away towards Egypt Hagar and Ishmael travel. They enter the wilderness of Beersheba. Happiness and home is behind • desolateness, dreariness, lonely journeyings, imminent dangers from the wild beast; and fierce hordes of men, with Egypt, before them. . Hagar; with bread dry and water spent, losing her way, waits for some one to guide. Unable to proceed she and her son sink down to die, to perish in the scorching heat from that most fe~rful of all deprivations, water. Hagar, with bitter memories of lost happiness and unjust treatment crowding, cannot bear the sight of her son's woe and sound of his moaning, therefore removes to a slight distance, that she might not see bis death nor <listurb it as she sought to ease her poor heart with tears. Oh, what morn! beauty blossoms in the desert in the maternal love of this outcast bondwoman. No human <'ye detects it, but God notices and bears her voice, and that of the child. Then comes the direction from heaven, and the promise, " I will make of him a great nation." We are told immediately afterwards in the brief record concerning Ishmael that" God was with the lad," nnd so the promise was fulfilled. We notice God's care evenfor an Ishmael, for one who would appear to be outside all covenant blessings. He was one whose "hand was to be against every man, and every man's against him" (eh. xvi. 12). God manifested care, however, to this Ishmael- 1 BY PRESERVING HIS LIFE. He heard his cry in distress. He knew his needs. God always knows our needs; whence to supply them, and where to find us even in the wilderness. A well of water is unexpectedly pointed out to the mother. Her eyes were opened to see its whereabouts. So God teaches many a mother, that she may lead her children to the well of living water. Every life preserved is only through the mercy of God. "In his hand our breath is" (Dan. v. 23). There is a well for bondsmen as well as free. God's living well is to be reached in any position of life. It is near to as when we think it far off. "The word is nigh thee, in thine ]1eart," &c. (Rom. :x. 8). If we are to see the treasure, .o.ur spiritual un_derstanding must be quickened, our "eyes opened" by the Holy S1;>mt. If we desire to kno-:v the way and well of life, we can pray for that openmg. Only as we have tins spiritunl sight and life can we rejoice in the present existence, in our preservation. God preserved Ishmael that he might know him. II. Gc,D ADVANCED HIM IN Lll'E. He was with him as he grew up, nnd gave him favour in the sight of others. God is ever seeking by hi_s Holy Spirit to n~ould tho character of tl,e worst for good. If we ha"\-·e any prospenty and grow up to mfluence, we should remember that it is from God. The darkest hour for Ishmael ho.d ushered in the clawr1ing of the brightent day. God knew what he would do with Ishmael. I~hmael is to founcl a nation. It is remarkable that he was the ancestor of the same number of tribes as ,vas Israel (eh. :x:xv. 16). He found various scattered people in the Arabian desert, but the tribes descended from him seem to hnve absorbed all otl1ers. What an honour to be the founder of a house, n dynasty; how much more of a nation ! This God granted to an Ishmael. III. Goo GAVE HIM SKILL. "He became nn archer." He had to learn to clefend himBelf, and secure for himself, by God's help, a position. The fighting power is not the highest, but man has always had to protect himself before he could make progress in civilisation. Alas, when he supposes himself to be civilised he often clings to tho old habit, and still loves the fighting. The archers, like IHhmael, h;i.vc tLcir sphere as well as the shepherds, like Isaacs. The fiery defenders of faith and the controversial champions of the truth have their sphere as well ae the pious, plodding pastors of Christ's flock. If men have skill for the one thing, let them not despise the powers of others. We have nil to learn to appreciate diversity of talents, and to remember that skill in any work is the outcome of independence, resolution, and energy. Ishmael hnd been endowed with these by God. IV. GoD FURNISHED ISHMAEL WITH A PLACE OF HABITATION. He gave to him the desert for hie domain. Here he might roam and pitch his tent at his own suggestion. God knew that the hot blood of his Egyptian mother, which coursed in nis veins, would find its most fitting sphere in the desert. Instead of mingling with gentle herdsmen, he bnd to dwell among the fierce and untrained spirits of the desert. He became an ancestor of those who despised town life, o.nd who were hardy and frugal enough to exist where others would have perished. Thus to Ishmael, the desert, with its widespread, sun-scorched sands, its scant herbage, ite infrequent wells and scattered oases, became a fitting home. God chose for him his dwelling-place, and defined for him the bounds of his habitation. And is it not best for us to leaYe ourselves in God's hands? He knows best where to place any of us, and what work to give us to do, what sphere to fill. We might prefer the green pasture anrl hills flowing with milk and honey of the Cano.an of prosperity, but the desert of trial o.nd loneliness may be the best for training our spirits. We may have losses to endure outwardly, but if we can acquire a spirit of content and faith, that is great gain. That spirit will lead us to so.y, " He shall choose our inheritnnc·e for us." V. GOD ALSO INSURED ISBMAEL'S HONOUR AMONG BIS DRETBREN. He was to" dwell in the presence of hie brethren" (eh. xvi. 12). Though cast out by Abral1am, he was not ea.at off by God or cut off from all interchange with others. We find (eh. xxv. 6) that Abraham gave portions to the sons of his second wife, Keturah, am\ sent them awny. Doubtless he gave a portion to Ishmael, for we find him uniting with Isaac in the funeral obsequies of bis father (eh. :x:xv. 9). The two sons were not nt enmity now. Further, he seems to have kept up his union with his brother, for bis daughter Bo.sbemath (eh. x:x:xvi. 3) married Esau, Isaac's son. Thus two families in the line of promise, but who hnd cast themselves out-Esau hy his indifference, and Ishmael by his mocking-were united. Thus, although of fierce aml fiery nature, Ishmael "dwelt in the presence of his brethren." God was with him. He had a shorter life than Iso.o.c. Ishmael died o.t 130 years old, Isaac at 180. Evidently the nctive, restless, wandering, hazardous life was more wearing and consuming than the calm and meditative life of the pastoral Isaac. But when he died God cared for him as well o.s for Isaac, only his purposes with respect to Isaac were different. Isaac was an ancestor after the flesh of the Messinh, but Ishmael had not thnt honour. Still we must not think that God hnd cast off Ishmael, nnd left him utterly o.nd everlastingly to perish. Our God cares for those outside the pnle of the Church, even as for those within. The former hnve not tuken up their privilege~, nor seen bow Christ loves them. They are suffering great loss, and are in clanger of further loss, but God cares for and pities them. He wills not the death of a sinner. He pitied the people of Nineveh, sent them o. warning, and gave them space for repentance. He healed o. Naamo.n; sent his prophet to dwell with a woman of Sarepta, nnd so conferred honour upon her; and he brought II Nebuchadnezzar to hi~ right mind by o. judicious infliction. All this was mercy shown outside the pale of Iernel to those who would be nccounted as Ishmo.elites. Oh, how much more widely flow.a the channel of Divine mercy and love than we imagino I How little we conceive the depth of the Father's love to all his creatures I In every heart he is seeking to find o. reflection cif his image. By the side of every soul, however much of nn lahmaelite, he is seeking by his Holy Spirit to walk, that he mny win back to the fold of Jove nnd mercy. Oh, ye who think yourselves too sinful to have a shnre in the Divine compassion, see God's treatment of nn Ishmael. Remember thnt Christ came "not to call the righteous, b11t sinners to repentance." God is merciful even to thoughtless sinners, aml gives streams in the desert. If this be the spirit of our God and Saviour, should it not teach t•s to take nn interest in nil? As the sun when setting in the west throws 1ia goMen nn i purple rays not only over the broad ocenn, THE F.OOK OF GENEi:;ts. trR. XXI. 22-84. but on the dank ditches of the meadows and the puddles of the street, so should wo remcmb('r that there is no heart so depraved but tl1e love of God ir. Christ may light it up. If only we looked at our fellows thus, with deeper sympathy, we should see them ~n to Christ.-H.
