entries.title: GEN 21:22–34
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - Abimelecli and Abraham, or ancient covenante,·s. I. THE P0I.ITICAL ALLIANCE, I. Tlte co-ntemplated object. Pence. Wh1Lt modern monarch~ mo~tly desire nt the close of exhausting campaigns is here sought before campaign~ begin. 2. Tlte covenanting parties. Two powerful princes, in their conduct exemplifying the spirit o.f unity 1Lnd pence which should bind together private persons in their dnily intercourse, as well as kings and 111Ltions in their political alliance. 3. The impelling motives. Worldly policy may hnve urged Abime\ech to cement n league with the powerful chieftain in his neighbourhood, but religious affinity would also seem to have exercised an influence in drawing him to seek the friendship of one who o.ppoared to enjoy celestial protection. Good men mostly desire to have the ~11ints ns friends, and even the wicked can perceive an odvanto.ge in being allied to the righteous. Abraham's acquiescence in the king's proposal was no doubt dictated oy o. peaceable disposition, 11 sense of equity, o. spirit o.f contentment, o.nd o.n unwavering confidence in God. 4. The public ceremonial. The alliance was contracted (1) by menns of amicable conference, and (2) with the so.nctions of religion. II. THE FRIENDLY REMONSTRANCE, I. The palpable inj1trJ.I, The herdsmen of the king had o.ppropriated Abraham's well. God's people, though expected meekly to suffer wrong, cannot always help seeing that it is wrong they suffer. Nor ard they called upon to bear what by lnw-ful means they nre nble to redress. A goo! mo.n is entitled to ha careful of his property, to preserve it from damo.ge, protect it from theft, and recover it when stolen or lost. 2. The mistaken charqe. Abraham, thinking the herdsmen had acted on their master's orders, reproved Ah1melech. This, however, was ILn error, which shows (1) that 11 person cannot always be held responsible for wlllLt his servants do, (2) that it is wrong to judge on insufficient evidence with reference to the cho.rnclers and conduct of otl:ers, and (3) that in making charges or preferring complaints it is well to avoiJ both heat of temper and severity of language. 3. 'l'he satisfactor,11 explanation. Abimelech declared himself perfectly unacquainted with tfie wrong which had been done to Abraham, 11nd immed'ately returned the well, which discovers how easily mi•und(.'rstnnding8 mi11;ht be 282 fllE BOOR OF GENESIS. [cu. x:m. 1-19. removed if, instead of harbouring enmity, men would resort to friendly conferenco. It is as much the duty of him who has a grievance to reveal it, as it is the duty of him who has caused tl,e grievance to remove it. 4. The prudent meas,.ere. Abraham gnve Abimelech. seven ~we lambs.as a witne~s that he h~d digged the well, and conscqucn1 tly had _a right to its_possession. Se~rmngly betraying a secret suspicion of the prmce s veracity, the act aimed at preventmg any recurrence of the grievance nnd in this light it appears to have been regarded by Abimelech. Good men should not only rectify the wrongs they do to one another, but adopt all wiso precautions against their repetition. IIT. THE PLEASING RESULT. 1. Peace e,stablished, Abimelech and Phichol having accomplished their mission, returned to Philistia. "Blessed are the peace-~akers" and "beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that publishcth peace." 2. Peace com111,emorated. .Abraham instituted two memorials of the important transactions, nnming the well Beersheba, and planting a tamarisk beside his tent. It is good to remember God's mercies, of which national and civil quietude is one of the grentest, and it is becoming to erect memorials of both privileges and obligations. 3. Peace enjoyed. .Abraham called on the name of the everlasting God. .As a planter of tamarisks, the patriarch has been styled the father of civilisation; it is more important to remark that he never neglected to worship God himself and publish his salvation to others. Happy they who can do both in peace I

entries.content: -A covenant between the patriarch and the Philistine king. .Abraham a sojourner in that land, afterwards the troubler of Israel ; for his sake ns discipline, for their sakes as opportunity. 1. entries.title: GEN 22:15–18

entries.content: -And the angel of the Lord onlled unto Abraham out of heaven the second ti.me,-the object of the first call ha·dng been to arrest the consummation of the fatal deed which threatened Isaac's life, and to declare the Divine satisfaction with the patriarch's complete spiritual surrender of his son, the purpose of the second was to renew the promise in roward for his fidelity and obedience-and said, By myself have I sworn, - by my word (Onkelos) ; by my name (Arabic) ; equivalent to by himself, by his soul (Jer. lL 14), or by his holiness (.Amos iv. 2)-an anthropomorphism by which God in the most solemn manner pledges the perfection of his Divine personality for the fulfilment of his promise ; an act which he never again repeats in his intercourse with the pRtriarchs. The oath here given to Abraham (frequently referred to in later 1-cripture: eh. xxiv. 7; xxvi. 3; I. 24 ; Exod. xiii. 5, 11 ; xxxii. 13 ; xxxiii. 1 ; Isa. xlv. 23; Heh. vi. 13) is confirmed by the addition of-saith the Lord,-literally, the utterance qf Je!UJvah ,· like the Latin ait, i,uzuit Doinin11,s, the usunl prophetic phrase accom• panying Divine oracles (cf. Isa. iii. 15 ; ~zck. v. 11 ; .Amos vi. 8), though occurrin~ II) the Pentateuch ouly here and in Num. xiv. 28-for because thou bast done thia thing, and haat not withheld thy son, thine only son (vi,d,e supra, ver. 12; from y;hicl, the LXX., Syriac, and Samal'itan insert here the _words "from me"): tbat in blessing I WJ!l bless thee, and, multiplying, I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven, and as the sand which is npon the sea shore; -:-)iterally, upon the_ lip of the sea; a repeti_tion and accumulation of the promises prcv10usly made to the patriarch concerning his seed (cf. eh. xii. 2, 3; xiii. 14-16 ; xv. 5 ; xvii. 1-8), with the special amplification following-and thy seed shall poBSess (i. e. occupy by force) the gate of his enemies;- shall conquer their armies and capture their cities (Keil, :Murphy); though that the spiritual sense of ent.e1in" in through the doorway of their susceptibilities in com·crsion (Lange)isnot to beoverlookedmaybe inferred from the appended prediction-and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (vide eh. xii. 3, where "families of the ground" occur as the cr;uirnlent of "nations of the earth") ; because thon hast obeyed my voice. Origiually unconditional in its grant, the promise is here distinctly declared to be reuewed to him as one who, besides being jnstifieJ and taken into covcnnnt with Jehovoh, had through trial and obedience attained to the spiritual patriarchate of a numerous posterity.

entries.title: GEN 22:1–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: --Mount Mo1'iah, 01' tlie mount of sac,ri.jice. I. AnRADA11's TRIAL, 1. Divine in its origin. However explained, the appalling ordeal through which the patriarch at this time passed was expressly created for him by Elohim. Only he who made the human heart can adequately search it ; and he alone who has nperfect understnnding of the standard of moral excellence can pronounce upon the intrinsic worth of his creatures. 2. Unexpected in its coming. After oil that hnd preceded, it might have been anticipated thot not only were the patdarch'R trials over, but thnt the need for such discipline in his case no longer existed. It shows that neither length of yenrs nor ripeness of grace, neither conscious enjoyment of Divine favour nor previous experience of suffering, can exempt from trial or pince beyond the need of testing; and that mostly " temptations" come nt unexpected times, and in unlooked-for wnys, 3. Sevei·e in itsform. Trials to be efficient must be gradunted to the strength of those they design to test. Only 11 temptation of great force conlcl. be of service in the case of morn! hel'oism like Abraham's. The intensity of the strain put upon his soul by the astounding order to make n holocaust of Isaac simply baffles description. l<~ven on the supposition that Abraham wos not unfamiliar with the practice of offering human victims, as it prevailed among the C1111aanites and enrly Chaldreans, painful doubt must have insinuated itself into hi~ mind (1) I\B to the chnrncter of Jehovah, who in making such 11, barbuo1rn awl i11h11ma11 demand might se,;m little snpe1;or to the heathen dcitio8 nwnncl ; (2) as to 286 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. xxIJ. 1-19. his own enjoyment of the Divine favour, which could scar,Jely fail to be staggered by s~1?h an excruciating sta~ to his natural affection; but, (3) and chiefly, 1\9 to the stab1h_ty of the promise, winch reason could not but pronounce impossible of fulfilment 1f I~aa~ must_be put to death. Yet, overwhelming as the trial we.a, it was-4. Need:(111 in i# deS'lr,_n. The great covenant blessing was still conditioned on the t'xercrne by the patnarch of full-hearted trust in the naked word of God. Not until that standpoint had been reached by Abraham in his spiritual development was he able to become the parent of Isaac ; nnd now that Isaac was born there was still the danger lest Isaac, and not the naked word of God, should be the ground of the patrinrch's confidence. Hence the necessity arose for testing whether Abraham could resign lsnac and yet cling to the promise. II. AnRAHAM's VICTORY. 1. The splendour of it. The tremendous act of selfimmolation was performed not without pain, else Abraham must have been either more or less than hums.n, but (1) with unhesitating promptitude-" Abraham rose up e3:rly ~n the morning," and" went l1?to the pla~e of which God had told him;" (2) with literal exactness-" Abraham laid the wood m order, and bound Isaac his son and laid him upon the altar on the wood;" (3) in perfect sincerity-" Abraham strekhed forth his hand to slay his son;" yet (4) without ostentation-Abraham went alone with his son to the mount of sacrifice. 2. The secret of it. This was faith. He accounted that, tl10ngh Isaac should be slain, God was able to raise him up again from the dead. Hence, though prepared to plunge the knif-e into his son's breast and to reduce his beloved form to ashes, he "staggered not at the promise." ' III. ABRAH.!M's REWARD. 1. The deliverance ofIsaac. (1) The time of it. At the moment when the sacrifice was nbout to be consummated, neither too soon for evincing the completeness of Abraham's obedience, nor too late for effecting Isaac's preservation. (2) The reason of it. Because the piety and faith of the patriarch were sufficiently demonstrated. God often accepts the will for the deed. (3) The manner of it. By the substitution of a ram, a type of the Lord Jesus Christ, through whose atoning death the Isaac of the Church is delivered from condemnation, (4) The teaching of it. If Abraham's surrender of Isaac was a shadow of the sacrificing love of the eternal Father in sparing not his only Son, nnd the bound Isaac typical of the Church's condemned condition before the sacrifice of Christ on Calvary, e.nd the substituted ram was emblematic of him who, though he knew no sin, was mnde n sin offering for us, the deliverance of Isaac was symbolic both of the resurrection life of Christ and of the new life of his redeemed people. 2. The confirmation of t!ie Uessing. (1) A renewal of the promises-of a numerically great, territorially pro3perous1 and spiritually influential posterity, and more particularly of that distinguished seed in whom all the families of the earth should be blessed; (2) a specification of the ground on which they were held, viz., the patriarch's believing obedienco to the Divine commandment; and (3) a solemn oath in guarantee of their fulfilment. Lessons :-1. The certainty of trial. 2. The omnipotence of faith. 3. 'l'ho blessedness of obedience.

entries.title: GEN 22:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Abraltam'a perfect fauh. "Now I know that thou fearest God, eecing 1hou Jiast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me." "The word of God," says Coleridge, "speaks to man, and therefore it speaks the language of the children ?f men. Tliis has to be kept in mind in studying the remarkable incident recorded ID this chapter. When God is represented tlB "tempting" Abraham, it only mel\ns that he tried or tested him. I. THE TESTING OF FAITH. Abraham was to be the head of the faithful nnd t.ype of tlio justified, therefore it was essential lie sho~ld ~e tested. Entire ?bedience i~ the test of perfect faith.. Abraham had shown Ins faith when ~e _left h_1a own lond, and when he waited patiently for a eon ;_ now he has to show it m a d1fferen~ way. In the two former testings he had a promise to rest on; now he mm:1t go far without any p1 omise to buoy him np in the perplexing eea of trial. "Take now thy s~n," &c. Surely there is some mistal,e I Mu~t Abral1am offer n humnn ancrifico? Tl11s event CB, XXII. 1-19.) 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. 287 ----- ------ ha.q perplexed many, and they have only escaped from the difficulties preserilc<l by regarding the event--(1) As exceptional for the purpose of securing a unique type of the future sacrifice of Christ. (2) As never intended to be actually carried out, God having foreseen the faith of his servant, and having determined at the right moment to interfere and prevent any disaster. There is also a miraculous element in the narrative, both in the special voice and the ram caught in the thicket. Some have thought that the impulse was from Abraham's own mind-that, seeing human sacrifices around, he wished to rise above all others in devotion to the one God. Had this been the case, the Scriptures would not have represented the testing as from God. Ir. that age a father's right to do as he would with his son was as unquestioned as his right to do what he would with his slave. The command of God was not out of harmony with this idea, but it helped to correct the mistake. A single act of such selfsacrifice becomes of the highest value; it is even a means of education to the world. God elicited the highest exerciee of faith, but not the blood of Isaac. What it must have cost the patriarch to submit to the Divine command I ,vith one blow he must slay his boy and his own ardent hopes. The only gleam of light was in the thought that God ,vho first gave Isaac could also restore him from death. This is indicated in the words 110 uttered to the young man, " We will come again to you." Tradition says that the mount was the same on which Adam, Abel, and Noah had offered sacrifice. Here possibly Abraham found an altar to repair or rebuild. Isaac helps in rebuilding the altar and in arranging the wood. Silent prayers ascend from father und son. Isaac wonders where the lamb is to come from. lie finds out when his father has bound him and laid him on the altar. The knife gleams aloft, and, but for the arresting voice, would have been plunged in Isaac. The test was satisfactory. II. Gon's MANIFEST APPROVAL OF THE PATRIARCH'S FAITH AND PERFECT OBEDIENCE. 1. It was by a voice from heaven. 2. It was manifested also by the way in which God took away any pain consequent on obedience to his command. It is remarkable how those who appear to have little faith can become, when trial falls, perfectly submissive to the Divine will. 3. The approval was seen also in the way in which God provided a sacrifice. 4. And God repeated hie promise of blessing, confirming it by a solemn covenant. "By myself have I sworn," &c. No such voice comes to us, and no such promise is audibly given; still we can have, in the inner calm of fue soul, an evidence of the Divine approval. When our faith is strongest, after passing through some trial, we get a clearer view of the glory of God's working, both in our lives and in the world. What approval have we ,von? Does not Abraham put us to shame? Too many will laud the obedience of Abraham who will never try to emulate it. Abraham was glad to have his Isaac spared ; so would the Father have been, but he gave up his "only-begotten, well-beloved Son" for us. Our readiness to accept and follow the Saviour given is only another way of showing how wo bear the testing of faith. " Thy will be done" should be the ntternnco of each believer. Perfect faith in the heo.rt should be exhibited by perfect obedience in lifo.-H.

entries.title: GEN 22:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie Lamb of God. 11 And Abraham called the name of that placo Jehovah-jireh." The key to this narrative is John i. 29. It sets forth in type the way of salvation. Whether Abraham understood this we need not inquire. The losson is for us. Isaac, i. e. laughter (cf. Luke ii. 10), the child of promise (Rom. ix. 7), type of "the children of the kingdom," is yet condemned to die (cf. Rom. v. 12). So in Egypt the Israelites were not exempted; God's gift to them was a way of escape. What is that way? (cf. Micah vi. 6). Every oge of the world has asked this question. A sense of separation from God has led to many efforts for its removol. Hence sacrifices, offerings, austerities, &c., but all in vain (lleb. x. 4). Still the soul asked," Where is the Lamb?" the effectual sacrifice for sin. 'l'ho answer of prophecy, i. e. God's answer, "God will provide himself a lamb" (rf. John i. 29; viii. 56). Man has no claim upon God, yet hie need is a plea (cf. Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7). We know not what was in Abraham's mind; perhaps ho was escaping from the direct answer, unable to utter it; perhaps there was II hope that God ·would in some way preserve or restore his son (cf. Heh. xi. 19). There nro many instances of prophrcy unconscionsly uttcrrd (cf. John xi. 50), ls:iac was buur:d- THE BOOK OF GE~ESIS. [en. XXII. 1--HI. type of man's helplessness to escape from the curse (cf. Luke iv.18), orfrom the law of sin in the members. The law of God of itself can only condemn. It can only be fulfilled by one "·ho loves God ; but he who is not at peace with God cannot love l,im. The sncrifice was now complete as far as Abraham could offer it. He had cas_t ~own self-will (cf._ Matt. xxvi. 39) ; he had sacrificed himself (Rom. xii. 1). Tln~ 1s ~he state of mmd of a)l others most prepared to receive blessings (rf. 2 Kmgs 1v. 3-6): "Lay not tlnne hand upon.th~ lad." God's purpose our deliverance (Rom. nu. 1). The work of the law, bnngmg home the conviction of sin is the prelude to the knowledge of life (cf. Rom. vii. 10-13)-life throuo-h de;th. God's way of deliverance (Isa. liii. 6). The type, the ram caught in the thicket. the antitype, Christ fulfilling the Father's will (Mntt. xxvi. 54; Mark xv. 31). Tl.Je practical application of this shown in brazen serpent (John iii. 14). Marvellous love of God (Rom. v. 8). We had no claim on him, yet he would _not that we should p~rish (Ezek. xxxiii. 11). He wanted, for the fulness of his blessedness that we ,1,ould partake of it, and therefore Christ came that he might die in our st~ad • and now in him we are dead (2 Cor. v. 4). Do not dilute the truth by saying he died for belie"ers only. This is to miss the constraining power of his love. If there is a11y doubt of his death being for each and all, the gospel is no longerfelt to be "whosoever will" (Rev. xxii. 17). Behold the Lamb. We need not now to say, 11 God will pro"\'ide; " he has provided (1 John ii. 2). The universe could not purchase that propitiation. No efforts could make thee worthy of it, yet it is freely offered to thee today. And mark what that gift includes (Rom. viii. 32)-the help of the Holy Spirit (Luke xi. 13), wisdom (James i. 5), help in trials (1 Cor. x. 13), peace (Rom. viii. 33), needs of this life (Luke xii. 30). Bring all thy sins, thy wants, thy hindrance11 to the mercy-seat (Heb. iv. 16). The Lord will see, will look upon thy need; and ere thy prayer is offered be has provided what that need requires.-M. Yers. 15-19.-The great trial and the great revelation. In such a history the representative character of Abraham must be remembered. He was tried not only !c- his own sake, but that in him all the families of the earth might be blessed. I. The PREPARATION for this great grace. God end Abraham recognising each nther ; the servant called by name, responding with the profession of readiness for ubedience. II. The COMMANDMENT is itself a secret communication, a covenant. Do this, and I wi11 bless thee; follow me in this journey "as I tell thee," and thou shalt see my salvation. III. The simple, childlike OBEDIENCE of the patriarch is reflected in the quiet demeanour of Isaac bearing the wood of the burnt offering, type of Jesus bearing his ,·roes, inquiring for the lamb with lamb-like innocence and patience. "They went both of them together" (vers. 6 and 8)-" together" in the beginning of the journey, "together" in the end, in the trial and in the blessing. IV. FAITH which accepts the will of God and takes up the DiYine mission WILL f'OllMIT THE FUTURE TO TEE GRACIOUS PROVISION ON WHICH IT DEPENDS. "My son, God will pro"\'ide himself a lamb for a burnt offering" (ver. 8). Already Abraham was saying, "The Lord will provide." We say it sometimes with a fearful burden upon our heart; but when we go steadfastly and hopefully forward we say it at last with the remembrance of a great deliverance sending its glory along the way of our future. V. THE TRlAL OF 'l"HE TRUE HEART IS OFTEN STRETCHED OUT TO ITS LAST EX· 1"REMITY, that the revelation which rewards faithfulness may be the more abundant ~nd wonderful (vers. 9, 10). We must take God at his word, otherwise we shall not experience the promised deliverance. "Take thy son, and offer him there'' (ver. 2). " And Abraham stretched forth hie hand and took the knife to sli1y his son." What else could he do? The commandment must be obeyed. The obedience must be "good and perfect and acceptable" 11s the will of God. VI. AT THE POINT OF ENTIRE SURRENDER ArrEARB THE ANGEL, is heard the voice of relief, the assurance of acceptance, the change in the method of obedience, the topenecl eyes, the provided sacrifice, THE RETURNING JOY 01' 6ALVATION (Yers. 11-13). Tl,erc iH a hlindness of self-sacrifice which leads to n sight of im111<':i~urnble joy, r,1,1. xx:u. 20-2-t] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. ---------------------- - ---------- Abrnlwm saw nothing before him but the plain path of obedience; he went on, l\nd nt last i; lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold" the self-sacrifice changed into peaceful offering of an appointed substitute (ver. 13) " in tlie stead ofliis son." VII. THE CLIMAX OF OUR EXPERIENCE AND 01' DIVINE MERCY BECOMKS TO ns A NEW NAME OF JEHOVAH. \Ve know him henceforth by that knowledge of fact. Jehovah-jireh (the Lord will provide) : as it is said to this day, In the mount of the Lord it shall be provided" (or seen) (ver. 14). 1. Not before the mount, but in the mount; therefore go to the summit and wait. 2. What the Lord will provide will be better ev"y way than what we could provide. 3. The offering on the mount is tlie great provision, the whole burnt offering for the sins of the world, by which the true humanity is redeemed and the true "joy" (" Isaac," laughter) is retained. 4. TLe last name of Jehovah which Abraham gave him was Jehovah the Ev"lastiff?.; now he adds to that name that which brings the Everlasting into the sphere of daily life-"Jehovah-jireh, the Lord will provide." We name that name when we rea,cl,, the mount where the great sacrifice was provided-Mount Moriah, Mount Calvary. 5. The end of the great trial and obedience was a renewal, a solemn republication, of the covenant. "God could swear by no greater; he aware by himself' (Heh. vi. 13). On the foundation of practical faith is built up the kingd-0m of heaven, which thf' Lord swears Bhall include all nations, and be supreme in all the earth. The notes of that kingdom are here in the history of the patriarch-(1) acceptance of the u-ord of God, (2) self-sacrifice, (3) faith instead of sight, (4) withholding nothing, (5) perseverance to the end. Beersheba became now a new place to .Abraham, for ho carried to the well and grove which he had na.med after the oaths of himself and .Abimelech the remembrance of the Divine oath, on which henceforth he rested all his expectations. .Alter this the man in whom a.II nations she.II be blessed looks round and finds the promise being already fulfilled, and his kindred spreading widely in the earth.-ll. entries.title: GEN 23:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Sarah was an hundred and aeven and twenty years old (literally, arvl the livlJIJ of Sarah were an hundred and twenty and seven years); so that Isaac must have been thirty-seven, havillg been born in his mother's ninetieth year. Sarah, as the wife of Abraham and the mother of believers (Isa. Ii. 2 ; 1 Pet. iii. 6), is the only woman whose age is mentioned in Scripture. These were the years of the life of Sarah-an emphatic repetition designed to impress the Israelitish mind with the impo1tance of remembering the age of their ancestress.

entries.title: GEN 23:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Sarah died in Xirjath-arba -or city of Arlia, Abraham having again removed thither after an absenco of nearly forty years, during which interval Murphy thinks the reign of Arba the Anakite may have commenced, though Keil postpones it to a later period (cf. Josh. xiv. 16). The ae.me is Hebron-the original name of the city, which wa.s supplanted by that of Kirjath-arba, but restored at the conquest (Keil, Hengstenberg, Murphy; vide eh. xiii. 18)- in the land of Canaan-indicating that the writer was not then in Palestine (' Speaker's Commentary') ; perhaps rather designed to emphasise the circumstance that Sarah's deathoccurred not in the Philistines' country, but in the promised land (Rosenmiiller, Keil, Murphy). And Abraham oame- or went; i)>,91 (LXX. ), venit (Vulgate); not as if he had been absent nt l:er death (Calvin), either in Beersheba, where ho retained a location (Clarke), or in Gerar, whither he hnd gone to sell the lands and other properties ho held there (Luther), or in the po.sturo grounds adjoining Hebron (Keil, Murphy) ; but aa addressin~ h~mself to tho work of mourn• ing for his deceased wife (Vntablus, Rosen• CII. XXII). 1-20.) THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 291 miillor), or perhaps as going into Sarah's tent (Meimonides, Ainsworth, Wordsworth, 'Speaker's Commentary') - to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her. "To arrange for the customary mourning ceremony " (Keil) ; the first verb, i~i;, (cf. u,paoa~w), referring to the beating of the breast as 11. sign of grief (cf. 1 Kings xiv. 13); and the second, iJ:?f, to flow by drops, intimating aquieter 11.nd more moderate sorrow. Beyond sittingon theground and weepingin presence of (or upon the face of) the dead, no other rites are mentioned as having been observed by Abraham; though afterwards, ns pl'Jlctised among the Hebrews, Egyptians, and other nations of antiquity, mourning for the dead developed into an elaborate ritual, including such ceremonies as rending the garments, shaving the head, wearing sackcloth, covering the head with dust and ashes (vide 2 Sam. iii 31, 35; xxL 10; Job L 20; ii. 12 ; xvi. 15, 16). Cf. the mourning for Patroclus (' II.,• xix. 211-213).

entries.title: GEN 23:4

entries.content: -I am a stranger and a sojourner with you. The burning of corpses was a practice common to the nations of antiquity ; but To.citus notes it ns characteristic of the Jews that they preferred interment to cremation ('Hist.,' v. 5). The wish to make Sarah's burying-place·his ciwn i;iossession has been traced to the inslinchvo desire ~hat most nations have evinced to lie in !1TOtmd belonging to them• selves (Rosenmlilfer), to an intention on the part of the patriarch to give a sign of his right and title to the land of Canaan by purchasing a grave in its soil-cf. Isa. xx:ii. 16 (Bush), or simply to anxiety that his dead might not lie nnburiecl (Calvin) ; but it was more probably due to his strong faith that the land would yet belong to his descendants, which naturally led him to crave a restin"•place in tho, soil with which tho hopes ofboth himself and people were identified (Ainsworth, Bush, Kalisch). That I may bury my dead out of my eight-decay not suffering the lifeless corpse to remain a fit spectacle for grief or love to gaze on. Vern. 5, 6.-And the children of Heth answered Abraham, saying unto him, Hear us, my lord. My lord (Adoni) = sir, monsieur, or mein herr. One acts as the spokesman of all; the number changing from plural to singula.r, The LXX., reading 1:(-1;, instead of iS, after the Samaritan Codex, render µ,j a,i,p,E, Not so, my lord; but hear us. Thou art a mighty prince among us. Literally, a prince ofElohim; not of Jehovah, since the speakers were heathen whose ideas of Deity did not transcend those expressed in the term Elohim. According to a familiar Hebrew idiom, the phrase might be legitimately translated as in tho A. V.-cf. "mount.tins of God," i. e. great mountains, Ps. xxxvi. 6; "cedars of God," 1·. e. goodly cedars, Ps. lxxx. 10 (Calvin, Kimchi, Rosenmiiller, 'Speaker's Commentary'); but, as employed by the Hittite chieftains, it probably expressed that they regarded him as a prince or phylarch, not to whom God hnd given nn elevated nspcct (Lange), but either whom God hnd appointed (Gesenius), or whom Go,l manifestly favoured (Kalisch, Murphy). Thi~ estimate of Abraham strikingly contrasts with that which the patriarch had formed (var. 4) of himself. In the choice of our sepulchres bury thy dead ; none of us will withhold from thee his sepulchre, but that thou mayest bury thy dead. This remarkable offer on the part oftho Hittites '.fhomson (' Land and-Book,' p. 578) regards as having been merely compliment, which Abraham was too experienced nn Oriental not to understand. But, even if dictated by true kindness and generosity, the proposal was one to which for many reasons-faith in God, love for the dead, and respect for himselt being among the strongest-the patriarch could not accede. With perfect courtesy, therefore, though likewise with rcspoctl'ul firmness, ho declines their ofl'er.

entries.title: GEN 23:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - And Ephron anawered Abraham, saying untohim, Mylord, hearken unto me : the land is worth four hundred shekels of silver. The word "shekel," from shakal, to weigh, here used for the first time, was not a stamped coin, but a piece of metal of definite weight, according to Exod. xxx. 13, equal to twenty gerahs, or beans, from garar, to roll. Coined money was unknown to the Hebrews until after the captivity. In the time of the Maccabees (1 Ma~. xv. 6) silver coins wvre struck bearing tlie inscription ',tt-,~' ',p~. Accordin a to Josephns (' Ant.,' iiL 8, 2) the sheke in use in his day was equal to four Athenian drachmai; and if, as is believed, these were one-fifth larger than the old shekels coined by Simon Maccabeus, the weight of the latter would be equal to three and one-third drachma, or two hundred grains, reckoning sixty grains to a drachm. It is impossible to ascertain the weight of the shekel current with the merchant in the time of Abraham; but reckoning it at a little less than 2s. 6d. sterling, the price of Ephron's field must have been somewhat under £50 ; e. very considerable sum of money, which the Hittite merchant begins to depreciate by representing as n trifle, saying, Whe.t is the.t betwixt me and thee 1--words which aro still heard in the EE1St on similar occasions (vide 'Land and Book,' p. 678)-bury therefore thy dead.

entries.title: GEN 23:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the field, and the cave that is !therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a burying-place by the sons of Reth. The palpable diserepancy between the statements of the Hebrew historian in this chapter concerning the patriarchal sepulchre and those of the Christian orator when addressing the Jewish Sanhedrim (Acts vii. 16) has been well characterised as pra;gravu q_'IJ,(Edam et perardua, et quorundam,iud:icw ine:r:tricabili,s '}UQiStio (Pererius). Of course the Gordian knot of difficulty may be very readily cut by boldly asserting that a mistako has been committ.ed somewhere ; either by Stephen, the original speaker, under the impulse of emotion confounding the two entirely different stories of Abraham's purchase of llfachpelah and Jacob's buying of the field near Shechem (Bede, Clarke, Lange, Kalisch, Alford, and others) ; or by Luke, the first recorder of the Martyr's Apology, who wrote not the ipsissim,a verba of the speech, but simply his own recollection ofthem (Jerome); or by some subsequent transcriber who had tampered with the original text, as, e. g., inserting Appaap, which Luke and Stephen both had omitted, ns the JHlminativo to wvq,,aro (Beza, Calvin, Bishop Pearr,e\, 'fhe last of these hypotheses would n~t indeed be fatal to the inspiration of the record ; but the clnims of either Luke or Stephen to be authoritative teachers on the subJect of religion would be somewhat hard to maintain if it once were admitted that they hn~ blun~ered on a. plain point in their ?Wn national htStory. And yet it is doubtful if any of the proposed solutions of the problem is perfectly satisfactory; such as (1) that the two plll·chases of Abraham and Jacob are here intentionally, for the sake of brevity, compressed into one account (Bengel, Pererius, Willet, Hughes); or (2) that Abraham bought two graves, one at Hebron of Ephron the Hittite, as recorded by Moses, and another at Shechem of the sons of Hampr the father ofShechem (Wordsworth); or (3) that the words "which Abraham bought for a sum of money" should be regarded as a parenthesis, and the sentence read as intimating that Jacob and the fathers were carried over into Shechem, and (afterwards) by the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem interred in Abraham's sepulchre at Hebron (Cajetan). Obvious difficulties attach to each of them ; but the facts shino out clear:enough in spite of the encompassing obscurity, viz., that Abraham bought a tomb at Hebron,·in which first the dust of Sarah was deposited, and to which afterwards the bodies of himself, Isaac and Rebek:i.h, Jacob and Leah were consigned, ,vhile Joseph and the twelve patriarchs, who a.II died in Egypt, were brought over to the promised land and buried in Jacob's field at Sbechem.

entries.title: GEN 23:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -T/ie deatli and burial of Sarah. I. TRUE RELIGION SANCTIFIES NATURAL BELATIONSllIPS. Those who know themselves blessed of God do not only feel thnt their human affections are precious and true, but do, in obedience to his will, preserve the greatest respect for their bodily frame, and for their dead who died in the Lord, and whose dust is committed tenderly to his keeping, II. THE PEOPLE OF Goo WERE UPHELD DY FAITll IN THEm CARE FOB TlIE DEAD. They looked beyond the grave. Some say there is no evidence of the doctrine of immortality in the Old Testament until nfter tho captivity. Surely .Abralrnm's feelings were not those of one who sorrowed without ltope. T110 purchase of tlie field, the securing possession for all time of the burying-place, pointed to faith, not the lnck of it. Where there is no sense 0£ immortality there is no reverence for tho dead. III. The PURCHASE OF THE FIEl,D was not only its security, but a testimony to tho heathen thnt the people of God held in reverence both the memory of the dead nnd the rights of the living. All social prosperity hns its root in religious life.-R.

Those who know themselves blessed of God do not only feel thnt their human affections are precious and true, but do, in obedience to his will, preserve the greatest respect for their bodily frame, and for their dead who died in the Lord, and whose dust is committed tenderly to his keeping, II. THE PEOPLE OF Goo WERE UPHELD DY FAITll IN THEm CARE FOB TlIE DEAD. They looked beyond the grave. Some say there is no evidence of the doctrine of immortality in the Old Testament until nfter tho captivity. Surely .Abralrnm's feelings were not those of one who sorrowed without ltope. T110 purchase of tlie field, the securing possession for all time of the burying-place, pointed to faith, not the lnck of it. Where there is no sense 0£ immortality there is no reverence for tho dead. III. The PURCHASE OF THE FIEl,D was not only its security, but a testimony to tho heathen thnt the people of God held in reverence both the memory of the dead nnd the rights of the living. All social prosperity hns its root in religious life.-R.

entries.title: GEN 23:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Lessons from the se-pulchre. "And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a burying-place." Abraham's first 11nd only possession in Cannan, a sepulchre. The importance of the purchase appears in the careful narrative of the transaction. For himself he was content to live as a stranger and pilgrim (cf. 1 Pet. v. 7) ; hut Sarnh's death lod him to acquire a burying-place. Deolining the offer to use any of the sepulchres of the people of the land (cf. the separation at death between God's people nnd aliens), he bought the field and tl-e cave, nnd,inrefully prepared the evidence of the purchase. 29G THE MOK OF GENtStS. [en. XXII". 1-9. The purchase showed his faith in God's truth; one of the branches of Adam's tempt• ation (Gen. iii. 4). It had been promised that his seed, aftor dwelling in n land not theirs, should return nnd possess that whereon he stood (cf. Jer. xxxii. 14, 15). Type of entrance into rest nfter pilgrimage (cf. 2 Cor. v. 1). It showed also his faith inn resurrection (cf. Ps. xvi. 10), The desire thathe and his family should lie in the same sepulchre speaks of a life beyond the present. Parted by death, they were one family still. Sarah was to him '' my dead." There was n link between them still. The Iiv.ing ,md dead etill one family. Doctrine of communion of saints (cf. Matt. xxii. 32). Death was the gate of life (cf. 1 Thess. iv. 16). Canaan a type of the rest which remaineth ; Abraham of the "children of the kingdom," pilg·rims with n promise. No rest here. Life full of uncertainties. One thing sure, we must die. But- I. \V& ENTER THE IIEAVENLY REST THROUGH DEATH; 'l'HE CITY OF Goo THROUGH THE VALLEY OF BACA. Here we walk by faith. Great and glorious promises for our encouragement, that we may not make our home here ; yet we know not whai we shall be, Sight cannot penetrate tbe curtain that separates t.irne from eternity. Thus there is the trial, do we walk by faith or by sight? We instinctively shrink from death. It is connected in our mind with sorrow, with interruption of plans, with breaking up of loving compnni-onship; but faith bids us sorrow not as those without hope. It reminds that it is the passing from whnt is defective and transitory to what is immortal. Here we are trained for the better things beyond, and our thoughts are turned to that sepulchre in which the victory over death was won; U1c-nce \\·e see the Lord arising, the pledge of eternal life to all who will have it. II. TIIE SEPULCHRE WAS MADE SURE TO ABRAHAM. In time he should enter it ae c,ue of the company gathered there to await the resurrection day; but meanwhile it was his. And if we look upon this as typical of our interest in the death of Christ, it speaks of comfort and trust. He took our nature that he might " taste death for every man." His grave is ours (2 Cor. v, 14). We are "buried with him," 11 planted together in the likP.ness of his death." The fact of his death is a possession that cannot be taken from us (Col. iii. 3, 4). He died that we might live. If frail man clings to the tomb of some dear one; if the heart is conscious of the link still enduring, shall we not rejoice in our union with him whose triumph makes us also more than conquerors? III. THE FIELD AND CAVE. How small a part did Abraham possess in his lifetime, but it was an earnest of the whole; he felt it so, and in faith buri~d his dead (cf. Gen. l. 25; Heh. xi. 22). An earnest is all we possess here, but still w~ have an earnest. In the presence of the Lord (John xiv. 23), in tho peace winch he gins, in the spirit of adoption, we have the "substance of things hoped for," n real fragment and sample of the blessedness of heaven.-M.

entries.title: GEN 24:2–4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Abraham said 11nto hie eldest servant of hie house, that ruled ever all that he l;.ad,-literally, to ltis se,-vant, the old man, ai,cient or ehler, qf kia house, the ruler over all which (sc. Lelouged) to 1,i11i, The term Ji?.t (an old man) is in most languages employed as a title of honour,-• cf. sheikh, aenatus, yipwv, presbyter, signor, seigneur, seiior, sir (Gesenius, p. 252),---:and is probably to be so understood here. Ehezer of Damascus, upwards of half a century previous regarded as heir presumptive to Abraham's house (eh. xv. 2), is commonly considered the official meant, though the point is of no importance - Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh : and I will make thee swear. This ancient form or adjuration, which is mentioned. ng:dn o~ly in chap. xlvii. 29, and to which notlung analogou~ can elsewhere be discoverod,-the practice alleged to exist among the mo<lern J,;gyptian Bcdouins ofplacing the band upon the membrum virile in solemn forms of asseveration ·not forming an exact pare.l_lel,- was probably originated by the patriarch, ell. XJ:l'I'. 1-!J.] TUE nooK OF GF,NESIS The thigh, llS the source of posterity (cf. eh. xxxv. 11 ; xlvi. 26 ; Exod. i 5), has been regarded as ~inting to Abraham's future descendants (Keil, Kalisch, Lange), and in particular to Christ, the promised seed (Theodoret, Jerome, Augustine, Luther, Ainsworth, Bush, Wordsworth), and the oath to be equivalent to a swearing by him that was to come. By others the thigh bas been viewed as euphemistically put for the generative organ, upon which the sign of circumcision was placed, and the oath as an adjuration by the sign of the covenant (Jonathan, Jarcbi, Tuch). A third interpretation considers the thigh as symbolising lordship or authority, and the placing of the band under it as tantamount to an oath of fealty nml allegiance to a superior (Aben Ezra, Rosenmilller, Calvin, Murphy). Other explanations are modifications of the above. By the Lord (Jehovah; sinre the marriage to which this solemn adjuration was preliminary was not an ordinary alliance, such as might have taken place under the providence of Elohim, but the wedding of the heir of the promise), the God of hea.ven, a.nd the God of the ea.rth (a clause defining Jebovab as the supreme Lord of the universe, and therefore as the sole Arbiter of human destiny), that thon shalt not take a wife unto my sonnot investing him with authority to provide a wife for Isaac in the event of death carrying him (Abraham) off before his son's marriage, but simply explaining the negative side of the commission with which he was about to be intrusterl. If it evinced Isaac's gentle disposition and submissive piety, that though forty years of age he neither thought of marriage, but mourned in devout contt,1uplation for his mother (Lnnge), nor offered resistance to his father's proposal, but suffered himself to be governed by 11 servant (Calvin), it was also quite iu accordance with nncient practice that parents should dispose of their children in man-iago (cf. eh. xxviii. 2)-of the daughters of the Canaanitea, a.mong whom I dwell. Being prompted to this partly by that jenlousy with which all pastoral tribes of Shemitic origin have been accustomed to gunrd the purity of their rnce by intermarriage (Dykes; cf. Thomson, 'Land and Book,' p. 591), and pnrtly no doubt by his perception of the growing licentiousness of the Cnnaanites, ns well us his knowledge of their predicted doom, though chiefly, it is probable, by n desire to preserve the purity of the promise<l seed. Intermarriage with the Cnnaanitcs was aftcrwnrds forbidden by tho lllosaic legislation (Exod. xxxiv. 16; Dent. vii. 3). But (literally, for, i. e. the former thing wust not be douo because this must be done) thou eba.lt go unto my country (not Ur of the Chnldces, Lut the region heyond the Euphrates generally), and to my kindred, and ta.ke a wife unto my son Isaac. Though enforced by religions considerations, this injunction to bring none but a rehtive for Isaac's bride "was in no sense a departure from established usages and social laws in regard to marriage" (' L'lnd and Book,' p. 591).

entries.title: GEN 24:6–8

entries.content: -And Abra.ham said, Beware thou-literally, be1oarefor th!lselj; the pleonastic pronoun being aJdeJ by way of emphasis (cf. eh. xii. 1; xxi. 16; xxiL 5)- tha.t thou bring not my son thither &lain. Literally, lest thou cause my wn to 1·et1trn thither; Abrnbam speaking of Isaac's going to Mesopotamia as a return, either because he regarded Isaac, though then unborn, as having come out with him from Mesopotamia, cf. Heh. vii. 10 (Wonlsworth), or because be viewed himself nuu his descendants ns n wbolo, as in eh. xv. 16 (Rosenmiiller). The Lord God of heaven, who took me from my father's ho11Be, and from the house of my kindred,--'lfide eh. xiL I. This was tho first consideration that prevented the return of oither himself or his sou. Having emigrated from l\Jesopotomia in obedience to a call of Heoven, not without" like instruction were they at liberty to return-and who spake unto me,-i. e. honoured me with Divine communications (1tidd supra)-and (in particular) tha.t sware unto me,-vide eh. xv. 17, 18; tho covenant transaction therein recorded having nil the force of nu oath (cf. rh. xxii. 16)-saying, Unto thy seed will I give this land. Here was a second considemtion that negatived tho idea of Jsa.ne's return,-he was the Gou-nppointl',\ heir of the soil,-1md from this, in conjunction with tho former, he nrgne<l thnt the Divine promise was certain of follilmc11t, and that nccordingly the mission for n bri,lu would be successful. He shall send hid a.ngel before thee,-i. e. to lcnJ and protect, ns was afterwords promised to Jsrnol (Ex0<L xxiii. 20), nnd to the Christion Church (Usr, 288 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [l·n. xxn·. 1-9. i 14)-and thou shalt take a wife unto my son from thence (mennini;(, thy mission shall be successful). And if the woman will not be willing to follow thee, then shalt thou be clear of this my oath (i. e. at liberty to hold thyself as no longer under obligation in the matter ; thy responsibility will at that point cease and determine) : only bring not my son thither again- or, observing the :,rder of the ~ebrew words, only my son !n-mg not a.gain to that place; with almost fc1·erish entreaty harping on the solemn refrain that on no account must Isnao leave the promisccl land, Rince in that would ha the culmination of unbeliefnnd disobedience.

entries.title: GEN 24:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -No tm'1ling back. "And Abraliam said unto him, Beware thou that thou bring not my son thither again." Abraham's care to prevent tho lenvcn of idolatry entering his family (cf. Exod. :x:xxiv. 16; 1 Cor. xv. 33; James i. 27). Worldly wisdom would have led him to seek a wife for his son among the families of Cannan, ~o us to givo him a firmer footing in the land; but he 11olcmnly charged his steward, in sending him on e. mnrringe embassy, not to clo this (cf. 1 Kings xi. 3; 2 Cor. vi. 14). A wifo was to be sought from his brother's THE DOOR OF GENESIS. [ct-1. XXIV. 10-28 family. Out of the earnestness of this godly desire came the trial of his fuith. An obvious difficulty; what if the damsel should not be willing to follow a etrnnger? There had been little intercourse between the families. The ne,1 s in eh. :xxii. 20 was plainly the first for many years. Must Isaac go in person to tnke a wife from her father's !1ouse? Muc~ might be urged in fav9ur of this. If the presence of Isaac were of importance, might he not return for a little, though Cannan was his appointed home? Was it not hindering the very thing Abraham desired to refuse to do so? Was it not unreasonable to look for a blessing and yet to negledt obvious means £or obtuining it? Not for a moment would Abraham listen to the suggestion. At God's call h~ h~d left M_esopotam!a for ever. To send his son b~ck would be contrary to the pnnc1ple of his whole hfe. It would be to put expediency above faith, to distrust God's promise, ta think his will chnngeable (cf. 1 Kings xiii. 19). Contrast the faithlessness of the Israelites in their wilderness journeys. Abraham would not allow e,·en ~ temporary return. They " in their hearts turned back ngain into Egypt" (cf. Luke 1x. 62). I. IN A GODLY LIFE TITERE IS OFTEN A TEMPTATION TO TURN BACK FOR A LITTLE. With a laudable aim, some step which seems likely to lead to it is not quite what in itself we know to be right. To gain the means of doing good, some little departure from truth may seem almost necessary. In the eagerness of some plan of usefulness the time for prayer can hardly be found, or the ordinary daily duties of life seem to interruptthe greater and higherwork; or, to gain an influence overthe gay and worldly, it may seem the course of wisdom to go, a little way at lenst, with them. And is not a Christian, under the law of liberty, freed from strict observance of the letter? Does not that savour of the spirit of bondage? Nay," to obey is better than sacrifice." Ahrnys danger when men seek to be wiser than God (Prov. xiv. 12). "\Ve cannot foresee the difficulties of returning. II. TnuE FAITH POINTS TO IMPLICIT OBEDIENCE. Can we not trust God to order all-not only the ends towards which be would have us strive, but the means to be used? We are to live by el"'ery word of God, not by some special saying only. Promise and precept, instrnction and direction, are alike his words, by which every Rtep should be guided. It is want of faith which leads to departure from obedience ; want of full truBt in God which leads to ways of fancied wisdom. We have to do with efforts, not with results; these are in God's hnnd. Where obedience is not in question we rightly use our juclgment; reason was given us to be our guide, but not tu take the guidance out of God's hands.-M.

entries.title: GEN 24:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he made his camels to kneel down-" a mode of expression taken from actual life. The action is literally kneeling ; not stooping, sitting, or lying uown on the side like a horse, but kneeling on his knees ; and this the camel is taught to do from his youth" (Thomson, 'Land iind Book,' p. 592)-without the city by a well of water. "In the East, where wells nre scarce and water indispensable, the existence of a well or fountain determines the site of the village. The people build near it, but prefer to have it outside the city, to avoid ,;he noise, dust, and confusion always occurring at it, especially if the place is on the highway" (lbul. ). At the time of the evening, even the time that women go out to draw water. Literally, that women that draw go forth. "It is the work of females in the East to draw water both morning and evening ; and they may be seen going in groups to the wells, with their vessels on the hip or on the shoulder" (Roberts' 'Oriental Illustrations,' p. 27). "About great cities men often carry water, both on donkeys and on their own backs; but in the country, nmong the unsophisticated natives, wome:n only go to the well or the fountain; and often, wlien travelling, have I seen long files of them going nnd roturning with their pitchers "at the time when women go out to draw water" (Thomson, 'Land and Book,' p. li92).

entries.title: GEN 24:12–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said,-commcncing his se!lrch for the m11iden by prayer, !ls he closes it with thanksgiving (ver. 26)-a beautiful exnmple of piety and of the fruits of Abmhllm's cure for the souls of his household, eh. xviiL 19 (Wordsworth)-O Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day. Litemlly, cause to meet (or come before) me, i. e. what I wish, the maiden of whom I am in quest ; hence , iuiow11ov 1vavTiov ,µov, make the way prosperous before me (LXX.); less accurately, occurre obsecro mihi (Vulgate). And show kindneBB unto my m11ster Abraham. 'l'he personal humility and fidelity displayed by this aged servant are only le~s remarkable than the fervent piety and childlike faith which discover themselves in th~ method he adopts for finding the bride. Having cast the matter upon God by prayer, RB a concern which specially b~longed to him, ho fixes upon a sign by which God should enable him to detect the bride designed for Isaac. Behold, I stand here by the well of water ;- literally, Behold me standing (cf. .er. 43) -and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water (vule on ver. 11, and cf. eh. xxix. 9; Exod. ii. 16) : a.nd let it come to pass that the damsel-ll!ET, with the vowels of the Keri ; the word used for .Abraham's young men (cf. eh. xiv. 24; xviiL 7; q. v.). In the Pentateuch it occurs twenty-two times, "'ithout thefeminine termination, meaning a girl (vide eh. xxiv. lG, 28, 55; xxxiv. 3, 12; Dent. xx. 15, &c.); a proof of the antiquity of the Pentateuch, and of this so-called Jehovistic section in particular, since in the latter books the distinction of sex is indicated by the affix ;-, being appended when a girl is intended ('Speaker's Commentary'); but this happens at least once in the Pentateuch (Dent. xx..ii. 19)-to whom I shall say, Let down thy pitcher, I pray thee, that I may drink; and she shall say, Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also :-the sign fixed upon was the kindly disposition of the maiuen, which was to be e,inccu in a particular wuy, viz., by her not only acceding with promptitude to, but generously exceeding, his request. It is probable that tho servant was led to chooso this sign not by his own natural tiict and prudence, but by that Divine inspiration and guidance of which he had been assured (ver. 7) before setting out on his importnnt mission-let the same be she that thou hast appointed for thy servant Ise.ao. "The three qualifications in the mind of this venerable domestic for n bride for bis master's son are o. pica.sing exterior, a. kindly disposition, and the approval of God" (Murphy). And thereby-Iv TOVT'f' (LXX.), per hoe (Vulgate) ; but rather, by her, i. e. the damselshall I know the.t thou hast showed kindneaa unto my master. ••

entries.content: -And it co.me to pass (not certainly by accident, but by Divine arrangement), before he had done speaking, that, -his prayer WllS nnswered (cf. Iso.. !xv. 24; Do.n. ix. 20, 21). From vcr. 46 it appears that the servant's prayer WllS not articulately spoken, but offered "in bis heart ;" whence the LXX. add,., Tp o,aa,oiq. auTou-behold, Rebekah oame out, who was born to Bethuel, son or Mi.J.cah, the wife of Nabor, Abraham's brother (vide eh. x.xiL 23), with her pitcher -the cad (cf. ~aooc, cadus) was n pail for drawing water, which women were accustomed to carry on their shoulders ; it wa~ this sort of vessel Gideon's men employed (Judges vii. 20) -upon her shoulder - iu exact correspondence with Oriental customthe Egyptian and the negro can-ying on the head, the 8yrian on the shoulder or lhd THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (en. liXIV, 10--28.• hip (vid.e Thomson, 'Laud and Book,' p. 592). VeT. 16.-And the damsel was very fair to look upon. Liternlly, r,ood of countenance, like Sarah (eh. xii. ll) and Rachel (eh. xxix. 17; cf. eh. xxvi. 7 of Rebekah). A virgin. Bethulah, i e. one separated and secluded from inteTcom-se with men ; from bathal, to seclude (ef. Deut. xxii. 23, 28; 2 Sam. xiii. 2, 18). :Neither had any man known her. A repetition for the sake of emphasis, rather than because bcthulah sometimes applies to a. married woma.n (Joel i. 8). And she went down to the well,-" nearly all wells in the East aTe in wadys, and have steps down to the water" (Thomson, 'Land and Book,' p. 592)-and filled her pitcher, and came up-probably wholly unconscious of the old man's admiration, though by no means unprepared for his request, which immediately followed.

entries.title: GEN 24:17–19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the servant ran to meet her, and said, Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher (a request which was at once complied with). And she said, Drink (and with the utmost politeness), my lord (and with cheerful animation): and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink. "Rebekah's address to the servant will be given you in the exact idiom by the first gentle Rebekah you ask water from ; but I have never found any young lady so generous as this fair daughterofBethnel" ('Thomson, 'Land and Book,' p. 592). And when she had done giving him drink, she said, I will draw water for thy camels also, until theyhave done drinking-thus proving that the kindly disposition within her bosom was "not simply the reflex of national customs, but the invisible sun beaming through her mind, and freely bringinq forward the blossoms of sterling goodness ' (Kalisch).

entries.title: GEN 24:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough (or gutter made of stone, with which wells were usually provided, and which were filled with water when animals required to drink), and ran again unto the well to draw water, and drew for all hi■ camels. "At one point we came upon a large village of nomade Bedouins dwelling in their black tents. For the first time we encountered a shepherd playing on his reeden pipe, and followed by nu flock. He was leading them to a. fountaiu, from which a maiden was meanwhile drawing water with a rope, and pouring it into a large stone trou?b. She was not so beautiful as Rebekah" ( In the Holy Land,' by Rev. A. Thomson, D.D. p. 198). •

entries.title: GEN 24:21

entries.content: -And the man wondering at her -gazing with attention on her (LXX., Vulgale, Gesenius, Furst); amazed and astoniEhed at her (Rosenmiiller, Delitzsch, Keil, Lange, Calvin)-held his peaoe, to wit-i. e. that he might know-silence being tho customary attitude fo1 tho soul in either ox• pecting or receiving 11, Divino communication (cf. Levit. x. 3; I's. xxxix. 2; Acts xi. 18) -whether the Lord had made his journey prosperous ornot. This inward rumination obviously took place while the whole scene was being cnaetea before hiseyes-the beautiful you_ng girl filling the.water-troughs, and the thirsty camels suckmg up the coolin" drink. _The lovel!ness. of mind e.nd body: both which ho desired 111 Isaac's bride, was manifestly present in Rebekah ; but still the questions remained to be determined, Was she one of Abraham's kindred 1 was she single i and would she follow him to Canaan ?-points of moment to the solution of which ho now proceeds.

entries.title: GEN 24:22–27
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking,-" If it is remembered that camels, though endowed in an almost marvellous degi·ee with the power of enduring thirst, drink, when an opportunity offers, e.n enormous quantity of water, it will be acknowledged that the trouble to which the maiden cheerfully submitted requiredmore than ordinarypatience"(Kalisch) -that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight,-the CB was neither a J?endant for the ear (LXX., Vulgate) nor a Jewel for the forehead (A.V., margin), but a. ring for the nose (ver. 47), the side cartilage, and sometimes the central we.II, of which was pierced for the purpose of admitting it (cf. Ezek. xvi. 11, 12). Such rings a.re still worn by Oriental women, and iu particular "the nose-ring is now the usual engagement present among the Bcdouins" (Delitzsch), The Weight of that presented to Rebekah was one lli2::;!, or half (Be. shekel), from lli2;, to divide-and two bracelets for her hands of ten skekels weight of gold;- the i•r,,¼', from i~'i, to bind or fasten, meant a circle of gold for the wrist or arm. So favourite a.n ornament is this of Oriental ladies, that sometimes the whole arm from wrist to elbow is covered with them ; sometimes two or more are worn one above the other ; and not unfrequently are they so numerous and heavy as almo&t to appear burdensome to the fair owners (Kalisch)- and said, Whose daughter art thou 1 tell me, I pray thee : is there room in thy father's house for us to lodge in1 The production of the bridal presents, and the tenor of the old m11n's inquiries, indicate that a.lrcady he entertained the belief that he looked upon the object of hie search. All dubiety was dispelled by Rebekah's answer. And she said unto him, I em the daughter of Bethuel the son of lllilcah, - to show that she was not descendecl from N,1hor'ij .'.llT. XXIV. 10-28.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 303 concubine (cf. vor. 15)-whioh she bare unto Nabor. This appears to have been tho stage Rt which the jewels W01"0 presented (ver. 47). She said moreover UDto him, We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in. It was now conclusively determined, by her answering all the pre-nrrangcd criteria, that the Lord had heard his prayer a.nd prospered his way, and thnt the hcnvenappointed bride stood before him. And the man bowed down his head, and worshipped the Lord. The first verb expressing reverent inclination of the head, and the second complete prostration of the body, and both combining "to indicate the aged servant's deep thankfulness for the guidance of the Lord." And he said, Blessed be the Lord God of my master Abraham (on the import of ';J~,i1 vide eh. ix. 26), who bath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth :-literally, who hat!,, not taken away his grace (i.e. the free favour which be.~tow~) and his truth (i. e. the faithfulness which implementspromises)/rCi77! (=from thehonso of, as in Exod. viii. 8, 25, 26 ; Gesenius) my master (cf. Ps. lvii. 3 ; cxv. l ; Prov. :xx. 28)-1 being in the way, the Lord led (or, hath led) me to the houae of my master's brethren. Yer. 28.-And the damsel-1JliiJ (vide on ver. 16)-ran (leaving the venerable stranger in the act of devotion), and told them of her mother's house-a true touch of nature. With womanly instinct, discerning the possibility of a love-suit, she imparts the Joyful intelligence neither to her brother nor to her father, but to her mother and the other females ofthe household, wholived separately from the men of the establishment-these things - in particular of th11 arrival of a messenger from Abraham. Perhaps also tho nose-jewel would toll its o,vn tale.

entries.content: -A bride for tlie heir.-2. .Eliezer and Rebekali, or the jindinr, of tlie bride. I. THE MATRIMONIAL EMBASSY, I. The departure from Hebron. With promptitude and alacrity, as became a servant executing the instructions of a master -attended by a cavalcade of ten camels and their drivers, as ambassadors of princes are wont to signalise their dignity by ample retinues; and laden with the choicest of his master's goods as presents for the bride, since they who go to woo must not neglect to carry gifts-the venerable steward issued forth upon his mission. 2. The iourney northwards. Up the Jordan valley towards II the Eye of the East" would probably be the route followed by Eliezer of Damascus ; thence closely skirting the spot whore in after yeors Tadmor in the wilderness arose with its palaces and temples, now magnificent in their ruins, till at length, crossing the Euphmtes, he would reach Aram of the Two Rivers. 3. Tlie arrival at Haran. If the time at which the patriarchal envoy reached the city of Nabor, viz., at sunset, when the maidens sally forth to draw, was an indication of the guiding hand of Providence, perhaps the spot at which he halted and partially unloaded his weary camels, viz., at the well, was a testirnoniol to his own shrewd sagacity, which discerned that for meeting with the virgins of the district, and in particular the females of Nahor's family, no better place could be selected than the city well, which was besides the customary restingpince for travellers. II. Tm: PRAYER AT THE WELL. I. Iu reverent humility. Not only does he adore the Divine greatness, but, leaving himself altogether out of account, he bespenks an interest in the Divine favour entirely as an act of kindness to his master. 2. Its childlike simplicity. He proposes a test by which he may be able to recognise the bride whom God has selected for his master's son. In doing so he practically casts the matter over upon God, asking him in the fashion indicated to point out the object of his search, thus exemplifying the very spirit of the Christian rnle, "In everything by prayer and supplication let your requests be made known unto God." 3. Its immediate answer. "Before he had done speaking, Rebekoh came out" to the well, and acted precisely os he had desired that the bride should do. It was a striking illustration of the promise, 11 Whiles they are yet speaking I will hear." III. THE MEETING WITH IlEDEKAH. 1. A description of licr person. As to parentage, the daughter of Bethuel; in respoct of condition, of virgin purity; with regard to appearance, very fair to look upon; concerning education, trained to domestic duties. 2. An account of lu:1· kindness. Coming up from the well, she graciously complios with the servant's request to be allowed to tako a draught from 'l'HE BOOK OF GE~ESIS. [rn. XXII'. 10-28. her pitcher. _Then ~ith w:inning sweetness she promptly offers to fill the stone troughs for his weaned ammals. And finally, when asked her namo, she with ingenuous frankness tells it, aQding, in reply to a request for lodging, that in Bethuel'B house there was not only room for him~elf and camels, but sumptt1ous hospitality for both. Such spontaneous acts of kindness to an unknown and nged stranger hPspoke a tender and susceptible heart within the breast of the fair Hebckah. 3. T/1,! imrresswn which she made on Eluz~. (1) Her appearance arrested him and mado him run t~ meet h~r (ver. 17) with his pre-arrang·ed request. Clearly this o!d man !~ad a singular chs~ernment of cl~ara~ter a~ well as a quick eye for beauty. (2) Her kmdness touched _!nm, and made lum silent m wonder (ver. 21), struc,k. dumb with amazement at her mmute fulfilment of every one of his stipulated conditions. (3) Her invitati~n overp~wered him, ?ausing ~im to bo:V his _head and worship (ver. ~G), admowledgmg Gods goodness m so quickly leadmg !um to the house of his master's brethren, and so unmistakably pointing out the bride. Learn-1. The fidelity and devotion to the interests of masters and mistresses "hich should be evinc,ed by servants. 2. The spirit of prayer and supplication wliich Christians should display in all the perplexing and difficult paths of life. ;I, Tl,c kind of brides which young men should select, viz., maidens distinguished hy Hrhekah's amiable and obliging disposition, eYen should they not be a-ifted with ncbckab's grace of form. ., HO:'!IILIES BY VARIOUS AUTHORS. \-er. 21.-Eliezer, or a W'lje--seel,:er. "And the man wondering at her held Iii~ peace, to wit whether the Lord had made his way prosperous or not." "The man " spoken of was probably the Eliezer of Damascus mentioned in eh. xv. 2. He had been s~lected by Abraham to be his heir, but of course when Isaac was born he could not hold that position. He became honoured and trusted as "the eldest servant of (Abraham's) house, who ruled o,er nll that he had" (eh. x.xiv. 2). To him was committed the delicate business recorded in this chapter; and the way in which it wns executed was just that which would be expected from one who bad so won the confidence of .Abraham as to be selected as heir. '\Ve cannot but admire the thoughtfulness of .Abraham for bis son. He sought to prevent Isaac from being brought under the polluting influence of the Canaanitish people in the midst of whom he dwelt. He also desired to prevent Isaac from going back to the country from which he had Limself been Divinely led. Hence he sends his steward to select from among his kinured one who shall be a suitable life-companion for his son. He takes an oath of his steward that he will in no wise permit a wife to be taken from among the Canaanites, or lead Isaac to Mesopotamia again. The mission of Eliezer was indeed difficult and delicate. We must not think of it according to the customs of our land, In Oriental nations to this day it is the practice to employ a third person to negotinte a marriage behveen those who seem by report to be suitable for such relationship. Eliezer undertook the affair with every desire to gratify his master, and to serve well even the one who had supplanted him in heirship. We cannot too highly praise "the man" for his unselfishness, or too warmly admire the devoutness which characterised bis whole conduct. ' I. HE SEEKS BY PBAYEn SUCCESS FBOM Goo. The prayer recorded here wns probably not the fil'l:lt offered with respect to the subject. His mission was not only delicate, but rather indefinite. He is sent to the relations of his master to choose from among them a wife for Isaac. He knows that much of the satisfaction of Abraham and welfare of Isaac will depend on hie right performance of the du_ty. He feels the responsibility resting upon him, and makes every nee~ful preparation for discharging it. He starts on the camels prepared, and carries with him presents Huitable. After a long journey he arrives at a city in Mesopotamia wher~ dwelt Nahor, bis master's brother. It is eventide when he reaches the well outside the city. The graceful daughters of tbE city, with pitcherij poised on their sl1oulders1 nre just coming forth to draw water for their households. The camels turn their 101,g necks and weary eyes in the direction of thA approaching maiden8. They know tl.u~t 011 their arrival the dry troughs, which only tantalised thirst, will he filled. The Cll, XXIV. 10-28.] 'l'HE BOOK Ol.<' GE}.ESIS. 305 shn.cle from the palms a.va.ils not now to break the fierce rays of the a11n SP,l);ing ~o rapidly in the west. Long shndows are over the landscape. Eliezer stands with the golden light about him. He feels that this may be the moment of great import. Clasping firmly his hands, and lifting fervently his face heavenward, he breathes ihe beautiful prnyer, "0 Lord God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and show kindness unto my master Abraham." It was-1. Brief prayer, becauso there was not time to say much more, but it was most appropriate. He asked for what he felt he needed. He did not use prayer as a mere mystical method of pleasing God, but as the expression of a felt need. This is true prayer. God does not want fine words, long sentences, and wearying repetitions. None are heard for their much speaking. 'fhat is a heathenish notion. God is not glorified by the length of time we remain on our knees, or the number of things we can crowrl into a certain time. The longest prayers are often the most unmeaning. ThiR i8 true of prayers in the home and in the Clrnrch. Brief, earnest, sincere prayer is that which wings its way to heaven. When Peter was sinking in the waters his cry was brief and pointed enough: "Lord, save; I perish." 2. Eliezer did not hesitate to ask God's guidance in respect to a subject which many would have accounted as quite within the scope of their own judgment to decide. Many also would have thought it beneath the notice of God. Many would have made their way direct into the city to Nahor's house to choose for themselves. And many would have left the matter to be decided by chance; but Eliezer seeks guidance from God. Only those who are ignorant of the value of trifles, of their relative power, orwho are ignorant of the fact that there are no trifles but which may become all-important circamstances, would think of such an affair as that Eliezer had in hand, as benellth God's notice. If not beneath God's notice, it may be the subject of prayer. Many who contemplate forming relationships might with the greatest advantage imitate the example of Eliezer in this case, and seek direction from God. Were this the practice there would be fewer unhappy marriages. Eliezer, in carrying out hie master's wish, seeks success from God. II. NOTICE' BOW Gon OVERTAKES OUR PRAYERS. At the most opportune time the ateward prays. He committed his way unto the Lord at the juncture when he felt he needed the guidance. God honours the man's trust. 11 It came to pass that before he had done speaking Rebekah came out." She was the very one whom God had appointed. She knew not that she wa.s moving to fulfil the intention of God. In her acts and in her words she wa.e doing that which was in bam1ony with the sign the man had asked. Courteously, on being asked for a draught from her vessel, she had offered even to draw for the camels also. In the first one addressed Eliezer had the answer to his prayer. Cf. Isa. Ix. 54: 11 Before ye cnll I will answer," &c. ; and Dan. ix. 23: "At the beginning of thy supplication the commandment came forth." We lose much of the comfort of prayer because, a.fter having put up a lletition, we either forget to look for the answer, or because we have but a semilelief in the power of prayer. If prayer be a reality to us, it is no loss so in God's eight. Some put up prayers in the spirit which seems to say, "Now I will see whether God will answer that." God is not to be subject to mere testinge. Christ Rhowcd that, when on earth he refused to gratify the curiosity or submit to the testings the Pharisees prepared for him. Where God is perfectly trusted the answer will, in some way or other, overtake, or even anticipate, the prayer. III. SEE now THE RAPIDITY OF THE ANSWER STAGGERS DELIEF. II He, wondering a.t her, held hie pence," waiting to know whether the "Lord had made his journey prosperous or not." God had not only answered speedily, but in tho ma.nner desired. Sometimes he sends the answer, but in a way so different from that we expected, that we discern not the fact that we have an answer. But what heavenly telegmphy is here I No soonerthe petition sent than the answer is given. Tho very correijpondence between the sign desired and its rapid fulfilment only sets Eliczer speculating as to whether it may not have been simply a very remarkable coincidence rather than a Divine response. Meanwhile he nets as though he believed. He offers to Reheknh the gifts which indicated already his business. He offers such llR shall hecomo iho character of his nrnster, who was princely in his possessions ns well ns position. Ho offer~ and waits. The man "held his peace." lle knows that if Go1l has auswere,1 QF,~ 1'HIS. X S06 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (cu. XXIV, 29-60. in part ne will also answer fully. God's dealings should always induce awe and patient waiting. He will often surprise us with the blessings of goodness. In our lives we have probably known like surprisingly rapid answers to prayer. Wo hrn-e even disbelieved in the answer. What if God had withdrawn. the help or blessing gi.-en because received in such unbelief I There are time11 when wo, like Eliezer, and like the Israelites on the shores of the Red Sea, have t> be still and know that the Lord is God. Then God's action staggers belief. IV. SEE HOW GRACIOUSLY Goo CONFIRMS ms SElWANT's WONDERING HOl'E, Elicze1 inquires of the maiden whether there is room in her father's house for him to lodge. After the manner of the Orientals, she readily replies, "We have both straw and provender enough, and room to lodge in." He follows Rebekah. Laban acts as host in place of his father Bethucl. He welcomes Eliezer heartily. "Come in, thou blessed of the Lord," &c. Eliezer enters and attends to the wants of his men and camels, but will not attend to his own until he has unburdened his mind. He tells of his errand, of the meeting '11-ith Rebekah at the well, of his praying, of the speedy an8wer, and of the sign fulfilled. Laban and Bethuel are surprised, and see in it God's hand. They say, "The thing proceedeth from the Lord; we cannot speak unto thee good or ill" Then the man"bowed his head and worshipped." .Rebekah consented to accompany him and become the wife of Isaac, his master's son, Everything fell out better than the steward could have expected; he could only sec in it God's band, God's mercy in guiding him and in confirming l1is hope. 1. God is as 'll'i!ling to answer us as to answer Eliezer of Damascus. 2. Prayer can overcome difficulties that seem insurmountable. When the cup of sorrow is not removed the strength is given to bear it, and so prayer is answered. If the way we expected does not open up in answer to our supplication, another and better is sw-e to be made plain. Prayer also "makes the darkened cloud withdraw." 3. When in tl1e other world we look at our past life, we shall all see that God had answered all prayers that it would have been for our good to have answered, and that in others the witbholdment has been kindliest response. There we shall "bow our heads and wor,;hip" him who made our earthly journey prosperous, and who had brought tis to ihe "city which bath foundations." Whatever, then, our. anxiety, trial, perplexity, let us lay all before God. If we are.earnestly trying for the salvation of members of our own family, or for the advancement of God's kingdom, let us by prayer a11d 6upplication make our requests known to God, and ho will send us an answer of peace, even as he did to Eliezer.-H.
