entries.title: GEN 24:30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Laban's eye of greed. "And when he saw the bracelets," &c. One thing moved Laban to offer hospitality to a stranger-the vision of gold on his sister's form. J. COVETOUSNESS MAKES A MAN CALCULATING WHEN APPEARING TO DE GENEROUS. Laban had not been so pressingly urgent in bis invitation if be had not cherished a hope of further advantages. He was a chnrlish man. He said, "Come in, than blessed of the Lord," &c., because he saw that which was to him the greatest sign of blessing-wealth. Laban helped the more readily to ungird Eliezer's camels because he hoped thereby to loosen the girdle-purse of his visitor. He had the eye of greed. Ile could not see anything valuable belonging to another without wishing; to possess it. 11. COVETOUSNESS MAKES A MAN, GENERALLY, SHORT-SIGHTED WITH RESPECT TO Rl:1 OWN BEST INTERESTS. Laban gave Eliezer a bad impression of himself. The latter would soon see through such a man as Laban. Ile showed this when he gave presents not only to the sister and mother, but to the brother (ver. 53). He knew that it would not be advisable to overlook Laban. Eliezer knew be could be bought. Laban, when treating with Jacob, was just ns short-sighted. He gave Leab and Rachel to Jacob as wives only after years of service for which he stipulated. He changed Jacob'e wages ten times. Through his greed be at last lost Jacob. He confessed how greRt II helper Jacob had been. "The Lord bath blessed me for thy sake" (eh. xxx. 27). Jacob would not tarry with him, and even the daughters were glad enough to got Rway from such a father. Covetousness is opposed to our temporal and eternal interests. We lose by it the respect of others here und of God hereafter. 111. COVETOUSNESS IS EVER INDIIJ'FF:RENT TO THE RIGHTFUL CLAIMS 011' OTHERS. It will ignore those cluime altogether, if possible. 1. We find Laban thus ignored tho influence of his father throughout the whole transaction. Perhaps Bethuel was infirm or aged, but he is, consistently with the character of Laban, thrust into the b:1ckground. Laban also takes all presents, and there is no mention of any being given to hie father. 2, We find also he was in great measure indifferent to the happines8 of his sister. He was subtle in tongue, and spoke of the Lord arranging things, bui he believed in the arrangement because his family was the gainer. A good chance is offered by the Damascene stranger, nnd Rebekah soon saw that it was n foregone conclusion that she should go with him. Covetousness will mnke pnrents cnreless as to the physical, mentRI, and moral well-being of their children, and employers cnrelose of the state of tlu,ir servants. It is covetousness also that lends mnny to spread temptations, too strong to be resisted, before others, and one nation to get rich out of that which is sapping the life-blood of another. IV. COVETOUSNESS NEVER SATISFIES, AND OFT :!!AKES MEN MOST MISERABLE. "Ho that is greedy of gain troubleth his house." "Envy is rottenness to the bones." Misers perish in the midst of plenty. niches possessed, the desire for morn i,i generally intensified. The desire is no more checked than a lamp is extinguished by added oil. V. COVETOUSNESS IS SURE, SOONER on LATER, TO DE ltEDUKED. Tito greed in Lnbnu'e eye which glistened at tho eight of the golden ornamc11t,i on hi:1 TUE nooK OF GENESIS. [,;n. XXIV. 6L-G7. sister's form deepened wiLh the passage of years, Ai hat, in hie pursuit of Jacob, he was rebuked by God in a vision, and afterwards by the man ho had wronged. Learn, therefore, that medium prosperity is better than great riches gained by greed. Despise not the comforts of life, but live for something higher. What is gained in the world is speedily gone. If we gain much and ruin our souls, we sh1lll uot only be rejected by God, but shall bitterly condemn ourselves,-H.

entries.title: GEN 24:31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Laban, the solu:it-Ous host. "Wherefore standest thou without?" The character of Laban has been well explained by Blunt in his 'Coincidences.' It is one of consistent greed. He was sincere in inviting Eliezer because he saw tho bracelets on his sister's orrn, and expected still further favours from a guest who can so lavishly bestow gifts. Christ asks us to enter his king·dom, but he expects notl1ing from us in return but love. We may adapt this inquiry of Lo.ban to souls e.s yet outside the Church. • I. THE POSITION OCCUPIED. "Without." Probably they have no realised pardon, no enjoyment in religion, no future prospects of joy. Life is a dread mystery to them. They are saying, "\Vho will show us any good?" They may be just awakened spiritually, like the Philippian jailor. They may be under the condemnings of law and conscience, and in dread of the consequences of sin. !'hose within the true Church know in whom they have believed, and rejoice in forgiveness and the prospect of heaven. They are no longer outside the gates of memy. We may be in o visible Church without being of Christ's fold. It is penitence, faith, o.nd character that determine our position, and not birth, rank, or ceremonial observances. ll. THE REASONS WHEREFORE MANY RETAIN A POSITION OUTSIDE THE CHURCH. 1. Accustomed to the state, and unwilling to change. They are like the prisoner who, nfter many years' imprisonment in the Bo.stile, wo.s liberated, and went forth only to find all bis friends gone and himself a mere burden to society. He went back ancl entreated to be allowed to retain his cell until he should pass out of the world. 2. Many, because they are ignorant of the fulness of Divine mercy. 3. Others, becauso they think there is so much to be done ere they can be fitted to be received within, and are looking to their own efforts to prepare themselves. 4. Many, because they fear their opportunity of admittance is past. 5. Others, because undecided as to whether they shall give up the pleasures of the world for the privileges of Christian fellowship. 6. Others, because they lack faith in their faith ond its power to justify. 7. Many stand outside because they think themselves o.s secure outside as within. They forget that Christ demands open confession, o.nd that to be united openly to his Chnrch is one way of confessing his name before men, Let there be o. person!\! and searching inquiry, ",VI1erefore standest thou without?" The invited guest passed within, and found his highest expectations more than realised, becaW!o God "bud prospered hiij joumey."-H.

entries.title: GEN 24:61–67
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.A bride for the heir.-4. Rebekalt and Isaac, or the wedding of tlte bride. I. THE PENSIVE DRIDEGROOM. 1. Mourning for his mother. Isnac•~ meditatio~ clenrly includes this. Good mothers, w~en they die, should be deeply nnd affectionately sorrowed for by grateful nnd lovmg sons. A son who loves hi~ mother living forgets not to lament her dead. The best testimonial of filial piety is to know thnt e. son tenderly regards hie mother while she lives, nnd cherishes her memory when she is gone. 2. MU8ing on liis bride. This too the langunge will ndmit. Sc11rcely could the thought of Eliezer'e mission be excluded from Isaac's mind. Doubtless he would often, during the interval of hie ubeence, have his silent wonderings about its return with the God-provided spouse. Almost certninly too his pra.yern would nscend to heaven on her behalf. He who asks a wife from God is most likely to receive one, and he who frequently pro.ye for the wife of his youth is most likely to love her when she comes. Note that Isanc's moarnings and musings ware in tll':, field at eventide. While any place and time will suffice for heart exercises, some plnees nnd times are more suitable than others, and none more so than the solitud~ of nature and the darkening of eve. II. THE VEILED DRIDE. Springing from her camel at the sight of her intended husband, "she took n veil and covered herself." The actions indieated-1. Rebekali's politeness. Etiquette required both. It was satisfactory nt least that Isaac was nbuut to receive as his wife a lady, one ncquainted with the gentle urnrmers of the day. Refinement, while desirable in nil, is specially beautiful in woman. Elegance of manners are only second to beauty of fonn in a bride. 2. Rebekaks modesty. Nothing can palliate immodesty in any, least of all in the gentler sex. Hence, not only should maidens be educated with the greatest possible nttention to the cultivation of pure and delicate emotions, but nothing sho1tld ever tempt them to cast aside that shield of maidenly reserve which is one of their surest protection~. in the midit of life's dangers and seductions. " Isaac brc,ught her into his m?ther Snr~h-s tent, and thus mstalled her m the honours ns well as invested her with the pnv1leges of matron of his house. I_Y. !HK HAPP! HOME. _1. !,saac loved Rebekah. "So oug·bt husbands to love their wives as theu own bodies (Ephes. "· 28). It is their duty· it ought to be their happines~ ; it certainly will pro\'e their interest. 2. Rebekah domforted Isaac. So oug:lit wives not merel,r "to revercn:e their \1usbands" (Ephes, v. 33), but to soothe their 80rrows, cure their cares, and dispel their despondencies. Learn-I. That the son who sorrows for a mother will likelyprove a husband that ea~ lo,e a wife. 2. That maidens' chafms are moi,t attrac~i!e whe~ seen through a ,·CJI of modesty. 3. That those marnages are most uusp1c1one which are made by God. 4. That those homes are happiest where husband and ,vife love and comfort 011e another. IIOMILIES DY VARIOUS AUTHORS. \·er. 63.-Isaac £1t the .field. "And Isaac we11t out to meditate in the field. at eYentide." Isaac was OI!e of the less prominent among the patriarchs. He seems le have lacked energy of character, but there was great devoutness. His life was like n toned picture, lacking garish colouring, but having a depth of interest. Possibly the fact that an uplifted knife had once gleamed death upon him, and that be Lad so narrowly escaped, may have had great influence in giving n sober tinge to bis life. Not only so, but training by such a father as Abraham must have inculcated a ready obedience to God's will, and a constant desire to know that will. In tl,e passage above we have- I. A GODLY BADIT INDICATED. 11 Went out to meditate "-to pray. There is I\ great difference between reverie and meditation. 'fhe one is aimless dreaming, the other, thought tending to an object. Prayer is the thought expressed. Meditation is the "nurse of prayer." Meditation stirs up the spiritual fire within. It brings us nearer to the Divine. It should be cultivated as a lmbit rather than be left to spasmodic impulses. II. A PLACE WELL ADAPTED TO PRAYER SELECTED. The field or open country, where we can get away from men, is the place for fellowship with God. A free prospect lets God's power be more plainly seen. It is an advantage to get out to sea, and, leaning over the bulwark of a vessel, to realise the width of the world, the ,astness of the universe and greatness of God. We should seek some pince where we can specially realise the presence and power of God. "Enter into thy closet" ie a command which many find it difficult to obey. At school, in business houses, there is little or no provision for solitary meditation; but with n book in hand the believer may in spirit get alone with God. III. THE TIME CHOSEN FOR PRAYER WAS MOST FITTING. Isaac went into the field at eventide. When the fret and toil of the day were over; when the sun was setting, glorified by crimson clouds, or shaded by the purplish haze ; when the blossoms were closing, and flocks were being folded; when the moon was just sh~wing, and the stars beginning to shine out; when a hush was over J?atnre and e~ter111g into the soul-then Isaac sought to pray; then he sought to realise the certnmt.J; of the Divine promises and the faithfulness of the Divine performance. The time accorded well with his own feelir~ga. He still mourned for his mother (ver. 67). Rorrow makes solitude congenial. Moreover, he was anticipating a change of state. He knew his father had sent Eliezer to seek for him a wife from among his own kindred, end he may have been praying that God would send him a suitable partner for life. \Vhile he was praying the answer was appronching. entries.title: GEN 25:1–11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The last days ofAbraham. I. AnnAHAM's OLD AGE. 1. The talcing of a second wife. (1) Her name: Keturah, recorded because of her relationship to Abraham. Connection with God's people confers honours as well as privileges. (2) Her marriage: of the second degree. Succeeding to Sarah's mr.!riage bed, Ketural, did not succeed to her social status. Neither did her issue possess legal claim to Abraham's inheritance. Concubinage, though permitted, was not necessarily approved by God. (3) Her children: numerous and (in some instances) distinguished. The common seed of the flesh may often be more enlarged than the 11pecial seed of grace; but the descendants of good men, other things being equal, • are likelier to come to honour than the families of the wicked. 2. The making of his will. (1) Isaac, the son of Sarah, be constitutes his heir, in accordance with tho Divine counsel, not attempting to interpose on behalf of Ishmael, his first-born. Primogeniture may involve certain rights in the world ; itbas no superiority in grace, or in the Church. (2) The sons of Hagar and Keturah he endows with portions from his ample pastoral wealth before he dies, and sends away to settle as independent nomads in the unoccupied territory lying on the east of Palestine, thus providing for the prosperity of his children and the peace of his family after he is gone-two things which pious parents should as far as possible secure before they die. II. .ADRAHAM's DEATH. 1. Before deatk The age to which the patriarch had attained was-(1) Numerically great, viz., 175 years. Mark the tendency of piety to prolong life (Pa. miv. 12). (2) Morally good. Neither beautiful nor desirable in itself, when associated with corresponding ripeness in grace old age is both delightful to look upon and pleasant to enjoy (Prov. xvi. 31). (3) Completely satisfying. He had experienced the Divine goodness and mercy for 175 y~ars, hnd God's covenant established with himself and family, beheld Isaac born, married, and, the father of two promising sons, and seen Sar~h away before him to the better !and; now he had no desire left unfulfilled but one, v1z.1 to depart. 2. At deatli. His end was peaceful; he "breather! out bis spirit''. into the ~ar,de o~ Jehovah. .~o did Isaac (eh. xx..xv. 29), Jacob (ch.xlix. 33), David (Pe. m1. 5), Chnst (Luke xxm. 46). "Mark tlte perfect, and behold the upright" (Pe. xxxvii. 37).. 3. After.d~atli. He was gathered to hie people-a significant intimation of (1) the immntenahty ?f the soul; (2) the conscious existence of the soul nfter death ; (3) the g~~hennp of pious souls into one society beyon~ tho grav?; (4) the mutual r~cogn1t10n of tho glorified· (5) the complete separation of the nghteous from the w10ked. III. A BRAIIAM's FUNERAL. 1. The chief mournen. Whether Kotural1's boys were present at the n:ffecting ceremonial iR not stnted, but the prominent positions were occupied by Ishm 1cl and Isaac. It is a duty which surviving children ?~e deceased parents to see their remains deposited with reverence in the gra...-e, nnd 1t IS beautiful when fr,i.ternal estrangements arc removed round I\ father's tomb. 2. The place of sepulture. The cave of Machpelah had three attractions for the CII. XXV. 12-18.] 'fln} BOOK Oli' GENESlS. patriarch: it was in the p:.-oin:ecd land, it was his own tomb, and it container! the dust of Sarah. 3. The bereaved son. Isaac, from his sensitive disposition and the unexciting character of his occupation, would feel hie father's loss more keenly than Ishmael. Perhaps this explains the statement of ver. 11. It is God's special care to comfort orphans (Ps. xxvii. 10). Learn-I. That though secondary wives are not agreeable to the word of God, second marriages are not against the will of God. 2. That good men ought to mako a just disposition of their temporal affairs before they die. 3. That whether God's saints die soon or late, they are always satisfied with living. 4. That in whatever sort of tomb a saint's dust may lie, his immortal spirit goes to join the company of just men made perfect. 5. That the loss of earthly parents is more than com• pensated by the blessing of a father's God.

HOmLETICS. Yers. 12-18.-The gene?·ations of IslimG£-l, or the biograp/iy of a prince. I. THE l'RINCE's NA.ME. Ishmael. 1. The si,gniji,cance of his name. "God hears." entries.title: GEN 25:19–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -T/te childless pair. I. THE DISAPPOINTED HUSDAND. 1. Tlte grievous ajftiction. Rebekah, the wife of Isaac, was barren. Though neither uncommon nor unjust, this was to Isaac (1) a specially severe affliction, from its long continuance, from his love for Rebekah, from his own natural desire of offspring, but cl,iefly from his faith in the promise; (2) a highly beneficial a~iction, serving to instruct and discipline his faith as to the true character of the cluldren of the promise, to refine and intensify his affection for Rebelmh, to purify and elevate his own spiritual life and to enable him to realise his complete dependence on the grace of God. 2. The earnest intercession. "Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife." Isaac's supplication was (1) directed to the right quarter, since "children are the heritage of the Lord;" (2) conceived in the right spirit, the word "entreated" implying earnest and repeated application to the heavenly throne; (3) stated in.the right way, wit!, plainness and simplicity of speech; and (4) seconded by the nght l,elpAr, Rebekah, nccorrling to one reading of the text., joining her entreaties with her husband's. Husbands and wives should be help.era, not hinderera, of each other's prayers. 3. Tlie gracious response. "The Lord was entreated of Isaac, and Rebekah conceived." Noto the character of God as the Hearer of prayer, the habitual practice of God, which is to listen to his people's Rupplications, the power which belongs to prayer of being able to prevail with God, and the special virtue which resides in united prayer (Matt. xviii. 19). II. Tm: ANXIOUS wun,:. 1. The un"!'onted experie-Me. In two respects the pregnancy of Rebekah was unusual. First, she had never conceived before ; and secondly, the attendant sensations were uncommon. Greatmercies are often accompanied by great discomforts to prevent gracious souls from resting in the gifts and neglecting the Giver. 2. The remarkable interrogatum. "Rebekah went to inquire of the Lord." Her conduct was remarkable for the impatience it di~playecl, the piety it evinced, the faith it implied. If in her querulous exclamation there was sin, in her seeking to God with her anxiety there were grace and faith. 3. The mysterious oracle. This contained three distinct announcements: the first hopeful, that Rebekah should be the mother of twins; the second painful, that, besides being mutually antagonistic from their birth, her two sons should develop into hostile nations ; the third unusual, that the elder should serve the younger. III. THE HAPPY MOTHER. 1. ller days were fulfilled. A special mercy which pregnant mothers can appreciate. 2. Her sons were born. Another cause of rejoicing to a mother (John xvi. 21). (1) Their names. "Esau and Ja.cob." Names of men are sometimes prophetic of both character and condition. (2) Their birth : remarkable for the singular phenomenon by which it was accompanied. Jacob's holding of Esau's heel was intended to foreshadow the early character of Jacob, his future over-reaching of Esau, and his ultimate precedence in grnce. N.B The first in nature is often last in grace. Between nature and grace there is perpetual antagonism. The great achievements of gracious souls have sometimes fore- Hhadowings in nature. (3) Their nppearnnce. Esau red like n. hairy cloak; Jacob catching Esau's heel. The boy is oft the father of the man. 3. Her husband was spared. "Isaac was threescore years old when she bare them." A third mercy not n.lways granted to mothers, to retain their husbands to participate in their run.ternal joys (1 Sam. iv. 19). Lenrn-1. That children in a home are n special mark of Divine favour. 2. That anxious wives and mothers should carry their troubles to God's throne. 3. That the future histories and destinies of children are known to God, if not to their 1iarents. 4. That mothers of families have peculiar joys as well as special sorrows.

entries.title: GEN 25:27–34
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The twin 'brothers. I. THE GROWING LADS. 1. .Diverse in daily calling. Esau elected to follow the adventurous and roving life of a hunter; Jacob, the simpler and lees exciting occupation of keeping sheep. The principles that guided their respective choices are not explained ; but, like the selection of trades by other inexperienced youths, these were doubtless due to physical constitution, mental temperament, the influence of example, the effect of parental counsel, and above all the over-ruling providence of God. Cf. Cain and Abel (eh. iv. 2). 2. Unlike in personal character. Esau was a wild man in disposition no less than in action, a youth of strong animal propensities and essentially mundane proclivities. Jacob, without being religious, was quiet, sedate, fond of home life, and studious of peace, though not without a vein of duplicity in his soul's texture. This diversity in character, not due to parentage, birth, or education, which in both were alike, modern ~cience would expl11in by molecular arrangement. Biblical theology goes a step behind, and traces it to God (Rom. ix. 11). 3. .Divided in parental favour. Esau was loved by Isaac, Jacob by Rebekah. Besides being sinful in itself-scarcely anything can justify partiality in parental affection-the conduct of Isaac and Rebekah was more than likely hurtful to the lads, leaving on their consciences a sense of injustice, estranging them from each other in fraternal regard, nnd helping them unconsciously to fulfil the untoward destiny of mutual rivalry a.nd jealousy already predicted for them. II. THE TIRED BUNTER. 1. His fa.mishing condition. I£ Esau was really foint, it indicated too great eagerness in following his sports. Even in honourable callings and profitable pursuits moderation is a duty. Rom. xii. 11 will assist traders and merchants to preserve the golden mean between slothfulness and slavishness in business. If E,j(lu was not renlly faint, but only fatigued and hungry, it was an instance of exaggerated talking which with some is common, but by a.II should be avoided. 2. His ravenous request. This indicated an impatient spirit, which the words attempt to reproduce--a spirit characteristic of ill-b11le.nced natures, resulting in most instances from unsubdued selfishness, betraying frequently into sins 11nd foults that might otherwise be avoided, and at all times ill-befitting noble souls a.nd renewed he11rts. It Ill.so discovered II gluttonous appetite. The glutton's god is his belly, the glutton's temple his kitchen, the glutton's high priest his cook, the glutton's ritu11l, Let us ee.t and drink. Let saints beware of gluttony (Prov. xxiii. 2). III. THE DESPISED BIRTHRIGHT. 1. The base proposal. " Sell me this day thy birthright." Jo.cob's desire to deprive Esau of his right of primogeniture w11s envious, unbrotherly, and, in the light of the pre-natal oracle, imp11tient and unbelieving. The conditions of s11le were mee.n, ex11cting, e.nd selfish. That Jacob's conduct w11s the fruit of grace or faith is difficult to credit, though God, who often works with despicable instruments, over-ruled it for the accomplishment of his own designs. 2. The foolish answer. "Behold, I am at the point to die: and wh11t profit shall this birthright do to me?" An ejaculation discovering both contempt £or spiritual and doubt of future things ; the very essence of epicureanism, whether ancient or modern. 3. The unholy oatli. "Swear to me this day ; 11nd he aware unto him." On the p11rt of both giver 11nd receiver this w11s wrong. Neither nad Esau right to part with his birthright until God in his providence took it from him; nor had Jacob the right to 11ccept th11t t>irthright until God tra.nsferrod it to his h11nds. 4. The unequal ezchange. Jacob got the birthright; Esau got tho pottage. Esau the type of many who accept the devil's bargain of the world (mostly an infini tcsimal fragment of it) for a soul. 0ENF.SIS. y !U2 THE BOOK OF uENESIS. [ell. XXV. 27-34.

entries.title: GEN 25:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Esau, the spiritually indifferent. "What profit shall the birthright do to me? " There was very much in Esau which would be greatly admired. He was of good humour, off-handed, manly, open, daring, and fond of field sports. He, and not Jacob, would in society have carried off the palm. He was a fair sample of a worldling. He knew nothing of the consecration of heart to God, or of spiritual aspirations. In the narrative we see how he showed indifference to the birthright, which carried with it certain spiritual advantages. He came in faint from the field, and the wafted odour of Jacob's savoury lentils filled him with longing. For a share in a mess of pottage he parted with his birthright. l. THE UNilENEWED HEART AI.WAYS UNDERVALUES MATERIAL, NATURAL, AND SPinl'l'UAI, DT.ESSINGS. We may enjoy all the blessings God may shower upon us and not think of them as coming from God. We undervalue the gift of life, and the various means by which God has arranged that life shall be sustained. 'i'hen we forget that God preserves to us reason and the power of acquiring knowledge, But there are spiritual advantages analogous to those which Esau despised which we may treat indiiferently. 1. .Authority and honour as the firstborn. 2. .A. double portion of his father's possessions. 3. The privilege of the priesthood. Evidently the eldest son acted as the priest of the family in offering the sacrifices, and the priestly garb was kept for him. It was this that Rebekah had by her, and which she put on Jacob to deceive Isaac. 4. The peculiar biessing of his father, which was bestowed with solemnity. A covenant was ratified by eating, and hence Isaac sent out Esau .to prepare venison; but Rebekah forestalled him. 5. Inc)uded in that blessing of Isaac was the promise made by God to Abraham, and which was to he handed on from one generation to another. It was for this Jacob longed. He rightly appraised the spiritual advantages connected with it. Though there was much that was mean in his character at first, he had these spiritual desires and faith in God not possessed by his brother. These brothers were twins, yet how diverse their character. It may have been that Ja.cob, knowing he was of equal age, felt he had an equal right to be accounted the firstbom. This may be said by way of excuse for that which otherwise would appear outrageous and mean. Probably when Esau said he was "at the point of death " he only meant it in the same way that we say "we are dying of hunger." Jacob asked the transfer because he knew his brother cared little about it, and because ho may have heard him express his indifference to it. Jacob could not have t.aken it by violence, and Esau should have refu~ed the suggestion with al! OB. XXV 27-34.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 323 emP.hatic "no; " say, " I will rather dio than pflrt with that.•· Esau may have even smiled at Jacob for caring so much about that which was of such little worth to hiir A deprnved heart made him profane, indifferent, ungrateful, and rash. II. A TIME IS SURE TO COME WHEN THE GOOD WE UNDERVALUED BECOMES OF GREATEST WORTII, AND WIIEN IT MAY BE BEYOND oun REAC11. It was probably about twenty years after Esau had parted with his birthright that Isaac felt one day that his end was approaching, and desired to bless hie son before he died. He was ignorant of the transfer which had been made. Esau deceived his father. He ignored a solemn compact. He would now rob bis brother. He comes back perspiring and exhausted from the field, thinking that anyhow he has earned his father's blessing. He finds that Jacob has acted in his right and obtained the blessing. His own mother frustrates him, believing that she was acting rightly for her son Jacob. We can see ho1v questionable were her doings, but we must not measure her nor Jacob by present moral standards. Esau weeps, "What, no blessing for thy firstborn?" He gets a blessing, but not the best. Deep his regret. Ho sees now his folly in its true light. "No place for repentance," &c. means no chance of repairing the mischief. Thus things done thoughtlessly in youth may have fearful after-consequences. Neglect of educational advantages, incurring of debt, acquirement of habits, rejection of appeals, and withstanding religious impressions. As the icicle freezes one drop at a time, so character is gradually formed. It depends on the water as to what the icicle will be. If muddy and tinged, the frozen mass will not be transparent; clear or thick, it is frozen and fixed, and will never be altered until dissolved altogether. Where are the warm rays that are to change our character? Esau sought to change his father's mind, but it was useless. Our heavenly Father is always willing to forgive if there be true repentance, but bis forgiveness may not conquer the fixed evil habit. So long as there ie life none should despair. See how David sinned, but he repented too. Esau lacked contrition. His sorrow was only remorse. ,vhat if we are risking the lose of some great spiritual advantage like to Esnu's I We shall discover it on the death-bed or at the judgment bar. There is then a serious warning-!. To those who are trifling with religion. Can you push the cross aside, and laugh on Calvary's mount? 2. To those hardening their hearts in neglect. An old man once said to me, "It is no use talking of religion to me now; I am past it. There was a time once when I felt, but now I cannot." 3. To those who think it will be easier to repent and do the right later in life. God promises pardon when we repent, but ho does not promise to prolong life. Probably there is not one present who has not heard this warning before, therefore it is to be feared it will be as unavailing as the preceding. Oh, Holy Spirit, forbid that it should.-H.

entries.title: GEN 25:34
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Neglect of heavenly things. "Thus Esau despised his birtliright." Strange and sad that truths so important as those bearing on eternal life, even where believed, often exercise so slight influence. Yet so it is. How many like to hear the go~pel in its fulness, and to be warned against neglecting it, yet in their lives show little of its power (Ezek. xxxiii. 32). How many live, content to know truth, forgetting that nil our daily life tells for good or ill on our eternal life, and that opportunities arc passing away. How many, believing that in every being there is a soul to be saved or lost, can yet see multitudes living in ungodliness without effort or even prayer for their recovery (cf. Luke xix. 41). Is not the spirit of Esau in these? He is called (Heh. xii. 16) a "profane person." Yet no crime or great fault is laid to his charge. There is an attractiveness in his character. We see in him an impulsive, thoughtless man; not what would be called a bad son ; his father's favourite; having some regard to his parent's wishes (eh. xxviii. 8, 9); but swayed by passing things, and without self-denial. Hungry and weary with the chase, he craved the food he saw (cf. Matt. iv. 3). But the price? His birthright, tho claim f.o a special benediction, the domestic priesthood (cf. Exod. xxii. 29), wero as nothing. He did not realise their value (cf. Heh. xi. 1). Tho present was everything (cf. 1 Cor. xv. 32). The pleasant, genial, headloug man is pronounced" profane." Observe- L THE GRADUAL EFFECT OD' SELF-INDULGENCE (cf. Matt. xix. 24). The birthright despised not through sudden temptation or any marked step of sin, but by worldly T2 824 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. No sharp line to tel_l.when_ dang;-r be,~·ms. Thmgs perf~ctly allowable, even laudable, may choke spmtual life•. Evc_n rn good work the mmd may be so engrossed in the work itself that commun~on with God fades, There is need of habitual self-denial (John vi. !)8) ; o_f keepmg gua_rd over the tendencies of daily life ; of definite aims, not passmg w1Shes ; of makmg personal communion with God an essential part of each day's work. ii. 1:EE DEADENING _EFFECT IN REL~TION TO REPENTANCE. "Time enough" ie IL fatal mistake (Acts xx1v. 25; 2 Cor. v1. 2). So far as we know Esau never repented Even when Jacob received the blessing he was sorry, but there was no real change· no confC'ssion of error. Self was still the ruling power. ' III. TrrE CALL TO ?ONSIDER _ou~ BIRTB:RIGHT (Rom. viii. 17; 1 John iii. 2). Not n;ierelJ a fu~ure bless!I'l:g·. Tlunkmg of_ 1~ thus leads to its being left out of view. Now there 1s reconc1hation, peace, spmt of adoption, the Spirit's witness in our hearts, freedom of access in prayer, imd promises to be realised in growing likeness to Christ and communion with him. Few would deliberately postpone to the end of life th~ claiming theiz: birthright and ma.king sure of it, the work of repentance and faith, and the casting away what has lnndered. But many without set purpose do delay. Each time the call is put away is a victory for the tempter.-M.

entries.title: GEN 26:1–6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A good man's perplexity. I. T11& CONTEMl'LATED JOUn~EY. 1. /l8 projected destination. Egypt. Renowned for fertility, the land of the Pharaohs was yet no proper resort for the son of Abraham, the heir of Canaan, and the friend of God. It was outside the land of promise ; it bad been to Abraham a scene of peril, and itwas not a place to which he was directed to turn. Considerations such as these should have operated to deter Isaac from even entertaining the idea of a pilgrimage to Egypt. But the behaviourof this Hebrew patriarch is sometimes outdone by that of modern saints, who not simply project, but actually perform, journeys, of pleasure or of business, across the boundary line which sepnrateij the Church from the world, into places where their spiritual interests are endangered, and that too not only without the Divine sanction, but sometimes in express violation of that authority. 2. Its ostensible occasion. The famine. A severe trial, especially to a flock-master. It was yet by no means an exceptional trial, but one which had occurred before in the experience of the inhabitants of Canaan, and in particular of hie father, and might possibly recur to himself, just as life's afllictions generally bear a singular resemblance to one another (1 Cor. x. 13; 1 Pet. iv. 12). It was not an accidental trial, but had been appointed and permitted by that Divine wisdom without whose sanction no calamity can fall on either nation or individual, saint or sinner (Deut. xxxii. 39; Pa. !xvi. 11 ; Amos iii. 6). And just as little was it purposeless, being designed to initiate Isaac in that life discipline from which no child of God can escape (Acts xiv. 22; Heh. xii. 11; James i. 2, 3). 3. Its secret inspirat·wn. Unbelief. J ehovnh, who had given the land to Isaac, could easily have maintained him in it notwithstanding the dearth, had it been hie pleasure not to provide a way of escape. Had Isaac not at this time been walking somewhat by sight, it is probable his thoughts would not have turned to Egypt. Most of the snint's doubtful trnnsnctious nnd dnngerous projects have a secret connection with the spirit of unbelief which causes to err. II. TnE DIVINE INTERPOSITION. 1. Prohibiting. " Go not down into Egypt." That Jacob subsequently went down to Egypt in obedience to Divine instructions is no proof that Isaac would have been blameless had he gone down without them. Abraham did so, but it is not certain that God approved of his conduct in thnt matter. Besides, though it could be shown that Abraham incurred no guilt and contructed no hurt by residence in Egypt, it would not follow that his son mig·ht venture thither with impunity nnd without sin. Hence the proposed journey was interdicted. So God in his word debars saints from going down to the unspiritunl nnd unbelieving world to endamage or imperil their souls' higher interests. 2. Prescribing. " Dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of: sojourn in this lnnd." It is always safest for the saint in seasons of perplexity to we.it for and to follow the light from heaven. Sufficient guidance God has promised, through his Spirit, by l1is word, and in hi<1 providence, to enable gracious ones who wait upon his tenching to detect the path of duty and the pince of safety. 3. Promising. For Isanc's enconragemont the various promises of the Abrahnmic covenant are repeated, renewed, and confirmed to himself for his father's snke; embracing promises of the Divine presence-" I will he with thee "-nnd the Divine blessing-" and will bless thee;" in which lntter are comprehended the inheritnnce,-" nil these countries,"-the seed,-" I will make thy seed to multiply,"-and the universnl snlvation-" in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed," which had been promised and gunranteed to Abraham by oath. So has God given to believers " exceeding great and precious promises" for Christ's sake, because of the covenant made with him, on the ground of the obedience rendered, and for the merit of the sncrifice presented, by him. III. THE FILIAL OBEDIENCE. "Isaac dwelt in Gerar," hnving removed thither in compliance with th11 Divine instructiona Like Abraham's, lsanc's obedien"9 'llr'ns- S26 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. (on. XXVI. 7-11. l. ,/J,finute, exactly following the Divine prescription. 2. ProinJJt, putting into immediate execution the Divine commandment. 3. Patient, remnming in the lnnd of the Philistines till God in his providence indicated it was time tf) remove. So should Christ's followers obey. HOMILIES BY VARIOUS AO rHORS. time of sojourn among the Philistines. The events of his intercourse with the Abimelech of his day resemble those of the former patriarch, though there are differences which show that tl1e recurrence is liiswrical. I. Gon REPEATS HIS LESSONS that they may make the deeper impression. The intention of the record is to preserve a certain line of IJwine guidance. Isaac h'od in the footsteps of .Abraham. We have Isaac's wells, oaths, feast, Shebah-nll follo~ing close upon those of the preceding generation. II. The SAME PRESERVATION OF THE COVENANT RACE in the midst of heathens confirms that covenant. The same lesson of special provide:ntial protection and blessing is thus repeated and enforced. .A.gain the same contrast of man's infirmitywitlt God's unchar1,gecible:ness. The perversity of the fleshly-minded man forming a marriage connection with heathen people, and bringing grief of mind to his parents, reveals the distinctness of the world from the kingdom of God.-R.

entries.content: -And the men of the place (i. e. the inhabitants of Gerar) asked him (literally, a.sked, or made inquiries; probably first at each other, though nltimntely the interrogations might reach Isaac himself) of bis wife (being in all likelihood fascinated by her beauty); and he said,-falling into the same infirmity as Abraham (eh. xii 13 ; xx. 2)-She is my sister:-which was certainly an equivocation, since, although sometimes used to designate a female relative generally (V'ide eh. mv. 60), the term "sister" was here designed to snggest that Rebekah was his own sister, born of the same parents. In propagating this deception Isaac appears to have been actuated by a simile.r motive to that which impelled his father-for he feared to say, She ismy wife; lest, said he (sc. to himself, the words describing the good man's secret app:ehensions), the men of the place should kill me for Rebekah ;-the historian adding, as the explanation of his fears-because she was fair to look upon (vide eh. xxiv. 16).

entries.title: GEN 26:7–11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A good man's transgress-ion. I. A LIE TOLD. 1. An unmitigated lie. It was scarcely entitled to claim the apology of being whot Abraham's falsehood was, on equivocation, Rebekah not being faaac's half-sister, but cousin. 2. A deliberate lie. Asked about his relations to Rebekah, he coolly replies that they are sister ond brother. He had no right to suppose his interrogators had ulterior designe against Rebekah's honour. 3. A cowardly lie. All'falsehoods spring from craven feor-fear of the consequences that may flow from telling the honest truth. 4. A dangerous lie. By his wicked suppression of the truth he wasguilty ofimperilling the chastity of her whom he sought to protect. Almost all falsehoods are perilous, and most of them are mistakes. 5. An unneceJJsary lie. No lie ever can be necessary; but least of all could this have been, when God had already promised to be with him in the land of the Philistines. 6. An unbeliemng lie. Had Isaac's faith been active, he would hardly have deemed it needful to disown his wife. 7. A wholly wmkless lie. Isaac might have remembered that twice over his father had resorted to this miserable stratagem, and that in neither instance had it sufficed to avert the danger which he dreaded. But lies generally are wretched hiding-places for endangered bodies or anxious souls. II. A LIE DETECTED. 1. God by his providence assists in the detection of liars. By the merest accident, as it might seem, Abimelech discovered the true relationship of Isaac and Rebekah; but both the time, place, and manner of that discovery were arranged by God. So the face of God is set against them that do evil, e'l"en though they should be his own people. 2. Liars commonly nssist in their own detection. Truth alone is sure-footed, and never slips; error is liable to stumble at every step. It is difficult to maintain o disguise for any lengthened period. The best fitting mask is sure in time to fall off. Actions good in themselves often lead to the detection of crimes. III. A LIE REPROVED. The conductof Isaac Abimelech rebukes-1. With prom_ptitude. Sending for Isaac, he charges him with his sin. It is the part of a true friend to expose deception whenever it is practised, ond, provided it be done in a proper spirit, the sooner it is done the better. Sin that long eludes detection is apt to harden the sinning heart and sear the guilty conscience. 2. With.fidelity. Characterising it os (I) o surprising inconsistency on the part of o good m11n like Isaac; (2) a reckless exposure of his wife's person, which wos for from becoming in a kindly husband ; and (3) 11n unjnstifioble offence against the people of the lnnd, who, by his carelessness and cowardice, might hove been led into grievous wickedness. 3. With forgiveness. Thot Abimelech did not intend to exact punishment from Isanc, or even cherish resentment against him in consequence of his behaviour, he proved by charging his people to beware of injuring in any way eilher Isaac or Rebekah. It is good oncl beautiful when mercy se11sons judgment, nnd the reproofs of friendship nre accompanied by messages of love.

entries.title: GEN 26:12–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.A good mam,'a prosperity. I. WHENCE IT PROCEEDED. 1. T¼ industry Qf Isaac. "Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfo1d." An intimate connection subsists between diligence and prosperity. (1) Ae there ie no harvest without a seed-time, eo there is no increase of wealth without the putting forth of personal labour in its acquisition (cf. Prov. x. 4; xiii. 4; xxviii. 19). (2) Ae by God's appointment harvest follows seed-time, so commonly "the hand of the diligent maketh rich" (cf. Prov. xiii. 4; xxi. 5; xxviii. 19). 2. The blessing of God. "And the Lord blessed him." As without Divine assistance the best contrived and most laboriously applied means may fail in the accumulation of material goods, so with heavenly succour the least likely instruments can achieve success. The harvests of the farmer depend more upon the goodness of God than upon the excellence of the plough (cf. Ps. cxxvii. 1, 2). II. IN WHAT IT BEBULTED. 1. The envJJ of the Philistines. Envy, one of the works of the flesh (Gal. v. 19 ; Jamee iv. 6), 11 frequent characteristic of evil men (1 Cor. iii. 3; Titus iii. 3), an occasional infirmity of pious souls (1 Cor. iii. 3; Phil. i. 15; 1 Pet. ii. 1), and straitly forbidden by the law of God (Exod. xx. 17; Ps. xxxvii. 1; Jamee v. 9), is commonly excited by observing the prosperity of others (Pa. xxxvii 7 ; lxxiii. 7 ; Eccles. iv. 4 ; cf. Rachel and Leah, eh. x:n:. 1, 15 ; Joseph's brethren, eh. xxxvii. 4--11, 19, 20; Acts vii. 9; Miriam and Aaron, Num. xii. 1-10; the princes of Darius, Dan. vi. 4), is usually accompanied with some degree of hatred (Cain, eh. iv. 4--8 ; Sarah, eh. xvi. 5, 6 ; Laban, eh. xxxi. 5), 11nd inevitably tends, as in the case of the Philistines, to hostility, secret or open. 2. The ~ci.()'11, of .Abimelech. The growing power of the patriarch had filled the monarch s mind with alarm. Interpreting the character of Isaac by his own, he conceived it impossible to possess large resources without using them to acquira dominion over othere. Modem kings and statesmen are scarcely further advanced, the prosperity of neighbouring empires being commonly regarded as a menace to the liberties of their own. It is the mission of Christianity, as regards both nations and individuals, to show how power of every kind can be possessed without injury, and wielded with advantage, to the highest interests of others. III. How IT WAS ILUNTAINED. By-1. Patience, or the exhibition of it. meek and unresisting spirit in submitting to injury. Whon Abimelech requested him to lenve the town of Gerar, he left. When the Philistines filled up his futher's wells, he quietly dug them out ngain. When tho herdmen of Gerar wrangled with his shepherds nbout a spring, he simply go.ve it up, and sought another; nnd when this too was disputed, he retired and sank n third. And all the ,vhile his flocks anti. herds kept on multiplying. A beautiful example of the spirit which Christ hue enjoined (Matt. v. 39-42), and of the promise which Christ has mnde (Matt. v. 5) to hie followers. 2. Perseverance, or tho diligent exercise of means in selecting pasture grounds nnd digging wells; not permitting himself to be discouraged by the o,.iposition of his neighbours, but, while peacefully allowing himself to he despo1led, steadily nttending to bis business. An illustration of thut quiet, determined, nnd unwearied application which often contributes more to success in life than brilliant abilities. 3. Piety, or the grateful recognition of God's hand in putting an end to the irritation and annoyance of his neighbours, and giving him at last a comfortable settlement at Rehoboth. It is grace in God which affords quiet neighbourhoods to reside in, easy circumstances to live in, and hopeful futures to trust in ; and it is piety in us to acknowledge that grace. Learn-1. That there is only one royal road to material prosperity, viz., diligence and devotion. 2. That if material prosperity can procure comforts, it is 11lso attended by drawbacks. 3. That material prosperity is often thrown away in litigation when it might be preserved by submission. 4. Thnt material prosperity should 1tir the heart's gratitude to God, 3/10 'l'HE BOOK 01!' GENESIS. [cu. XXVI. 23-35 II0MILIES BY VARIOUS AUTHORS.

entries.title: GEN 26:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Diggi,n[(, wells of salvation. "And he removed from thence, and digged another well. ' Historically, an instance of a meek and quiet spirit in contact with the world. ,vells precious. Often formed with much labour. Herdsmen of Gerar took what Isaac had digged. Twice he yielded for the sake of peace. Then l?e digged another, and for it they st~ove !lot: His example (cf. Matt. v. 39 ; 1 Cor. v1. 7). But we may also observe a typical s1gmficance. Wells,fountains sources of " living wnter" (Isa. xii. 3 ; Zech. xiii. 1) connected with spiritual blessi~gs (cf. 1 Cor. x. 4 with John iv. 14, and vii. 39). I. ISAAC DIGGED, to find "the gift of God" (common Eastern name for water). The gift is from God alone (Isa. xliv. 3 ; Zech. xii. 10). His will to bless appears through the whole Bible-in the first formation of man, and in care for the salvation of sinners (Luke xix. 10). But many, though thirsty, do not seek living water. They have not peace. Separation from God brings unrest (Isa. lvii. 20). But the cause is not believed, and the way of comfort not loved. Many try all ways to find peace except the right one. They will follow preachers, or take up systems, or join associations. Bat Christ's word is "Come unto me." Again, many will not dig ; content merely to wish. God who bestows the gift has appointed means (Matt. xi. 12). These do not really desire a work of grace in their souls. Want to be made safe, not to be renewed ; to be delivered from fear, bat not disturbed just now. Hence do not search their Bibles (Ps. cxix. 130), or pray for the Holy Spirit (Ezek. xxxvii. 9), or care for the salvation of others (1 John iii. 17). It is God's will- we should dig. He may send a blessing unsought. But usuallyhe works through means. The Bible, prayer, the Lord's table, Christian converse, Christian work (Prov. xi. 25), all are as wells, means for getting the water of life; nothing in themselves, yet rnade effectual where the blessing is desired. IL HINDRAN'CES. Let none expect to possess wells of salvation without. They fonn the trial of faith (1 Pet. i. 7). From those who love not God. A Christian member of a worldly family, or cast among careless associates, meets many hindrances. They may be open or veiled ; in opposition or in mistaken kindness. And time for prayer is intruded on, and work for God is hindered, and a constantopposing influence is felt to chill the love of God. Or the hindrance may be from within. In prayer the mind overpowered by intrusive thoughts ; besetting sins constantlygaining the victory ; our spirits not in harmony with the "still email voice." Remember it is God's will through trial to give victory (1 Cor. x. 13). Amalek fought against Israel (Exod. xvii.) as the herdsmen strove against Isaac, but the way of victory was the same in both instances-trust and perseverance. Ill. DIGGED ANOTHER WELL (Gal. vi. 9). Will the Lord fail his people though surrounded by hindrances? le some means of grace debarred ? Is some line of Christian work, some way of Christian progress, closed against thee ? Dig another well. Seek and pray for other channels in which to consecrate thy life. Perhaps tlie real foe hindering thee was self-will, and God has helped thee to put down self. Jesus cried, 11 Come unto me and drink." Whatever be the well, he is the source of its spring. Make it clear to your own heart that you are pressing to him. Tell God that it is indeed so. Then in some fonn or other the prayer, 11 Spring up, 0 well," sbnll have an abundant !lnswer.-M.

entries.content: -And thef said, We saw certo.inly-litero.lly, seeing we saw, i e. wo essuredly perceived, or, we have indeed dis- Eovered (vide Ewe.Id's 'Heb. Synt.,' § 312). Abimelech and his ministers first explain tho mDtive which has impelled them to solicit o. renewal of the old alliance-that the Lord was with thee :-the use of Jehovah instead of Elohim, as in eh. xxi. 22, docs not prove that this is a Jehovistic elabor• ation of the earlier legend. Neither is it necessary to suppose that the term Jehovah is o. Mosaic translation of the epithet employed by Abimelech (Rosenmiiller). entries.title: GEN 26:23–35
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.A good man's environment. I. IsAAC AND JErrovAn. 1. Jelwvali's grace to Isaac. (1) Revealing his presence. "The Lord appeared unto him." Similar discoveries are now made to saints in "night" seasons, nnd at locnlitios liko BeersbeLa, previously consecrated by gracious revelations of himself. (2) Proclaiming Lis character. "I am the God of thy father;" on nppellation that must lmve sounded dear to Abraham's son, but not more than the God of our Lord Jesus Christ is to Christians. (3) Comforting his servant. " Fear not, for I om with thee." So a Christian bas the best right to preserve equanimity nmid life's vicissitudes nnd tribulations, Christ's command (Matt. x. 31 ; Luke xii. 32) ; and the best reason, Christ's presence (Matt. xviii. 20; xxviii. 20). (4) Renewing his promises. "I will bless tLee and multiply thy seed." God renews his promises when he reYives their impressions on the heart, which he does for his own glory ns the faithful PromiHer, and for his people's comfort as necessity requires. 2. Isaac's gratitude to Jehovah,. (1) Building an altar; on net expressive of Isaac's personal uevotion (1 These. v. 18). (2) Invoking God's name; referring to the public recital of God's goodness (vide eh. xii. 8). It becomes saints to remember God's mercies (Pa. xlviii. 9 ; ciii. 1, 2), and to speak of them to others (Pa. !xvi. 16 ; lxxviii. 4). (3) Pitching a tent and digging o well ; indicative of Isaac's confidence in God. Grateful acknowledgment of past mercies, public celebration of present mercies, Lope~ul expectation of future mercies, are duties incumbent •1pon all, but especially on samts. OH, XXVIJ, 1-14,] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 333 , II. Js.uo AND AnIMELECH. _1. Awmelech's request of Isaac. (1) Tbe nature of 1t: 11 demnnd for a forma~ alliance confirmed by the sanctions of religion. "Let there be now an oath betwut us, nnd let us make a covenant with thee." (2) The object of it: his own rather than Isaac's protection. "That thou wilt do us no hurt." Most men suspect their neighbours sooner than themselves. C'hristianity requires saints to be as careful of their neighbour's interests as of their own (Phil. ii. 4). (3) The motive of it: partly selfish fear, and partly a recognition of Isaac's goodness. "Th?u a~t no~ the blessed of the Lord." 2. Isaac's_ receptwn of Abimelech. (1) Cautious rnquuy, "Wherefore come ye to me?" It 1s prudent to try injurious men before we trust them. (2) Generous entertainment. "He made them a feast." Overlooking, as became a good man, their too favourable account of themselves, he gave them welcome to his hospitable board. God's people should not be censorious even in judging enemies; when obliged to suffer, they should forget as well as forgive injuries, and never should they disdain overtures for peace, though made by those who have done them wrong. 3. Solemn adjuration. "And they aware onu to another." Though religion does not lie within the sphere of politics, politics lie ,vithin the sphere of religion. Nothing should be done by agood man that he cannot sanctify by the word of God and prayer (Col. iii. 17, 23). 4. Peaceful dism-issal. "Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.'' Those who come for pence should never go without peace, It is the saint's interest as well as duty to follow after peace (Matt. v. 9). No sooner had Isaac dismissed Abimelech and his mi11i-sters, than hie servants came with tidings of their successful operations in sinking a well. Peace-makers seldom fail to find a recompense (James iii. 18). III. ISAAC AND ESAU. 1. Esau's sinful ma:rri,age. (1) He took more wives than one, which was against the fundamental law of marriage (eh. ii. 24; M11tt. xix. 5); (2) be married Canaanitish women, which was against the will of God, as expressed by Abraham in regard to Isaac's marriage, and doubtless also by Isaacwith reference to Eeau's ; and (3) he acted contrary to·his parents' counsel in the matter, which was a violation of that filial duty which he owed his aged parents. 2. Isaac'a bitter grief. (1) Deeply seated as to its intensity, being bitterness of spirit (Prov. xviii. 14); (2) truly religious as to its character, being occasioned chiefly by the circumstance that Esau'e ill-assorted marriages were not such as Heaven could approve; and (3) sympathisingly shared by Rebekah, whose motherly bosom was also stricken with sorrow at her son's impiety. Learn-I. That God's gracious visits to his people are always admirably suited to their needs in respect of time, place, nnd manner. 2. That when a mnn's ways please God he maketh even his enemies be at peace with him. 3. That while a wise son maketh a glad 4ther, a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother.

entries.title: GEN 27:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to paH, that when laaao was old,-nccordin~ to the gcnernllynccepted cnlculation, in his one hundred and thirty-seventh year, Joseph, having been introduced to Phamoh in his thirtiethyear(eh. xii. 46), nad hnving been thirty-nine years of nge (eh. xiv. 6) when his father, aged ono hundred and thirty (eh. xlvii. 9), came down to Egypt, must have been born before Jacob w11s nine~-ono; consequently, as his birth occurred m the fourteenth year of Jacob's sojourn in llfosopotnmia (cf. eh. xxx. 25 with xxix. 18, 21, 27), Jacob's flight must have taken place when he wo.s eeventysevea, But Jacob was born in Isnac's sixtieth yenr (eh. xxv. 26); hence Isaac was now one_hundred a.nd thirty-seven. [cu. XXVII. 1-14 xxxi. 41)-and his eyes were dim,-litcrally, 1oere jailing in st1·ength, hence becoming dim (1 Sam. iii. 2). His failing sight, and probably the recollection that Ishmael, his half-brother, had died at 137 (if that was Isaac's age at this time; ~•ide supi-a), occasioned tho suspicion that his mrn end could not be remote, though he lirnd forty-three or sixty-three years longer, according to the calculation adopted, expiring at the ripe age of 180 (i,-ide eh. =. 28).

entries.title: GEN 27:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now therefore take, I pra.y thee, thy wea.pons,-the word "weapon" signifying a utensil, vessel, or finished instrument of any sort (cf. eh. xx:iv. 53 ; x:xxi. 37 ; xlv. 20). XXV. 28.

entries.title: GEN 27:1–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The stolen blessing: a domestic drama.-1. Isaac and Rebekah, or plotting and C()?tnte:rJ?lotting. L TnE SCHEME OF Is.u.o. 1. Its sinful object. 'fhe heavenly oracle having with no uncertain sound proclaimed Jacob the theocratic heir, the bestowment of the patriarchal benediction on Esau was clearly an unholy design. That Isaac, who on Mount Moriah had evinced such meek and ready acquiescence in Jehovah's will, should in old age, from partiality towards his firstbom, or forgetfulness of Jehovah's declaration, endeavour to thwart the Divine purpose according to election affords a melancholy illustration of the deceitfulness of sin even in renewed hearts, and of the deep-seated antagonism between the instincts of nature and the designs c,f grace. 2. Its secret character. The commission assigned to Esau does not appear to have been dictated by any supposed connc-ction between the gratification of the palate, the reinvigoration of the body, or the refreshment of the spirit and the exercise of the prophetic gift, but rather by a desire to divert the attention of Rebekah from 11uppoeing that anything unusual was going on, and so to secure the necessary privacy for carrying out the scheme which he bad formed. Had Isaac not been doubtful of the righteousness of what he had in contemplation, he would never have resorted to manrouvring and secrecy, but would have courted unveiled publicity. Crooked ways love the dark (John iii. 20, 21). 3. Its urgent motive. Isaac felt impelled to relieve bis soul of the theocratic blessing by a sense of approaching dissolution. If it be the weakness of old men to imagine death nearer, it is the folly of young men to suppose it farther distant than it is. To young and old alike the failure of the senses should be a premonition of the end, and good men should set their houses in order ere they leave the world (eh. m. 6; 2 Kings xx. 1; Isa. =viii. 1). 4. Its inherent weakness. That Isaac reckoned on Rebekab's opposition to his scheme seems apparent; it is not so obvious that he calculated on God's being against him. Those who meditate unholy deeds should first arrange that God will not be able to discover their intentions. II. THE STRATAGEM OF REBEKAH. 1. The design was legitimate. Instead of her behaviour being represented as an attempt to outwit her aged, blind, and bed-ridden husband (for which surely no great cleverness was required), and to stealthily secure the blessing for her favourite, regard for truth demands that it should rather be characterised as an endeavour to prevent its surreptitious appropriation for Esau. 2. The inspiratwn was religious. Displaying a considerable amount of woman's wit in its conception and execution, and perhaps largely tainted by matemal jealousy, Rebekah's stratagem ought in fairness to be traced to her belief in the pre-natal oracle, which had pointed to Jacob as the theocratic heir. That her faith, however mixed with unspiritual alloy, was strong seems a just conclusion from her almost reckless boldness (ver. 13). 3. The wickedness was inexcusable. Good as were its end and motive, the stratagem of Rebekah was deplorably wicked. It was an act of cruel imposition on a husband who had loved her for well-nigh a century; it was a base deed of temptation and seduction, viewed in its relations to Jacob-the prompting of a son to sin against a father; it was a signal offence against God in m11ny ways, but chiefly in the sinful impn.tience it displayed, and in the foolish supposition that his sovereign designs needed the assistance of, or could be helped by, human craft in the shape of female cunning. III. THE RIVAL AC00MPLICEB. 1. The confederate of Isaac. The guilt of Esau consisted in seeking to obtain the birthright when he knew (1) that it belonged to Jacob by Heaven's gift, (2) that he had parted with any imaginary title he ever had to expect it, (3) that he was utterly unqualified to possess it, and (4) that he was endeavouring to obtain it by improper means. 2. The tool of Rebekah. That Jacob in acting on_ his mother's counsel was not sinless is ~vinced br the.fa~t t~at be (1) perceived its hazardoua nature (vers. 11, 12), (2) discerned its cnmmahty, and yet (3) allowed himself to carry it through. Lessons :-1. The wickedness of trying to subvert the will of Heaven-exemplified in Isaac. 2. The sinfulness of doing evil that good may come-illustrated by the OB. XXVII. lli-29.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 337 cond~ct of Rebek~h. 3. The criminaJity of following evil counsel, in opposition to the light of consc1ence and the restramts of Providence-shown by the conduct of both Esau and Jaoob,

entries.title: GEN 27:24–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said (showing that a feeling of uneasy suspicion yet lingered in his mind), Axt thou my very son Esaut Luther wonders how Jacob wasable to brazen it out ; adding, "I should probablyhave run away in terror, and let the dish fall ;" but, instead of that, he added one more lie to those which had preceded, saying with undisturbed composure, I am-equivalent to an English yes; upon which the blind old patriarchrequested that the proffered dainties might be set before him. Having partaken of the carefully-disguised kid's flesh, and drunkan exhilarating cup of wine, he further desired that his favourite son should approach his bed, saying, Come near now, and kiss me, my son-a request dictated more by paternal affection (Keil, Kalisch) than by lingering doubt which required reassure.nee (Lange).

entries.title: GEN 27:27
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he came near, and kissed him. Originally the act of kissing had a symbolical character. Here it is a sign of affection between a parent and a child ; in eh. xxix. 13 between relatives. Itwas also atoken of friendship (Tobit vii. 6; x. 12; 2 Sam. xx. 9; Matt. xxvi 48; Luke vii 45; xv. 20; Acts xx. 87). The kissing of princes was a symbol of homage (1 Sam. x. 1; Pa. ii. 12; Xenoph., 'Cyrop.,' vii 6, 32). With the Persians it was a mark of honour (Xenoph., 'Agesil,' v. 4). Tho Rabbine permitted only three kinds of kisses- the kiss of reverence, of reception, and of dismiseal The kiss of charity was practised among disciples in the early Christian Church (Rom, xvi. 16; 1 C0r. xvi. 20; 2 Cor. xiii. 12; 1 Thcss. v. 26 ; 1 Pot. v. 14 ; vide Kitto'e ' Cyclopedia,' ut. Kissing). And he smelled the smell of his raiment,-not deliberatoly, in order to detect whether they belonged to a shepherd or a huntsmnn (Tuch), but accident.ally while in the net of kissing. The odour of Esau's garments, impregnatnd with the fragrance of the aromatic herbs of Palestine, excited the dull sensibilities of the nged prophet, suggesting to his mind pictures of freshness and fertility, and inspiring him to pour forth his promised benediction -and blessed him (not a second time, the statement in ver. 23 being only inserted by anticipation), and said,-the blessing, as is usualinelevatedpro1>heticutterances,assumes a poetic and a.ntistrophical form (cf. Esau's blessing, "l"ers. 39, 40)-See, the smell of my son is as the smell of afield-the first clause of the poetic stanza. cleo.rly connects with the odour of Esau's raiment e.s that which had opened the fount ofprophetic song in Isaac'a breast, so far at least e.s its peculiar form was concerned ; its secret ins_puation we know wasthe Holy Ghostoperating through Isaac's faith in the promise (vide Heb. xi. 20)- which the Lord hath bleBBed. The introduction of the name Jehove.h instead of Elohim in this second clause proves that Isaac did not mean to liken his son to an ordinary well-cultivated field, but to "b. field like that of Paradise, resplendent with tr11ces of the Deity-an ideal field, bearing the same relation to an ordinary one as Israel did to the heathen-a kind of enchanted garden, such as would be realised at a later period in Canaan, as far e.s the fidelity of the peoplo permitted it" (Hengstenberg).

entries.title: GEN 27:15–29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The stolen blessing: a domestic drama.-2. Isaac and Jacob, or tlze successj1tl stratage;m, I. JACOB s DECEPTION OJI' lsAA0. Jacob's pcrsonation of Esau was-I. Deftly pepared. 'rhe ingenious Rebekah, having dressed him in the fragrant festal robes of the princely hunter, covered his smooth skin with the soft, silky hide of the camel-goat, and put into his hand the simulated dainty dish which she had cooked. It is a melancholy thing when either woman's wit or man's sagacity is prostituted to unholy ends. 2. Boldl'lf avowed. Entering hie father's tent, and approaching within easy reach of the mvnlid's couch, at the same time imitating Esau's intonations, the heartless impostor calls upon his aged parent to arise and eat of his son's venison, in response to hie father's inquiry olso openly declaring himself to be Esau; in which was a fourfold offence-against his venerable father, against his absent brother, against himself, and against God. Never is a lie, and seldom is a sin of any kind, single or simple in its criminality. That scheme cannot be a good one of which the first act is a lie. 3. Persistently maintained. In the face of his father's searching interrogation, careful exnmination, nnd mnnifest trepidation, Jncob brazens out the imposture he had begun, covering his first falsehood by a second, and his second by a third, in which he verges on the limits of blasphemy, allowing himself to be handled by his aged parent without betraying by a word or sign the base deception he was prnctieing, and at length capping his extraordint1ry wickedness by a solemn asseveration of his identity with Esau that cnrried with it in the hearing of Isaac much of the impressiveness and weight of an oath,-" I am thy very son Esau I" It is amazing to what depths of criminality those may fnll who once step aside from the straight paths of virtue. 4. Completely successful. Critical as the ordeal was through which he passed, he was not detected. So God sometimes allows wicked schemes to prosper, accomplishing hie own designs thereby, though neither approving of the.schemes nor holdingthe schemers guiltless. II. !Bile's BENEDICTION OF JACOB. The patriarchal blessing which Isaac uttered was-I. Divinely inspired as to its origin. It was not within the power of !so.no to either conceive or express it in any arbitrarily selected moment, or in any particular way or place thnt he might determine. Least of all was it the production of Isaac's ordinary faculties under the physical or mental impulse of delicious viands or paternal affection. It was the outcome of an unseen afflatus l.'f the Divine Spirit upon the venerable patrinrch'e soul (Heh. xi. 20). 2. Providentially directed as to its destinatuYTI,. Intended for the firstbom, it was prono1~nced upon the younger of his sons. Had Rebekah and Jacob not interposed with their miserable trick, there is reW!on to suppose thnt God would hnve di8co,·erecl means of defeating the miRgui,lcd z 2 840 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH, XXVII, 30-40, patriarch's design; perhaps by laying an embargo upon hia lipa, as he did on Balaam (Numb. xxii. 38); perhaps by miraculously guiding his speech, as afterwards he guided Jacoh's hands (eh. xlviii. 14). But none the less is the Divine finger discernible in carrying the heavenly blessing to its predestined recipient, that he does not interfere with Rebekah's craft, but allows it, beneath the guidance of his ordinary providence, to work out its appropriate result. 3. Ruhly laden as to its contents. It embraced-(1) Material enrichment, represented by the dew, corn, and wine, which may also be regarded as symbolic of spiritual treasures; (2) personal ad- ;ancement in the world and the Church, foreshadowing both the political supremacy 1rnd ecclesiastical importance to which Israel should afterwards attain; (3) spiritual influence, emblematic of the religious priesthood enjoyed first by the Hebrew people as a nation, and latterly by Christ, the true Seed of .Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob. 4. Absolutely permanent as to its duratwn. Though Isaac subsequently learnt of the deception which had been practised towards him, he felt that the wor<ls he had spoken were beyond recall. This was proof decisive that Isaac spake not of himself, but as he was moved by the Holy Ghost. His own benediction, uttered purely by and from himself, might, and, in the circumstances, probably would, have been revoked; the blessing of Jehovah transmitted through his undesigned act he had no power to cancel. Learn-1. That those who attempt to deceive others ure not unfrequently themselves deceived. 2. That those who enter on a sinful course may speedily sink deeper into sin than they intended. 3. That deception practised by a son against a father, at a mother's instigation, is n monstrous and unnatural display of wickedness. 4. That God can accomplish-his own designs by means of man's crimes, without either relieving them of guilt or himself being the author of sin. 5. That the blessing of God maketh rich and addeth no sorrow therewith. 6. That the gifts and calling of God are without repentance,

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Isaac answered and said unto Esau (repeating the substance of the blessing already conferred on Ja.cob), Behold, I have made himthy lord,-litero.lly, behold, a lord (vide ou ver. 29) have I constituted him to thee; lsanc hereby intimating that in pronouncing the words of blessing he hail been speaking under a celestio.l impulse, nnJ. therefore with absolute authority-and all hia brethren have I given to him for servants (for the fulfilment vide 2 Snw. viii. 14), and with corn and wine have I sustilined him :-i e. declared that by these he shall be sustained or supported (cf. \'Cl", 28) -and what shall I do now unto thee, my BOD 1 Yer, 38.-And Eaa\~ 6aid unto his father, Hast thou but one blessing, my father l Not as desiring either tho reversal of tho :patriarchnl sentence upou Jacob, which ho appears to ho.ve understoo,l to be irrevocnblo, or an extension of its gracious provisions, so e.s to include him as well as Jacob; but as soliciting such n benediction ns would pince him, at least in respect of temporalities, on o.
