[cu. xxvn. 80-40. though recognising it, he was willing to let it go :Bless me, even me also, 0 my father, And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept (cf. Heb. xii. 17). "'rhose tears expressed, indeed, sorrow for his forleiture, but not for the sinful levity by which it had been incurred. They were ineffectual (i. e. they did not lead to genuine repentance) because Esau was incapable of true repentance" (vide Delitzsch on Heb. xii. 17). Yer. 39.-And Isaac his father (moved by the tearful earnestness of Esau) answered and said unto him, - still speaking under inspiration, though it is doubtful whether what he spoke was a real, or only an apparent, blessing- (mde infra)- llehold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the ea.rth, and of the dew of heaven from above. Literally, from (lt,,) the fatness/!3 (or fat places) of the earth, and from the dew of heaven; a substantial repetition of the temporal blessing bestowed on Jacob (ver. 28), with certain important variations, such a.a the omission of plenty of corn and wine at the close, a.nd of the name of Elohim at the commencement, of the benediction (Vulgate, Luther, Calvin, Amsworth, Rosenmilller, •Speaker's Commentary') ; though, by a.ssigning to the preposition a privative rather than a partitive sense, it is readily_transformed into "amodifiedcurse"-behold, au;ay /!'om thefatness/!3 ofthe earth, &c., shall thy d'lllelling be, meaning that, in contrast to the la.nd of Canaan, the descendants of Esau shculd be located in a sterile region (Tuch, Rnobel, Kurtz, Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch,Murphy). In support ofthis latter rendering it is urged (1) thatitisgrammatically admissible ; (2) thatitcorrespondswith the present aspect of ldum:ea, which is "on the whole a dreary and l!D.productive land;" (3) that it agrees with the preceding statement that every blessing had already been bestowed upon Jacob; and (4) that it explains the play upon the words "fatness" and "dew," which are here chosen to describe astate ofmatters exacUy the opposite to that which WELS dcclarod to bo tho lot of Jacob. On the other l1and, it is felt to be somewhat arbitrary to assign to tho preposition a pnrtitivo sense in ver. 28 and n privativo in ver. 39, Though called in later times (Mai. i. 3) a. we.ste and desolate region, it may not ho.ve been originally so, or only in comparison with Co.naan; while according to modem travellers the glens and mountain terracesofEdom, covered with rich soil, only want an industrious population to .:onvert the entire region into "one of the wealthiest, a.a it is one of the most picturesque, countries in the world."

entries.title: GEN 27:40
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And by thy sword shalt thou live,-literally, upon thy sword shalt th011, be, i e. thy maintenance shall depend on thy sword; a prediction that Esau's descendants should be a warlike and tumultuous people of predatory habits (cf. Josephus, B. I., iv. 4)-and shalt serve thy brother;-a prediction afterwards fulfilled (cf. 1 Sam. xiv. 47 ; 2 Sam. viii 14 ; 1 Kings x:i. 16 ; 2 Kings xiv. 7-10; 2 Chron. XL 22-25)- and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from oft' thy neck. The verb ,~,. used of beasts which have broken the yoke and wander freely about (Gesenius, Furst), appears to hint at an incessant restlessness onthepart ofEdom whileunder Israel'syoke which should eventually terminate in regaining their independence. The exact rendering of the clause is obscure1 but perhaps means that when Edom shoUld roam about as a freebooter (Lange), or should revolt (Alford), or should toss, shake, or struggle against the yoke (Vulgate, Keil, Hengstenberg, •Speaker's Commentary), he should succeed. Other renderings are, when thou shalt bear rule (Kimchi), when thou shalt repent (Je.rchi), when thou shalt be strong (Samaritan), when thou prevailest (Muryhy), when thou shalt truly desire it (Kalisch), when thou shalt Eull down (LXX.); because thou art restless (Hii.vernick).

entries.title: GEN 27:30–40
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -ne stalen blessing: a domesti,c drama.-3. Isaac and Esau, fJ1" the hunter's lamentation. I. Isuc's STARTLING DISCOVERY. 1. Unexpectedly made. The return of Esau from the hunting-field with a dish of venison was a sudden and most unpleasant revelation to the aged patriarch, showing that in some inexplicable manner he had been out-manCJluvred, and, as it were, constrained against his will to bestow the blessing upon Jacob. So in common life it is not unfrequently seen that the u1:::ixpected is that which happens, that wicked schemes prove abortive, that the deceiver is himself deceived-" the engineer hoist on his own petard,"-and ihot men are often made the involuntary and unconscious instruments of furthering the will of Heaven. 2. Tremhlingly received. Apprehending what had taken ploce the blind old invalid " feared a great fear exceedingly/ saddened with an inward horror, uot through disappointment at the failure of his scheme, or indignation nt the wicked c-raft a.nd heartleas duplicity of Rebekah's favourite, but alarm at hie own on. x.xvu. 30-40.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 343 sinful intention which God bad thus manifestly seen and thwarted. It is well when the soul trembles a.ta discovery of its own wickedness. Gracious souls dread nothing more than ste.nding on the verge of sin. 3. Pathetwal,ly a,cknr.noledged. "Thy brother ea.me with subtilty, and bath taken a.way thy blessing;" and, "I ha'\'"e blessed him: yea, and he shall be blessed." It becomes parents to commiserate their children's misfortunes, and especially to sorrow if they miss the blessings of salvation. They who lack these, even when they do not wish to obtain them, are objects of profoundest pity. 4. Meeldy acquusced in. Recognising the hand of God in the remarkable transaction in which he had been an e.ctor, with true humility and faith the venerable patriarch bowed before the will of the Supreme. Neither Esau's prayers and tears, nor his own paternal affections, could stimulate so much as a wish to undo what had been done. To a truly pious heart the will of God is final. "Thy will be done " is the language of faith. II. EsAu's SINGULAB BEHAVIOUR. 1. His lntter lamentation for him8elf. Esau's grea.t and exceeding bitter cry " wa.s expressive not of heartfelt grief for his sinful levity in pa.rting with the birthright, or guilefnl beha.viour in attempting to secure the blessing; but (1) of deep mortification at being over-reached by his crafty brother; (2) of remorseful chagrin at not recovering the blessing he had practically s~endered in the sale of the birthright; (3) of earnest desire to induce Isaac to revoke the words he had spoken. The repentance which he sought carefully with tears (Heb. xii. 17) was not his own change of heart, but his father's change of mind. 2. His wrathful indignation against his brother. "Is he l)Ot rightly named Jacob? for he bath supplanted me thesetwo times." Astatementnot quite accurate; but nngry men are seldom remarkable for accuracy of statement; a statement a.lso expressive of hatred against Jacob, and incensed brothers often call each other bad names. Good men should be angry and sin not. Indignation, even when righteous. should be restrained. 3. His tearful request to liisfather. "Bless me, me nlso, 0 my father I " Having lost the blessing of the covennnt, be was still desirous of possessing some sort of blessing. Wicked men often covet the materinl advantages of religion who have no desire to eharo in its spiritual enrichments. Ill lsilc's SOLEMN DECLARATION. 1. OJ Esau's subjection to Jacob. "Behold, I have made him thy lord." A prediction of (1) politicnl subordination, ofterwards fulfilled in the conquests of Israel; nnd (2) of possible salvation to Esau and his descendants through believing recognition of the spiritual ascendancy of Jacob and his seed. 2. Of Esau's portion from God. (1) A fat soil. God appoints to all men, individuafs and nations, the bounds of their habitation. Inhabitants of fertile regionshave n specinl call to thankfulness. (2) A roving life. Though the warlike character of Esau's descendants was of God's appointment and permission, it is no just inference that savnge tribes are os useful o.s those of settled and improved ho.bits, or that God does not desire the cllifusion of civilisation and the elevation of the ro.ce. (3) Ultimo.ta independence. Though eome nntions have been plo.ced in subjection, it is God's will tho.t o.11 should aspire to freedom. Revolt, rebellion, insurrection o.ro sometimes a people's highest duty. LessO'T/,8:-1. The blessing of the covenant is not of him that willeth or of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy. 2. Those who despise God's salvation in youth cannot always obtain it in manhood or age. 3. Those who finally come short of eternal life will ha.ve no one to blame but themselves. 4. No one need sue in vain for Heo.ven's favour, since the blessing is not now for one, but for all. 5. There is a difference between l?enitence and remorse. 6. Though no man co.n hopl.l to cho.nge the mind of God, it lB within the power of a.II men to desire o.nd to effect n change upon their own heo.rts. 7. The prediction of n nation's or a person's futuru does not interfere with the free operation of the human will.

entries.title: GEN 27:33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's deceit. Esau supplanted. In this familiar no.rrative the fol• lowing points mny be distinguished:- .I. Isuc's ERROR-connecting a solemn blessing with mere gratification of th~ senses, neglect of the Divine word, favouritism towards the son leFS worthy. 3H TllE BOOK OF GENEsts. Ccn. Xlt\rII, 30--40. II. JAcoB's 601lTILTY and selfishness. The birthright had been sold to him; he might have obtained the blessing by fair agreement. His fear of Esau lay at the root of his deceit. One sin leads on to another. Those who entangle themselves with the world are involved more and more in moral evil. III. REBEKAH's AFP'F:CTI0N was perverted into unmotherly partiality and unwifely treachery to Isaac. The son's guilt rested much on the mother's shoulders, for she laid the plot and prepared the execution of it. All were sad examples of aelfassertion destroying the simplicity of faith. And yet-- IV: THE COVENA:NT Goo over-rules the weakness and error of_his people. The blessmg was appomted for Jacob. Although pronounced by an instrument blind foolish, sinful, deceived, it yet is the blessing, which, having been lodged in Isaac' must pass on to the true heir of Isaac, who, according to the promise and prediction: is Jacob. V. The lower character and standing of Esau·and hie inferior blessing represents the distinction between THE CHOSEN PEOPLE AND THOSE WHO, WHILE NOT INCLUDED IN THE COMMONWEALTH OF lsB.AEL, may yet by connection and intercourse with it derive some portion of the Divine benediction from it. Both in pre-Christian and Christian times there have been nations thus situated. Vl The LATE REPENTANCE of the supplanted Esau. He found no possibility of avertini; the consequences of his own error (Heh. :xii. 17), no place where repentance would av'ail to recover that which was lost. The "great and exceeding bitter cry " only reveals the shame, the blessing taken away. Those who, like Esau, despise their place in the fawily of God are driven out into the fierce opposition of the world; "by their sword" they must live and "serve their brethren," Vil THE END OF DECEIT IS HATRED, passion, fear, flight, individual and family disorder and suffering. Yet again the merciful hand interposes to over-rule the errors of man. Jacob's flight from Esau's hatred is his preservation from ungodly alliance with heathen neighbours, and the commencement of a wholesome course of discipline bywhich his character was purged of much of its evil, and his faith deepened and developed.-R.

entries.title: GEN 27:36
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Unfaitlifulness in believers. "Is not he rightly named Jacob?" Jacob, lsrnel-.bow widely difl'erent the thoughts suggested by the two names. Both tell of success. But one is the man of craft, who takes by the heel to trip up. The oilier, as a prince of God (cf. Luke i. 15), prevails through believing prayer. Yet Jacob became Israel, and Israel had once been Jacob. The plant of faith has often to struggle through a hard soil. To understand the lessons of his life, remember-I. In contrast to Esau, he was a man of faith. His desire was for a future and spiritual blessing. He believed that it was to be his, and that belief influenced his life. But-2. His faith was imperfect and partial in its operation, and this led to inconsistencies (cf. Matt. :xiv. 29, 30; Gal. ii. 12). Naturally quiet, his life was passed chiefly at home. Godly influences undisturbed by outward life taught him to worship God, and to prize his promise. But he had not proved his armour (cf. 1 Cor. x. 12); and, as often happens, the object of hie foit.h wna the means of his trial. His father's purpose in favour of Esau shook his faith (cf. 1 Pet. iv. 18). He yielded to the suggestion to obtain by deceit what God had promised to give (Isa. !ix. 1), and earned his brother's taunt, "Is not he rightly named Jacob? " Yet it does not appear that he was conscious of having failed in faith. Consider- !. TrrE DANGER OF SELF-DECEIVING (cf. Ezek. :xiii. 10). One brought up among godly influences may seem to possess faith. Ways of faith, hopes of faith, may be familiar to him. He may really embrace them, really desire a spiritual prize. But 110t without cause are we warned (1 Cor. :x. 12). Some plan of worldly wisdom, some point of self-seeking or self-indulgence, attracts him; only a little way; not into anything distinctly wrong. Or he falls into indolent self-sufficiency. Then there is u shrinking from close walk with God. Formality takes the place of confidence. All way seem outwardly well ; but other powers than God's will are at work within. And if now some more searching trial is sent, some more distinct choice between God and the world, a self-satisfying plea is easily found. And the self-deceit whiob CD. XXVlt. 41~40,] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 345 led to the foll makes it unfelt. And the path is lighted, but not from God (Isa. 1. 11). II. THE HARM DONE TO OTHERS BY UNFAITHFULNESS OF CnRISTIAN9 (cf. Rom. ii. 24; xiv. 16). The world is quick to mark inconsistencies of believers. They form an excuse for the careless, a :plea for disbelieving the reality of holiness. .And for weak Christians they throw the rnfluence of example on the wrong side (cf. 1 Cor. viii. 9). Deeds have more power than words ; and tho course of a life may be turned by some thoughtless yielding. Nor can the harm be undone even by repentance. The failure is visible, the contrition and seeking pardon are secret. The sins of good men are eagerly retailed. The earnest supplication for pardon and restoration are known to few, and little cared for. The man himself may be forgiven, and rise stronger from his fall ; but the poison in the soul of another is still doing its deadly work. III. THE WAY OF SAFETY, Realise the living Christ (Ephes. iii. 17). Rules of themselves can do little; but to know the love of Christ, to beaJ it in mind, is power.-M.

entries.title: GEN 27:41
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Esau hated Jacob-a proof that he was not penitent, however disap, pointed and remorseful (cf. Obad. 10, 11 ; 1 John iii 12, 16)-becaue of the bleSBing wherewith his father ble11ed him :-notwithstanding the fact that he too had received an appropriate benediction ; a display of envy u well as wrath, another proof of liis ungracious character (Gal v. 21; James iv. 6)-a.nd Esau ea.id in his hea.rt,--i. e. secretly resolved, though afterwlLl'ds he must have communicated his intention (vide ver. 42)-The days of mourning for my father a.re a.t ha.nd. The LXX. interpret a.a a wish on the part of Esau that Isaacmight speedily die, in order that the fratricidal act he con• templated might not pain the old man's heart ; another rendering (Kalisch) under- Htands him to eo.y that days of grief were in store for his father, o.s he meant to slay his brother; but the ordinary translation seems preferable (Rosenmiiller, Keil, Murphy, et alii), tho.t Esau only deferred tho oxecution of his unholy purpose because of the neo.r 11pproach, o.s he imagined, of his father's death. Isaac, however, lived upwards of forty years after this. Then will I slay my brother Jacob. That which roconcilell Isaac nnd Ishmael (eh. xxv. 9), the death of a father, is here mentioned as the event which would decisively aud finally part Esau and ,lacob. Esau's murderous mtention Calvin I regards o.s o. clear pr?of_of the 1;10~-rcal!ty of liis repentance for b1S sm, the rns1ncenty of his sorrow for his father, and tho intense malignity of his b<Lte against his brother.

entries.title: GEN 27:42
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And these (literally, the) words or Esau her elder sonwere told to Rebekah: -uot likely by revelation (Augustine), but by some one to whom he h!'-d made known his secret purpose (Prov. XXIL 11)-and she aent and called Jacob her younger son (to advise biw of his danger, being apprehensive lest the passionate soul of the enraged hunter should find it difficult to delay till Isaac'a death), and said unto him, :Behold, thy brother Esau, a.a touching thee, doth comfort himself, purposing to kill thee. Literally, behold thy brother Eaau talci'Tl.(J vengeanc6 upon thee (the hithpael of er:,~ meaning properly to comfort oneself, hence to satisfy one's feeling of revenge) lYIJ l,·illing thea. The translations a>TuX,i (LXX.) a.nd minatur {Vulgn.te), besides being inaccurate, are too feeble to express the fratricidal purpose of EsalL Vora. 43-46.-Now therefore, my son, obey my voice; - i. & be guided by my counsel; a request Rebekah might perhaps feel herself justified in making, not only by het maternal solicitude for Jacob's welfare, but also from the successful issue of her previous stratagem (vide on ver. 8)-a.nd arise, fiee thou-literally, flee for thyself (cf. eh. xii. 1; Numb. xxiv, 11; Amos vii. 12)-to Laban my brother to Hara.n (vide eh. xi. 31 ; xxiv. 29) ; and tarry with him a few days,-litorally, days some. The few days eventually proved to be at least twenty years (vide eh. xx.xi. 88). It is not probable that Rebekah ever again beheld her favourite son, which was a signal chastisement for her sinful ambition for, nnd 11artiality towards, Jacob-until thy brother's fury turn away; until thy brother's anger turn away from thee,-tho rage ofEsau is hero described by two different words, the first of which, il:;)IJ, from a root signifying to te warm, suggests tho heated and inflamed condition of Esau's sod, while the second, i:i~,, from l:]~1$, to breathe through the nostrils, depicts the visible manifestations of that internal fire in hard end quick breathing-and he forget thnt which thou hast done to him. Rebekah apparently had conveniently OO• 34.6 THE DOOK 01<' GENESIS. [cH, XXVll. 41-4.0. come oblivious of her omi share iu the transacti0n by which Esau had been wronged. Then will I send, and fetch thee from thence -whkh she never did. Man proposes, but God disposes. Wb.y should I be deprived also of you both in one day! I. e. of Jacob by the hand of Esau, nnd of Esau by the hand of the avenger of blood (eh. iL 6 ; cf. 2 Sam. xiv. 6, 7; Calvin, Keil, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch), rather than by his own fratricidal a.et, which would for ever part him from Rebekah (Lange).

entries.title: GEN 27:46
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Rebekah said to Isaac (perhaps already discerning in the contemplated flight to Haran the prospect of a suitable matrimonial alliance for the heir of the promise, and secretly desiring to suggest such a thought to her aged husband), I am weary of my life because <\f the daughters of Heth :-referring doubtless to Eso.u's wives (cf. eh. nvi. 36)-ifJaoob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, suoh as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me 1 Litemlly, for wlw,t to me life, i. e. what happiness can I have in living I It is impossible to exonerate Rebekah altogether from a charge of duplicity even in this. Unquestionably Esau's wives may have vexed her, and her faith may have perceived that Jacob's wife must be sought for amongst their own kindred ; but her secret reason for sending Ja~ob to Haran was not to seek a wife, ea she seems to have desired Isaac to believe, but to elude the fury of his incensed brother.

entries.title: GEN 27:46
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Rebekah, the disappointed. "Whatgood shall my life do me? " Rebekah as a mother doubtless promised herself much joy in her children. They grew up. Esau becomes wayward, Jacob becomes a wanderer. Rebekah yielded to favouritism (ver. 13), and schemed to carry her point. She cherished a treacherous spirit, and led Jacob to ein. She was ambitious not for herself, but for Jacob. This is like woman ; she 1ives in others. She was reckless us to results, but when they came she found them bitter. " She loved Jacob more than truth, more than God." This was idolatry. No wonder she utters the exclamation, "What good shall my life do me ?" She was a disappointed woman. Her favourite son was in hiding from the wrnth of a wronged brother, and Esau was induferent towards her and angry. If life is not to be a disappointment we must beware of- L UNSCRUPULOUS SCHEMING. JI. AFFECTIONS TJIAT OARE MORE FOR HAPPINESS THAN HONOUR. III. OF IDOLATRY, COVETOUSNESS, AND NEGLECT OF Goo's CLAIMS. IV. OF IGNORING THE RIGHTS OF OTHERS. V. OF IGNORANCE AS TO THE TRUE ELEMENTS OF SUCCESS. Rebekuh began well. Her advent unto the encampment was o. "comfort " to Isnnc. She seems to have been "weary of life," and nsks "whut good it shall do her." Some who ask at this dny "whether life is worth living" may find nsuggestion in Rebeknh's conduct ns to the reuson wherefore they nsk the question.-H.

entries.title: GEN 28:1

entries.content: -And Isaao (recognisingthewisdom o.nd propriety of Rebek11b's suggestion that a bride should now be sought for him whom God hnd so unmistak11bly declared to bo the heir of the theocratic promise) called Jacob (to bis bed-side), and blessed him,-in enlnrged form, renewing the benediction previously given (eh. xxvii. 27)-and said unto him, Thou shalt not take a wife of the dnughters ofCanaan (cf. eh. mv. 3). Intermarriage with the women of the land wns n:pressly forbidden to the theocrntic heir, while his attention WIIS directed to his mother's kindred.

If yet nlive, P.cthuel must hnve been very oh!, since he was Isaac'~ cousin, nnd probably born mnny years UP· fore the son of .A.brahnm-and take thoo a. wife from thence-though Isaac's wifo was found for him, ho does not think or imitating Abraham ond despatching nnother Eliezer in search of n spouse for Robckah's son. Probably be saw tl1at Jncob coulcl nttond to 3!8 THE BOOK OF GENESt!t [en. xx,•111. 1-9. that business sufficiently mthout 11.SSista.nce from others--i>f the daughters of Laban thy mother's brother (vide eh. xxiv. 29). "Isaac appears to entertnin no doubt of Jacob's success, u-bicb might be the more probable since the same reason which kept Jacob from marrying in Can,111.n might prevent Laban's daughters from ooiag marrioii in Haran, the worshippers of the Lord being few" (Inglis). Y~. 8.-And God Almighty-El Shaddai (mde eh. xvii. 1)-bles■ thee,-the Abrahamic benediction in its fullest form was given byEl Shaddai('IJUie eh.xvii. 1-8)-and make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, that thou mayest be-literally, and thou shalt become (or grow to)--amultitude-an assembly, or congregation, or crowd called together, from a root signifyiug to cell together (Gcsenius), or to sweep up together (Fiirst) ; corres~onding to lrc>-.1J11ia in Greek-of people. , er. 4.-And give thee the blessing of Abraham,-i. e. promised to Abraham (vide eh. xii. 2 ; ::a.ii 17, 1S). The additions of TOV 1rarpo, µov (LXX. ), 7':l)( =TOU 1raTpiii; aov (Samaritan), are unwarranted-to thee, and to thy seed with thee; that thou mayest inherit the land wherein thon art a stranger, -literally, the land of thy sojournings (eh. xvii. B)-which God gave unto Abrahamby promise (cf. eh. :xii 7 ; xiii 15; xv. 7, 18; xvii 8).

entries.content: - .And Isaac sent away Jacob (Rebekahonlycounselled, Isaaccomm11nded)1 and he went to Padan-aram unto Laban, son of Bethuel the Syrian (1;ido Hosea xii 12), the brother of Rebekah, .Tacob's and Esau'■ mother. entries.title: GEN 28:6–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -When (literally, and) Esau saw that Isaao had blessed .Taoob, and sent him away to Padan-aram, to take him a wife from thence; and that as he blessed him he gave him a charge,-litorally, in hu bl6S8fr1g him (forming a parenthesis), and lie commanded him-saying, Thou she.It not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan; and that (literally, and) .Jacob obeyed his father and his mother, and was gone (or went) to Padan-aram; and Esau seeing that (more correctly, saw that) the daughters of Canaan pleased not (literally, were evil in tl,,e eyes of) Isaao hie father; then (literally, and) went Esau unto Ishmael (i. e. tho family or tribe of Ishmael, aiming in this likely to please his father), and took unto the wives which he had (so that they were neither dead nor divorced) Mahalath (called Bashemath in eh. xxxvi. 3) the daughter of Ishmael (and therefore Esau's half-cousin by tho father's side, Ishmael, who was now dead thirteen years, having been Isaac's half-brother) Abraham's son, the sister of Nebajoth,-Ishmael's firstborn (vid6 eh. xxv. 13}-to be hie wife.

entries.title: GEN 28:1–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob and Esaie, or diverging paths. I. JAcoB'e JOURNEY TO PADAN-ARAM. 1. The pa.tit ofdldy. Entered on in obedience to his mother's wish and his father's commandment, it was an evidence of filial piety. It is the token of a good son that he "hears the instruction of his father, and forsakes not the law of his mother" tProv. i. 8). Sons come to mature age should respect and, where not inconsisteI.lt with allegiance to God, yield submission to parental authority (Prov. vi. 20; Mai. i. 6 ; Ephes. vi. 1-3). 2. The path ofblessi,ng. The benediction already bestowed upon Jacob was repeated with greater amplitude and tenderness before he left the patriarchal tent. Happy the youth who enters upon life's journey carrying on his head and in Lis heart a father's blessing I much more who goes forth beneath the canopy of Heaven's Lcnediction I and this ie ever the experience of him wl10 travels by the way of filial obedience. Pious children seldom foil to come to hc-nour, and never want the favour of the Lord (Pe. xxxvii. 26; Prov. iv. 20-22; viii. 32). 3. The path of promue. In addition to Lis fother's blessing and the Alruighty's benediction, Jacob carried with him as he left Beersheba the promise of a seed a!1d an inheritance to be in due time acquired; and in like manner now ha.a the eamt exceeding great and preciot..R promises to cheer him in his heavenward pilgrimage, promises the full realisation of which is attainable only in the future (John x.iv. 2; 1 Pet. i. 4). 4. The path of lwpe. Sad and sorrowful ns Jacob's heart mu?t have been as he kissed hi~ mother ar.d bade farewell to Isaac, it wae at least eustamed by pleasant expectatio'1. Gilding the horizon of his future was the prospect of a wife to love as Isaac had loved Rebekah, and to be the mother of the seed of promise. So the pathway of the children of promise, though often painful, arduous, and pro• tracted, is always lighted by the star of hope, and always points to a bright and beautiful beyond. • II. EsAu'e MARRIAGE WITH MABALATH. 1. Tiu way of ai1i. His former wive■ OH, X.XVIII. 10-22.) THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 349 being neither dead nor divorced, the conduct of Esau in adding to them a third was wrong. 2. The way ofshame. In the selection of lshmael's daughter he hoped to please his father, but was apparently indifferent about the judgrnent of either Rebeknh or Jehovah. Daring transgressors, like Esau, rather glory in their shame than feel abashed at their wickedness. 3. The way of sorrOUJ. If not to himself, at least to his pious parents, this fres~ matrimonial alliance could not fail to be a grief. The daughter of Ishmael was certainly better than a daughter of the Hittites being al~ost as neBr a relative on Isaac's side as Rachel and Leah were on Rebekah'~; but, unhke Rachel and Leah, who belonged to the old family stock (the Terachites) in Mesopotamia, Mahalath descended from a branch which had been removed from the Abrahamic tree. Learn-I. The care which pious parents should take to see their sons well married. 2. The piety which children should delight to show to their parents. 3. The connection which subsists between true religion and prosperity. 4. The inevitable tendency· of sin to produce shame and sorrow, 5. The wickedness of violating God'A law of marriage.

entries.title: GEN 28:1–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Life with, and life without, God. The divergence of the two representative men ie seen in this short statement of their marriage relations. I. Domestic life under the blessing of God and apart from that blessing. 2. The true blessing ie the blessing of Abraham, the blessing which God has already provided, promised, and secured. 3. The heir of the blessing must be sent away and learn by experience how to use it. 4. The disinherited man, who ·has scorned his opportunity, cannot recover it by his own devices. Esau is still Esau. Polygamy was suffered, but never had the blessing of God upon it.-R.

entries.title: GEN 28:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And J'acob went ont from :Beersheba, - in obedience to his father's commandment to seek a wife (ver. 2), but also in compliance with his mother's counsel to evade the wrath of Esau (eh. LTI'ii. 43; er. Hosea xii. 12. On Beersheba vide eh. :x:xi. 81 ; xxvi. 33-and went towards Haranprobably along the route traversed by Abrahnm's serv1mt (cf. eh. xxiv. 10).

entries.title: GEN 28:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he lighted npon a certain plaoe,-Iiterally, he struck upon the place; i. e. either the place )lest suited for him to rest in (Inglis), or the place opJ>ointed for him by God (.Ainsworth, Bush), or more prob11bly the well-known place afterwards mentioned (Keil, Wordsworth, 'Speaker's Commentary'). Situated in the mountains of Ephraim, about three hours north of Jernsalem, it was not reached after one, but after several days' journey (r.f. eh. xxii. 4)-and tarried there all night, because the sun was set;-being either remote from the city Luz when overtaken by darkness, or unwilling to enter the town ; not because he hntcd the inhabitants (Josephus), but because be was 11 stranger-and he took of the atones of that plaoe,-i. e. one of the stones (vide ver. 18). "The track (of pilgrims) winds through an uneven valley, covered, 11s with gravestones, by large &hcets of biiro rock ; some few here and there standing np like tho cromlechs of Druidical monuments" (Stanley's 'Sinai and Palestine,' p. 219 ; cf. 'Lectures on Jewish Church,' p. 59)-and put them for his pillows,-literolly, and put for his head-bolster, the word signifying that which is at the henu of any one (cf. 1 Sam. xix. 13 ; :x:xvi 7, 11, 16 ; 1 Kings xix. 6)- and lay down in that place to sleep (cf. eh. xix. 4 ; 1 S11m. iii. 6, 6, 9).

entries.title: GEN 28:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he dreamed. This drenm, which has been pronounced " beautifully ingenious," " clever," and "philosophical," the work of a Inter Hebrew poet, anu not ofJacob (De Wette), was not wonderful considering the state of mind and body in which he must have been-fatigued by trove!, s,Hldened by thoughts of home, doubtless meditating on hi~ mother, anu more than likely pondering the great beneJiction of his agcJ and, to all appearance, dying father. Yet while these circumstance~ may account for the mental fmmework of the dream, the dream itselfwas Divinely sent. And behold a ladder-the rough stones of the mountain appearing to form themselves into a vast staircase (Stanley, Bush) - set np on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: -symbolically intimating tho fact of a real, uninterrupted, ~nd close corr11nunica\io11 Lo· 350 THE DOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. .lXYIII, 10-22. t:wecn hea,cn and earth, and in particular between God in his glory and man in bis solitude and sin-and behold the angels of God-literally, the 'TMSSl!11.{lers of Elohim, i e. the angels (Ps. ciii. 20, 21 ; civ. 4 ; Heh. i. H)-ascending and descending on it -m·d.e John i. 51, which shows that Christ regarded either the ladder in Jacoh's vision as an emblem of himself, the one Mediator between God and man (Calnn, Luther, .Ainsworth, ' Speaker's Commentary,' Murphy), or, what is more probable, Jacob himself as a type of him, the Son of man, in whom the lfring intercourse between earth and heaven depicted in the vision of the angel-trodden sfaircase was completely fulfilled (Hengstenberg, Ilaumgnrt<ln, Lange, Bnsh).

entries.title: GEN 28:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And,behold,-"the dream-vision is so glorions that the narrator represents it by a threefold i1,~;'J "(Lange)-the Lord stood above it,-the change in the Divine name is not to be explained by assigning vers. 13--- 16 to the Jehovistic editor (Tuch, Bleek) or to a subsequent redactor (Davidson), since without it the Elohistic document would be ahrnpt, if not incomplete (Kalisch), but by recalling the fact that it is not the general prondence of the Deity over his creature man, but the special superintendence of the God of .A.braham and of Isaac over his chosen people, that the symbolic ladderwas intended to depict (Hengstenberg)-and said, I am the Lord God of Abraham thy father, and the God ofIsaac:-thus not simplyproclaiming his personal name Jehovah, but announcing himself as the Elohlm who had solemnly entered into covenant with his ancestors, and who had now come, in virtue of that covenant, to renew to him the promises he had previously given them-the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed-given to Abraham, ea. xiii. 15 ; to Isaac, e:h. xxvi. 3.

entries.title: GEN 28:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth,-promised to Abraham, eh. xiii. 16; to Isaac, under a different emblem, eh. ::uvi. 4-and thou shalt spread abroad (literally, brea/c forth-) to the west, and to the east, to the north, and to the south :-(cf. eh. xiii. 14; Dent. xii. 20). In its ultimate significance this points to the world-wide universality of the kingdom of Christ (llforpby)-and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed (vide eh. xii. 3; xviii. 18; xxii. 18 (.A.braham); xxvi. 4 (Isaac).

entries.title: GEN 28:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And, behold, I am with thee,- spoken to Isaac (eh. xxvi. 24); again to Jacob (eh. xxx:i. 3) ; afterwards to Christ's cli~ciples (Uat.t. x:xviii. 20)-and will keep thee in all pla.cc:s whither thou goeet,-literally, in all thou goest =in a.11 thy goings (cf. eh. xlvili. 16; Ps. cxxi. 5, 7, B)-and will bring tb11e age.in into thi11 land ;-e']Uivalent to an intimation tlmt his present journey to Padan-aram was not without tho Divine sanction, though apparently it ha.cl been against the will of God that Isae.o should leave the promised land (vide eh. xxiv. 6, 8)-for I will not leave thee,-a promise afterwards repeated to Israel (Dent, xxxi. 6, 8), to Joshua (eh. i. 5), to Solomon (1 Chron. xxviii 20), to the poor and needy (Isa. xli 17), to Christians (Heb. xiii 7)- until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of-cf. Balaam's testimony to the Divine faithfulness (Numb. xxiii. 19), and Joshua's (eh. xxi. 45), and SCllomon's (1 Kings viii 66). It is impossible, in connection with this sublime theophany granted to Jacob at Bethel, not to recall the similar Divine manifestation vouchsafed to .Abraham beneath the starry firmament at Hebron (vide eh. xv. 1). Yer. 16.-And Jacob awe.ked out of his sleep (during which he had seen and talked with Jehovah), and he said, Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not. Jacob does not here learn the doctrine of the Divine omnipresence for the first time (Knobel), but now discovers that the covenant God of Abraham revealed himself e.t other than consecrated places (Roscnmiiller, Keil, Lange, Murphy); or perhaps simply gives expression to his astonishment at finding that whereas he fancied himself a.lone, he was in reality in the company of God-se plus adeptum esse quam sperare ausua ]'u:isset (Calvin). Yer. 17.-And he was afraid,-so were .Moses (Exod. xx. 18, 19), Job (eh. xlii 5, 6), Isaiah (eh. vi. 6), Peter (Lnke v. 8), John (Rev. L 17, 18), at similar discoveries of the Divine presence-and said, How dreadful is this place !-i. e. how to be feared I how awe-inspiring I ,po/Jipo, (LXX.), terribilis (Yulgate)-this 1s none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven. Not literally, bnt figuratively, the place where God dwells, and the entrance to his glorious abode (Keil); the idea that Jacob wrui "made a.ware by the dream that he had slept on one of those favoured spots singled out for a future sanctuary, and was fearful that he had sinned by employing it for a profane purpose" (Kalisch), being fancifnL ••

entries.title: GEN 28:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jaco!J rose up early in the morning (et: eh. xix. 27; xxii 3), and took the stone that he had. put for hi.a pillows (vide supra), and set it up for a pillar -literally, set it up, a pillar (or something set upright, hence e. statue or monument); not as an object of worship, a sort of fetish, but as e. memorial of the VIBion (Calvin, Keil, Murphy; cf. eh. xxxi. 45 ; xxxv. 14 ; Josh. iv. 9, 20 ; xxiv. 26 ; 1 Sam. vii. 12)-and poured oil upon the top of it. Quasisignum consecrationis (Calvin), and not becnuso he "11. XXVIII, 10-22.) THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 351 regarded it as in itself invested with any degree ofsanctity. The worship ofsacredstones (Bretylia), afterwards prevalent among the Greeks, Romans, Hindoos, Arabs, and Germans, though by some (Kueneu, Oort ; vide 'The Bible for Young People,' vol. i. p. 231) regarded as one of the primeval forms of w'brship among the Hebrews, was expressly interdicted by the law of Moses (cf. Exod. xxiii. 24 ; xxxiv. 13; Levit. xxvi. 1 ; Dent. xii. 3 ; xvi. 22). It was probably a heathen imitation of the rite here recorded, though by some authorities (Keil, Knobel, Lange) the Brotylian worship is said to have been connected chiefly with meteoric qtoncs which Wero supposed to have desccn.J.ed from some divinity; as, e. g., the stone in Delphi sacred to Apollo ; that in Emesa, on the Orontes, consecrated to the sun ; the angular rock at Pessinus in Phrygie. worshipped es hallowed by Cybele; the black stone in the Kaaba at Mecca believed to have been brought from heaven by the angel Gabriel (vide Kalisch in loco). That the present narrative was a late invention, "called into existence by a desire " on the part of tho priests and prophets of Yahweh (Jehovah) "to proclaim the high antiquity of the sanctuary at Bethel, e.nd to make a sacred stone harmless " (' The Bible for Young People,' vol i. p. 231), is pure assumption. The circumstance that the usage here mentioned is nowhere else in Scripturo countenanced (except in eh. xxxv. 14, with reference to this same pillar) forms asufficient pledge of the hi§h antiquity of the narrative (vide Hiivemicka 'Introd.,' § 20).

entries.title: GEN 28:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - And he called the name of that place Bethel - i. e. house of God. Rosenmiiller and Kalisch find a connection between Bethel and Bmtylia, the formor regarding Bretylia as a corruptio_n of Bethel, and the latter viewing Bethel as the Hebrnised form of Bretylion. Keil objects to both that the interchange of .,. in /3a1Tv'A1ov and 9 in {3a,9~X would be perfectly inexplicable. On the site of Bethel (Beitin) vide eh. xii. 8. But the name of that city was cRlled Luz at the first. Originally the Cannanitish town, built nccording to Calvin after this event, was called Luz, or "almond tree,'' a name it continued to benr until tho conquest (Judgcs i. 23). From the circumstances recorded in the na1Tative, Jncob called the spot where he slept (in the vicinity of Luz) Bethel-the designation aftorwnrds extendina to the town (eh. xxxv. 6). Until the co~quest both titles appear to have been used-Luz by the Cnnaanitcs, Bethel by the Israelites. When the conquestwns completed the Hebrew name wes substituted for the Hittite, the sole sur•rivor of the captured city building another Luz in another part of the country (vide Judges i. 26).

entries.title: GEN 28:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jacob vowed a vow,- not in o.ny mercenary or doubtful spirit, but as an exprossion of gratitude for the Divine mercy {Calvin), as the soul's full and free acceptance of the Lord to be its own God (Murphy), as the instinctive impulse of the new creature (Candlish)-sa.ying, If (not the language of uncertainty, but equivalent to "since," or "forasmuch as;" Jacob by faith both appropriating and anticipating the fulfilment of tho preceding promise) God (Elohim; for the reason of which vide infra) will be with me,-as he has promised (ver. 15), and as I believe he will-and will keep me in this way that I go,-a particular appropriation of the general promise (ver. 15) -and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on (i. e. all the necessaries of life,included,though notspeciallymentioned, in the preceding promise), ao that I come again to myfather's house-also guaranteed by God (vcr. 15), and here accepted by the patriarch-in peace (i. e. especially free from Esau'savengingthreats); then shall the Lord be my God-literally, and Jehoval. will be to me for Elohim (Rosenmiiller, Hcngstenberg, Keil, Kalisch, 'Speaker's Commentary'), though the received translation is not without support (LXX., Vulgate, Syriac, Calvin, Michaelis, Lange, Murphy, Wordsworth) ; but to have bo.rgnined and bartered with God in the way which this suggests before assenting to accept him as an object of trust and worship would hnve been little less than criminal. Accordingly, the clause is best placed in the protosis of the sentence, which then practically reads, "if Elohim will be Jchovnh to me, and if Jchovah will be to me Elohim" (vide Hengstcnberg, 'Introduction,' vol. i. p. 358).

entries.title: GEN 28:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And (or then, the npodosis now commencing) this stone which I he.ve set for a pillar (vide on ver. 18) shall be God's honse - Bethel, meaning that he would afterwards erect there an altar for the celebration of Diviue worship - 11 resolution which WQS subsequently carried out (vide eh. xxxv. 1, 15). "The pillar or cnim or cromlech ofBethel must have been looked upon by the Israelites, and may bo still looked upon in thought by us, ns tho precursor of every "house of God " that has since nriscn in the Jewish and Christian world-the temple, the cathedral, the church, the chnpel ; llny moro, of those secret places of worshif thRt are marked by no nnturnl beauty nn, seen by no humnn cyo-tho closet, tho catncomb, the thoroughfore of the trne worshipper" (Stnnley's 'Jowish Church,' lcct. iii. p. 60), And of all the.t thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee. Litornlly, giving I will give the tenth (cf. eh. xiv. 20). Tho case of Jacob 111fords nnother proof thllt tho prnctico of voluntary tithing was known and observed antecedont to the time ofMoses !152 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cH. XXVIII. 10-22.

entries.title: GEN 28:10–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's dream. Where revelations had been vouchsafed it wa11 supposed thnt they would be repeated. The stony pillow on which the weary head rested may be changed by the visitation of Divine grace into the meeting-place of heaven nnd enrth. The morning beams brenking in upon the shadowy refuge of the night are transfigured into a dream of covenant blessing. The ladder set up on the earth, the top of it reached to heaven. .Angels of God on the way of mediation, ascending, descending, carrying up the wants and services of the man of God, bringing down the messages of consolation, the vouchsafements of help and deliverance. "Debold, the Lord stood above it," as the source of nil the blessing, standing ready to work for his chosen. ThiR is the first direct communication of Jehovah to Jacob, the first in a long line of revelations of which be was the recipient. It is a renewal of the covenant made to his fathers, it is a republication of the promises. Butwe require to hear the Lord say to us," I am with thee, I will not leave thee," especially when we are nlreody on the journey of faith, when we are obeying the commandment of God, and of the father and mother speaking in his name. Such a place as Jacob found may be mode known to us- I. IN PROVIDENTIAL INTERPOSITIONS. We journey on through the wilderness and lig·ht upon a certain place where we think we are only among stony facts, where we can find but e. harsh welcome; but the Lord is in the place, though we know it not till he reveals himself. Then we cry with trembling gratitude, This is the house of God, &c. II. IN SEASONS OF RELIGIOUS OPPORTUNITY. The ordinary and customary is lifted up by specie.I gift of the Spirit into the opened heaven, the visiting angels, the vision of the throne of God. "The house of God, the gate of heaven." Such may be the awaking of our soul in the sanctuary of our own private devotions or of our publio worship. III. Jacob is .iL TYPE OF THE LORD'S PEOPLE REGARDED AS A WHOLE. The Church has often laid itseif down upon the stones ana slept with weariness in its passage through the desert, and the Lord has revealed the laddes of hiR covenant, connecting GE.NESIB. A A 354 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. XXVIII. 10--22. together that Yery pince and time of hardship with the throne of grace nnd glory, and the ascending and descending angels. IV. Jesus himself employed this dream of the patriarch as A TYPICAL PROPilEOY 011' THE KINGDOM OF Gon. " Heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man," the true Jacob, the Prince prevailing with God-and with men (John i. 51). The cross is the ladder of mediation, It was sP-t up of the earth. It w:is not of earthly origin as a means of atonement, but its foot wns on the earth as 1t came forth out of the method and course of earthly history in connection with Divine counsels. Its top reached to heaven, for it was a Divine Mediator whose sacrifice ""as offered upon it. Angels of God ascended and descended upon the ladder, for only through the atoning merit of Christ is angelic ministration maintained. It is for them" who shall be heirs of salvation." At the summit of the cross, representing the whole mediatorinl work of Christ, is the Lord standing, speaking his word of covenant, and stretching forth his right hand on behalf of his people. Resting at the foot of the cross we hear the voice of a faithful Guido, saying, "I will not leave thee," &c. In every place one who is conscious of surrounding covenant mercy can say, "This is none other but the house of God," &c.-R.

entries.title: GEN 28:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A stairway to heaven. "And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven." Jacob in fear of hie life leaves home. The last..kiss of his mother is taken. During the µay Jacob goes forward cheerfully. Night comes on at length. The path is no longer distinct. The wind moans sadly. A sense of loneliness creeps over him. Fear of Esau haunts him. He sees the figure of his brother behind this shrub and that rock. Had Esau outrun to murder him in that lonely spot? He trembles at every shadow, and shudders at every sound. He thinks of the God of his father and mother, and prays. He lies down in the desert; a furze-bush is his only shelter, and a stone his hard pillow, He looks up into the dark vault all glittering with the silent stars. More intense becomes his loneliness, for the stars have no voice for him. Plotting and far-seeing Jacob had deep borne-longings, mystic inquirings, and a wealth of affection in hi8 natnre. Of snch God can make something; to such God can reveal something. To idolatrous, carnal Esaus how little can Go.d make known. Selfishness hinders. Here in the desert Jacob draws his camel-hair robe more tightly over his feet, and dreams of parents and home, and heaven and God. It might surprise us that he could have such sweet dreams when he was fleeing from the one whom he had undoubtedly WTonged. God would over-rule the wrong, and therefore sent him this vision, I. ALL HAVE DREAMS OF A HEAVEN. A heaven is that for which all men are -seeking, whether sou"ght in the way of business, or pleasure, or politics, or literature. Even sceptics have their heaven in their doubt and intellectual pride. That which is our highest object is our heaven. As water cannot rise_ above its level, so the heaven of some cannot be above their thoughts. There will be a future state answering to the highest longings of the believer, a place of existence in glory far beyond anything here. II. ACTUAL COMMUNICATION WITH HEAVEN IS POSSIBLE. One author (Hazlitt) says, "In the days of Jacob there was a ladder between heaven and earth, but now the heavens are gone further and become astronomical." True ecienc_e opens up an infinite number of worlds and densely-peopled spaces. Material discoveries lessen the sense of spiritual realities. It need not be so, If the universe is great, how great also is the soul, which can embrace in its thoughts the universe I And it is in the soul that God can and does reveal heaven. Peace, hope, love is the spirit of heaven, and that is revealed by Christ. Purify the spirit and heaven comes near, III. EARNEST EFFORT 1B NEEDED TO MAINTAIN COMMUNICATION WI1'H HEAVEN, In the dream of Jacob he saw a picture of hie own struggling ascent in life. Angels might flit up and down, but man had to struggle and put forth earnest effort to maintain the union. Early in life the ascent seems easy. A mountain never appears so far 1.o its summit as it is in reality. As we go on we become more conscious of the difficulties in the way of maintaining the open communications. Often we find ourselvef! with heads between our hands, pondering whether we shall ev.ar ovorcorne the evil and attain to the good. OH. XXVIU, 10-22.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 355 IV. THERE IS ALWAYS HELP ll'ROM THE HEAVENS IN THE EFFORT TO MAINTAIN TIIE COMMUNIOATION. A voice comes to Jacob. A promise of guidance and support was given. Christ in his conversation with Nathaniel shows us how all good comes through him. In Christ all goodness centres. All heaven rays out from him in ibe pardon nnd reconciliation 110 has brought. He is the Word made flesh. He is the Divine voice from above. Through him the Holy Spirit is given, and that Holy Spirit shows us things to come, makes heaven plain, and the way direct. One day we shall be called to follow tho way the angels go, and after death shall ascend that stairway which "slopes through darkness up to God."-H.

entries.title: GEN 28:15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Goil's providential care. "Behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest." Among things believed, bnt not sufficiently realised, is the truth of God's constant overruling care. We can trace cause and effect a little way, then lose the chain, and feel as if it went no further, as if events had no special cause. This a common evil in the life of Christians. Its root, walking by sight more than by faith. Jacob-what made him try craft? Did not trust God fully. Had no habit of faith. But God had not forgotten him. And as he slept on the stone at Bethel the reality of God's presence was made known to him (Isa. xliii. 2; Matt. xxviii. 20) and recorded for our learning. I. GOD DOES ALWAYS WATCH OVER AND GUIDE. The ladder was not a new thing; it had existed always. The vision showed what exists everywhere (2 Kings vi. 17). The ladder shows the truth which should stamp our lives. God is love, and love means care. This is for all. Not our Jove that causes it. Our love, trust, life spring from that truth. The living God is close to us. His hand touches our lifa at every point. How is it that we nre unconscious of this? 11 GoD's WORKING IS HIDDEN AND SILENT. Jacob was startled to find him near. Because year by year the world goes on as before, unbelievers deny God's active presence, worldly men think not of it, and even godly men sometimes forget; for we cannot see the tqp of the ladder. But God, there, directs all. III. HIS PURPOSES ARE ACCOMPLISHED DY MANY AGENTS. Many angels, messengerlil (Pe. civ. 4; Heh..i. 14); natural agents, the elements, &c. ; human agents, men good and bad. alike carrying out his will; spiritual beings (Ps. x:ci. 11). How often those who pray for spiritual blessings forget that co=on things also nre ruled by God. Thus a great dooi; of communion is closed. IV. BUT THERE IS BO MUCH CONFUSION IN THE WORLD. We often cannot trace God's hand. How often is trust confounded, wise schemes frustrated, earnest selfdenial in vain; prayers, real and intense, without apparent answer. Nay, these are but seeming confusions, to teach the lesson of faith. Through all these, by all these, God's purposes are surely carried out. One great truth is the key of all-the love of God revealed in Christ. .This is the ladder from which he proclaims, 11 Lo, I am with thee" (cf. Rom. viii. 32). He who wrought out redemption, can he fail? v. GoD'B GOVERNANCE IS ll'OR OUR SALVATION, in the fullest sense of the word, giving us the victory over evil. God was with Jacob. He had been from the first, though not recognised. He was so to the end. Not giving uninterrupted prosperity. Me.ny a fault and many a painful page in his history ; but through all these he was led on. The word to each who will receive it--" Behold, I am with thee." Not because of thy faith, still lees of thy goodness. Oh that every Christian would practise trust (Ps. v. 3); bearing our Father's voice, "Commit thy way unto the Lord," and gladly believing " the Lord is my Shepherd."-M. Vore. 18-22.-The grateful retrospect and the consecratedprospect. I. THE TRUE Lill'E is that which starts from tho place of fellowship with God nnd commits tho future to him. We can always find a pillar of blessed memorial and consecration. The Bethel. 1. Providential care. 2. Religious privilege. 3. Special communications of the Spirit. God with us as a fact. Our pilgrimage a Bethel all through. II. THE TRUE 1'ESTIMONY that which erects a stone of witness, a Bethel, where others can find God. 1. Pers()'fl,(J,l. The pillow of rest the pillar of praise. 2. Practical. The testimony which speaks of the journey and the traveller. III. THE TRUJ! COVENANT, 1. Coming out of fellowship. 2. Pledging the future AA2 856 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. XXIX. 1-14. at the house of God, and in sight of Divine revelation. 3. Dleased exchange of gifts, confirmation of love. Jehovah keeping nnd guiding and feeding; hie servant sen"ing him and giving him a tenth of all he received, The pntriaroh'e vow was the result of a di~tinct advance in his religious life. The hope of blessing became the covenant of engagement, service, worship, sacrifice. The highest form of religious life is that which rests on a solemn vow of grateful dedication at Bethel. The end lilefore us is ' our Fathers house in peace."-R.

entries.title: GEN 29:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Then J'acob went on his journey (literally, lifted up h-is feet-a w,i.phic description of travelling. Inspired by ne,v l1opes, and conscious of loftier aims than when he fled from Beersheba, tho louely fugitive departed from Bethel), and came into the land of the people of the eastliterally, the land ofthe sons ofthe east, i. e. Mesopotamia., about 450 miles distant from Beersheba.

entries.title: GEN 29:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A.nd he looked (either to discover where he was, or in search of water), and behold a well in the field,-not the well at which Eliezcr's caravan halted, which was a well for the village maidens, situated in front of the town, and approached by steps (vide eh. xx:iv.), but a;well in the open fieltl for the use of flocks, and covered at the time of Jacob'e arri,al with a huge stone-and, lo, there were three flocks of sheep lying by it. A frequent Oriental scene (cf. eh. x:xiv. 11 ; Exod. ii. 16). " Who that has traveiled much in this country has not often arrived at a well in the heat of the day which was surrounded with numerous flocks of sheep waiting to be watered ! I once saw such a scene iu the burning plains of NorthemSyria, Half-naked, fierce-looking men were drawing up water in leatherbuckets; flock after flock was brought np, watered, andsent away; autl after all the men had ended their work, then several women and girls brought up their flocks, and drew water for them. 'l'hus it was mth Jethro's daughters; and thus, no doubt, it would have been with Rachel if Jacob had not rolled away the stone and watered her sheep" (' Land and Book,' p. 589). For out of that well they watered the :flocks: and a in-eat ston.e was upon the well's mouth. T, Most of the cisterns are covered with a large thick, flat stone, in the centre of which n hole is cut, which forms the mouth of the cistern. This hole, in ,nany instances, we found covered with a heavy stone, to the removal of which two or three men were requisite" (Robinson, ii. p. 180).

entries.title: GEN 29:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And thither were all the 11.ocks gr.thered. "Fifteen minutes later we came to a large well in a valley among the swells, fitted up with troughs and reservoirs, with flocks waiting nround" (Robinson, iii. p. 21). And they rolled the stone from the wall's mouth, and we.tered the sheep, and put the stone age.in upon. the well's mouth in his place. From the middle of ver. 2 the wortls are parenthetical, the watering of the flocks not having taken place till Rachel had arri,ed (ver. 9) and Jacob had uncovered the well (ver. 10).

entries.title: GEN 29:4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A.nd J'acob said unto them (tho shepherds of the three flocks), My brethren. (a friendly salutation from one who was himself e.shephertl), whence be ye 1 Anticipating that their reply woultl reveal his whereabouts. And theysaid, Of Haran are we. This could scarcely fail to remiud Jacob of God's promise to guide him in his journey.

entries.title: GEN 29:5
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said unto them (with the view of discovering his kinsmen), Know ye Laban the son of Nahor '1-i. e. the grantlson, Laban's father having been Bethuel,who, however, here, as in eh. xxiv., retires into the background. And they said, We know him. The language of the shepherds being Chaldman (vide eh. xxxi 47), Jacob, who spoke Hebrew, was ablo to converso with them either because he had learnt Chaldee from his mother (Clericus), or, as is more probable, because the dialects were not then greatly dissimilar (Gosman in Lange).

entries.title: GEN 29:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -An.d he said unto them, Is he well 1 Literally, is there peace to him? meaning not simply bodily health, but all mannerof felicity; iry,aivu (LXX.); sanusne est f (Vulgate). Cf. the Christian se.lutation, Pa.t: vob-iscum. And they said, He is well (litera1I1, peace): and, behold, Rachel- " Ewe' (Gesenius)-his daughter cometh with the sheep.

entries.title: GEN 29:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -A.nd he se.id, Lo, it is yet high day (literally, the day is yet great, i. e. much of it still remains), neither is it time that the cattle should be gathered together (i. e. to shut them up for the night): water ye the sheep, and go and feed them-being desirous to get the shepherds a.way from the well that he might meet Rachel alone (Keil, Lange, Murphy), though perhaps his worda with as much correctness may be traced to that prudent and industrious ho.bit of mind which afterwardsshone forth so conspicuously in himself, antl which instinctivrly caused him to frown upon laziness and inactivity (Stnrke, Kalisch, B118h),

entries.title: GEN 29:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And they said, We cannot,-not because of any physical difficulty (Kalisch), since three men could easily have accomplishedwhatJo.cob byhimselfdid,butbecause they had agreed not to do so (Rosenmiiller, Murphy), but to wait-until all the flocks be gathered together (when the wateringwas done at once, instead of o.t so many different times), and till they roll the stone from the well'smouth ;-more correctly rendered, and (sc. then, i. e. when the flocks are assembled) they (i. e. the shepherds) roll away the atone -then (or, and) we water the sheep. The object of watering the flocks collectively may have been, as above stated, for convenience, or to prevent the well from being opened too frequently, in which case dust might rapidly accumulate within it (Kalisch), or perhaps to secnre an equal distribution of the water (Murphy).

entries.title: GEN 29:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: Andwhile he yet spake with them (literally, he yet speakingwiththem), Rachel came with her father's sheep: for she kept th~m-or, she was a shepll'erdess, the part. i1~1 being used o.s a substantive (Gesenius, 'Lex.,' sub. nom.).

entries.title: GEN 29:10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, when J'acob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother,-"the term mother's brother is not unintentionally repeated three timesin this verse to describe with the greatest possible stress thnt Jacob had met with his own relations, with " bis bone aml his flesh" (Knliscb) - and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother (Jacob from the first takes particular notice of Labnn's flock perhaps regarding them as a sign of Laban s wealth. If Lo.ban's d1mghter hnd her attractions for the son of Isaac, so also bad Laban's sheep), that J'acob went near, and rolled the stone from the well'smouth (probnbly disregarding the shepherds' rule to wait for the gathe1ing of all the flocks, unless, indeed, Rachel's was the last), and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother. The threefold repetition of this phrase does not prove that Jacobo.ctecl in all this purely as a cousin (Lange). The phrase is the historian's, nncl Jacob had not yet informed Rachel of bis no.me.

entries.title: GEN 29:11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -ADd J'acob kissed Rachel,-in demonstration of his cousinly affection, If Jacob bad not yet di.ticovered who he was to tho fair shepherdess, bis behaviour must have filled her with surprise, even allowing for the unaffected simplicity of the times ; but the fact that she does not resent his conduct as o.n undue liberty perhaps suggests that he had first informed her of his relationship to the inmates of Laban's house (Calvin). On kissing vide eh. xxvii. 26- !lnd lifted ~p his voice, and wept-partlyfor JOY at findmg his relatives (cf. eh. xliii. 30 ; xlv. 2, 14, 15) ; partlf in grateful acknowledgment of God's kmdness in conducting him to his mother's brother's house.

entries.title: GEN 29:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And J"acob told (or, had told, ut supra) Rachel that he was her father's brotber,-as Lot i.~ uuled Abraham's brother, t~ougb in realit) his nephew (eh. xiii. 8 ; xiv. 14, 16)-and that he was Rebekah's son (this clause would explain the meanina of the term "brother" in the former): and she ran and told her father. Like Rebekah, believing the stranger's words and running to report them, though, unlike Rebekah, first relating them to her father (cf. eh. xxiv. 28).

entries.title: GEN 29:13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, when Laban heard the tidings (literally, heard the hearing, or thing heard, i. e. the report of the arrival) of J'acob his sister's eon,-he acted very much as he did ninety-seven years before, when Abraham's servant came to woo bis sister (eh. xxiv. 20, 30)-that (literally, and) he ran to meet him, and embraced him, -so nitemo.rdsEsau did Jacob (eh. xxriii 4), and Jacob the two sons of Joseph (eh. xlviii. 10)-o.nd kissed him, and brought him to his house-thus evincingthe same kindness o.nd hospitality that hnd che.r.icterised him on the previous occasion. And he (Jacob) told Laban all these things-what hismother bad instructed him to say to attest his kinship (Cnlvin) ; the things relnted in tho immediate context (Keil); more likely the entire story of bis life, and in particular of bis exile from homo, with its co.use and object (Rosenmilller, Kalisch, Lange).

entries.title: GEN 29:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Labanea.id untohim(giving utterance to tho impression Jo.cob's recital bo.d produced upon his mind), Surely thou ort my bone and my flesh-i. e. my blood rclation (cf. Judges ix. 2 ; 2 8nm. v. 1). Lo.b:m meant that Jacob bnd satisfoctorily proved himself Robekah's son. And he abode with him the space of a month-literally, a month ofdays (cf. eh. xli. 1; Numb. xi. 20), or II month as ro~rds time, "the second substantive deso.ibmg the general notion of which the first is nspecification" (Ii:Rlisch).

entries.title: GEN 29:1–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob at the well of Haran: a romantic adventure. I. JACOB'B 'MEETING WITH THE SHEPHERDS, 1. Tlie yrO'IJidential discovery. The well in the field with the three flocks of sheep lying by it ennbled Jncob to ascertain hie whereabouts, nncl ultimntely l~d to his finding Rachel. God guides the steps of his 558 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. XXIX. 1-14. people without interfering with the ordinary course of nature, simply directing them in the exercise of sense and intellig·ence; and doubtless Jacob recognised in his lighting on the Haran well a first instalment of that celestial guidance he had been lately promised. Saints should practise the art of discerning the movement of God's finger in the minutest and commonest events of life. 2. The friendly conversation. Saluting the shepherds as his brethren, i. e. as masters of a common craft, Jacc:b gathers from their frank communications that he was on the outskirts of Baran, in which bis uncle Laban was a prosperous and wealthy citizen, and that hie cousin Rachel was on the road to that very well beside which he stood with a flock of her father's sheep. Great is the virtue of asking questions, especially when they are prefaced with politeness. Seldom anything is lost, but frequently much is_ gained, by courteous inquiries. 3. The prudent counsel. Observing his friends disposed to indolence, and perhaps desirous of meeting Rachel alone, Jacob recommends them to uncover the well, water their flocks, and drive them off again to pasture, since much of the day yet remained. If it was their advantage he sought, his advice was good; if it was his own interest he served, the stratagem was ingenious. God's people should be wise as serpents, but harmless as doves, . II. JACOB's FIRST SIGHT OF RACHEL. 1. The gallant action. The lovely shepherdess arriving made a deep impression on her cousin's heart. Springing to bis feet, he rolls the stone from the well's mouth, fills the troughs, and waters Laban's sheep-impelled thereto, shall we say, as much by consideration for the fair girl who attended them as for the rich flock-master who possessed them. Kindly acts proceeding from loving hearts are sometimes largely assisted by the attractions of their recipients. 2. The lO'IJing salutation. "And Jacob kissed Rachel." If before explaining who he was, it must have taken her by surprise even in those unconventional times; but it is probable he may have first announced his name, in which case bis behaviour was only in accordance with the manners of the -age. Suitable expressions of affection to friends beseem both grace and nature; 3. The irrepressible emotion. "And Jacob lifted up his voice and wept"-expressive both ·of joy at finding his relatives, and of gmtitude for God's goodness in guiding him to the house of his mother's brother. Unexpected good and eminent providences kindle transports of delight in gracious souls. 4. The important communication. "Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's brother, and that he was Rebekah's eon: and she ran and told her father." Friends, and much more Christians, meeting on life's journey, should with frankness discover themselves to each other, and give each other hearty welcome. III. JAcoB's INTRODUCTION TO LADAN. 1. The uncle's reception of his nepltew, "Laban ran to meet his sister's son, and embraced him,.and kissed him, and broug·ht him to bis house." Kinship and kindness should ever be allied. Laban's hospitality to Jacob was grounded on the fact of their relationship. So is Christ'li entertainment of his people based upon the circumstance that they are" members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones." 2. The nephew's return to ltis uncle. Ingenuous confidence-" Jacob told Laban ,all these things"-and faithful service. I! isimpl_ied in ver. 15 that during the month Jacob abode with La~an he s_erved m k~epmg Laban's sheep. God's people should endeavour as far as m them hes to reqmte the kindnesses of relatives and friends.

entries.title: GEN 29:15

entries.content: - And Laban said unto Jacob (probably at the month's end), Jlecause thou nrt-litcrally, is it not that th-Ou art (cf. eh. xxvii. 36; 2 Sam. xxiii. 19)-my brother, -my kinsman (vide on ver. 12)-shouldest thou therefore serve me for nouJht t (literally, and th()'IJ, serves& me gratuitously) tell me, what shall thy wages be I A proof of Le.ban's generosity and justice (Kalisch); of his selfishness llDd greed (Keil) ; of his prudence and sagacity in opening up the way for a love-suit (Lange).

"If nnthentic l1istory was not in the wny, Lenh, as the mother of Judah, nnd of the Davidic lllessinnic line, ought to h11vo carried off the 1/rize of beauty after Sarah and Rebekah (Lange).

entries.title: GEN 29:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jaoob loved Rachel (it is more tlian probable thnt this was an illustration of what is known ns "love at first sight " on the part of Rachel as well us Jncob) ; and said, I will serve thee seven years for Rachel thy younger daughter. Hoving no property \\ith which to buy his wife, 11ccording to Oriental custom (Kalisch), or to give the usual dowry for her to her father (Keil),-cf. eh. xxiv. 63; xxxiv. 12; 1 Sam. xviii. 25,-Jacob's offer was at once accepted by his grasping uncle, though ho was that uncle's "brother" (ver. 15).

entries.title: GEN 29:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban said, It is better that l give her to thee, than that I should give her to another man. Orientals commonly prefer alliances within the circle of their own relatives. Burckhardt, Volney, Layard, and Llllle testify that this is still the case among the Bedouins, the Druses, and other Eastern tribes. Abide with me-- a formal ratification of the compact on the part of Laban.

entries.title: GEN 29:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jacob served-hard service (eh. xxxi. 40, 41), in keeping sheep (Rosen xii 12)- seven years for Rachel. Tho purity and intensity of Jacob's affection was declared not a.Ione by the propose.I of a seven yenrs' term of servitude,-11. long period of waitingfor 11.manoffifty-seven, ifnotseventy. seven, years of age,-but also by the spirit in which he served bis 11varicious rehltive. MllDy as the days were that req_uired to intervene before he obtained possession of his bride, they were rendered happy hy the sweet society of Raebel. And they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her. "Words breathing the purest tenderness, nnd expressingmore emphatically than the flowery hyperboles of romantic phrnseology the deep attachment of un uf• fectionute heurt" (Kalisch); words too which show the lofty apprecintion Jncob butl of the persona.I worth of his future bride.

entries.title: GEN 29:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jacob said unto Laban (who, though the term of servitude hud expired, appeared to be in no hosto to implc• ment his pnrt of the bargain), Give me my wife (i e. my 11filanccd wifo, ns in Dent. xxii. 23, 24; lliatt. i. 20), for my days are fu.llllled (i.e. my tC11Jl ofsorvico is completed), that I may go in unto her-quo sigmficat intactam adhuc esse virginem (Cnlvin); a proof that Jacob's love was pure and true.

entries.title: GEN 29:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban (unnble to evade or delay tho fulfilment of his ngreemeut with Jacob) gathered together all the men of the TRE BOOK OF GENESIS. [err. XltlX. 16-30. place (not the entire population, but the princifal inhabitants), and made a feasta "m1shteh," or drinking (cf, eh. xix, 3), i. e. a wedding banquet (cf, bride-ale = bridal), which commonly lasted seven days (Jndges xiv. 10; Tobit xi. 18), though it appears to have varied according to the circumstances of the bridegroom.

entries.title: GEN 29:23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him. The deception practised on Jacob was rendered possible by the fact that the bride was usuallv conducted into the marringe chamber veiled ; the veil being so long and close as to conceal not only the face, but much of the person (vide eh. xxiv. 65). And he went in unto her. The conduct of Laban is perfectly intelligible as the outcome of his sordid avarice; but it is difficult to understand how Leah could acquiesce in a proposal so base as to wrong her sister by marrying one who neither sought nor loved her. She must herself have been attached to Jacob; and it is probable that Laban had explained to her his plan for bringing about a double wedding.

entries.title: GEN 29:24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban gaveUDto his daughter Leah Zilpe.h-" the Dropping" f (Gesenius), "Myrrh-juice" (Furst) - his me.id (according to Gcsenius the ,rnrd is closely connected with an UDused root signifying to spread out, hence a maid-servant) for an handmaid. This was in accordance with Oriental custom (vide eh. xxiv. 61). That Leah obtained only one damsel need not be RScribed to Labe.n's parsimonious character, but to hisalready-formed intention to bestow a second on Rachel

entries.title: GEN 29:25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah. If Jacob's deception, even with the veiled bride, may still be difficult to understand, it is easy to perceive in Leah's substitution for Rachel a clear instance of Divine retribution for the imposition he had practised on his father. So the Lord oftentimes rewards evil-doers according to their wickedness (cf. 2 Sam. xiL 10-12). And he said to Laban (who, Calvin conjectures, had given Jacob a splendid entertainment the night before to make him say nothing about the fraud), What is thia thou ha.et done unto met did not I serve with thee for Ra.chel 1 wherefore then hast thou beguiled me 1 It says much for Jacob that he did notseek to repudiate the marriage. Perhaps he saw the hand of God in what had bappcned, and probably considered that, though he had chosen Rachel, God had se• lccted Looh as his "ife, If so, it must be set to Ja.cob's credit that at the coll of God, thus providentially addressed to him, ho was prepared to sacrifice his best affections to the claims of religion and duty. It is not Jacob, but Lsbnn, ,vho proposes that he should also marry Rachel.

entries.title: GEN 29:26

entries.content: -And Laban so.id, It must not be so done-tl1e future expresses the thougl1t that the custom l1as grown into nstrongmoral obligation (Kaliscl1)-in ourcountry(Hebrew, place), to give the younger before the firstborn. The same custom exists among tho Judians (Rosenmiiller; cf. Roberts, 'Oriental Illustrations,' p. 34), Egyptians (Lane), and other Oriental countries (Delitzsch).

entries.title: GEN 29:27
