entries.content: -Fulfil her week, -literalJy, makefull the week of thi,s one, i. e. of Leah, if Leah was given to Jncob on the first night. of the festivities (Calmet, Rosenmiiller, Keil, Kalisch, L:mge, Ainsworth); but if Leah was married at the close of the seven days, then it must referto Rachel's week (Bush, Murphy) -and we (including Labal).'s wife and eldest son, as in eh. xxiv. 50, 55) will give thee this also (i. e. Rachel) for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years. Almost every motive that is mean, base, and desP.icable appears in this behaviour of Labnn's; 1f he attached little vnlue to his daughters' affections, he had a keen apprecio.tion of Jo.cob's qualities as a shepherd.

entries.title: GEN 29:28
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. Literally, the week of this one, eitherof Leah orof Rachel, as abovo. Rosenmiiller, assigning the first week (vcr. 27) to Leah, rnfers this to Rachel ; but tho expression can scarcely have two different meanings within the compass of two verses. And he ga.ve him Rachel his daughter to wife also. The polygamy of Jacob, though contrary to the law of nature (eh. ii. 21-25), admits of some palliation, sine& R,ichel was the choice of his affections. 'fhs marriage of sisters was o.ftenvards decfarecl iucestuous (~e_vit. xviii. 18).

entries.title: GEN 29:29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah-" Bashful," "Modest" (Gcsenius)-his handmaid to be her maid.

entries.title: GEN 29:30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he went in also unto Rachel,and heloved also Rachel more thanLoah (implyin~, however, that Leah had a place in his affect1ona), and served with him yet seven other years. The seven years cunningly exacted for Leah was thus the second fraud practised upon Jacob (eh. xxx. 26; xxxi. 41; Hoseo. xii. 12). Oil. XXlX. 15-30.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 361

entries.title: GEN 29:15–30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob and Laban, or the deceiver decdved. I. JAcoB's CONTRACT WITH LABAN. 1. 1'he promiaed service-seven years of pastoral !l8Sistance. (1) Freel1 offere1l. '· I will serve thee seven years." Contracts are leg11.!ly and morally invalid where f,c.:ldom in the promiser does not exist. (2) Faithfully rendered. Jacob II served seven years," as he had stipulated. Voluntary engagements should be deemed sacred. (3) Readily accepted. Laban both appreciated' Jacob's merits as a shepherd and regarded Jacob's terms as easy. If Le.ban's words in closing with Jacob's offer did not indicate his guile, they were at least evidence of his greed. (4) Harshly exacted. Jacob testifies as much on leaving Laban. Covetous souls do not shrink from making hard bargains even with relatives and friends. 2. The stipv:Jated wages-Rachel in marriage as a wife. This part of the contract was- (1) Eagerly desired by Jacob. "Jacob loved Raebel," who was beautiful both in face and form. It is not sinful either to appreciate or desire personal symmetry and grace in those to whom we yield our affections. Female loveliness, though it may enkindle love, need not render the heart that loves less pure. (2) Patiently waited for byJacob. This was a testimony to the purity, tenderness, and strength of Jacob's affection. Besides transforming seven years into a few days, and ma.king pleasant and lightsome labour of what would otherwise have been galling bondage, it enabled him to wait God's time for receiving his bride. (3) Cheerfullyassented to by Laban. "It is better that I give her to thee than that I should give her to another man." Yet--(4) Guilefully withheld by Laban. Avaricious men seldom scruple at deceiving others for the sake of profit. Greed of gain is commonly accompanied by guile of men. II. LABAN's DECEPTION 0l!' JACOB. 1. The just request. 11 Give me my wife." "The labourer is worthy of his hire," and the servant is entitled to his wages. 2. The marriagefestival. "Laban made e. feast." Seemingly assenting to his nephew's request, the crafty uncle prepares a wedding banquet. Feasting and rejoicing are both becoming and allowable in connection with marriage celebration!!. 3. The subat,ituted bride. Either at the end of the first day or at the close of the festivities, "Laban took Leah and brought her," veiled nnd in silence, to the bridal chamber. For the wickedness of Laban in breaking his promise, defrnuding bis nephew, wronging his younger daughter, and practically prostituting his elder, excuse is impossible ; for Leah's acquiescence in her father's plot explanation, though not npology, may be found in her manifest love for Jacob, and perhaps in her belief that Laban had secured Jacob's consent to the arrangement. The man who could sell one daughter's affections nnd sacrifice nnotber's would not stick at deceiving both, if he could. 4. Tlie discovered fraud. "In the morning, behold, it wns Leah." The day manifests whnt the night hides-the sins of men; and the light of the great day will disclose what the darkness of time conceals. 6. The lame excuse. Interrogated by Jacob, Laban offers in extenuation of his heartless deception that popular custom demanded the marriage of an elder sister before a younger. So public opinion, prevailing habit, universal practice, are often pied in apology for offences against the Inw of God. But the conventional maxims of society are of no weight when set against Divine commandments. 6. The rigliteo113 retribution. Though indefensible on the part of Laban, the substitution of Leah for Rachel was a deserved punishment of Jacob. Having wronged Esau his brother, he is in turn wronged by "u brother"-Laban. Having substituted the younger (himself) for the older (Esau),.ao is recompensed by ho.ving the older put into the pl11ce of the younger. Ae Isaao knew not when he blessed Jacob, so Jacob knows not when he marries Loah. As Jacob acted at the instigation of his mother, Leah yields to the suggestion of her fo.ther. 7. The amicable settlement. Jacob celebrates the week of festival for Leah, nnd then receives Rachel as o. wife, engaging to serve another term of seven years for her who had lightened the labour of the previous seven. If Jacob's conduct evinced sincere attachment to Rachel o.nd peaceful disposition towardii Laban, it displayed doubtful regard for the law of God. 362 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. [vu. XXIX. 15-80.

entries.title: GEN 29:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie JJOW(!I' of true aJfection,. "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel," &c. I. THE INWARD SPRING OF THE OUTWARD LIFE, Power of the heart over the will, over the circumstances, over flesh. 'l'ime measured by the motions of our thought. The world needs to be taught that the material rests on the immaterial. II. THE SERVICE OF LOVE THE CONSECRATION AND CONSUMMATION OF HUMAN ENERGY.. Christ the highest object of affection. The life of his servant cornpa.red withthe life of selfish caprice. III. THE GREAT EXUfPLE OF LOYE SUGGESTED. Jacob I\ type of Christ; Rachel, of his Church. He served for her. His love made obedience, even unto death, his delight. IV. SPECUL TRIAL BAS ITS SPECIAL REWARD, Jacob served doubly for Rachel; but his service was amply paid afterwards, although for a time the veil of disappointment hid the purpose of Gcd. While Leah, as the mother of Judah, was the true ancestress of Messiah, still it was in Joseph, the son of Rachel, that Jacob's heart wns satisfied, 8Ild that the history of the kingdom of God was most manifestly carried on and its glory set forth, .As in the CW:le of Sarah and Rebekah, so in that of Rachel, the birth of the representative seed is connected with special beatowments of grace.-R. Ver. ro.-Christ's love for the Church. ".And Jacob· served seven years for Rachel." On the surface this is a step in Jacob's training, in the fulfilment of God's promise at Bethel. It shows a new feature in his character. We see. not the man of cunning devices, but one full of pure, self-sacrificing love. Fourteen years of service willingly given to purchase, according to Eastern custom, his bride. But Jacob's love suggests the deeper and purer love of Christ for the Church. Rachel a type of the Bride; a shepherdess and" fairest among women" (Cant. i. 7, 8); sharer of the sufferings of the Church (Jer. x.xxi. 15; Matt. ii. 18; Rev. xii. 17). For the Church's sake (Ephes. v. 25) Christ "served" (Phil. ii. 7) ; became a Shepherd (John x. 11); with his service and life-blood," obedient unto death," he purchased her (.Acts :x:x. 28), to unite her to himself for ever. I. THE LORD "SERVED II BECAUSE BE LOVED BIS CHURCH. In condescending to unite himself with human nature ; in bearing the infirmities of childhood and stoie of subjection ; in bearing the contradiction of sinners and the wrath of God. And still in standing and knocking (Rev. iii. 20); in bearing with half-hearted believers (2 Pet. iii. 9); in pleading with and for the wayward (1 John ii. 1; 2 Cor. v. 20); in seeking and following individual sheep. The love which led to this was free, not deserved or purchased. Rachel brought no dowry to Jacob. The Church has of its own no spiritual wenlth (Isa. lxiv. 6 ; Rom. iii. 23). The Bridegroom had to s:inctify and cleanse it. By nature unholy, at variance with God's will; yet, knowing this, he loved it (cf. Rom. viii. 35). For love to Rachel Jacob g·ave the la~our of fourteen years. For the Church Christ grudged nothing-gave himself. Sacnfi_ce 11 mark of true love. How many will not sacrifice anything-will not leave a gam, a companion, an amusement-to "win Christ." In the garden bis human nature shrank from the bitterness of the cup, but he persevered. Why? . II. THE LORD "SERVED" THAT BE MIGHT UNITE us TO HIMSELJI'. Mar11age, the closest earthly tie, used as a type. No mere removal of condemnation satisfied ~hat love, nor even our being made happy; he became such as we are, that we might become such as he is. '£he Church is his Bride (Ephes. v. 27; Ilev. xxi. 9), sharer of his kingdom (Rev. iii. 21; xx. 4), of his blessedness and glor;r (J_ohn ~vii: 22-24). And this belongs to its humblest and wealcest member. A un10n m this li£e (Cant. ii. 16; John xv. 4); peace in committing all cares to him, even our own steadfastness (Jolm x. 28; Rom. viii. 35; Heh. xiii. 6). A union after our departure more close (Phil. i. 23). Here we see dimly (1 Cur. xiii. 12). The conditions of I?ortnl life hinder clear visions (Exod. xxxiii. 20). The law of sin in our members lnnders perfect union. Then no impediment (Luke x.xiii. 43). Union perfected after the resurrection (1 Thess. iv, 7). The body, which now limits consoioua union, shall OH, XXIX. 31-35.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 363 then minister to its completeness. his human nature. Not till then shall we be perfectly like him in III. HE "SERVED" THAT WE MIGHT HAVE CONFIDENCE IN ms LOVE. Jacob's love not shaken by time, or by the deceit practised upon him, a type of Christ's. Often forgetful, _often faithless, we might well think, How dare I trust to a love so often neglected? But his love is not wearied out (Isa. xlix. 15). He has graven us with the nail-prints on his hands. His word is etiTI, "Look unto me; " trust my love (Pa. xxxvii. 5).-M.

entries.title: GEN 29:31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: And when the Lord saw-literally, and Jehovah saw. As Eve's son was obtained from Jehovah (eh. iv. 1), and Jehovah visited Sarah (eh. xxi 1), e.nd was entreated for Rebekah (eh. xxv. 21), so here he a.gain interposes in connection with the onward development of the holy seed by giving children to Jacob's wives. The present section (vers. 31-35) is by Davidson, Kalisch, and others o.ssigned to the Jehovist, by Tuch left undetermined, o.nd by Colenso in several parts ascribed to the Elohist. Kalisch thinks the contents of this section must have found a pince in the earlier of the two documents-that Leah was hated,-i. e. less loved (cf. Mal i. 3)-he opened her womb (cf. 1 Sam. i. 6, 6; Ps. cxxvii. 3) : but Rachel was barren-as Sarai (eh. xi. 30) and Rebekah (eh. xxv. 21) had been. The fruitfulness of Leah and the sterility of Rachel were designed not so much to equalise the conditions of the sisters, the one having beauty and the other children (Lange), or to punish Jacob for his partiality (Keil), or to discourage the admiration of mero beauty (Kalisch), but to prove that "the origin of Israel was to be a work not of nature, but of gmce" (Keil).

entries.title: GEN 29:32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Leah conceived, and bare a son, and she called his name Reuben (literally, Reit-ben, Behold a Son I an expression of joyful surprise at the Divine compnssion) : for she said, Surely the Lord hath looked npon my affliction. Though not directly contained in the term Reuben, the sense of these words is implied (Kalisch). As Leah's child was an intimation that she had been an object-of Jehovah's compassion, so did she expect it to be II means of drawing towards herselfJacob's affection. Now therefore (literally, for now) my husband will love me. She was confident in the first flush of maternal ;joy that Jaeob's hell.l't would turn towards her; she believed thot God had sent her child to effoct this conversion of her husband's affections; and she regarded the birth of Reuben as a. signal proof of the Divine pity.

entries.title: GEN 29:33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she conceived again, and bare a son (probably the following year) ; and said, l!ecaUBe the Lord hath heard that I was hated (the birth of Reuben had obviously not answered Lcah's expectations in increo.sing Jacob's love), he hath therefore given me this son also (the faith and piety of Leah are as conspicuous as her affection for Jacob) : and she called his name Simeon -i. e. Hearing, because God had heard that she was hated (ut supra).

entries.title: GEN 29:34
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she conceived again (say, in the third year of her m,miage), and bare a son; and said, Now this time will my husband be joined unto me,-ili?, to join, is the root from which comes 1)2 (Levi), bcr son's name-becaUBe I have born him three sons : therefore was his name called Levi- Associated, or Joined.

entries.title: GEN 29:35
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she conceived again, and bare a son (possibly in the fom1:h year of marriage, nnd in Jacob's eighty-eighth year of n.ge, he having been seventy-seven when ho arrived in Haran, and eighty-four when he was united to Laban's daughters) : and she said, Now will I praise the Lord. Well she might ; for this was the ancestor of the promised seed (Murphy). There cannot bo a doubt that her excellence of character ns well as eminence of piety eventually wrought a change upon her husband (vide eh. xxxi. 4, 14 ; xlix. 31). Therefore she called his name Judah (i. e. Praise); and left bearing. Literally, stood still, i. o. ceased, J1·om bearing. Not altogether (eh. xxx. 16); only for a time, "th11t sho might not be untluly lifted up by her good fortune, or attributo to the fruitfulness of her own womb wl11tt the faithfulness of Jehovah, the cove1111nt God, hnd bestowed uron her" (Keil.)

entries.title: GEN 29:31–35
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Leali and Racliel, or the two wives. I. RACIIEL TIIE DELOVED, "Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah." That Leah was not hated in the sense of being regarded with aversion, the numerous family she bore to Jacob proves; tbut 864 THE BOOK OF GEN~S1S. [en. xicx. 1-11', she occupied a lower place than Rachel in her husband's nffections ie explicitly declared. This preference of Rachel to Leah was-1. NaJ,ural in Jacob. Rachel had been his he~rt•s choice from the first, while Leah had been thrust upon him against his inclination. But even had this been otherwise, as no man cnn serve two masters, so can no h_i.sband love two wives equally-an argument against polygamy. 2. Painfi!l to Leah. Had Leah loved Jacob less than she manifestly did, it is doubtful 1f the undue regard sbo,vn to Rachel would not have inflicted a grievous wound upon her wifely heart; but, entertaining towards him an affection strong and tender, she yeamed for a larger sl1are of his esteem, and at each successive child's birth gave utterance to a hope that he would yet be joined to her. No heavier blow can be dealt by a husband to the tender heart of a loving wife than to withdraw from her his love, or even to be cold and indifferent in its expression. 3. Sinful in th.e sight of God. Though not so beautiful as Rachel, Leah was yet entitled to an equal share with her in Jacob's affection. Equally with Rachel she was Jacob's wife. It was Jacob's sin that he had married her at all when he did not either love or desire her. On detecting the fraud he should have instantly repudiated the engagement. But having publicly ratified the contract with Leah by fulfilling her WP,ek, he owed to Leab a full share of his affection as a husband. Nay, though not the wife his inclination had selected, there is reason for believing that Leah, rather than Rachel, was the bride God had chosen (Leah was the ancestress of the Saviour); hence doubly was Jacob bound to love Leah equally with Rachel. II. LEAII THE FRUITFUL. W11ile Rachel enjoyed the highest place in Jacob's affection, she was "barren "-a grievous affliction to one who might possibly be the mother of the promised Seed. The fruitfulness of Leab was-1. Expr_essly caused by God. The Lord, who had decreed temporary barrenness for Rachel the fair, opened the womb of Leah the despised; neither to compensate Leah for the loss of Jacob's love, nor to punish Jacob for his sinful partiality; but to manifest his power, to show that children are the heritage of the Lord, to vindicate his sovereignty, to attest th::i.t God giveth families to whomsoever he will, and to suggest that the line of promise was designed io be not the fruit of nature, but the gift of grace. 2. Thankfully a.clcn,owledged by Leah. While cherishing the hope that her children would eventually unite Jacob's heart to her own, she delightedly recognised her exceptional fruitfulness as a special mark of Jehovah's favour, and gave expres~ion to her gratitude in the naming of her sons: Reuben, see, a son! Simeon, heanng; Le,i, joined ; Judah, praise. 3. Enviously belield by Rachel. This appears from the opening statement in the ensuing chapter; and this, though perhaps as natural as Leah's sense of pain at Rachel's preference by Jacob, was yet as sinful as Jacob's excessive partiality towards herself. Learn-1. The sinfulness and sorrow of having more wives at once than one. 2. The wickedness of wedding where one does not love. 3, The sovereignty of God in giving and withholding children. 4. The cruelty and criminality of showing partiality towards those who possess an equal claim on our affections. 5. 'l'he duty and profit of remembering and ackncwledging family mercies.

entries.title: GEN 30:1
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Envy working in Go<l:s people. "Rachel envied her sister." Jacob's love for Rachel a type of Christ's love for his Church. We cannot doubt that his love was returned. There was thus the chief element of conjugal happiness. But her sister, less favoured in this, had a blemiing which was denied her, ancl "Rachel envied her sister." It was not that she feared to lose her husband's love. Of that she had abundant proof. It was a selfish sorrow. Her husband's children were growing up, but they were not hers. Racbel's envy bas its counterpart among Christians. Love for Christ may take the form of selfish zeal ; unwillingness to acknowledge or rejoice in work for God in which we take no part. In the spiritual history of the world a blessing often seems to rest upon means irregular or unlikely. Where efforts that promised well have failed, God makes bis own power felt ; and many think this cannot be right (cf. John ix. 16), and would rather have the work not done than done thus (cf. Numb. xi. 28; Mark ix. 38). Contrast the spirit of St. Paul (Phil. i. 18). Examples of this: unwillingness to rejoice in good done by some other communion, or some other party than our own ; inclination to look at points of difference rather than at those held in common; the work of others doubted, criticised, or ignored; eagerness to warn against this or that. Self lies at the root of this. Perhaps the harvest of another seems to diminish ours. Perhaps our own thoughts are to us the measure of God's plans (cf. l\lark xiv. 4). Men see the outside of others' work, and judge as if they knew both the motives and the full results. Yet with this there may be much real zeal nnd love for the Lord. The failure lies in the want of complete acceptance of his will. To rejoice in work for Christ, by whomsoever done, is not inconsistent with decided views as to the objects to be aimed at, and the means to be used (1 These. v. 21). 1. We are callerl to enlarge the household of God ; to be the means of making enemies into children (cf. Ps. lxxxvii. 4, 5) through producing faith (cf. John i. 12). Each responsible for the faithful use of the powers given to us, and bidden to exnmine ourselves as to sincerity. But the visible results are as God pleases. Here a test of singleness of mind. Can we rejoice in success of a work in which we have no share, or when another's success appears greater than ours? (Gal. v. 26). 2. As an exercise of unselfishness, be careful not to provoke envy by parading distinctive peculiarities (Rom.xii. 18}or exalting our own work. 3. Be not discouraged that work of others seems more blessed (John iv. 36, 37). Faithfulness is within the power of all. It is that which God regards (Matt. xxv. 21). The result we cannot judge of here. The fruit delayed may prove a greater blessing.-M.

entries.title: GEN 30:22–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - And God remembered Rachel (cf. eh. viii. 1 ; 1 Sam. i. 19), and God hearkenedto her,-as to Leah (ver.17)- and opened her womb-as he had previously done to Leah (eh. xxix. 31). Rachel's barrenness had not continued so lon" as either Sarah's or Rebekah's.. And she ~onceived, and bare a son; and said, God he.th taken away my reproach-i. e. of sterility. 'l'he ma~drakcs of Leah having proved inefficac1ous, Rachel at length realises that child;en are God'.s gift, and this thought sufficiently explams the use of the term Elohim. And she called his name Joseph ;-1:}P.i~, either,"lie takes away," with allusion to the re_moval of her reproach, or, "he shall add," With reference to her hope of another son. Perhaps the first thought is not obscurely hinted at, though the second appears from tho ensuing clause to have occupied the greater prominence in Rachel's mind-and said, The Lord - Jehovah ; e. trace of the Jehovistic pen (Tuch, Bleek, et alii) ; rather an outcome of the higher spiritual life of Rachel, who had now got emancipated from all such merely human devices ns resorting to mandrakes, and was able to recognise her complete dependence for offspring on the sovereign grace of tho covenant God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob (Hengstenberg, Keil)-shall add to me another son.

entries.title: GEN 30:14–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.The BtO'f"1/ of the mandrakes. I. A YOUNG CHILD'S INNOCENCE, "Reuben found mandrakes ID the field, and brought them to his mother." Nature with its beautiful sights and harmonious sounds, possesses a wonderful fascinatio~ for the infant mind. In proportion as man sinks beneath the power of sin does he fall_ out o~ sympathy with God's fair world. Strong and tender is the bond of Jove wL,ch 1;1111tes a child to its mother. The true depositary for a child's treasures is the moth~r s lap, for a child's joys and sorrows the mother's heart. Yet a child's inexpenence and simplicity may sometimes ea.use a parent to err, thongh the true OH, XXX. 14-24.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 361} srmrce of temptation lies in the parent, and not in the child. "To the pure all things ru o rum; but to them that are defiled is nothing pure." 11. A GROWN WOMAN'S BUPERSTITION. " Give me of thy son's mandrakes." Rachel ohviouely shared the popular belief that Reuben's fragrant herbs would have an influence in removing her sterility. It is useless inquiring how such a notion criginated. Superstitions commonly arise from mistaking as cause and effect what are only coincident occurrences. Of more importance it is to note that Rachel wfls of mature years, had be~n born an_d nui:tured in wh~t ma)'. be regarded as a religions home, was now the wife of an mtelhgent and pious (1f also encompassed with infirmities) man, and yet she was the victim of delusive beliefs. In this Rachel was perhaps scarcely to be charged with blame. Superstition is essentially e. fault of the intellect resulting from defective information. But Rachel erred in calling superstition to her aid in her unholy rivalry with Leah ; all the more when she knew that God alone could remove her reproach. III. A JEALOUS WIFE'S BARGAIN. On the part both of Rachel and Lee.h it was a miserable compact; e.nd a pitiable spectacle it surely was, that of two rival wives contracting with one another about their husband's society. Rachel disposes of Jacob for a night in consideration of a handful of mandrakes, and Leah counts herself entitled to Jacob's favours as a boon which she had purchased with Reuben'ii yellow apples. Not to speak of the humiliation in all this to Jacob, and the continual misery to which he must have been subjected between his ardent sister-wives, think of the wretchedness it must have entailed upon the women themselves, and the dispeace it mnst have brought into the rival homes. .A more powerful condemnation of polygamy it will be difficult to find, or a more signal illustration of the retribution which sooner or later follows on the heels of transgression. IV. A SOVEREIGN GoD's DECISION, The two wives were seemingly uncertain whether to ascribe virtue to the mandrakes or not. God determined the problem in a way that must have fully convinced them. 1. That the mandrakes could not remove sterility he demonstrated by allowing Rnchel's barrenness to continue at least two years longer, though she had made use of Reuben's apples, and by opening Leah's womb without them. 2. That he alone could bestow offspring on married people he showed by remembering Rachel in his own time, and causing her reproach to depart. • Learn-1. That things and persons innocent and pleasant in themselves may lead astray. 2. That out of small occasions great events may spring. 3. That much infirmity may cling to good men and women. 4. That things desirable in themselves may be sought in wrong ways. 5. That God's hand should be recognised in the giving or withholding children.

entries.title: GEN 30:22–24
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The life of faith and its reward. The Scripture teaches us to put the £nets of common life in the light of God's countennnce. The true foundation on which family welfore rests is God's faithfulness and favour. The intense desire of the Hebrew women for children, especially sons, a testimony to the Divine covenant; the original promise pervading all the national life. I. The birth of Joseph a REWARD OF FAITH AND ANSWER TO PRAYER, God remembers, though we think he forgets. Reproach may lie awhile on the true believer, but is taken away at last. Syrophenicinn woman ; seeming neglect calls out stronger expression of faith. Pray without ceasing. II. BLESSINGS WAITED FOR are the more appreciated and the richer WHEN THEY COME. " Joseph" a type of him who, though he was sent after many prophets and long tarrying, was greater than all his brethren. The Rachel, the true beloved, the chosen bride, the Church in whom the true Jacob finds special delight, waits and prays. When God shall show that he has remembered and hearkened, the elect one shall be abundantly satisfied. " God hath to.ken away my reproach." III. All experience of Divine faithfulness is a great help, in looking forward, to cherish expectation. "The Lord shall add to me another son." We ask for more when we know that our prayer is heard.-R. Thus far the historian simply narrates the fact of the patriarch's prosperity, and the steps which led to it, "without expressing approb&tion of his conduct or describing his increasing wealth as a blessing from God. The verdict is contained in what follows" (Keil).

entries.title: GEN 30:25–43
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: ~acob and Lahan, or craft versus greed. I. JACOB's RESPECTFUL REQUEST OF LAllAN. At the close of fourteen years' harsh and exacting service, Jacob desires permission to take hie wives and children and return to Canaan. The motives which induced him were probably-I. The termination of hie contract, which released him from a servitude both galling and oppressive. 2. The remembrance of God's covenant, which had assigned him the land of promise as his true inheritance. 3. The joy occasioned by the birth of Rachel's child, whom he seems to have regarded as the theocratic heir. 4. .A desire to provide for his now rapidly-increasing household. IL JAcoB'e SELFISH HINDRANCE BY LAllAN. That Jacob's uncle and father-in-law was unwilling to acquiesce in his departure and solicitous to ret&in him was due to- 1. His appreciation of Ja.cob's qualities as a flock-master. Jacob felt he could appeal to "the service he had done" for the past fourteen years. 2. His discovery of a latent connection between Jacob's presence and his own augmenting prosperity. Laban, poor enough before his nephew's arrival, had shrewdly noted that the day of Jacob's coming had been the day of fortune's turning in his ~avo~r, and tha~, wherever his clever "brother" went, flocks and herds broke out beside him. 3. Hui secret hope of effecting easy terms with Jacob. Though ostensibly willing to ta~e him at hie own price, he was clearly calculating that he would_not have much d1~- ficulty in over-reaching the man whom already he had cheated m the matter of !us daughters. III. JACOB1 B BEM.ABKABLE CONTRACT WITH LABAN. He agrees to serve a third time with Laban on condition of receiving all the speckled and spotted, ringstraked and brown, e.nimals that Le.ban's flocks might produce, after ell of those sorts had been previoullly rt:moved. 1. The proposal of such a singular condition on the part of Jacob was an act not of folly, but of faith, being tantamount to a committal of his cause to God instead of Laban. 2. The acceptance of it on the p&rt of.Laban was a pitiful display of greed, and a proof that the bygone years of proseenty had both awakened in his soul the insatiable demon of avarice and extmgwshed any spark of kindly feeling towards Jacob that may have once existed in his breast. IV. JACOB'e CUNNINO BTRATAOEM AOAINBT LABAN. 1. The nature of it. Thie was the employment of a triple artifice: (1) by means of pilled rods to produce particoloured animals in Le.ban's flock; (2) on securing these, so to use them as to increase their number; and (3) to direct the animals in such n fashion that the Cli, XXXI. 1-21.j THE BOOK OF GEN'ESIS. 373 l!ltronger and healthier portion of the flock should be his, and the feebler Laban·~. 2. The BUCCeBB of it. That Jacob's stratagem did not fail is apparent; but how far it wo.s due to the particular expedient employed cannot be so easily determined. Tho.t impressions me.de upon the minds of sheep at rutting time affect the fcetus seems II well-established £net; but the extraordinary rapidity with which brown and speckled animali; were produced appears to point to the intervention of a special providence in Jacob's behalf. 3. 'l'he rightness of it. That in what Jacob did there was nothing fraudulent may be inferred from the fact that he acted under the Divine approval (eh mi. 12), and made use of nothing but the superior knowledge of the habits of anitnals whichhe had acquired through hie Jong experience in keepingsheep. V. JACOB's ULTIMATE ADVANCEMENT OVER LAFAN. This comes out with greater prominence in the ensuing chapter; the present notices his Rmazing prflSf,erity. "The man increased exceedingly; " and, in spite of Laban's craft and avarice combined, eventually eclipsed him in the possession of flocks and herds. Leam-1. The attractive influence of home, both temporal and spiritual. 2. The danger of material prosperity-exemplified in Laban. 3. The wisdom of trusting God in all things, even in secular callings. 4. The value of all kinds of knowledge, but especially of the best. 5. The advantage of having God upon our side in all our bargains-notably when dealing with the selfish and mean. 6. The right to use all lawful means to preserve our interests-particularly against such as would invade them. 7. The possibility of the last outstripping the first-in the Church as well as in the world.

entries.title: GEN 30:43
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's hutory an illustration of the blending together of the natural and the supernatural in God:s dealings. ".And the man increased exceedingly," &c. I. The PROMISE TO GUIDE, protect, and bless fulfilled in connection with the employment of ordinary faculties and instrumentalities. Jacob's craft partly natural, but in this instance specially assisted that he might be helped in an emergency. The 11 supplanter" in this case represented the better cause. II. HUMAN DEVICES only apparently, and not really, thwart the purposes of God. Jacob represents the people of God. The victory is appointed them. Their interests must be served by the kingdoms of this world, though for a season the advantage appears on the side of the mere calculating, selfish policy. The true wisdom is that which cometh from above. III. INCREASE in the best sense is God's promise. It will be sent as he wills and when he wills, but will be found the true answer to prayer and the true manifestation of love. On all that belongs to us the blessmg rests. Spiritual prosperity carries with it 1111 other. Though the individual may be called to suffer for the sake of the community, the promise to the Church must be fulfilled. "It is our Father's good pleasure to give us the kingdom." "The meek shall inherit the earth."-R.

H)-and all his goods which he had gotten,-Recush, literally, acqui-sition, hence substance, wealth in general, from racash, to acquire (vide eh. xiv. 11, 16, 21 ; xv. 14), which, however, is more specifically described as-the cattle ofhis getting, which he had gotten (both of the above verbs, kanah and racash, being now employed) in (i. e. during his stay in) Padan-aram, for to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.

entries.title: GEN 31:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban went-or, Now Laban had gone, probably to the other station, which was three days' journey from Jacob's flocks ('llide eh. xxL 36; and cf. eh. x:xxi. 22)-to &hear his sheep. fo this work he would probably be detained several days, the time of shearing being commonly regarded as a festal season (cf. eh. xxxviiL 12 ; l Sam. x.xv. 4 ; 2 Sam. xiii. 23), at which friendly entertainments weregiven. Whether Jacoli's absence from the festivities is to be explained by the dissension existing between Lim and Laban, which either caused him to be uninvited or led him to decline the invitation (Kurtz), or by the supposition that he had first gone and subsequently left the banquet (Lange), the fact that Laban wo.s so i,ngo.ged afforded Jacob the opportunity he desired for making bis escape. And B.acb.el had stolen (or, "and Rachel stole," 11.vniling herself likewise of the ol?portunity presented by her father's absence) the images that were her father's. The teraphim, from an unused root, taraph, si~nifying to live comfort.1,bly, like the Sanscnttrip, Greek rp,1m11, Arabic tarafa (Gesenius, Furst, sub voce), appear to have been smnll human figures (cf. eh.. xx.xi. 34), though the image in 1 S_nm. XIX. 13 mut have been nearly life. size, or at least a full-sized bust, sometimes made of silver (Judges xvii. 4), though commonly constructed of wood (1 Sam. xi.x. 13 -16); t~ey were worshipped ea go~s (,icl'w;\.a, LXX.; idola, Vulgate, cf. eh. x.xn. 30), consulted for oracles (Ezek. xxi. 26 ; Zech. x. 2), and believed to be the custodians and promoters of human happiness (Judges xvili. 24). Probably derived from the Ammieans (Furst, Kurtz), or the Chaldeans (Ezek. xxi. 21, Kalisch, Wordsworth), the worship of ~raphim was subsequently denounced as idolatrous (1 Sam. xv. 23 ; 2 Kings xiii. 24). Cf. with Rachel's act that ascribed to 1Eneas:- " Effigies sacrm divilm, Phrygiique Penates, Quos mecum a Troja, mediisque ex ignibus urbis, Extuleram" (Virg., '1En.,' iiL 148-160). Rachel's motive for abstracting her father's teraphim has been variously ascribed to a desire to preventher father from discovering, by inquiring at his gods, the direction of theirflight (Aben Ezra, Rosenrniiller), to protect herself, in case of being overtaken, by an appeal to herfather'sgods (Josephus), to draw her fatherfrom the practice ofidolatry (Bazil, Gregory, Nazianzen, Tbeodoret), to obtain children for herself through their assistance (Lengerke, Gerlnch), to preserve a memorio.l of her ancestors, whose pictures these ter..- phim were (Lightfoot) ; but wo.s probably due to avarice, if the images were made of precious metals (Pererius), or to a taint of superstition which still adhered to her otherwise relirous nature (Chrysostorn, Calvin, 'Speakers Commentary'), causing her to look to these idols for protection (Kalisch, Murphy) or consultation {Wordsworth) on her Journey.

entries.title: GEN 31:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Jo.cob stole away unawares to Laban the Syrian, - literally, stole tM heart of Laban the Sy1-ian, i. e. deceived his mind and intelligence, like rr:X,1rrEt11 1100v, Hom.,' II.,' xiv. 227 (cf. vers. 26, 27); hence= ir:pv,j,, (LXX.); so Calvin, Rosenmiiller, Keil, Gesenius, and others. Longe fancifully understands by the henrt of Labau which Jacob stole either Laban's daughters or his favourite Rachel. Gerlach contrasts Jacob's stealing withthat of Rachel, in which Jacob had no part. 'l'he exact import of Jacob's stealing is declnred by the worde that follow-in tho.t he told him not (Lange 11.nd Bush intorrret 11.itJ impersonally, ea eignifyiug in thtit or because It was not told; but in this among expositors they stand alone) that he :11.ed.

entries.title: GEN 31:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -So (literally, and) he :11.ed with (literally, and) all that he had; and he rose up, and paseed over the river,-i. e. the Euphrates, which was called by preeminence the river (cf. 1 Kings iv. 21 ; Ezra iv. 10, 16)-and set his face toward the mount Gilead. 1ll~J, according to Geseniu~, "the hard, stony region," from on unused quadrilateral root, signifyin$ to be hard, though, according to the historian (by a slight change in the punctuation), "The hill, or heap ofwitness," from the transaction recorded in verses 45-47, which name it here proleptically receives, was not the mountain-range to the south of the Jabbok, now styled Jebel JilM (Gesenius), Jebel-es- Ssalt (Robinson), Jebel osha (Tristrarn), since Jacob had not yet crossed the river, but that upon its northern bank, called Jebel Ajlun, and sitnated near 1.fahanaim (Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch, Porter).

entries.title: GEN 31:1–21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's flight from Laban. I. THE HO'!IEWARD DESIRE. The longing to revisit Canaan, which six years previously Laban's exactions and Joseph's birth (eh. xxx. 25) had combined to inspire within the heart of Jacob, returned upon him with an intensity that could no longer be resisted. Accelerated in its vehemence partly by the interposed delay to which it had been subjected, pnrtly by his further acquaintance with the meanness and craft of his uncle, and partly by his own rapidlyaccumulatingwealth, it was now brought tc> a head by-1. The calumnious remarks of Laban's sons. Inheriting the sordid and avaricious nature of their parent, they were filled with envy at the remarkable prosperity which had attended Jacob during the past six years. If good men are sometimes "envious at the foolish," it is not surprising that wicked men should occasionnlly begrudge the success of saints. Then from sinful desires they passed to wicked thoughts, occusing Jncob of having by superior craft out-manceuvred their designing father, and appropriated the flocks nnd herds that ought to have been his; which, however, was a manifest exaggeration, since Jacob had not token away all their father's "glory," and an unjustifiable calumny, since it was not Jncob's stratagem, but God's blessing, that had multiplied the parti-coloured flocks. And lastly, from witked thoughts they advanced to evil words, not only accusing Jacob in their minds, hut openly vilifying him with their tongues, adding to the sin of private sl1mder that of public defamation-conduct which the word of God severely reprehends (Prov. xxx. 10; 1 Cor. vi. 10; Titus iii. 2; James iv. 11). 2. The manifest displeasure of Laban. During the fourteen yeMs that Jacob kept the flocks for Rachel and Leah, Laban regarded him with evident s&tisfnction; not perhaps for his own sake, but for the unprecedented increase in his (Laban's) pastoral wealth which had token place under Jacob's fostering care. He wns even disposed to be somewhat pious so long as the flocks and herds continued multiplying (eh. xxx. 27). But now, when at the end of six years the relative positions of himself and Jacob are reversed,-when J11cob is the rich mnn and he, comparatively speaking at lenst, the poor one,-not only does his piety towards God disappear, but his civility towards m&n does not remain. There are many Labans in the Church, whose religion is but the shadow that wnits upon the sun of their prosperity, and many Labans in the world, whose amiability tow.ards others is only the reflection of their complncent feeling towards themselves. 3. T!te explicit command of God. Twenty years before, at Bethel, God had promised to bnng Jncob buck again to Cana&n, o.nd now he issues formal instructions to bis servnnt to return. As really, though not ns visibly nnd directly, God orders the footsteps of 1111 his children (Ps. xxxii. 8; xxxvii. 23). If it is well not to run before God's providence, as Jacob would have done had he returned to Canaan at the end of the fourteenth year, it is also well not to lag behind when that providence has been clearly made known. 'l'he assurance given to Jacob of guidance on his homeward journey is extended to all who, in their daily goings forth, obey the Divine instructions and follow the Divine leadings. II. THE CONFERENCE IN TIIE FIELD. 1. Tlte e:xplanatwn of Jacob. Three contrasts completo tho sum of Jncob's announcements to his wives. First, between the 378 THE BOOR OF GENESlR [en. xxxr. 1-21. growing displeasure of Laban their father and the manifest favour of the Elohim of his father (ver. 5); second, between the unwearied duplicity of their father, notwithstanding Jacob's arduous service, nnd tl1e ever-watchful protection of God &g!linst his injurious designs (vers. 6, 7) ; and third, between the diminishing herds of Laban and the multiplying flocks of himself, Jacob, both of which were traceable to Divine interposition (vers. 8, 10, 12). After enlarging on these contrasts, he informs them of the Divine!y-given order to return (ver. 13). 2. 1'lie answer of Rachel and Leah. Acknowledging the mean and avaricious spirit of their father, who had not only sold them as i,Jr..ves, but unjustly deprived them of the portions to which, as the daughters of a chieftain, they were entitled (vera. 14, 15), they first confoss that Jacob's wealth was nothing more than it would have been bad they been honourably dowered at the first; second, recognise the hand of God in thus punishing their father and restoring to their husband what was practically his; and, third, encourage him to yield complete and prompt obedience to the Divine commandment (ver. 16). III. THE HASTY DEPARTURE. In this there were four things discernible. 1. Faith. In setting his face towards Canaan ho was acting in obedience to Divine instructions; and respect unto God's commandments is an essential characteristic of living faith. 2. Love. In determining " to go to Isaac bis father" he was actuated by a true spirit of filial piety. 3. Wisdom. In stealing away unawares to Laban, while Laban was providentially detained at the sheep-shearing, there was commendable prudence, which, i{ possible, a good man should never lack. 4. Sin. Not indeed on Jacob's part, but on that of Rachel, who, taking advantage of her father's absence, carried off his Penates or household images. Learn-1. That the love of country and friends is deeply implanted in the human breast. 2. That it is a great trial for worldly men to see good fortune go past their doors. 3. That the love of money, or the greed of gain, is the l"Oot of every kind of evil. 4. That the promises of God, however long delayed, are certain of fulfilment. 5. That loving husbands should consult their wives in all important steps in life. 6. That daughters should avoid speaking ill of parents, even should those parents deserve it. 7. That wives should always study to encourage their husbands in doing God's will. 8. That those who flee from oppression should seek for safety in paths of God's appointing. 9. That thriving and prosperous sons should not forget their parents in old age. 10. That daughters should not steal from their fathers, even to the extent of pilfering worthless images.

entries.title: GEN 31:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Teraphim. "Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's." This the first direct mention of images in connection with worship, tho~gb tradition llpeak.s of Nimrod as an idolater (cf. Josh. x.x.iv. 2). Laban calls them his god~ (ver. 30); yet he and his family knew the Lord. His use of them was a corruption of worship. I. THE IMAGES. Teraphim. Had some resemblance to the human form (1 Sam, xix. 13). Of different sizes and materials. The manna~ of t~1eir use not_very cl~ar, but used in some way for worship. Apparently not as mtentional l"~belhon agamst God. Rather ae a help to worship him, but a help chosen in self-w1ll. It was the error forbidden in the second commandment ; a departure from the way of Abel, Noah .Abraham • tho device of a soul out of harmony with spiritual things, and unabl e to realis; God's presence in worship (cf. ~xod. x~!i. 4; Jud~es viii. 27; xvii. 3 • 1 Kings xii. 28). "'e live in midst of tlungs clanmng attention. Necessities of life compel it. .And the go~d- effect_of d_iligence is quiclt_l_.r felt. 'fhis n~t evil, but becomes a snare unless spmtual hfe vigorous (Matt: xm. 22 ; 1 Cor. vn 29-31). The habit of Jooldl'.g earthward grows. The walk wit~ Go_d becomes l~ss close. Then unreality in worship. Then t!1e attempt _by material_ aids_to reconcile worship with an unchanged life. Hence, m the old time, teraph1m ; m our days, will worship. ll, TEE EFFECT OF THIS ON THE MORAL CllARACTER AND ON TllE SPIRI'l'UAL LIFE; exemplified in Laban, Compure him as presented in ~h. xxiv. with what he now oppetlrs. Thero ho is hospitable, frank, 11nd Iibernl; here he is sordid, ungenerous, deceitful even to hie own nephew. There he acknowledges the Lord as the Guide of actions (eh. xxiv. 60, 61); here he speaks of "the God of your father," and of 11 my gods." The love of wealth had made God no longer first in his thoughts (cf. Ps. x. 4; Phil. iii. 19). Thus worship became a thing of times and seasons, a thing separate from daily life, and therefore possessing no influence on daily life. So in the Christian Church great nttentio,i to external aids and extravagant symbolism were the resources of a pervading spirit less spiritual tliar,in times before ; and these too often were as clouds hiding the foce of God. .III. RACHEL'B ACT, Stole teraphim. Why? Some have thought to wean her father from them. More probably wished to make use of them. Had not escaped her father's influence. Hence the want of a submissive spirit (cf. eh. x.xx. 1 with 1 Snm. i. 11). The evil spread in Jacob's household (eh. xxxv. 2). The necessity for innking a stand against it (Josh. xxiv. 23). IV. THE LESSON FOR OUR TIMES. The second commandment meets a real danger in every age,-of leaning upon secondary means in religious service. Teraphim no longtir tempt U"• But amid whirl of active life, danger of leaning too much on outward impressions for spiritual life ; of cultivating the emotions in place of spiritunl earnestness (Pa. cxxx. 6; Matt. xi. 12); of putting religious services (1 Sam, xv. 22) or work (Matt. vii. 22) in place of walk with God. Amid much apparent religious activity the striving against self (Luke ix. 23) and growth in grace may become languid (1 John v. 21).-M.

entries.title: GEN 31:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The separatwnfrom Laban. "And Jacob stole away unawares to Laban the Syrian," &c. A great lesson on- I. THE EVIL OF DISSIMULATION. Hatred and wrong the fruits of crafty ways. Family dissensions where the things of this world uppermost. Separo.tione which are made in the spirit of dependence on God rend no true bond, but rather strengther. affection. . .:II. THE F0RBEABA.NCE OF Goo. No justification of Laban, much imperfection in Jacob ; yet the shield of Divine patience and mercy thrown over the man who vowed the vow of service, in whom his grace would yet be abundnntly revealed. Laban's nction controlled by God. He forbad the evil design. He stilleth the enemy and the nvenger. "Take thou heed that thou speak not to Jacob either good or bad " (ver. 29). "Touch not mine anointed," &c. When we are doing God's work nnd walking towards his chosen end we may leave it with him to speak with those who would hinder or ha1m us.-R.

entries.title: GEN 31:26–30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -.4.nd Laban (ossuming & tone of injured innocence) said to J'acob, What hast thou done, that thou hast stolen away unawares to me, - literally, and (meaning, in that) tltou luut stolen myheart (vide supra, ver. 20 ; and cf. ver. 27)-and carried away (vide ver. 18) my daughters, as captives taken with the sword! Literally, as captives of the sword, i e. invitis parentibus (Rosenmiiller) ; language which, if not h_y-pocritical on Laban's part, was certainly hyperbolical, since he had already c,inced the strength of his parentcl affection by selling his daughters to Jacob ; and besides, so far ns it concerned either Jacob or his wives, it was quite untrue, Rachel and Leah having voluntarily accompanied their husband in his flight. Wherefore didst thou flee &way secretly,-literally, wherefore didst tltou hide thyself to.flee away; tq,;i (niph.), with an inf. following, corresponding to the similar construction in Greek of >.av9avuv with a part., and being correctly rendered in English by an adverb (vide Gesenius, 'Gram.,' § 142)-and ste&l away from me (literally, and steal me, ut supra); &nd didst not tell me, th&t I might (literally, and I would) have sent thee &way with mirth, and with songs, - in Oriental countries those about to make a long journey are still sent away cantionibus et musicorum instrumentorum coMentu (Rosenmiiller)-with tabret,-the toph was a drum or timbrel, consisting r,f a wooden circle covered with membraM. and fumishecl with brass bells (like the modern tambourint), which Oriental women beat when dancing (cf. Exod. xv. 20; Judges xi. 34; Jer. xxxi. 4)-and with !Larp 1 For a description of the kinMr see cl1. iv. 21. And h&at not suffered me to kiss my sons (i. e. the children of Leah and Rachel) and my daughters 1 It is perhaps judging Laban too severely to pronounce this complete hypocrisy end cant (Alford, Bush, Candlish, Gerlach), but equally wide of the truth is it to see in Laban's conduct nothing but generosity_of feeling (Kalisch) ; probably ~here was a mixture of both pater- ~al affection nnd crafty dissimulation (Delttzsch). , Thou h&at now done foolishly in so doing. 'l'he charge of fotly in Old Testament Scriptures commonly carries with it an imputation of wrong-doing (cf. 1 Sam. :riii. 13 ; 2 Sam. xxiv. 10). It is in the power of my hand-so the phrase ~~~jj, ''J! (cf. Deut. xxviii. 32; Neh. v. 5; Micah ii. I) is rendered by competent authorities (Gesenius, Flirst, Rosenmiiller, Kalisch Murphy, et alii), with which agree /,rxvE~ •i x•ip pov (LXX.), and valet manus mea (Vulgate), though the translation "My hand is for God," i. e. my hancl serves me as God (cf. Job xii 6; Hab. i ll), is by some preferred (Keil, Knobel, Jacobus)-to do you hurt: but the God of your fa.ther-the use of this expression can be rightly regarded neither ns a proof of Elohistic authorship (Tuch, Bleek, Colenso, Davidson) nor as a. sign of Laban's spiritual degeneracy (Hengstenberg, Wordsworth), since it is practically equivalent to Jehovah (vide eh. xxviii 13), but is probably to be viewed as a play upon the sound and sense of the preceding clause, as thus:-" It is in the El of my hand to do you evil, but the Elohim of your father spake to me." Another instance of this play upon the sound and sense is to be found in vers. 19, 20-" Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father's ; and Jacob stole the heart of Laban the Syrian" (cf. Quarry on Genesis, p. 498)-spake unto me yesternight, ea.ying, Take thou heed th&t thou speak not to Jacob -literally, guard orkeep theeforthyseif(the pleon. pron. being added ut supra, ver. 24) from spealcing with Jacob-either good or b&d (vide on ver. 24). And now, though thou wouldest needs be gone (literally, going tlwu didst go =thou hast indeed gone), because thou sore longedst after thy father's house (literally, because desiring thou didst desire. 'l'he verb 1:Ji;)f, to be po.le (whence I:]~~. silver, so called from its pale colour), expresses the idea of pining away nnd languishing through stronginward longing), yet wherefore hast thou stolen my gods 1 Laban had probably gone to consult his teraphim and so discovered their loss. Augustine cnlls attention to this as the first Scripture reference to benthen gods, ancl Calvin probably supplies the right explanation of the sense in which they were so styled by Lo.ban, non quia deitatem illic putaret ease inclusam, OB. XXXI. 22-44.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 381 ,ed quia in lwwYrem deorum imagines illaa ,olebat,· velpotius quod Deo sacrafa<:turua, vertebat se ad illaa ima,ginea (cf. Exorl. xxxii. 4; 1 Kings xii. 28). "This complaint of Laban, that his 'gods were stolen,' sbowctnthe vanity of such idolatry" (Ainsworth). Cf. Judges vi. 31; xvi. 24; Jer. x. 5, 11, 15. Vcrs. 31, 32.-And Jacob answera,1-" in an able and powerful speech" (Kalisch}- and said to Laban (replying to his first interrogation as to why Jacob had stolen away unawares), Because I was afraid : for I said (sc. to myself), Peradventure (literally, lest, i. e. I must depart without informing tl.tee lest) thou wouldest (or shouldest) take by force-the verb signifies to strip off as skin from flesh (vide Mic. iii. 2), and hence to forcibly remove-thy daughters from me (after which, in response to Laban's question about his stolen gods, he proceeds). With whomsoever thou fi.ndest thy gods, let him not live. If Jacob meant he shall not live, but I will slay him with mine own hand (Aben Rzra), let God destroy him (Abarbanel), I give him up to thee to put to death (Rosenmiiller), let him instantly die (Drusius), he was guilty ofgreat unadvisedness in speech. Accordingly, the import ofhis words has been mollified by regarding them simply as a prediction, "he will not live," i. e. he will die beforehis time(Jonathan),a predictionwhich, the Rabbins note, was fulfilled in Rachel (vide eh. xxxv. 16, 18); or by connecting them with clause following, " he will not live before our brethren," i. e. let him be henceforth cut off from the society of his kinsmen (LXX., Bush). Yet, even as thus explained, the language ofJacob was precipitate, since he ought first to have inquired at his wives 11nd children before pronouncing so emphatically on a matter of which he was entirely ignornnt (Calvin). Before our brethren-not Jacob's sons, but Le.ban's kinsmen (ver. 23)-disoern thou-literally, e.xamine closelyfor thyself, the hiph. of,~~ (to be strange) meaning to press stron~ly into a thing, 1,, e. to perceivo it by findmg out its distinguishing characteristics (vida Fiirst, sub voce)-what is thine with me, and take it to thee. For (literally, andl,- J'aoob knew not that Raohel had stolen them-othorwise he would have spoken with less heat and more caution.

entries.title: GEN 31:33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Laban. wen.t into J'aoob's ten.t, and into Leah's tent, and into the two maid-servants' tents ;-the clause affords an interesting glimpse into tho manners of the times, showing that not only husbands and wives, but also wives among themselves, possessod separate esl:ablishments)-but he ~ound them not. Then went he out of Leah's tent (he probably commenced with Jacob's nnll thoso of tho hand-maids, e.11d afterwards passed into Leah's), and entered into Rachel's tent-last, because she was the favourite. Cf. eh. xxxiii 2, in which a similar partiRlity towards Rachel is exhibited by Jacob (l7'ide Thomson's 'Land and Book,' i. 37C).

entries.title: GEN 31:34
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now Rachel had taken the images (teraphim), and put them in the camel's furniture, - the camel's furniture was not stramenta cameli (Vulaate), "the camel's straw" (Luther), but the camel's saddle (LXX., Onkelos, Syriac, Calvin, Rosenmiiller, Keil, and others), here called 111, from i1f, an unused root signifying either to go round in a circle, hence to run (Gesenius), or to be firmly wound together, hence to be puffed up as a bolster (Fi\rst). The woman's riding-saddlo was commonly made ofwicker-work and had the appearance of a basket or cradle. It was usually covered with carpet, and protected against wind, rain, and sun by means of a canopy and curtains, while light was admitted by openings in the side (cf. Gesenius, sub voce; Kalisch in loco). "'fhat which is now customary among the Arabs consists of a large closed basket-work, with a place for sitting and reclining, and awindow at tl.te side ; one of this kind hangs on each side of the camel" (Gerlach)-and sat upon them. "To us the picture of Rachel seated upon the camel furnihue is true to life, for we have often seen its counterpart. The saddle-bags and cushions which were to be set upon the camel lay piled on the floor, while she sat upon them" (Yan Lennep, quoted by Inglis, p. 254). And Laban searched-the word means to feel out or explore with the hands (cf. eh. x.xvii. 12; Job xii. 25)-all the tent, but found them not.

entries.title: GEN 31:35
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she said to her father,- " covering theft bv subtlety and untruth" (Kalisch), nnd tbus proving herself 11 true daughter of Labnn, as well as showing with how mnch imperfection herreligious chnracter was tainted-Let it not displease my lordliterally, let it not burn with anger (10~. from i"l~,:J, to glow, to burn) in the eyes of mylord(Adoni)-that I caDJ1otriseup before thee;-Oriento.l politeness required children to rise up in the presence of their parent~ (vide Levit. xix. 32; and cf. 1 Kings ii. 19). Hence Rachel's npology we.e not unnecessnry -for the custom of women-(liternlly, tht way of women; 11 periJ?hre.sis for menstruation (cf. eh. xviii. 11) which, under the law,required females, as ceremonially unclean, to bo put apart (Lovit. xv. 19). Thnt, prior to the law, this particnlnr statute concerning women was in force nmong tho Arnmro:ms nppenrs from tho present instance ; nnd that it wus not exclusively Jowish, but shared in by other I\Rtioua of antiquity, is the opiniou 382 THE BOOK OF ttENESIS. [CH, XXXI. 22-44, of the best authorities (vide Kurtz, 'History of the Ole1 Covenant,' § 79 ; 'Sacrificial Worship of the Old Testament,'§ 213; Keil in loco; both of ,vl1om quote Bahr's •Symbolikof the Mosaic Cultus,' ii. 466). Roberts mentions that under similar circumstances mth Rachel no one in India goes to the fomple or any religious ceremony (' Oriental Illustrations,' p. 37)-is upon me. It is just possible R.-ichel may have been speaking the exact truth, though the probability is she was guilty of fabrication. And he searched (everywhere except among the camel's furniture, partly from fear of defilement, but chiefly as regarding it impossible that Rachel in her then state would sit upon his gods), but foUlld not the images (teraphim). The three times repeated phrase "ho found not," emphasises the complet~ness of Laban's deception.

entries.title: GEN 31:36–42

entries.title: GEN 31:22–44
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Lahan'spursuit of Jacob. I. THE HOSTILE PREPARATION. Leaming of bis son-in-law's departure, Laban at once determines on pursuit; not alone for tl!e purpose of recovering his household gods, but chiefly with the view of wreaking his pent-up_ veng~ance on Jacob, whom ½e now regarded as the spoiler of his fortunes, and if possible to capture and detam the much-coveted flocks and herds which he considered had been practically stolen by his nephew. Mustering his kinsmen by either force or fraud,-by command enjoining those belonging to his household, and by misrepresentation probably beguiling such as wereindependent of bis authority - he loses not a moment, but starts upon the trail of the fugitives. Worldly men ~re seldom slow in seeking to repair their lost fortunes, and angry men are seldom laggard in exacting revenge. It is only God's vengeance that is slow-footed. II. THE DIVINE INTERPOSITION. Six days the wrathful Laban follows in pursuit of Jacob, and now the distance of one day is all that parts him from the fugitives. In a dream by night be is warned by Elohim to speak neither good nor bad to Jacob. The incident reminds us of the Divine superintendence of mundane affairs in general, and of God's care for his people in particular; of the access which God ever has to the minds of bis dependent creatures, and of the many different ways in which be can communicate bis will ; of his ability at all times to restrain the wrath of wicked men, and check the hands of evil-doers, who meditate the spoiling of his Church or the persecution of hie Raints. Ill THE STORMY INTERVIEW. 1. The pompous harangue ofLaban. Laban gives way to-(1) Passionate reproach; chargmgJacob with having clandestinely departed from bis service and violently carried off his daughters, in the first of which Jacob did nothing WTong, while the second was a pure exaggeration (vide ver. 16). (2) Hypocritical affection; declaring that Jacob, bad he, Laban, onlyknown, might have been sent away with public demonstrations of rejoicing, while Rachel and Leah might have carried with them a parent's kiss, if not a father's blessing. But if Jacob's leave-taking would in any way have excited Laban's jubilation, it is doubtful if this would not have been traceable less to Laban's regard for his son-in-law than to Laban's anxiety about his flocks, which, in the absence of the spoiler, he might hope would become prolific as before : while as for Laban's love for his daughters, one might fairly claim indemnity for suspecting an affection so recent in its origin, and so palpably contradicted by his previous behaviour. (3) Boastful assertion ; passing on, like all weaknatures who love to he considered formidable, to brag about his power to inflict injury on Jacob (ver. 29), and to hint that he only forbears to do so out of respect for God, who had appeawd to him on the previous night. (4) Direct accusation; ere he closes his oration, deliberately impeaching Jacob with having abstracted his teraphim. 2. Tlie ingenuous response of Jacob. In this are discernible virtues worthy of imitation, if alao infirmities deserving reprobation. If Jacob'e candour in declaring the reasons of his flight (ver. 31) and willingnees to r6.9tore to La.ban whatever property belonged to him (ver. 32) are examples to be copied, on the other hand, the over-confident assertion that no one had Laban·s gods, 11nd the over-hasty imprecation on any who should be found possessing them, are 1:ot to be commended. IV, THE FRUITLESS SEARCH. 1. The musing gods. On the nature, probable origin, and uses of the teraphim see Exposition, ver. 19. The existence of these silver or wooden images in Laban's tent was a proof of the reliITTous declension if not complete apostasy, of this branch of the family of Tera!~ Scripture ne~er represents idolatry as an upward effort of the human heart, as o.furtherdeveloprnent in the onward evolution of the son! (Sir J. Lubbock on the' Origin of Civilisation ' p. 256); but always as a deterioration, or a retrogression, or a falling away of the Irn:rian spirit from its rightful allegiance. The lose of Laban's manufactured deities was a ridiculous commentary on the folly of worshipping or trusting in a god that could be st<;>len-a complete reductio ad absurdum of the whole superstmcture of idolatry (cf. 1 Kings xviii. 27; Ps. cxv. 4, 8; Isa. xliv. 19; xlvi. 6, 7; Jer. x. 5). 2. The an;cious devotee. Invited by Jacob to make a search for his lost teraphim, Laban beg-ins with Jacob's tent, then with the tents of Bilhah and Zilpah, after which he passes into Leah's, and finally comes to Rachel's; but everywhere his efforts to recover his gods ore defeated. What a spectacle of infinite humour, if it were not rather of ineffable sadness-a man seeking for his lost gods I The gospel presentR us with the opposite picture-the ever-present God seeking for his lost children. 3. The lying daugliter. I£ the conduct of Raebel in carrying off the images of her father was open to serious question (vide Exposition, ver. 19), her behaviour towards her father in the tent was utterly inexcusable. Even if she spoke the truth in describing her condition, she was guilty of bare-faced deception. This particular passage in Rachel's history is painfully suggestive of the disastrous results of worldliness and irreligion in the training of children. Laban's craft and Laban'R superstition had both been factors in Rachel's education. 4. Tlte decdved parent. Worse than being disappointed in his gods, Laban was dishonoured by his daughter. But what else could he expect? Laban was only reaping as he had sowed. I\Iarvellous and appropriate are God's providential retributions. V. THE PASSIONATE INVECTIVE. It was now Jacob's tum to pour out the vials of liie wrath upon Laban, and certainly it burned all the hotter because of its previom1 suppression. 1. He upbraids Labn.n with the unreasonableness of his persecution (ver. 36). 2. He taunta Laban with the fruitlessness cif his search (ver. 37). 3. He reminds Laban of the faithful service he had given for twenty yenrs (vers. 38-41). 4, He recalls the crnfty 11ttempts to defraud him of which Labon had been guilty (ver. 41 ). 5. He assures Laban that it was God's gracious care, and neither his lionesty noraffection, that had prevented him from being that day a poor man instead of a rich emir (ver. 42). 6. He somewhat fiercely bids Laban accept the rebuke which God had addressed to him the previous night. VI. THE AMICABLE SETI1.EMENT. Doubtless much to Jacob's surprise, the wrnth of Laban all at once subsided, and a proposal came from him to bury past animosities, to strike a covenant of friendship with one another, and to part in peace. The seven days' journey, a:ffording time for •reflection; the Divine interposition, inspiring him with fear; the mortification resulting from his fruitless search, convincing him that he had really overstepped the bounds of moderation in accusing Jacob; the voice of conscience within his breast ra-echoing the words of Jacob, and declaring them to be true; and perhaps the sight of his daughters at Inst touching a chord in the old man's heart ;-all these may have contributed to this unexpected collapse in Laban; but whether or not, Jacob, as became him, cordially assented to the proposition. Lessons:-1. The reality of God's care for his people~illustrated by the appearances of Elohim to Jucob and to Lo.ban. 2. The misemble outcomi, of n worldly lifeexemplified in Laban. 3. The efficacy of n soft answer in turning away wrnthproved by Ja.cob's first response. 4. The difficulty of restraining angry speech within just bounds-exemplified by both. 5. The folly of idolatry, as seen in Laban's lost teraphim. 6. The evil fruits of bad par~ntal training, as they appear in Rachel. 7. The proper way of ending quarrels-exhibited hy Laban and Jacob in their covenant agreement. GENF.~TS. C 0 386 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XXXI. 45-55.

The most that ean l.,e reasonably inferred from the term Jegar-sahadutha is that Aramaic was the language of Mesopotamia (R~eenmiiller) ; besides this expression there ll! no oth~r evidence that Laban and Jacob conversed m different dialects; while it is certain that the word Mizpah, which was probably a~o spoken by Laban, is not Chaldee or Aramaic but Hebrew. Laban) said, Th11 I.ord~ehovah; a proof that vers. 49, 60 are e. The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge'-the verb is plural, either because Laban regarded the Elohim ofNahor os diJferentfrom the Elohim ofAbraham(Roscnmiiller, Keil, Kalisch, Wordsworth, 'Speaker's Commentary'), or because, though acknowledging only one Elohim, ho viewed him as maintaining several and distinct relations to the persons named (cf. Laban here invokes his own hereditary Elohim, the Elohim of.Abraham's father, to guard his rights and interests under the newly-formed covenant; while Jo.cob in his adjuration appeals to the Elohim of.Abmha.m's son. entries.title: GEN 31:45–55
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -G~leed and lrlizpah, OT the covenant ofpea.ce. I. Tm: COVENANT MEMORIALS, I. . ·The pillar of remembrance. The erection of the stone slab appears to have been the act of Jacob alone, and to have been designed to commemorate the important transaction about to be entered into with Laban. It is well to keep note of those engagements we make with our fellow-men in order to their punctual fulfilment; much more of those we make with God. It does not appear that any name was given to the'· column, and this may have been because it was intended chiefly for himself. 2. The pile ofwitness. This was the work both of Laban and Jacob, wl1ich they conjointly performed through the instrumentality of their brethren ; and being of the nature of a public monument, it was further characterised by a name- Laban calling it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob styling it Galeed, both expressions signifying heap of witness, and perhaps both of them naming it Mizpah, or watchtower, from the nature of the oath which they both took on the occasion. Men who are truly sincere in their covenant engagements are never afraid to bind themselves by public attestations of their good faith, though it is certain that of all men these least require to be so bound. II. THE COVENANT WORDS. 1. The solemn engagements. On the one hand Lnban undertakes never to pass the stone heap on Gilead to do injury to Jacob-not mentionino- the pillar, which was purely of Jacob's construction, and therefore supposed to ha~e a religious significance solely for Jacob; ond on the other hand Jncob record~ his vow never to cross the pillar and th!l pile to inflict wrong on Laban, and in addition, as Laban might be injured in bis daughterswithout crossing the forbidden line, never ~ afflict Rachel and Leah by taking other wives besides them. The engagement on JOth sides is to abstain from doing injury of any sort to each other ; and to this nil men are bound by both natural and revealed religion without the formality of an oath ; and much more than·other men, are Christians taken bound by God's grnco and Christ's blood to live peaceably with all men and be nt peace omongst tl1emselves. 2. Tlte impressive oaths. If it is dubious whether Labun appealed to God or only to the stone-nenp to witness his sincerity in promising not to harm Jucob, it is certain t.hat he appealed to God to keep a strict eye on Jacob (ver. 49), and inn sem:-supe~- '5titious way united the Goe! of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of thou •• • cc2 388 THE DOOK OF GENESIS. [UI. XXXI, 45-55 fathers, to judge between them. Jacob does not mention either pilo or pillar, but fWears by the fear of his father Isaac. III. THE COVENANT ACTIONS, 1. Tlie sacr{fice, The offering of sacrifice was esRential to the fonnntion of a covenant. As between God and man, it virtually proclaimed that God could enter into amicable relations with sinful man only on the basis of an atonement. As between man and man, it was equivalent to un ucknowledgment by the covenanting parties that both required to be covered with the blood of propitiation, That Jacob, and not Laban, offered sacrifice intimates that these truths were already in some degree appreciated by Jacob, though possibly they were not understood by Laban. 2. The feast. In making this feast Jacob may only l,a"'e been following the example of his father Isaac, who similarly entertained Abimelech and his statesmen at Beersheba on the occasion of the treaty which wa~ there formed between them ; but the sacrificial fe~st afterwards became an important element in the Mosaic cultus, and was designed to express the idea of house and table fellowship between the covenanting parties. IV. THE COVENANT RESULTS, 1. The ki.ss of reconciliation. It is not certain that Laban kissed Jacob when be prepared for his departure in the morning; perhaps that was too much to expect; but he kissed Rachel and Leah and their children. It was a sign of forgiveness not alone to them, but through them also to Jacob. 2. The pakrnal benedu:twn. Laban, whose better nature appears to have returned ns the result of the covenant, or of the feast, or of the contemplated parting with his daughters, poured out bis feelings in a farewell blessing on their heads. It is the last we hear or see of Laban in the Scripture ne.rrative. Let us hope it was the renval of early kindness and piety in the old man's heart.

entries.title: GEN 31:51–55
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Final coven,,ani between Jacob and Laban. I. ENTIRE SEPARATION FROM TEMPTATION IS TBE ONLY SAFETY. Very imperfect knowledge in the Mesopotamian family. Rachel's theft of the household gods a sign of both moral and ~piritual deficiency. The religion of Jacob and his descendants mast be preserved from contamination. Intercourse with the unenlightened and unsanctified, though 11ecessary for a time and in some degree, must not be suffered to obscure the higher light, or surround us with practical entanglements which hinder our faithfulness to God. I!. WHEREVER THE SPIRITUAL LIFE IS FEEBLE IT IS WELL THAT THERE SHOULD DE SOLEMN PU1!LIC ACTS OF COVENANTAND TESTIMONY. We want the Galeed and the Mizpah, the heap of witness and the watch-tower of faith. Many united together in the covenant, and thus became witnesses in whose presence the oath was taken. We are J,elpcd to faithfulness by the publicity of our vows. But the higher the spiritual life, the less we shall call in material things to support it. Jacob with Laban is not the true Jacob. A.11 dependence upon the symbol and rite is more or less compromise. !II. THE CONTACT OF THE HIGHER FORM OF RELIOION WITB THE LOWER ONE, OF 'l'HE MEANS OF PREPARING THE WORLD FOB THE '!'RUTH. Laban and hie family types of the lower order of religious knowledge and life. The covenant between the father• in-law and son-in-law in the name of the God of Abraham and the God of Nabor points to a rising light in the Mesopotamian family. We may be sure that the influence of Christianity will be supreme wherever it is brought face to face with men's religions. That influence may be embodied in matters of common life, in covenants between man and man, in laws and commercial regulations and social arrangements. IV. THE SEED OF THE DIVINE LIFE 1B PLANTED IN THE SOIL OF NATURE, BOT REVEALS ITS SUPERIORITY TO NATURE ilY BRINGING ALL THINGS AND JIIEN UilTO SUBJECTION 1'0 ITSELF. Jacob, Rachel, and afterwards Joseph, present to the Spirit of God elements of character which require both elevation and renovation. The grace is given. On a natu:al foundation inherited from others God rears by his ~race a lofty structure. The crafty and the thoughtful are often nearly allied. It 1s one of the spiri1u,i! danger~ to wLie;J, specially energetic und E:;Ubtle minds are exp06eJ, that tl.cy may so easily fall into an abuse Gf their superior mcnta,l q,niekneE~ :o the illjnry of thei1 OR. UXII. 1-~lJ.) TilE BOOK OF crn}n:sts. 389 moral purity nm! simplicity. Jac-ob ond Laban making their covenant togetl,er, and erecting their witnessing monuments, are another illustration of the homoge which even very imperfect chorocters pay to the God of truth. They appeal to him, and they do so in the presence of o world which they know will justify God, and not the sinner. The God of Abraham, the God of Nahor, the God of Isaac, judged between them. Jacob offered·sacrifice upon the mount, and invited bis brethren to a sacrificial banquet ; and it was in that atmosphere of mingled reverence for God and human affection that the heir of tlie covenant bade farewell to all that held him in restraint, and set his face once more towards the land of promise.-R.

entries.title: GEN 32:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: And the messengers returned to le.cob, saying, We came to thy brother Esau, and also he cometh to meet thee_(vide eh. xxxiii. 1), and four hundred men with him. That Esau was attended by 400 armed followers was a proof that he had grown to be a powerful chieftain. If the hypothesis be admissible that he had already begun to live by the sword (eh. xxvii 40), and was now invading the territory of the Horites, which he afterwards occupied (Delitzsch, Keil, Kurtz), it will serve to explain his appearance in the land of Seir, while as yet he had not finally retired from Canaan. That he = with such a fonnidable force to meet his brother has been set down to personal vanity, or a desire to show how po,)·erful a prince he had become (~yra, Menochm_s); to fraternal kindness, which prompted hrm to do honour to hiq brother (Poole, Colvin, Clarke), to a distinctly h_ostile inteutio!1 (Willet, Ainsworth, Candlish), at least 1f circumstances should seem to call for vengeance (Keil), though it is probable that Esau's mind on first hearing of his brother's nearness,' was simply excited, .and "~n .that waverinu state which the slightest mc1dent might s~othe into good will, or rouse into vengeance" (Murphy).
