entries.content: -A.nd Jacob said,-the combined beauty and power, humility and boldness, simplicity and sublimity, brevity an<l comprehensiveness of this prayer, of which Kalisch somewhat hypercritically complains, that it ought to have been olfered before resorting to the preceding precautions, hns baen universally recognisecl-O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, the Lord-Jacob's invocation is addressed not to Deity in general, but to the, living personal Elohim who had taken hh fathers Abraham and Isaac into covenant, i. e. to Jehovah who had enriched them with promises of which he was the heir, and wl10 had specially appeared unto himself (cf. eh. xxviii. 13 ; xxxi. 3, 13)-which se.idst unto me, Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred, and I will deal well with thee: -here was a clear indication that Jacob had in faith both obeyed the command and embraced the promise made known to him in Haran-I am not worthy of the least of (literally, I am l/1$8 than) all thol mercies, and (of) all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant;-tho profouncl humility which these words b1·eatho is n sure indication that the character of Ja.cob had either undergone a great inward transformation, if that was not experienced twenty years before at Bethel, or had shaken off the moral and spiritual lethargy under which he too manifestly laboured while in _the sr.rvice of Laban-for with my stafl:' (i. e. possessing nothing but my stnlf) I passed over this Jordan (the Jo.bbok was situated near, indeed is a tributary of the Jordan); and now I am become two bands (or Machnnoth). entries.title: GEN 32:1–23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Mahanaim, or preparing for Esau. I. THE ANGELIC APPARITION. 1. The time when it occurred. (1) After Jacob had concluded a covenant of peace with Laban. Celestial visitations of a peaceful and encouraging character a.re never vouchsafed to those who are living in a state of enmity with their fellow-men. 'Phe troubled sea reflecte not the ehining foce of heaven, and neither does the wrathful soul invite approaches of God. (2) When Jacob was proceeding on his way to Canaan. The road which Jacob now pursued was the path of duty, inasmuch as it had been prescribed by God, and led to the covenant inheritance; and only then need the saints expect to meet with either God or bis angels, when they are walking in the way of his commandments, and making for the better country, even an heavenly. 2. The impression which it niade. Whether completely su1Tounding him, or divided into two companies, one on either eide of him, Jacob's angelic visitors, from their number, their orderly array, their military dispositions, assumed the appearance of a heavenly army lying encamped over against his own ; and the sight of the t'IVo companies immediately suggested the ejaculation," This is God's host," and caused him to name the place Mahanaim. 3. The purpose which it served. For :m enumeration of the different ends which this sublime vision is supposed to have been intended to subserve the Exposition may be consulted. 'l'he greatestprobability attaches to that which regards it as having been designed to prepare Jacob for his rapidly-approaching interview with Esau. It was fitted to remind him of the heavenly reinforcements that are always at hand to succour saints in their extremities (cf. 2 Kings vi. 17; Ps. xxxiv. 6; Zech. ix. 8; Heh. i. 14). II. THE FnIENDLY EMBASSY. 1. The despatch of the messengers. (1) Their <lestination-to Mount Seir, to Esau; (2) their instructions-to inform Esau of Jacob's prosperous estate and immediate return; (3) their design-to deprecate the wrath of Esau, and find grace for Jacob in his sight. 2. The return of the messengers. (1) Their alarming report-that Esau was on the way with 400 men ; (2) the terror it produced-Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed; (3) the o.cta to "·l,ich it Jed-stratagem, supplication, conciliation. III. Ts:E SUDDEN STRATAGEM. Jacob divided the people that were with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two bands. 1. An evidence of Jacob's seifpossession. The fear in~pired bf Esau's approach had not been so _gr~at as to make liim lose command of his faculties. Men that have God upon the1r side should not allow themselves to be thrown by evil tidings into excessive trepidation (Ps. xxvii. 1-3; Rom. viii. 31). 2. A proof of Jacob's prudence. The division ofhis compo.ny into two bands afforded to one at least of the portions a chance of escaping the sword of Esau. Though contrary to the Divine word to resist evil, it is not wrong to use all lawful endeavours to a,•oid it. 3. A testimony to Jacob's chivalry. In a. time of danger lie thinks of the safety of others, of the women and children, rather than of himself. 4. A sign of Jo.cob's meekness. He contemplates not armed resistance to the onset of his infuriated brother, but prepares by peaceful means to elude at lea.et the full force of bis attack. IV. TrrE EARNEST PRAYER. Characterised by-1. Lofty faith. Jacob addresses l,imsel£ to God as to a living personality, and not as to an impersonal force; to the God of the covenant,-" 0 God of my father Abraham," &c.,-o.nd not simply to God in the abstract, as the inscrutable power that presides over men and things, und bases his appeal upon the promises which God in virtue of that covenant had extended to himself. 2. Profound ltumility. He not only acknowledges tho CIJ. Pl:irn, duect, ar,tless, and confiding, it is snch a prayer as n lovrng child might breathe rnto a mothers ear when driven hy impending danger to seek shelter in her bosom :-" Deliver me, I pray thee from the hand of Esau my brother: for I fear him." . ' V. THE C0N~~~IAT0RY rRESEN;- "A '!la~•s gift make~h room for him," says Solomon (Prov. xvm. 16); and agarn, "A gift 1n secret pac1fieth anger, and a reward in the bosom strong wrath" (Prov. xxi. 14). The gift of Jacob to his brother was-1. Handsomely prepared. It was munificently and generouR!y selected from the best of the flocks and herds in his possession. 2. Skilfully arranged. The sheep, goats, camels, asses, kine that composed it were drawn up in a series of droves, which were despatched in succession under the care of as many drivers. 3. Promptly despatched. The measures just recited were adopted on the very day that Ja.cob's messengers returned, and the several droves despatched upon their journey ere the nij?ht fell. 4. Peacefully designed. They were meant to appease the wrath of Esau. Lessons:-1. The ministry of angels. 2. The courage inspired by true religion. 3. The value of prayer. 4. The use of a present.

entries.title: GEN 32:24–32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Peniel, or tlie mysterious contest. I. THE DEscnlM'ION OF THF. STRUGGLE. 1. The scene. The north bank of Jabbok (vide Exposition). 2. 'l.'he time. Night; the most suitable season for soul exercises, such as self-examination (Ps. iv. 4), meditation (Ps. ]xiii. 6), devotion (Luke vi. 12). 3. The circumstances. Jacob was alone. In solitude the human soul discovers most of itself, and enjoys most frequent interviews with God (Ps. Jxxvii. 6; Dan. x. 8; John xvi. 32). 4. J.'11e combatants. (1) Jacob: by nature the supplanter, by grnce the heir of the covenant; who in early life by craft had overreached his brother Esau in the matters of the family birthright and theocratic blessing, and who had now, by tho despatch of his munificent present to " my lord Esau," renounced both, so far at Jenst as renunciation was possible, i. e. in respect of materinl and temporal advantages. (2) A man, i. e. one who in outward appearance wore tho form of a mnn, though in reality" the visible revealer of the invisible God" (Dclitzsch); the angel of Johov11h, who hncl previously appeared in like guise to Abraham at Mamre (eh. xviii. 1), and who subsequently, in the fulness of the times, incarnated himself as the \Vorel made flesh (John i. 14). 5. 'l.'lie combat. (1) Its commencement. When precisely thi!I mystc,rious conflict began, and how Jacob wus engaged at the moment of tho unknown wrestler's approach, are points upon which the narrative is silent, though it is probable that Jacob was employed in fervent supplication, and that, without knowing how, he suddenly became conscious of being involved in u close phpical etrugglo with a poweiful nntagonist. Perhaps this was designed to suggest that God's approaches to the praying soul are mostly sudden and inexplicable (cf. John iii. 8). (2) Its character. 'l'hongh unque~tionably depicted in the narrative as a THR BOOK OF GENESIS. [er:. xx:m. 24-39. Yerit~ble contest between two l)uman beings, it i~ appnrent that underlying the pLys1cal struggle., and_ r:lated to 1t as_ the sub~tanco to the shadow, ns the soul to the body, "·n~. another spmtual _contendmg c~rned on by means of prayers and tears (Hosea xu._ 4). (3) Its_contmuance. Degi~ning proba?ly at midnight, it was protracted unt.il dawn, a c1rcumstar.ee sugg·eshve of Jacobs earnestness and determinnt.ion, and yet attesting the severe character of ell true spiritual conflicts and the extraordinary difficulty o~ achi~vin~ vi~tories wi~h God (Matt. xii. 12).' (4) Its course. Four stages are discernible m tins mystenous strnggle. (a) The wrestlers appear to be equally balanced in their strength and skill, sothat the stranger finds him- ~elf unabl_e _to preY~il against Jacob, and laying his_finger on h!s adversary's hip, puts 1t ont of JOmt-a lnnt to Jacob that though seemmgly the victory inclined towards liim, it was due not so much, or even at all, to his wisdom and prowess but rather to the stranger's g-raco and good-will (b) Jacob having thus been' disabled hiA myst~ri?us antagonist, as i~ owning that the mastery rem~ined with him, req~ests pern11ss10n to depart, allegmg as a reason that the ascending dawn proclaimed the day's retnrn, and called to other duties-a valuable reminder that religion has other necessary works £or God's saints besides devotion and contemplation; but Jacob who by this time recognised his antagonist as Divine, objected to his departure with~ out confirming the blessing he hnd formerly received at Bethel-and this, the personal rec~ption and enjoyment of the blessing of the covenant, should be the end and aim of all the saint's contendings with God and communings with Heaven. (c) Inquiring Jacob's name, the Divine adversary now discovers his true personality by authoritatiYely changing that r.ame to Israel, prince of El, in token of his victory--'- an outward symbol of the completed spiritual renovation which had taken place in Jacob since God first met with him at Bethel. (d) Probably excited, or i;piritually elevated, by what had just transpired, Jacob ventures, either with holy boldness or with unthinking curiosity, to inquire after his heavenly antagonist's name, but is answered that in the mean time he must rest satisfied with the blessing which was then and there pronounced. It was either a rebuke to Jacob's presumption, or, and with greater probability, a reminder that even holy boldness has its limits, beyond which it rnay not intrude. (5) Its close. Suddenly and mysteriously as the stran~er came did he also disappear, leavingJacob in possession of the blessing indeed, hut also of a dislocated limb. So God :frequently accompanies spiritual enrichment with material and temporal deprivation, in order both to evince his own sovereignty and to keep hie saints humble (cf. 2 Cor. xii. 7). (6) Its commemoration. Dy Jacob, who called the place Peniel; by Jacob'e descendants, who to this day eat not of the sciatic nerve in animals they kill £or food. II. THE REALITY OF THE STRUGGLE. The question arises whether the cont~st just described had an objective reality (Hiivernick, Kurtz, Murphy, Alford, &c.), or partook of a purely subjective character, being in fact an allegorical description of a spiritual conflict in the soul of ~acob (Kalisch), o: a wrestli!1g which took pla~e only in a dream (Hengstenberg), or man ecstasy (Delitzsch, Keil, ~ange), for the 1de~ of its being a myth (Bohlen, De Wette, Oort, Kuenen) may be discarded. 1. Agamst the notion of a dream-vision it is sufficient to remark that if Jacob's wrestling was n dream, so also were his ,·ictory and his blessing dreams. Besides, limbs do not usually become dislocated in dreams. 2. To read the passage as an allegory is both forced and unnatural, and "little better than trifling with the sacred narrative " (Alford). 3. There is no insuperable objection to the idea of an ecstasy, provided it is not intended to exc:lude the objective manifestntion; yet, 4. There docs not seem sufficient reason for departing from the obvious and literal sense of the pussoge, according to which there was a bond fide corporeal c?ntes~ betwee_n ~ac~b and tli_e angel of Jehovah in human fo:m; £or (1) the n~rrat1ve ~•ves no 111d1~at:0!1 tlrnt 1t was designed in this part to be mterpreted otherwise th~n literally ond lllslonce~ly, as in the surrounding context; (2) unl_ess on the hyp_othes1s that the supernatural_ 1s ~he unreal,there is no imperatfre necessity why exccpti_on sh~uld be taken ~o th~ ohJec~1va character of this remarkable struggle; (3) the d1slocation of Jacobs tlugh pomts to en actual physical contest; and (4) the other events in the narrative appear to require that the historic credibility of Jacoh's wrestling be maintained. Ill. TrIE SIGNIFICANCE or THE STRU<.GLE. '!'hat a momentous crisis lmd nrisen in Jacob's history is universnlly admitted. He wo.s now returning to the lond of Canann II man of mnture age, being in his ninety-seventh year, and of a singularly diversified experience, both n11tural and spiritual. In his early life he had twice supplanted Esau by means of croft, depriving him of his birthright and blessing, and now he was on the eve of meeting that formidable brother whom he had wronged. That the prospective interview filled him with ulann is explicitly declared (eh. :x.xxii. 7); but it likewise drove him to take refuge in prayer, in which exercise it is scarcely doubtful he was engaged when his mysterious assailant approached. What then did this extraordinary combat signify in the spiritual consciousness of Jacob? Putting together those views which do JJot necessarily exclude one another, and which appear to contain an element of truth, it may be said thnt this remarkable experience through which the patriarch passed at Jabbok was designed to have a threefold bearing. 1. On his/ear of Esau. Apprehensive of his brother, he now learns th~t not Esau, but Jehovah, was his real adversary (Keil, Kurtz, Gerlach, Candlish), 111,<i that before he can ever hope to triumph over Esau he must first conquer God. 2. On his retention of the blessing. Having previously, 11s he thought, obtained the birthright and its accompanying blessing by means oE carnal policy anrl worldly stratagem, he now discovers that it cannot be received, or, if he renounced it in the act of homage done to Esau (Lange), cannot be recovered except directly fro1n th11 lips of God; and by means of earnest cries and entreaties (Keil)-a truth taught him, according to Kurtz, by the dislocation of his thigh, which caused him to discontinue his corporeal wreslling, and resort toprayers and tears. 3. Onhis personal chararter. Jacob during all his past career, from his birth, when he caught l,is brotl,er by the heel, to l1is last years in Haran, when he overreached the crafty and avaricious Laban, having been a person who sought to overcome by means of self-reliance ~nd personal effort, it was now designed to teach him that, as the heir of the covenant, the weapon;i of his warfare were not to be carnal, but spiritual, nnd that his advancement tu the place prede~tined for him of pre-eminence over his brethren was to be bronght about by earnest reliance upon God (Murphy),

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he (the introduction of the pronoun giving emphasis to the statement) passed over before them (i. e. passed oninfront of them, thus chivalrouslyputting himself in the place of danger), and bowed himself to the ground-not coIUplctely prostrating the body, asAbraham did in eh. xix. 1, but bending forward till the upper part of it became parallel with the ground, a mode of expressing deep reverence and respect, which may be seen to lifo in Oriental countries at the present day (Roberts, 'Orient11l Illustrations,' p. 41)-seven times (not in immediate succession, but bowing and advancing), until he came near to his brother. The conduct of Jacob was dictated neither byartful hypocrisy nor byunmanly timidity; but by true politeness and a sincere desire to concili11to. And as such it was accepted by Esau, who ran to meet him, and, his better· feelings kindling at the sight of his longnbsent brother, embraced him, and fell on hia neck, and kiased him-as Joseph afterwords did to Benjamin (eh. xlv. 14, 15), though the puncta e:ctmordinai-ia of the Masorites over the word "kissed" seem to indicate either that in their judgment Esau was incapable of such fraternal affection (Delitzsch, Kalisch), or that the word was suspicious, Origen appearing not to he.ve found it in his codices (Rosenmiiller, Keil), unless indeed the conjecture be correct that the word waa marked to draw attention to the power of God's grace in ch1mging Esau's heRrt (Ainsworth). entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw

entries.title: GEN 33:12
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Worldly companionship. ".A.nd he said, Let us tnke our journey, and let us go, and I will go before thee." The offer probably made with kindly intention. No sign of bitterness in Esau's feelings; but ignorance of the necessities of Jacob's march. Jacob knew it was not possible with safety (cf. Ps. cxxxvii. 4; 1 Pet. iv. 4). Reminds us of the attitude of many worldly persons towards Christinns. "The carnal mind is enmity ogainst God." Yet worldly men may havo sincere regard for Christian men; bear unconscious testimony to excellence of Christianity. And here a danger to Christions. Let us journey together. I like you ; you are unselfish, trustworthy. And why not? Because in journeying with Esau ho must be leader, or he would cease to be Esau. The world's good-will does not mean a chnnged heart. Without any pronounced dislike to higher aims, it shares them not, and knows not anything more real than earth. Thero is a journey wo all t,ike in company: in the thousand ways in which men are dependent on each other ; in tl1e courtesies nnd good offices of life ; in what belongs to our position as citizens or hmily men, But in wh:\t constitutes the rof\l\ of life-its stamp am! ,lircl'lion, ih D D2 404 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. XXXIV. 1-81. motives and aims-no union. We have another Leader (Hel,. xit 2), The pillar of fire led Israelites not according to human judgment. I. TH1s DOES NOT IMPLY KEEPING ALOOF FROM MEN, OR FROM RUMAN INTERESTB. Wo are called to be the salt of the earth. It is an error to shrink from contact with the world as dangerous to us. This of old led to monasticism. But there may be a 6piritual solitude even when living in the throng of a city. In secular matters refu~ing to take_an interest in_ wha~ ?Ccupie~ others (c~. Luke yi._31), as if God had nothmg to do with these; or m spmtual tlungs avo1dmg Chnst1an intercourse with those who do not in all points agree with us ; or being engrossed with our own spiritu~1welfare, and turning a,vay from all concern for the welfare of others (cf. I Cor. 1x. 20-22). II_. IT DOES IMPLY A REAL CONSCIOUSNESS OF BEING REDEEMED, set free, bought with 8 pnce; OF HAVING A DEFINITE WORK TO DO FOR Goo, WITH WHICH NOTHING MUST INTERFERE; a real way to walk in, from which nothing must make us turn aside. And in order to this, watchfulness over self, that in seeking to help others wo oursch·es are not ensnared. III. SOME WAYS IN WHICH TRE WORLD IN ITS FRIENDSHIP TEMPTS CHRISTIANS, 1. By the plea, there is no harm in this or that. We must not think that all actions can he brought to an absolute standard of right and wrong. This is the spirit of legality, the spirit of bondage, and leads to partial service instead of entire dedication (cf. Luke xv. 29). Loyalty to Christ must direct the Christian's life; desire not merely 1o 11\'oid direct disobedience, but to use our time and powers for him who loved us and gave himself for us. 2. By the display of good feelings as the equivalent of Christian gnces. Esau's kindliness and frankness are very attractive. Yet he was a " profane person ; "not because of his anger or any sinful act, but because he thought little of God's blessing. 3. By making Christians familiar with worldly aims and maxims, and thus insensibly blunting their spiritual aspirations. The way of safety is through prayer for the Holy Spirit's help, to maintain the consciousness of Christ's presence.-M.

entries.title: GEN 34:1–31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tlie tragedy at Shechem. I. DINAH AND SHECHEM. 1. A young girl's indiscretion. "Dinah went out to see the de.ughtere of the land." If Dinah'e object was to witness the manners of the people, 11he we.e guilty of objectione.ble curiosity; if to exhibit herself, of distressing vanity ; if to mingle in their entertainments, of improper levity; and for all these reasons, considering the character of the family to which she belonged, and the wickedness of the people with whom she mingled, of exceedingly heinous sin. 2. A young princis wickedness. Shecbem saw her, and took her, and lay with her, e.nd defiled her. The sin of Shechem had many aggravations. It was done by a prince, whose very rank should have preserved him from such degradation. Those whom God makes elevated in station should make themselves eminent in virtue. Goodness should always e.ccompany greatness. Then it was done without the least excuse, since Shechem wa.e at liberty by God's law and man's to have a wife whenever he desired. Again, it was done against a young and comparatively helpless girl whom circumstances had placed within his power. Further, it was done in violation of the laws of hospitality, which required him to protect, rather than to injure, a stranger's good name. And, lastly, it was done to one belonging to a family whose members were invested with a high degree of sanctity. Still the crime of Shechem was not without its extenuations. First, he loved the maiden whom be had dishonoured. Second, he offered the reparation of an honourable marriage. Third, he treated her with kindness while Le detained her in his palace. II. JACOB AND HIS soN3. 1. The impression made on Jacob by Dinah's misfortune. (1) He held bis peace; in stupefaction, in sorrow, in meditation, in indecision. (2) He sent for his sons, who, as recognised guardians of their sister, were entitled to be consulted in all that concerned her welfare. 2. Tlie effect produced on Jacob's soiia by their suter's shame. (1) They were grieved for what had happened-for Dinah's, for their father's, for their own sake. (2) They were angry n.t its perpetrator; not so much, however, for the sin ho had committed, as for the fact that he had committed it against Jacob'e de.ughter. Ill. JAcon's soNs AND HAMOR's soN. 1. Tlie honourable proposal of Shechem First through the medium of hie father, and afterwards in his own person, ho solicits Jacob and his sons to give him Dinah in marriage, and to enter in turn into matrimonial alliances with them, offering as e.n inducement unrestricted liberty to settle, trade, and acquire property in the land, and promising to po.y whatever dowry or gift might Le demanded for the damsel. 2. The deceitful reply of Jacob's sona. First they declared it impossible that Dinah should become the wife of one who wns uncircumcised. Then they consented to the proposition on condition thnt Hamor, Shechem, and th~ Shechemite~ would submit to circumcision. And yet nil the while it was only part of a deep-laid plot for exacting revenge, IV. HAMOR AND THE SBECBEMITEs. 1. 1'/ie condition prescribed by Jacob's sons explained. This was dooe by the ruling sovereign nnd the crown prince in a public assembly convened at the city gate. 2. T/i,e condition accepted by the Shechemites. Trusting to the good faith of the Hebrew strangers, they assented to the proposition thnt all the male inhabitants should be circumcised, and in good faith it was carried out by both prince nnd people. V. THE SONS OF JACOB AND THE SHECHEMITES. 1. Tli,e massacre of the inhabitants by .Dinali's brethren. Three dnys after, when, in consequence of the painful operation to which they had submitted, the male part of the population was unable to stir in their defence, Simeon and Levi, confident of success in their nefarious deed, fell upon the unsuspecting city, and slew all the males. It was a heartless, rutbless, treacherous, diabolic massacre, fit to rank with the St. Bartholomews and Glencoc~ of modern times. 2. The spoliation of the city by Jacob's sons. If Simeon nnd Levi were alone responsible for the massacre, the sacking of the city was the work of all the brethren (Joseph and Benjamin doubtless excepted). Not only did they make captives of the wives and children, but they carried off every live thing they could find of any value; and not only did they ransack the houses, from the palace to the cottage, but they appear to have stripped even the very dead. The annals of uncivilised warfare scarcely record a more atrocious crime. VI. JACOB AND DrnAH's BRETHREN. 1. Tlie feeble reproof of Jacob. Be only complains that their cruel deed would cause his name to be abhorred in the lnnd, anrl perhaps lead to their extermination ns a people. For the different views that have been entertained of Jacob's words the Exposit.ion may be consulted. 2. The ins1tfficient reply of .Dinah's brethren. Shechem certainly had wronged Dinah, but he never meant to treat her as a harlot. Learn-I. The danger of unrestrained social intercourse between the Church allfl the world in genernl, and in particular between the daughters of the pious and the sons of the ungodly-exemplified in Dinah, who, going to see the danghters of the land, lost her fair fame, and brought trouble on her father's house. 2. The misery of yielding to unholy passion-illustrated in Shechem, whose unbridled lust bore bitter fruit to all concerned: to Dinah dishonour, to Jacob shame and sorrow, to Jacob's sons the thirst for revenge, to Hamor and the Shcchemites as well as to himself overwhelming retribution. 3. The wickedness of which good men when left to themselves may be guilty-exhibited in the conduct of Jacob's sons, who in this lamentable affair were chargeable with treachery, sacrilege, murder, spoliation, oppression. 4. The possibility of the innocent suffering with and for the guiltyshown in the massacre of the Shechemites for the sin of Shechem. 6. The certainty that a man's worst foes are often those of his own household-of which the case of Ja.cob wns n melancholy instance, whose name wns more dishonoured by his sons' atrocities than by his daughter's misfortune.

entries.title: GEN 34:30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Anger um·utrai'Md. "And Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, Ye have troubled me." It was not merely the fear of retaliation by neighbourino- tribes. He felt the act was wrong (eh. xlix. 5---7); God's blessing could not rest upon it (cf. Ps. xxxiv. 7); and he and his family were involved in that wrono- (cf. Josh. vii. 13 ; 1 Cor. xii. 26). But was not the anger of Simeon and Levi just? No doubt there was cause, and no doubt a measure of righteous indignation. But (1) thev thought more of the wrong against themselves than of the sin against God (ver. 31). (2) Their anger was unrestrained by mercy, or even by justice (ver. 25). (3) It led them into acts of sin-deceit, murder, robbery. (4) It was soiled by selfish gain (ver. 27). Anger may be right; but need of special watchfulness (Ephes. iv. 26). For under its influence the heart is not in a state fitted to judge; and much danger of self-deception, of mistaking a selfish for a godly anger. I. A JUST CAUSE FOB ANGER DOES NOT EXCUSE ITS EXCESS, Anger may be called for (1) as a protest againstwrong ; (2) to deter others from wrong. But vengeance, retribution, belongs to God (Rom. xii. 19). He alone has the knowledge to apportion it, looking both to the past and to the future. But anger tempts to retaliation (Matt. v. 38). The wrong fills the mind. Our own errors and acts of wrong (cf. John viii. 7), and the plea, Thine anger brings harm to the innocent, are unheeded. The fact that there was cause for anger blinds to its real nature; for unrestrained anger is in truth an offering to self-love. The plea, of zeal for right and of godly indignation may seem sincere ; but "ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of." II. A JUST CAUSE FOR ANGER DOES NOT EXCUSE WRONG-DOING. God's laws cannot be set aside. And he who takes on himself the office of judge should be especially watchful not to transgress (Ps. xxxvii. 3). To do wrong on the plea of doing God's work is to distrust his providential care (Rom. xii. 19-21). It is to do evil that good may come; a form of being drawn aside by our own lusts (cf. 1 Sam, :xxiv. 7; x:xvi. 9). Such acts of wrong are especially evil in Christians. They are " o. city set on an hill." Men nre ever ready to point to their errors as excusing their own. Men see and judge the act, hut cannot estimate the provocation, or, it may be, the sorrow, for a hasty action. Ill. WoBKS DONE IN ANGER HINDER THE WORK Oil' THE CHURCH. That work is to draw men together in one (John xvii. 21). The power by which this is done is love. The love of Christ reflected in us (1 John iv. 7). Love wins men's hearts, reason only their minds. And the presence of angerhinders love ; not merely in him against whom it is directed ; like a stone thrown into still water, it distmbs its surface fnr and wide. IV. THE POWER BY W!WlH ANGER MUST DE CONTROLLED, Dwelling on the work and example of Christ. He bore all for us. Is not wrath rebuked in the presence of his patience? And if as a II strange work''. we are c?netra~ed _to indignation, must we not watch and pray that no selfish feeling may mmgle with it; and, knowing in how many things we offend, that we be "slow to wrath," ready to forgive, and ever II looking unto Jesus" ?-M.

entries.content: -And they gave unto Jacob all the strange gods-Rosenmiiller thinks these mUBt have been many, since the histori,an would not otherwise have used the tenn ',j -which were in their hand (i. e. which they possessed), and nil their earrings which were in their ears;-i. e. those emplayed for purposes of idolatrous worship, which were often covered with allegorical figures and mysterious sentences, ancl supposecl to be endowed with a talismanic virtue (Ju<lgcs viii 24 ; Isa. iii. 20 ; Hosea ii. 13)-and Jacob hid them-having probably first destroyed them, since they do not appear to have been ever after sought for or resumed by the parties who gave them up (Hughes) -under the oak which was by Shechem. entries.title: GEN 35:1–15
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Bethel revisited. L JACOB's JOURNEY TO BETHEL. I. The occasion of the journey. The c1ime of his sons had made it necessary that Jacob shoulrl leave Shechem o.nd its neighbourhood; but it is doubtful if in the circumstance~ Jacob would have thought of going to Bethel without an express invitation from Heaven, which, however, he got. 2. The object of the journey. This was stated bv the Divine communication which Jacob received to be the fulfilment of the vo,~ which twenty years before he had made to erect an altar on the spot where he enjoyed the vision of the ladder and the angels. Vows do not lose their obligatory character by lapse of years. Men may, but God never does, forget the promises which are made to him. Hence the counsel of the Preacher (Eccles. v. 4, 5). 3. Thepreparati()'fl, for the journey. The removal of the strangegods-(1) Was needful if God wo.s to be sincerely worshipped by Jacob and his household. The necessity of having no other gods but Jehovah was nftenvards enjoined upon Israel as a nation. In the gospel the le.w is equally imperative, God and Christ demand the undivided homage of the human heart. (2) Was counselled by Jacob to his honsehold. It is well when heads of families have the ability as well as inclination to direct thei1 children and dependents in the duties of religion. (3) Was cheerfully assented to by Jo.cob's household. The silver and wooden images (the teraphim) that Rachel had abstracted from her father's tent, the idolatrous objects that the Shechemites may have brought with them, and the earrings that were in their ears, were at once and completely given up, and by Jacob's own hand buried beneath the oak of Shechem. (4) Was symbolised in ,Tacob's household by the acts of washing and putting on of clean apparel. Under the law corporee.l ablutions and beautified habiliments were typical of spiritual renovation and the putting on of the righteousness of the saints (cf. Ezek. x.xxvi. 25; Heh. x. 22; Jude 23; Rev. xix. 2). 4. 'l'he experience of the journey. Wherever the travellers went they found themselves unmolested, and the cities round about them alarmed, and afraid to pursue. The terror of Elohim was upon the people of the land, and thus the care of Jehovah was around Ilia saints. 5. The completion of the journey. Jacob and all the people that were with him came to Luz m the land of Canaan, which is Bethel. Many journeys are begun that never end. Some that promiije well at the outset are ovenvhelmed in disaster before they terminate. It 1s only he who keeps Israel that can preserve a good mrn's going out and coming in. II. JAcoB's RESIDENCE AT BETHEL. 1. The building of an altar. This was on the part of Jacob (1) an act of obedience, since it was done in accordance with Divine instructions (ver. 1); (2) an act of justice, inasmuch as it was executed ia fulfilment of a vow (eh. xxviii. 22) ; (3) an act of gratitude, being designed to give expression to Jacob's thankfulness for God's mercies (vers. 3, 7). 2. Tlte deatlt oj Deborah. (1) Her life-work: Rebekah's nurse. (2) Her death: this must have taken place o.t an advanced age. (3) Her burial : the place of sepulture was on the slope of Bethel hill, beneath the shadow of a wide-spreading oak. (4) Hermemorial: the tree was named Allon-bachuth, oak of weeping. 3. Tlteappearanceof .Elohim. (1) The blessing renewed (ver. 9;) (2) the new name confirmed (ver. 10) ; (3) the promises repeated (ver. 11). 4. The erec,i()'fl, of a pillar. The old column having probably been thrown down, this was (1) set up as a memorial of the interview with God which had just been enjoyed ; (2) employed as an altar for the worship of Elohim-" he poured a drink offering thereon;" and (3) co11secrated as an object of reverential rt1gard by pouring oil thereon. 5. The renaming of the place. 'fhe name given twenty years previously is renewed, Bethel (ver. 15), with a slight modification, El-Bethel (ver. 7), to connect it with the altar Just erected. Leam-1. That good men sometimes require to be reminded by God of their duty. 2. That acts of Divine worship should be preceded by heart purification and lifo reformation. 3. entries.title: GEN 35:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's preparation for acceptable woraHp. "Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be ye clean, and change your gannente: and let us arise, and go up to BetheV' "When thou vowest a vow, defer not to pay it," says Ecclesiastes(eh. v, 4); butJacobhad deferred. He made a vow atBethel, and he seems afterwards to have ignored it. If he thought of it, a number of things had been ever ready to present themselves as excuses for delay. His faithful services given constantly to Laban, hie efforts to make good hie position in the land, and then to avert 1he anger of Esau, had apparently absorbed so much of hie attention that he had forgotten his vows. These solemn promises had been made at a very critical period of his life, and. God had not forgotten them. He reminds Jacob of them in a very emphatic manner. Jacob had failed to see in the circumstances in which he was placed with respect to the people among whom he dwelt that there was a hint of neglected duty. God permitted Jacob to be made uncomfortable that he might be made considerate. The way in which his sons· had treated the Shechemites had brought him into great danger. He and all his were likely to be cut off by these enraged inhabitants of the land. He is reminded of the danger in which he was once placed from the vengeance of Esau. The similarity of the circumstances forcibly and very naturally tum his thoughts to the One who alone can be his defence. 'l'hus circumstances and Divine communications impel to the performance of duty. How merciful is God in his treatment of souls I how he leads the wanderer back to duty I Jacob, when about to strike hie tents and remove to Bethel, wishes that his sons o.nd servants should go up with him, e.nd the.t they should go up in the right spirit. He therefore so.ye to them, "Put away the strange gods," &c. 1. NEGLECTED DUTY IS A HINDRANCE TO APPROPRIATE AND ACCEPTABLE WORSIIIP. Thut Jucob should have been obliged to give such an injunction to hie household ehows that he bad not sufficiently kept before his sons and servants the duty they owed to God. He he.d allowed himself to strive for worldlysuccess until they might have even imagined that he wns no better than the rest of them or their neighbours ; but deep down in the heart of this man was o. reverence for God and a desire to do his will. His neglect to carefully instruct hie sons bad borne bitter fruit. Had he instilled into his sons ideas more in o.ccordance with the character of the God he served, they would not have taken such mean methods as are mentioned of revenging themselves on those theybad come to dislike, His neglect necessitates the sudden nnd difficult effort now put forth to induce hie sons to seek with him to serve God. He feels that he cannot rightly worship God unless his children and household nre with him in spirit. He wishes to foster in them a belief in his own sincerity. To huve one in 11 family looking on indifferently or sneeringly is death to successful worship. Ja.cob's neglect had led to carelessness by his sons of the Divine service. llo could not himself enter heartily on the service until he hnd discharged, in 11 measure, his duty us guide nnd instructor to his family. II. ANOTHER HINDRANCE IS THE ATTACHMENT TO OBJECTS WRONGLY HELD IN REVERENCE, The sons of Jacob had o.dmitted false gods into their affections. Idolatry was rife among them. Even his wife Rachel had so much foith in her father's idols that she stole them when she left borne. The sons caught the spirit of the mother, o.nd indulged in the worship of strange gods. Perhups they worshipped secretly the gods which Rachel cherished, or they may have given udomtion to the idols they found among the spoils of the Shechemites. They may have had little images which they carried about with them, as many superstitious Christians curry tho crucifix. Amulets and charms they seem to have worn on their hands uncl in their ears, all indicating superstition, false worship, and wrong ideas. God is spoken of in the Bible as "jealouR." This is with. respect to worship given to represent,. utions of gods having no existence. The jealousy is right, becauso it would ho an evil thing for man himself to think there were many gods, or to select his own god. When, in after ages, the doscendnnts of these son~ of Jacob yielded to the 8ill of (16 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. XXXV. 16-29, worshipping other gods, ten of the tribes wero swept away, and Lave never been redisco,-ered. Indeed the stream was tainted in sourcE , and II grew no purer na it rolled along." When Achan brought the Babylonish garment into the camp of Israel, the chosen of God could not stand before their enemies, but when it was rcmo,·ed they were again victorious. So strange gods must be removed from our homes and from our hearts, or we can never be successful in the conflict ao·ainst sin or in the acceptability of the worship we offer. It is for each Christian to~earch hi~ soul, and to see whether there is any desire, habit, or practice which in the least militates ngainst the worship of God. Many who were incorporated with Jacob's household were Syrians, who brought their evil practices with them. When any enter God's Church they must leave behind them the practices of the world· nor possessions nor position must be the gods then worshipped. "If any man lo;e the world, the love of the Father is not in him.'' III. THE HARBOURING OF ANY SPECIAL SIN WILL BE A SURE HINDRANCE. The sons of Jacob had not only outward false objects of reverence, but inward evil propensities. They were treacherous, cruel, lustful, envious, murderous. See how they treated the Shechemites, and in after years their own brother Joseph. What scandalising, jealousy, and even opposition, are found in some homes I How hard it is to alienate sinful habits from the heart and the home I how hard to get the right tone for devout service in the home I Certain habits of temper, ridicule, sarcasm will chill and check all won;hip. Jacob urged his sons to be "clean,"-pure,-" to change their garments." They had need to do the latter, for they had been spotted with the blood of the men they had murdered. Jacob meant that they were,to put on the g'arments kept for the worship of God. Rebekah had garments by her in which Esau as eldest son worshipped God, and which she put on Jacob. It is probable that it was the practice under the patriarchal dispensation to perform certain ceremonial ablutions prior to entering on the solemn worship. 11 Cleanliness is next to godliness." It leacls to it. The need of purity in the worship of God is thus indicated by ablutions and change of garments. But how easily we may have the outward without the inward. We need cleansing in the holy fountain opened by Christ, and to be clothed by his righteousness. IV. A great hindrance to successful worship is l:IAVING LOW IDEAS OF THE DIGNITY OF TJIE ACT' AND THE MAJESTY AND HOLINESS OF HIM WHOM WE WORSHIP. God must be made to appeargreat to us. He is" high and lifted up." He made not only these frames of ours, but this vast universe. He is worshipped by worlds of intelligent spirits, and has been worshipped from the depths of eternity. He is holy and full of majesty. Shall we be indifferent as to the duty or the mode of worship? What o. marvel that we should be permitted to have fellowship with our Crea.tor I If we have it, it must be in the way and place he appoints. For Jacob it was at Betha_), for the Jews at Jerusalem, for Christians o.t the cross. To Jacob and the Jews 1t was by annual sacrifices, to us it is by the offering of Christ "once for all."-H.

entries.title: GEN 35:16–29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -From Bethel to Mamre. I. THE DEATH OF RACHEL. 1. Thd travailing woman. Raebel, overtaken by the pains of childbirth, had hard labour. In every instance an inheritance derived from mother Eve (eh. iii. 16) the eorrow of maternity was in her case providentially intensified; perhaps by b~r advanced age,. or by t~1e discomforts of travel, or by feeb\e~ess ?f health, or posoibly by special appomtment of God as a rebuke for her rnordmate desire for children (eh. xxx. 1), or as_ a means of shortening her I_ife. 2. '!'lie comforting midwife. Though her name 1s not recorded, wherever tlus pathetic story is recited there shall her kindly offices to the dying Rachel be remembered. Chosen to' assist Rachel in her bodily struggle, she was likewise helpful to Rachel in her soul's conflict. Sympathising with the sufferer in her pain, she sought to minister comfort to the droop~ng h~art in_ its despondency.. The.y who tend the sick and dying should be tender m then feelings and hopeful m their words, as well aa skilful and gentle in their acts. 3. The departing mother. Though Rnchel's child was born, Rachel herself died; in which were some circumstances of sadness, as (1) that it happened on a journey,-" in the way to Ephrath,"-and near its end-" there was but a little way to come to Ephrath," where it is likely Jacob bad intended to rest a while for Rachel's convenience; (2) that it occurred on the occasion of her confinement, death in child-bed being a comparatively rare experience in the history of mothers, though, considering the severity of the ordeal, it is o. special mercy that any mothers survive; and (3) that it removed her from her newly-born son, than which no greater grief can agitate a dying mother'a henrt, and the thought of which perhaps gave added poignancy to the bitter anguish with which she named her child Ben-oni-the son of my sorrow. Yet in Rachel'e death were certain elements of gladness, as (1) that she died in the presence of her husband, Jacob being by her couch to catch her latest breath ; (2) that she died not before she gave him another son, to be to him whom she loved a Benjamin, though to herself Ben-oni ; and (3) that she died in the hope of a glorious immortality, her soul departing to.the better country, even an heavenly. 4. The bereaved liusband. (1) Cheering the drooping heart of bis dying wife. This is probably tho correct view to be taken of what otherwise interpreted cannot fail to seem strangely inconsistent-Jacob's naming Rachel's child Benjamin, the son of my right band, the son of my aJfection, of my prosperity, a token of good hope and happy fortune, while Rachel called him Benoni. " In vain the broken-hearted father-refusing to take in the terrible fact passing under bis eye-determined to be sanguine to the last, and let no evil omen touch either mother or child-whispers hope in the dull ear of death, and welcomes the last pledge of an undying love as no "son of sorrow," but "the son of the right hand" (Candlish). (2) Burying the lifeless body of his beloved spouse, which doubtless he would do with reverent affection and with heart-felt mourning. (3) Erecting a pillar above her lonely grave-to demonstrate bis affection for her who slept beneath, to show that though she lay not in the family tomb, she was not forgotten, and to mark the last resting-place of an ancestress of Israel, II. THE SIN OF REUllEN. 1. The enormity of Reuben's wickedness. The act which be committed was that of incest, since Bilhah had been the wife of Jacob. It was asin punishable by death under Moses' law (Levit. xviii. 8), .and such a sin as should not be named among Christians (1 Cor. v. 1). It is not likely that Bilhah was innocent in this matter, but it is certain that Reuben was guilty of heinous transgression. 2. The impresswn i~ pr?duced 07!- Jaco~. "Is~ael heard." We m~y suppl_y the hiatus by saymg, (1) W1th mexpress1ble gnef-gl'lef that a son and wife of his ~hould have committed such a horrible iniquity; (2) with bitter shame-was this to be the end of all God's mercies to hie house, and of all hie efforts to piously direct hie household? (3) with silent submission, ns recognising God's ho.nd in the dispensation. More bitter and crushing was this last stroke than tho death of Rnchel or even the ravishment of Dinah; and Jacob's silence under it may be interproted as the sil1Jnce of devottt resignation:-" I was dumb, because thou didst it;" Ill. THE DEATH OF Isuc, 1. He waa spared to see liis son's i·etum. "Jaco!> ea.me unto leaac hie father unto Mamre" at leaet a consiclerable period before liifl death. According to calculations (mile Exposition), Isaac eurv1ved tl,e sale of Joeeph thirteen yea.re. Hence Jacob'e coming home must have taken place while 11111.nc had yet many years to live. It is a mercy 'which Goel does not grant to all, to see their children and their children's children around them before they die. 2. He was privileged to reach a good old age. "The days of Isaac were an Iiuntlrect and fourscore yea.re." Piety hne a special tendency to prolong life (Ps. xxxiv. 12), while the wicked live not half their days (Pe. Iv. 23). 3. lie was favoured witlt a peaceful and a blessed end. "Isaac gave up the ghost, and died, and was gathered unto his people." See Homily on the death of Abraham (eh. xxv. 8). 4. Jle was honoured with a decent and respectful funeral. "Esau and Jacob buried him." entries.title: GEN 35:16–29
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: These family records mingle well with the story of God's grace. The mother's "Benoni" is the father's "Benjamin." Out of the pain and the bereavement sometimes comes the consolation. A strange blending of joy and sorrow is the tale ·of human love. But there is a higher love which may draw out the pure stream of peace and calm delight from that impure fountain. Jacob and Esau were separated in their lives, but they met at their father's grave. Death is a. terrible divider, but a muter too. Under the shadow of the great mystery, on the borders of an eternal world, in the presence of those tears which human eyes weep for the dead, even when they can weep no other tears, the evil things of envy, hatred, revenge, alienation do often hide themselves, and the better things of love, peace, brotherhood, nmity come forth. Jacob was with Isaac when he died, and Esau came to the gmve.-R. § 10. THE GENERATIONS OF ESAU (CR, XXXVI. 1-XXX\'ll, 1).

entries.title: GEN 37:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Esau aeparatesfrom Jacob. I. GOD REQUIRES ENTIRE DEVOTEDNESe AND FA1TH. Edom is allied to the true kingdom, butis not one with it. We may keep in mind the relationship between the descendants of the two brothers, that we may learn the more clearly to distinguish the true heirs of the blessing. II. entries.title: GEN 37:31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -lJelayinfulfilment ofGo<ls promiaes. Between two stoges of the history of the covenant family stands the genealogy of Esau's descendants. The text sug• gests a contrast between their course and that of the family of Jacob. On the deatl1 of Isaac Esau departed from Canaan with family and possessions (cf. eh. xxvii. 40). The desert and the valleys of Seir were more attractive than quietness of Cannan. Prosperity, such as he cared for, attended him. Among his family we rend of dukes, or heads of tribes, and of kings. And whnt of the line ofpromise ?-king~ foretold to them (eh. xvii. 6; xxxv. 11). Yet while kings were reigning in Erlom, Israelites were slaves in Egypt or wanderers in the desert. Is God slack to fulfil hi~ word? (1 Pet. iii. 4). This is often o. trial to believers (Ps. lxxiii. 3). But God's promises are sure, though the time may seem long. The fulfilment of promisrs of great hlessings has almost always been slow, as we count it. Abraham waited long (eh. xii. 2). It was long ere tho kingdom of Israel arose; far longer ere the promise of a Saviour fulfi.'.led (eh. iii. 15; Gal. iv. 4); and still we wnit for the Lord's return. The same huth appears in nature. Great nnd precious things are of 11low growth (cf. Mark iv. 5). .Doctrinal lessons :-1. Delay serves for the trial and strengthening of faith. Fnith grows by enduring trial. Mark how often the faith of eminent saints hns been tried. Without faith we cannot please God; for faith believes God's truth and love, and embruces his will. Unbelief charges God with untruth (eh. iii. 4; 1 John v, 10). TIIE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. xxxnt. 2-11 Even in believers a leaven of unbelief may be at work. Trials are sent to cause faith to ?evelop into othe;__graces _(James i.~). 2. What springs up quickly is apt to fode quwldy (cf: Exod. m. 11 _with Hagg,u 1. 2). Danger lest what seemM to be faith be mer~ly feeling. .3•.The time that seems ~o lol'!g is not mere delay, but preparation. 'While the seed lies m the earth a process 1s gomg on, though unseen, without which the perfect plant could not be formed. Compare the expression "the fulness of time" (Gal. iv. 4), and the way in which all previous history prepared the way for the coming of Christ. These lessons apply equally to God's dealings with the world and with individuals. .Practical lessons.~1. Encouragement if dishe!lrte~ed by slow progress of Christ's kmg-dom: much labour am?ng the heathen with little apparent result; or many e;fmts at home, ye_t ungod_hness not _checked. We have promises (Isa. Iv, 11; 1 Cor. xv. 58). In his own time God will make them good. 2. In like mnnner if our own striving for personnl holiness, or for good of others, snems to have little success. \\'.e require the training of ~isappointment to _chec.k pride (2 Cor. xii. 7), and God will see to the result (Gal. v1. 9). 3. To bear m mmd that we are but instruments in the Lord'~ hand (1 Cor. iii. 6). Every work to be performed "looking unto Jesus'' (2 Cor. xn, 10).-M. § 11. THE GENERATIONS 01!' entries.title: GEN 37:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Now (literally, and) Israel loved J'oseph more than all his children (literally, sons), because he was the son of his old age -literally, a 8m ofold a,ge (was) M to him; not a son possessing the wisdom of advanced years (Onkelos), but a son born in his old age (Rosenmilller, Keil, Kalisch, et alii), which was literally true of Joseph, since he wasbom in his father's ninety-firstyear. Yet as Joseph was only a year or two younger than the children of Bilbah and Zilpah, and as Benjamin was still later bom than he, the application of this epithet to Joseph has been explained on the ground that Benjamin was at this time little more than a child (Keil), and had not much come into notice (Murphy), or perhaps was not born when this portion of the narrative was originally written (' Speaker's Commentary'); or that Joseph had obtained the name before Benjamin's birth, and that it had clung to him after that event (Inglis). Josephus(' Ant.,' ii. 2, I) gives another reason for Jacob's partiality which is not inconsistent with the statement in the text, viz., the beauty of his person and the virtue of his mind, cui rE r1)v roii awµaro, Euyivuav, ,:ai oui ,J,vxij~ ap,nk. And he made him a coat of many colours -literally, a coat (kithoneth, from kathan, to cover ; vide eh. iii. 21) of ends (Keil, Lange), i. e. a tunic reaching to the ancles, and with sleeves reaching to the wrists, anti commonly worn by boys and girls of the upper ranks (Josephus, 'Ant.,' vii. 8, I ; 2 Sam. xiii. 18), or II coat of pieces (Kalisch, T. Lewis, Wordsworth); hence a variegated garment, -x•rwv 1rou:/~o, (LXX.), tunica polymita (Vulgate), a coat of many colours (Murphy, 'Speaker's Commentary'). The whole of the captives are clnd in pnrti-colourcd garments, nnd tho tunic of this ind.ividunl in particular mriy bo cnlled " 11 coat of many colours' (Thomley Smith, 'Joseph nnd his Times,' p. 12). It has been supposed that Jacob's object in confcrrinit this distinction on Joseph was to mark him out ns the heir to whom the forfeited birthright of Reubon (I Chron. v. 1) was to be transferred (Kurtz, Lnnc.e Gerlach,Bush,Wordsworth,'Speaker's Com m'ontnry,' &c.); but tho hi~torian only mentions it as a token of affection, such as was customnry in those times for princes to bestow upon their subjects, and parents on their children (vide 'l.'homlcy Smith, 'Joseph nnd his Times,' p. 11). entries.title: GEN 37:5
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And loseph dreamed a dream (in which, though, e.s the sequel shows, intended as a Divine communication, there was nothing to distinguish it from an ordinary product of the mind), and he told it to his brethren:-not in pride, since there is no reason to suppose that Joseph e.s yet understood the celestial origin of his dream, but in the simplicity of his heart (Kalisch, Murphy), thongh in doing so he was also guided, unconsciously it may be, but still really, by an overruling providence, who made use of this very telling of the dream as a step towards its fulfilment (Lawson)-and they hated him yet the more-literally, and they added aqain to hate him.

entries.title: GEN 37:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he said unto them, Hear, I prayyou, this dream which I have dreamed.. Though Joseph did not certainly know that his dream was snpernatural, he may have thought that it was, the more so as dreams were in those times commonly regarded as mediums of Divine communication ; and in this case it was clearly his duty to impart it to the household, and all the more that the subject of it seemed to be for them a matter of peculiar importance. In the absence of information to the contrary, we are warranted in believin" that there was nothing either sinful or off;nsive inJoseph's spirit or manner in making known his dreams. That which appears to have excited the hostility of his hrethren was not the mode of their commui:.ication, but the character of their contents.

entries.title: GEN 37:2–11
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Josephinliisfather'shouse. I. JOSEPH EMPLOYED WITH ms BRETHREN. 1. With them in tlie sense of as well as them. That is to say, Joseph no more than the other sons of his father was trained to indolence. It is the duty of parents to educate their children in some useful and honourable calling. Even when not required for procuring daily bread, it is of advantage as a means of withdrawing one from temptations which would otherwise beset him, while it largely enhances the enjoyment of existence, and enables one to contribute more or less directly to the sum of human happiness. Adam, Noah, Abraham, !sane, and even Laban, nil hrought up their sons to honest toil. 2. Witli them in the sense of lil.:e tltem. Thnt is, he was, ns they bad been before him, instructed in the business of a husbandman and shepherd. There is evidence that Jacob combined the callings of an agriculturist ns well ae sheep-farmer, and trained his boys to sow and reap and bind sheave11 ns well ns tend the flocks and herds on his estate. From this, however, it were wrong to argue that all the children in a family should be trained alike, or put to learn the same craft or profession. In J11cob's day and Josepb's there was little choice of openings for young men who had aspirations nbove the crook or the plough. But in these times the avocations of men are as diverse as their gifts ; and in 1111 respects it is better-more beneficial to society at large, and more advantageous for the individual-that a wise discrimination be exercised by parents and guardians in selecting spheres of labour for those d~endent on or intrusted to them that shall be suited to their gifts and tastes. 3. With them in the sense of betride them. Joseph accompanied his brethren when they tended the flocks or reaped the ripened grain, and in particular associated himsel£, for reasons suggested in the Exposition, with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpab. It was IL privilege which Joseph enjoyed that he did not need to go from home to learn his trade; and doubtless Joseph's amiable disposition would make the society of bis father's sons more agreeable tc him than the company of strangers. II. JOSEPH PREFEBBED ABOVE HIS BRETHREN. 1. By his/ather. (1) The ground 430 TliE BOOK 01<' GENESIS. [en. XXXVII. 2-11. of Jacob's partiality for Joseph. He was the son of Jacob's old age. However this expression may be explained ('lli,de Exposition), the amount of it seems to be diat Joseph had come to gladden Jacob's heart after a considernble period of waiting, and at a time when Jacob was beginning to feel himself an old man. Hence more than to any of his other children Jacob's affections went out to the firstborn of Rachel, and this affection could not fail to strengthen after Rachel's death. It is just possible also that it was kept alive and fostered by a. reminiscence of Rachel'a beauty, which he saw reproduced in the well-proportioned frame and finely-cut features of the growing lad. Anyhow, Jacob's fondness for Joseph was palpable· and without affirming that it was right, it may at least be contended that it wa~ natural, the more especially when Josepl11 s piety is contrasted with the notorious wickedness of Jacob's other sons. (~) The exhibition of Jacob's partiality for Joseph. Many parents who find themselves in Jacob's situation, drawn to one child more than another in their families, make an effort at least to conceal n preference which in their inmost hearts they cannot but feel to be justifiable. But Jacob, with a sad lack of prudence, displayed his superior estimation of Rachel's son by presenting him with a rich and valuable coat of ends or pieces (vide Exposition). As might have been expected, such a. mark of preference was distasteful to his other children, and, had it not been for Joseph's superior character, might have been morally hurtful to Joseph himself. As it was, it was no kindness to .Joseph, but only a foolish gratification to Joseph's father. 2. By God. Joseph was honoured to receive dreams prophetic of his future greatnesl!. The first, the dream of the bowing sl1eaves, was a Divine foreshadowing of his advancement above his brethren ; and the second, the dream of the nodding orbs, of his elevation above all the members of his family. Even had they not concerned himself at all, to have been made the recipient of Divine communications was an honour; much more when theso communications related to his own exaltation. This preference of Joseph was unquestionably gracious, but it was also natural (1 Sam. ii. 30) III. JOSEPH HATED DY HIS DRETHREN. 1. The cause of their liatred. This was-(1) The superior place which he enjoyed intheir father's affection (ver. 4). Parents may here observe the danger of cherishing, and especially of manifesting, a preference of one member of the family above another. Unless in very exceptional circumstances, all are equally entitled to a father's care and a mother's love. (2) The supetior piety he displayed above themselves. It is difficult to credit the actors in the Shechemite and Dothan tragedies with anything in the shape of religion. Certainly they were not looked upon as exemplary characters by those who had the misfortune to live beside them. Out of their father's sight they shook off any little restraint which his presence may have inspired. Their scandalous behaviour became the talk of every neighbourhood they chanced to visit; and Joseph hearing it, as in duty bound, reported it to Jacob. Not that the mere reporting of it at home would much concern these reckless youths. Possibly it would exasperate their minds againsttheir brother. But the thing which would incense them most would be the disinclination which he showed to run with them into the same excess of riot. (3) The superior honour he received from God. The brethren clearly enough understood the dreams to contain a prognostication of Joseph'e future, else why did they allow themselves to become inflamed with anger on account of a foolish boy's fancies ? At least they believed Joseph regarded them in this light, and they hated him on that account. 2. The progress oftheir hatred. (1) They omitt~d to give him the.customary ~alutati_on of Shalem. It is a bad sign when a man declines to exchange fnendly greetmgs with hie neighbour, and much more with hie. brother. (2) They passed on to deep and bitter hatred. They hated him yet the more fo~ hie ~reams and bis word~. _E:,:il passions have a tendency to grow, an~ sh_ould be mpped m the b':1~- Obst0;pri'fl,cipi71. (3) They envied him ; the fierce mahgmty of their enraged spmte burnmg 111 their bosoms, suffusing their countenances with ominous Io·oke and angry scowls, an? generally expressing itoelf in dislike, irritation, and annoyance. 3. The end of. tliew hatred. It was impossible that the gathering storm should continue long without bnrsting. All things wundane, evil as well as good, strive after completeness. " Lust, when it bath conceived, bringeth forlh sin: sin, when it is finiehed, bringeth fo1ih death' (James i. 15). Hence, "whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer" JI!, XXX\'11. 2-lJ.] 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. 431 (1 John iii. 15); initially in thought, nnd nltimntely, granting time and opportunity, in deed. The murderous feeling of Joseph's brethren very speedily found occasion to become the fratricidal net.

entries.title: GEN 37:2–4
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: --Joseph aJ, lwme. "Joseph, being seventeen years old," &c. Picturesque 8Ccne is the encampment ofJacob. How well thedark camel-hair tents harmonisewith the general character of the spots in which they are pitched. Peace and purity should dwell there. Ten men of the tribe of Jacob are most depraved, but their characters only threw into brighter prominence that of Joseph. It ie probable that Jacob gave greater attention to the training of Joseph than to that of hie brethren, He showed favouritism also. His act of giving him a garb of varied colour may not altogether have been so foolish and weak as sometimes it has been supposed to be. It was simply an ordinary Eastern way of indicating that Joseph was to be the future leader and sheik of the encampment. Think of Joseph's home life, and learn- I. THAT AT HOME WE SHOULD, LIKE JOSEPH, LEARN TO PREPARE FOR FUTURE LIFE. Doubtless Jacob would tell Joseph of the promises of God to Abraham, of the tradition of the Deluge and the Fall ; probably also of his own fleeing from home, and his dream in the desert, when he saw "the great altar-stair sloping through darkness up to God," and the angels ascending and descending. Jo11eph always afterwards has great faith in dreams. No book had he. 'l'he Bible was not written. Traditions and oral teaching formed his mental training. II. AT HOME WE SHOULD ALWAYS HAVE SOME EMPLOYMENT. His father loved him too dearly to allow him to grow up in habits of idleness. He learned to handle the crook and to become a faithful messenger. No work is to be despised, for all may be a preparation for fntnre usefulness. III. AT HOME WE SHOULD NOT WILLINGLY BE WITNESSES OF WRONG-DOING. The lives of Joseph's brethren were sinful, and their doings deceitful. Some things he is obliged to know about of which itis dangerous to keep silence. The welfare of the whole tribe was being riFked by the elder brothers, and Joseph, fearing that, tells his father, or seeks counsel that he may be strengthened to resist evil influence. IV. AT HOME WE MAY HAVE GLOWING VISIONS OF TIIE FUTURE. The two dreams concerning the sheaves, and the sun and moon and stars; brought hate from his brethren, hut they had an influence on Joseph's after life. They were remarkably fulfilled. Vil'e all have some such visions. We build " castles in the air." The stern realities of life tone down our dreams. It is well to have some such dreams. Without them few make any advance in life. \Ve are not to be like mere senseless stones, but growing plants. Better is it to bear fruit than to wait to become only the sport of circumstances.-H.

entries.title: GEN 37:12–25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph among his brethren at IJothan. I. THE FRIENDLY MISSION. 1. Its local destinatioii. This was Shechem, at a distance of sixty miles from Hebron, where Jacob had previously resided for a number of years and acquired a 1,rnall estate (eh. xxxiii. 18, 19), where Jacob's sons had committed, afew years befor11 the terrible ntrocity which made the name of Israel stink throughout the land (eh: xxxiv. 26-30); and where now Joseph's brethren were shepherding their flocks ha,ing gone thither either on account of the excellent pasture, or in order to b~ beyond the reach of Joseph and his tale-bearing, or perhaps with a mind to keep an eye on their father's estate. 2. Its kindly intention. . Joseph was despatched to this important sheep-station in the north to inquire after the welfare of his brethren. That Jacob should have sent a son so tender and beloved on a journey so arduous and an errand so fraughtwith danger to himself, considering the well-known hostility ('f his brethren towards him, if a proof of Jacob's want of consideration, was also a mark of his parental solicitude for his sons' behaviour, as well as a sign of his ;1pprehensions for their safety, venturing, as they had, to revisit the scene of their former crimes, and perhaps it may be added, an indication of his desire to effect a reconciliation between Joseph and his brethren. 3. Its cheerful susception. Though realising better than bis father did the perilous character of the enterprise, in consequence of knowing more exactly than his father the depth of malignant feeling entertained towards him by hie bn,thren, Joseph did not hesitate to comply with his father's instructions, but, making nothing of the long journey, and keeping silent as to the risks of increased hatred, if nothing more, which he must have known that mission would entail upon him, cheerfully replied, Here am I. What o bright example of true filial piety and obedience I 4. Its successful completion. Arriving at Shechern, he first failed to find his brethren, and then lost his way, but ultimately, on being directed by a stranger, discovered them at Dothan. The perseverance of Joseph in carrying through his father's commission may be profitably studied, as a pattern to all to whom any sort of work, but more especially Christian work, is intrusted. JI. THE DIABOLICAL CONSPIRACY. 1. Its innocent occasion-the approach of Joseph in his long-sleeved and long-skirted tunic. Likengunpowder train that has been carefully prepared, and only wants the application of a spark to produce an explosion, the brethren of Joseph were only needing some trifling incident to elicit all the frniricidal hate which was already growing in their bosoms, and that incident waa supplied by the sight of the coat of ends. Itwas a striking illustration of how gre11t results frequently proceed from apparently insignificantcauses (James iii. 4, 6). 2. Its murderous clwracter. It aimed at the destruction of Joseph's life. With unexampled unanimity, not a voice wa~ raised against the proposal (perhaps mnde by Simeon) to kill him aod cast his lifeless body into a pit. The proposal of Reuben must have been understood by the others as only a more excruciatingly cruel way of inflicting death, vii., by starvation. See here in Jacob's family n development of cm. XXXVII 12-25.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 4.35 the same spirit of murder aa existed in Adam's, Like Cain, the sons of Jacob were of that wiclced one, and slew (in intention at least) their brother, and for the Rame reason (1 John iii. 12). 3. Ita impious desig11,--to spoil hie dreams. From this it is evident that theyregarded hie dreams as a. Heaven-sent prognostication of hie future grea.ineea; else, if they regarded them as purely boyishfancies, why should they have felt annoyed at what was eo evidently groundless? Hence, in seeking to prevent the realisation of hie dreams they were actually fighting against God. But it is just precisely in proportion ae wicked men eee God's hand in any prophecy or programme that they take. measures to insure its defeat (cf. 1 Sam. :x:.ix. 1 ; 2 Kings vi. 14). 4. Its ruthless e.xecution. They took him and cast him into a pit. The crime was perpetrated (1) with insolent humiliation-they stripped the poor lad of his pretty coat; (2) with violent brutality-they caet him into the pit; Jeremiah waa leL down by cords (Jer, :xxxviii, 6) ; (3) with relentless cruelty-they heeded not his outcries and entreaties (eh. xiii 21, 22); and (4) with exquisite cold-bloodedness-having <le- ~patched their infernal business, with infinite nonchalance the ruffians sat down to eat bread, to regale their appetites after o. good day's work. Reuben, in aome respects not a person to be greatly admired, weak and vacillating in hie character, and easily drawn aside by stronger natures into sinfol courses, appears in this matter to have been the only one of Joseph's brethren in whom the natural affections of a brother were not completely overborne. Though he wanted the courage to resist his stronger-minded brothers, he seems to have conceived the purpose of saving, if he could, the life of Joseph. So far the stratagem was good, only it was-2. Timidly planned. The narrative would almost seem to convey that Reuben in the first onset of his opposition to his brother's nefarious intentions had succeeded in wresting Joseph from their hands, Had he at that moment asserted himself with vigour and boldness, as became the firstbom of the house, he might have saved Joseph altogether. But, alas, true to his feeble and pusillanimous character, he allowed himself to be overcome by the clamours of his fiercer-natured brethren, and only proposed that instead of imbruing their hands in Joseph's blood they should inflict on him the horrors of starvation. In making such a proposal of course Reuben hoped to be able to effect his deliverance, in which he might have succeeded, had he acted with promptitude and decision. But instead his stratagem wne-3. Weakly carried through. Where Reuben was when his brethren were comforting their hearts with.a.dinnerafter Joseph's consignment to the cistern, and concocting the matter of his sale, the narrative does not say ; but most likely he was by himself, deliberating, and resolving, and hesitating, and delaying, instead of acting. Hence his stratagem was-4. Completely defeated. By the tin1e he had got his mind made up to act it was too late. When he returned to the pit Joseph was gone, and, like many another procrastinator, he could only bemoan his own folly. HOMILIES BY VARIOUS .AUTHORS.

entries.title: GEN 37:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Josepli leaving home. "Go, I pray thee, seo whether," &c. Joseph left home unexpectedly. He knew not wl1en he left it to seek hie brethren that he would never come back again. After a longer journey than he anticipated Joseph finds his brethren. I. Like many leaving home, Joseph MET WITH ll'AITHFUL GUIDES. There are gonerally companions, teachers, ministers to help. II. Like many leaving home, Joseph FELL INTO BNAREB. He could not help him- ~elf. The snares were not such as were willingly entered. The wicked entrapped l1im. On this youth, far frotn home,defenceless, and kindly-intentioned, nine cowardly men fell. Ill. Like many away from home, Joseph FOUND THAT Goo CARED Fon HIM WHEN ms EARTHLY FATHER COULD NOT. Reuben was the means of saving him from death, Sold into slavery, he was still on the highway to eminence. Wo have to bewaro of hateful nnd murderous thoughts, remembering" that he that hateth his brother is" (so I' I' 2 43G THE BOOK OF GENESIS. Leu. xxxvu. 26-36. far ns intent goes) " a murderer." In all journeyings we have to commit our way unto the Lord, and he will guide and defend.-H. Yers. 20, 21.-Coa's pi·ovuknce and man's i·espon.sibili,ty. I. Goo's PURPOSES CAR• RIED OUT BY MEN IRRESPECTlVE OF 'l'HEIR OWN PLANS. The word to Abraham (eh. x,·. 13) does not seem to have been thought of by Jacob. After long wandering he seemed to be settled in Canaan. But God was bringing to pass his word. Jacob's injudicious fondness for Joseph, the anger and murderous design of his brethren (cf. John xi. 50; Acts iii. 17), Reuben's timid effort for his deliverance (cf. Acts v. 38), Judah's worldly wise counsel (cf. Luke xiii. 31), Joseph's imprisonment by Potiphar, the conspiracy in Pharaoh's household, were so many steps by which the sojourn in Egypt was brought about. So in the founding of the Christian Church. The writing on the cross (John xix. 20) pointed to three separate lines of hist11ty, two of them pagan, which combined to bring about the sacrifice of Christ and the spread of the gospel. So in the case of individuals. God's promises are sure (2 Cor. i. 20). There may seem to be many hindrances, from ourselves (Ps. !xv. 3) or from circumstances; but no cause for doubt (Luke xii. 32; xxii. 35). Unlikely or remote causes are often God's instruments. The envy of the Jews opened for St. Paul, through his imprisonment, a door to the Gentiles which otherwise he would not have had (Acts xxL 28; Phil. i. 13). IL IT IS NO EXCUSE FOR WRONG-DOING THAT IT HAS WORKED GOOD (cf. Rom. iL 19). The cruel act of his brethren brought about the realising of Joseph's· dreams, his greatness in Egypt, the support of the whole family during the famine, and the fulfilment of God's word; but not the l6ss was it wrong (eh. xiii. 21; cf. Matt. XXYi, 24). Moral guilt depends not upon the result, but on the motive. God has given the knowledge of redemption to move our will, and the example of Christ and the moral law to guide our lives. The fulfilment of his purposes belongs to himself. He needs not our help to bring it to pass. It is not his will that we should forsake his immutable rules of right and wrong, even for the sake of bringing on the fulfilment of prophecy. Much evil has sprung from neglect of this-e. g. the maxim, Faith need not he kept with heretics. God's will and promise, Ps. xxxvii. 3-5. III. To EACH ONE THEBE IS A HISTORY WITHIN A HISTORY. Our actions lead to their appropriate results (Gal. vi. 8) at the same time that they tend to carry out God's purposes, whether we will or not. Each one is a factor in thegreat plan which in the conrse of ages God is working out (John v. 17). Men such as they are, wise or ignorant, guided by the Spirit or resisting him, loving or selfish, pressing upwards or following worldly impulses, all are so directed by a power they cannot comprehend that they bring about what he wills (Pa. ii. 2-4). But along with this there is a history which concerns oureelvee, which we write for ourselves, the is1mes of which depend immediately upon ourselves. To each a measure of time, knowledge, opportunity has been given, on the use of which the line of our course_ depends. Nothing can turn aside the course of God's providence ; but upon our fa1thfulnese or unfaithfulness depends our place and joy in it. Hence encouragement to work for Christ, however small our powers (1 Sam. xiv. 6). The little is accepted as well as the great; and as "workers together with him" (2 Cor. vi. 1) our work cannot be in Yain.-M.
