entries.title: GEN 37:26–36
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph carried by Midianites to Ev,ypt. I. THE INll'AMOUS SALE. 1. The wi,cked proposal. "Come, and let us sell him.' By whatever motives Judah was actuated, the notion that either he or his brethren had a right thus to dispose of Joseph's life was not simply nn open violation of the Divine law which constituted all men with equal rights, and in particular made every man his brother's keeper, not his brother's destroyer or proprietor, but a hideous discovery of the utter perversion of moral nature which had taken place in the case of Joseph'e brethren, So low had they now sunk, that they were become not alone without humanity, but without natural affection as well. 2. Tlie double reason. (1) The advantageous character of the proposed transaction is exhibited by Judah, who doubtless understood the sort of arguments that would weigh most powerfully with his brethren. Simply to assassinate the hated stripling and conceal hie blood might indeed gratify their feelings of revenge, but would not do much to enrich them. Might it not be possible to dispose of him more profitably than by the coarse way of killing him? 'l'hen (2) the humane aspect of the proposed transaction is pathetically dwelt upon by Judah,-" he is our brother and our flesh,"-in which perhaps may also be det"cted Judah's subtle knowledge of human nature, in reasoning that mon who cared nothing for the claims of humanity and brotherhood in themselves might be induced to do a little cheap philanthropy by sparing Joseph, nfter they ha.d first been made to see that it would likewise be profitable. Judah's last rernnrk was n master-stroke which overbore every vestige of opposition: "his brethren were content." 3. T!ie favourable opporlunity. Many wicked schemes are happily never carried through because the opportumty is wa11ting-thanks to Divine providence I But, on the other hand, thousands of nefarious crimes are born of the opportunity-thanks to 1.be sinful ingenuity of the fallen heart I The scheme of Judah was clearly suggested by the providential circumstance that at the moment an Ishmnelitish cam.van was passing by on its way with gums and spicery to Egypt. That camvnn wns God's ch:iriot sent to convey Joseph to the throne of Egypt. Judah naked his l,retbrcn to Ree in it a piison van to take their brother into slavery in Egypt. Wicked men and G?d may often seem to play at cross purposes with one _another, but ~od always tnumph8. Man propQBes; God disposes. 4. The accomplislied transaction. "They o!.I. xxxvu. 26-3G.J THE DOOK OF GEN'ES1S. 4$9 drew and lifted Joseph up out of tho pit, and sold him to the Midianites for thirty pieces of silver." The first recorded specimen of a transaction which has frequently been repeated in the history of mankind. Slave markets have often imitated, but seldom surpassed, the wickedness of which Joseph'e brethren were guilty. It wns not simply a fellow-creature that they sold, but a brother; and they had not even the poor apology of getting a good bargain, as they sold him for twenty shekels-little over forty shillings I 5. The unf(J'reseen result. Joseph's purchasers convey11d him into Egypt, and sold him, as probably his brethren expected; it is scarcely likely they nnticipated he would find hie way into so honourable service as that of a high officer of state. Dut God was taking Joseph thereby a step nearer to his predicted elevation. II. THE DOLEFUL TIDINGS. 1. The ominous B?Jmbol. The coat of ends, the token of a father's love for his darling son, the insensate ruffians, after dipping it in blood, caused to be conveyed into their father's presence by the hands of a swift-footecl messenger. This was rather a proof of their cowardice than of their consideration for Jacob's feelings. 2. The pretended ducovery. The bearer of the blood-stained tunic was directed to say that the brethren had found the robe, and to ask, with expressions of their deep concern, whether or not it was the coat of his beloved son. Their intention we cannot think was to stab their father's heart, bat to mislead his judgment. 3. The e:r:pected inference. As they designed, the old man conclurled that his son was devoured: 11 Joseph is without doubt rent in pieces." Seldom do villains' plots succeed so well. III. THE SORROWING PARENT. 1. The biller grief. The depth and tendemess of Jacob's mourning for his lost son was-(1) visibly expressed: "he rent his clothes, and put snckcloth on his loins;" (2) long continued: 11 he mourned for his son many days;" nnd, if we accept n proposed reading of the last clause of ver. 35, (3) lovingly shared: ''his fother," the blind Isaac, who still survived, "wept for him" -for Rachel' s dead child and Jacob's lost son. 2. The ineffectual consolation. " All hie sons and alJ his daughters rose up to comfort him ; but he refused to be tomforted." For this Ja.cob was (1) to be excused, since his comforters were mostly hypocrites, whose proffered consolations must have sounded strangely hollow in his enrs; but also (2) to be blamed, since although God in his providence harl taken away Joseph, that was no reason why he should give way to despairing grief. Not so did Abraham when be thought of losing Isaac.

entries.title: GEN 38:1–30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The house of Judah: a family record of sin and sltame. I. THE WICKEDNESS or ER AND ONAN. 1. Early. On any hypothesis Er and Onan can have been little more than boys when they were man-ied, and yet they appear to have arrived at a remarkable precocity in sin. Nor was it simply that they had shed ~he i_nnocence and purity of youth, but they had also acquired a shameful J?roficiency m vwe. Young scholars are mostly apt learners, especially in the devil's school. 2. Unnatural. Though not described, the wickedness of Judah's first son had relation to some perversion of the ordinance of marriage; that of his second is plainly stated to have been uncleanness and self-pollution. Neither against nature nor contrary to grace are the endearments of the married state, but every act outside of the Divine permissions concerning woman is both. 3. Heinous. The act of Er is characterised as "wicked in the sight of the Lord," while that of Onan is said to have displeased the Lord. Hence it may be reasonably inferred that the essential criminality in both cases was the same. They were both perversions of a natural ordinance. They both militated against the purity and development of the theocratic family. Both indicated a contemptuous unbelief in the promise of the covenant, and a sacrilegious disregard for the calling of Israel as the progenitor of tl,e promised seed. Hence both were deserving of Divine reprobation. 4. Disastrous. The tendency of all sin is ruinous, both for body, soul, and spirit. Whether as a natural result of indulgence in vice, or as a direct punitive visitation from God, Er and Onan were consigned to premature graves; and this, it should be noted by young persons of both sexes, is the almost inevitable consequence of indulgence in secret vice, and'in particular of the practice of which Onan was guilty. Yielded to, it debilitates the physical constitution by a wasting of the vital powers, it impairs the mental faculties, it corrupts the moral nature, it sears and petrifies the conscience, and finally, what might have been a fair specimen of noble and virtuous manhood or womanhood it covers up, a poor, wasted, shivering skeleton, beneath the clods of il,e ,·aUey, causing it to lie down among the sins of its youth. II. THE BIN OF 'l'AMAn. The conduct of Judah's daughter-in-law, the young widow of Er and Onan, though not without its extenuations, in having been partly pro\'oked by Judah's reluctance to marry her to Shelah, and partly inspired by a desire to take her place among the ancestresses of the promised seed, was yet in many respects reprehensible. 1. She discovered impatience. Although Judah did manifest a temporary unwillingness to give her Shelah for a husband, she might l,ave reasoned that, after losing two sons, it was not unnatural that he should hesitate about exposing a third to the same riRk of destruction. 2. She manifested unl.,eliej. I£ Tamar did regard herself aa wronged, as most undoubtedly she w11s, instead of taking measures to right herself, she should have left her cause to God, who had already vindicated her against the wickedness of her youthful husbands, and who in his own time and way would doubtless have interposed to assert her P!erogative as a widow belonging to the family of Israel. 3. She practised deceptwn. Laying aside her widow's garments, and assuming tha attire of n harlot, she took her station at the gate of Enajim, 9n the way to Timnntl1, nnd pretended to bo 11 prostitute, Tamar mnnifeatly was not a woman of refined and delicate sensibilities; but then she was a Canaanite, and had been the wife of Er and Onan1 who were not calculated to improve her modesty. 4. She was g,iilty of temptatwn. It ia true the narrative does not represent her as having been guilty of solicitation, like the "foolish woman" described by Solomon (Prov. vii. 6-23; ix. 14-18). Perhaps she knew that Judah would not require solicitation; but if so, she was all the more guilty in placing temptation in Judah'a way. 5. She committed ince:;t. The guilt of an incestuous connection which rested on Judah unconsciously she had knowingly nnd willingly taken on herself. III. THE TRANSGRESSIONS OF JUDAH. More numerous, if not more heinous, than those of either hie sons or his daughter-in-Jaw were the offences of Judah. Jacob's fourth son sinned-1. In marrying a Canaanituh wife. Though Judah's marriage with Shuah's daughter was blessed by God, who made it fruitful, it does not follo,v that it was approved by God. 2. In withholding Shelah from Tamar. Although it does not appear as yet to have been commanded that in default of issue a widow should be married by her deceased husband's brother, it is obvious that Judah recognised that it should be so, both by his own act in giving Onan to Tamar after Er·~ death, and by his own subsequent confession with regard to Shelah (ver. 26). 3. In deceiving Tamar. Instead of frankly telling her that he did not intend his thin! ~on to become her husband, he bound her to remain a widow, and sent her home to her father's house (instead of keeping her in his own) under the impression that Shelah was only withheld from her on the score of youth. 4. In committin(J sin witli Tamar. Though in reality Judah committed incest, yet so far as his intention went it was only adultery, or fornication. Yet all forms of unchastity are forbidden in the law of God. And it gives !I very low conception of the morality of Judah that he, a member of the consecrated family of Israel, who had himself been manied, should have so openly, and deliberately, and coolly turned aside to seek the company of a common strumpet, as he imagined Tamar to be. Judah should have acted on the J?rinciple afterwards stated by Paul (1 Cor. vii. 9). 5. In condemning Tamar. "Brmg her forth, and let her be burnt," said the indignant patriarch. It is obvious the sentence was excessive in its severity. It was not imperative, else it could not have been remitted; and a recollection of his visit to Timnath three months pre• viously should have inclined him to lean to mercy's side. But the virtuous Angelo~ of society always procure indulgence for themselves by damning their fellow-sinners (l,feas'ltre for Measure, .Act II.). Scripture counsels differently (Matt. vii. 3; Ilom. ii. 22; Gal. vi. 1).

entries.title: GEN 38:12–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Judah's sin with Tamar. I. COMMITTED. 1. Suddenly. It was occasioned by the sight of a supposed courtes!ln. Much evil enters by the eye (cf. 2 Sam. xi. 2). Great need for the prayer of David (Pa. cxix. 37), 2. Openly. Judah wne in the company of Hirah, bis friend, when he beheld Tamar sitting in the gate of Enajim, and, without attempting to hide it from his frieRd, went to seek her society. Shamelessness in sin betokens gre!lt depravity. 3. Wilfully. Though in n mnnner surprised by the temptation, Judah w11e not inadl'ertently betrayed into commission of his sin with Tamar, but, on the contrary, went about it in n remarkably deliberate manner. 4. lne:r:cU&ably. There was no reason why J udnh should not hnve sought !I second wife to succeed Shuah'sdaughter, rather than consort with prostitutes. II. DETECTED. 1. Quickly, No doubt Judah thought he hnd heard the last of his indiscretion on the way to Timnath; but lo I in three short months his guilt is rliscovered. Not every offender is so speedily arrested ; but sooner or Inter detection is inevitable for all. "Be sure thy sin will find thoe out." 2. Unexpectedly. Judah never imagined that his own signet, and chain, and staff would be produced as witnesses 11g11inst him; and criminals never can be sure from what quarter testimony ehnll nrise to condemn them. 3. Completely. There was no possibility of Judah's evading the charge of To.mar. By 110 sort of ingenuity could he repudillte the articles of dress with which probably his household were fnmiliar. 4. P'ltblicly. At tho very moment when Tamar was produced for execution Judah was oblig-,d to confess his guilt in presence of his a~sembled household; and in like mnnncr will the wickccl yet be openly convicted in the sight of an assembled world. 446 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cu. XXXIX. 1-6. III. CONFESSED. _1. Candul.ly. Found out, Judah did not attempt either to deny or to palliate his guilt, but frankly acknowledg·ed that Tamar's condition was due to him. 2. Promptly. Nor did he hesitate to own his guilt, but immediately confessed ~hat.he had done. 3. Pe:n,itently. This we may infer from the statement of the lnstonan that the offence was not again repeated. IV. FORGIVEN. It does not fall within the scope of the historian's design to indi• cate whether Judah obtained mercy; but this may be reasonably concluded from- 1. T!ie pro'f'!,ptness of hi.s co,ifessi,on. 2. The sincerity of liis penitence. 3. The reality of his fauh-as evinced by the fact that he wns reckoned among the nnces• tors of our Lord.

entries.title: GEN 38:27–30
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Tamar's twins. I. POINTS OF RESEMBLANCE. (1) The offspring of the snme parents; (2) the fruit of the same sin; (3) the gift of the same God. II. PorNTs OF DISTINCTION, (1) The order of their birth; (2) the import of their names; (3) the purpose of their lives-the first being an ancestor of the promised seed. HOMILIES BY VARIOUS .AUTHORS. Ch. x:a:viii.-.The goodness and severity of God. These occurrences in the family of Judah would seem (1) to betoken the retributive }udgment of God, and (2) illustrate his grace. Joseph is Jost, and still Divinely protected. Judah is a wande1er from his brethren, a sensual, self-wille_d, degenerate man; yet it is in the line of this same wanderer that the promised seed shall appear. The'whole is a lesson on the evil of separation from the people of God. Luther asks why such things were placed in Scripture, and answers, (1) That no one should be self-righteous, a11d (2) that no one should despair, and (3) to remind us that Gentiles by natural n:ght are brothers, mother, sisters to our Lord; the word of salvation is a word for Lhe ·whole v.•orld.-R.

entries.content: -And his master saw tho.t the Lord (Jehovah) was with him-this does not imply that Potiphar was acquainted with Jehovah, but s1mplv that he concluded Joseph to be under the Divine protectionand that the Lord (Jehovah) ma.de all that he did to prosper in his hanll. That which led to the conviction of Potiphar concerning Joseph was the remarkable success which he saw attending all his efforts nnd undertakings. • Vor. 4.-.And J'oseph found graoe in his aight,-vide eh. vi. 8; xviii. 3 ; xix. 19; xxxix. 21. Most men aro plertsed with a good servant. Even Laban had no objections to Jacob so long as lie divined that Jehovah w11s multiplying his flocks for Ja. cob's sake (eh. xxx. 27)-nnd he served him (i. e. ho waited on Potiphar, or nctcd as his personal attendant and comptroller of his f1ouschold): and he (i. e. Potiphar) made him overseer over. his house,-a position co1Tesponding to that occupied by Eliezer in the household of Abraham (eh. xxiv. 2). ,Egyptian monuments attest the existence of such an officer in wealthy houses at an early period ; a tomb at Kum-el-Ahmar exhibiting the account books, writing materials, and clerks that pertain to the office of a stewo.rd, and anotheratBeni-hassan,besidesdisplayiug his accustomed inlplements, styling him the Overseer (Wilkinson's 'Ancient Egyptians,' vol.i. p. 372,ed. 1878;Hengstenberg's'Egypt and tbe Books of Moses,' p. 24). A sepulchral inscription belonging to the period of the eleventh dynasty also mentions among the officers comprising the household of Amcni the chancellor Athorsi, the barber Khentikhrati, the slave Gefohapi, the lady's maid Khui, the steward Ameni, the steward Santit (vide 'Records of the Past;' vol. vi. p. 3). Joseph had also, after his exaltation, a ruler or sieward of his house (cf. eh. xliii 16, 19 ; xliv. 1)-and all that he had he put into his hand=literally, and all which was w hiin he gave into Ms hand, i. e. he intrristed to ,Toseph's care). Ver. 6,-Alld it came to pass from the time that he had made (literally, from lltat time he made) him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, that (literally, and) the Lord (Jehovah) blessed the Egyptie.n's house for.J'oseph's sake (cf. eh. xxir. 12); and the bleasing of the Lord (Jehovah) was upon all.that he had in the house, and in the ~eld. It is observable that throughout this chapter, when the historian is speaking in his own name the term Jehovah is used to designate the Supreme Being (cf. ve:ra: 21! 23), '!"~ereas when Joserh replies to his mistress it LS the word Eloh1m which he employs, the reason of which is sufficiently obvious.

entries.title: GEN 39:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: And· (accordingly, encouraged by the admirable success attending Joseph's management) he left all that he had in J'oseph's hand (i. e. gave him unrestricted. control over all his temporal affairs) ; and ha knew not ought he had (literally, he knew not anything with him, i. e. he shared. uot the care of anything along with him), save the bread which he did eat. This was necessitated by the laws of caste which then prcvo.iled among the Egyptians, and in particular by the fact that "the Egyptians might not eat with the Hebrews" (eh. xliii. 32). And Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured-literally, beautiful in form and beautifitlinappearance, likehis mother Rachel (eh. xxix. 17).

entries.title: GEN 39:1–23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph in tlie house ofPotiphar. I. PURCHASED AS A SLAVE. 1. A sad lot. Worse even thnn being kidnapped by strangers, Joseph had been first sold by his brethren; carried into Egypt, he had there been exposed for sale in a slavemarket; and now, as if he had been a beast of burden or a captive taken in war, he had .been a second time purchased for money. Few fortunes are more touchingly sorrowful or more deeply humiliating than this which was now measured out to Jacob's youthful son. 2. A common lot. Happily in ourland, nnd indeed wherever the gospel prevails, it is not a spectacle that can now be beheld-that of men trafficking in each other's flesh. But in those days the horrors of the auction block were not unfrequent sightR, and Joseph, in being sold and bought like goods and chattels, was only experiencing a fate which had been undergone by mo.ny previous to his times, and has by myriads been suffered since. 3. An appointed lot. As everything on earth is, so was Joseph'e sad and sorrowful estate assigned him by Heaven; and the recognition of thi-s doubtless it wns by Joseph that prevented him from murmuring, and apparently inspired him with a cheerful confidence, even in the darkest times. II. EMPLOYED AS A sEnVANT. 1. Eminently prospero11,11. (1) The extent of thi~ prosperity. All that he iid prospered. Everything he put his hand to o.ppenred to thrive. Success seemed to wait upon him like his shadow. It is seldom such n measure of good fortune is meted out to any of God's people on the earth, or even of the devil's children. For the first they would probably be spoiled by such indulgence, while for the second they mostly fail in the conditions that are needfnl for such distinction. (2) The means of this prosperity. That Joseph was attentive, diligent, and conscientious in the performance of his household duties, ns well us faithful nnd devoted to the interests of his master, may be reasonably inferred, since success seldom waits upon tho negligent, the idfo, or the unprincipled. (3) Tho 44.8 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XXXIX. 1-6, source of this prosperity. The historian is careful to note tho.t the true mainspring of Joseph's, as of e,ery other person's, prosperity was the Divine blessing on his labours. "The Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand." 2. GreaUy re• ,oarded. Joseph was-(1) Noticed by his master. It is a pleasure to true nnd faithful servants when those they serve regard their ,vork with favourable obscrvntion. (2) Accepted by his master. It says a g·reat deal for Potiphar that he treated Joseph kindly, even though it was largely on account of his excellent qualities ns a servant. (3) Promoted by his master. From being humble valet to the great man's person, he was exalted to the high position of steward or comptroller of the great man's house. (4) Trusted by his master. Everything connected with the management of Potiphar's establishment, in his mansion and on his farm, was unreservedly committed to the care of Joseph. Potiphar troubled himself about nothing "save the bread which he did eat." Ill. BLESSED AS AMAN. 1. He enjoyed Divine companionship in his sad captivity. " The Lord was with him ; " a compensation rich enough to be set against the miseries of bondage and exile, as God's people, when similarly situated, have not unfrequently experienced (cf. Acts xvi. 25; 2 Tim. iv. 17). 2. He obtained Divine assistance in his arduous duties. When the circumstances of Joseph's lot might have induced despondency, indifference, inaction, carelessness, and inattention, Divine grace so upheld and cheered him that he was able to go abouthis duties with alacrity and cheerfulness, so that everything he turned his hand to succeeded. 3. Ho received Dimne favour in the eyes of his master. For Joseph himself to have ~ecretly known that God approved of his person and behaviour would have been nn ample consolation to his sad heart; but to obtain tbe good-will of Heaven so conspicuously that even his heathen master could not avoid observing itwas surely n sig-nal honour. 4. He attracted Divine blessing towards his fellow-men. "The Lord hlessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake." Here was a. clear experience by Joseph of the truth of the .A.brahamic blessing (eh. xii. 2, 3). In this also Joseph was an eminent type of Christ. Lessons :-1. Patience under suffering. 2. Contentment with one's lot. 3. Fidelity in service. 4. The secret of prosperity. 5. The obligations of masters towards serva'.1ts. 6. The value of religion to a workman. 7. The profit of a pious servant.

entries.title: GEN 39:1–23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Sunsliine and shadow. I. THE BRIGHTENING SKY. The advancement of Joseph in the house of Potiphar. 1. To Joseph's sense it was a lightening in his bondage. 2. To Joseph's faith it was the smiling of Jehovah's face. 3 To Joseph's hope it V'as the dawning of a better day. II. THE THREATENING CLOl'D. The temptation of Joseph by his mistress. Here was-1, An assault upon his virtue, which, unless it were overcome, would deprive l1im of Jel1ovah's favour, and consequently put an end to any prospect he might have of deliverance; and, 2. An attack upon his safety, which, however it resulted, whether in Lis defeat or his victory, would likely terminate his enjoyment of his master's fa,·our, if not altogether cost him his life. III. THE FALLING DARKNESS. The accusation of Joseph by his mistress. 1. Tbouo-h untrue, it was almost certain to be believed. 2. If believed, it would certai~Iy involve him in punishment. 3. If deemed deserving of punishment, he would almost certainly be put to death. IV. TnE: STARLIGIIT NIGHT. The history of Joseph in the prison. 1. He hod not been executed, but only imprisoned. 2. God was with him in the dungeon, ns he hud been in the palace. 3. If the favour of his master had been lost, the confidence of liis keeper had been gained. 4. Misfort_une might seem to be always_ lying in wait for him, but, on the other hand, prosperity appeared to be ever followrng close upon his heels. HOMILIES DY VARIOUS AUTHORS. Ch. xxxix.-T/ie ?-igldeous rr.wa. Again the word of the Lord tries Joseph, but not so much now as the word of prophecy, but ns 1he word of command, the doctrine of righteousncsa. "The Egyptian's houeo is blessed for Joe<'ph's snke.'1 11 The Lord was with Joseph, and be was a prosperous man." A lesson on the true method of prosperity. A prosperous man is one who has the Lord with him- 1. To give him favour with fellow-men. 2. To teach him wisdom, and put things into his hand. 3. To give him the faculty of rule, and dispose others to trust him entirely. 4. To keep him pure from the vicious besetments of the world, both by his own personal chastity and by his courage and self-command in hours of temptation. 6. Dy delivering him when he is entangled in the meshes of the evilminded. The bad woman's determination is thwarted. Mercy is shown him in the prison. 6. By making him a messenger of peace and truth, even in the very prisonhouse of shame and misery. Notice again the elevation of Joseph's character. 1. His love of God. 11 How can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" 2. His lov~ of man. "My master hath committed all to me "-bow can I wrong him so? 3. His C(Yfl,fide:ru;e in the blessing of God on the upright and holy life. He knew that God would vindicate him. 4. His self-control. His circumstances were fearful temptation. Had he not been a virtuous man in his heart of hearts, he would have succumbed, and then pleaded, as so many do, the power of the flesh and of the tempting circumstances. Notice also how these characteristics do help one another when they are in the character, and bow, when a man casts himself upon God, God makes the way of escape. Joseph was safer in prison than he was in his master's house.-R.

entries.title: GEN 39:7
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Ancl it came to pass after these things, - Josepb had by this time been nearly ten years in Potiphar's house ('Vide eh. xii. 46)-that his master's wife cast her eyes (lasciviously) upon Joseph ; ancl she saicl, Lie with me. According to monumental evidence (Wilkinson's 'Ancient Egy:ptinns,'vol.i.p. 392, ed. 1878; Hengstenberg s 'Egypt and the Books of Moses,' i. 25 ; Kalisch, p. 631) and historical testimony (Herod., ii. 111), Egyptian females, even though married, were distinguished for licentiousness nnd immorality, and were not condemned to live in seclusion (Bohlen), but ,rnre nllowed freely to mix in promiscuous society, which facts perfectly account for Joseph's temptation by bis mistress.

entries.title: GEN 39:16–18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And she laid up his garment by her (literally, by her side), until his lord came home (literally, until the coming ofhu lord to hu house). And she spake unto him according to these words, saying, The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us (here she charges her husband with being indirectly at least the cause of ihe alleged affront ,vhich had been put upon her), came in unto me to mock me: -" she seemed too modest to speak in plain terms of Joseph's crime (Lawson) -and it ea.me to pass, as I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me and :fled out (i. e. went forth into the street, ut supra).

entries.title: GEN 39:19
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass, when his master heard the words of his wife, which she spake unto him, saying, After this manner (literally, according to these 1cords) did thy servant to me; that his wrath was kindled. A papyrus consisting of nineteen pages of ten lines of hieratic writing (purchased from Madame D'Orbiney, and presently in the British Museum), belonging _probably to the nineteenth dynasty, contains a tale of two brothers, in which incidents occur very similar to those here narrated. While the two are ploughing in the field, the elder sends the younger brother, who appears to have acted in the capacity of general superintendent, to fetch seed from the house. "AD.d the younger brother found the wife of the elder sitting at her toilet." . . . . " And she spoke to him, saying, What strength there is in thee ! indeed I observe thy vigour every day. Her heart knew him. . . , She seized upon him, and said to him, Come, let us lie down for an instant. Betterfor thee ...beautiful clothes.'' "The youth became like a panther with fury on account of the shameful discourse which she had addressed to him. •AD.d she was alarmed exceedingly." . , . " Her lrnsband returned home at e,ening, according to his daily wont. He came to the house, and he found his wife lying as if murdered by a ruffian.'' lnquirina the reason of her distress, he is answer;8 as Potiphar was answered by his deceitful spouse. ".And the elder brother became like apanther; , , . he made his dagger sharp, and took it in his hand " (vide ' Records of the Past,' vol. ii p. 139).

entries.title: GEN 39:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Joseph's master took him, and put him into the prison, - literally house of endos1we; sohai·, from sahai·, to encircle, meaningprobablya turreted, arehed, or rounded building for tho r.nn.finoment of prisoners-a placewhere the king's prisoners (i. e. State offenders) werebound: and he was there inthe prison. This, which someregard as having been a mild punishment(Delitzsch, Keil), since, according to Diodorus Sieulus, tho laws of the Egyptians were specially severe in their penalties for offences against women, is represented by a Hebrew psalmist (Ps. cv. 18) as having been accompanied with bodily tortures, at least for a time ; for his speedy elevation to a place of trust within the prison almost gives countenance to the idea (Kurtz, Lange, &c.) that Potiphn,r did not believe his wife's story, and only incarcerated Joseph for the sake of appearances. That Joseph was not immediately punished with death is not improbable (Bohlen), but exceedingly natural, since Joseph was Potiphar's favourite (Havernick).

entries.title: GEN 39:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -But (even if Joseph was harshly treated in the tower of.Heliopolis) the Lord -Jehovah (videon ver. 5)-was with Joseph (v'ide ver. 2), and shewed him mercy (literally, extended kindness unto him), and gave him favour in the eyes of the keeper (or captain) of the prison (or round house).

entries.title: GEN 39:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And the keeper of the prison (captain of the round house, or chief officer of the tower) committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners that were in the prison; and whatsoever they did there, he was the doer of it-literally, and all that they (the prisoners) were doing there, he was the person doing it, or attending to it; i. e. the keeper gave him charge to see that the /risoners obeyed whatever orders were issue for their regulation ; and, having implicit confidence in Joseph's probity, the keeper of the prison looked not to anything that was under (or in) his hand (i. e. he did not trouble himself about anything intrusted to Joseph) ; beoause the Lord (Jehovah) was with him, and that which he did, the Lord (Jehovah) made it to prosper.

entries.title: GEN 39:7–23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Josepli and t!te wife of Potipliar. I. THE GREAT TEMPTATION. l. The time of it. Never perhaps had Joseph's prospects been brighter since he lefthis father's house than towards the close of that decade of years which he spent in the Egyptian officer's employ; and yet then it was that, like a thunderbolt shot from a clear sky, a fierce temptation burst upon him. 2. The occasion of it. Thiewas the beauty of Joseph'e person. Things innocent and lovely in themselves may sometimes mI, XXXIX. 7-23.] 'rHE BOOK OF GENESIS. 451 be n source of danger, and, if not guarde<l against, a cause of sin, to their possessors. In particular the good looks of men and women are often snares to others 11s well as fraught with peril to themselves, as the cases of Sarah (eh. xii. 14), Rebekah (eh. xxvi. 10), and Dinah (eh. xxxiv. 2)testify. Hence beauty of the person should neither be too eagerly coveted nor too proudly worn by either sex, as by each its charms in the other should be moderately admired, and its allurements earnestly resisted. 3. The form of it. The special trial to which the young man Joseph was no\V subjected partook of the character of an assault upon his chastity. It is, however, a mistake to suppose that a good man is always assaulted at the point where he is weakest. On the contrary, it is one of the devil's blunders that, in directing his attacks against saints, be for the most part mistakenly selects the point where they are strongest. Joseph was permitted to be assailed by his lascivious mistress not because his own personal virtue was doubtful, but because in that direction he was best prepared to repel the fiercest onset of temptation. 4. The strervjtk of it. There were elements in this assault upon Josepb's virtue which were calculated to impart to it a vehemence that in ordinary circumstances, i. e. with persons of less robustness of moral principle than Joseph, must have proved overwhelming. These were-(1) The person by whom it was directed, viz., Joseph's mistress, the wife of a high officer of state, whose smile might have turned the head and intoxicated the heart of a young man who was only her slave. (2) The vehement importunity with which it was urged, his mistress speaking to him day by day, and even by act as well as word endeavouring to prevail. (3/ The convenient opportunity which was almost always presented, seeing that Josephs master was mostly absent, and the domestics often out of the way. (4) The danger he might incur by offending one so high in rank as his master's wife. (5) The advantages he might expect to reap from complyi11g with her pleasure. II. THE SPLENDID VICTORY. 1. The manner of Joe!\ph's refusal. (1) Promptly, without the slightest hesitation or appenrance of dallying with the tempting bait. Had Joseph hesitated, be might have.been lost; bad he trifled with the forbidden fruit, he might have plucked and nte. (2) Firmly. There ,vas no sonnd of m1vering or indecision nbout the reply of Joseph. It was not the answer of II man who was only half-hearted in putting away from him a thing which be secretly desired. In Joseph's II no" therewas the clear, full-toned ring of a man who had made up his mind intelligently and finally. (3) Kindly. Joseph behaved towards his mistress with as much tenderness as his moral indignation and disgust at her behaviour would allow ; his considerateness shining out conspicuously in this, that he studiously endeavoured to be as much as possible out of the unhappy womnn's sight, in the hope, doubtless, that her unholy passion might abate. (4) Bravely. Joseph was prepared to run any risk rather than accede to the baRe proposal of his mistress, as was proved by his fleeing from the house without his doublet, when tho impudent woman sought by catching hold of him to secure compliance with her request. 2. The reason of Joseph's refusal. (1) The greatness of the trust reposed in him by his muster. Potiphar hnd committed everything to his (Joseph's) care; and how then could he repay with treachery so e.bominable a confidence so grent? (2) The extent of tho power delegated to him. Potiphar bad kept back nothing from him except his wife ; how then, having privileges so extElnsive, should he covet the one thing forbidden? (3) The sacredness of the relationship existing between his rni8tress nnd Potipht1r. 11 Thou nrt his wife ;'' and by the covenant of marriage thou belongest to him only, and not to me. (4) The heinousness of tho sin of which ho would be guilty. "How can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" III. THE REMARKABLE REWARD. 1. The slander of hismistress. The <lisnppointerl Jtrumpet, thirsting for revenge, resolves upon accomplishing the ruin of tho fair youth of whom the moment before she affected to be enamoured. But indeed nil illicit passion, whether gratified or baulked, has a tendency sooner or later to become transformed into hate. Laying up the garment which Joseph had indiscreetly dropped in his haste, she makes use of itto trump up acharge againstJoseph of having attempted a violation of her chastity. There is no length to which the fierce resentment of a wicked woman will not proceed against those who have incurred her hate. It will commonly go hard with her 1f out of a atre.w her infernal ingenuity cannot G G 2 452 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XXXIX, 7-2,i, manufacture a rope wherewith to strangle her victim. 2. The wratli of his master Potipha.r, as was natural, at first felt inclined to believe his wife and to suppose that Joseph ha? foully betrayed t~e trnst reposed in his honour. In this, of course, he ncted_has~1l.y, ~nd therefore sinfully. Even from the nearest and the dearest reports affecting mJunously the characters of others should not be accepted without investigation. Bt!t that secon? thou~hts prevailed with Potiphar, who, remembering the bad reputation of Egyptian ladies generally, and knowing something possibly of the slenderness of his own wife's virtue, as well as recalling the previous high character of Joseph, began to doubt the truth of what was alleged against his favourite and to think it more likely that his wife lied than that Joseph sinned, has been inferr~d from the circumstance that Joseph was not forthwith remitted to the executioner's block but only committed to the tower. 3. The mercy of his God. As before, Jehovah w:ent ~t~ Joseph to the prison, an_d comf?rted hi~ with gracious thoughts concerning Ins affiwtron, with speedy favour m the sight of his keeper, so that the severity of his confinement was considerably mitigated, and with ultimate promotion to a position of trust within the prison, the charge of all the criminals being committed to his care. And finally, the Lord made him prosperous and successful as before in all hie undertakings.

entries.title: GEN 39:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph in slavery. "But the Lord was with Joseph," &c. Men would have thought, as they looked on the Hebrew slave, that he was God-forsaken. Not so. God blessed him. This was evidenced in the character he developed. The Lord was with him. I. DISCRETION, THE RESULT OF A BENSE OF THE DIVINE PRESENCE, He did not betray trust, or presume on the confidence placed in him, or the kind treatment he received ; nor did he unwisely run into danger. II. DILIGENCE, THE OUTCOME OF A BENSE OF THE DIVINE PRESENCE. Toil kept off much temptation. If a slave by circumstances, he will yet do what he can to benefit his master. He worked rmder apparently hopeless conditions. III. DEVOUTNESS, THE CERTAIN CONSEQUENCE OF A BENSE OF THE DIVINE PRESENCE. Joseph lived as rmder the eye of God. Hence when special temptations came he repelled them in the Divine strength. "How can I do this great wickedness?" &c. Joseph was neither to be persecuted out of hie religion nor enticed from it. Thie is the brightest chapter in Joseph's life. He would not sin against himself, nor against God, 'l'l•ho was with him.-H.

entries.title: GEN 39:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Gor!s presf:Me with his servants. Joseph in slavery, yet the Lord was with him (cf. Rev. i. 9). Twice stated in this chapter. Outward prosperity is no test of God's presence (cf. Rom. v. 3; 2 Car. xii. 9), Often in times of trial God's presence is most clearly felt. When nil dark below, the eye is drawn upwards. The world's good seen to be unprofitable (James iv. 4). There is a sense in which God is always with all. He guides men's actions and course of life, whether they will or not. But while unbelief derives no comfort from this (Zeph. i. 12), the knowledge of his presence gives peace to his people (Isa. xxvi. 3-12). I. CHARACTER OF HIM WITH WHOM GOD WAS THUS PRESENT. A Godward mindliabitually living as in the eight of God, though left alone (cf. Gal. iv. 28). ~'ulfilled what his hand found to do. God's will was his rule of life. He resisted temptation (James i. 12); was faithful in the charge committed to him, tho~gh ~ot of his own choice. Did not look upon the wrong he had suffered as excusmg hun from fidelity. This faithful spirit can spring only from thorough belief in God's love and care (1 John iv. 19). II. THE BLESSING OF GoD'B PRESENCE EXTENDED TO EVERY PAR1' OF HIS LIFE. Not merely in the fact of his being carried to Egypt (cf. Acts xxiii. 11), but in ~very incident God's hand is seen. His management of Potiphar'e affairs was a traming for rule over Egypl His unjust accusation was a step towards his standing bef~re Pharaoh. His experience in prison prepared him to be the deliverer of o. nation (cf. Heb. ii.,18; iv. 15). Thus God's presence is something better and higher tha;.1 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 458 merely a prosperous course. It is the certainty that everything that happens is ordered by infinite wisdom and love-is a step towards the fulness of joy (Deut. viii. 2). This holds good in spiritual experience not less than in temporal. .A Christian is often led through times of darkness. Communion with God seems to be interrupted (Ps. lxv. 3; Rom. vii. 24). Temptation, opposition, difficulty in prayer make the soul sad. Yet the Lord is not absent ; and these are all parts of the training by which he is preparing his servant for the fulness of blessing. III. HE WITH WIIOM THE LORD ABIDES (John xiv. 23; Rev. iii. 20) IS A BLEssmo TO OTHERS. So it was with Joseph. Potiphar, the jailer, Pharaoh, the Egyptian nation, were blessed through him. There is no such thing as keeping a blessing to ourselves; the very attempt destroys it as a blessing. Temporal possessions and powers, used selfishly, become vanity. They pass away, and leave no good, no joy behind, And so with spiritual good, He who has experienced the grace of God must caTe for others, or his own state will suffer (Prov. xi. 24). The more we partake of the mind of Christ, the more we learn that wherever ho leads us, it is that we may be channels of blessing to others.-M.

entries.title: GEN 39:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph asprison warder. "And the keeper of the prison committed to Joseph's hands all the prisoners that were in the prison," &c. Joseph is unjustly treated and thrown into prison. Here he makes the best of circumstances. He gains the confidence of the keeper. The keeper of the State prison is glad to find one like Joseph, to whom he can delegate much toil and responsibility. I. DUTY DISCHARGED IN A SYMPATHETIC SPIRIT. He admits many to prison, and feels for all. He sees that it is but a step from the presence-chamher of Pharaoh to a vile prison. To those who found higher places slippery, nnd those who found the temptations of poverty too strong, he shows his pity. His own bitter separation from friends makes him sympathetic. II. DUTY DISCHARGED IN A CHEERFUL SPIRIT. Generally ho had a smile for the prisoners. They looked for it, and responded to it. The heart can give to the sad that which is better than gold-n cheerful helpfulness. Our gloom can lay extra burdens on others. III. DUTY DISCHARGED IN A COURTEOUS SPIRIT. He would not trample on those alrendy fallen. He inquires even into the cause of the sadness of the prisoners, and interprets for them drenms which bud perplexed them. His own dreams had made him nt one time elate, but they Reem as yet far from being fulfilled. Still this only lends him to be more courteous to those who mny also be doomed to disappointment. The sympnthy, cheerfulness, and courtesy of Joseph mnde him eventually prime minister of Egypt.-H. •

entries.title: GEN 40:1–23
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph in the round house.at Heliopolis. I. THE PRISONERS AND 'J'HEIR ATTENDANT. f. The prisoners. (1) Their rank. They were high officers of state-the chief of the butlers and the •hief of the bakers, i. e. the principal cupbearer and Court purveyor. (2) Their offence. They had sinned against their lord the king of Egypt; in what way it is of no importance to inquire, since "we would have beard nothing about them had their story not been connected with that of Joseph" (Lawson), though the Rabbis allege that they had been detected in 1111 attempt at poisoning their master. (3) Their pur.ishment. "The king'1:1 wrath is !lll the roaring of a lion," and" as mesRengers of death" (Prov. xix. 12; xvi. 14); and the two offenders were immediately arrested and thrown into prison, committed to the keeping of the captain of the round house, where Joseph was bound. (4) Their privilege. Their punishment was tempered with clemency. In consideration of cu. Xl,. 1-23.J THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 457 their official rank, the governor of the tower appointed Joseph to wait upon them and act 01 their servant. 2. Their attendant. In this new capacity Joseph behaved himself wisely and with discretion. With regard to his illustrious companions in misfortune, he-(1) Served them faithfully. "Joseph had been unjustly enslaved, unjustly imprisoned, unjustly detained in his prison, and yet he declined not the work enjoined by hie master" (Lawson). Joseph appears to have always acted on the principle commended by the royal preacher (Eccles. ix. 10), and on that recommended by Christ (Luke xiv. 11). "Joseph was o. better man than the men whom he served. He was sprung from noble ancestors, and knew that he would one day be exalted above them; but at this time he cheerfully performed to them every service in his power" (Lawson). (2) Sympathised with them sincerely. Though bearing hie own misfortunes with unmunnuring resignation and manly fortitude, because sustained by God's grace and the possession of truly religious principles, the amiability of Joseph'e nature led him to commiserate his fellow-prisoners who had no such inward supports and consolations as were enjoyed by him. In particular on one occasion mentioned in the text he was so struck with their dejected countenances that he feelingly inquired the cause of their sadness. (3) Directed them wisely. Leaming that they were troubled on account of dreams which they had dreamt overnight, and of which they could not find the explanation, he piously exhorted them to look to God for the desired interpretations. II. TrIE DREAMS AND THEIR INTERPRETATIONS. 1. The dreams-(!) Agreed in tlie time when they occurred, happening on the same night; in the impressions they produced, filling the hearts of both dreamers with forebodings; in the person by whom they were explained, Joseph giving equally the key to both; and in the interval required for their fulfilment, only three days being allowed for the accomplishment of each. (2) Differed in tl1e imagery of which they were composed-that of the butler consisting of a tableaux in which himself and his royal master appeared beneath the shadow of a blooming vine, Pharaoh sitting on his throne, and himsel£ pressing the ripe clusters into Pharaoh's cup and setting it on Pharaoh's hand ; and that of the baker representing himself also engaged in the performlLnce of hiH officinl duties, bearing into Pharaoh's presence three wicker baskets of pastries and confections, out of the uppermost of which the birds came to ent ;-in the character of the events which they foreshadowed-the butler's dream prognosticating speedy restoration to his butlership, and the baker's dream rno!lt ominously pointing to early execution. 2. Their interpretations. These were-(1) Revealed by God. Joseph did not claim to be able of himself to interpret the significance of either of the dreams, but explicitly affirmed thnt to do so was exclusively the prerogative of Elohim. (2) Declared by Joseph. Thus Joseph was authenticated as a prophet of the Lord in that hellthen land. (3) Fulfilled by Pharaoh. Pharaoh wns no doubt unconscious that he wns accomplishing a Divine prediction. So Goel is able to accord to men the completest liberty of action, and yet realise his own sovereign purpose. Exactly as Joseph had interpreted, both as to time and as to results, the dreams came true. III. TJIE INTERPRETER AND BIS REWAl!D, ]. T!te interpreter's request. Joseph desired in return for his services to the butlor tlrnt II word should ho spoken for him to the king by that officer when restored to his occupation, in tho hopo that it might lead to his release from confinement. For this comluct Joseph has been blamed by some censorious critics; but (1) his request was natural. '!'hough required lo encluro the crosses laid on him by Divine providence with meekness and resignation, ho wa3 under no obligation to stay a moment longer in prison than he could justly help, but was rather bound to use all legitimate means to insure his deliverance. The11, (2) his request was moderate. He did not ask much at the butler's hand in return for his own great service, only that hi6 name should ho mentioned to Pharo.oh. Joseph was not exacting in his demands. Again, (3) his request was touching. As ho tells the butler, in the hope of moving him to pity, he was a stranger in a strange land, who had been forcibly abducted, though he does not say by whom. What a token of the kindly charity and truly forgivir.g spirit cherished by Joseph towards his brethren I And finally, (4) his request was just. He had done nothing to deserve imprisonment in that or ony other dungeon. 2. Tlie interpreter's reward. "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him,' This must have been (1) a pni11ful 458 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XL, 1-23. experience to Joseph, probablyas cruel and unkind a blow as any he had yet reoeived as certainly it wns (2) a monstrous iniquity on the part of the butler, indicating ~ callous, ungrateful, 11nd truly base disposition, though unfortunately it is (3) a frequent occurrence in human life. • . Learn-I. That God's saints are sometimes thrown lby Divine providence into companionship with the worst of men. 2. That the exceilent of the earth are often foun? fillin~ the _very_ humblest situations. 3. T_hat God has many different methodsof d1scovenng his mmd to men. 4. That God 1s able to fulfil his own predictions. 5. That wicked men sometimes meet their deserts in this life. 6. That God's people should sympathise with and succour their fellow-men. 7. That they who do good to others should hope for nothing again.

entries.title: GEN 40:8
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The interpreter of God's message. We cannot but not_ice the importance often assigned in the Bible to dreams, as channels of revelation from God. The dreams of Jacob and of Pharaoh, and passages such as Deut. xiii. 1 and Joel ii. 28, show this. It may be that in the absence of the written word, which in ite completeness is our heritage, God's message was. thus given to them in portions.. Applying this thought to the circumstances of the text, we see men who had received a message from God which they believed was of importance ; but they ccmld not understand it, and they are sad because there is no interpreter, I. THE DEEP IMPORTANCE OF Gon's MESSAGE. How many questions does life present ! What and where are we? Whither going? What lies beyond the present? I see that all things decay; yet on all sides life from death. Is there such revivo.l for me? Can the active, thinking spirit be as though it _had never be~n-passed from existence ere the frail body began to decay? And 1f there be a hfe beyond the present, what ia its nature? and w~at the preparation for it?_ Ve.inly does human wisdom try to answer these quest10ns. He who made all thmgs alone. can explain his works (Ps. xciv. 9-12), and the Bible is his answer to our qu~st1ons, wherein he tells us what we are, for what created, and how to fulfil the obJect of our being (Ps. cxix. 105). II. But WE NEED AN INTERPRETER. It may be asked, Why? The Bible is open. Its words are such as any one can understand. This is true, us fur ~ regards fe.cts, 'l.lld precepts, and doctrines. There is a knowledge of the wo•'l which the natural OH, XL. 1-23.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 459 man can attain to ; but the Holy SJlirit alone can so open it as to make it " the power of God." It is one thing to know the doctrines of sin and of salvation, and quite another to know ourselves ns sinners, and Christ as the Saviour. The one puffs up with pride of knowledge, the other leads to the one Foundation. Tl,ere is no more dangerous snare than of ignoring this work of the Holy Spirit. Too often men do not believe their need of it, and do not believe in his help. And thus the Bible is found dull, and its teaching departed from in daily life. III. How To GET THE INTERPRETER'S HELP. "Tell me." Think of our Lord watching hie disciples in the boat. So he watches over thee, ready to help. Hast thou found it so? Hae the light of God's love entered thy heart? It is the special work of the Holy Spirit to guide into all truth (John xvi. 13); not in solving mysteries and hard questions, but in revealing Christ to the heart. Have you sought this; sought with expectation the full gift; sought to know Christ (Phil. iii. 10), and the transforming power of belief in his love? Will you seek ? There lies the difficulty-the want of earnestness. Men seem afraid of being earnest. But it is the earnest (Matt. xi. 12, /3,aarai) who enter the kingdom of hea,en,-M. remember Joseph, but forgat him." "I do remember my faults this day." Good men have sometimes had to bear painful imprisonments. Think of Bunyan and Baxter shivering behind the bars of a narrow cell, where light and air were almost excluded, and where disease and death held sway. How much brightness, however, has broken at times from behind piison bars I We might not have had the' Pilgrim's Progress,' unless Bunyan had been incarcerated on the banks of the Ouse. Nor might the patience e.nd kindness of Joseph's disposition have shcne out so brilliantly but for his prison life. In a work entitled 'Five Years' Penal Servitude' a most vivid description is given of how the criminals of the clever and cultured class have to mingle and work with those of ignorant and most sensual type. Defaulting cashiers have to undergo the same trea.tment a.s cowardly garotters a.ml desperate burglars. Breaking the law brings e.ny under its rigorous clutches, anrl levels all distinctions of class or education. Thus Joseph, a. Hebrew slave, although not o. criminal, would be despised by the chief butler of Pharaoh, but the bLttler had to associate with him. Indeed the former became his superior in prison, nncl was in n position to render to a State official certain kindness. l. THE FORGETFUL INGRATE, This man wa.s a courtier, a permitted adviser of the Pha.moh of Egypt, but he is sent to the common prison. Joseph gives him much cheer, attention, and kindness. He seeks in every way to relieve the monotony of prison life, nnd becomes a. prophet and religious helper. He sees the butler one da.y sa.d of countenance, and lenrns the reason. Readily he, by Divine help, interpreted the perplexing dream, His words are verified. The chief butler was doubtless profuse in his thanks and promises, but we see how he kept them. Perhaps the forgetfulness was convenient. Ho did not wish, after his restoration, to remind his monarch-even by making a request-of his having been formerly in disfavour. He possibly never intended to ma.ke any effort, unless it should be a gain to himself. He is a very different ma.n in prison and out. This is tho way of men in life. Favours slip from the memory like floods from n smoothly-worn rock. We might here possibly find out certa.in things in our own conduct which would indicate a similar forgetfulness of favours. For example, Christ cnme as the good Jos~ph to share our captive state. Think of whe.t love he showed in bearing- so much euffeiing for us. Do not put aside the thought of it ns not being definitely for you. It was for ea.eh one, as if there were none other for whom to suffer. Some have not believed, have not come out from prison, but have preferred the darkness to light, have thought that the atonement was all unnecessary. They c,innot understand how evil is their state until brought out of it. A beg·gar would not be troubled about his patches o.nd rags in the common lodging-house; but let him be taken into a room of decently-arro.yed people, ancl he then feels the difference, and shudders a.t his degraded appenrance. When once brought into Christ's light we see from what we hove been saved, and should be grateful to him. Some have been brought into union with him, nnd afterwards have declined from his we.y. Dangerous state. 460 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. l.LI. 1-45. We should blame others who were ungrateful; what if we have been I The longer action is postponed, the deeper the ingratitude, and the less likelihood is there that the favour will be felt. The longer postponed, the harder to acknowledge. Thus the butler may have hesitated to speak of Joseph because he would have to reveal his own ingratitude. Possibly he hoped Joseph was dead. Not so; Joseph lives. Forgotten by man, he is not forgotten by God. God will yet bring the forgetful one and his benefactor face to face. II. AROUSED MEMORIES. Wonderful is that faculty of the mind whereby we can imagine ourselves to exist in the past. Some have weak memories, others strong, Some have memories for places and thoughts, others for dates, figures, and words. 'Whether memory be strong or weak, the power of association is such that at times facts Jong past will be brought back most vividly. Revisiting plnces of interest, traversing certain countries, will bring to memory past friendships, and perhaps even subjects of conversation formerly held there. A house in which one has been born or trained becomes a complete history in time. Certain seasons arouse memories of the past, as birthdays, wedding days, Christmas time, or Easter. Certain circumstances also arouse memory. Pharaoh's perplexity concerning his dream forcibly reminded the butler of bis morning of sadness in the prison. "I do remember," &c. The butler implied that he repented of his sins and of his forgetfulness. He may not have been very sincere, but as a courtier he introduces a subject in that way. Let us remember our faults, our inconsistencies as Christians, our hesitation to confess Christ, our excusing ourselves on the ground of the doings of others. Let us be plain with ourselves. Let us not see the motes in the eyes of others, and forget the beams in our own. Let us remember them that we may be humbled, may gain experience of bow to e.void them in the future, may gain strength to resist, may gain pardon for past faults, and learn thereby more of the infinite forbearance and love of God, who is so willing to blot out our transgressions, and even the memory of our sins.-H.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And it came to pass at the end of two full years (literally, two years of days, i. e. two complete years from the commencement of Joseph's incarceration, or more probably o.fter the butler's liberation), that Pho.re.oh-on the import of the term vide eh. xii. 15. Under what particular monarch Joseph came to Egypt is a question of much perplexity, and has been variously resolved by modern Egyptologers in favour of-1. Osirtasen I., the founder of the twelfth dynasty, a prosperous and successful sovereign, whose name appears on a granite obelisk at Heliopolis (Wilkinson, '.Ancient Egyptians,' i. 30, ed. 1878). 2. Assa, or Assis, the fifth king of the fifteenth dynasty of Shepherd kings (Stuart Poole in Smith's 'Bible Diet.,' art. Egypt). 3. Apophis, a Shepherd kingofthe fifteenth dynasty, whom all the Greek authorities agree in mentioning as the patron of Joseph (Osburn, 'Monument.al History,' vol. ii eh. 2; Thornley Smith, 'Joseph and bis Times,' p. 42). 4. Thotbrnes III., a monarch of the eighteenth dynasty (Stanley Leatbes in Kitto's 'Cyclopecha,' p. 744). 5. Rameses III., the king of Memphis, a ruler belon~g to the twentieth dynasty (Bonomi in The Imperial Bible Diet.,' p. 488; Sharpe's 'History of Egypt, vol. i. p. 35). It may assist the student to arrive at a decision with respect to these contending aspirants for the throne of Pharaoh in the time of Joseph to know that Canon Cook (' Speaker's Commentary,' vol. i. p. 451), after an elaborate and careful as well as scholarly review of the entire question, re• gards it as at least "a very probable conjecture" that the Phare.oh of Joseph was Amenemhe. III., "whois represented on thelately• discovered table of Abydos as the last great king of all Egypt in the ancient empire (tho last of the twelfth dynasty), and as such receiving divine honours from his descendant Rameses"-dreamed. "For the third time are dreams employed as the agencies of Jo. seph's history: they first foreshadow his illustrious future ; they then manifest that the Spirit of God had not abandoned him even in the abject condition of o. slave and a prisoner; and lastly they are made the immediate forerunners of his greatness" (Kalisch). And, behold, he stood by the rivor-i. e.. upon the banks of the Nile, the term il-tl (an Egyptian word signifyin~ great river or canal, in the Memphitic dialect yaro, in the Sahidic yero) being used almost exclusively in Scripture for the Nile (Exod. i. 22 ; ii. 8; vii. 15; Gesenius, 'Lex.,' p. 826). This OH. XLI. 1-45.) THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 461 \vas the common name for the Nile a.mong the E~tia.ns, the sacred being HO!pi (Ca.non Cook m 'Speaker's Commentary,' p. 485).

entries.title: GEN 41:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And, behold, there ea.me up out of the river seven well-favoured kine and fa.t- 11.eehed. According to Pluta.rch and Clement of Alexandria., the heifer wa.s regarded by the ancient Egyptians as e. symbol of the earth, agriculture, and the nourishment derived therefrom. It was therefore natural that the succession of seven prosperous years should berepresented byseven thriving cows. That they appeared ascending from the river is explained by the circumstance that the Nile by its annual inundations is the ea.use of Egypt's fertility (cf. Hiivemick, •Introd.,' § 21). A hymn to the Nile, composed by Euna. (according to the generality of Egyptologers a contemporary of Moses), and tnmslatcd from a. papyrus in the British Museum by Canon Cook (who ascribes to it an earlier date than the nineteenth dynasty), describes the Nile as "overflowing the gardens created by Ra., ... giving life to all animals, ... watering the land without ceasing ... Lover of food, bestower of corn . . . Bringer of food I Great Lord of provisions ! Cree.tor of all good things !'' (vide •Records of the Pe.st,' vol. iv. pp. 107, 108). And they fed in a. mea.dow-lnl$f, iv r,;"Ax.11 (LXX.),literally, in the Nile or reed grass. The word ~nis appears to be an Egyptian tenn descriptive of any herbage growing in a. stream. It occurs only here and in ver. 18, and Job viii. 11.

entries.title: GEN 41:3
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And, behold, seven other kine came up after them out of the river, illfavoured and lea.n-11.eshed. The second seven cows, "evil to look upon,'' i. c. bad in appenrance, and "thin (beaten small, dakotli, from dakak, to crush or beatsmall) of flesh,'' also proceeded from the rh·er, since a failure in the periodico.l overflow of the Nile we.s the usulll cause of scarcity nnd famine in Egypt. And stood by the other kine upon the brink of the river. The use of the term lip, n~r;,. for brink, common enough in Hebrew (eh. xxil. 17: E.x:od. xiv. 30: 1 Kings v. 9), occurs also in a papyrus of the nineteenth dynasty, "I sat down by the lip of the river,'' which appears to suggest the impression tho.t the verse in the text was written hy one who was equally fe.milio.r with both languages (Canon Cook in •Speaker's Com• mentary,' p. 485).

entries.title: GEN 41:4

entries.content: -And the ill-favoured and lean- 11.eshed kine did eat up the seven wellfavoured and fat kine-without there being any effect to show that they had ea.ten them (ver. 21). So (literally, and) Phare.oh a.woke.

entries.title: GEN 41:5
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And he slept and dreamed the seoond time (that same night) : and, behold, seven ears of oorn oa.me up upon one stalk, rank (i. e. fat) a.11cl good. Thill clearly pointed to the corn of the Nile valley, the truicumcompositum, which bears seven ears upon one stalk. The assertion of Herodotus, t~at the Egyptians counted it a disgrace to live on wheat and barley (ii. 36), Wilkiuson regards as incorrect, since "both wheat and barley are noticed in Lower Egypt long before Her?d~tus' time (Exod. ix. 31, 32), and the pamtmgs of the Thebaid prove that they were grown extensively in that part of !he country ; they were a'!long the offerings m the temples ; and the kmg, at his coronation, cutting some ears of wheat, afterwards offered to the gods as the staple production of Egypt, shows how great a value was set on a grain which Herodotus would lead us to suppose was held in abhorrenco" (Rawlinson's •Herodotus,' vol. ii. p. 49).

entries.title: GEN 41:6
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them-literally, hum!, up of the eait, C'7i? being put poetically for the fuller C'ii? IJ-17. It has been urged that this displays a gross ignorance of the nature of the climate in Egypt (Bohlen), since a wind directly east is rare in Egypt, and when it docs occur ill not injurious to vegetation ; but, on the other hand, it is open to reply (1) that direct east winds may be rare in Egypt, but so are dearth and famine such as thnt described in the narrative equally exceptional (Kalisch); (2) that the Hebrews ho.ving only nnmes to describe the four principal winds, the kaclim might comprise any wind blowing from on easterly direction (Hengstenberg) ; and (3) that the south-cast wind, "blowingin the months of Ilforch and April, is one of the most injurious winrls, and of longest continuance" (Ho.vcrnic~. Hengstenberg quotes Ukert as saying, "As long as the south-enst wind continues, doors nnd windows nre closed ; but. the fine dust penetmtes everywhere; everything dries up; wooden vessels warp nnd crack. The ther, mometer rises suddenly from 16° 20', up to 30° 36°, and even 38°, Rcaumur. This wind works destrnction upon everything. The grass withers so that it entirely perishes if this wind blows Ion~" (' Egypt aml tho Books of Moses,' p. l0J.

entries.title: GEN 41:9–13
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Then spake the chief butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults this day :-literally, my faults I (sc. am) remembering to-day; but whether he understood by his faults his ingratitude to Joseph or his offence against Pharaoh commentators are not agreed, though the latter seems the more probable-Pharaoh waa wroth with his servants,-literally, broke out against them (vide eh. xl. 2)-and put me in ward in the captain of the guard's house -literally, put me in custody of the lwuse ' of the captain of the slaughterers (cf. eh. xl. 3)-both me and the chief baker: and we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he· we dreamed each man according to the interpretation of bia dream (vide eh. xl. 5). And there was there with ua a young man, an B'ebre~, servant .~o the captain of the guard (vi.de eh. xxxvn. 36); and we told him (sc. our dreams), and he interpreted to us our dreams ("llide eh. xl. 12, 13, 18, 19); to each man accor_ding to bis dream he did interpret. And 1t came to paaa, as he interpreted to us, so it was i me he (not Pharaoh, but Joseph) resto1;ed unto mine office, and him he hanged {vide eh. xl. 21, 22).

entries.title: GEN 41:14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Then Pharaoh aent and oalled .Joseph, a.nd theybrought him hastily (literall,:v1 caused him to run) out of the dungeon (vuu eh. xl. 16): and he shaved himself,- this was exactlyin accordance with Egyptian custom (Herod. ii. 36). Wilkinson statos that "the custom of shaving the head o.s well as beard wns not confined to the priests in Egypt, but WM general amongall classes " (Rawlinson's 'Herodotus,' vol. ii. p. 49 ; cf. •Ancient Egyptians,' vol. ii. pp. 330-332, ed. 1878). That the verb is not more exactly defined by a term following, such as the head (Numb. vi. 9), the beard (2 Sam. x. 4), but stands alone (the only instance of its intransitive use), appears to suggest that the writer was familiar with the ctractica of shaving (vide Havernick, 'Intro .,' § 21)- and che.nged hie raiment,-as required by the customs of Egypt ("llide Hengstenberg's ' Egypt,' p. 30 ; cf. eh. xxxv. ~)-and came (or went) in unto Pharaoh.

Pharaoh) informs Joseph that the professional interpreters a.ttached to the Court (the chartummim, or masters of the occult sciences) could give him no idea. of its meaning. Vor. 25.-And Joseph said unto Pharaoh (tho inability of the magicians to read the dream of Pharaoh was the best proof that Joseph spoke from inspiration), The drell.lll of Pharaoh is one (i. e. the two dreams have the same significance) : God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do (literally, what the. Elohim is doing, i. e. is about to do he causeth to be seen by PharMh).

entries.title: GEN 41:26–32
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Proceeding with the interpretation of the dream, Joseph explains to Pharaoh that the seven good kine and the seven full ears point to a succession of seven yeara of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt which were already coming (ver. 29), after which there should a1ise seven years of famine, in which all the plenty should be forgotten in the land, and the famine should consume, or make an end of, the land (ver. 30), and the plenty should not be known i.n the land by reason of (literally, from the face of, used of the efficient cause of anything, hence on account of) that famine following- literally, the famine, that one,after(things have happened) so,· adding(ver. 32), And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice (literally, and as for the dm.ibling of the dream to PharMh twice); it is because the thing is established by God,-literally, the word (or thing spoken of) is firmly fixed, i. e. certainly decreed, by the Elohim- and God will shortly bring it to pass-literally, and hastening (is) the Elohim to do it. The name is very common on Egyptian monuments (Hengstenberg's 'Egypt and the Books of Moses,' p. 32)~prieet-or prince (Onkelo~), as in 2 Sam. viii. 1B, where the word r::,::i, as explained by 1 Chron. xviii 17, means a principal minister of State, though the probability is that Poti-pherah belonged to the priestly caste in Egyptof On- or Heliopolis, •HX10111roX,c (LXX.) 1 the name on the monuments being ta-Ra or pa-Ra, house of the sun. "The site of Heliopolis is still marked by the massive walls that surround it, and by a granite obelisk bearing the name of Osirtasen I., of the twelfth dynasty-, dating about 3900 years ai:;o" (Wilkinson in Rawlinson's ' Herod., ii. p. 8). The priests attached to the temple of tho sun at Heliopolis enjoyed the reputation of being the most intelligent and cultured historians in Egypt (Herod., ii. 3). That a priest's daughter should have married with a foreign she,Pherd may have been distasteful to the preJudices of an intolerant priesthood (Bohlen), but in the case ofAsenathand Joseph itwas recommended by sundry powerful considerations. 1. Though a foreign shepherd, Joseph was a descendant of Abraham, whom a former Pharaoh had recognised and honoured as a prince, and ' The Story of Saneha,' a hieratic papyrus belonging to the twelfth dynasty, shows that Eastern foreigners might even bocome sons• in-law to the most powerful potontates under the ancient empire (vide lforords of the Past,' vol. vi pp. 135-150). 2. Though & foreign shepherd, Joseph was at this time graud vizier of the realm, with absolute control of the lives nm! fortunes of its people (vide ver. 44). 3. Though a foreign shepherd, he was obviously afavourite ofPharaoh, who, besides beingmonarch of the ree.lm, was the recognised head of the priestly caste, over whom, therefore, he exercised more than a merely external authority. 4. Though a foreigv OH, XLI. 1-45,] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 4G6 shepherd, he was circnmciseu, which, if this rite was already observed in Egypt, and did not originate with Joseph, would certainly not prove a bar to the contemplated alliance (vide Canon Cook in 'Speaker's Commentary,' vol. i. p. 480 ; Kurst, 'Hist. of Old Covenant,'§ 88; Hengstenberg, 'Egypt and the Books of Moses,' pp. 32-35). As to the probability of Joseph consenting to become son-in-law to a heathen priest, it may suffice to remember that though marriage with idolaters was expressly forbidden by patriarchal commandment (eh. xxiv. 3; xx:viii. 1), and afterwards by Mosaic statute (eh. xxxiv. 16 ; Deut. vii. 3), it was sometimes contracted for what seemed a perfectly adequate reason, viz., the furtherance of the Divme purposes concerning Israel, and apparently too with the Divine sanction (cf. the cases of Moses, Exod. ii. 21, and Esther, eh. ii. le); that Joseph may have deemed the religion of Egypt, especially in its early symbolical forms, as perfectly compatible with a pure monotheistic worship, or, if he judged it idolatrous, he may both have secured for himself complete toleration 1md have felt himself strong enough to resist its seductions ; that Asenath may have adopted her husband's faith,though on this, ofcourse, nothing can be affirmed ; and lastly, that the narrator of this history pronounces no judgment on the moral quality of Joseph's conduct in consenting to this alliance, which, though overruled for $ood, may have been, considered in itself, a sm.
