entries.title: GEN 47:1–10
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob and his sons before Pliaraoh. I. JosEPn's BRETHRE~ BEFORE PHARAOH (vers. 1-6). 1. Their arrival announced (ver. 1). "My father and brethren are come out of the land of Canaan, and bahold they are in the land of Goshen." 2. Their persons presented (ver. 2). "He took some of his brethren, even five men, and presented them to Pharaoh." The import of this selection of five is explained in the exposition. 3. Their occupations declared (ver. 3). In answer to the king's interrogation they replied that they were shepherds. They had no dosire to deceive, although they had learnt that persons of their trades were not commonly regarded with favour, Joseph indeed had convinced them that in this instance honesty would be the best policy ; but even had it been precisely the reverse there is no reason to suppose they would have attempted any sort of prevarication. 4. Their purpose eXJ>lained (ver. 4). It was not their intention to settle permanently in Egypt, but only to find in it a temporary shelter during the years of famine. But while man proposes God disposes. 5. Their wi,sh. stated (ver. 4). "Now, therefore, let thy servants dwell in Goshen." Though Joseph might have had sufficient power to accord them this favour, it was only courteous to ask it from Pharaoh. "Honour to whom honour is due," is the dictate of right feeling as well as of true religion, and men seldom find themselves the losers by practising politeness. 6. Their request granted (ver. 6). Pharaoh at once responJe,1-" The land of Egypt is before thee ; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwall; in the land of Goshen let them dwell." Nay, Pharaoh even exceeded their desires or expectations. 7. Their promotion indicated (ver. 6). "If thou knowest any men of activity among them, make them rulers over my cattle." "Seest thou a man diligent in business? ho shall stand before kings I" II. JosEPH's FATrrEn BEFORE PHARAOH (vere. 7-11). 1. The old man's blessing. "And Jacob blessed Pharaoh." Thie was (1) a vnlnuble gift. Once before he had sent a present to one whom he regarded as of vice-regal dignity; but now, when standing in the royal presence, he does not think of material offerings, but presents what must ever be beyond rubies, the intercession of n snintly heart with God on a. fellow-creature's behalf. I£ the effectual fervent prayer uf a righteous man availeth much, the simple Lenediction of an aged saint cannot profit little. (2) Earnestly given. This was shown by the promptitude with ,which it was bestowed. Immediately the venerable patriarch is ushered into the royal presence he Lreake forth into the language of benediction, as if the inward emotion had just been trembling on the heart's lip and ready at the first agitution to overflow. And he for whom he prays w11s a benefactor indeed, but a. monarch and II heathen; and so 111'8 Christ's people taught to pray for nil men, £or kings and such as 11re in authority, for unbelieving us well as believing, and not £or friends and benefactors solely, but likewise for enemies and persecutors. (3) Solemnly confirmed. Spoken on the first entrance to the regal mansion, it was tremblingly re-uttered on rleparture. Never before had such II prayer been heard within 11n Egyptian palace. Yet the halls of princes no more than the hovels of peasants are unsuitable for intercessions nnd supplications. J~verywhere and always should be the saint's motto in regard to prayer. 2. The old man's history. Gazing with tender interest on the venerable form of the patriarch as, leiming on the arm of hie son, he softly steps 11cross the threshold of the magnificent reception hall, the royal Pharaoh, probably struck with his aged and feeble appearance, kindly inquires, "How many are the days of the years of thy life?" to which Jacob with equal circumlocution, with perhaps a little of the garrulousness that is so natural and becoming in the old, but also with a true touch of pathos, replies, "The days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years; few and evil have the days of the years of my life been, and have not attained unto the days of the years of the lives of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage," Uis cJ;istence on the earth be characterises as having been-(1) A filO THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [cH. XLVIJ. 1-10. perpetual pilgrimage, a constant wandering, a continual sojourning, which in his case it had really been - from Beersheba to Padan-aram from Pndan-nrarn to Canaan, from one location in the land of promise to ano ther, and finally from Canaan to Egypt-but which is no less true of all men's lives• "here we have no continuing city.". (2) A_ short pi_lgrimag·e. Adding them up o:1e by ono, the days of the years of his p1lgnmage might seem to be many; but in the retrospect they appeared what they really were, few and soon numbered; as life which to the ;young i? prospect l?oks long, to the old in _retrospect is ever short. ' How amazing 1s the difference winch a change of standpoint produces in the view which the mind takes of man's exi_ste_nce ~n the earth, as of_ other things I and how important that we should bear this m mind when numbering our days I (3) A sad pilgrimnge. Not only had the days of Jacob's years been few, but they had o.lso been evil, filled wit.h trouble, sorrow, and vexation, more even than that of any of his predecessors. It was one more testimony to the fact that not only is man born unto trouble as the sparks fly upward, but that it is only through much tribulation that a child of God con enter the kingdom. Learn-I. That prudence becomes a counsellor. This was strikingly exemplified in Joseph's conduct in presenting his brethren before Pharaoh. 2. That honesty advances a suppliant. In the long run Joseph's brethren were better served by their perfect integrity and straightforwardness in Pharaoh's presence than they would have been b) .rosorting to duplicity and equivocation. 3. That piety adorns the old. How beautiful does the character of Jacob, the aged wanderer, appear as it stands before us in Pharaoh's palace, in the westering sunlight of his earthly pilgrimage I "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness."

entries.title: GEN 47:9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The ducipline of life. Few and evil, yet 130 years; and how many blesRings temporal and spiritual ha<l been received during their course. We need not 1mppose him untbankful. But blessings do not of themselves make a man happy. Some worm may be at the root. And in Jacob'a case early faults cast a shadow over his whole lifo. The remembrance of early deceit, his natural shrinking from danger, bis family cares, his mourning for Rachel (eh. xlviii. 7) and for Joseph. gnve a tinge OB. XLVII 11-27.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. of melancholy not entirely to be taken away even by receiving hie son as it were from the dead. The retrospect of hie life seemed that of a EJUffering man. I. ABIDING BORROW JS THE FRUIT OF EARLY FAULTS, THOUGH REPENTED OF (1 Cor. xv. 9). It does not necessarily imply separation from God, or doubt of personal salvation. I£ 11 a godly sorrow," it works repentance, i. e. a more complete turning to God. But just as early neglect of the laws affecting bodily health produces a lasting effect, however carefully these laws may be attended to in after years, so neglect of God's moral and spiritual laws produces sorrow, varying in kind, antl in the channel by which it comes, but bearing witness to the truth of God's uncea11ing watchfulness. II. THE DISCIPLINE OF LIFE 18 NOT IN ANGER, BUT FOR OUR PURIFICATION. Thus suffering may be a blessing. But for sorrow Jacob might have sunk into taking his ease. His besetting danger was worldly carefulness (eh. xxx. 41). So sorrow, from outward circumstances or from inward reflection, often brings us nearer God. It teaches the vanity of eartl:: that we may realise the blessedness of the inheritance above ; that frail and weary we may cling more closely to the promises of the rest which remaineth (Heh. iv. 9). III. THIS LIFE IS INTENDED TO BE APILGRIMAGE, NOT A REST. Its blessedness consists not in present enjoyment, but in preparation £or the rest to come (Luke xii. 20, 21). We are reminded that there is a goal to be reached, a prize to be won (1 Uor. ix. 24 ; 1 Pet. i. 3-9), and that the time is short, that we may put forth all our efforts (Eccles. ix. 10) to overcome besetting faults and snares of worldliness. A pilgrim (Heh. xi. 14) is seeking a country not yet reached. The remembrance of this keeps the life Godward. True faith will work patience and activity; true hope will work cheerfulness under hindrances, and, if need be, under sufferings. And the love of Christ (John xiv. 2, 3), and the consciousness that we ,ire his, will constrain us "to walk even as he walked." For what are you striving? to lade yourself with thick clay ? To gain honour, renown, admiration, bodily enjoyment? or as a pilgrim (Num. x. 29) walking in Christ's way, and doing Christ's work ?-M.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And J'oseph placed his father and his brethren (i. e. gave them a settle- :nent, the import of which the next clause explains), and gav!I them a possession (i. e. allowed them to acquire property) in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses,-either that district of Goshen in which Jacob o.nd his family first settled (Michaelis, Rosenmtille1·), or, what seems more probable, the land of Goshen itself (LXX., Keil, Hengstenberg, Knlisch, et alii), being so named proleptically from the town Rameses, which was subsequently built (Exod. i. 11), or, if the town existed in the time of Joseph, and wns only afterwards fortified by the lsro.elites, deriving its designation from the name of its chief city-as -Pharaoh had commanded.

entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And there was no bread in all the land ; for the famine was very sore (literally, heavy), so that the land of Egypt and all the land ofCanaan fainted (literally, was exhausted, had become languid and spiritless) by reason of the famine. entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And .Joseph bought all the land of Egyptfer Pharaoh; for the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them: so (literally, and) tbe land became Pharaoh's. From this it may be concluded that originally Pharaoh had no legal claim to the eoil, but that the people had a valid title to its absolute possession, each man being regarded as the legitimate proprietor of the portion on which he had expended the labour of cultivation.

entries.title: GEN 47:21
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And as for the people, he removed them-not enslaved them, converted them into serfs aud bondmen to Pharaoh (LXX.,Vulgate), butsimplytransferred them, caused them to passover-to cities-not from cities to cities, as if changing their populations (Onkelos, Rosenmiiller, Knlisch), but either from the country districts to the towns (Targums Jonathan and Jerusalem, Lange, Schumann, Gerlach, Murphy), or nccording to the cities, i. e. in which the grain had been previously collected (Keil)-from one end of the borders of Egypt even to the otherend thereof. Not that the peoplewere transported from one side of the country to the other as a high stroke of policy to complete their subjugation (Jarchi, Grotius, Rosenmilller, Kalisch, and others), but that throughout the fand they were moved into the nearest cities, as a considerate and even merciful arrangement for the more efficiently supplying them with food (Calvin, Keil, Lange, Wordsworth, Speaker's Commentary).

entries.title: GEN 47:22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -0nly the land of the priests (so the LXX., Vulgate, and Chaldee render cohen, which, however, sometimes signifies a. prince) bought he not; for the priests had a portion-not of land (Lange, Kalisch), but of food (Keil, Murphy)-assigned them ot Pharaoh (not of Joseph, who must not, therefore, be charged with the sin of extending a State allowance to au idolatrous priesthood), and did eat their portion which Pho.re.oh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands,-that is, in consequence of the State aliment which they enjoyed (during the period of the famine) they did not require to alienate their lands; Vern. 23, 24.-Then Joseph so.id unto the people, Behold, I have bought you this day and your land for Pharaoh : lo, here is seed for you, and ye shall sow the land. This proves the time to have been the last year of the famine; and since the people obtained seed from the viceroy, it is reasonable to suppose that they would also have their cattle restored to them to enable them to till the ground. And it shall come to pe.ss in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part Ullto Pharaoh, and four parts she.11 be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them ofyour households, and for food for your little ones. 'l'his verse is a sufficient refutation of the oft-preferred charge that Joseph had despoiled the Egyptians of their liberties, and converted a, free people into a horde of abject slaves. Slave-ownersare not usually content with a tax of only twenty per cent. on the gross revenues of their estates. Nor does it seem reasonable to allege that this wa~ an exorbitant demand on the part eitherofJoseph orofPharaoh. Ifin the seven years of plenty the people could alford to part with a fifth part of their produce, might not an improved system of agriculture enable them, under the new r~gulations, to pay as much as that in the shape of rent, and with quite as much case I At all events the people themselves did not consider that they were being subjected to any harsh or unjnst exaction.

entries.title: GEN 47:25
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And they said, Thou hast saved our lives (literally, thou hMt kept us alive): let us find grace in the sight of my lord (i. e. let us have the land on these favourable terms), and we will be Phe.re.oh's servants. " That a sort of feudal service is here intended-the service of free labourers, not bondmen-we may learn from the relationship of tha Israelites to God, which was formed after the plan of this Egyptian model" (Gerlach). -

entries.title: GEN 47:26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And J'oseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day (i. e. the day of the narrator), that Phare.oh should have the fifth part ; except the land of the priests only, which Deco.me not Pharaoh's. The account here given of the land tenure in Egypt, viz., (1) that after the time of Joseph the kingsof Egypt became lords paramount of the soil, (2) that the only free landholders in the countrywere the members of the priestly caste, and (3) that the population generally occupied their farms at the uniform fixed rent of one fifth of their yearly produce, is abundantly corroborated by the statements of Herodotus (ii. 109), that Sesostris divided thesoil of Egyptamong the inhabitants, "assigningsquare plots of equal size to all, and obtaining his chief revenue from the rent which the holders were required to payhim yearbyyear;" ofDiodorusSiculus (i. 73), that the land in Egypt belonged either to the priests, to the king, or to the military order; and of Strabo (nii. 787), that the peasants wero not Iandownera, but occupiers of rateable land; as also by the monuments, which represent the king, priest~, and warriors alone as having landed property (Wilkinson, Keil}. Dr. Robinson quotesamodernparallel to thisactofJoseph's, which both illustrates its nature and by way of contrast exhibitsitsclemency. Up to the middle of the present century the people of Egypt had been the owners as well a.s tillers of the soil. " By a single decree the Pasha (Mohammed Ali) declared himself to be tho sole owner of all lands in Egypt; and the people of course became at once only his tenants at will, or rather hisslaves." "The modern Pharaoh made no exceptions, an(l stripped the mosques and other religious an(l charitable institutions of their landed endowments as merciles.slyas the rest. Joseph gave the people seed to sow, and required for the king onlya fifth of the produce, leaving fourfifths to them as theiruwn ; but now, though sr.ed is in like manner given out, yet every villageis compelled to cultivate two-thirds of its lands with corn and other articles for the Pasha, nnd also to render back to him, in the form of taxes and exactions in kind, a large proportion of the produce rem:iining after" (' Biblical Researches,' i. 42).

entries.title: GEN 47:11–27
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseplt's poli-cy in Egypt. I. TowAn.ns THE IsnAELITES. 1. He gave th= a seUlement in Goshen. Though in one sense the land of Goshen wns Pharaoh's grant, it is appnrent from the Mtory that they owed it chiefly to the wise and prudent mnnngement of Joseph that they found themselves located in the fattest corner of the land. In thus providing for them Joseph had without doubt nn eye to their enrichment, to their sepnrntion ns n people from the Egyptian inhabitants of the lnnd, nnd to their convenience when the day came for their return. Thus we see an evidence of Joseph's fervent piety. 2. He supplied tltem wit/1 f()od while tlie famine lasted. That he did so without charges to them tho narrative oxplicitly asserts. Nor can Joseph's right so to provide for his own household bo legitimately challenged, tho more especially that it wne owing purely to his wise administration that the king's granaries were filled with corn. That Joseph did so was a proof of his natural affection. 3. He allowed them to acquire possessions. That is to say, he secured them in their rights of property while they resided among strangers. He cast around them the protection of the lnw nil the same as if they had been Egyptian8. This was n testimony to Joseph's political eqnity. II. TowAnns THE EGYPTIANS. 1. Josepli's policy descril,ed. (1) Defore tho coming of the famine. Joseph gathered up a fifth part of the prod11ce of tho hncl ond stored it up in granaries ag,iinst the succeeding yours of fnmino, paying dunl,tless for wliat ho took, and affording the inhabitants of the country an example oE economy and foresight. (2) During the continuance of the famine ho resolu the GENF,RJS, L L THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [en. XLVII, 28-31. grain which he had previously collected; in the first instance, for money; in tho second instance, when the money failed, for horses and cattle; and in the third instance, when nothing remained between the people and starvation, for their lands and their persons.. (3) At the close of the famine Joseph returned to the people their lnnds, along with seed, and of necessity also cattle for its cultivation, exacting from t.!iem in return as rei:it a fifth part of the produce, the same proportion that he hnd hfted from th~m durmg the_seven prospe:ous yea!-s. 2. Joseph a policy_clialleng~d- It bas been vigorously assailed, (1) for its seventy; oloquent wnters d1latino- with much indignation on its arbitrary, oppressive, tyrannical, and ferocious character representing Joseph as little other than a semi-royal despot who little reeked of'the Jives and liberties of his grovelling subjects so long as he could aggrandise himself and his royal patron; (2) for its injustice, being very different treatment from that which had been measured out to the Israelites, who wore strangers and foreigners in the land, while they (the Egyptians) were the native population; and (3) for its impiety, Joseph having sinfully taken advantage of the necessities of the people to reduce them by one bold stroke to a condition of abject and helpless slavery. 3. Joseph's policy defende,d, (1) The alleged severity is greater in appearance than reality, since it is ctrtain that Joseph did nothing harsh in selling corn for money so long as people bad it, or horses and cattle when money failed, and it cannot be fairly proved that Joseph did not give them full value for their lands. (2) The imputation of pc.rtiality will disappear if it be remembered that Joseph's brethren were only expected to be temporary settlers in Egypt, and besides were few in number, so tl,at a gratuitous distribution of corn amongst them was not at all an unwarrantable exercise of philanthropy, whereas to have pauperised a whole nation would have been to inflict upon them the greatest possible injury. (3) The charge of having enslaved a free people may be answered by stating first that the nan-ative when fairly construed implies nothing more than that Joseph changed the land tenure from that of freehold to a rent charge, and that for the convenience of supporting the people while the famin~ lasted be distributed them (i. e. the country folks) among the cities where the grain was stored; and secondly, that instead of complaining against Joseph as the destroyer of their liberties, the people applauded him as the saviour of their lives.

entries.title: GEN 47:13–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: The policy of Joseph is faithfully employed for his monarch. The advantacre taken of the people's necessities to increase the power of the throne is quite Ea~tern in its character-not comn:iended t? general imitation, but permitted to be carried out through Joseph, because 1t gave him greater hold upon the government, and perhaps wrought beneficially on the whole in that early period of civilisat_ion. The honour of the priesthood is a testimony to the sacredness which the Egyptians attached t0 religious persons and thing~. The earliest nations were the most religious, and there is no doubt that the universality of religion can be traced among the tribes of the eaiih. An atheistic nation never has existed, and never can E"Xist, except as i11 France, at a re,·olutionary period, and for a short time.-R.

Jacob) must die (literally, and the days ofIsrael to die c/Jrew near): and he called hie son .Joeeph, and ea.id unto him, If now I havefound grace in thy eight (not as if Jacob doubted Joseph's affection, lMlt simply as desiring a last token of his love, perhaps also as lllleonsciously recognising his son's greatness), put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh,-an ancient form of adjuration (cf. eh. xxiv. 2)-and dee.I kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt. entries.content: -llut I will lie with my fathers, and thou she.It carry me out of Egypt, end bury me in their burying-place. The request of the venerable patriarch, while due in some respect to the deeply-seated instinct of human nature which makes men, almost universally, long to be bw'ied in ancestral graves, was inspired by the clear faith that Canaan was the true inheritance of Israel, and that, though now obtaining a temporary refuge in Egypt, his descendants woulu eventually return to the land of promise as their permanentabode. And he (i. e. Joseph) said, I will do e.e thou hast said-literally, accordi7VJ to thy word.

entries.content: -And he (i. e. Jacob) said, Swear unto me (in the manner indicated in ver. 29). And he (i. e. Joseph) awe.re unto him. And (having conclude,l this tonchin" and impressive ceremonial) Israel bowed hkself upon the bed's head. Though supported hy many eminent authorities (Ch~idee Paraphrase, Symmachus, Vnlgate, Calvin, Willet, Rosenmiiller, Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch, &c., &c.), the present renderi.ug is not entirely free from difficulty, since not until the next chapter is there any mention of Jacob's sickness; while in fa~our of the reading, "And Israel bo,vecl himself on the top o[ his staff" (LXX.), it may be urgecl (1) that it is adopted by the writer to tL.e Hebrews (Heb. xi. 21), (2) that the Hebrew wonls for staff anu bed differ only in the punctuation, and (3) that the action of leaning on hi3 staff was quite as suitable to Jacob's circumstances as turning over and bowing on his bed's head.

entries.title: GEN 47:28–31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: - Jacob's residence in Egypt. I. JAcon's PEACEFUL OLD AGE. "And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen yeara." After an eventful and chequered pilgrimage of 130 years, during which Jacob had made large experience of the ills of life, having encountered adversity in forms both more numerous and severe than are allotted to most, be had at length rencbed a happy harbour of rest in the calm contemplative evening of old age, exchanging the anxieties and toils of his previously wandering condition for a hoine of ease and comfort in the fat land of Goshen, and bidding· farewell to all his past tears and sorrows in the enjoyment of the tender care and rich love of Joseph, Racbel's son. Verily, with this old weatherbeaten tmveller it had become light nt eventide. It is noticeable that Jacub lived as long ll time in Egypt as Joseph bnd spent in Jacob's home in Ca.naan-scventeen yenrs-thus receiving an ample recompense for the affection he had 11\Vishctl on his son. Let parents be encouraged thereby to love and care for their children in the tender yenrs of infancy and youth; and let children see in Joseph nn example of the rich return which they ebould give their parents, cherishing nmid the infirmities o.f nge those who have watched over them, and loved them, and prayed for them with so much solicitude and affection. II. JACOB'S APPROACHING DISSOLUTION. "The time drew nigh that Israel must die." It wns a time that Israel had now for some considerable period been nnticipating. When be stood before Pharaoh be informed that auguGt but benevolent monarch that he reckoned his earthly pilgrimage ns g·ood as closed. At least his words imply that he bad no expectation of living to the age of his revered nncestors. Consequently he was not surprised, though he perceived that death wns rapidly gaining ground upon his feeble steps. Perfectly nwnre that it was nppointecl w1to ull men once to die, be hod been piously, while reposing beneath the shadow of Joseph's wing, reckoning up the number of his own d1tys in particular, and bad found that the allotted span was nearly passed. Nor does it appear that he was alarmed by the knowledge of thnt melancholy fact. Tho man who had fought with God and pre- 1•ailed was not likely to be dismayed by the prospect of engaging with the king of terrors. He who had been so long in the enjoyment of Jebovah's friendship and salvation would scarcely regard it as a hardship to be translated to Jehovah's presence. Let the saints learn to number their days that so thC'y may apply their hearts LL2 616 'l'HE BOOK OF GENESIS. [CH. XL\'11. 28-31. to heavenly wisdom; to live in habitual contemplation of tho end, that they may not be afraid when doath comes, and to cultivate that holy alliance with the God of ealvation which will e~able them to say, "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were chssolved, we have a building of God an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." ' III. JAcon's DYING REQUEST. "Bury me not in Egypt; but I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying-place." This request was addressed to his son Joseph, whom he had hastily summoned to his side. It is not quite certain that at this moment Jacob was confined to bed, or that he was actually so near his decease as he imagined. Tho probability is that he survfred for some little while longer, but that with the knowledge that his departure from ihe e-arth could not be long delayed, he desired to leave his last instructions for his funeral with his honoured and beloved son. Accordingly, in a conversation he explained that he was anxious that Joseph should convey bis remains to the £ad1i1y vault at Hebron, and lay them beside the dust of Abraham and Isaac. It was a natural desire that the old man should seek to sleep among his kindred; but the wish had a higher origin than simply the instincts of nature. Canaan was the Godgiven inheritance of hintself and his descendants ; and though as yet a long interval must elapse before his children could enter on its possession, he would manifest his faith in the Divine promise by laying his bones in the sacred soil. It becomes God's people to imitate the patriarch in still holding on to God's sure word of promise, although the fulfilment should be long delayed, and in particular to remember that as with Jacob so with them, God's best promises will be realised not on earth, but in the better country, even an heavenly. IV. J ACOB's DEEP A:-IXIETY. ".And he said, Swear unto me," It might have been supposed that Joscph's word of promise, "I will do as thou hast said," would be sufficient to allay the aged patriarch's apprehensions, but it we.a not. Remembering the old form of oath which .Abraham had employed in connection with Eliezer, he imposed it on his son, as if to bind him by the holiest obligations to fulfil his last request. Joseph, we may be sure, would have honoured his aged parent's wish without the additional ceremony of swearing; but inasmuch as it was not necessarily rinful, and it would tend to dispel his father's fears, he consented to the proposal, "and be sware unto him." Jacob perhaps might have dispensed with the oath, e.nd certainly Christians should be satisfied with a simple II yea" or II nay," remembering that whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil; but sons may learn from Joseph to bear with an aged parent's infirmities and to humour his inclinations, when these are not sinful. V. JACOB's SOLEMN wonsmr. "And Jacob bowed himself upon the bed's head," or II worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff." But whatever was the exact position of the patriarch, his exercise was devotion. With reverent inclination of Lis aged head he poured out his soul in grateful adoration to his God, who bo.d enabled him so successfully to arrange everything connected with his funeral that he had now nothing left to do but die. .And in this too the patriarch might ndvo.ntageously be followed by his spiritual children. Happy they who before being summoned to put off this tabernacle are able to say, 11 Father, I have finished the work thou gavest me to do I" It is a special mercy for which they may well give God thanks.

entries.title: GEN 47:28–31
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jacob's appreliension. I. WHAT IT WAS. 1. It was not anxiety about temporal support, for that had been generously made sure to him by his son Joseph. 2. It was not concern about thefuturefortunes ofliisfarnil11, for these had been graciously taken under God's protection. 3. It was not uncertainty as to his own personal acceptance with Jehovah, for of that he had long ago been assured. 4. It was scarcely even/ear ofliis apJ?_roacliing death, for besides being a thought with which Jacob had long been familiar, to a weary pilgrim like him the event itself would not be altogether unwelcome. 5. It wus dread lest his lifeless body should be interred in Egypt, far from the graves of his ancestors in the holy land. II. WHENCE IT AROSE. 1. Fromthedeeply-seatedinstinctinhumannature, which makes men wish, if possible, to sleep beside their fathers and friends. Though religion teaches us to believe that every spot on earth is in a manner holy ground, yet it does not induce a spirit of indifference as to the last resting-place where wo shall lie. 2. From afirmfaith in tlie Divine promise that his descendants should yet return to Canaan. Even if Jacob did not anticipate that this would immediately occnr, if, as is probable, he had already dark forebodings that the period of exile and servitude spoken of by Jehovah to Abraham was about to commence, he wns yet able to detect nsilver lining in the cloud, to see the happy time beyond, when bis children, in accordance with the promise "I will surely bring thee up again," should return home to their presently abandoned inheritance. III. How rr WAS REllOVED. 1. By Joseph's promise. Requested by his aged parent to convey his body back to Canaan, when the life hnd departed, Joseph solemnly engages to carry out that parent's wishes to the letter. "I will do as thon hast said.'' 2. By Joseph's oatli. As if to remove every possible ground of apprehension, the old man further binds his son by an nppenl to heaven. "And he said, Swear unto me; and ho (Joseph) swnre unto him." The venerable patriarch's anxieties were 1tt an encl. "And Israel bowed himself upon the bed's Lend."-\V.

entries.title: GEN 48:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Joseph said unto his father, Not so, my father: for this is the Jirstborn; put thy right hand upon his head. "From .roseph's behaviour we cannot certainly infer that, like Isaac, he loved the firstborn better than the youngest; but be was sorry that an honour was not given to the eldest which l1e would naturally expect, and bestowed on the youngest who did not expect it, and who would not h;ve been hurt by the want of it" (Lawson). Yer. 19.-And his fa.ther refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly (literally, and over against thal; Cl?~~. the strongly adversative particle, signifying that which stands in front of, or opposite to, another thing) his younger brother shall be greater than he (cf. Numb. i. 33 with i. 35 ; ii. 19 with ii. 21), and hia seed shall become a multitude of nationsliterally, shallbeafulncss ofnations. In the time of llfoses this prediction begnn to realise itself. In the first censuswhich took place in tho wilderness the tribe of Ephraim ba.d 40,500 men, while that of Manasseh could only reckon 32,200; in the second the numbersreceived a. temporaryalteration, Ephraim counting only 82,500, and Manasseh 62,700; but after the conquest the ascendancy of Ephraim was restored, so tha.t she easily assumed the lead among the ten northern tribes, a.nd acquired a name and a.n influence only second to that of Juda.h•(cf. Judges iv; 5; v. 14; viii.; xii.). • Yer. 20.-And he (i. e. Ja.cob) blessed them tha.t day, saying, In thee (i. e. in Joseph, who is still identified with his sons) shall Israel (the nation) bless, saying, God (Elohim, the supreme source of all blessing) make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh : and he set Ephraim before Manasseh- " in the position of his hands, and the terms of the blessing" (Keil). Yer. 21.-And Israel (Jacob) said unto Joseph, :Behold, I die: but God (Elohim) shall be with you, and bring you again unto the land of your fathers. "For Joseph and his childrena great promiseand dispensation" (Lange). Yer. 22.-Moreover (literally, and) I have given-or, I give (Keil), I will give (Kalisch), the preterite being used prophetically as a fu~re, or even as a present, the event being regarded, from its certainty, as already accoJDplished. It is thus not absolutely clear that Jacob here alludes to any past transaction in his own personal history-to thee one portion-literally, one shoulder, or ridge, or elevated tract of land, c:;ir:, ; unam parlem (Yulgate), with which agree several of the ancient versions (Onkelos, Syriac)-.above thy brethren, which I took-or take (Keil), or shall take (Kalisch)-out of the hand of the Amorite-a general name for the inhabitants of Canaan (vide eh. xv. 16)-with my sword and with my bow. As Scripture has preserved no account of any military exploit in tho historyof Jacob such as is here described, the patriarch's language has been understood as referring to the plot of ground at Shechem which Jacob J>Urchasedof Hamor the father of Shechem (eh. xxxiii. 19), and as signifying either that he had captured it by sword and bow, in the sense that his sons at the bead of his armed retainers had put the inhabitants of the town to the sword, and so taken possession of ihe entire district (Calvin, Rosenrniiller, Murphy); or that, though he had peacefully paid for it, he yet required at e ellbHequent period to recovel" OU. Jt seems, however, better to regard the worde as a prophetic utterance pointing forward to the conquest of Canaan, which Ja.cob here represents himself, in the persons of his descendants, as taking from the Amorites by means of sword a.nd bow, and as intimating that the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh would receivea doul;,le portion of the inheritance, the word Cl~~ being prob'.l.blydesigned to conveya hint that the tract to be in future assigned to Joseph's descendants would bo the region round about the ancient city Shechem (Ainsworth, Keil, Kalisch, Lange, &c.).

entries.title: GEN 48:1–22
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Jac.,b's dying utterances. I. AN or.o MAN'S SICK-BED. "It came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick." In this the venerable patriarch-I. Suffered an experience that is common to all. For nearly three half-centuries had this weather-beaten pilgrim been able to maintain himselE erect amid the numberless vicissitudes of life. Strong, healthy, vigorous, and active too, he appears to have been until now, notwithstanding the peculiarly trying an,l chequered career through which be had passed. But all the while, the rolling years, us they glided softly by, had been touching him with their invisible fingers, anrl leaving on him their ineffaceable impressions, imperceptibly but surely relaxing his corded muscles, whitening and diminishing bis manly locks, loosening his joints, making his step less lithe and firm, and generally draining away his strength. And now, at length, he had arrived where all men must, sooner or later, come, if they have a death-bed at all, no matter how bright may be their eye, or how ruddy their countenance, or how stalwart their frame, or how herculean their strength, to that period of infirmity and sickness that precedes dissolution. 2. Enjayed a privile(Je accordecl to fe:w. Immediately that he had fallen sick, a messenger, despatched from Goshen, carried tidings to the vice-regal palace in the great metropolis, and Joseph, his beloved Ron, accompanied by his two boys, Ephraim and Manasseh, at once descended to express his sympathy and lend his uid. Not to many is it granted, in this world of separations and bereavements, to have all their family around them when they breathe tl1eir last, or to Lave their Josephs even, to put their hands upon the sinking eyelids, and gently close them in the sleep of death. Venerable pilgrim I Much afflicted in thy riper years, thou wast greutly comforted in thy latter days. 11. AN OLD PILGRIM'S REMINISCENCES. Learning of Joseph's urrival, the aged father musters his rapidly failing strength, and, recognising within his withered bosom the stirrings of the old prophetic spirit, prepares himself, by sitting upright in hi8 bed, for delivering whatever communication should be put into his trembling lips. C:.1sting his thoughts back upon the past with that fond delight with which the aged recall the story of their younger yeurs, he relates to Joseph-I. /Iow El Sltaddai liad appeared to Mm at Luz, or Bethel, in the l11nd of Co.ntrnn, as he returned from Mesopotamia. 2. What God had promised him on th11t memorable occasion, that he should grow into a multitude of people, who should eventunlly possess the laud, adding by way of parenthesis, at this stage, that in view of tllllt inheritance to come he intended to adoptthe sons of Joseph as his own ; and 3. The great ajfliction thathacl .1tappened to him almost immediately after in the loss of Rachel, Joseph's mother, to whose premature death and uffecting burial "in the way of Ephrath" the old man, even at that long distance of time, cannot refer without emotion. "As for me, Rachel died upon me in the land of Canaan in the wuy." Ill. AN OLD SAINT'S DLI;:BSING, It is probable that, though Jacob had already referred to Joseph's sons, l,e had not yet been conscious of their presence, for "the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not sec." At length, however, discerning unfamiliar forms in the chamber, and ascertaining they were Ephraim an,! Mano.sseh, he proceeds to give them his patriarchal benediction. 1. Tlte actions of the patriarch. (1) Requesting his gro.ndchildren to be brought to his bedside, ho tenderly embrncee them, nnd kisses them with ull o.n old mnn's affection, ut the samu 522 THE DOOK 01•' GENESIS. [CH, XLVIII. 1-22. time giving special thanks to_ Elohim for his suverabundant mercy in permitting him to see Joseph's sons, and Ins beloved Rachels offspring. (2) Guiding his hands wittingly, he ~ets them crosswise upon his grandsons' heads, tho rig·ht hand upon that of.Eplrnnm, the y~unger, and the left hand upon that of Manasseh, the elder. Supposing tha_t the patz:iarch had ~rred, Joseph endeavours, by changing· his father's hands, to rectify the nnstake, saymg, 11 Not so, my father: for tl1is is the firstborn • put thy righ~ hand upon his head." But the old man replies, thinking perhaps at th~ moment of himself and Esau, when they came before Isaac for his blessing II I know it, my son, I know it," but refuses to complywith his son's suggestion. 2.' The contents ofthe blessing. (1) The blessing upon Ephraim, This was the heirship of the theocratic blessing, the right of primogeniture, the place and power of the firstborn. " Truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations." (2) The blessing upon Manasseh. 11 He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great." (3) The blessing upon both. "The angel who redeemed me from all evil bless the lads "-a promise of spiritual blessing for themselves; and "In thee shall Israel bless, saying "-a promise of ~piritual influence with others. (4) The blessing upon Joseph. Joseph was blessed in the blessing of his sons, by their adoption into Jacob's family,-" My name shall be named upon them, imd the name of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac;" and by their reception of a double portion of the inheritance,-" Moreover, I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword an<l with my bow." IV. AN OLD PROPIIET's PREDICTION. "Behold, I die ; but God shall be with you; and bring you again into the land of your fathers." 1. T!te timewlien itwas uttered. ,vhen Jacob was on the eve of death. It is not at all improbable thatthe soul's vision of unseen (celestial and future) things becomes clearer as the obscuring veil of this mortal flesh wears thin; but the power of apprehending things to come, which Jacob in this instance displayed, was not due to such intensified spiritual penetration. Neither is it necessary to suppose that he received at-this moment any special supernatural communication. Simply, he directed his dying gaze to the sure word 0£ promise. 2. The substance ofwhat it said. It announced nothing more than God already promised, viz., that he would continue with Jacob's descendants in Egypt, and eventually bring them up again to Canaan. 3. The guaranteeto wltichitpointed. This was implicitly contained in the expression, "the land ofyour fathers." Canaan had been given in covenant to Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob; and hence of necessity it would ultimately be restored -to their seed according to the terms of the covenant.

Yers. 8, 4.-Reubon, thou art my first• THE TIOOK OF GENESIS. [en. entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Joseph is afruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whoso branches run over the wa.11-literally, sonof afntit tree, Joseph ; son ofafruit tree at the well; daughters rwn (each one of them: 11ide Gesenius, 'Grammar,' § 146, 4) 011er the wall. The structure of the clauses, the order of the words, tho repetition of the thoughts, sup~ly o. glimpse into the fond emotion with which the aged prophet approached the blessing of his belovedson Joseph. Under the image of a frnit treo, probably a vine, as in Ps. lxxx., planted by a. well, whenco it draws forth necessary moisture, and, sending forth its young twigs or offshoots over the support• ing walls, he pictures tho fruitfulness and prosperity which should afterwards attend the tribes of Ephraim e.nd Manasseh, as the twofold representative of Joseph, with perhaps a backward glance e.t the service which Joscph had performed in Egypt by gathering up and dispensing the produce of the land for the salvation of his family and people. The archers he.ve sorely grieved him, e.nd shot o.t him, and hated him-literally, the?J provoked hirn, and shot at, and laid snares for him, m,as_ters of arrows, though Kalisch translates Ulil, and they assembled in multitudes, which yields a sense sufficiently clear. It is sometimes alleged (Keil, Lange, 'Speake1·'s Commentary') that the words contain no allusion to the persona.I history of Joseph, but solely to the later fortunes of tho tribes of Ephraim o.nd Manasseh ; but even if they do point to tho subsequent hostilities which Joscph's descendants should incur (Josh. xvii. lG-18; Judges xii. 4-6), it is almost morally certain thnt the imago of the shooting archers which he selects to depict their adversaries was suggested to his mind by the early lot of his beloved son (Calvin, OH. But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty Gou of Jacob. Notwitlu!tanding the multitudinous and fierce assaults which had been ma(lo on Joseph, lie had risen superior to his adver- Haries; his bow had continued firm aml unbroken (cf. 1 Sam. ii. 4 ; ,fob xii. 19 ; xxxiii. 19), and his arms had bum rendered active and flexible-neither il!,,Xi,91/ Ta ,,,upa {3pa- ,c:uivwv x••piic auTwv (LXX.), dissoluta sunt vincula brachiorum et manuum (Vulgatc), as if Joseph's enemies were the subjects referred to ; nor, " Therefore gold was placed upon his arms " (Onkelos, Rashi, and others), refen'ing to the gift of Pharaoh's ring-by the hands of the Mighty Ono ofJacob, i. e. God, who had proved himself to be Jacob's Mighty One by the powerful protection vouchsafed to his servant. The title here nscribed to God occurs afterwards in Isa. i. 24. From thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel. If the claus6 is parenthetical, it may signify either that from the time of Joseph's exalt.'ttion he became the shepherd (who sustained) and the stone of (i. e. the rock which supported) Israel (Oleaster), or thatfrom God, the MightyOneofJacob, Joseph received strength to become the shepherd and stone of Israel (Pererius, .Ainsworth, Lawson, Patrick, and others), in which capacity ho served ns a prefiguration ofthe Good Shepherd who was also tobecometheRockorFoundationofhisChurch (Calvin, Pererius, Cnndlish, &c.) ; but if the clause is rather co-ordinate with that which precedesand thnt which follows, as the introductory particle IQ nppears to suggest, then the words "shepherd and stone of Iaraol" will apply to God, nnd the sentiment will be thnt the httnds of Joseph were made strong from the hnnds of the Mighty One of Jacob, from there (i. e. from there where is, or from him who is) the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel (Keil, Knlisch, Murphy, Gerlnch, Lnnge, et alii). Even by the God of thy father, who shnll help thee (liternlly, /T&m the God of thy father, and he shall help thee, i. o. who sho.11 help thee); and by the Almighty, who shall bleBB thee-literally, and with (sc. the 11.id of) the Almighty, and he shall bless fhee. It is unnecessary to chango n~1 into ',~l (LXX., Vulgatc, Samnritan, Syriac, Ewald), or to insert lr.> before n~, ns thus, n~~ (Knobel, Rosonmiiller, Kalisch), sinco n~ may be understood bore, as in eh. iv. 1 ; v.'• 24, in the sense of helpful communion (Keil)-with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lieth under, bleBBinge of the breasts, and of the womb. "From the God of Jncob, nnd by the holp of foe Almi"hty, shoi1IJ. tho rain nnd J.cw of heaven (eh. x.XYii. 28), 11nd fountain~ nud Q~NEBIS. brooks which spring from the great deep or the abyss of the earth, pour their fertilisin" waters over Joseph's land, so that cverythin~ that had womb and breast should bccomo pregnant, bring forth an,! suckle" (Keil). The blessings of thy father have prevaifocl above the blessings of my progenitors unto the utmost bound of the everlasting hills. The meaning is, according to this renJerin" which some adopt (the Tar6 '11ms, Vulgat;, Syriac, Saaclia.~, Rosenmiiller, Lange, Mnrphy, et alii), that the blessings which Jacoh pronounced upon Joseph surpassed thoso which he himself had rccei,ed from Abraham and Isaac, either as far as the primary monntains towered above the earth (Keil, Mnrphy), or, while exceeding the bcnc,lic:ions of his ancestors, those now <lclive1·eJ by himself would last while the hills endurccl (Rosenmiiller, 'Spcakel"s Commentary'). B11t the words may be othenvise rentlered : "The blessings of thy father prevail over, nre mightier than the blessings of the mountain~ of eternity, the delight, oc glory, or loveliness of the hills of eternity" (LXX., Dath". l\Iichaelis, Gesenius, Bohlen, Kalisch, Gerlach, and others); and in favour of this may be adduced the beautiful parallelism between the last two clauses, which the received translation overlooks. They shell be on the head of Joseph, and on the crown of the head of him tha.t we.s separate from his brethrenliterally, of him, the separatccl (from na::ar, to separate)fromhis brethi-cn (Onkelos, Rashi, Rosenmiiller, Keil, nnd others), though by some different renderings nre prefeJTed, as, e. q., the crowned among his brethren (LXX. Vor. 27.-Benja.min shall ravin a.s a. walf (literally, a wolf, he shall tear in pieces): iu the morning he shall devour the prey, nnd e.t night he shall divide the spoil. entries.title: GEN 49:1–33
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -The patriarchal bleIJsing, or tlie last words of Jacob. I. THE soNs OF LEAR. 1. Tiu blessing on Reube:n. (1) A declaration of Reuben's natural precedence, as the first-born in Jacob's family, the beginning of Jacob's strength, and therefore the legitimate heir of Ja.cob's house. (2) A proclamation of Reuben's deposition from this honourable position : 11 Boiling as water, thou shalt not have the precedence," i. e. the birthright is taken from thee, and assigned to another. (3) A i,tatement of Reuben's sin, as the reason of this forfAiture of the firsthorn's place: "because thou wentest up to thy father's bed : then defiledst thou it; he went up to my couch." 2. The bleIJsings on Simeon and Levi. It is only by a species of irony that the words pronounced on the authors of the Shechem massacre can be styled a blessing. (I) The patriarch expresses his abhorrence of their atrociou~ wickedness, describing them with a refined sarcasm as brethren, confederates in sin as well as the offspring of common parents, characterising their swords, or their compacts, or their rage, or their machinations, according to the translation adopted, as instruments of violence, and shudderingly recoiling from the least association with two such reckless murderers, who in their wrathful fury spared neither man nor beast: "Man they slew, and ox they houghed." (2) He pronounces a solemn cµrse upon theirsin. Not upon themselves, it is noticeable, but upon their deed, meaning that while God might mercifully pardon transgressors such as they had been, he could not do otherwise than renal his wrath against appalling wickedness like theirs. (3) He allots to them n punishment appropriate to their offence: "I will_ divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel." 3. The bleIJsing upon Judah. Recalling probably the part which his fourth son had played with reference to Benjamin, Jacob fervently declares that Judah should be-(1) The admiration of his brethren: "Judah, thou art 110 whom thy brethren shall praise;'' and II thy father's children shall bow down unto thee." (2) The terror of his foes: 11 thy hand shall be in the neck of thine enemies;" "Judah is a lion's whelp," &c. (3) The ancestor of the Messiah, whose character he defines by the term Shiloh, whose advent he marks by the time: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver (or ruler's staff) from between !,is feet, until Shiloh come ;" and the result of his appearance: 11 unto him shall the gathering of the people be." (4) The possessor of a prosperous do1:1ain, whose vin~-trees should be abundant, and whose pasture grounds should be fertile. 4. The blessing on Zebulun. With allusion to the import of his name, Jacob prophesies that Leah's sixth son should be the ancestor of a flourishing community devoted to commercial pursuits, with a territory reaching towards the sea-coast, where ships should come to load nnd unload their cargoes of merchandise. 5. The blessing on Issac/tar. The last mentioned son of Leah, though the fift~ in the_order of birth, the patriarc~ predicts sho1;1ld develop into a powerful and sagacious tnbCl, capable of great exertion nnd warhko achievements but addicted to pastoral pursuits, and so fond of luxuriant repose, that for the sake ~f resting among his sheepfolds and in his fnt meaclows he shonlcl be willing to fulfil the mute anticipation of his name, and render tribute to his more heroic brethren. II. THE SONS OF TIIE CONCUDINEB, 1. The blessuig on Dan. Danwas the firstborn of Bilbnh, the mnid of Rachel; and concerning him the patriarch annonnces-(1) That though the child of n secondary wife, his descendants shoulrl attain to the position of an independent nnd self-governing tribe : " Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel"; (2) That if not ns a tribe, yet ns individuals, and if not permanently, yet occasionally, they should manifest the qualities of sudden, nnc:i.::- pected, and even treacherous attack that were so remarkably characteristic of the horned serpent; (3) '!'hat he should enjoy, in all the perils to which he might in future be exposed, the gracious succour of Jehovah-a thought which appears to elevate the speaker's soul to the contemplation of another and higher keeper, who was yet to come to heal the fatal bite of that great serpent the Devil, who had injected his mortal virus into the race. 2. The blessing on Gad. The firstborn of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, obtains the next place in the order of the sons, and concerning him it is declared with a threefold play upon his name, which signifies a troop, th11t-(l) He will be sore pressed on every side by troops of marauding foes; but that-(2) He will in the end prove himself to be victorious over the fiercest and the boldest. 3. The blessing on Asher. The happy one should be the occupier of a territory exceeding fertile, and capable of yielding rich and dainty fruits for royal tables. 4. The blessing on Naphtali. Naphtali was Bilhah's child, which Rachel named in honour of her triumphant wrestling or contending with her sister; and for him were reserved the gifts of a graceful exterior, agile movements, and attracti,·e speech both in eloquence and song. III. THE SONS OF RACHEL. 1. The blessing on Josiph. With a fulness and tenderness of paternal emotion like that with which already he had spoken of Judah, the expiring patriarch declares the fortunes of Joseph, setting forth-(!) The general prosperity that awaited him, representing him as the son (or offshoot) of a fruit-tree planted by a well, and rushing up into such luxuriance of growth that its branches (or daughters) overhung the walls that gave it support; (2) The severe adversity to which in early years be had been exposed, and of which in future his descendants should have experience, comparing him to one whom the archers shot at and bated, nnd fiercely persecuted; (3) 'rhe heavenly succour which had enabled him to overcome his bitter trials, nod which would yet advnnce his children to safety, viz., the assistance of the mighty God of Jacob, the Shepherd and Stono of Israel, the God of hie fathers Abraham and Isaac ; (4) The wealth of Benediction that should descend upon the bead of him who bad been separated from his brethren, viz., blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that Iieth under, blessings of the breasts and of the womb, blessings that should surpnss those bestowed on any of his progenitors, or, according to the more correct rendering,that should outlast the everlasting hills. 2. The blesaing on Benjamin. Though latest born of Jncob's family, he should not be the least important, but should show himself possessed of a. warlike and adventurous disposition, causing him with eagerness and animation to take the field against the foe, and to desist not from battle till he could lead back his legions as rejoicing conquerors, enriched with the spoils of glorious victory. Learn-I. That God is the great arbiter of human destiny. 2. That each mnn's sphere in life, as well as each nation's place on earth, is ndaptcd to his or its peculiar character. 3. That thoug·h fore-appointod nnd fore-known, the destinies of men and nut.ions are freely wrought out by themselves. And-4. That in Providence ns well o.s Grace, it often happens that tho first becomes last, nnd the last first.

entries.content: -The coming of Sltiloli, Remarkable agreement of ancient interpreters, Jewish ns well as Chdstian, to consider this a prophecy of Messiah. The former of special value, as being before the event. The Targum of Onkelos renders the po.ssnge, "until Messio.h comes, whose is the kingdom." l\Iany others equally distinct. The colonising instinct of the Greeks making their language almost universal; the contnct of Greek and Jewish learning at Alexandria and elsewhere, by which the heathen language was made capable of e:i::prc~sing Divine truth ; the widespread power and organisation of the Romane, by which m so many ways the fulfilment of prophecy was brought about (Luke ii. 1; John xix. 36, 37). • III. To redeem mankind, both Jews and Gentiles (Pe. xlix. 15; Isa. xxxv. 4-10; John x. 1G; Gal. iv. 5). To bear the sins of mankind (lea, !iii. 11, 12; 2 Cor. v. 14; 1 Pet. ii. 24). To teach his people the way of life (Deut. xviii. 15; Matt. :x:i. 27; John iv. 25). To reign over hie people (Dan. ii.-44; Rev. xi. 15). To give them 'rictory (Ps. xliv. 5 ; 1 John v. 4; Rev. xii. 11), • IV. LESSO?\ OF ENCOURAGEMENT. Why doubt God's acceptance of thee P or bis readiness to help? Mark hie desire that all should bc saved (Ezek. xviii. 32 ; 1 'rim. ii. 4). llfork how this is the ruling principle running through the whole Dible. •The work of Christ was no newly devised thing, but" that which wasfrom the beginning·" (1 Pet. i. 20). All our imperfections, all our weakness of faith is known to God, yet such aR we arc, he bids us trust in Christ's work. Judah himself was a very imperfect character. His descendants not lees so. Yet of them the text was spoken, "Be not afraid, only believe."-M.

entries.title: GEN 49:18
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -God's salvation. I. WHAT IT IB. Deliverance from evil, succour against foes, victory over sin and death. II. WHENCE IT COMES. The primal fountain is Jehovah, the covenant God of. the believer. The salvation of the gospel is God's in its original conception and proclamation, in its subsequent procurement nnd donation, in its ultimate development and consummation. III. How IT IS OJJTAINED. Not by merit, or by works, but by believing, and waiting and hoping. "He that believeth shall be saved." "The Lord loveth them that hope in his mercy." "It is good for a man both to hope, and to quietly wait for the salvation of the Lord."-W.

entries.title: GEN 50:1

entries.content: -And Joseph fell upon his fa.ther'a face, and wept upon him, e.nd kissed him. Joseph had no doubt closed the eyes of his revered and beloved ;parent, ns .God .l1ed promised to the patn.arch that he would (eh. xlvi 4), and now, in demoastrntion both of the intensity of his love and of the bitterness of his sonow, he sinks upon the couch upon which the lifeless form is lying, bending over the pallid countenance with warm tears, and imprinting kisses of affection on the ~old and irresponsive lip. entries.title: GEN 50:2
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Joseph commanded hisservant~ the physicie.ns-litcrally, the healers, Cl11i!l~10, from !:(~~. to sow ~ogether, to mend, hence to heal, a clnss of persons which abounded in Ancient Egypt, each physician being only qualified to treata. single disorder (Herod., ii 84). The medical men ofEgypt were held in high repute abroad, and their assistance was at vano118 times required by persons from other countries, e.s, e. g., Cyrus and Darius (Herod., iii. 1, 132). Their knowledgo of medicines was extensive, nnd is referred to both in sacred (Jer. !xvi. 11) and profane (Homer, 'Odyssey,' iv. 229) Wl'itings. The Egyptian doctors belonged to the sacerdotal order, and were expected to know all things relating to the body, e.nd diseases and remedies contained in the six last of the sncrod books of Hermes. Accord. in~ to Pliny (vii. 66), the study of medicine ongino.ted in Egypt (vide Wilkinsonin Rawlinson's 'Herodotus,' vol. ii pp. 116, 117), 'fhe physicians employed by Joseph were those attached to his own household, or the court practitioners-to embe.lm his father : -litere.lly, to spice orsea.son(the bodyol) his father, i e. to prcparo it for burial by menus of aromatics ; -ut aromatihus condircnt (Vulgate); h>ra1/ua11a1 rov .rarlpa avrov (LXX.), which is putting part of a proceeding for the whole (Tayler Lewis). According to Herodotus (ii 86), the embalmers b,ilonged to 11 distinct hereditary class or guild from the ordinary physicians ; but either their fonnntion intc such a sep11rate order of practitioners wns of Interorigin (Hengstenberg, Kurtz, Kalisch), or Jacob was embalmed by the physicians instead of the cmbalmers proper because, notbeing an Egyptian, he could not be subjected to the ordinary treatment oftho embalming art(' Speaker's Commentary')- and the physicians embalmed Isra.el. The method of preparing mummies in Ancient Egypt has been elaborately described, both by Herodotus (ii. 86) and Diodorug Siculus (i. 91), and, in the m11in, the accuracy of their descriptions has been confirmed by the evidence derived from the mummies themselves. According to the mo,t expcnsivo process, which cost one talent of silver, or nbout £250 sterlin~, the brain was first ex. tracted through the nostrils by merns of a crooked piece of iron, the skull being thoroughly cleansed of any remaining portions by rinsing with drugs ; then, through 11n o_pening in the left side made with a sharp Ethiopian knife ofngateor offlint, the viscera were removed, the abdomen being afterwarJs purified with palm wine and an infusion of aromatics; next, the disembowelled corpse wns filled with every sort of spiccry except frankincense, and the opening sewed up ; after that the stuffed form wns stcepeu. for seventy days in natrum or snbcarbona.tc of soda obtained from the Libyan desert, ancl sometimes in wo.x and tanning, bitumen o.lso boing employed in later times ; and finally, on the expiration of that period, which wos scrupulously observed, the body was washed, wrapped about with lincu bamlages, smeared over with gum, clecorntc,l with amulets, sometimeswith a network ofporcelain bugles, covered with a linen shroud, nnd, in dno course, trnnsferrccl to a mummy caso (vide Wilkinson's ' .Manners aml Customs of tl10 Al1cient E~tians,' yo!. iii. p. 471, eel, 1878; Rnwlinson s 'Herodotus,' vol. ii. pp. 11S- 123),

entries.title: GEN 50:7–9
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And Joseph went up to bury his father: and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh (i. e, the chief officers of the roy11l palace, n.s tho next clause explains), the elders of his house (i. e. of Pharaoh's house), and all the elders of the land of Egypt (i. e. the nobles e.nd State officials), and e.11 the house of Joseph, and his brethren, and his father's house: only their little ones, and their 11.ocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen. And there went up with him (as an escort) both chariots and horsemen: and it we.a a very great company. Delineations of funeral processions, of a most elaborate character, may be seen on the monuments. A detailed and highly interesting account of the funeral procession of an Egyptian grandee, enabling us to picture to the mind's eye the scene of Jacob's burial, will be found in Wilkinson's ' Manners and Customs of tho Ancient Egyptians,' vol. iii. p. 444, eel. 1878. First servants led the way, carrying tables laden with fruit, cakes,'flowers, vases of ointment, wine and other liquids, with three young geese and a calf for sacrifice, chairs and wooden tablets, napkins, and other things. Then others followed bearing daggers, bows, fans, and the mummy cases in which the deceased and his ancestors had been kept previous to burial. Next came a table of offerings, fauteuils, couches, boxes, and 11, chariot. .After these men appeared with gold vases and more offerings. To these succeeded the bearers ofa sacred boatand the mysterious eye of Osiris; as tho god of stability. Pl11ced in the consecrated boat, the heo.rse containing the mummy of the deceased was drawn by four oxen and by seven men, under the direction of a superintendent who reguluted the march of the funeral. Behind tho hearse followed the male rela.tions and friends of the deceased, who either bea.t their breasts, or gave token of tl1eir sorrow by their silence and solemn step as they w11lked, leaning on their long sticks ; and with these the procession closed.

entries.title: GEN 50:10

entries.content: -And they came to the threshing-11.oor of Atad. 'l'h8 threshing-floor, or goren, was a large open circular area which was used for tmmpling out the corn by means of oxen, and wos exceedingly convenient for the accommodation of a !11rgo body of people such us accompanied Joseph. Tho goren at which the funeral p11rty halted was named Ata<l (i. e. Buckthorn), either from the nnme oa. L. 1-14.J THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 537 of the ownor, or from the quantity or buckthorn which grew in the neighbourhood. Which is beyond Jordan-literally, on the other side of the Jordan, i. e. west side, if the narrator wrote from his o,m standpoint (Jerome, Drusius, Ainsworth, Kalisch, 'Spoaker's Commentary,' Wordsworth, et alii), in which case the funeral train would in all probability follow the direct route through the country of the Philistines, and Goren Atad would be situated somewhere south of Hebron, in the territory (afterwards) of Judah ; but east side of the river if the phrase must be interv.reted from the staniipoint of Palestine (Clericus, Rosenmiiller, Hengstenberg, Kurtz, Keil, Lange, Gerlach, Ha.vernick, Murphy, antl others), in which case the burial procession must have journeyed by the wilderness, a.s the Israelites on a latter occa.sion did, -and probably for not dissimilar rea.som. In favour of the former interpretation may bo claimed ver. 11, which says the Cana.a.nites beheld tho mourning, implying seemingly that it occurred within the borders of Cana.an, i. e. on the west of the Jordan ; while support for the latter is derived from ver. 13, which appears to state that after the lamentation at Goren Atad the sons of Jacob carried him into Canaan, almost necessarily involving the inference that Goren Atad was on the east of the Jordan ; but vule infra. If the former is correct, Goren Atad was probably the place ,vhich Jerome calls Betagla tertio ab H~- richo lapide, duobus m.illibus ab Jordane; if the latter is correct, it does not prove 11 post-Mosaic 1111thorship (Tuch, Bohlen, &c.), since the phrase appears to have had an icleo.l usage with reference to Cana.au iu addition to the objective geographical one (Hengstenberg 'on the Genuineness of the Pentatouch,' vol. ii. p. 260 ; Keil's 'Introduction,' vol. i. p. 189 ; Kalisch ' on Genesis,' p. 776). And there they mourned with a gree.t and very sore le.mentation. The Egyptians wore exceedingly demonstr11tivo and vehement in their public lamentations for the dead, rending theii garments, smiting on their breo.sts, throwing dugt and mud on their heads, calling on the deceased by name, and chanting funeral dir~es to the music of a tambourine with the tinkling plates removed (Wilkinson's 'Ancient Egyptians,' vol. iii. p. 440, ed. 1878). entries.title: GEN 50:1–14
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Thefuneral ofJacob. I. Tun: PRIVATE SORROW. 'rhat a great 11nd good man like Jacob, the father of a numerous family, the nncestor of an important people, the chieftain of an influential tribe, the head of the Church of God, should depart this life without eliciting from some heart a tribute of sorrow, is inconceivable. That any of his sons witnessed the last solemn act of this great spiritual wrestler, when he gathered up his feet into his bed und yielded up his spirit into the hands of God, without a tear and without a pang of grief, although it is only the emotion of Joseph that is recorded, is whut we cannotfor a moment believe. Less demonstrative than was thut of Joseph, less deep too, probably, since the heart of Joseph appears to have been peculiarly susceptible of tender emotions, we may yet snppo8o that tho grief of Joseph's brethren wus not less real. II. THE PUDLIC MOURNING. In accordance with tho custom3 of the time~, anJ of 638 THE BOOK OF GENESIS. [OH. L. 1-14. the country, it was needful that a public ceremonial should be observed, in honour of the dend. Accordingly, Joseph, as the first step required by the usages of the people amongst "-hom he lived, gave instructions to his court physicians to embalm his father. For details as to the process, which orcupied a period of forty days the Exposition maybe consulted. Then, along with tl:is, for seventy days, peculiar ~ites supposed to be e~pressive of the heart's grief,_such as rending the garments, smiting the breast, throwmg dust upon the head, calling on the deceased, were maintained with the assistance of friends, neighbours, and professional mourners. III. TnE FUNERAL rROCESSION. 1. Tlie train ofmourners. This consisted of the state and court officials of Pharaoh's house, and of the land of Egypt, the members of the houses of Joseph and his brethren, and atroop of horsemen and charioteersfor protection on the journey. 2. The line of march, This wns either straight north, through the country of the Philistines, if Goren Atad was south of Hebron in Judea, or it was round 3:bout by the way of the wilderness, if the halting-place was east of Jordan. 3. The ktmentation at Goren Atad. This was intended as a special demonstration before burial, and was conducted with such vehemence as to arrest the attention of the Canaanites, wbo called the place in consequence, Abel-Mizraim; i. e. the plain or the mourning of Mizraim. 4. The advance to Hebron. It is more than probable that the Egyptians, who had accompanied the funeral procession from Goshen, remained behind at Goren Atad, while Joseph and bis brethren bore the patriarch's body on to Hebron. IV. THE SOLEMN INTERMENT. His sons bw·ied him in the ancestral vault of Machpelab. Reverently, affectionately, tearfully, yet hopefully, let us hope, they laid the weary pilgrim down to sleep till the resurrection morn beside the dust of bis own Leah, and in the company of Abraham, and Sarah, and Isaac, and Rebekah. Itmust have been an affecting, as surely it was a sublime spectacle, this coming home of an aged exile to lay his bones in his native land, this returning of the heir of Canaan to claim his inheritance, this laying down of the last member of the great .patriarchal family among the other inmates of Macbpelab. With the burial of Jacob, the first patriarchal family was complete, and the tomb was closed. The members of the second household slept at Shecbem.

entries.title: GEN 50:16
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -And (under these erroneous though not unnatural apprehensions) they sent a messenger unto Joseph,-literally, they charged Joseph, i. e. they deputed one of their number (possibly Benjamin) to carry their desires to Joseph-saying, Thy father did command before he died, saying(though not recorded, tho circumstance here mentioned may have been historically true), So shall ye say unto Joseph, Forgive, I pray thee now, the trespass of thy brethren, and their sin; for they did unto thee evil (nothing is more inherently probable than tho.t. the good man on his death-bed did request his sons to beg their brother's pardon): and now, we pray thee, forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father. Joseph's brethren in these words at once evince the depth of their humility, the sincerity oftheir repentance, and the genuineness of their religion.
