entries.title: GEN 50:15–26
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -Th.e last of tli,e house of Jacob. I. Josgprr AND HIS BRETHREN (vers. 15-18). 1. Tiu unworthy suspu:ion. _After Jacob's death, Joseph's brethren began to fear lest he should seek to revenge lumself on account of his early injuries. It was perhaps natural that such an apprehension should arise within their breasts considerin~ the enonnity of the wic!;:edness o~ which they had been guilty; but remembenng all the tokens of Joseph B love which already they had received it was surely unkind to Joseph to suffer such a thought for even a moment to find 'a lodo-- ment in their breasts. ~- T~efriendly_emliassage. . Deputin~ Benjamin, it is thought, to be the bearer of their wIShes, they mstructed him to renund Joseph of their dead father's desire that be should forgive the evil he had suffered at their hands, and to solicit an express assurance from his own lips that it was so. 3. The voluntary humilwtion. Vvhether they allowed their messenger to return or followed close upon his heels cannot be certainly concluded. But they appear to have resorted in a body to Joseph's palace, and placed themselves unconditionally in his power; "Behold, we be thy servants," meaning," Do with us what seemeth good in thy sight." 4. Tlie generous assurance. As they desired, he explicitly declared, though with tears at their unkindness, that they had no cause whatever to anticipate bis anger, that he was not in God's place that he should seek to punish them for a sin which had turned out so providentially for good, and that on the contrary be would continue to noarish them and their little ones so long as they remained in Egypt. II. JOSEPH AND HIS CHILDREN'S CHILDREN. 1. The children of Ephraim. He lived long enough to see the children of Ephraim's grandchildren born into this sinful world, and then he died at the good old age of 110 years. 2. Tlie children of Manasseh. He saw the offspring of Manasseh's son born, and either adopted into his own family, or brought up in his own house. III. JosErH AND TIIE nousE OJ!' IsnAEL. 1. Joseph's premonition of approaching death. "J·oseph said unto his brethren,"-i. e. the descendants of his brethren, his actual brethren having in all probability predeceased him,-" I die." Along with this Joseph recalled to their minds the sacred promise that God would eventually vmit them and cause them to return to their own land. It is well when death approaches to remember God's promi~es. The thoughts of God are very euita~le for dying hours. 2. Joseph's pi-eparatwn for deatli. He took an oath of the cluldren of Israel that they would carry up his bones to Canaan, in this following the example and imitating the faith of his revered father Jacob. 3. Josepli's falling asleep in death. "Joseph died, the son of an hundred and ton years." He had lived n shorter life than any of the four great preceding patriarchs; but his life had been eminently honoured and useful, and his death, we may be sure, would be beautifully calm and peaceful. 4. Joseph's body_ after d~ath. ~t was embalmed, and t\10 mummy put into a coffin for better preservation, until the time approached when 1t could be taken for consignment to the holy land. Learn-1. How difficult it is to shake oneself free from the evil consequences of sin, even after it bas been forgiven. 2. How painful to a loving heart it is t_o be ~uspected of cherishing a feeling of reye~ge. 3. How gene~ousJ:i,; God_ sometimes rewards his servants on earth, by perm1ttmg them to see cluldren s cl11ldren, born und brought up, and sometimes also broug-ht into the family of his Church. 4. How peacefully a child of God can die; and 5. How hopefully he oug-ht to look forward to the re,rnrrecti0n CD, L. 15- -26.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 541

entries.title: GEN 50:20
entries.author: Thomas Whitelaw
entries.content: -lntended bane an unintentiooal boon. "Ye thought e~·il against me; bnt God meant it unto good." Joseph must have been deeply pained by the mistru,t of his brethren. 'fhcy implied that it was only out of consideration for his father that ho had heon kind to them. Yet Joseph had forgiven them. They could not so easily believe in the forgiveness; just as man now is forgiven by God, but he has the greatest difficulty in believing in the reconciliation. Joseph's brethren sent a messenger unto him, probably Benjamin. They who had once sold Joseph as a slave now offer to be his slaves. The offer is to him humiliating. Moreover, it is great pain to him. To a noble soul designing only good to others there is no greater offensiveness than to have his doings viewed with suspicion. Joseph repudiated the mistrust, and refused the offered self-enslavement. lie assures his brctliren of full forgiveness in words which must have been as softest balm to wounded spirits. In a spirit of the highest magnanimity he tries even to make them view with complacency the result of their wrong-doing. In the text we have the "grand golden key to the whole of his life's history." Notice howl. INTENDED DANE OFTEN BECOMES UI,INTENT!ONAL BOON. Evil works evil to others, out sometimes good. Intended evil is overruled by God when he has some good object in view. "Man proposes, God disposes." God always knows what the result of certain actions will be. If they are good actions they work in line with his will; if evil, be overrules them. If the horse keeps the road it feels not the rein, but iE it will turn aside, the sharp bit roust draw it back again. Whatever speculation therd may be abont our absolute freeness, we feel that we are free. It is the glory oE God to be able to trust with freedom a being with such great powers for moral evil, like man. He would teach us to use our wills, by giving us full freedom. \Ve frequently pain him by our misuse and our abuse of our powers. \Vhat evil we deviso and strive to carry out! The brethren of Joseph even intended murder, and modified it by selling their brother into slavery. They acted more cruelly than some of tlrn roen-stealers of Africa, The latter steal strangers to sell them, but these ten men sold their own brother. They thought they were rid of him. Egypt was a long way off; Joseph was but a weakling, and might soon perish. They would be free from his presence, and could divide their guilty gains. They hardened themselves again8t his tears and entreaties; nnd even in malicious spite were ready to slay the weeping youth because be did not appreciate their considerateness in selling him into slavery instead of killing him outright. It was an evil deed. Those who looked on could see no good to come out of it. There were, however, several great results. 1. He was personally advanced in life, and was able to make the best of it. 2. lie saved thousands o.f people from perishing, and among them his own family. 3. He was the means of bringing Israel into Egypt, where it developed as a people. Its deliverance gave occasion to the mightiest display of Divine power. 4. He became a type of tho Messiah-rejected of men. Thus we know not the results of any of our acts. God can overrule, to the development of charBCtcr and spiritual power, circumstances seemingly most opposed to our best interests. God knows what is best. He could break the plans of the evil in pieces. Instead of this he oft confounds the wicked by letting them see that the ends they did not desire have been attained in spite of their opposition, nnd even by the very existence, that the intended bane becomes un unintentional boon. 'rI1us Joseph's brothers found it, and bowed their heads. II. THERE ARE SEVERAL LESSONS TO DE LEARNED FROM THE WAY IN WllICil, BY Goo's 0VERRUI,ING, INTENDED DANE BECOMES A DOON. 1. It is ll dangerous thing to scheme ngai11st others. Especially is it a d11ngerous thi11g when a good ml\n is tho object of the attack. It is likely to be checked 11nd to recoil, " A greater power than we can contradict may thwart our plans," There are 11 thousand che.nces of check or change. l\Ien have so noticed this that even n French moralist suicl, "I do not know what hidden force it is that seems to delight in breaking up human plans just at tho moment when they promise to turn out well." Yea, there is n "hidden force," ever watchful, ever balancing human 11ctions1 ever ordaining, either in this w1nhl or tho 111ext1 the just meed of praise or blame, or retribution or rcwnn.l. Thoy excommuni~ l!ated hnn, they sent othe1:s to entrap !nm.. ~hey ~ucceeded at length in nailing him to the cross. They can-1ed out their evil mtentions ; but that cross became the throne of the Saviour's power, ihe salvation; and the death of Christ became the life of ~he world. They went by wagging th.eir he!ds,_but at Inst they had to wring their hands. They themselves were left m theu· srn, and their "houso left unto thC'm desolate," while unto the Christ they hated all men are being drawn. 2. That God OYerrnles evil ·s no license to do evil. Many would say," Let us do evil that good may come." This would suit carnal nature. They would suy, 11 Sin is not 80 firent an evil, since God can overrule it." To t~lk like this would be like throwing dust 111 our own eyes when we have reached an emmence from whence we might behold 11 beautiful landscape. It would be like n youth who, seeing a gardener prunino- trees should take a knife and cut and slash all the trunks. Or, it would be like th~ net of one who, seeing how an artist ha~ wrought inn ~ic~ure some blunder into o. beauty, sho1;1ld take a brush an~ streak with bl~ck the bnllrnnt sky. We are not at liberty to sm tl1at God may brmg good out of 1t. 3. That God overrules evil should make ~s feel oitr dependence on him. If we could succeed in good without him, if all wo mtendcd to do could surely be calculated upon, we should become proud. It is well that God sometimes even breaks up our good plans in order that we may learn this 1esson. Vve might even intend g·ood without him otherwise, and that would lead tu evil in ourselves. But we are dependent on him to check the evil of our own lives and of others' intentions. 4. It should make us hopeful also with respect to our affairs. Surely out of this thought we may get "royal contentment," as knowing we are in the hands of a noble protector, "who never gives ill but to him who dese1·ves ill." 5. It should make us hopeful with respect to the order and destiny of the world. In some way, far off, God's glory may be advanced, even by the way in which he will han subdued, by Christ, all things unto himself. 6. Intended good is not always a benefit to those for whom intended. God intends good to men, and provides a way to bless, but men refuse. See at what a cost the way has been provided. Those who refuse are under worse condemnation. "It were better for them not to have known tLe way of righteousness than, after they have known it, to turn from t);ie holy commandment delivered unto them." 7. We must all face our wrong-doing some time or other. ,ve shall find that the evil we have sown has prod1:1ced a harvest of weeds, which we shall have sorrowfully to reap. We ought to pray earnestly, "Deliver us from evil."-H.

entries.content: -The lesson,s of a life. Joseph's life remarkable for the variety of his experience, e.nd for the consistency of his character through all. A man full of human sympathy, who also walked with God. Here the charm of hie history. We can thoroughly enter into his feelings. In his boyhood, deservedly loved by his father, and on that very account hated by his brethren (1 John iii. 13); in his unmerited sufferings; in his steadfast loyalty to God and to his master;_in hie exaltation and the wisdom with which he ruled Egypt; and .in Lis forgiveness of those whd had sold him as a slave, we feel for him and with him. Bnt Joseph died. His trials and his triumphs passed away. The scene where he had played so conspicuous a p□ rt is filled by other forms. And ho who was tLe means of saving a nation must sbRre the lot of the most commonplace life. One event happens to all (Eccles. ii. 15). I. THE UNCERTAIN TENURE OF EARTHLY GOOD. No care can keep away misfortune, not even care to walk uprightly before God. Sin brings sorrow sooner or later; but it is a great mistake to think that all sorrow springs from faults committed (Pa. hxiii. 5). Joseph's slavery was because his Godward life condemned his brothers and made them angry. His being thrown into prison was because he would not yielcl to temptation. '!'his often a stumbling-block. If God really marks nil that is rlone wl,y are !,is most faithful servants often so sorely smitten? We can neither deny'the fact nor trace the reason of the stroke. Enough to know that it is part of Gud's plan (Heb. xii. 6), to fit us for the end of our being. As Christ wns perfected Ly suffering (Heb. ii. 10), so must wo be. And just because to benr the cross is needful for a follower of Christ (Matt. xvi. 24)-and ibis is not tho endurance of OH. L, 15-26.] THE BOOK OF GENESIS. 5-13 suffering CLt our own choice, but the willing receiving of what God is pleased tc send-the uncertainty of life gives constant opportunity for that submission to his will which is the result of living faith. II. TnE ONE END OF ALL LIVING (Exod, i. 6). How varied soever the outward lot, wealth or penury, joy or mourning, one day all must be left behind. To what purpose then is it to labour for good, or to dread impending evil? Can we no! remember many whose name was much in men's months, full of youthful vigour or mature wisdom? And they are gone, and the world goes on as before. Joseph, embalmed in Egypt with almost royal honours, ,vas as completely separated from nll his wealth and power as if ho had never possessed them. Others filled his plac'l and occupied his gains, in their tum to give them up, and awake from the dream of possessions to join the company of those who have left all these things behind. And 1s this all? Has life nothing worth striving for? Is there no possession that we can really regard as our own ? III. LIFE BAS ABIDING TREASURES. Was it nothing to Joseph that he possessccl and showed a forgiving spirit (Matt. vi. 14, 15), and singlenes~ of heart, and earnest benevolence, and watchful consciousness of God's presence? These are treasures the world thinks little of. But these are treasures indeed, mimstering comfort without care. And when earthly things slip from the grasp these abide, reflections of the mind of Christ, anc:l telling of his abiding in the soul (Rev. xiv. l;l).-M.
